profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-06T13:38:24.815+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command
Later Student Tiāntāi
The Sīmǎ clan
were from Wēn County in Hénèi.
Xuānwáng Yì obtained the government of Wèi,
passed it to Jǐngwáng Shī,
and reached Wénwáng Zhāo,
who was first enfeoffed as Duke of Jìn.
Since Wēn County was originally Jìn territory,
it was therefore taken as the name of the state.
Shìzǔ Wǔ Huángdì, Part One, Volume One
His personal name was Yán,
courtesy name Ānshì,
surname Sīmǎ,
grandson of Xuānwáng Yì,
and eldest son of Wénwáng Zhāo.
Wénwáng's temple name was Tàizǔ,
so the Emperor's temple name was Shìzǔ.
According to the rules for posthumous names: "Subduing and quelling calamity and disorder is called 'Wǔ' (Martial)."
First year of Tàishǐ
(yǐyǒu, 265) In this year, in the twelfth month,
he formally accepted the abdication and changed the era name.
This was still the second year of Wèi's Xiánxī era.
1 Spring,
third month.
The ruler of Wú sent the Grand Master of Splendid Happiness Jì Zhì and the Leader of the Court Gentlemen for the Five Services Hóng Qiú
to come together with Xú Shào and Sūn Yù to return the courtesy visit.
Shào and Yù's mission to Wú is seen in the previous year of the previous scroll.
There were those who said that Shào praised the excellence of the Central State,
so the ruler of Wú became angry,
recalled him,
and killed him.
2 Summer,
fourth month.
Wú changed its era name to Gānlù.
At that time, because sweet dew was reported to have descended at Jiǎnglíng, the era name was changed.
3 Fifth month.
The Wèi Emperor bestowed special honors upon Wénwáng,
meaning banners, chariots and horses, music and dance, and ceremonial caps and robes,
all followed the rituals of an emperor.
His heir was called the Crown Prince.
4 Guǐwèi day,
a general amnesty was declared.
5 Autumn,
seventh month.
The ruler of Wú forced Jǐng Huánghòu to commit suicide,
and relocated the four sons of Jǐngdì to Wú;
soon after, he killed the two elder ones.
The ruler of Wú demoted Jǐnghòu
and enfeoffed his four younger brothers;
the affair is seen in the previous year of the previous scroll.
Elder,
pronounced zhǎng.
6 Eighth month,
Xīnmǎo day.
Wénwáng died.
The Crown Prince succeeded as Chancellor of State and Prince of Jìn.
7 Ninth month,
Yǐwèi day.
A general amnesty was declared.
8 Wùzǐ day,
appointed Wèi's Minister over the Masses Hé Zēng as Chancellor of Jìn;
Guǐhài day,
appointed the Chariot and Horse General Sīmǎ Wàng as Minister over the Masses.
9 Yǐhài day,
buried Wénwáng at the Chóngyáng Tomb.
Examination of Discrepancies says: The Jìnshū Annals of Wén records it as
"Guǐyǒu" day;
now follow the Wèizhì Annals of the Prince of Chénliú.
10 Winter,
the Wú Commander of Xīlíng Bù Chǎn
Xīlíng
was Yílíng.
In the first year of Huángwǔ of the ruler of Wú Quán, Yílíng was changed to Xīlíng,
and the commandery seat of Yídū was located there.
The ruler of Wú followed this,
and sent the Imperial Secretary Dīng Gù and the General on the Right Zhūgé Jìng to guard Jiànyè.
Chǎn
was the son of Zhì.
During the time of the ruler of Wú Quán,
Zhì was Commander of Xīlíng.
Zhì,
pronounced zhì.
11 Twelfth
month,
Rénxū day.
The Wèi Emperor abdicated the throne to Jìn;
Wèi's Yuándì was then twenty years old.
The year was gùndūn shàngzhāng.
Wèi's Wéndì first received the abdication from Hàn,
passed through five reigns,
and lasted forty-six years before perishing.
Jiǎzǐ day,
he moved out to reside at Jīnyōng City.
Jīnyōng City was at the northwest corner of Luòyáng City.
Holding the Emperor's hand,
he wept and sobbed uncontrollably,
saying:
"On the day I die,
I will surely be a loyal subject of Great Wèi."
Bǐngyín day,
the Prince ascended the emperor's throne,
declared a general amnesty,
and changed the era name.
Only at this point was the era name changed to Tàishǐ.
Dīngmǎo day,
he honored the Wèi Emperor as Prince of Chénliú,
and established his palace at Yè.
Established,
means to take up residence.
All imitated the precedents from the beginning of Wèi.
See scroll 69, first year of Huángchū of Wèi's Wéndì.
Posthumously honored Xuānwáng as Emperor Xuān,
Jǐngwáng as Emperor Jǐng,
and Wénwáng as Emperor Wén;
honored the Queen Dowager as Empress Dowager.
Enfeoffed the imperial granduncle Fú as Prince of Ānpíng,
imperial uncles Gàn as Prince of Píngyuán, Liàng as Prince of Fúfēng, Zhòu as Prince of Dōngguǎn, Jùn as Prince of Rǔyīn, Róng as Prince of Liáng,
and Lún as Prince of Lángyá;
younger brothers Yōu as Prince of Qí, Jiàn as Prince of Lè'ān, and Jī as Prince of Yān;
also enfeoffed seventeen others including the Minister over the Masses Wàng and others all as princes.
Wàng
was the son of Fú.
The Emperor enfeoffed the various princes,
using commanderies as their states.
Fiefs of twenty thousand households were great states,
establishing upper, middle, and lower three armies,
with five thousand soldiers;
ten thousand households were secondary states,
establishing upper and lower armies,
with three thousand soldiers;
five thousand households were small states,
establishing one army,
with five hundred soldiers.
The princes did not go to their states,
but held office in the capital.
Zhòu,
pronounced zhòu.
Including,
pronounced cóng.
Guǎn,
pronounced guān.
Róng,
pronounced róng.
Yān,
pronounced yān.
Appointed Zhèng Chōng as Grand Tutor,
Wáng Xiáng as Grand Guardian,
Hé Zēng as Grand Commandant,
Jiǎ Chōng as Chariot and Horse General,
and Wáng Shěn as Chariot and Horse General;
the remaining civil and military officials were promoted in rank and advanced in nobility to varying degrees.
Yǐhài day,
appointed the Prince of Ānpíng Fú as Grand Steward,
and Commander of All Military Affairs Within and Without.
The Jìn Treatise states: Grand Steward, Grand Tutor, and Grand Guardian
were the offices of the Three Dukes of Zhōu.
At the beginning of Jìn, because of the taboo on Jǐngdì's name,
and also adopting official titles from the Zhōu Guān,
the Grand Steward was established to replace the responsibilities of the Grand Preceptor,
his rank was increased to that of the Three Excellencies,
and together with the Grand Tutor and Grand Guardian, they were all considered Superior Dukes.
Grand Marshal
was an ancient office.
The Hàn system placed it above the Great General and the Chariot and Horse General,
to replace the duties of the Grand Commandant,
so it was always set up alternately with the Grand Commandant,
not concurrently.
By the time of Wèi, there was a Grand Commandant,
while the Grand Marshal and Great General each became separate offices,
ranking above the Three Excellencies.
Jìn followed this system,
with the Grand Steward, Grand Tutor, Grand Guardian, Minister over the Masses, and Minister of Works as Civil Dukes;
the Left and Right Grand Masters of Splendid Happiness and Grand Masters of Splendid Happiness who opened their own offices
held rank equivalent to Dukes,
wore the Jìnxián cap with three beams,
and a black headcloth.
The Grand Marshal, Great General, and Grand Commandant were Military Dukes;

the Chariot and Horse General, Chariot and Horse General, General of the Guards, General Who Calms the Waves, General Who Pacifies the Army, Protector-General, General Who Guards the Army, General of the Center, the Four Campaigning Generals, the Four Guarding Generals, General Soaring Dragon, General Who Directs the Army, General of the Upper Army, General Who Assists the State, and other Great Generals who opened their own offices
held rank equivalent to Dukes,
all wore military caps,
and plain black headcloths.
Also appointed the Chariot and Horse General Chén Qiān as Great General,
together with the Minister over the Masses, Prince of Yìyáng Wàng, and the Minister of Works Xún Yǐ,
making eight dukes in total,
established simultaneously.
The Emperor, taking warning from the weakness of the Wèi house due to isolation,
thus greatly enfeoffed the imperial clan,
and entrusted them with official duties.
He also decreed that all princes could personally select the senior officials within their states;
only the General of the Guards, Prince of Qí Yōu did not dare,
and in all cases requested instructions from above.
12. The Emperor issued an edict lifting the restrictions on the Wei imperial clan,
and abolished the requirement for military commanders and senior officials to provide hostages.
The Wei dynasty had imposed strict prohibitions on the imperial clan,
and they were also barred from holding office;
now these restrictions were removed.
Additionally, all generals on campaigns and senior officials serving in the provinces
had been required to leave hostages in the capital;
this practice was also abolished.
(Regarding the term "jiàng" [general],
it is pronounced as "liàng."
The term "zhì" [hostage],
is pronounced as "zhì.")
13. The Emperor, succeeding the harsh and extravagant legacy of the Wei dynasty,
sought to correct it with benevolence and frugality.
Tàicháng Chéng Xǔ Qí,
was the son of Xǔ Yǔn.
In the Jìn dynasty, the Tàicháng, Guānglù Xūn, Wèiwèi, Tàipú, Tíngwèi, Dà Hónglú, Zōngzhèng, Dà Sīnóng, Shǎofǔ, Jiāngzuò Dàjiàng, the three ministers of the Empress Dowager, and Dà Chángqiū,
were all ranked as high ministers,
each with officials such as Chéng, Gōngcáo, Zhǔbù, and Wǔguān.
Court discussions considered that Qí's father had been executed,
(Qí's father, Xǔ Yǔn, was executed;
this matter is recorded in the 76th volume, in the first year of the Gāoguì Xiānggōng Zhèngyuán era.)
(Regarding "cháo" [court],
it is pronounced as "zhí yáo fān.")
and requested that he be sent out to serve as an external official;
the Emperor, however, recalled Yǔn's longstanding reputation,
praised Qí's talent,
and promoted him to Cíbù Láng.
(The Wèi Shàngshū department had a Cíbù Láng,
which the Jìn dynasty retained.)
An edict ordered that green hemp be used instead.
14. For the first time, remonstrance officials were established,
with Sànqí Chángshì Fù Xuán and Huángfǔ Táo appointed to these positions.
Since the Qín and Hàn dynasties, there had been Remonstrance Grand Masters,
as Zhèng Chāng said,
"officials whose title signifies remonstrance."
The Eastern Hàn had Remonstrance and Discussion Grand Masters.
The Wèi dynasty did not reinstate them.
The Jìn dynasty used Sànqí Chángshì to rectify omissions and correct faults,
which was the function of remonstrance officials.
(Fù Xuán was the son of Fù Gàn.
Fù Gàn
was the son of the Hàn dynasty's Fù Xiè.)
He submitted a memorial stating:
"I have heard that when the ancient kings ruled the world,
education and transformation flourished from above,
and pure discussion was practiced below.
Recently, Emperor Wǔ of Wèi favored legalist methods, and the world valued punishment and names;
Emperor Wén of Wèi admired openness and freedom, and the world despised integrity and restraint.
Subsequently, the moral fabric was not upheld,
(Regarding "shè" [uphold],
it means to rectify.)
referring to figures like Hé Yàn and Ruǎn Jí.
(Regarding "cháo" [court],
it is pronounced as "zhí yáo fān.")
Now Your Majesty has ascended the throne and received the mandate,
promoting the transformation of Yáo and Shùn,
yet you have not yet elevated clear-minded and courteous ministers to strengthen moral integrity,
nor have you dismissed empty and vulgar scholars to punish impropriety.
Therefore, I still dare to speak out."
The Emperor praised and accepted his words,
ordering Xuán to draft an edict for promotion,
but he was still unable to bring about reform.
15. Initially,
the Hàn dynasty's Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Sīmǎ Jūn
(Jūn's deeds are recorded in the 50th volume, in the second year of the Hàn Āndì Yuánchū era.)
gave birth to Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu Jùn,
Jùn gave birth to Jīngzhào Yǐn Fáng,
and Fáng gave birth to Xuāndì.
(This records the lineage of the Sīmǎ family,
setting the stage for the establishment of the ancestral temple below.)
1. In spring,
first month,
on Dīnghài,
the Wèi ancestral temple was used to sacrifice to Zhēngxī Fǔjūn and those below him,
together with Jǐngdì, making seven shrines in total.
(Shěn Yuē's records state: At the beginning of the Jìn dynasty, sacrifices were made to Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn, Yùzhāng Fǔjūn, Yǐngchuān Fǔjūn, and Jīngzhào Fǔjūn,
along with Xuān Huángdì, Jǐng Huángdì, and Wén Huángdì, forming three zhāo and three mù.
At that time,
Xuān Huáng had not yet been elevated,
and the position of Tàizǔ was vacant,
so six generations were worshipped,
together with Jǐngdì, making seven temples.
The rituals were based on Wáng Sù's theories.)
2. The Emperor honored
Jǐngdì's wife, Lady Yáng, as Jǐnghuánghòu,
and she resided in Hóngxùn Palace.
3. On Bǐngwǔ,
the Empress, Hóngnóng Yángshì, was established;
the Empress
was the daughter of the Wèi dynasty's Tōngshì Láng Wénzōng.
(At the beginning of the Wèi Huángchū era,
the Zhōngshū department established the positions of Jiān and Lìng,
and also established Tōngshì Láng.)
4. The ministers memorialized:
"The Five Emperors
are actually the Heavenly Emperor,
but the royal energy varies with the seasons,
hence there are five different names.
From now on, the seats of the Five Emperors should be removed from the Míngtáng and the southern suburban altar."
This was approved.
The Emperor,
being the maternal grandson of Wáng Sù,
meant that in matters of suburban sacrifices,
the officials mostly followed Sù's opinions.
(The Zhōulǐ states: When sacrificing to Hàotiān Shàngdì,
one wears a great fur robe and a ceremonial cap;
it is the same for sacrificing to the Five Emperors.
Zhèng Xuán believed that Hàotiān Shàngdì referred to
the Heavenly Great Emperor,
the North Star, Yàopò Bǎo.
The Five Emperors
are the spirits of the essence of the Five Elements,
namely: the Green Emperor Língwēi Yǎng,
the Red Emperor Chìbiāo Nù,
the Yellow Emperor Hánshūniǔ,
the White Emperor Báizhāo Jǔ,
and the Black Emperor Zhīguāng Jì.
Hence, there arose the theory of the Six Heavens.
The Six Heavens
refer to the supremely pure and empty substance,
which is actually one;
but when considering their functions of nurturing and giving birth in the five seasons,
they are distinguished into five,
hence the Six Heavens.
Based on their substance above,
they are called Heaven;
Heaven is a term for substance,
hence it is said of Heaven,
Heaven,
means the summit.
Based on their nurturing function,
they are called Emperor;
Emperor is a term for virtue,
hence the Máo Shī Zhuàn states: "As careful and discerning as an emperor."
Wáng Sù refuted this,
arguing that the Five Emperors are not Heaven,
and only used the text of the Jiāyǔ,
stating that Tàihào, Yándì, Huángdì, Shǎohào, and Zhuānxū, the Five Emperors,
are the Five Human Emperors.
The Jìn ministers, following Sù's theory,
believed that the Five Emperors are the Heavenly Emperor,
and that the royal energy varies with the seasons,
so although their names differ into five,
they are actually one deity.
Therefore, in the Míngtáng and southern suburban altar,
the seats of the Five Emperors should be removed,
and the titles of the Five Essences in the five suburban sacrifices should be changed,
all to be called Hàotiān Shàngdì.
This was approved.)
(Regarding "wàng" [king],
it is pronounced as "yú kuàng fān.")
5. In the second month,
the restrictions on the Hàn imperial clan were lifted.
After the Wèi replaced the Hàn,
the various Liú clans were restricted;
now these restrictions were removed.
6. In the third month,
Wú sent Dà Hónglú Zhāng Yǎn and Wǔguān Zhōngláng Jiàng Dīng Zhōng to offer condolences and sacrifices.
(This was due to the mourning for Wéndì.)
(Regarding "lú" [Hónglú],
it is pronounced as "líng rú fān.")
7. Wú's Sànqí Chángshì Wáng
Fān,
who was noble and upright in character,
was unable to flatter and comply with orders,
which displeased the Wú ruler.
Sànqí Chángshì Wàn Yù and Zhōngshū Chéng Chén Shēng consequently slandered him.
When Dīng Zhōng returned from his mission,
the Wú ruler held a grand assembly of ministers,
and Fān, heavily intoxicated, collapsed.
The Wú ruler suspected he was feigning,
and had Fān carried out.
After a short while,
he was summoned back.
Fān was fond of maintaining dignified demeanor,
and his movements were calm and composed.
The Wú ruler was greatly enraged,
shouted to his attendants to behead him in front of the hall,
then went out,
and ascended Lái Mountain.
(The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: South of Wǔchāng city is Lái Mountain,
which is Fán Mountain.)
The Wú ruler Sūn Hào ascended it,
and had his close attendants throw Wáng Fān's head down for tigers to fight over.
(They acted like tigers leaping and wolves fighting, biting and gnawing,
and the head was completely shattered.)
Dīng Zhōng advised the ruler of Wú, saying:
"The north lacks preparations for defense and warfare;
Yìyáng can be attacked and taken."
Yìyáng County,
during the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Rǔnán Commandery;
Emperor Wén of Wèi separately established Yìyáng Commandery.
Advised,
read as shuì.
General of the West Pacification Lù Kǎi said:
"The north has recently annexed Bā and Shǔ,
and sent envoys to seek peace;
this is not because they seek aid from us,
but because they wish to accumulate strength and await the right moment.
The enemy's power is currently strong,
and to seek victory by taking chances
shows no benefit."
Although the ruler of Wú did not send out troops,
he subsequently broke off relations with Jìn.
Kǎi
was a clansman of Lù Xùn.
8 In summer,
the fifth month,
on the Rénzǐ day,
Bólíng Yuángōng Wáng Shěn passed away.
9 In the sixth month,
on the last day, Bǐngwǔ,
there was a solar eclipse.
10 During the mourning period for Emperor Wén,
the officials and people all followed expedient regulations,
removing mourning garments after three days.
After the burial,
the Emperor also removed his;
however, he still wore plain caps and ate simple food,
grieving and emaciating himself like one in mourning.
In autumn,
the eighth month,
the Emperor was about to visit the Chóngyáng Mausoleum,
and his ministers memorialized, saying,
"The autumn heat has not yet subsided,
and we fear the Emperor's grief may cause injury."
The Emperor said:
"We shall be able to pay respects at the mountain mausoleum,
and our health will naturally be fine."
He also issued an edict saying:
"Emperor Wén of Hàn did not allow the whole empire to fully grieve,
which was also the ultimate modest intention of an emperor.
Emperor Wén of Hàn's testamentary edict is seen in the fifteenth scroll, the seventh year of his later reign.
Zhēn Déxiù said: Emperor Wén's edict
was the beginning of shortened mourning.
However, the original text was established for the officials and people;
Emperor Jǐng was the successor ruler—
how could he, based on this, shorten his mourning!
How heartless to have no mourning garments!
Let it be discussed to follow the journey in mourning attire.
The ministers shall follow the old regulations."
The Minister of Works Péi Xiù memorialized:
"Your Majesty has removed mourning garments and then worn them again;
this is not in accordance with righteousness.
If the ruler wears mourning garments but the ministers do not,
we would not dare to feel at ease."
The edict said:
"We are concerned that our feelings cannot reach that far;
what does clothing matter!
This means we are concerned that the feelings of grief and longing do not reach,
not that clothing is important.
Reach,
read as qǐ,
means to stand on tiptoe.
How can we lightly go against this?"
Thus it was stopped.
General of the Central Army Yáng Hù said to Fù Xuán:
"The three-year mourning period,
even for the noble, should be fully observed—
this is ritual.
The three-year mourning period
extends from the Son of Heaven down to the common people;
meaning even with the Son of Heaven's nobility,
he should also be able to fulfill his filial thoughts by observing the three-year mourning.
Our ruler is extremely filial;
although his mourning garments were taken away,
he actually practices mourning rituals.
If, because of this, the laws of the former kings are restored,
would that not be good!"
Xuán said:
"Exchanging months for days
has been practiced for several hundred years;
exchanging months for days
is a mistaken theory of Hàn Confucians;
see the annotation in the fifteenth scroll, the seventh year of Emperor Wén of Hàn's later reign.
It is difficult to implement."
Hù said:
"If we cannot make the whole empire follow the ritual,
at least let the ruler observe the full mourning period—
would that not be better!"
Xuán said:
"If the ruler does not remove mourning garments but the empire does,
this would mean there is only father and son,
and no longer ruler and minister."
Thus it was stopped.
On the Wùchén day,
the ministers memorialized requesting to change garments and resume regular meals;
the edict said:
"Whenever we think of the underworld,
and cannot complete the rituals of wearing coarse hemp and mourning belts,
Zuǒzhuàn: When Qí's Yàn Huánzǐ died,
Yàn Yīng wore coarse mourning hemp and a mourning belt.
Dù Yù's annotation says: Coarse hemp
is hemp with seeds,
chosen for its coarseness.
Coarse hemp,
read as jū.
How much more so when it comes to eating rice and wearing brocade!
This would only agitate our heart,
not soothe it.
We originally come from a scholarly family,
and rituals have been passed down for a long time;
how could we suddenly change these feelings toward our lord in a single day!
There are already many who follow;
you may try to reflect on Confucius's reply to Zǎi Wǒ's words.
The Analects: Zǎi Wǒ asked:
'The three-year mourning period,
one year is already long enough.
If a gentleman does not practice rituals for three years,
rituals will certainly decay;
if he does not practice music for three years,
music will certainly collapse.
The old grain is already gone,
the new grain has already risen;
one year is enough.'
Confucius said:
'If you eat that rice,
wear that brocade,
would you feel at ease?'
He said:
'At ease.'
Confucius said:
'If you feel at ease,
then do it.'
After Zǎi Wǒ left,
Confucius said:
'Yú is unkind!
A child is born and for three years,
only then is it free from its parents' embrace.
The three-year mourning period
is the universal mourning of the world.'
The Book of Etiquette and Ceremonial says: The father
is the child's heaven.
Reflect,
read as xǐng.
Thus, he wore plain garments and observed the three-year mourning period.
Your servant Guāng remarks: The three-year mourning period,
extending from the Son of Heaven down to the common people,
is the ritual classic of the former kings,
unchangeable for a hundred generations.
Emperor Wén of Hàn, following his own mind and not learning,
changed antiquity and corrupted rituals,
severing the kindness between father and son,
damaging the righteousness between ruler and minister;
later emperors could not deeply maintain feelings of grief,
and their ministers flattered and fawned,
with none willing to correct it.
As for Emperor Wǔ of Jìn, alone he corrected and practiced it by his innate nature,
and can be called an extraordinary worthy ruler;
but Péi, Fù, and their like,
obstinate and ignorant mediocre ministers,
accustomed to routine and playing with old ways,
could not support and follow his goodness—
what a pity!
The Classic of Filial Piety says: In serving his superior, a gentleman
supports and follows his goodness,
and corrects and saves his faults.
The annotation says: Support,
means to uphold.
11 Wú changed its era name to Bǎodǐng.
This was because a large ding was obtained there, so the era name was changed.
12 The ruler of Wú appointed Lù Kǎi as Left Chancellor,
and Wàn Yù as Right Chancellor.
The ruler of Wú disliked people looking at him,
and when ministers attended an audience,
none dared to raise their eyes.
Lù Kǎi said:
"There is no way for ruler and minister not to recognize each other;
if something unexpected suddenly happens,
we would not know where to go."
The ruler of Wú then allowed Kǎi to look at him,
but others remained as before.
Only Kǎi could look at him,
others still could not look.
The ruler of Wú resided in Wǔchāng.
The people of Yángzhōu had to travel upstream to supply provisions,
suffering greatly from this.
Wú's Wǔchāng belonged to Jīngzhōu,
while Dānyáng, Xuānchéng, Pílíng, Wú, Wúxīng, Kuàijī, Dōngyáng, Xīndū, Línhǎi, Jiàn'ān, Yùzhāng, Línchuān, Póyáng, and Lúlíng all belonged to Yángzhōu.
Therefore, they suffered from traveling westward upstream,
going against the current to supply provisions.
Both public and private resources were exhausted and depleted.
Lù Kǎi submitted a memorial stating:
"Now that the four borders are at peace,
we should focus on nurturing the people and enriching resources.
Yet instead, we indulge in extreme extravagance and desire;
without disasters, the people's lives are exhausted,
without action, the state's wealth is depleted.
I privately worry about this.
In the past, when the Hàn dynasty declined,
three states stood in a tripartite division;
now Cáo and Liú have lost the Way,
and both have been taken by Jìn.
This is clear evidence from recent times.
I, in my foolishness, only regret for Your Majesty the state's affairs.
Wǔchāng's land is dangerous, barren, and rocky,
unfit for a royal capital.
Moreover, a children's rhyme says: 'Rather drink Jiànyè's water,
than eat Wǔchāng's fish;
rather return to Jiànyè to die,
than stop to dwell in Wǔchāng.'
This rhyme arose from the suffering of traveling upstream to supply provisions.
It sufficiently illustrates the people's hearts and Heaven's intent.
Now the state lacks even a year's reserves.
The Book of Rites, 'Royal Regulations' states: A state without six years' reserves is called precarious;
without three years' reserves, it is said the state is not a state.
How much more so without even a year's reserves!
The state shows signs of exposed roots,
using a tree as metaphor.
The reason a tree can grow and multiply
is because it has roots and trunk.
If the roots gradually become exposed,
then its foundation will be uprooted.
No one shows any concern for this.
In the time of the Great Emperor (Sūn Quán),
the palace women and various weavers numbered less than a hundred.
Since Emperor Jǐng's time,
they have reached over a thousand.
This is an extreme drain on resources.
Furthermore, the ministers on the left and right,
generally are not the right people.
Forming cliques to support each other,
harming the loyal and concealing the worthy,
these are all those who corrupt governance and harm the people.
I wish Your Majesty would reduce and cease the various labors,
abolish harsh and oppressive measures,
select and release palace women,
purify and select the hundred officials.
Then Heaven will be pleased and the people will submit,
and the state will enjoy eternal peace."
Though the ruler of Wú was displeased,
due to Lù Kǎi's longstanding reputation,
he specially tolerated him with favor.
Textual analysis note: Chén Shòu said:
"I have repeatedly met people from Jīngzhōu and Yángzhōu,
and obtained twenty matters that Kǎi admonished Sūn Hào about.
Broadly inquiring among Wú people,
most say they have not heard of Kǎi having this memorial.
Moreover, examining its text, it is extremely blunt and direct,
fearing it was not something Hào could tolerate.
Some believe Kǎi kept it in a box,
not daring to publicize it.
When he was ill and in distress,
Hào sent Dǒng Cháo to inquire what he wished to say,
and thus he handed it over.
Its truth or falsehood is hard to ascertain,
therefore it is not recorded in the main text;
however, admiring its pointing out of Hào's faults,
sufficient to serve as a warning for later generations,
it is copied and placed beside Kǎi's biography."
Now it is not adopted.
13 In the ninth month,
an edict stated:
"From now on, even if there is an imperial decree desiring something,
or a memorial has already been approved,
but if it is inconvenient for the matter at hand,
none may conceal the true situation."

According to the Annotated Rivers Classic: Lèxiāng city is in Chánlíng county of Nánpíng commandery,
with the Jiāng River flowing north of it,
and the Jiāng River also flows eastward past the north of Gōng'ān county.
Sòng Bái said: Lèxiāng is the land of the state of Rǔ during the Spring and Autumn period,
and its city was constructed by Lù Kàng,
located within the borders of Sōngzī county.
The Jìn Geographical Records state: Xìnlíng county belongs to Jiànpíng commandery.
Shěn Yuè said: It is suspected to have been established by Wú.
The Annotated Rivers Classic records: the Jiāng River flows from Kuí city eastwards,
passing south of Xìnlíng county,
and further east passes south of Yílíng county.
Yílíng,
is Xīlíng.
Lèxiāng city lies east of present-day Jiānglíng prefecture in Sōngzī county,
north of Lèxiāng city,
with sand banks in the Jiāng River,
and the opposite bank is shallow enough to ford,
making it a strategically important place.
Kàng, observing many deficiencies in the governance of the Wú ruler,
submitted a memorial stating:
"I have heard that when virtue is equal, the multitude overcomes the few;
when strength is paralleled, those in peace dominate those in danger.
This is why the six states were annexed by Qín,
and western Chǔ was subdued by Hàn.
Now, the enemy occupies not only the region of Guānyòu,
but west of the Hónggōu,
whereas our state lacks external alliances to support us,
and internally, we are not strong as western Chǔ.
Governance is decaying,
and the common people remain ungoverned.
The reason people depend on,
merely using the Yangtze River, lofty mountains as the borderlines of our territory,
this is ultimately a passive defense strategy,
not what the wise prioritize.
Every time I think of this,
I find myself unable to sleep at night,
nor can I eat at meals.
It is the duty of a service to the ruler,
to be honest even if it offends.
I have respectfully composed seventeen strategic recommendations."
It is said that the seventeen recommendations were lost and are not recorded.
Lǐ Xù, due to failure in Jiàn'ān,
killed the leading general Féng Fěi,
and withdrew the army.
Initially, Hé Dìng had sought marriage for his son with Xù,
but Xù refused.
Consequently, Dìng accused Xù of unjustly killing Féng Fěi,
forcibly returning the army,
and then executed Xù along with Xú Cún and their families,
and burned Xù's body.
Dìng also ordered each general to present imperial hunting dogs,
at that time translated as guarding translators,
costing ten thousand coins to capture rabbits for the kitchen;
the people of Wú blamed Dìng,
but the ruler of Wú regarded him as loyal and diligent,
granting him the title of marquis.
Lù Kàng submitted another memorial:
"Small-minded people do not understand reason and morality,
their views are shallow,
even if they exhaust their loyalty and efforts,
they are still unfit for responsibility,
let alone when their deceitful hearts are deeply ingrained, and their loyalties and hatreds easily sway!"
The Wú ruler did not listen.
In June,
on the day Wǔwǔ,
Hú Liè fought the Xiānbēi Túpó Shùjīnéng at Wànhú mound.
Shùjīnéng's ancestor, Shòutián, was still in utero when his mother Xiāng Yèshì was asleep and gave birth within her bedding.
The Xiānbēi called bedding 'Túpó,' thus adopting it as the family name.
By the time of Southern Liáng's Túpó Wūgū,
he was the fifth-generation grandson of Shùjīnéng.
Wànhú mound was located in the Aneast-river water region,
northeast of Āndìng commandery in Gāopíng county.
He was killed.
Commander of Yōng and Liáng provinces military affairs, Fúfēng Wáng Liàng sent General Liú Qí to rescue him,
but Qí hesitated and did not advance.
Liàng was demoted to General of the Pacified West,
and Qí was sentenced to death.
Liàng petitioned,
"The responsibility for the loss in command belongs to Liàng,
I beg to bear the punishment of death."
The decree stated,
"If the blame does not lie with Qí,
there should be another guilty party."
Thus, Liàng's official position was stripped.
Appointing Shàngshū Lè Lìng Shíjiàn as acting General of the Western Territories,
overseeing military matters in Qín province,
Lè Lìng county,
during the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Píngyuán commandery,
later divided to belong to Lè Lìng country.
Shùjīnéng's troops grew strong,
Jiàn instructed Governor of Qín province Dù Yù to send troops to attack him.
Yù believed that the enemy had the advantage of victory and their horses were well-fed,
while the official troops were increasingly eager,
suggesting a significant effort to transport fodder and supplies,
and wait until spring for an offensive.
Jiàn presented Yù's delay in military initiatives,
summoning him in a barred carriage to the court circle,
to discuss a reprieve.
At that time, Yù's authority as Consort of the Currents,
resulting from eight discussions,
was purchased with a marquisate.
Ultimately, he could not overcome.
In the autumn,
in July,
on the day Yǐsì,
the Chéngyáng Wáng Jǐngdù passed away.
On the day Dīngwèi,
Rǔyīn Wáng Jùn was appointed as Grand General of the Western Defense,
overseeing all military affairs in Yōng, Liáng, and other provinces,
stationed at Guānzhōng.
In the winter,
in November,
the crown prince was established as the king of Rǔnán.
The younger brother of the Wú ruler, former General Xiù, was made governor of Xiàkǒu,
the Wú ruler disliked him,
and rumors spread among the people that Xiù would be plotted against.
Xiù, the grandson of Wú ruler Quán's younger brother Kuāng,
fearful,
fled with his family and personal soldiers overnight, numbering in the hundreds.
In December,
Xiù was appointed General of Rapid Cavalry,
with an opened residence, equal to the Three Excellencies,
and was made Duke of Huìjī.
He was richly rewarded to attract the people of Wú.
This year,
Wú issued a general amnesty.
Initially,
the Wèi people settled the five divisions of the Southern Xiōngnú in various commanderies of Bìng province,
living mixed with the people of China.
Since the Eastern Hàn, the Southern Xiōngnú were divided among several commanderies in Bìng province,
the Wèi merely divided their people into five divisions.
This is mentioned in volume sixty-seven of Hàn Xiàn Dì's Jiàn'ān twenty-first year.
At that time, the left division governed over ten thousand settlements,
residing in former Zíðū county of Tàiyuán;
the right division over six thousand settlements,
residing in Qí county;
the southern division over three thousand settlements,
residing in Púzǐ county;
the northern division over four thousand settlements,
residing in Xīnxīng county;
the central division over six thousand settlements,
residing in Dàlíng county.
They adopted the surname Liú.
Initially,
Emperor Gāo of Hàn gave his daughter in marriage to the Chányú,
hence they called themselves the grandchildren of the Hàn,
adopting the surname Liú.
In spring,
in January,
Xiōngnú's Right Wise King Liú Měng rebelled and fled beyond the frontier.
The Inspector of Yù province, Shíjiàn, was accused of falsely claiming Wú military achievements with inflated headcounts,
the decree stated:
"Jiàn holds an important ministerial position,
entrusted by me.
Yet he deceives at low levels,
is this justified!
Such is spoken here.
He shall never be employed again."
3. A man from Wú named Diāo Xuán fraudulently augmented a prophecy text, saying:
"Yellow banners and purple canopies
appear in the southeast;
in the end, the one who will possess All-under-Heaven
is the lord of Jīng and Yáng."
The Surname Genealogy states: The surname Diāo
descends from Shù Diāo, a senior official of Qí.
I note: How could Shù Diāo have descendants!
The "Biographies of Money-Makers" in the Book of Hàn mentions a Diāo Jiān.
The Jiāngbiǎo Chronicle states: Xuán was sent to Shǔ,
obtained Simǎ Huī's discussions on fate, destiny, and calendrical calculations,
and thus fraudulently augmented the text to deceive the people of Wú.
See,
read xiàn as xiàn.
On the last day of this month,
[the ruler of Wú] launched a major military expedition from Huálǐ,
Huálǐ is west of Jiànyè.
They proceeded westward from Niúzhǔ.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: Niúzhǔ lies on the border between the counties of Gūshú and Wūjiāng.
Today, thirty lǐ north of Dāngtú County in Tàipíng Prefecture is Niúzhǔ Mountain.
At the foot of the mountain is Niúzhǔ Jetty,
facing the Héngjiāng Crossing in Hé Prefecture.
Dù Yòu said: Niúzhǔ Qí is present-day Cǎishí in Dāngtú County.
[The ruler of Wú] did not listen.
The Dōngguān Director,
was in charge of collating books and records and compiling accounts.
Guān,
read guān as guàn.
Huá,
read huá as huà.
Hé,
read hé as hè.
The roads were sunken and ruined,
the soldiers, clad in armor and bearing weapons,
a hundred men together pulled one chariot,
nearly dying from the cold and freezing,
all said:
"If we encounter the enemy,
we will immediately turn our weapons around."
Zhòu dispatched troops to meet King Wǔ of Zhōu in battle at Mùyě,
the front ranks turned their weapons around and attacked those behind them,
and were defeated.
So they returned.
The Emperor dispatched Wàng, Prince of Yìyáng, to command the central army of twenty thousand and three thousand cavalry to station at Shòuchūn to prepare for them.
Hearing that the Wú army had retreated,
he then disbanded them.
4. In the third month,
on Bǐngxū,
the Yuán Duke of Jùlù, Péi Xiù, died.
5. In summer,
the fourth month,
Táo Huáng, Governor of Jiāo Prefecture of Wú, attacked Dǒng Yuán, Grand Administrator of Jiǔzhēn,
and killed him;
Yáng Jǐ appointed his general Wáng Sù to replace him.
Textual Analysis states: Huáng's biography says:
"Taking them by surprise,
he went straight to Jiāozhǐ."
Note: Yuán was the Grand Administrator of Jiǔzhēn,
not of Jiāozhǐ.
The Huáyáng Records of States states:
"Yuán died of illness,
Yáng Jǐ then replaced him with Wáng Sù."
Note: According to the Basic Annals of Emperor Wǔ,
"In the fourth month,
Dǒng Yuán, Grand Administrator of Jiǔzhēn, was attacked by Yú Sì, a general of Wú,
his army was defeated,
and he died."
Then Yuán did not die of illness.
Probably, although Jǐ appointed Sù to replace Yuán,
before Sù reached the commandery, Yuán had died.
6. The Hú of Běidì raided Jīnchéng,
Qiān Hóng, Governor of Liáng Prefecture, campaigned against them.
The various Hú all rebelled internally,
and together with Shù Jīnéng besieged Hóng at Qīngshān.
The Continued Hàn Treatise states: Qīngshān is within the boundaries of Shēnluán County in Běidì Commandery.
Xián said: Qīngshān is in present-day Qìng Prefecture,
there is the Qīngshān River.
Textual Analysis states: Cuī Hóng's Spring and Autumn Annals of the Sixteen States, Biography of Tūfǎ Wūgū, says:
"His ancestor Shù Jīnéng was originally a Xiānbēi from Héxī.
During the Tàishǐ era,
he killed Hú Liè, Governor of Qín Prefecture,
and beheaded Qiān Hóng, Governor of Liáng Prefecture."
The Basic Annals of the Jìn Emperor states:
"The rebel tribes killed Hú Liè,
the Hú of Běidì killed Qiān Hóng,"
neither mentions the Xiānbēi.
Probably, speaking of the various tribes rebelling internally,
then the Xiānbēi are also among them.
Or perhaps the Hú of Běidì were Shù Jīnéng.
Previously,
Grand Marshal Chén Qiān said to the Emperor:
"Hú Liè and Qiān Hóng are both brave but lack strategy,
stubborn in their own views,
they are not talents for pacifying the borders,
they will bring shame upon the state."
At that time, Hóng was Governor of Yáng Prefecture,
and often did not comply with Qiān's orders.
At that time, Qiān, as Grand Marshal, commanded the various armies of Yáng Prefecture,
and garrisoned Shòuchūn.
Thereupon [the Emperor] summoned Hóng back,
and once he arrived,
soon again appointed him Governor of Liáng Prefecture.
Qiān secretly sighed,
believing he would certainly be defeated.
The two men indeed lost the harmony of the Qiāng and Róng tribes,
their armies were defeated and they themselves perished.
Campaigns continued for years,
and only then were they barely pacified.
The Emperor then regretted it.
7. In the fifth month,
[the Emperor] enfeoffed his son Xiàn as Prince of Chéngyáng.
8. On Xīnchǒu,
Wàng, Prince of Yìyáng, died.
9. Jiǎ Chōng, Palace Attendant, Imperial Secretary, and General of Chariots and Cavalry,
had been favored and entrusted with authority since Emperor Wén's time.
When the Emperor was Crown Prince,
Chōng contributed significantly,
the matter is seen in scrolls 77 and 78, the Annals of Wèi.
Chōng was an artful flatterer,
and together with the Grand Commandant, Acting Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince, Xún Yǐ,
the Jìn Treatise states: The Emperor, considering the Crown Prince's position to be exalted,
ordered the various Dukes to hold the positions of the two Tutors.
Because their original positions were esteemed,
they therefore either acted or concurrently held the posts.
Yǐ,
read yǐ as yǐ.
Ānpíng County,
in the Former Hàn belonged to Zhuō Commandery,
in the Later Hàn belonged to the Principality of Ānpíng,
in Jìn belonged to Bólíng Commandery.
Dǎn,
read dǎn as dǎn.
The court and the populace detested him.
The Emperor asked the Palace Attendant Péi Kǎi about the gains and losses of the present time.
He replied:
"Your Majesty received the Mandate,
all within the Four Seas follow your influence.
The reason [your virtue] is not yet comparable to Yáo and Shùn
is simply because people like Jiǎ Chōng are still at court.
You should attract worthy men from All-under-Heaven,
to broaden the way of governance,
and should not show people favoritism."
The Palace Attendant Rèn Kǎi of Lè'ān and the Governor of Hénán, Yǔ Chún of Yǐngchuān, were both at odds with Chōng.
Chōng wanted to remove them from their close positions.
Close positions,
refers to Palace Attendant.
Rèn,
read rén as rén.
They should be in the Eastern Palace;
the Emperor appointed Kǎi as Junior Tutor of the Crown Prince,
but he remained Palace Attendant as before.
The Jìn Treatise states: Rèn Kǎi, Palace Attendant,
was personally respected by the Emperor.
He was made to concurrently hold the Junior Tutor position,
probably a temporary arrangement.
Looking at this,
then Chōng wanted to use a scheme to distance Kǎi.
The Emperor was worried about it,
Kǎi said:
"We should obtain a prestigious and weighty minister with wisdom and strategy to pacify and oversee it."
The Emperor said:
"Who would be suitable?"
Kǎi thereupon recommended Chōng,
Chún also praised him.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on Guǐyǒu,
[the Emperor] appointed Chōng as Commander of the Various Military Affairs of Qín and Liáng Prefectures,
remaining Palace Attendant and General of Chariots and Cavalry as before;
Textual Analysis states: The Spring and Autumn Annals of the Thirty States and the Jìn Spring and Autumn Annals
place Chōng's departure in the second month of the eighth year.
Note: According to the Basic Annals of Emperor Wǔ,
Chōng's departure was in this month.
Probably the two Spring and Autumn Annals, because the Crown Prince's marriage was in the second month of the eighth year,
led to this error.
10. The Wu Grand Commander Xuē Xǔ
and Táo Huáng, along with an army of one hundred thousand,
jointly attacked Jiāozhǐ.
When the city ran out of food and reinforcements were cut off,
it fell to Wu.
Yáng Jì and Máo Jiǒng were captured.
Huáng admired Jiǒng's bravery and strength,
and wanted to spare his life;
but Jiǒng plotted to kill Huáng,
so Huáng executed him.
Xiū Zé's son Yǔn
cut open Jiǒng's belly while he was still alive,
removed his liver,
and said:
"Can you still be a rebel now?"
Jiǒng still cursed him, saying:
"I regret not being able to kill your Sūn Hào!
Your father is a dead dog!"
Yǔn's father Zé had been killed by Jiǒng,
see the fourth year above.
Textual Analysis: The Hàn Jìn Chūnqiū states:
"Initially,
Huò Yì sent Yáng Jì and Máo Jiǒng to garrison Jiāozhǐ,
making an oath with them: 'If the enemy besieges the city and you surrender before one hundred days,
your families will be executed;
if after one hundred days,
reinforcements have not arrived and the city falls,
I will bear the blame.'
Jì and the others had not held out for one hundred days
when their provisions were exhausted.
They begged to surrender to Huáng,
but he refused,
and instead supplied them with grain to continue defending.
All his generals advised Huáng: 'Huò Yì is already dead,
so he certainly cannot rescue Jì and the others.
We should wait until their allotted days are full,
and then accept their surrender.
This way, they will be without fault,
and we will gain righteousness.
Internally, it instructs our people;
externally, it shows kindness to neighboring states.
Would this not be good?'
When Jì and the others' time limit was reached and their provisions were exhausted,
and reinforcements had not arrived,
he then accepted their surrender.'"
The Huáyáng Guózhì, however, says:
"Jì and the others were captured when the city fell and were imprisoned.
Jì vomited blood and died,
and Jiǒng died cursing the enemy."
The two accounts contradict each other,
and cannot be reconciled.
Yet the Jìn Táo Huáng biography records both.
Considering that Sūn Hào was suspicious and cruel,
it is unlikely that Huáng dared to supply grain to the enemy.
I now follow the Huáyáng Guózhì.
The Wu forces captured them,
and Jiǔzhēn and Rìnán both surrendered to Wu.
Wu issued a general amnesty,
and appointed Táo Huáng as Governor of Jiāozhōu.
Huáng pacified and subjugated the Yí and Liǎo tribes,
and the entire province was pacified.
11. In the eighth month,
on the day Bǐngshēn,
Chéngyáng King Xiàn died.
12. Four commanderies from Yìzhōu and Nánzhōng were separated to establish Níngzhōu.
Níngzhōu took its name from the Jiànníng commandery,
and governed the four commanderies of Jiànníng, Xīnggǔ, Yúnnán, and Yǒngchāng.
13. In the ninth month,
the Wu Minister of Works Mèng Rén died.
14. In winter,
the tenth month,
on the first day, Dīngchǒu,
there was a solar eclipse.
Textual Analysis: The Sòngshū Wǔxíngzhì records an eclipse on the fifth month, Gēngchén,
but not one on the tenth month, Dīngchǒu.
The Jìnshū Annals and Astronomical Treatise record an eclipse on the tenth month, Dīngchǒu,
but not one on the fifth month, Gēngchén.
I now follow the Jìnshū.
15. In the eleventh month,
Liú Měng invaded Bìngzhōu,
and the Inspector of Bìngzhōu, Liú Qīn, defeated him.
The Jìn Treatise states: Bìngzhōu does not take its name from the Wèi River,
nor is it named after Héng,
but is called Bìng
because it lies between two valleys.
It governed Tàiyuán, Shàngdǎng, Xīhé, Lèpíng, Yànmén, and Xīnxīng.
According to the Jìn Treatise,
based on the Zhōulǐ, the sacred mountain of Bìngzhōu is called Héngshān.
The Chūnqiū Yuánmìngbāo says: The constellation Yíngshì flows into Bìngzhōu,
which is divided into the state of Wèi.
16. When Jiǎ Chōng was about to depart for his post,
the high officials gave him a farewell feast at the Xīyáng Pavilion.
Xián's note: The Xīyáng Pavilion was west of Hénán city.
Xù said:
"You are the Prime Minister,
yet you are being controlled by one man.
Is that not shameful!
However, regarding this departure,
it is truly difficult to refuse.
The only way is to arrange a marriage with the Crown Prince,
then you can stay without having to refuse."
Chōng said:
"But who can I entrust this idea to?"
Xù said:
"Allow me to speak of it."
He then said to Féng Dǎn:
"With Lord Jiǎ going far away,
we will lose our influence;
the Crown Prince's marriage is not yet settled.
Why not advise the Emperor to take Lord Jiǎ's daughter!"
Dǎn agreed.
Initially,
the Emperor intended to take Wèi Guàn's daughter for the Crown Prince.
Chōng's wife Guō Huái bribed the attendants of Empress Yáng,
to have the Empress persuade the Emperor to take her daughter instead.
The Emperor said:
"Duke Wèi's daughter has five desirables,
Duke Jiǎ's daughter has five undesirables: The Wèi family line is virtuous and has many sons,
and she is beautiful, tall, and fair-skinned."
The five desirables: Virtuous lineage,
first;
many sons,
second;
beauty,
third;
tall,
fourth;
fair-skinned,
fifth.
The five undesirables
can be inferred by analogy.
Shùi,
read as shuō, with the meaning of persuasion.
Zhǒng,
read as zhǒng, meaning lineage;
same below.
She is ugly, short, and dark-skinned."
The Empress persistently requested it,
and Xún Yǐ, Xún Xù, and Féng Dǎn all praised Chōng's daughter as exceedingly beautiful,
and furthermore talented and virtuous.
The Emperor then complied.
Chōng was kept in his former post.
This sets the stage for the Jiǎ clan bringing disorder to Jìn.
17. In the twelfth month,
Zhèng Mào, Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, was appointed Minister of Works,
but Mào firmly declined and did not accept.
18. This year,
the Duke of Ānlè, Liú Shàn, died.
19. Wu appointed Fàn Shèn, Governor of Wǔchāng from Guǎnglíng, as Grand Commandant.
The General of the Right, Sīmǎ Dīng Fèng, died.
According to Dīng Fèng's biography,
for his merit in rescuing Shòuchūn, he was appointed General of the Left;
after executing Sūn Chēn,
he was appointed Grand General,
with the additional titles of Left and Right Protector;
he jointly welcomed the Wu ruler Sūn Hào,
and was promoted to Grand Marshal of the Right and Army Supervisor of the Left.
He should be recorded as Grand Marshal of the Right and Army Supervisor of the Left.
20. Wu changed the next year's era name to Fènghuáng.
The era name was changed because phoenixes were said to have gathered in the Western Park.
1. In spring,
the first month,
the Army Supervisor Hé Zhēn attacked Liú Měng,
repeatedly defeating him.
He secretly used benefits to lure Liú Měng's Left Division commander Lǐ Kè.
The Left Division
was one of the five divisions.
Shuài,
read as shuài, meaning commander.
2. In the second month,
on the day Xīnmǎo,
the Crown Prince married Jiǎ.
She was fifteen years old,
two years older than the Crown Prince.
She was jealous, crafty, and manipulative,
and the Crown Prince was infatuated with her but also afraid of her.
On the Rénchén day (the 3rd),
Prince Ānpíng Xiàn, Sīmǎ Fú, passed away,
at the age of ninety-three.
Fú was loyal and cautious by nature.
During the period when Xuāndì (Sīmǎ Yì) held power,
Fú often deliberately withdrew and diminished his own role.
Later, during the occasions of depositions and enthronements,
he never participated in the planning;
Emperors Jǐng (Sīmǎ Shī) and Wén (Sīmǎ Zhāo), because Fú was a senior member of the clan,
also did not dare to pressure him.
During these times of depositions and enthronements,
Fú was gentle yet able to uphold correctness.
The events are recorded in the 76th scroll, under the first year of the Zhèngyuán era, and the 77th scroll, under the first year of the Jǐngyuán era.
The imperial favor and courtesies shown to him were especially great.
At the Yuánhuì assembly,
an edict permitted Fú to ride in a carriage up to the palace hall,
and the Emperor would greet and bow to him at the zuò steps.
The zuò steps,
are the eastern steps,
the master's steps.
Shàng (to ascend),
is pronounced shí zhǎng fān;
the same applies below.
The Emperor personally raised a cup to offer him long life,
following the etiquette of family members.
Each time the Emperor bowed,
Fú would kneel to stop him.
Although Fú received such respect and favor,
he did not consider it an honor,
and often wore a worried expression.
On his deathbed,
he left instructions stating:
"I, Sīmǎ Fú, styled Shūdá, a loyal scholar of the Wèi state from Hénèi,
am neither like Yī Yǐn nor like the Duke of Zhōu,
neither like Bó Yí nor like Liǔ Xià Huì,
but in establishing myself and practicing the Way,
I have remained consistent from beginning to end.
I should be dressed in ordinary clothes of the time,
and placed in a plain coffin for burial."
An edict bestowed upon him the Dōngyuán Wēnmíng secret burial objects.
Fú Qián said: The Dōngyuán Wēnmíng
is shaped like a square lacquered barrel,
open on one side,
painted with lacquer,
with a mirror placed inside it,
which is suspended above the corpse,
and covered together during the grand encoffining.
Shī Gǔ said: Dōngyuán,
is the name of an office,
subordinate to the Shǎofǔ,
which is in charge of making these objects.
The secret objects,
are a catalpa wood coffin,
because they are funerary objects,
they are kept secret.
All followed the precedent of Prince Dōngpíng Xiàn of the Hàn;
see the 46th scroll, under the eighth year of the Jiànchū era of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn.
The objects provided,
were not used at all.
On the 4th, the Emperor was discussing affairs with Right General Huángfǔ Táo.
In the fifth year of the Tàishǐ era,
the position of General Zhènjūn was abolished,
and the positions of Left and Right Generals were reinstated.

'To rely on chaos and act recklessly is called chǒu,'

The Emperor, by decree, granted him the posthumous name Xiào.
Granting a posthumous name by decree
means not following the Erudite's proposal,
but bestowing the name through an imperial edict.
14 The former Colonel Director of Retainers, Fù Xuán, passed away.
Textual analysis notes: Xuán's biography states:
"In the fifth year,
he was promoted to Grand Coachman,
then transferred to Colonel Director of Retainers.
When Empress Jǐngxiàn passed away,
he was dismissed for disputing positions and insulting a Secretary.
He died soon after."
However, Empress Jǐngxiàn passed away in the fourth year,
so Xuán's biography is mistaken.
Whenever he had an impeachment to submit,
even if it was dusk,
he would hold the white tablet,
adjust his hairpin and belt,
(from the *Wénxuǎn*: Rèn Fǎng's impeachment of Cáo Jǐngzōng says: I respectfully present this white tablet for your attention.
Lǚ Xiàng's commentary states: Tablet,
means a brief memorial.
The *Jìn* records state: In ancient times, officials held tablets,
and would write matters on them,
hence they often wore hairpin brushes;
the modern white brush
is a remnant of this practice.
Officials of the third rank and above in the Five Departments wore them.
Belt,
refers to a leather belt,
the ancient pán belt.)
Impeach,
pronounced hù gài fān,
also hù dé fān.
He would sit and wait until dawn;
because of this, the nobility was awed and fearful.
The *Zhōu* official Shīshì
taught the sons of the state's nobility.
The commentary states: Sons of the nobility,
are the sons of kings and dukes,
who do not hold official positions.
Fear,
pronounced zhī shè fān.
Xuán was on good terms with the Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Cuī Hóng from Bólíng.
Emperor Ān of Hàn divided Ānpíng
to establish the Bólíng commandery.
He enjoyed bluntly pointing out others' faults to their face,
but never spoke ill of them behind their backs.
People respected him for this.
15 The Xiānbēi leader Shù Jīnéng had long been a border threat.
Shù Jīnéng began his raids in the sixth year of Tàishǐ,
and by now it was the ninth year.
Court discussions all considered military campaigns to be serious matters,
and that the barbarians were not a major concern.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Shù Jīnéng attacked and captured Liáng Province.
Liáng Province's seat was at Wǔwēi.
The Emperor faced the court and sighed:
"Who can campaign against these barbarians for me?"
The Military Supervisor Mǎ Lóng stepped forward and said:
"If Your Majesty can appoint me,
I can pacify them."
The Emperor said:
"If you can certainly pacify the bandits,
why would I not appoint you?
It depends on your strategy!"
Lóng said:
"I wish to recruit three thousand brave men,
regardless of their origin.
Those who respond to the recruitment,
may come from the fields,
or from the army camps,
or be fugitives,
or slaves.
I will not question their origins.
The barbarians will not be difficult to pacify."
The Emperor approved.
On the day Yǐchǒu,
he appointed Lóng as Campaigning Against Barbarians Protector of the Army and Grand Administrator of Wǔwēi.
The high ministers all said:
"Our existing troops are already numerous,
we should not arbitrarily establish rewards for recruitment.
Lóng is a minor officer speaking recklessly,
he is not to be trusted."
The Emperor did not listen.
Lóng recruited those capable of drawing a bow of four jūn or drawing a crossbow of nine shí.
Thirty jīn make one jūn,
four jūn make one shí,
one shí is one hundred twenty jīn.
Mark,
means to indicate.
He obtained three thousand five hundred men.
Lóng said:
"This is sufficient."
He also requested to personally go to the armory to select weapons.
The Armory Director argued angrily with Lóng.
The *Jìn* records state: The Armory Director
was under the Commandant of the Guards.
From the Eastern Hàn through Wèi and Jìn,
the Palace Assistant Imperial Clerk was the head of the Censorate.
Impeach,
pronounced hù gài fān,
also hù dé fān.
"I am to give my life on the battlefield,
yet the Armory Director issues me decayed weapons from the Wèi era.
This is not in accordance with Your Majesty's intent in employing me."
The Emperor ordered that Lóng take whatever he wished,
and additionally provided him with three years' worth of military supplies before sending him off.
2 Earlier,
the Southern Chányú Hūchúquán had appointed his elder brother Yúfúluó's son Bào as Left Worthy Prince.
When Emperor Wǔ of Wèi divided the Xiōngnú into five tribes,
(the five tribes are mentioned in the sixth year of Tàishǐ in the previous scroll.)
Bào's son Yuān
was exceptionally talented from a young age.
He studied under Cuī Yóu from Shàngdǎng,
and was widely learned in the classics and histories.
He once said to his fellow students Zhū Jì from Shàngdǎng and Fàn Lóng from Yànmén:
"I have often felt ashamed for Suí Hé and Lù Jiǎ's lack of military prowess,
and for Jiàng Hóu and Guàn Yīng's lack of literary talent;
Suí Hé and Lù Jiǎ encountered Emperor Gāo but could not establish achievements worthy of marquisates,
Jiàng Hóu and Guàn Yīng encountered Emperor Wén but could not promote education in schools.
Is this not regrettable!"
Suí Hé and Lù Jiǎ,
were Suí Hé and Lù Jiǎ.
Jiàng Hóu and Guàn Yīng,
were Marquis Jiàng Zhōu Bó and General Guàn Yīng.
When he grew up,
he had long arms good for archery,
possessed extraordinary physical strength,
and had a majestic appearance.
He served as a Hostage Son in Luòyáng.
Wáng Hún and his son Jì both held him in high regard,
and repeatedly recommended him to the Emperor.
The Emperor summoned him for an audience,
and was pleased with him.
Jì said:
"Yuān has great civil and military talent.
If Your Majesty entrusts him with affairs in the southeast,
Wú will not be difficult to pacify."
Kǒng Xún and Yáng Yáo said:
"If he is not of our kind,
his heart must be different.
(From the *Zuǒzhuàn*,
Lǔ's Jì Wénzǐ said:
"Shǐ Yì's records state: If they are not of our kind,
their hearts must be different.")
Yáo,
pronounced yú zhāo fān.
Therefore, he should not be given heavy responsibilities."
When Liáng Province fell,
the Emperor asked Lǐ Xǐ about a general.
He replied:
"If Your Majesty can indeed mobilize the masses of the five Xiōngnú tribes,
grant Liú Yuān the title of a general,
and have him lead them west,
Shù Jīnéng's head can be taken and displayed within days."
Kǒng Xún said:
"If Yuān indeed beheads Shù Jīnéng,
then the troubles in Liáng Province will only become deeper."
The Emperor then stopped.
Dōnglái Wáng Mí came from a family that had held the rank of two thousand piculs for generations.
Shì Yǔ states: Mí was
the grandson of Wáng Qí, the Grand Administrator of Xuāntù in the Wèi dynasty.
He was skilled in horsemanship and archery,
and the people of Qīngzhōu called him
"the Flying Leopard."
The recluse Dǒng Yǎng from Chénliú, upon seeing him, said to him:
"You delight in chaos and calamity;
if there is trouble in the world,
you will not remain a gentleman-official."
This meant he would become a bandit.
Chǔ (處) is pronounced chǔ.
Hǎo (好) is pronounced hào.
Lè (樂) is pronounced lè.
He said to Mí:
"Wáng and Lǐ were recognized because of their local connections—
Wáng Hún was from Tàiyuán,
Lǐ Xǐ was from Shàngdǎng,
both from the same region as Yuān.
They are merely enough to cause trouble for us."
Thereupon, he sighed and wept.
Qí Wáng Yōu heard of this
and spoke to the Emperor, saying:
"If Your Majesty does not eliminate Liú Yuān,
I fear Bīngzhōu will not remain peaceful for long."
Wáng Hún said:
"The great Jìn is just now winning over foreign customs with trust;
why kill a hostage prince over unfounded suspicions?
How lacking in magnanimity and tolerance!"
The Emperor said:
"Hún's words are correct."
It happened that Bào died,
and Yuān replaced him as Left Division Commander.
The affairs of Liú Yuān begin here.
The history states that Jìn was about to face turmoil.
Shuài (帥) is pronounced shuài.
3 In summer,
the fourth month,
a great amnesty was declared.
4 The hostage obligations for commanders of private troops and below were abolished.
At the beginning of the Emperor's reign,
the hostage obligations for commanders of private troops were abolished;
now, the hostage obligations for supervisors of private troops were also abolished.
Zhì (質) is pronounced zhì.
5 The Grand Administrator of Guìlín in Wú, Xiū Yǔn, died.
Guìlín was a Hàn county,
belonging to Yùlín Commandery.
In the third year of the Fènghuáng era of Wú's ruler Hào,
Guìlín Commandery was established separately.
The supervising commanders Guō Mǎ, Hé Diǎn, and Wáng Zú, among others, were from long-standing military families
and were unwilling to be separated.
It happened that the ruler of Wú was conducting a census of the households in Guǎngzhōu,
and Mǎ and others, taking advantage of the people's unrest,
gathered a crowd, attacked, and killed the Governor of Guǎngzhōu, Yú Shòu.
Mǎ proclaimed himself Commander of Military Affairs for Jiāo and Guǎng Provinces,
sent Diǎn to attack Cāngwú,
and sent Zú to attack Shǐxīng.
In the first year of the Gānlù era of Wú's ruler Hào,
Shǐxīng Commandery was established from the southern part of Guìyáng Commandery.
In the eighth month,
Wú appointed the Army Advisor Zhāng Tì as Chancellor,
the Niúzhǔ Commander Hé Zhí as Minister over the Masses,
and the Bearer of the Gilded Mace Téng Xiū as Minister of Works.
Before they were installed,
Xiū was instead appointed Governor of Guǎngzhōu
and led ten thousand men along the eastern route to attack Guō Mǎ.
Mǎ killed the Grand Administrator of Nánhǎi, Liú Lüè,
and drove out the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu, Xú Qí.
The ruler of Wú also sent the Commander of Xúlíng, Táo Jùn, with seven thousand men.
Xúlíng was opposite Dòngpǔ on the riverbank.
During the time of Wú's ruler Quán,
after Lǚ Fàn's defeat at Dòngpǔ,
Wèi's Zāng Bà crossed the river to attack Xúlíng,
but Quán Cóng and Xú Shèng repelled him.
Also, Huà Hé was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xúlíng,
so Xúlíng was likely the name of a station.
Because it faced the river crossing,
Wú established a commander to guard it.
The Nán Xúzhōu Jì states: Jīngkǒu was originally called Xúlíng,
located in the western district of Dāntú County, at Jīngkǒu Village.
6 In Wú, there was a ghost-eye vegetable that grew in the home of the artisan Huáng Gǒu;
there was also a "buy vegetable" that grew in the home of the artisan Wú Píng.
The Wú Zhì states: The ghost-eye vegetable
climbs around jujube trees,
growing over ten feet long,
with stems four inches wide
and three-tenths of an inch thick.
The buy vegetable
is four feet tall, two-tenths of an inch thick,
shaped like a loquat,
with stems one foot eight inches wide,
the lower stem five inches wide,
leaves growing on both sides,
and green in color.
Wú had a Director of the Eastern Lodge.
Guān (觀) is pronounced guàn.
The buy vegetable was called the "calm-worry grass."
The ruler of Wú appointed Gǒu as Attendant of the Mushrooms Gentleman
and Píng as Calm-Worry Gentleman,
both with silver seals and blue ribbons.
According to Hàn regulations,
silver seals and blue ribbons
were worn by officials of the fully two thousand picul rank.
The ruler of Wú, whenever feasting with his ministers,
would order them all to become thoroughly drunk.
He also appointed ten court gentlemen as overseers of faults.
After the feast concluded,
each would report the shortcomings and errors of the others.
Any glance of displeasure or mistaken word
would be reported without exception.
For major offenses, punishment or execution was imposed;
for minor ones, they were recorded as crimes.
Some had their faces skinned,
others had their eyes gouged out.
As a result, superiors and subordinates became estranged,
and no one exerted their full effort.
The Inspector of Yìzhōu, Wáng Jùn, submitted a memorial stating:
"Sūn Hào is debauched, cruel, and rebellious;
he should be swiftly attacked.
If Hào were to die suddenly
and a worthy ruler were established in his place,
then they would become a formidable enemy.
I have been building ships for seven years—
in the eighth year of Tàishǐ,
Jùn began building ships,
and by now it has been seven full years.
I am seventy years old;
death could come any day.
If any one of these three factors goes awry,
it will be difficult to achieve our goal.
I sincerely hope Your Majesty does not miss this opportunity."
The Emperor then resolved to attack Wú.
It happened that General Āndōng Wáng Hún submitted a report that Sūn Hào intended to march north,
and the border defenses were all on alert,
so the court instead discussed launching the campaign the following year.
Wáng Jùn's Army Advisor Hé Pān, who was on a mission in Luòyáng,
submitted a memorial stating:
"Hào certainly will not dare to come out;
we should take advantage of the alert
to launch a surprise attack—it would be very easy."
Dù Yù submitted a memorial stating:
"Since the intercalary month began,
(This year had an intercalary seventh month.)
the enemy has had no troops to move upward.
Wú, from Jiànyè, has raided Huái and Xiāng,
all moving from downstream up the river.
(Up,
read as shàng with the rising tone.)
This is the desperate plan of the bandits;
their strength cannot secure both ends,
so they will certainly defend east of Xiàkǒu to prolong their survival.
(When a person's eyes cannot see,
and breath cannot be drawn,
they are unmistakably dead.)
Their capital is left empty.
Yet Your Majesty, misled by others,
is about to abandon this grand strategy,
allowing the enemy to cause future calamities.
This is truly regrettable.
If launching the campaign might lead to defeat,
then not launching it would be acceptable.
But now, the plan is well-prepared,
ensuring completeness and security.
If it succeeds,
it will lay the foundation for lasting peace;
if it fails, it will only waste a few months' time.
Why hesitate and not give it a try!
If we must wait until the year after next,
(Xū means to wait.)
the situation will not be as favorable as usual,
and I fear it will become even more difficult.
Now we have a perfectly safe plan,
with no risk of collapse.
My mind is truly decided,
(Liǎo means determined.)
not ambiguous or unclear.
(Àimèi means unclear.)
After a full month without a response,
(Lěi, read as lì ruì fān.)
Dù Yù submitted another memorial:
'Yáng Hù did not first seek broad counsel from the court officials
but secretly plotted this strategy with Your Majesty,
which has led to many differing opinions among the courtiers.
In all matters, one should weigh the advantages and disadvantages.
For this campaign, the advantages are eight or nine out of ten,
while the disadvantages are only one or two,
amounting to nothing more than failure.
Even if we ask the court officials to describe the shape of defeat,
they cannot do so.
It is simply that the plan did not originate from them,
and the credit will not belong to them,
so they are ashamed of their earlier mistaken statements and stubbornly cling to them.
These words expose the true hearts of Jiǎ Chōng, Xún Xù, Féng Dǎn, and others.
Dissenting opinions arise sharply;
although people's minds differ,
it is also because they rely on imperial favor without considering future consequences,
thus lightly agreeing or disagreeing.
Since autumn,
the signs of attacking the enemy have become quite apparent.
If we halt now,
Sūn Hào might become frightened and devise a plan,
moving the capital to Wǔchāng,
further repairing the cities south of the river,
relocating the residents far away.
Then the cities would be unassailable,
and the countryside would offer nothing to plunder.
By next year, our plans might be too late!'"
The Emperor was playing wéiqí with Zhāng Huá.
(The Bówùzhì states: Yáo invented wéiqí to teach his son Dānzhū.
Some say: Shùn, because his son Shāngjūn was foolish,
created wéiqí to teach him.
The method requires intelligence to master.)
Huá pushed aside the board, folded his hands, and said:
"Your Majesty is sagely and martial;
the state is wealthy and the army strong.
The ruler of Wú is licentious and cruel,
killing the worthy and capable.
To attack him now
would require little effort to secure victory.
I urge you not to doubt this!"
The Emperor then approved it.
He appointed Huá as Minister of Revenue,
to plan and manage transportation and supplies.
Jiǎ Chōng, Xún Xù, and Féng Dǎn vehemently opposed it.
The Emperor grew furious,
and Chōng removed his cap to apologize.
The Vice Director Shān Táo withdrew and told others:
"Unless one is a sage,
external peace inevitably brings internal worries.
(This is a saying from Fàn Wénzǐ, a senior official of Jìn in the Zuǒzhuàn.)
How could this not be part of the calculation!"
Shān Táo, as a high official,
did not speak openly at court but withdrew to tell others,
likely seeking to align himself with Jiǎ Chōng.
In winter,
the eleventh month,
a massive campaign against Wú was launched.
Zhènjūn General Lángyé Prince Shì was sent to Túzhōng,
Āndōng General Wáng Hún to Jiāngxī,
(now Hézhōu, taking the Héngjiāng crossing route.)
Píngnán General Hú Fèn to Xiàkǒu,
Zhènnán General-in-Chief Dù Yù to Jiānglíng,
Lóngxiāng General Wáng Jùn and Bādōng Supervisor Lǔguó's Táng Bīn down to Bā and Shǔ.
The forces totaled over two hundred thousand from east to west.
Jiǎ Chōng was appointed as Envoy with Credentials, Bearer of the Yellow Axe, and Grand Commander.
(Emperor Wén of Wèi appointed Cáo Zhēn as Commander of Internal and External Military Affairs,
bearing the Yellow Axe.
In the fourth year of Emperor Míng's Tàihé era,
Sīmǎ Yì campaigned against Shǔ,
with the additional title of Grand Commander.
This followed Wèi's system.)
(King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
holding the Yellow Axe in his left hand.
The Yellow Axe is an imperial instrument,
not for exclusive use by subjects,
hence 'borrowed.')
(Shǐ, read as shū lì fān.)
Chōng firmly argued that attacking Wú was unfavorable
and claimed he was too old and frail
to shoulder the commander's responsibility.
An edict stated:
"If you do not go,
I will lead myself."
Chōng had no choice
and accepted the credentials and axe,
leading the central army south to station at Xiāngyáng,
coordinating all armies.
Mǎ Lóng crossed the Wēn River westward.
(East of Wǔwēi is the Wēnwéi River.)
Lóng found the mountain paths narrow and confined,
so he created flat-sided carts.
(Xiá is the same as narrow.
With flat cart sides, they could travel narrow paths.
Biǎn, read as bǔ diǎn fān.)
He mounted wooden shelters on the carts
to shield against wind and rain
and defend against arrows and stones.
After traveling over a thousand lǐ,
they inflicted heavy casualties.
(Commentary: Lóng's biography says:
'Sometimes magnetic stones were piled along the road;
the enemy wore iron armor
and could not advance.
Lóng's soldiers all wore rhinoceros hide armor,
unaffected,
so the enemy thought them divine.'
This account seems too fanciful
and likely unreliable.
I say magnetic stones attracting iron armor
is plausible in principle.)
News was cut off,
and the court grew anxious,
some fearing he was lost.
Later, Lóng's envoy arrived at night.
The Emperor clapped his hands joyfully
and the next morning
summoned his ministers, saying:
"Had I listened to all of you,
we would have lost Liángzhōu."
He then issued an edict granting Lóng credentials
and appointed him Xuānwēi General.
(Shěn Yuē's records: Wèi established forty general titles,
Xuānwēi being the second.)
The Xiānbēi chieftain Cùbá Hán Qiě Wànnéng led over ten thousand households to surrender.
In the twelfth month,
Lóng fought a major battle with Shù Jīnéng,
killing him;
Liángzhōu was thus pacified.
8 The emperor issued an edict inquiring among the court officials about the strengths and weaknesses of governance.
Fù Xián, the Left Chief Clerk of the Minister over the Masses, submitted a memorial stating,
(Jìn Dynasty Records: The Minister over the Masses added one Left and one Right Chief Clerk each.)
(Cháo,
pronounced zhí yáo.)
"The insufficiency in both public and private resources is due to the excessive number of established offices.
In the past, there were only four military governors,
but now, including supervising armies, they exceed ten.
(At the beginning of the Wei dynasty, military governors were established for various armies:
in the southeast to guard against Wú,
in the west to guard against Shǔ,
and in the north to guard against the northern tribes.
Based on their seniority and prestige, they were given titles such as Zhēng, Zhèn, Ān, and Píng,
totaling only four.
Later, additional appointments were made,
including the military governor for the defense of Yèchéng,
the military governor for Qín, Yōng, and Liáng,
the military governor for Liáng and Yì,
the military governor for Jīngzhōu,
the military governor for Yángzhōu,
the military governor for Xúzhōu,
the military governor for Huáiběi,
the military governor for Yùzhōu,
the military governor for Yōuzhōu,
and the military governor for Bìngzhōu,
making ten in total.
Those of lower seniority served as supervising armies.)
The number of provincial inspectors today is nearly double that of the past.
(At that time, there were inspectors for Sī, Yù, Xú, Yǎn, Jīng, Yáng, Liáng, Yì, Níng, Jiāo, Qín, Yōng, Liáng, Jì, Yōu, Bìng, and Qīng—eighteen in total.)
(Jǐ,
pronounced jū xī.)
During the Yuánshǐ era of the Hàn dynasty,
there were 13,233,612 households
and a population of 59,194,978.
This was the peak of the Hàn dynasty.
At the beginning of Emperor Huán's reign,
there were 26,070,906 households
and a population of 50,066,856.
After Wèi annexed Shǔ,
in the fourth year of the Jǐngyuán era,
when combined with Shǔ's statistics,
there were 943,423 households
and a population of 5,372,891.
Thus, the population was only about one-tenth of the Hàn dynasty's,
and the number of households was even less.
Empty military offices were established,
often numbering in the hundreds,
yet they contributed nothing to the palace guards.
The nobles of the five ranks
idly maintained their own staff.

(Military offices refer to titles such as Piāoqí, Chēqí, Wèi, Fúbō, Fǔjūn, Dūhù, Zhènjūn, Zhōngjūn, Diǎnjūn, Shàngjūn, Fǔguó, Lǐngjūn, Hùjūn, Zuǒ‧Yòu Wèi, Xiāoqí, Yóujī, Zuǒ‧Yòu‧Qián‧Hòu Jūn, and various other general titles.
The staff of the five-rank nobles:

kings established tutors, friends, literary scholars, chief stewards, commandants, grand ministers of agriculture, left and right regular attendants, gentlemen attendants, directors of documents, sacrifices, guards, and schools, deputy directors of documents, secretaries, commandants, marshals, heirs, secondary sons, overseers of tombs and temples, receptionists, grand masters of the palace, retainers, and directors of the household.
Dukes, marquises, and below also maintained staff,
varying in size according to the state,
with no fixed regulations.)
All these are burdens on the people,
which is the reason for their impoverishment.
The most urgent task today
is to reduce offices, lighten labor duties,
and ensure that both the government and the people focus on agriculture."
Fù Xián
was the son of Fù Xuán.
At that time, there was also a proposal to halve the number of officials in provinces, commanderies, and counties to promote agricultural work.
Xún Xù, the Director of the Central Secretariat, believed
that "reducing officials is not as good as reducing offices,
reducing offices is not as good as reducing administrative tasks,
and reducing administrative tasks is not as good as cultivating a clear and tranquil mind.
In the past, when Xiāo Hé and Cáo Shěn served the Hàn dynasty,
they upheld a policy of tranquility,
and the people enjoyed peace and stability.
(This is recorded in the twelfth volume, in the second year of Emperor Huì of Hàn's reign.)
They suppressed empty talk,
simplified documents and cases,
overlooked minor strictures,
pardoned small faults.
Those who sought profit by frequently changing established norms
were inevitably punished.
This is what is meant by reducing administrative tasks.
Merging the Nine Courts into the Imperial Secretariat
and transferring the responsibilities of the Orchid Terrace to the Three Ducal Offices
is what is meant by reducing offices.
(The Nine Courts refer to the courts of the Nine Ministers.
At the beginning of the Hàn dynasty, the Nine Ministers each had their own responsibilities.
After the Eastern Capital era,
the various bureaus of the Imperial Secretariat took charge of many affairs,
and the Nine Ministers became largely ceremonial positions.
Therefore, it was proposed to merge them into the Imperial Secretariat.
The Orchid Terrace refers to the Censorate.
The Three Ducal Offices refer to the offices of the Three Dukes.
In the Hàn dynasty, the Chancellor had a chief clerk and an inspector,
while the Imperial Counselor had a deputy and attendant censors
responsible for investigating and reporting illegal activities.
Therefore, Xún Xù proposed transferring the Orchid Terrace's duties to the Three Ducal Offices.)
If all officials in the empire were reduced by half,
I fear that the numerous civil and military officials
and the duties of commanderies and states
vary in difficulty and complexity,
and cannot be treated uniformly.
If vacancies arise,
they will inevitably need to be refilled,
and this could lead to even greater proliferation.
This is a matter that cannot be taken lightly."
Punctuated by Wáng Chóngwǔ, reviewed by Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí.
Compiled by Sīmǎ Guāng
by imperial decree.
Later Student Tiāntāi
Middle Reign of Emperor Shìzǔ Wǔ
First Year of Tàikāng
(Gēngzǐ, 280 AD) In April of this year,
the era name was changed.
1 Spring,
first month,
Wú declared a general amnesty.
2 Dù Yù advanced toward Jiānglíng,
Wáng Hún marched out from Héngjiāng,
attacking Wú's garrisons and border posts,
and wherever they went, they triumphed.
In the second month,
on the Wùwǔ day,
