People at the time called them the 'Three Yángs'.
Many of the old ministers were sidelined and dismissed.
Shān Tāo repeatedly offered admonitions and remonstrances,
and although the Emperor knew of this, he could not change his ways.
2. Initially,
the Xianbei chieftain Mòhùbá began moving from beyond the frontier to settle north of Jíchéng in Liáoxī.
Jíchéng was located within the boundaries of Chānglí County.
Later, the Mùróng clan established Jíchéng County.
In the eighth year of the Zhēnjūn era of Emperor Tàiwǔ of the Tuòbá Wei dynasty,
Jíchéng was merged into Lóngchéng County of Chānglí Commandery.
The "Zǎijì" records: Mòhùbá followed Emperor Xuān in attacking the Gōngsūn clan and was meritorious,
and was appointed as the "King Who Leads Righteousness."
He first established his state north of Jíchéng.
The "Wèi Shū" states: During the time of Emperor Huán of Hàn,
the Xianbei chieftain Tánshíhuái divided his territory into eastern, central, and western sections.
The leaders of the central section were named Kēzuì, Quèjū, Mùróng, etc.,
serving as great commanders.
This was the beginning of the Mùróng tribe.
The "Zǎijì" records: Mòhùbá established his state north of Jíchéng.
At that time, in Yān and Dài, many people wore "bùyáo" crowns.
Mòhùbá saw them and liked them,
so he gathered his hair and donned such a crown.
The various tribes thus called him
"Bùyáo."
Later, the pronunciation became corrupted,
and it became "Mùróng."
Another account says: He admired the virtue of the Two Principles (Heaven and Earth),
and continued the appearance of the Three Luminaries (sun, moon, stars),
thus taking Mùróng as his clan name.
I consider the "bùyáo" explanation far-fetched;
the alternative account,
that after the Mùróng clan gained the Central Plains,
their ministers and followers fabricated this explanation.
Mùyán begot Shèguī,
who moved to the north of Liáodōng.
For generations they submitted to the Central Plains,
repeatedly joining in campaigns and earning merit,
and were appointed as Great Chányú.
In winter, the tenth month,
Shèguī began raiding Chānglí.
Chānglí
was the Jiāolí County of Hàn,
belonging to Liáoxī Commandery.
During the Eastern Hàn, it belonged to the Liáodōng Dependent Chief Commandant.
In the fifth year of the Zhèngshǐ era of Wèi,
the Xianbei submitted internally,
and the Liáodōng Dependent Chiefdom was re-established,
setting up Chānglí County to settle them,
later establishing Chānglí Commandery.
The Mùróng clan began here.
"Kǎoyì" states: The Imperial Annals say
"Mùróng Huì."
According to Fàn Hēng's "Yān Shū Wǔxuān Jì":
"Huì
was born in the fifth year of Tàishǐ,
at age fifteen,
his father, the Chányú Shèguī, died."
This was the fourth year of Tàikāng.
The raid this year
should have been by Shèguī.
3. Eleventh month,
on the Rényín day,
the Duke of Gāopíng, Wǔgōng Chén Qiān, passed away.
"Kǎoyì" states: The Imperial Annals say
"Grand Marshal."
According to records, Qiān resigned his position in the third year of Xiánníng,
and returned to his residence as the Duke of Gāopíng.
4. This year,
the Governor of Yángzhōu, Zhōu Jùn, moved his garrison to Mòlíng.
The Wèi dynasty's Yángzhōu was administered from Shòuchūn.
After Jìn pacified Wú,
it was moved to Mòlíng.
Yáng (扬) means: the energy south of the river is impetuous and vigorous,
its nature is light and soaring.
Also said: the region has much water,
and the water waves soar.
It governed Dānyáng, Xuānchéng, Huáinán, Lúlíng, Lújiāng, Pílíng, Wú, Wúxīng, Kuàijī, Dōngyáng, Xīn'ān, Línhǎi, Jiàn'ān, Jìn'ān, Yùzhāng, Línchuān, Póyáng, Nánkāng,
a total of eighteen commanderies.
There were frequent rebellions and raids,
and Jùn suppressed them all;
he treated the elderly with guest rites,
sought out the talented and virtuous,
applying both authority and kindness,
and the people of Wú were pleased and submitted.
1. Spring,
first month,
on the Dīngchǒu day, the new moon,
the Emperor personally performed the suburban sacrifice south of the capital.
After the ceremony,
he sighed and asked the Colonel-Director of Retainers, Liǔ Yì:
"To which Hàn emperor can I be compared?"
He replied:
"Emperor Huán and Emperor Líng."
The Emperor said:
"How could it be that bad?"
He replied:
"Emperor Huán and Emperor Líng sold offices, but the money went into the state treasury.
Your Majesty sells offices, but the money goes into private households.
Speaking from this,
you are perhaps not as good."
The Emperor laughed heartily and said:
"In the times of Emperor Huán and Emperor Líng,
such words were not heard.
Now I have a forthright minister,
so I am certainly better than them."
"Kǎoyì" states: The "Treatise on Geography" says:
"In the first year of Tàikāng,
the Colonel-Director of Retainers was abolished,
and Sīzhōu was established."
Yì's biography:
"Yì served as Colonel-Director of Retainers.
The Emperor once performed the southern suburban sacrifice.
After the ceremony,
he asked Yì."
But it gives no year or month.
"Jìn Chūnqiū" places the question to Yì in this month,
but does not mention Yì's official position.
According to Yì's biography,
"In the sixth year,
he was transferred from Colonel-Director of Retainers to Left Vice-Director of the Imperial Secretariat."
Perhaps this year it had not yet been changed to Sīzhōu.
I now follow Yì's biography.
Yì, as Colonel-Director of Retainers,
impeached and disciplined the powerful and noble,
showing no fear or favor.
"Shéng" means to correct by impeachment.
"Jiū" means to supervise.
Officials, upon reaching the palace gates,
would put away their ceremonial guides,
dismount from their carriages, and enter on foot.
For the Crown Prince to enter the palace gates with musical escort was considered disrespectful.
"Chuī" is pronounced chāngruì.
The Central Protector of the Army and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Yáng Xiù,
had old favor with the Emperor.
The matter is seen in the seventy-eighth scroll, the first year of Xiánxī of Emperor Yuán of Wèi.
"Xiù" is pronounced xiù.
He participated in confidential matters for over ten years,
relying on imperial favor to be arrogant and extravagant,
and repeatedly broke the law.
Yì impeached Xiù, stating his crimes deserved death.
The Emperor sent Prince Qí, Yōu, to privately plead with Yì for Xiù,
and Yì agreed.
The Metropolitan Official, Chéng Wèi of Guǎngpíng, directly rushed into the Protector of the Army's camp,
arrested Xiù's subordinate officials,
investigated and questioned them about secret matters,
first memorialized Xiù's numerous and disorderly crimes,
and then reported to Yì.
The Emperor had no choice
but to dismiss Xiù from office.
Not long after,
he was again allowed to perform duties without official rank.
Xiù
was the cousin of Empress Jǐngxiàn;
the Rear General, Wáng Kǎi,
was the younger brother of Empress Wénmíng.
Emperor Jǐng's Empress Yáng was posthumously titled Jǐngxiàn.
Emperor Wén's Empress Wáng was posthumously titled Wénmíng.
"Cóng" is pronounced cáiyòng.
Chóng was the son of Bāo.
These three men were all extremely wealthy,
competing to outdo each other in extravagance: Kǎi washed his pots with malt sugar,
Chóng used wax instead of firewood.
Wax is the dregs of honey.
Chóng made a brocade screen fifty lǐ long.
A "bùzhàng" screen is set up along a path to provide shelter and concealment, like today's "guàsī" screens.
Pepper is warm in nature and fragrant.
The "Běncǎo Tújīng" says: Red halloysite
comes from Shèyáng in Jǐnán and the northern slopes of Tàishān.
Sū Gōng said: I have not heard of it coming from Jǐnán or Tàishān;
it is found in Lúshì County of Guó Prefecture, Língchuān County of Zé Prefecture, and Chāngxiāng County of Cí Prefecture,
and also in the mountains of Yí Prefecture.
Nowadays it comes from Lù Prefecture,
with the bright and smooth-colored varieties being superior.
The Emperor once bestowed a coral tree upon him.
"Běncǎo": Coral
grows on the sea floor,
its branches bright and lustrous like red jade.
Kǎi showed it to Shí Chóng,
and Chóng immediately smashed it with an iron ruyi scepter.
An iron ruyi is a hand-held implement,
made of iron,
like today's "gǔduǒzi" mace.
Kǎi thought he was jealous of his treasure.
Chóng said:
"Don't be too regretful,
I'll repay you now!"
Then he ordered his attendants to fetch all the coral trees from his home,
six or seven of them three or four chǐ tall,
many comparable to Kǎi's.
Kǎi was bewildered and felt a sense of loss.
The Cavalry and Chariot Commander Sima Fu Xian submitted a memorial stating:
According to the Records of Jin: For generals below the rank of Piaoqi and all major generals who do not open their own offices and are not regional commanders holding imperial tallies,
one Chief Clerk and one Commander are appointed.
"In the governance of the world by the former kings,
eating meat and wearing silk
were all regulated.
In ancient times, the common people did not eat meat until they were fifty,
and did not wear silk until they were sixty.
Wearing,
pronounced yú jì fān.
is worse than natural disasters.
In ancient times, the population was dense and land was scarce,
yet there were reserves,
due to frugality.
Nowadays, the land is vast and the population sparse,
yet there is a shortage,
due to extravagance.
If you wish people to value frugality,
you should reprimand their extravagance.
If extravagance is not reprimanded,
it will become increasingly esteemed,
with no end in sight!"
2. The Minister of the Imperial Secretariat, Zhāng Huá,
was renowned for his literary talent and knowledge,
and his reputation was highly esteemed at the time.
Commentators all said that Huá should be one of the Three Excellencies;
the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Xún Xù, and the Palace Attendant, Féng Dǎn, deeply resented him for his strategy in conquering Wú.
It happened that the Emperor asked Huá:
"Who can be entrusted with affairs after my death?"
Huá replied,
"In terms of virtue and closeness,
none surpasses the Prince of Qí."
Because of this, he offended the Emperor's wishes,
and Xù slandered him as a result.
On the jiǎwǔ day,
Huá was appointed as the Commander of the military affairs of Yōuzhōu.
When Huá arrived at his post,
he pacified and governed both the barbarians and the Chinese,
and his reputation and prestige grew even more.
The Emperor again considered recalling him.
Féng Dǎn, while attending the Emperor,
casually mentioned Zhōng Huì,
and Dǎn said:
"Huì's rebellion
was largely due to Tàizǔ."
Huì's rebellion is recorded in the 78th volume, in the first year of the Xiánxī era of Emperor Yuán of Wèi.
Emperor Wén,
temple name Tàizǔ.
"What kind of talk is this!"
Dǎn removed his cap and apologized, saying:
"I have heard that a skilled charioteer must know when to tighten or loosen the six reins.
Therefore, Confucius restrained Zhòng Yóu for being overly assertive,
and encouraged Rǎn Qiú for being too timid.
This is recorded in the Analects.
These matters are also recorded in the Annals of Emperor Gāo of Hàn.
The five kings,
namely, Hán Xìn, Péng Yuè, Yīng Bù, and Lú Wǎn.
Emperor Guāngwǔ did not allow meritorious officials to participate in governance,
so they all preserved their fortunes and emoluments,
and none were executed or punished.
Below, there are differences in wisdom and foolishness,
but it is the restraint and encouragement,
the granting and taking away,
that make it so. Zhōng Huì's talents and wisdom were limited,
yet Tàizǔ praised him without limit,
placed him in a position of great authority,
and entrusted him with a large army,
causing Huì to believe that his plans were flawless,
and his achievements were beyond reward,
leading him to plot treason.
If Tàizǔ had recognized his minor abilities,
restrained him with proper rites,
checked him with authority,
and guided him with rules,
then rebellious thoughts would have had no way to arise."
The Emperor said:
"Indeed."
Dǎn kowtowed and said:
"Since Your Majesty agrees with my words,
you should consider the gradual formation of solid ice,
and not allow those like Huì to cause ruin again."
The Emperor said:
"Is there anyone like Huì today?"
Dǎn then dismissed the attendants and said:
"Your Majesty's planning ministers,
those who have achieved great merit for the empire,
hold regional commands,
and command armies—
they are all within Your Majesty's wise consideration."
The Emperor fell silent,
and from then on, he stopped considering recalling Huá.
3. In the third month,
General Ānběi Yán Xún defeated Mùróng Shèguī at Chānglí,
beheading and capturing tens of thousands.
4. The Duke of Lǔ, Jiǎ Chōng, was old and ill.
The Emperor sent the Crown Prince to inquire about his condition.
Chōng worried about his posthumous title and biography,
knowing well his own treachery and regicide.
He feared he would receive a bad posthumous title,
and could not escape the judgment of upright historians.
Biography,
pronounced zhù liàn fān.
"Right and wrong will become clear in time,
and cannot be concealed!"
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the gēngwǔ day,
Chōng passed away.
His eldest son, Límín, had died early,
leaving no heir.
His wife, Guō Huái, wanted to make Chōng's grandson by his daughter, Hán Mì, the heir.
Hán Mì
was the son of Chōng's son-in-law, Hán Shòu.
Heir,
refers to the legitimate grandson who inherits the grandfather's lineage.
According to Jin regulations,
for princes and dukes of commanderies, there are three ministers: the Gentleman of the Household, the Commandant, and the Grand Minister of Agriculture.
"The rites have no provision for an heir of a different surname.
To do so now
would cause our late lord to be ridiculed by later generations and feel ashamed in the underworld."
Huái did not listen.
Xián and others submitted a memorial,
requesting a change of heir,
but the matter was shelved without response.
Huái then submitted a memorial explaining,
claiming it was Chōng's dying wish.
The Emperor approved it,
and issued an edict stating:
"Unless one's merit is like that of the Grand Steward,
being the first enfeoffed and having no heir,
none may be compared to this."
When the Grand Master of Ceremonies discussed the posthumous title,
the Erudite Qín Xiù said:
"Chōng violated the rites and indulged his emotions,
disrupting the great order.
In the past, the state of Zēng raised the grandson of the Jǔ lord as heir,
and the Spring and Autumn Annals recorded, 'The people of Jǔ destroyed Zēng.'
Spring and Autumn Annals: In the sixth year of Duke Xiāng,
the people of Jǔ destroyed Zēng.
The Gongyang Commentary says: They took an heir from Jǔ.
A woman from Jǔ became the wife of the lord of Zēng,
and they established her offspring.
The Guliang Commentary says: The people of Jǔ destroyed Zēng,
but it was not a true destruction.
Establishing an heir of a different surname to preside over sacrifices
is the path to destruction.
This opens the source of disorder for the court.
According to the rules for posthumous titles: 'Confusing and disrupting the laws and measures is called Huāng,'
I request the posthumous title Huāng Duke."
The Emperor did not agree,
and instead gave the posthumous title Wǔ.
5. In the intercalary month,
on the bǐngzǐ day,
the Marquis of Guǎnglíng, Lǐ Yǐn, passed away.
6. The Prince of Qí, Yōu, grew increasingly virtuous and prestigious,
and Xún Xù, Féng Dǎn, and Yáng Yáo all disliked him.
Dǎn said to the Emperor:
"Your Majesty's edict ordering the feudal lords to go to their fiefs
should start with the closest relatives.
The closest relative is none other than the Prince of Qí.
Now he alone remains in the capital.
Is this appropriate?"
Xù said:
"All officials, inside and outside the court, are inclined toward the Prince of Qí.
After Your Majesty's passing,
the Crown Prince will not be able to ascend the throne.
If Your Majesty issues an edict ordering the Prince of Qí to go to his fief,
the entire court will surely oppose it.
Then my words will be proven true."
The Emperor agreed.
In winter,
the twelfth month,
on the jiǎshēn day,
an edict was issued:
"In ancient times, the Nine Commands made a lord,
some entered to assist the court's governance,
others went out to guard the frontiers.
The principle is the same.
The Palace Attendant, Minister of Works, and Prince of Qí, Yōu,
assisted in establishing the mandate and achieved merit,
toiling diligently for the royal house.
He is hereby appointed Grand Marshal and Commander of the military affairs of Qīngzhōu,
retaining his position as Palace Attendant,
and further honored with ceremonies,
with the responsible officials detailing and implementing according to old regulations."
The Prince of Rǔnán, Liàng, was appointed Grand Commandant, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, and concurrently Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
The Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, Shān Tāo, was appointed Minister of Education.
The Minister of the Imperial Secretariat, Wèi Guàn, was appointed Minister of Works.
The General Who Pacifies the East, Wáng Hún, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"Yōu is a close relative of great virtue,
comparable to the Duke of Zhōu.
He should assist the imperial court
and participate in governance.
Now, sending Yōu to his fiefdom,
granting him the empty title of Regional Commander,
without the actual authority to command troops or govern the region—
'command troops'
means to lead the army.
The *Book of Songs*, in the 'Hán Yì' section, says: 'To pacify the rebellious regions.'
This means to serve as a pillar.
I fear this does not align with Your Majesty's intention to honor the late Emperor and Empress Dowager Wénmíng's longstanding regard for Yōu.
The matter of treating Yōu is recorded in the second year of the Xiánníng era in the previous volume.
If he is overly favored,
it could lead to rebellious plots like those of Wú and Chǔ.
What kind of people were the Lǚ, Huò, and Wáng clans of the Hàn dynasty?
They were all such individuals!
Hún's meaning
is that Prince Qí should not be doubted,
and the three Yángs should not be trusted.
If the weight of matters is misplaced,
it will inevitably cause harm.
One must only rely on righteousness and seek loyal and virtuous men.
If one uses cunning schemes to suspect others,
even close relatives will be doubted,
let alone distant ones—
how can they be secure?
I humbly believe that since the position of Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince is vacant,
Yōu should remain to fill it,
and together with Prince Liàng of Rǔnán and Yáng Yáo, manage court affairs.
With the three of them holding equal positions,
they can adequately uphold justice,
avoiding both the danger of one side becoming overly dominant
and the loss of the kindness that comes from familial affection and benevolent care.
This is the most perfect plan."
Subsequently, Prince Jùn of Fúfēng, Senior Grand Master Lǐ Xǐ, Central Protector Yáng Xiù, Palace Attendant Wáng Jì, and Zhēn Dé all earnestly remonstrated;
the Emperor did not heed any of them.
Jì sent his wife, Princess Chángshān, and Dé's wife, Princess Chángguǎng, to enter the palace together,
kowtowing and weeping,
begging the Emperor to keep Yōu.
The Emperor grew angry
and said to Palace Attendant Wáng Róng:
"Brothers are the closest of kin.
Now, sending Prince Qí away
is my family matter.
How dare Zhēn Dé and Wáng Jì repeatedly send their wives here to wail at people!"
He then demoted Jì to the position of Chancellor of the National University
and Dé to Chief Minister of Ceremonies.
They were transferred from Palace Attendants to outer court officials.
He personally killed him with a blade;
the Northern Army Central Inspector,
a Hàn dynasty official,
was in charge of the five battalions of the Northern Army;
it was abolished during the Wèi dynasty.
In the fourth year of the Tàishǐ era,
the position of General of the Central Army was abolished,
and the Northern Army Central Inspector was established;
in the seventh year,
the Central Army Commander was also abolished and merged into it.
He declined due to illness and did not appear,
prompting officials to impeach Xiù,
who was demoted to Grand Coachman.
Xiù, filled with resentment,
fell ill and died.
Lǐ Xǐ also retired due to old age
and died at home.
During his time at court,
Xǐ shared clothing and meals
with his relatives and old friends,
but never privately appointed them to official positions.
People praised him for this.
7 That year,
Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Xuē Yíng died.
Someone asked Lù Xǐ of Wú Commandery:
"Is Yíng the foremost among the scholars of Wú?"
Xǐ replied:
"Yíng ranks between fourth and fifth;
how could he be the foremost!
Given Sūn Hào's tyranny,
the scholars of Wú
who remained silent and withdrawn,
hiding their talents and not serving,
are the foremost;
those who avoided high positions for humble ones,
accepting salaries in place of farming,
are the second;
those who earnestly served the state,
upholding justice without fear,
are the third;
those who adapted to the times,
occasionally offering modest contributions,
are the fourth;
those who were gentle, respectful, cautious, and restrained,
not leading in flattery,
are the fifth.
Beyond these,
they are not worth counting.
Thus, the highest scholars often fall into obscurity and avoid regret,
while the middling scholars gain fame and position but court disaster.
Considering Yíng's conduct and achievements,
how could he be the foremost!"
1 In spring,
the first month,
on Jiǎshēn,
Shàngshū Right Deputy Wèi Shū was appointed as Left Deputy,
and Prince Huǎng of Xiàpī was appointed as Right Deputy.
Huǎng
was the son of Fú.
2 On Wùwǔ,
the newly appointed Tà Kāng Bó, Shān Tāo, passed away.
In the third year of the Jǐngchū era of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
the officials and people of Dá County in Liáodōng who crossed the sea to reside within the borders of Qí Commandery
were established as Xīntà County.
3 The Emperor ordered the Minister of Ceremonies to deliberate on the honors and gifts to be bestowed upon Prince Qí.
The Erudites Yǔ Fū, Tàishū Guǎng, Liú Tūn,
Miào Wèi, Guō Yí, Qín Xiù, and Fù Zhēn submitted a memorial stating:
"In ancient times, Zhōu selected men of illustrious virtue to assist the royal house.
The Duke of Zhōu, Kāngshū, and Dān Jì
all entered court as the Three Dukes.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* records: Zǐyú, the Grand Invocator of Wèi, said: 'King Wǔ had eight younger brothers by the same mother;
the Duke of Zhōu served as Grand Steward,
Kāngshū as Minister of Justice,
and Dān Jì as Minister of Works.'
'Assist'
is read as 'zuǒ yòu.'
Dān
is pronounced 'nán.'
Their positions as territorial lords were of lesser importance.
During the Hàn dynasty, the feudal princes
ranked above the Chancellor and the Three Dukes.
Those who entered court to participate in governance
held concurrent appointments;
when they left for their fiefdoms,
they were not granted empty titles of the Three Departments as a mark of honor.
Among the Hàn feudal princes who participated in governance,
only Prince Cāng of Dōngpíng did so.
Thus, it is inappropriate for a close brother like him to hold the regular duties of Lǔ or Wèi;
if he is unworthy,
it is inappropriate to grant him vast territories
and establish him as the Prince of Dōnghǎi.
According to ancient rites,
the Three Dukes had no specific duties;
they sat and discussed the Way,
and it was unheard of for them to be burdened with regional responsibilities.
'Burdened'
means entangled.
Only then did King Xuān order Duke Mù of Shào to campaign against the Huáiyí,
hence the poem says:
'The Xú region did not rebel,
and the king said, "Return home."'
This appears in the poems 'Jiāng Hàn' and 'Cháng Wǔ.'
Now, the realm is pacified,
and the six directions are united as one family.
The Three Dukes should be frequently summoned
to discuss the foundations of peace.
Instead, he is sent away,
two thousand *lǐ* from the royal city,
violating the old statutes."
Sīmǎ Biāo's *Treatise on Commanderies and States* records: The State of Qí was 1,800 *lǐ* east of Luòyáng.
He was the son of Chún;
Tūn
was the son of Yì.
After Fū drafted the memorial,
he first presented it to Chún, who did not forbid it.
The matter was brought to Tàicháng Zhèng Mò and Bóshì Jìjiǔ Cáo Zhì.
The Continued Hàn Records state: There was one Bóshì Jìjiǔ;
originally it was the Púyè,
during the Restoration it was changed to Jìjiǔ.
Hú Guǎng said: The official title Jìjiǔ
all refers to the head of a particular position.
"How can one with such talent,
and such closeness [to the imperial house],
not be established as a pillar to assist governance,
but instead be sent far away to a coastal corner!
The prosperity of the Jìn house,
is it not in peril!"
He then submitted a memorial stating:
"In ancient times, those who supported the royal house from the side,
among the same surname was the Duke of Zhōu,
among different surnames was the Grand Duke [of Qí],
both resided at the court,
and for five generations were returned for burial [in the ancestral land].
The Lǐjì, Tángōng chapter says: The Grand Duke was enfeoffed at Yíngqiū,
but up to the fifth generation,
all were returned for burial in Zhōu.
The ancients said:
'When a fox dies, its head points towards its mound,
this is benevolence.'
Although the Five Hegemons arose in succession,
how can their governance be discussed on the same day as that of Zhōu and Shào!
This means the Five Hegemons arose in succession to honor the Zhōu house,
but cannot be discussed on the same day as the supportive governance of Zhōu and Shào.
Zhì (治),
is pronounced zhí lì fān.
How can it be exclusively possessed by a single surname!
One must uphold a mind of utmost impartiality,
sharing benefits and harms with all under heaven,
then one can long enjoy the state.
Therefore, Qín and Wèi desired to monopolize power and barely managed to last their own lifetimes,
while Zhōu and Hàn were able to share the benefits and employed both close and distant relatives,
this is clear proof from past events.
Zhì believed it should be as the Bóshì and others proposed."
The Emperor read it,
and was greatly angered, saying:
"Even Cáo Zhì does not understand my heart,
let alone all within the four seas!"
This means Cáo Zhì was originally the son of Wèi's Prince Sī of Chén, Cáo Zhí,
Zhí and Wèi Wéndì
were brothers.
How Wéndì restricted and controlled Zhí is well known,

"The Bóshì did not answer what was asked but answered what was not asked.

Yōu acted according to ritual in all his actions,

Xià,
hù yǎ fān.

2. Initially,
Chén Qún, because the Ministry of Personnel was unable to properly examine and evaluate the scholars of the realm,
thus ordered each commandery and principality to establish a Zhōngzhèng,
and each province to establish a Dàzhōngzhèng.
All were to be selected from among natives of the locality who held court office and were of abundant virtue and talent to serve as commissioners.
They were to rank and grade [candidates] into nine classes.
This matter is recorded in the 69th scroll, in the first year of the Huángchū era of Emperor Wén of Wèi.
If someone's moral conduct was deficient, their rank would be lowered.
The Ministry of Personnel relied on this to appoint and fill official posts for the hundred officials.
As this system was practiced for a long time,
the Zhōngzhèng sometimes were not the right people for the post,
and corruption and abuses daily increased.
Liú Yì submitted a memorial stating:
"Now, establishing the Zhōngzhèng
and fixing the nine classes
allows them to arbitrarily decide high and low,
holding honor and disgrace in their hands,
wielding the sovereign's power to reward and punish,
seizing the authority of the imperial court.
In public, they bear no responsibility for examination and verification,
and in private, they have no fear of being accused of slander.
Even if it is said that the ranking of high and low might be inappropriate,
in public, they are not held accountable for inaccurate evaluations.
They expose people's hidden faults,
going to all extremes,
yet in private, they do not avoid [accusations] for fear of being denounced.
[People] scheme and seek [rank] by countless means,
the custom of integrity and deference is extinguished,
and the practice of contention and litigation arises.
Your servant privately feels ashamed for the Sacred Court!
The establishment of the Zhōngzhèng
involves eight ways of harming governance: Ranking follows power and weakness,
right and wrong follow rise and decline.
For a single person,
their status can change within ten days.
The upper classes have no one from humble families,
the lower classes have no one from powerful clans.
This is the first.
Establishing provincial overseers
(provincial overseers
refer to Zhōngzhèng)
was intended to settle differences and achieve uniformity,
a unified consensus.
Now, the responsibility is heavy but the persons are treated lightly,
causing contentious and contradictory arguments to run rampant in the provinces and villages,
and sowing seeds of suspicion and enmity among high officials.
This is the second.
The original purpose of establishing the system of standards,
in creating the nine classes,
was that talent and virtue have superiority and inferiority,
and seniority has precedence and sequence.
Now, instead, superiority and inferiority are reversed,
precedence and sequence are inverted.
This is the third.
Your Majesty rewards good and punishes evil,
all judged according to law.
Yet solely for the establishment of the Zhōngzhèng,
entrusting them with the weighty responsibility for the entire state,
there is absolutely no safeguard of rewards and punishments.
Furthermore, people are prohibited from lodging complaints,
allowing them to act arbitrarily and willfully,
with nothing to fear or restrain them.
All those who suffer injustice,
harboring grievances and accumulated grievances,
cannot have them heard by superiors.
This is the fourth.
The scholars of a state,
at most number in the thousands.
Some may have migrated to other regions,
or seek sustenance from distant places
(meaning those whose clothing and food are insufficient,
sojourn in distant places to obtain sustenance).
How can their talents be fully assessed?
Yet the Zhōngzhèng, whether they know them or not,
must all grade and describe them,
gathering praise from the offices of the court,
accepting slander from circulating rumors.
Relying on oneself leads to the fault of ignorance,
listening to others leads to bias for this side or that.
This is the fifth.
Generally, seeking talented individuals
is for the purpose of governing the people.
Now, those who achieve results in office may be assigned to low grades,
while those who accomplish nothing in office may receive high rankings.
This suppresses actual merit and elevates empty reputation,
encourages superficiality and abolishes the examination of achievements.
This is the sixth.
Different offices require different people,
different tasks require different abilities.
Now, instead of describing what their talents are suitable for, they are merely ranked into nine classes.
Selecting people by class
may not match where their abilities lie.
Selecting people by description
is then limited by their original class.
This merely results in empty discussions.
(Empty,
meaning plain,
explaining 'plain meals' as meaning empty meals.
'Empty discussions'
is like empty talk.)
This is the seventh.
When the nine classes lower someone, they do not clarify their crimes;
when they raise someone, they do not list their good deeds.
Each follows their own likes and dislikes,
to advance their private interests.
How can the people of the realm not neglect virtuous conduct and instead zealously engage in personal networking?
This is the eighth.
From this perspective,
the official title 'Zhōngzhèng'
is in reality a den of corruption;
the system called the 'nine classes'
has these eight harms.
The failures of past and present,
none are greater than this!
This foolish minister believes we should abolish the Zhōngzhèng,
eliminate the nine classes,
discard the flawed laws of the Wèi house,
and establish anew a fine system for our generation."
The Grand Commandant, the Prince of Rǔnán, Sīmǎ Liàng, and the Minister of Works, Wèi Guàn, also submitted a memorial stating:
"The house of Wèi inherited the aftermath of chaos and disorder,
with scholars displaced and migrating,
and no means to conduct detailed examinations.
Therefore, they established the nine-class system,
roughly as a temporary basis for selection and appointment.
Now, the nine regions share uniform regulations,
and great transformation is just beginning.
Your ministers believe we should sweep away these inferior methods,
and all implement local registration
(meaning to determine based on permanent residence.
Determine,
pronounced dìng).
Taking one's place of residence as correct,
eliminating transient households,
and distant affiliation with other lands.
Completely abolish the Zhōngzhèng and nine-class system,
so that recommending the good and advancing the talented
each follows the discussions of the local communities.
Then ostentatious competition will naturally cease,
and each will seek [improvement] from within themselves."
The Literary Scholar of the Prince of Shǐpíng, Lǐ Chóng of Jiāngxià, submitted a memorial:
Since the time of Wèi,
each princely kingdom established one Preceptor, one Friend, and one Literary Scholar each.
Xià,
pronounced hù yǎ.
Submitted,

"Once the nine classes are abolished,
we should first allow freedom of migration,
permitting people to merge and settle together.
Then the substance of local registration can be implemented."
Although the Emperor approved of their words, in the end he was unable to make the change.

"Whenever discussing this matter with you,

In the tenth year of the Tàikāng era
(Jǐyǒu, 289)
1 In summer,
during the fourth month,
the Imperial Ancestral Temple was completed;
on the Yǐsì day,
a xiá sacrifice was held;
xiá
refers to a grand combined sacrifice.
The Gōngyáng Commentary states: What is the grand xiá?
It is a combined sacrifice.
How is this combined sacrifice conducted?
The spirit tablets of the dismantled temples are arranged before the Great Ancestor,
and the spirit tablets of the undismantled temples are all elevated,
to feast together with the Great Ancestor.
Xiá
is pronounced as hú jiá.
2 Mùróng Huī sent an envoy to request surrender;
in the fifth month,
an imperial edict appointed Huī as the Xiānbēi Commander-in-Chief.
Huī went to pay a visit to Hé Kān,
using the etiquette of a scholar-official,
wearing a headscarf and robe to the gate;
during the Wèi and Jìn periods,
when scholar-officials visited their superiors,
it was customary to wear a headscarf and a single-layer robe.
Gōu
refers to a single-layer garment.
Kān
is pronounced as kǒu hán.
Huī then changed into military attire before entering.
Someone asked him the reason,
and Huī said:
"If the host does not treat the guest with proper etiquette,
why should the guest bother?"
Upon hearing this,
Kān felt deeply ashamed,
and held Huī in high esteem and admiration.
Receiving a surrender is like facing an enemy;
a commander stationed at the border,
meeting foreign guests with a strong military presence,
is not excessive,
so why should he feel ashamed?
The Duàn clan
belonged to the Eastern Xiānbēi.
Dù Yòu said: Yǔwén Mòhuái originated from beyond the Liáodōng frontier,
and for generations served as the tribal leader of the Eastern Xiānbēi.
Duàn Jíliùjuàn of Túhé came from Liáoxī,
and due to turmoil,
was sold into slavery to Kùnù, the tribal leader of the Yúyáng Wūhuán.
Kùnù, impressed by his strength,
put him in charge of leading people,
and sent him to Liáoxī to seek sustenance,
where he recruited deserters and rebels,
eventually growing powerful.
According to my examination of the Jìnshū biography of Wáng Jùn: Duàn Jíliùjuàn
was the heir of Wùwùchén.
The Duàn clan had been powerful since Wùwùchén's time,
and had long been strong;
it is possible that Jíliùjuàn was captured during turmoil,
as such things could happen;
but since Wùwùchén was already able to serve as tribal leader,
it is unlikely that the clan's strength depended on his son's recruitment efforts.
Huī served them with humble words and generous gifts.
Duàn Guó Chányú Jiē married his daughter to Huī,
and they gave birth to Huàng, Rén, and Zhāo.
Thus, the Mùróng and Duàn clans became allied through marriage.
Shuò
is pronounced as suǒ jiǎo.
Chán
is pronounced as chán.
Qī
is pronounced as qī xì.
They relocated to Qīnghé Mountain in Túhé.
Túhé County
belonged to Liáoxī during the Former Hàn,
to the Liáodōng Dependent State during the Later Hàn,
was abolished during the Wèi and Jìn periods,
and merged into the territory of Chānglí Commandery.
Later, the Mùróng clan reestablished Túhé County,
and during the eighth year of the Zhēnjun era of Tàiwǔ of the Northern Wèi,
Túhé was merged into Guǎngxīng County of Chānglí Commandery.

At that time, Lún used the Eastern Palace as his Xiàngguó residence.
Lún engaged in battle repeatedly but was defeated,
with over a thousand dead.
Tàizǐ Zuǒshuài Chén Huī commanded the Eastern Palace troops to raise a clamor inside in response to Yǔn.
Zuǒshuài,
is the Zuǒwèi Shuài.
Bows and crossbows were fired together,
shooting at Lún,
arrows flying down like rain.
Zhǔshū Sīmǎ Suī Mì used his body to shield Lún.
The *Continued Hàn Records* state: The Shàngshū had thirty-six Section Láng,
each Section had three Zhǔshū.
This Zhǔshū Sīmǎ,
was likely an official subordinate of the Xiàngguó's residence,
appointed by Lún himself.
Suī,
is pronounced Xī suí,
a surname.
Lún's officials all hid behind trees to stand,
each tree was hit by several hundred arrows,
from Chén to Wèi.
Zhōngshū Lìng Chén Huái,
previously there was a Zhōngshū Lìng Chén Zhǔn,
"Huái"
is likely
a mistake for the character
"Zhǔn".
Wishing to support Yǔn,
he said to the Emperor:
"We should send out the White Tiger Banner to resolve the fighting."
The White Tiger Banner was used to command the army to advance and fight,
not to resolve fighting.
Chén Zhǔn likely, because the Emperor was平庸 and foolish,
requested the White Tiger Banner to command the troops,
hoping that when Lún's soldiers saw it,
they would think Yǔn's attack on Lún
was ordered by the Emperor,
and would then collapse on their own.
Otherwise, how could he support Yǔn?
Sīmǎ Dūhù,
also a Diànzhōng Jiàngxiào,
subordinate to the Two Guards.
Secretly swore to Sīmǎ Yìn:
"If we attain wealth and honor, I will share it with you."
Yìn then concealed a blank tablet and went out.
Blank tablet,
is a tablet without an edict written on it.
There was originally no edict,
but he took a blank tablet, concealed it, and went out.
Yǔn did not realize this,
opened his ranks to let him in,
dismounted from his carriage to receive the edict,
whereupon Yìn killed him.
He also killed Yǔn's sons, Qín Prince Sīmǎ Yù and Hàn Prince Sīmǎ Dí.
Several thousand people were implicated in Yǔn's rebellion and exterminated.
A limited amnesty was granted for Luòyáng.
Not a general amnesty for the realm,
but only for Luòyáng,
therefore it is called a limited amnesty.
Initially,
Sūn Xiù had once served as a minor official,
working under the Gentleman of the Yellow Gate Pān Yuè,
who frequently had him flogged.
Sūn Xiù
was from Lángyá.
Pān Yuè served as the Administrator of Lángyá,
and Xiù was a minor official
assigned to Yuè,
being cunning and self-satisfied.
Yuè despised his character,
and repeatedly had him flogged and humiliated.
(Regarding the memorial detailing Lún's crimes,
see the sixth year of Yuánkāng in the previous volume.)
Lǜzhū was skilled at playing the flute.
The Tàipíng Guǎngjì states: At the foot of Shuāngjiǎo Mountain in present-day Báizhōu, there is Lǜzhū's Well.
In the past, a daughter of the Liáng family was renowned for her beauty.
Shí Chòng, while on a mission to Jiāozhōu,
purchased her with three hú of pearls.
At the former residence of the Liáng family,
the old well remains.
It is said that those who draw and drink from it will inevitably give birth to beautiful daughters.
The local villagers, believing beautiful women to be of no benefit,
subsequently filled the well with stones.
Chòng refused to hand her over.
After the defeat of the Prince of Huáinán, Sīmǎ Yǔn,
Xiù accordingly accused Shí Chòng, Pān Yuè, and Ōuyáng Jiàn of supporting Yǔn in rebellion,
and had them arrested.
The Examination of Discrepancies states: Chòng's biography says:
"Chòng and Jiàn secretly learned of the plot,
and privately urged the Prince of Huáinán Sīmǎ Yǔn and the Prince of Qí Sīmǎ Jiǒng to plot against the Prince of Zhào Sīmǎ Lún."
If Chòng had indeed conspired with Yǔn,
after Yǔn's defeat,
Chòng should have been fearful and anxious.
He should not have been feasting upstairs
at the time of his arrest.
It is likely that Lún and Xiù, harboring old grievances, falsely accused and executed him.
Now, referring to Shí Chòng's biography:
"Sūn Xiù demanded Lǜzhū,
but Chòng refused.
Xiù, enraged,
then urged Lún to execute Chòng.
Chòng was feasting upstairs
when armored soldiers arrived at his gate.
Chòng said to Lǜzhū: 'I have now incurred guilt on your account.'
Lǜzhū wept and said: 'I shall prove my loyalty before you.'
Thereupon, she threw herself from the tower and died."
"These slaves covet my wealth, that is all!"
The arresting officer said:
"Knowing that wealth brings disaster,
why did you not disperse it sooner?"
Chòng could not reply.
Initially,
Pān Yuè's mother often reproached and admonished him, saying:
"You should know contentment;
must you ceaselessly pursue illicit gains?"
This was to warn Yuè against seizing opportunities for profit,
not knowing when to stop.
Fú Qián said: "Gān mò"
means speculating on success or failure.
Rú Chún said: Gaining profit is "gān,"
suffering loss is "mò."
"Gān"
is pronounced "gān."
Another interpretation uses water as an analogy:
It describes one who looks upon profit and rushes toward it,
not caring whether he is left high and dry on land,
or submerged and drowned,
he disregards all.
Yuè apologized to his mother, saying:
"I have failed you, Mother."
follows the entering tone of "ān."
Chòng's family property was confiscated.
The Chancellor of State Lún arrested the Prince of Wú, Sīmǎ Yàn, the younger maternal brother of the Prince of Huáinán,
intending to kill him.
The Grand Master of Splendid Happiness Fù Zhī disputed this in the court hall,
and many others remonstrated to stop it.
Lún then demoted Yàn to the rank of Prince of Bīntú County.
Bīntú County
belonged to the Liáoxī Commandery in the Former Hàn,
to the Liáodōng Dependent State Commandant in the Later Hàn,
and to the Chānglí Commandery in the Jìn.
The Prince of Qí, Sīmǎ Jiǒng, was promoted for his merit to General of Agile Cavalry.
The Jìn Treatise states: The General of Valiant Cavalry and the General of Agile Cavalry
were both miscellaneous titles of generals in the Hàn.
The Wèi established them as central army generals.
By the Jìn dynasty,
the Generals of the Center, Protector, Left and Right Guards, Valiant Cavalry, and Agile Cavalry constituted the Six Armies.
(He bore a resentful countenance,
which Sūn Xiù detected.
Moreover, fearing his presence within the capital,
Xiù had him sent out as General Who Pacifies the East,
to garrison Xǔchāng.
This sets the stage for Jiǒng's raising troops from Xǔchāng to campaign against Lún.)
15. Chén Zhǔn, Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, was appointed Grand Commandant,
overseeing the Department of State Affairs.
Not long after,
he passed away.
16. Sūn Xiù proposed conferring the Nine Bestowments upon Chancellor of State Lún.
None of the officials dared voice dissent.
The Minister of Personnel Liú Sòng said:
"In the past, when the Hàn bestowed them upon Wèi,
and Wèi bestowed them upon Jìn,
it was for a specific occasion,
not a practice to be universally applied.
It is said that the Nine Bestowments came only after abdication,
and are not part of the regular statutes.
Their achievements were of the utmost greatness,
yet none are recorded to have received the mandate of the Nine Bestowments."
(Referring to Zhōu Bó and Huò Guāng, who devised strategies to secure the Hàn house,
and it is not recorded they received the mandate of the Nine Bestowments.
This was to thwart
the treacherous schemes of Lún and Xiù.)
Considering Sòng a partisan of Zhāng Huá,
they intended to kill him.
Sūn Xiù said:
"Killing Zhāng and Péi has already damaged public opinion;
we cannot kill Sòng as well."
Lún then desisted.
Sòng was appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.
The Jìn Treatise states: The Grand Master of Splendid Happiness held the same rank as the Nine Ministers,
with a salary of fully two thousand dàn.
He wore a cap with two beams for promoting the worthy,
a black headcloth,
court robes for the five seasons,
and carried a pale green jade pendant.
The Examination of Discrepancies states: The Sānshí Guó Chūnqiū says:
"Lún's faction was greatly angered,
plotted to harm Sòng,
and Sòng, in fear,
took his own life."
Sòng's biography says:
"Sòng became Grand Master of Splendid Happiness,
and soon after died of illness."
We follow the biography here.
Furthermore, his son Sīmǎ Fū was additionally appointed General Who Comforts the Army.
The General Who Comforts the Army
was the title Emperor Wén used when appointing Emperor Wǔ,
who subsequently used it to replace the Wèi.
(Lún bestowing this upon his heir apparent—
what was his intention?)
After Emperor Wǔ received the abdication,
he established the General of the Center Army,
commanding the seven armies of the palace guard.
It was soon abolished,
but later reinstated.
Sūn Xiù was also appointed Palace Attendant, General Who Supports the State, and Chancellor of State's Army Major,
retaining his former position as Right Leader.
(Right Leader
refers to the Leader of the Right Guard.
Not relinquishing this post
was intended to keep control of the Eastern Palace troops.)
The troops of the Chancellor's residence were increased to twenty thousand,
equal to the palace guard.
Combined with the troops they had concealed,
the number exceeded thirty thousand.
In the ninth month,
the title of Minister over the Masses was changed to Chancellor,
and the Prince of Liáng, Sīmǎ Róng, was appointed to the position.
Róng firmly declined and did not accept.
Lún and his sons were all obstinate, vulgar, and lacking in discernment.
Xiù was cunning, greedy, and licentious.
Those with whom they collaborated
were all wicked and sycophantic individuals,
solely contending for glory and profit,
without long-term plans or deep strategies.
Their aims and interests were divergent,
and they mutually detested and envied one another.
Xiù's son Sūn Huì served as Colonel of Archers Who Shoot by Sound.
His appearance was short and ugly,
resembling the lowest of servants.
Yet Xiù had him marry the Emperor's daughter, the Princess of Hédōng.
(The historian remarks that Lún and Xiù, with the blade already at their necks,
still harbored illegitimate ambitions.)
17. In winter,
the eleventh month,
on the jiǎzǐ day,
Empress Yáng was installed,
and a general amnesty was proclaimed.
The Empress
was the daughter of Yáng Xuánzhī, a Gentleman of the Masters of Writing from Tàishān.
Her maternal grandfather was Sūn Qí, General Who Pacifies the South of Lè'ān,
who was on good terms with Sūn Xiù.
Hence, Xiù had her installed.
Xuánzhī was appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, Specially Advanced, and Regular Attendant of the Chancellery,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīngjìn.
The Jìn Treatise states: The Grand Master of Splendid Happiness,
when granted the silver seal and blue绶,
held the third rank.
With the addition of Specially Advanced,
his rank and salary became equal to those of the Grand Masters of Splendid Happiness of the Left and Right.
The Jìn established Xīngjìn Commandery,
located within the boundaries of the Táng dynasty's Hézhōu.
An edict summoned Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Zhào Xīn to serve as Grand Chief of the Autumn Harvest,
and appointed Chéngdū Nèishǐ Zhōngshān Gěng Téng as Yìzhōu Cìshǐ.
The various princely states of Jìn established the position of Nèishǐ,
analogous to the Chancellor of a princely state in Hàn times.
In the ninth year of the Tàikāng era of Emperor Wǔ,
the title Chancellor of the various princely states was changed to Nèishǐ.
Textual Analysis: The Imperial Annals record it as
"Gěng Shèng",
but the Collected Records and the Huáyáng Guózhì record it as
"Téng".
We follow the latter.
He was a relative by marriage of Empress Jiǎ.
Hearing of the summons,
he was greatly afraid,
fearing implication as a member of Empress Jiǎ's faction.
He secretly harbored the ambition to seize Shǔ.
He then emptied the granaries,
providing relief to the displaced people,
to win over the hearts of the masses.
Considering the Lǐ Tè brothers to be talented and martial,
and their followers all being from Bāxī,
the same commandery as Xīn,
(Lǐ Tè's followers were originally Bā Dī,
and Zhào Xīn was also from Bāxī.)
Tè and others relied on Xīn's power,
exclusively gathering crowds to become bandits,
causing the people of Shǔ to suffer from them.
(The matter of Tè and others entering Shǔ began in the eighth year of Yuánkāng, in the previous scroll.)
"The displaced people are fierce and rapacious,
the people of Shǔ are weak and timid,
the host cannot control the guests,
this will certainly become a source of rebellion.
They should be sent back to their original places of residence.
If they are left in this perilous territory,
(the land of Shǔ is rugged and perilous.
The displaced people originally resided in Qín and Yōng.
Yōng,
pronounced yòng.)
The province received the imperial edict,
dispatching over a thousand civil and military officials to welcome Téng.
At that time,
Chéngdū administered Shǎochéng,
while Yìzhōu administered Tàichéng.
Both cities were built by Qín's Zhāng Yí.
After Yí built Tàichéng,
the following year he also built Shǎochéng.
Tàichéng is the present-day inner city of Chéngdū Prefecture.
Shǎochéng had only the south, west, and north walls;
the east side was the western wall of Tàichéng.
Shǎo,
pronounced shào.)
Before he had departed,
Téng wished to enter the provincial seat.
Gōngcáo Chén Xún admonished:
"Now the enmity between the province and the commandery deepens daily.
(Province refers to Yìzhōu;
commandery refers to Chéngdū.
This refers to the enmity between Xīn and Téng.)
It would be better to remain in Shǎochéng to observe the changes,
issuing proclamations to the various counties to unite village defenses to prepare against the Qín Dī.
(Lǐ Tè and others were originally Bā Dī.
The people of Shǔ, because they had migrated to the borders of Qínzhōu,
thus called them Qín Dī.)
And inform Chén of Xīyí,
(referring to Xīyí Xiàowèi Chén Zǒng.)
that he is on his way and will arrive soon.
(Meaning Zǒng was coming to assume the post of Xīyí Xiàowèi and was about to reach Chéngdū.
Jìn established the Xīyí Xiàowèi in Wènshān,
the Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiàng in Guǎngzhōu,
the Nánmán Xiàowèi in Xiāngyáng,
and the Nányí Xiàowèi in Níngzhōu.)
Otherwise,
retreat and defend Qiánwéi,
crossing westward to Jiāngyuán,
to guard against unexpected events."
(Jiāngyuán County belonged to Shǔ Commandery in Hàn times.
Later, Lǐ Xióng established the separate Jiāngyuán Commandery.
Jìn changed it to Duōróng County,
and later changed it to Jìnyuán County.
The Táng districts of Jìnyuán, Qīngchéng, and Táng'ān in Shǔzhōu were all within the territory of Hàn's Jiāngyuán County.
Qián,
pronounced jiān.)
That day,
he led his troops into the provincial seat.
Xīn dispatched troops to intercept him,
and they fought at the West Gate.
Téng was defeated and died.
Textual Analysis: The Huáyáng Guózhì says:
"They fought at Xuānhuà Pavilion in Guànghàn,
and killed the messenger of the edict."
Considering that both the province and commandery administered Chéngdū,
it is unlikely they fought in Guànghàn.
Also, if Zhào Xīn had already fought Téng,
he should not have wanted to directly enter the provincial seat.
We now follow the Collected Records.
Only Chén Xún, with his hands bound behind his back, went to see Xīn,
requesting to die in Téng's place.
Xīn, considering his righteousness, granted his request.
Xīn also dispatched troops to intercept Xīyí Xiàowèi Chén Zǒng.
When Zǒng reached Jiāngyáng,
(Jiāngyáng County belonged to Qiánwéi Commandery in Hàn times.
Liú Zhāng separated the Jiāngyáng Commandery.
The Táng districts of Lúchuān and Miánshuǐ in Lúzhōu were within the territory of Hàn's Jiāngyáng.)
his Zhǔbù, Zhào Mó of Shǔ Commandery, said:
"Now that the province and commandery are at odds,
great turmoil is certain to arise.
We should hasten to proceed and join them.
Our office is a key military position.
Assisting the righteous and punishing the rebellious,
(meaning the Xīyí office commanded the key troops of Shǔ.
The righteous refers to Gěng Téng,
the rebellious refers to Zhào Xīn,
urging Zǒng to assist Téng in attacking Xīn.)
if you, Zǒng, further delay along the way,
by the time we reach the Yúfú Ford at Nán'ān,
(Nán'ān County belonged to Qiánwéi Commandery and had the Yúfú Ford.
The Táng district of Qīngshén in Méizhōu was within the territory of Hàn's Nán'ān County.
Sòng Bái said: Yìnglíng County and Zīguān County of Róngzhōu, and Lóngyóu of Jiāzhōu were all part of Hàn's Ānnán County.
Bǐ,
pronounced bì.
Fú,
pronounced fú.)
Mó said to Zǒng:
"Distribute wealth to recruit soldiers to resist and fight.
If we defeat the provincial army,
then the province can be taken;
(meaning if we defeat Xīn's army, then Yìzhōu can be captured,
and the criminals will be apprehended.)
If we retreat downstream,
we will certainly come to no harm."
(Meaning retreating downstream,
Xīn's army would be unable to pursue,
and there would certainly be no harm.)
"Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Zhào was angry with Marquis Gěng,
therefore he killed him.
He has no grievance with me,
why should I act like this!"
With troops approaching his front,
he still uttered such words—
Chén Zǒng was truly a mediocre man.
"Now that the province has risen in revolt,
he will certainly kill you to establish his authority.
Even if you do not fight,
it will be of no benefit."
He spoke until tears fell,
but Zǒng would not listen.
The troops then dispersed on their own.
Zǒng fled into the grass.
Mó donned Zǒng's official robes and fought to the death.
Xīn's troops killed Mó,
and seeing he was not the right man,
searched further and found Zǒng,
killing him.
(Sōu means to search.)
Textual Analysis: The Imperial Annals state:
"Xīn also killed Qiánwéi Tàishǒu Lǐ Mì and Wènshān Tàishǒu Huò Gù."
According to the Huáyáng Guózhì,
it was Qiánwéi Tàishǒu Lǐ Bì and Wènshān Tàishǒu Yáng Bīn,
not Mì and Gù.
The Collected Records also record
"Lǐ Bì".
The Annals are probably mistaken.
Xīn declared himself Grand Commander, Grand General, and Governor of Yìzhōu.
The historical commentary notes: In the "Jìn Chūnqiū" it is stated
"In the first year of the Tàipíng era,”
though other books do not record this,
so it is not accepted here.
He changed and replaced officials,
and when government officials were summoned,
no one dared not to come.
By "government officials,"
it is meant those appointed by the Jìn court.
"Summoned,"
phonetic reading Pi.
Four thousand riders, including Mǐ Fúchéng and Kuí Bó, defected to Xīn.
Xīn appointed Xiáng as the "Wēikòu General."
Shěn Yuè records: "Wēikòu General,"
the seventh of the forty titles.
He entrusted him as a confidant,
and had him recruit over ten thousand brave warriors from the six prefectures,
to block the northern route.
The six prefectures
refer to Tiānshuǐ, Lüèyáng, and others.
"Brave warriors"
refers to the strong and courageous among the refugees.
The northern route
is the road from Guānzhōng to Shǔ.
"Block,"
phonetic reading Dīng Guǎn.
Collated by Wáng Chóngwǔ, Biāodiǎn Róngzhào, Zǔ Nièchóngqí.
Sīmǎ Guāng
was ordered to edit.
Later Heavenly Tái of Studies.
Xiàohuì Emperor in the first year of Yǒngníng
(Xīnyǒu, 301), still the second year of Yǒngkāng.
In the first month, on the day Yǐchǒu,
Prince Lún of Zhào changed the era name to Jiànshǐ;
in April,
the Emperor reasserted his authority,
and changed the era name to Yǒngníng.
1. In spring,
in the first month,
the Imperial Secretariat Appointee in Andìng, Zhāng Guǐ, was appointed Governor of Liángzhōu.
Guǐ, seeing that times were difficult,
secretly aspired to secure Hésī,
thus he sought the position in Liángzhōu.
At the time, the region was troubled by bandits and insurgents,
while the Xiānbēi tribe raided;
upon Guǐ's arrival,
he made Sòng Pèi and Fàn Yuǎn his chief advisors,
and decisively defeated them,
establishing his renown in the western lands.
The Zhāng family’s tenure in Liángzhōu began here.
Alas!
In chaotic times, people seek personal preservation,
yet many fail despite their efforts.
The efforts of Dòu Róng and Zhāng Guǐ to hold Hésī
succeeded in securing their aim.
The attempts of Xiè Huì and Yuán Yǐ to safeguard Jīng and Xiāng
ultimately did not secure them.
Dòu Róng and Zhāng Guǐ
consistently dedicated themselves to serving the Hàn and Jìn,
hence they were naturally blessed with enduring fortune and to benefit their descendants.
Xiè Huì and Yuán Yǐ
sought to secure themselves by relying on geographical advantages,
but their intentions were misguided,
as Heaven did not favor them.
However, Liú Yān’s quest for governorship of Yìzhōu,
Yuán Shào's ambition for Jì territory,
and Shí Jìngtáng's desire for Hedong,
secretly planned immense goals;
yet their success or failure over time
was beyond mere calculation or foresight.
2. Chancellor Lún and Sūn Xiù had Officer Zhào Fèng falsely communicate that Emperor Xuān’s spirit commanded:
"Lún should promptly enter the Western Palace."
Sīmǎ Yì,
posthumously titled Emperor Xuān.
Lún appointed the Eastern Palace as the Chancellor's Office,
referring to the Western Palace as the forbidden inner court.
Wàng's grandson,
accustomed to flattering service,
was made Assistant Chancellor by Lún,
and he was sent to forcefully seize the Imperial seal,
draft the abdication edict,
and with Shàngshū Official Mǎn Fèn, carry the seal to
transfer the throne to Lún.
General of the Left Guard, Wáng Yú, and Forward Army General, Sīmǎ Yǎ, led armed soldiers into the palace,
informing the three departments of the situation,
demonstrating power and offering rewards,
so none dared to resist.
Zhāng Lín and others garrisoned and guarded all gates.
This refers to guarding the gates of the palace city.
On the day Yǐchǒu,
Lún, prepared with ceremonial attire, entered the palace,
taking the Imperial throne.
The historical commentary notes: In "The Spring and Autumn Annals of the Thirty States," it is said:
"When Lún intended to usurp the throne,
the King of Yìyáng, Wēi, showed the edict to Jī Shào, saying: 'The Sage's action follows that of Yáo and Shùn;
what do you think?'
Shào sternly replied, 'I will only die,
never will there be two allegiances!'
Wēi, infuriated,
drew his sword and left.
When Emperor Huì was moved to Jīnyóng city,
only Shào remained determined, not cooperating,
remaining resolute in Jīnyóng,
completely refusing communion with Lún,
and all who heard feared for him."
The "Jìn Shū: Loyal and Righteous Biographies" states:
"Lún usurped the throne,
and Shào served as Inner Court Official,
and upon Emperor Huì’s restoration,
he retained his position."
The two accounts differ,
so neither is accepted here.
"Restoration"
has
"restoration"
interpreted as
"appointment."
The era name changed to Jiànshǐ.
The Emperor left the Western Gate of Huálín to reside in Jīnyóng city,
the Western Gate of Huálín,
refers to the Western Gate of Huálín Garden.
On the day Bǐngyín,
the Emperor was honored as Grand Emperor,
the name Jīnyōng was changed to Yǒngchāng Palace,
and the Imperial Grandson was demoted to Prince of Púyáng.
The heir, Shí, was established as Crown Prince,
the son Fù was enfeoffed as Prince of Jīngzhào,
Qián as Prince of Guǎngpíng,
and Xǔ as Prince of Bàchéng,
all serving as Palace Attendants and leading troops.
Prince Liáng, Róng, was appointed as Zàihéng,
Hé Shào as Grand Preceptor,
Sūn Xiù as Palace Attendant, Director of the Central Secretariat, General of Agile Cavalry, and given the same honors as the Three Excellencies,
Yìyáng Prince Wēi as Director of the Central Secretariat,
Zhāng Lín as General of the Guards,
and the rest of their faction,
were all made ministers and generals,
ministers and generals,
meaning the various ministers and the various Colonels of the Palace Guard.
General,
is pronounced as Liàng.
They were too numerous to record;
down to the slaves and soldiers,
they were also granted noble ranks.
At each court assembly,
the hall was filled with those wearing the sable and cicada insignia,
the military cap,
also called the military headdress,
worn by various military officials.
Palace Attendants and Regular Palace Attendants added golden dang ornaments.
Attached cicadas formed the pattern,
and sable tails served as decoration,
called
the "Zhào Huìwén Crown."
Hú Guǎng explained: King Wǔlíng of Zhào imitated Hú clothing,
adorning the head with golden dang,
inserting sable tails in front,
as a mark of high office;
when Qín destroyed Zhào,
they bestowed this crown upon close ministers.
Yìng Shào's Hàn Officialdom says: Commentators say gold was chosen for its firmness and strength,
enduring a hundred refinements without loss,
the cicada dwells high and drinks pure dew,

(*Jìn Treatise*: The Emperor separated nine commanderies: Héngyáng, Chángshā, Xiāngdōng, Línglíng, Shàoyáng, Guìyáng from Jīngzhōu, and Shǐ'ān, Shǐxīng, Línhè from Guǎngzhōu,
and established Xiāngzhōu.
The Emperor's Annals say: Eight commanderies from Jīng and Jiāng were separated to form Xiāngzhōu.
The Annals and Treatise contradict each other.
We follow the Annals here.
Shěn Yuē also said: Eight commanderies were separated: Chángshā, Héngyáng, Xiāngdōng, Shàolíng, Línglíng, Yíngyáng, Jiànchāng from Jīngzhōu,
and Guìyáng from Jiāngzhōu,
to establish Xiāngzhōu.)
16. In the ninth month,
on *wùshēn*,
Lángyé Prince Ruì arrived at Jiànyè.
Ruì took his General Who Pacifies the East's Marshal, Wáng Dǎo, as his chief strategist,
trusted him wholeheartedly,
and consulted him on every matter.
Ruì's reputation had always been low,
and the people of Wú did not submit to him.
He stayed for a long time,
but no scholar-officials came to him,
and Dǎo was troubled by this.
Once, when Ruì went out to observe the purification festival,
Dǎo had Ruì ride in a shoulder-borne carriage,
with full ceremonial dignity,
and Dǎo and various famous figures all followed on horseback.
Jì Zhān, Gù Róng, and others saw this and were astonished,
and they came forward in succession to bow by the roadside.
Dǎo then advised Ruì, saying:
"Gù Róng and Hè Xún
are the leading figures of this land;
you should win them over to secure the people's hearts.
Once these two come,
then all will follow."
Ruì then sent Dǎo to personally visit Xún and Róng,
and both responded to the summons and came.
He appointed Xún as Neishi of Wúguó;
Róng as Army Controller,
(Army Controller
is Army Marshal.
His position was Army Controller,
this was an additional appointment.)
and consulted with them on plans and discussions.
He also appointed Jì Zhān as Army
Libationer,
Biǎn Kǔn as Gentleman of the Masters of Writing,
Zhōu as Assistant of the Granary Section,
and Liú Chāo of Lángyé as Retainer.
(Jìn princes' kingdoms had four Receptionists,
six Grand Masters of the Palace,
and ten Retainers.)
Kǔn
was the son of Biǎn Cuì;
(Biǎn Cuì appears in the second year of Tài'ān of Emperor Huì, in the previous scroll.)
and the great-grandson of Zhāng Zhāo.
(Zhāng Zhāo assisted Wú as a founding minister.)
"Be humble in receiving scholars,
frugal to ensure sufficient resources,
govern with tranquility,
and pacify both the new and the old;"
(new,
meaning those who came from the Central Plains;
old,
meaning the people of Jiāngdōng.)
(*shuō*,
read as *shuì*, *ruì* fan.)
When Ruì first arrived,
he often neglected affairs due to drink;
Dǎo admonished him.
Ruì ordered wine to be poured,
took the cup and overturned it,
and from then on abstained.
The history records that Emperor Yuán was able to employ Wáng Dǎo, which is why he prospered in Jiāngdōng.
17 Gǒu Xī pursued and attacked Jí Sāng,
breaking through his eight encampments,

Sāng and Shí Lè gathered their remaining troops,

but Jìzhōu Cìshǐ Qiáoguó Dīng Shào intercepted them at Chìqiáo,
and defeated them again.
Sāng fled to Mǎmù,
which is the Mǎmù in Chípíng.
According to Jìn records,
Yángpíng Commandery had a Lèpíng County,
which was Qīng County of Dōng Commandery in the Former Hàn,
renamed Lèpíng by Emperor Zhāng of the Later Hàn.
However, since Shí Lè intended to flee to Hàn,
this Lèpíng is not that one.
Also, Bīngzhōu had a Lèpíng Commandery,
established during the Tàishǐ era of Emperor Wǔ,
which was Liáozhōu in the Táng;
Lè fled to this place.
Gǒu Xī was appointed Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn and Dūdū of Qīng, Yǎn, and other military affairs,
Dīng Shào was appointed Níngběi Jiāngjūn and Jiān of Jìzhōu military affairs,
both were granted the authority to act with imperial credentials.
Xī repeatedly defeated powerful bandits,
his prestige and fame were immense,
he excelled at managing complex and demanding affairs,
and his application of law was severe and strict.
His maternal aunt relied on him,
and Xī provided for her very generously.
Her son requested to become a general,
but Xī refused,
saying:
"I do not pardon people with the king's law,
will you not regret it later!"
He insisted on requesting it,
so Xī then made him a Dūhù;
later he violated the law,
Xī, wielding his credentials, executed him,
his maternal aunt kowtowed to plead for his life,
but he did not listen.
Afterwards, he wore plain clothes and wept for him, saying:
"The one who killed you,
was the Cìshǐ of Yǎnzhōu,
the one weeping for his younger cousin,
is Gǒu Dàojiāng."
Gǒu Xī,
courtesy name Dàojiāng.
18 The Hú tribal chief Zhāng Bèidū, Féng Mòtū and others,
the leader of a Hú tribe,
was called Bùdà.
Yáng Zhènghéng said: Bèi,
pronounced bèi.
were encamped at Shàngdǎng,
Shí Lè went to join them,
and then persuaded Bèidū and others, saying:
"The Shànyú Liú is raising troops to attack Jìn,
Shànyú Liú,
refers to Liú Yuān.
Persuade,
shuì, pronounced shuì.
Shànyú,
pronounced chán.
Do you think you can ultimately remain independent?"
They said:
"We cannot."
Lè said:
"If so, then how can you not early on pledge allegiance to someone!
Now the various tribes have all already received rewards and recruitment from the Shànyú,
and they often gather to discuss,
wanting to betray the Bùdà and submit to the Shànyú."
Bèidū and others thought this was reasonable.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Bèidū and others followed Lè, riding alone, and submitted to Hàn.
The Hánwáng Yuān appointed Bèidū as Qīnhànwáng,
Mòtū as Dūdū Bùdà,
and appointed Lè as Fǔhàn Jiāngjūn, Píngjìnwáng,

The Wūhuán Zhāng Fúlìdù had two thousand followers,
encamped at Lèpíng,
Yuān repeatedly summoned him,
but could not get him to come.
Lè pretended to have offended Yuān,
and went to join Fúlìdù,
Fúlìdù was pleased,
and they became sworn brothers,
he had Lè lead various Hú tribes on raids,
and wherever they went, they were unstoppable,
the various Hú tribes feared and submitted to him.
Lè knew the hearts of the masses were attached to him,
so he took advantage of a gathering to seize Fúlìdù,
and said to the various Hú:
"Now that we are starting a great undertaking,
between me and Fúlìdù, who is fit to be the leader?"
The various Hú all recommended Lè.
Lè then released Fúlìdù,
and led his followers to submit to Hàn.
Yuān added to Lè the title Dū Shāndōng Zhēngtǎo Zhū Jūnshì,
and assigned Fúlìdù's followers to him.
The history records that Shí Lè's forces gradually grew strong.
19 Eleventh month,
on the first day, Wùshēn,

appointed Shàngshū Yòupúyè Hé Yù as Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn,

appointed Wáng Yǎn as Sītú.
Yǎn persuaded Tàifù Yuè, saying:

and his clansman Dūn as Cìshǐ of Qīngzhōu.
Kǎoyì says: Jìn Chūnqiū records:

Dūn to Yángzhōu,

Dūn's biography says,
he entered from Qīngzhōu to become Zhōngshū Jiān,

Bō died in the third month of the third year of Yǒngjiā,
this year Yuè was in Xǔchāng,
not in Luò,
therefore, we follow the Jìn Shū as definitive.
"Jīngzhōu has the solidity of the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
Qīngzhōu has the peril of the sea at its back,
you two are outside while I am in the center,
enough to form three burrows."
Zhànguócè: Féng Xuān said to Mèngchángjūn:
"A cunning rabbit has three burrows,
only then can it avoid death."
Later, Dūn and Chéng turned on each other,
Yǎn also died at the hands of Shí Lè,
where were the three burrows then!
Therefore, a loyal minister forgets his family for the state,
for if the state is secure, the family is also secure.
Lù Diàn's Pǐyǎ says: It is commonly said that rabbits dig burrows,
they must connect them through the backs of hills,
this is the so-called cunning rabbit with three burrows.
Spoken,
yǔ, pronounced yǔ.
He appointed Guō Shū as Biéjià,
and entrusted him with the affairs of the administration.
Chéng indulged in wine day and night,
not attending to administrative duties,
even though bandits and invaders were pressing from all sides,

Shū often earnestly admonished him,
believing he should cherish the people, nurture the troops,
and preserve the territory of the province,
but Chéng did not listen.
This sets the stage for Wáng Chéng's inability to protect Jīngzhōu.

Lèlíng County,

For,
wèi, pronounced wèi.
Former officials of Yǐng collected and buried him.

Dùzhī Xiàowèi,

duó, pronounced duó.

25. Initially, Grand Tutor Sīmǎ Yuè and Xún Xī were close friends.
Yuè invited him into the inner hall,
and they swore brotherhood.
Sīmǎ Pān Tāo advised Yuè, saying:
"Yǎnzhōu is a crucial strategic area.
Cáo Cāo used it to found his enterprise.
The events are recorded in scrolls 60 and 61.
Xún Xī is not a purely loyal subject.
If he remains stationed there for long,
calamity will arise in our very heart and belly.
If we transfer him to Qīngzhōu,
bestowing upon him a grander title,
Xī will surely be pleased.
You, my lord, can personally govern Yǎnzhōu,
manage the affairs of the various Xià regions,
and act as a protective screen for the imperial court.
This is what is called 'acting before disorder arises'."
Lǎozǐ said: When a situation is stable, it is easy to maintain;
before signs appear, it is easy to plan;
when it is fragile, it is easy to break;
when it is minute, it is easy to disperse.
Act before it exists;
govern before disorder arises.
Wěi (manage),
read as yú guì fān.
Xià (regions),
read as hù yǎ fān.
Cháo (court),
read as zhí yáo fān.
On the Guǐmǎo day,
Yuè appointed himself as Chancellor,
assumed the post of Governor of Yǎnzhōu,
and was made Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of Yǎn, Yù, Sī, Jì, Yōu, and Bìng provinces.
Dù Yòu said: In the Jìn dynasty, the posts of Minister over the Masses (Sītú) and Chancellor were interchangeable;
they were alternately established and abolished,
never coexisting.
It was not until the first year of the Yǒngjiā era that both posts were established simultaneously,
with Wáng Yǎn as Minister over the Masses,
and Dōnghǎi Prince Sīmǎ Yuè as Chancellor.
Xún Xī was additionally appointed Palace Attendant, granted the ceremonial axe (jiǎjié), and made Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of Qīngzhōu,
assuming the post of Governor of Qīngzhōu,
and enfeoffed as Duke of Dōngpíng Commandery.
From then on, discord arose between Yuè and Xī.
This sets the stage for Xī later issuing a proclamation enumerating Yuè's crimes.
When Xī arrived in Qīngzhōu,
he established his authority through harshness and severity,
carrying out executions daily.
The people of the province called him
the "Butcher Lord".
Dèng Zhǎn said: This means he killed people like a butcher slaughtering the six domestic animals.
Bó (Lord),
means chief.
Jǐ Zhí gathered a crowd of fifty to sixty thousand men,

Xī marched out and stationed at Wúyán to attack him.
Wúyán County
belonged to Dōngpíng Principality.
In the Táng dynasty, it was within the boundaries of Jìzhōu.
Jǐ Zhí's punishments and killings were even more severe than Xún Xī's.
Xún Xī attacked Zhí,
and defeated him.
Initially,
Liú Líng of Yángpíng,
was poor and lowly in his youth,
yet his strength could restrain a charging ox,
and his running could keep pace with a galloping horse.
Although people of the time found him extraordinary,
none could recommend him for office.
Líng beat his chest and sighed, saying:
Yīng,
means chest.
"Heaven!

It happened that Wáng Mí was defeated by Xún Chún,
and Líng was also defeated by Wáng Zàn.

enfeoffing him as Duke of Dōnglái;

Textual Analysis says: Huáyáng Guózhì records Wáng Xùn as the Administrator of Guǎnghàn becoming Regional Inspector of Níngzhōu.
However, at that time Guǎnghàn had already fallen to Lǐ Xióng.
Here we follow the biography of Xùn.
The Regional Inspector of Jiāozhōu, Wú Yàn, sent his son Wú Zǐ leading troops to rescue them.

Hǎo (friendly),

1. Spring,
first month,

killed him,

These events occurred the following year.
Here we follow the Spring and Autumn Annals of the Sixteen Kingdoms.

Xià,

Zhǐ,

Textual analysis notes: Liú Kūn's letter replying to the Grand Tutor's office said:

Considering that at that time Liú Yuān was strong and Liú Kūn was weak,
