He dispatched the Protector-in-Chief, the Qūyáng King Liú Xián, together with the General-in-Chief Who Subdues the North Liú Líng, General Who Pacifies the North Zhào Gù, and General Who Pacifies the North Wáng Sāng,
to encamp east at Nèihuáng.
Nèihuáng County
belongs to Wèi Commandery.
Yīng Shào said: Because Chénliú has a Wàihuáng,
therefore
"Nèi"
is added.
They campaigned east to Qīng Province,
and also to fetch their families.
Liú Yuān approved.
Initially,
the Colonel of the Eastern Yí, Bóhǎi man Lǐ Zhēn,
had an agreement with Wáng Jùn to jointly support the Jìn house.
Jùn harbored different intentions,
and Zhēn resented him.
When Hé Yǎn died,
see the 85th scroll, first year of Emperor Huì's Yǒngxīng reign.
He urged Zhēn to raise troops to punish Jùn.
Zhēn sent his son Lǐ Chéng to lead troops to attack Jùn.
According to the "Different Examination": In the "Yān History, Wáng Dàn Biography,"
"Chéng"
is written as
"Xián."
Here we follow the "Lǐ Hóng Biography."
Urge
is pronounced shuì ruì.
Páng Běn had long-standing enmity with Zhēn.
Taking advantage of the emptiness, he attacked and killed Zhēn,
and sent someone to kill Chéng in Wúlǜ.
Wúlǜ County
belonged to Liáodōng in Former Hàn,
to the Liáodōng Dependent State in Later Hàn,
and was abolished in Jìn.
Yīng Shào said: Lǜ
is pronounced lǘ.
It is what the "Zhōu Rites" calls
"the mountain Yīwūlǘ."
An edict appointed the Bóhǎi man Fēng Shì to replace Zhēn as Colonel of the Eastern Yí.
Páng Běn again plotted to kill him.
Shì's son Fēng Quān advised Shì to set an ambush and invite Běn,
arresting and beheading him,
and exterminating his entire family.
In the 1st year, spring,
on the 1st month,
Yǐchǒu, the first day,
a great amnesty was declared.
The Hàn ruler Liú Yuān established Shàn Zhēng's daughter as Empress.
Shàn Zhēng
was a Dí chieftain.
His submission to Hàn is seen in the previous scroll, second year.
Shàn
is pronounced shàn.
A great amnesty was declared.
He enfeoffed his son Liú Yì as the Běihǎi King.
He appointed the Chánglè King Liú Yáng as Grand Marshal.
3. The Han Dynasty's General-in-Chief of the Eastern Pacification, Shí Lè, crossed the Yellow River,
captured Báimǎ,
and Wáng Mí joined him with thirty thousand troops,
together they invaded Xú, Yù, and Yǎnzhōu.
In the second month,
Lè attacked Juànchéng,
killed the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, Yuán Fú,
then captured Cāngyuán,
and killed Wáng Kān.
He crossed the Yellow River northward again,
attacked the various commanderies of Jìzhōu,
and over ninety thousand common people followed him.
4. Chéng's Grand Commandant Lǐ Guó garrisoned Bāxī,
his subordinate Wén Shí killed Guó,
and surrendered Bāxī to Luó Shàng.
5. The Grand Tutor Yuè summoned the General Who Establishes Might, Qián Huì of Wúxīng.
(Wúxīng Commandery was established by dividing Wú Commandery and Dānyáng,
because it originated from Wúchéng.)
Huì,
(pronounced Huì).
Huì plotted to kill Dūn and rebel,
Dūn fled to Jiànyè,
and reported to Prince Lángyà Ruì.
Huì then rebelled,
advanced and invaded Yángxiàn,
(Yángxiàn County,
belonged to Kuàijī Commandery in the Former Hàn,
to Wú Commandery in the Later Hàn,
since the time of Wú,
it was divided and belonged to Wúxīng Commandery.
Xián said: The old city of Yángxiàn,
is south of Yìxīng County in Chángzhōu today.)
Zhōu gathered the local villagers,
and together with Yì and others, they jointly attacked Huì,
and beheaded him.
This was the third pacification of Jiāngnán.
(In the first year of Yǒngxīng of Emperor Huì, he attacked Shí Bīng,
in the first year of Yǒngjiā, he attacked Chén Mǐn,
and now he executed Huì,
thus three pacifications of Jiāngnán.)
Yìxīng Commandery was established in his hometown to honor him.
(At that time, Yángxiàn of Wúxīng, the western township of Chángchéng County, and Yǒngshì of Dānyáng were divided to form Yìxīng Commandery.)
6. Cáo Nì led troops east from Dàliáng,
everywhere he went, he captured,
then conquered Dōngpíng,
and advanced to attack Lángyà.
7. In summer,
the fourth month,
Wáng Jùn's general Qí Hóng defeated the Hàn Dynasty's Inspector of Jìzhōu, Liú Líng, at Guǎngzōng,
and killed him.
8. The ruler of Chéng, Xióng, said to his general Zhāng Bǎo:
"If you can obtain Zǐtóng,
I will reward you with Lǐ Lí's official position."
Bǎo then first killed someone and fled to Zǐtóng,
Hōng Qí and others trusted him,
and entrusted him with important matters.
When Luó Shàng sent an envoy to Zǐtóng,
Qí and others went out to send
him off;
Bǎo closed the gates from behind,
Qí and others fled to Bāxī.
Xióng appointed Bǎo as Grand Commandant.
9. In the six provinces of Yōu, Bìng, Sī, Jì, Qín, and Yōng, there was a great locust plague,
which consumed all the grass, trees, and the hair of oxen and horses.
10. In autumn,
the seventh month,
besieged the Administrator of Hénèi, Péi Zhěng, at Huái.
An edict ordered General Who Subdues Caitiffs, Sòng Chōu, to rescue Huái.
Lè and the Great General Who Pacifies the North, Wáng Sāng, intercepted and attacked Chōu,
and killed him;
the people of Hénèi captured Zhěng and surrendered him,
the Hàn ruler Yuān appointed Zhěng as Left Assistant of the Imperial Secretariat.
The supervising general of Hénèi, Guō Mò, gathered the remaining troops of Zhěng,
and made himself a fort master,
(small fortifications are called wù).
With the world at war,
people gathered and built forts to defend themselves;
without imperial orders,
they thus made themselves fort masters.)
General,
(pronounced jiàng).
11. Luó Shàng died in Bā Commandery,
an edict appointed the Administrator of Chángshā, Pí Sù of Xiàpī, to replace him.
(Genealogy: The surname Pí,
descended from Fán Zhòngpí.)
12. On Gēngwǔ,
the Hàn ruler Yuān fell ill;
on Xīnwèi,
he appointed Prince of Chénliú, Huānlè, as Grand Steward,
Prince of Chánglè, Yáng, as Grand Tutor,
Prince of Jiāngdū, Yánnián, as Grand Guardian,
Prince of Chǔ, Cōng, as Grand Marshal and Great Chányú,
all concurrently managed the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat.
A Chányú Terrace was established west of Píngyáng.
He appointed Prince of Qí, Yù, as Grand Minister of Works,
Prince of Lǔ, Lóng, as Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
Prince of Běihǎi, Yì, as Great General Who Assists the Army, concurrently Colonel of the Capital Province,
Prince of Shǐ'ān, Yào, as Grand Commander of Campaigns, concurrently Left Assistant of the Chányú,
the Commandant of Justice, Qiáo Zhìmíng, as Great General Who Champions the Army, concurrently Right Assistant of the Chányú,
the Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, Liú Yīn, as Left Deputy Director,
Wáng Yù as Right Deputy Director,
Rén Yǐ as Minister of Personnel,
Zhū Jì as Palace Secretary,
the Protector of the Army, Mǎ Jǐng, concurrently General of the Left Guard,
Prince of Yǒng'ān, Ān Guó, concurrently General of the Right Guard,
Prince of Ānchāng, Shèng, Prince of Ānyì, Qīn, and Prince of Xīyáng, Xuán, all concurrently Generals of the Martial Guard,
respectively commanding the imperial guards.
Initially,
when Shèng was young,
he did not like reading books,
only read the Classic of Filial Piety and the Analects,
saying:
"Reciting these and being able to practice them,
is sufficient,
why recite many but not practice them!"
Lǐ Xī saw him,
sighed and said:
"From afar, he seems easygoing,
but when near,
he is solemn like a strict ruler,
truly a gentleman!"
Yuān, because of his loyalty and sincerity,
thus entrusted him with important responsibilities on his deathbed.
On Dīngchǒu,
Yuān summoned Grand Steward Huānlè and others into the palace,
to receive the testamentary edict to assist in governance.
On Jǐmǎo,
Yuān died;
(Examination of discrepancies: The Spring and Autumn Annals of the Sixteen Kingdoms:
"On Dīngchǒu in the eighth month,
Yuān summoned Grand Steward Huānlè and others to receive the testamentary edict,
died on Jǐmǎo,
buried on Xīnwèi."
According to the perpetual calendar,
the first day of the seventh month was Rénxū,
the sixteenth day was Dīngchǒu,
the eighteenth day was Jǐmǎo,
the first day of the eighth month was Xīnmǎo,
there were no Dīngchǒu, Jǐmǎo, or Xīnwèi.
Xīnwèi was the eleventh day of the ninth month.
Probably Yuān died in the seventh month,
and was buried in the ninth month.
The Spring and Autumn Annals of the Sixteen Kingdoms is mistaken.)
Hé,
styled Xuántài,
was Yuān's legitimate son.
Hé was suspicious and jealous, showing no kindness.
The Director of the Imperial Clan, Hūyán Yōu,
the son of Yì,
because Yuān considered him lacking in talent and virtue,
was never promoted throughout his life;
the Palace Attendant Liú Chéng,
had always disliked the Prince of Chǔ, Cōng,
and the Commandant of the Guards, the Prince of Xīchāng, Ruì,
felt ashamed for not being included in the late emperor's final edict;
thus they conspired together,
and persuaded Hé, saying:
"The late emperor did not consider the balance of power,
allowing three princes to command strong troops within the capital.
Wéi,
means to consider.
The three princes,
refer to Prince Ānchāng, Shèng,
Prince Ānyì, Qīn,
and Prince Xīyáng, Xuán;
some say: the three princes,
refer to Prince Qí, Yù,
Prince Lǔ, Lóng,
and Prince Běihǎi, Yì.
Xíng,
read as xià mèng fān.
Wù,
read as wū lù fān.
Shuì,
read as shū ruì fān.
It is said that Cōng was stationed west of Píngyáng.
They said that great authority was not in their own hands,
and though they were placed above the officials and people,
their position was like that of a temporary lodger.
Zuò,
read as cú wò fān.
Hé,
was the nephew of Yōu.
He deeply believed them.
On the night of Xīnsì,
he summoned Prince Ānchāng, Shèng, and Prince Ānyì, Qīn, among others, and informed them.
Shèng said:
"The late emperor's coffin is still in the hall,
and the four princes have shown no signs of rebellion.
Cōng,
was the fourth son of Yuān,
hence called the four princes.
Some say: referring to Cōng, Yù, Lóng, and Yì.
What will the world think of Your Majesty!
Moreover, the great enterprise has just begun,
Your Majesty must not believe the words of slanderers and doubt your brothers;
if even brothers cannot be trusted,
who else can be trusted enough!"
Yōu and Ruì angrily said to him:
"Today's discussion,
leaves no room for a second opinion,
what kind of words are these from the Commander of the Army!"
They ordered their attendants to kill him.
After Shèng died,
Qīn, fearing, said:
"I obey Your Majesty's command."
On Rénwǔ,
Ruì led Mǎ Jǐng to attack the Prince of Chǔ, Cōng, at the Chányú Platform,
Yōu led Prince Yǒng'ān, Ānguó, to attack Prince Qí, Yù, at the Minister over the Masses' residence,
Chéng led Prince Ānyì, Qīn, to attack Prince Lǔ, Lóng,
and sent the Minister of Works Tián Mì and the General of the Martial Guards Liú Xuán to attack Prince Běihǎi, Yì.
Mì and Xuán, taking Yì with them, broke through the gates and fled to Cōng,
Cōng ordered his troops to don armor and await them.
Guàn jiǎ,
means to put on armor.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
They galloped back,
and together with Yōu and Chéng, attacked Lóng and Yù.
Yōu and Chéng suspected that Ānguó and Qīn had different intentions,
and killed them;
on that day,
they beheaded Yù.
On Guǐwèi,
they beheaded Lóng.
On Jiǎshēn,
Cōng attacked the Xīmíng Gate,
and captured it;
Liú Yuān made Píngyáng his capital,
and all the city gates were named after those of Luòyáng's city gates.
The vanguard followed him.
On Yǐyǒu,
they killed Hé in the western chamber of the Guāngjí Hall,
Liú Yuān had built the Guāngjí Hall in Píngyáng.
They displayed his head on a pole at the main crossroads.
The ministers requested Cōng to ascend the throne;
Cōng, considering that Prince Běihǎi, Yì,
was the son of Empress Dān,
yielded the throne to him.
Examination of discrepancies: The Records of the Jin Dynasty writes
"Yì".
According to the Spring and Autumn Annals of the Sixteen Kingdoms, it is written
"Yì",
now we follow this.
After a long time, Cōng agreed,
saying:
"Yì and the ministers are only doing this because disasters and difficulties are still severe,
and they covet my seniority.
This is a matter of the family and state,
how dare I decline!
When Yì comes of age,
I shall return the great enterprise to him."
Thus he ascended the throne.
Cōng,
styled Xuánmíng,
was the fourth son of Yuān.
He changed the era name to Guāngxīng.
He honored Lady Dān as Empress Dowager,
and his mother, Lady Zhāng, as Imperial Empress Dowager.
He appointed Yì as Imperial Younger Brother, concurrently holding the titles of Grand Chányú and Minister over the Masses.
He established his wife, Lady Hūyán, as Empress.
Lady Hūyán,
was the cousin of Empress Yuān.
He enfeoffed his son Càn as Prince of Hénèi,
Yì as Prince of Héjiān,
Yì as Prince of Péngchéng,
and Kuī as Prince of Gāopíng;
and still appointed Càn as General Who Pacifies the Army and Commander of All Military Affairs Within and Outside the Capital.
He appointed Shí Lè as Governor of Bìng Province,
and enfeoffed him as Duke of Jí Commandery.
13 The Dí chieftain of Línwèi in Lüèyáng, Pú Hóng,
was brave and resourceful,
and the Dí people feared and submitted to him.
According to the Records of the Jin Dynasty,
Lüèyáng Commandery had Línwèi County,
likely established during the Wei period.
The Records of the Jin Dynasty states: The ancestors of the Dí,
were descendants of the Yǒuhù clan,
and for generations served as chieftains of the western barbarians.
In Hóng's household pond, reeds grew,
reaching a length of five zhang and five chi,
with joints like bamboo,
and at that time, people all called it
"the Pú family",
thus they took it as their surname.
Later,
because Hóng saw in prophetic texts the words
"grass and fu shall respond to the king",
and also because his grandson Jiān had on his back the characters
"cǎo fù"
he changed his surname to Fú.
Hóng did not accept the appointment,
and proclaimed himself Protector of the Dí, Inspector of Qín Province, and Duke of Lüèyáng.
The affairs of Pú Hóng begin here.
14 In the ninth month,
on Xīnwèi,
they buried the Hàn ruler Yuān at the Yǒngguāng Mausoleum,
posthumously titled Emperor Guāngwén,
with the temple name Gāozǔ.
15 Many refugees from Yōng Province were in Nányáng,
and an imperial edict ordered them to return to their hometowns.
The refugees, because Guānzhōng was devastated and barren,
were all unwilling to return;
the General Who Conquers the South, Shān Jiǎn, and the General of the Southern Palace, Dù Ruí, each sent troops to escort them,
urging them to depart by the deadline.
Wáng Rú of Jīngzhào then secretly gathered strong men,
and at night attacked the two armies,
defeating them.
The two armies,
refer to the troops sent by Shān Jiǎn and Dù Ruí.
Hóu Tuō of Jīngzhào each gathered crowds to attack cities and towns,
killing magistrates and chiefs to respond to them,
and before long,
their numbers reached forty to fifty thousand,
proclaiming themselves Grand General, concurrently Governor of Sī and Yōng Provinces,
and pledged allegiance to Hàn.
16 In winter,
the tenth month,
the Hàn Prince of Hénèi, Càn, Prince of Shǐ'ān, Yào, and Wáng Mí led forty thousand troops to raid Luòyáng,
Shí Lè led twenty thousand cavalry to join Càn at Dàyáng,
defeated the Army Supervisor Péi Miǎo at Miǎnchí,
and then drove straight into the Luò River region.
Càn exited through Huányuán,
plundering between Liáng, Chén, Rǔ, and Yǐng.
Lè exited through the Chénggāo Pass,
according to the Records of the Jin Dynasty,
Chénggāo County in Hénán had a pass.
On Rényín,
they besieged the Administrator of Chénliú, Wáng Zàn, at Cāngyuán,
but were defeated by Zàn,
and retreated to station at Wénshí Ford.
According to the Imperial Annals,
Wénshí Ford is north of the Yellow River.
Also, according to the sixth year of Yǒngjiā,
Lè marched north from Gébēi,
reached Dōngyàn,
and sent Kǒng Cháng to secretly cross from Wénshí Ford to Fāngtóu,
to seize boats on the Xiàng River,
thus Wénshí Ford is northeast of Dōngyàn,
and southeast of Fāngtóu.
17 Liú Kūn personally led troops to attack Liú Hǔ and the Bái tribe.
The Bái tribe
were Xiānbēi.
Kūn attacked them because
Liú Hǔ and the Bái tribe had both submitted to the Hàn.
Yīlú sent his younger brother Fú's son Yùlǜ to lead twenty thousand cavalry to assist him.
They subsequently defeated Liú Hǔ and the Bái tribe,
slaughtering their camp.
Kūn and Yīlú swore brotherhood.
Kūn petitioned to have Yīlú appointed as Great Chányú,
and enfeoffed him as Duke of Dài with the Dài commandery.
At that time, the Dài commandery belonged to Yōuzhōu.
Wáng Jùn did not consent,
and sent troops to attack Yīlú.
Yīlú resisted and defeated them.
Because of this, Jùn developed a rift with Kūn.
Yīlú considered his fief to be too distant and isolated from his own state,
with no connection between the peoples,
so he led over ten thousand households of his tribe from Yúnzhōng into Yànmén,
and requested from Kūn the lands north of Xíng.
North of Xíng
means north of the Shíxíng Pass.
Xíng
is pronounced xíng.
Furthermore, wishing to rely on him for support,
Kūn relocated the populations of the five counties—Lóufán, Mǎyì, Yīnguǎn, Fánzhì, and Guō—south of Xíng.
Lóufán
was where the Xiōngnú resided.
Its location was south of the Northern River.
The present-day Lóufán commandery in Lánzhōu
is not the ancient Lóufán.
The Hàn dynasty's Mǎyì county
corresponds to the location of the Táng dynasty's Dàtóng Army.
The Hàn dynasty's Yīnguǎn county
was northwest of Gōuzhù.
Fánzhì county
was in the Wǔzhōu River valley.
Guō county
became the Píngkòu county of the Northern Qí's Běixiǎnzhōu.
Although these five counties still exist today,
none are located on the lands of the ancient counties.
Xíng
refers to the Xíng Ridge.
Xíng
is pronounced xíng.
Textual analysis notes: The Annals of Emperor Huái states:
"In the fifth year of Yǒngjiā,
eleventh month,
Yīlú invaded Tàiyuán,
and Liú Kūn relocated the populations of five counties for him to occupy.
In the sixth year,
eighth month,
on the xīnhài day,
Liú Kūn requested troops from Yīlú,
and petitioned to have Lú appointed as Duke of Dài."
The Biography of the Suǒlǔ in the Sòng Shū places this in the third year of Yǒngjiā.
The Jìn Chūnqiū places it in the fourth year of Yǒngjiā,
and furthermore states:
"Yīlú led over ten thousand households seeking refuge,
entering Yànmén from Yúnzhōng."
The Preface Annals of the Later Wèi place it in the third year of Emperor Mù,
which corresponds to the fourth year of Yǒngjiā.
According to Liú Kūn's collected works,
in the fourth year of Yǒngjiā,
sixth month,
on the guǐsì day,
he submitted a memorial to the Grand Tutor's office,
stating
"Lú was moved by the grace of the enfeoffment in Dài."
Therefore, we know it was before the sixth month of the fourth year.
Furthermore, Kūn's memorial to the Chancellor stated:
"Previously, Chējì, moved by Yīyí's merit in rescuing the province,
petitioned to enfeoff Yí as Duke of Dài with the Dài commandery,
and it was approved.
At that time, the imperial carriage was in Cháng'ān.
Coinciding with military affairs,
the roads were impassable,
so it was ultimately not implemented.
Lú entrusted me with the matter of the enfeoffment.
I, Kūn, indeed submitted the petition on his behalf,
reiterating Chējì's previous intention.
It was immediately approved.
An Attendant Gentleman-in-Waiting was sent to appoint Lú,
bestowing the seal, tally, and patent.
Jùn held this against me.
Enfeoffing a barbarian with a Huá commandery
was truly a breach of ritual.
However, it was done to remedy a crisis,
just as Jùn had previously enfeoffed Wùwùchén with Liáoxī.
This breach of ritual
was actually initiated by Jùn.
Jùn then contended with Lú over the Dài commandery,
raised troops to attack Lú,
and was defeated by him.
The origin of this tangled conflict
began here.
The Yànmén commandery had five counties north of Xíng.
Lú had recently annexed Chén's officials,
and his state was very powerful and prosperous.
He requested from me the lands north of Xíng.
Moreover, over thirty thousand households had been sent
and were scattered among these five counties.
They were already beyond my control;
furthermore, considering my own weakened and diminished situation,
having them gather together
was not inappropriate.
I therefore relocated the five counties north of Xíng to settle south of Xíng.
Lú, having moved,
somewhat encroached upon and pressured the western frontier fortifications and various military camps of Jùn.
Jùn, no longer tolerant of my peril and weakness, blamed and censured me."
Judging from this,
Lú did not come seeking refuge.
Kūn sent an envoy to speak with the Grand Tutor Yuè,
requesting to jointly send troops to attack Liú Cōng and Shí Lè.
Yuè was wary of Xún Xī and the Governor of Yùzhōu, Féng Sōng.
Yuè and Xī had a rift,
as recorded in the second year of the previous scroll.
Sōng was likely also not loyal to Yuè.
Yuè did not grant permission.
Kūn then declined Yīlú's troops,
and sent them back to their state.
Textual analysis notes: The Preface Annals of the Later Wèi state:
"Liú Kūn requested troops to rescue Luòyáng.
Emperor Mù sent twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to assist him.
The Prince of Dōnghǎi, Yuè, citing famine in Luòyáng,
did not permit it."
According to Kūn's memorial to the Chancellor:
"I, Kūn, devoted myself fully and exhausted my words,
forging an alliance in the north with Yīlú.
He then led a great host,
personally initiating a military campaign.
I immediately reported fully to the Grand Tutor,
earnestly stating my humble opinion:
the strategy for capturing the bandits,
that Cōng should be attacked promptly,
and Lè should not be left unchecked.
However, the Chancellor held a different view;
his concerns were not the same.
He was more worried about men like Xún Xī and Féng Sōng, and thus delayed the punishment of these two bandits.
He sent an envoy to restrain me,
dampening my sharp spirit.
I then disbanded my armor,
and sent Lú's host back to their state."
If Yīlú had indeed sent a host to aid Luòyáng,
how could Kūn's memorial not mention it!
Liú Hǔ gathered his remaining followers,
crossed the river westward,
and settled in the Sìlú River valley in Shuòfāng.
The Sìlú River valley,
located within the Shuòfāng frontier,
was later where the Tuòbá clan established the Sìlú commandery.
In the seventh year of Zhēnjūn,
it was merged into the Xiùróng commandery.
According to Wèi Shōu's Treatise on Geography,
Xiùróng county in the Xiùróng commandery had the Sìlú city.
He was enfeoffed as Duke of Lóufán.
18 On the rénzǐ day,
Liú Kūn was appointed General Who Pacifies the North,
Wáng Jùn was appointed Minister of Works,
and the Xiānbēi Duàn Wùwùchén was promoted to Great Chányú.
19 Famine and hardship in the capital grew increasingly severe day by day.
The Grand Tutor Yuè sent envoys with urgent military dispatches to summon troops from across the land,
ordering them to come to the capital's aid.
The Emperor said to the envoys:
"Tell the various regional commanders for me:
if they come today, they can still save us;
later, it will be too late!"
In the end, none arrived.
General Who Guards the South Shān Jiǎn sent his Protector Wáng Wàn to lead troops to aid the capital.
He encamped at Nièyáng.
Nièyáng county
belonged to the Nányáng commandery.
Yìng Shào said: It was located north of the Niè River.
Master Yán's annotation: Niè
is pronounced niè.
Rú Suì extensively plundered the Miǎn and Hàn regions,
and advanced to threaten Xiāngyáng.
Jiǎn barricaded himself within the city walls for defense.
The Governor of Jīngzhōu, Wáng Chéng,
Chéng was then governing Jiānglíng.
intended to aid the capital.
He reached Lízhǐkǒu.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Língshuǐ River connects upstream to Liángzhōu's Miǎnyáng county.
It flows east past Líxiāng county in the Xīnchéng commandery,
where it is called the Líshuǐ River.
It then flows east past the western mountains of Yíchéng,
where it is called Lí Creek.
It flows east and joins the Yíshuǐ River,
at a place called Lízhǐkǒu.
Yáng Zhènghéng said: Lí
is pronounced yí.
His forces scattered, and he returned.
Many at court proposed moving the capital to avoid disaster.
Wáng Yǎn considered it unacceptable,
and sold off carriages and oxen to calm the people's hearts.
Shān Jiǎn, pressured by Yán Nì,
moved his garrison from Xiāngyáng to Xiàkǒu.
20. Shí Lè led his troops across the Yellow River,
intending to head toward Nányáng.
Wáng Rú, Hóu Tuō, and Yán Ní, upon hearing this,
dispatched ten thousand soldiers to garrison Xiāngchéng to resist Lè.
Lè attacked them,
capturing all their troops,
and advanced to garrison north of Wǎn.
At that time,
Hóu Tuō held Wǎn,
and Wáng Rú held Rǎng.
Rǎng County,
during the Hàn Dynasty, belonged to Nányáng Commandery,
and during the Jìn Dynasty, belonged to Yìyáng Commandery.
Wáng Rú sent an envoy with generous bribes to Lè,
forming a brotherly alliance,
and persuaded Lè to attack Tuō.
Lè attacked Wǎn,
capturing it;
Yán Ní led troops to rescue Wǎn,
but arrived too late and surrendered.
Lè executed Tuō;
imprisoned Ní,
and sent him to Píngyáng,
absorbing all his troops.
He then advanced south to raid Xiāngyáng,
attacking and capturing over thirty fortified positions along the Jiāngxī region.
After Lè raided Xiāngyáng in the south,
he followed the Hàn River downstream,
attacking and plundering the Jiāngxī region.
He headed toward Xiāngchéng,
and Wáng Rú sent his younger brother Lí to launch a surprise attack on Lè;
Lè met and attacked him,
annihilating him,
and once again garrisoned the Jiāngxī region.
21. Grand Tutor Yuè, after having killed Wáng Yán and others,
as seen above in the third year of Yǒngjiā,
and also because the Hú raids were growing increasingly severe,
felt uneasy within,
so he donned military attire and entered the court for an audience,
requesting to campaign against Shí Lè,
and to pacify and gather forces in Yǎn and Yù.
The Emperor said:
"Now the Hú invaders are encroaching upon the outskirts of the capital,
and the people lack steadfast resolve.
The court and the altars of state
rely upon you,
how can you go far away and leave the foundation isolated!"
He replied:
"If I go out,
and by fortune defeat the bandits,
then the state's prestige can be restored,
which is still better than sitting and waiting for exhaustion and poverty."
In the eleventh month,
on the jiǎxū day,
Yuè led forty thousand armored soldiers toward Xǔchāng,
leaving behind Lady Péi, his heir apparent Pí, and Generals Lóngxiāng Lǐ Yùn and Right Guard Hé Lún to guard the capital,
to defend and oversee the palace and government offices;
he appointed Pān Tāo as Governor of Hénán,
to take overall charge of the remaining affairs.
Yuè submitted a memorial to have a mobile secretariat accompany him,
appointing Grand Commandant Yǎn as Army Supervisor,
and all court worthies of established reputation,
were made his subordinate officials,
while renowned generals and elite soldiers,
all entered his headquarters.
Consequently, the palace and government offices were left without guards,
famine grew increasingly severe day by day,
and corpses lay crisscrossed within the palace halls;
bandits operated openly,
and government offices and military camps
all dug moats to defend themselves.
Yuè moved east and garrisoned Xiàng,
appointing Féng Sōng as Left Marshal,
and personally assuming the role of Governor of Yùzhōu.
Prince Mào of Jìnglíng informed the Emperor and sent troops to attack Hé Lún,
but was unsuccessful;
the Emperor placed the blame on Mào,
and Mào fled into hiding,
managing to escape.
Mào,
was originally Prince Mào of Dōngpíng;
when the Emperor ascended the throne,
he was re-enfeoffed as Prince of Jìnglíng.
22. The Governor of Yángzhōu, Zhōu Fù, considering Luòyáng isolated and imperiled,
submitted a memorial requesting to move the capital to Shòuchūn.
Grand Tutor Yuè, angered that Fù had not first informed him but directly submitted the memorial,
was greatly enraged,
and summoned Fù and the Governor of Huáinán, Péi Shuò.
Fù refused to go,
and ordered Shuò to lead troops and advance first.
Shuò falsely claimed to have received Yuè's secret order,
and attacked Fù,
but was defeated by Fù,
and retreated to defend Dōngchéng.
Dōngchéng County,
during the Hàn Dynasty, belonged to Jiǔjiāng Commandery,
during the Later Hàn, belonged to the Principality of Xiàpī,
and during the Jìn Dynasty, belonged to Huáinán Commandery.
Sòng Bái said: Dìngyuǎn County of Háozhōu,
was the territory of Dōngchéng County during the Hàn Dynasty.
23. An edict was issued adding to Zhāng Guǐ the titles of General Who Guards the West and Commander of All Military Affairs in Lǒngyòu.
Examination of Discrepancies says: The Imperial Annals state
"General Who Pacifies the West."
According to the second year of Yǒngxīng of Emperor Huì,
Guǐ had already been appointed General Who Pacifies the West.
Now we follow his biography.
He was informed of the capital's famine and shortages.
Guǐ sent his Army Advisor Dù Xūn to present five hundred horses,
and thirty thousand bolts of felt cloth.
Felt cloth,
is cloth woven from fine hair.
Felt,
is pronounced tǎn.
24. Chéng's Grand Tutor Xiāng attacked Qiáo Dēng at Fúchéng.
Luó Shàng's son Yǔ and his staff had long disliked Dēng,
and did not supply him with grain.
The Governor of Yìzhōu, Pí Sù, was angry,
and wanted to punish them for their crime;
in the twelfth month,
Sù arrived at Bā Commandery,
and Luó Yǔ had someone kill Sù at night,
Jiànpíng Commandant Bào Zhòng killed Yǔ,
and Bā Commandery fell into chaos.
Xiāng, knowing that Dēng's provisions were exhausted and his aid cut off,
attacked Fú with increasing urgency.
The soldiers and civilians all smoked rats to eat,
and many died of starvation,
yet not a single person deserted or rebelled.
Xiāng's son Shòu was originally at Dēng's place,
so Dēng then returned him.
In the first year of Yǒngxīng,
Luó Shàng captured Xiāng's wife and his son Shòu,
who were thus at Dēng's place.
The three offices,
the Pacifying West General's Office, the Yìzhōu Governor's Office, and the Western Rong Colonel's Office,
were all concurrently held by Luó Shàng.
Supervisor,
is pronounced jiān.
25. Earlier,
the Emperor, because Wáng Mí and Shí Lè were encroaching upon the capital region,
issued an edict ordering Xún Xī to command the provinces and commanderies to campaign against them.
It happened that Cáo Ní captured Lángyá,
and in the north seized the Qí region,
his military power was very strong,
and Xún Chún closed the city gates and defended himself.
Xī returned to rescue Qīngzhōu,
and engaged Ní in successive battles,
defeating him.
In the first year of Yǒngjiā,
Xún Xī campaigned against Wèi Zhí,
leaving his younger brother Chún to guard Qīngzhōu.
26. This year,
the Governor of Níngzhōu, Wáng Xùn, arrived at his post,
and submitted a memorial appointing Lǐ Zhāo as Governor of Zhūtí.
At that time, Níngzhōu was externally pressured by Chéng,
and internally plagued by Yí bandits,
and its cities and towns were in ruins.
Xùn wore coarse clothes and ate simple food,
gathering the scattered and displaced,
tirelessly comforting and encouraging them,
and within a few years,
the province's territory was restored to peace.
He executed over ten powerful families who did not obey the law;
because the Wǔlíng Yí had previously been the leaders of the rebellion,
as seen in the eighty-fifth scroll, second year of Tài'ān of Emperor Huì.
Líng,
is pronounced líng.
Both inside and outside, they were awed and submitted.
27. The Hàn ruler Cōng, considering that he had ascended the throne out of proper order,
was suspicious of his legitimate elder brother Gōng;
taking advantage of when Gōng was asleep,
he made a hole in the wall,
stabbed and killed him.
The Han Empress Dowager Shàn died.
The Han ruler Cōng honored his mother, née Zhāng, as Empress Dowager.
The Shàn Empress was young and beautiful,
and Cōng had an incestuous relationship with her.
A younger man's illicit relations with an elder woman is called "zhēng";
an elder man's illicit relations with a younger woman is called "bào".
Shào,
pronounced as in the Shijing, zhào.
The Shàn Empress died of shame and resentment.
From this time, Yì's favor gradually declined,
but because of the Shàn Empress,
Cōng had not yet deposed him.
Empress Hūyán said to Cōng:
"The son succeeding the father
is the constant principle from ancient times to the present.
Your Majesty inherited the enterprise of Emperor Gāozǔ.
Liú Yuān,
temple name Gāozǔ.
After Your Majesty's passing,
Càn and his brothers will certainly be left with no seed."
Cōng said:
"True,
I should consider this slowly."
Hūyán said:
"If matters are delayed, changes will arise.
The Grand Imperial Younger Brother, seeing Càn and his brothers gradually growing up,
will certainly have thoughts of unease;
if by chance there are petty men sowing discord between them,
it is not certain that disaster will not break out today."
Meaning Yì would kill Cōng.
This sets the basis for Cōng killing Yì in the first year of Emperor Yuán's Jiànwǔ era.
"The distant should not come between the close.
The Sovereign already has intentions regarding the Prince of Hénèi;
why does Your Highness not avoid him!"
Yì said:
"At the end of the Héruì era,
the Sovereign himself considered the distinction between legitimate and secondary sons,
and yielded the great position to me.
I, because the Sovereign was older,
therefore deferred and supported him.
The empire
is the empire of Emperor Gāozǔ;
the elder brother ends and the younger brother succeeds,
why should it not be possible!
When Càn and his brothers are grown,
it will be just like today.
Moreover, among sons and younger brothers,
how much difference is there in closeness and distance?
How could the Sovereign possibly have such intentions!"
Cōng yielding to Yì is seen above.
Yì's words here certainly were not uttered in this year;
the Zizhi Tongjian, because of Hūyán's words,
consequently records them together.
Jǐ,
pronounced jū qǐ.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the Rénshēn day,
Xún Xī was defeated by Cáo Yí,
abandoned the city and fled to Gāopíng.
Gāopíng county,
formerly belonged to the State of Liáng,
under Jìn it became the Principality of Gāopíng.
The Sì River passes west of it,
and there is Mount Gāopíng.
The mountain is ten lǐ east-west,
five lǐ north-south,
and four lǐ high.
This mountain is the highest,
its summit is level,
therefore it is called Mount Gāopíng,
and the county also takes its name from it.
2 Shí Lè planned to secure and hold the region between the Jiāng and Hàn Rivers,
but his Army Counselor Commandant Zhāng Bīn considered it inadvisable.
At that time, the army suffered from famine and pestilence,
with more than half dying,
so they crossed the Miǎn River,
and invaded Jiāngxià.
On the Guǐyǒu day,
they captured it.
3 On the Yǐhài day,
Chéng's Grand Tutor Xiāng captured Fúchéng,
capturing Qiáo Dēng;
Grand Bǎo Shǐ captured Bāxī,
killing Wén Shí.
Thereupon, the Chéng ruler Xióng proclaimed a great amnesty,
and changed the era name to Yùhéng.
Qiáo Dēng was brought to Chéngdū,
and Xióng wished to pardon him;
but Dēng's words and spirit were unyielding,
so Xióng killed him.
4 Refugees from Bā and Shǔ were scattered throughout Jīng and Xiāng provinces,
and were repeatedly oppressed and harmed by the local people.
A Shǔ man named Lǐ Xiāng gathered a crowd and occupied Lèxiāng in rebellion.
This is another Lǐ Xiāng,
not the Lǐ Xiāng who was Chéng's Grand Tutor.
Lǐlíng county,
belonged to Chángshā commandery.
Tāo,
pronounced tǔ dāo.
During Emperor Huì's time, when Shǔ was in chaos,
they carved out the three counties of Huáróng, Zhōulíng, and Jiānlì from Nán commandery,
separately established the new county of Fēngdū,
and set up the commandery of Chéngdū as the fief of the Prince of Chéngdū, Yǐng.
Chéng pretended to agree but then attacked and killed them,
using their wives and children as rewards,
and drowned over eight thousand people in the river;
the refugees became even more resentful and angry.
Subsequently, Shǔ men Dù Chóu and others rebelled again.
Xiāng Province Army Counselor Féng Sù had a grudge against the Shǔ man Rǔ Bān.
Rǔ,
is a surname.
In the Shāng dynasty there were Rǔ Jiū and Rǔ Fāng,
in Jìn there were Rǔ Kuān and Rǔ Qí.
"The Bā and Shǔ refugees all wish to rebel."
Tiào believed this,
and wanted to exterminate all the refugees.
The refugees were greatly frightened,
and forty to fifty thousand households rebelled simultaneously,
and because Dù Tāo was highly esteemed in their homeland,
they jointly elected him as their leader.
Tāo proclaimed himself Governor of Liáng and Yì Provinces, concurrently Governor of Xiāng Province.
5 Péi Shuò sought aid from the Prince of Lángyà, Ruì.
Ruì sent General Yángwēi Gān Zhuó and others to attack Zhōu Fù at Shòuchūn.
Fù's forces scattered,
and he fled to Xiàng.
The Examination of Discrepancies says: The Annals of Emperor Huái records:
"On the Wùyín day,
Ruì ordered Zhuó to attack Fù at Shòuchūn,
and Fù's forces scattered."
It is unknown whether this was the day he ordered Zhuó, or the day of the attack, or the day of the scattering,
therefore it is left blank.
Fù died of worry and indignation.
Què,
was the son of Téng.
6 The Governor of Yáng Province, Liú Táo, died.
The Prince of Lángyà, Ruì, again appointed the An Army Advisory Chief Clerk Wáng Dūn as Governor of Yáng Province,
and soon added to him the title of Commander-in-Chief of the Various Military Affairs of the Campaigns.
Last year Dūn fled to Jiànyè.
7 On the Gēngchén day,
the Prince of Píngyuán, Gàn, died.
8 In the second month,
Shí Lè attacked Xīncài,
and killed the Prince of Xīncài, Zhuāng, Què, at Nándùn;
he advanced and captured Xǔchāng,
killing General Píngdōng Wáng Kāng.
9 The Dí leaders Fú Chéng and Kuí Wén rebelled again.
Fú Chéng and others had submitted to Luó Shàng,
see scroll 85, the second year of Emperor Huì's Tài'ān era.
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu.
Jiànpíng Commandant Bào Zhòng was sent to suppress them.
Zhòng took the opportunity to kill Hán Sōng,
and took personal command of the affairs of the three prefectures.
10. Dōng Hǎi Xiàoxiàn Wáng Yuè (the Prince of Donghai, posthumously titled Xiaoxian) had already developed a rift with Xún Xī.
This matter began in the second year of the Yongjia era, as recorded in the previous volume.
Xún Xī was furious.
He submitted a memorial requesting the heads of Pān Tāo and others.
He publicly declared:
"Sīmǎ Yuánchāo, as Prime Minister, has been unjust.
(Dōng Hǎi Wáng Yuè,
courtesy name Yuánchāo.)
How can Xún Dàojiàng (Xún Xī's courtesy name) be made to serve such an unrighteous man!"
He then issued a proclamation to the various provinces,
boasting of his own merits,
and enumerating Yuè's crimes.
Emperor Huái also detested Yuè's monopolization of power
and his frequent violations of imperial decrees.
The officers and soldiers Yuè left behind, such as Hé Lún,
plundered the high officials and nobles,
and even insulted and coerced princesses.
The Emperor secretly bestowed a handwritten edict upon Xī,
ordering him to attack Yuè.
Xī frequently exchanged documents with the Emperor.
Yuè grew suspicious.
He sent out roaming cavalry to spy in the Chénggāo area.
They indeed captured Xī's messenger and the imperial edict.
Yuè then issued a proclamation denouncing Xī's crimes.
He appointed his Attendant Officer, Yáng Mào, as Governor of Yǎn Province,
and ordered him, together with Pèi Dùn, the Governor of Xú Province, to jointly attack Xī.
Xī sent cavalry to arrest Pān Tāo.
Tāo fled under cover of night
and escaped.
Xī arrested the Minister Liú Zēng and the Palace Attendant Chéng Yán,
and executed them.
Yuè, overwhelmed by worry and indignation, fell ill.
He entrusted his affairs to Wáng Yǎn.
In the third month,
on the day Bǐngzǐ,
he died at Xiàng.
Textual Analysis (Kǎo yì) states: The Emperor's Annals record:
"In the first month of the fifth year,
the Emperor secretly ordered Xún Xī to attack Yuè.
On the day Yǐwèi,
Yuè sent Yáng Mào and Pèi Dùn to jointly attack Xī.
In the third month,
on the day Wùwǔ,
an edict was issued listing Yuè's crimes,
ordering the regional commanders to attack him,
and appointing Xī as Grand General.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
Yuè died."
Xún Xī's biography states:
"Xī issued a proclamation to the various provinces,
enumerating Yuè's crimes.
The Emperor, detesting Yuè's monopolization of power,
then ordered Xī to issue a proclamation to six provinces,
coordinating a major campaign.
Xī sent the proclamation to the various commanders.
The Emperor again secretly ordered Xī to attack Yuè.
Xī again submitted a memorial stating that when Lǐ Chū arrived,
he received the handwritten edict,
rolled up his armor and advanced rapidly,
and encamped at Cāngyuán.
In the fifth year,
the Emperor again issued an edict to Xī,
listing Yuè's crimes.
On the day the edict arrived,
it was to be proclaimed to the world,
and he was to lead Qí in a major campaign.
Xī's memorial stated that
he immediately sent Wáng Zàn to lead troops to Xiàng.
Yuè sent cavalry who captured Xī's messenger in the Chénggāo area,
thus creating a major rift of suspicion."
The Jìn Chūnqiū states:
"In the fifth year,
first month,
the Emperor sent Lǐ Chū with an edict ordering Xī to attack Yuè."
Analysis: If Yuè had already captured Xī's messenger,
then the Emperor could not have felt secure either,
and Pān Tāo, Hé Lún, and others could not have remained peacefully in Luòyáng.
Moreover, before Tāo and the others left,
the Emperor would not have dared to openly state that he was ordering Xī to attack Yuè.
The years, months, and events
are so inconsistent and contradictory.
Now, I place them all at the time of Yuè's death,
hoping this is not incorrect.
The multitude jointly recommended Yǎn as commander-in-chief.
Yǎn did not dare accept.
He yielded the position to Xiāngyáng Wáng Fàn.
Fàn also did not accept.
Fàn
was the son of Sīmǎ Wěi.
Thereupon, Yǎn and others together escorted Yuè's funeral cortege back to Dōnghǎi for burial.
Hé Lún, Lǐ Yùn, and others, hearing of Yuè's death,
escorted Lady Péi and the heir apparent, Sīmǎ Pí, eastward from Luòyáng.
The gentry and commoners in the city vied to follow them.
The Emperor posthumously demoted Yuè to the rank of District Prince.
He appointed Xún Xī as Grand General and Grand Commander,
overseeing the military affairs of the six provinces: Qīng, Xú, Yǎn, Yù, Jīng, and Yáng.
11. The officers and officials of Yì Province together killed the violent Bào Zhòng.
They petitioned for Zhāng Luó, the Administrator of Bā Commandery, to act as head of the Three Offices.
Luó fought against Wěi Wén and others and died in battle.
Wén and others drove off and plundered the officials and people,
and surrendered west to Chéng (the state of Chéng Hàn).
The civil and military officials of the Three Offices jointly petitioned for Wáng Yì, the Pingxi Army Marshal of Shǔ Commandery, to act as head of the Three Offices.
The remnant troops of Yì Province were naturally insufficient to advance and conquer.
Before a year had passed, the commander had changed five times.
This merely provided the Qín and Dī tribes with the means for annexation.
12. Earlier,
the Governor of Liáng Province, Zhāng Guāng, assembled the various commandery administrators at Wèixīng,
to jointly plan an advance.
Zhāng Yàn advocated, saying:
"Hànzhōng is desolate and ruined,
and close to the great bandits.
The task of recovering it
should await a hero."
Guāng believed Yàn had accepted bribes from Dèng Dìng,
leading to the loss of Hànzhōng.
(This matter is seen in the first year of Yongjia in the previous volume.)
He berated him and expelled him,
then executed him.
He trained his troops and advanced to battle.
After several years, he finally reached Hànzhōng.
He pacified and comforted the desolate and ruined land,
and the common people were pleased and submitted.
(Zhāng Guāng becoming Governor of Liáng Province is seen in the second year in the previous volume.)
13. In summer,
the fourth month,
Shí Lè led light cavalry in pursuit of the funeral cortege of Grand Tutor Yuè.
He caught up with them at Níngpíng City in Kǔ County.
(Kǔ County
belonged to Chén Commandery.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: Níngpíng City was north of the Shā River.
Originally, it was Níngpíng County of the Huáiyáng Kingdom in the Former Hàn;
the Later Hàn changed Huáiyáng to the Kingdom of Chén.
The Jìn abolished Níngpíng County,
but the old city remained.
Lǐ Xián's commentary states: The old city of Níngpíng
is southwest of present-day Gǔyáng County in Bó Prefecture.)
(Cavalry,
pronunciation qí jì fān;
same below.)
He deployed his cavalry to surround them and shoot,
and the over 100,000 officers and soldiers trampled each other like a mountain,
not a single one escaped.
He captured Grand Commandant Yǎn, Xiāngyáng Wáng Fàn, Rènchéng Wáng Jì, Wǔlíng Zhuāng Wáng Dàn,
Xīhé Wáng Xǐ, Liánghuái Wáng Xǐ, Qí Wáng Chāo.
(Xīhé Wáng Xǐ
was a descendant of Xīhé Miù Wáng Bīn, younger brother of Emperor Xuān.
Chāo
was the son of Qí Wáng Jiǒng.)
He made them sit under a tent,
and questioned them about Jìn affairs.
Yǎn fully explained the origins of the disasters and defeats,
saying the plans were not his own;
and furthermore said of himself that from youth he had no desire for officialdom,
and did not involve himself in worldly affairs.
He then urged Lè to assume the imperial title,
hoping to save himself.
Lè said:
"You entered court in your prime,
your fame covered the four seas,
you held positions of great responsibility—
how can you say you had no desire for officialdom!
The one who destroyed the empire—
if not you, then who!"
He ordered his attendants to escort him out.
The others, fearing death,
mostly made statements about themselves.
Only Xiāngyáng Wáng Fàn maintained a stern and dignified expression.
Looking around, he rebuked them, saying:
"In today's situation,
why all this confusion!"
Lè said to Kǒng Cháng:
"I have traveled the world extensively,
but I have never seen people like these.
Should they be spared?"
(Lè wanted to spare them,
because of their dignified and clear appearance.)
"They are all princes and dukes of Jìn,
they will never serve us."
Lè said:
"Even so,
we still must not put them to the sword."
At night,
he had men push over a wall to kill them.
(Jì
was the son of Jǐng Wáng Líng, younger brother of Emperor Xuān's son.
Xǐ
was the son of Dàn.)
He split open Yuè's coffin,
burned his corpse,
and said:
"This man is the one who brought chaos to the empire.
I am avenging the empire on him,
therefore I burn his bones to inform Heaven and Earth."
Hé Lún and others arrived at Wěncāng.
According to the Shuǐjīng,
the Wěi River
flows southeast past Chángshè County in Yǐngchuān,
splits into a branch that flows east past Xǔchāng County,
and then enters east into the city of Wěncāng.
Common people consider this river to be the Wèn River,
hence the name Wěncāng.
It is likely a storage depot along the Wěi River.
They were defeated in battle.
The heir of the Prince of Dōnghǎi and forty-eight princes of the imperial clan all perished under Lè.
The Examination of Discrepancies states: The Biography of the Prince of Dōnghǎi, Yuè, says
"thirty-six princes."
Here we follow the Imperial Annals.
Lǐ Yùn fled to Guǎngzōng.
Péi was captured and sold by others.
After a long time,
he crossed the river.
Earlier,
when Lángyé Prince Ruì was stationed at Jiànyè,
it was Péi's idea,
so Ruì was grateful to him,
treating him generously and providing support,
and having his son Chōng succeed Yuè.
14 Hàn's Zhào Gù and Wáng Sāng attacked Péi Dùn,
killing him.
Dùn was in Péngchéng at the time.
Dùn,
pronounced as tú sǔn fān.
15 Dù Tāo attacked Chángshā.
In the fifth month,
Xún Tiào abandoned the city and fled to Guǎngzhōu,
but Tāo pursued and captured him.

An edict ordered Qū Yǔn to station at Huángbái City to resist them.
8 Shí Lè sent Shí Hǔ to attack Yè.
Yè fell,
and Liú Yǎn fled to Lǐnqiū.
Lǐnqiū County,
under the Former Hàn, belonged to Dōng Commandery,
under the Later Hàn, belonged to Jìyīn Commandery,
under the Jìn, belonged to the Principality of Púyáng.
Xián states: The old city of Lǐnqiū
is north of present-day Léizé County in Pú Prefecture.
Shí Lè appointed Táo Bào as the Administrator of Wèi Commandery to pacify the area;
after some time,
he replaced Táo Bào with Shí Hǔ to garrison Yè.
Initially,
Liú Kūn appointed the Administrator of Chénliú, Jiāo Qiú, as the Governor of Yǎn Province.
Xún Fān also appointed Lǐ Shù as the Governor of Yǎn Province.
Lǐ Shù wanted to attack Jiāo Qiú,
so Liú Kūn recalled Jiāo Qiú.
After the fall of Yè City,
Liú Kūn again appointed Liú Yǎn as the Governor of Yǎn Province,
to garrison Lǐnqiū.
The former Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Xī Jiàn,
was famous from a young age for his integrity and moral conduct.
He led over a thousand households from Gāopíng to seek refuge and defend themselves at Yì Mountain.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: Yì Mountain is north of Zōu County,
and the town of Yì derived its name from it.
The mountain stretches twenty lǐ from east to west,
lofty and prominent, standing alone,
with piled rocks leaning against each other,
almost without soil.
Among the rocks are many holes and caves,
interconnected and penetrating,
often with spaces as large as several rooms,
commonly called
"Zékǒng" by the locals.
When encountering turmoil,
people would take their families into Yì Mountain.
Though external bandits were numerous,
they could not inflict harm.
During the Yǒngjiā era of the Jìn dynasty,
Xī Jiàn defended this mountain.
Today, south of the mountain is a large peak,
named Zōu Gōng Yì,
as mentioned in the Shī,
"possessing Fú and Yì."
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu fān.
Shǎo,
pronounced shì zhào fān.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
Yì,
pronounced yì.
He garrisoned Zōu Mountain.
Zōu Mountain
is in Zōu County of Lǔ Commandery.
Examination of discrepancies: In the collected works of Liú Kūn,
on the first day of the eleventh month of the second year of Jiànxīng,
which was Rényín,
he wrote in a letter to the Chancellor:
"Although Jiāo Qiú comes from a humble background,
he has both civil and military courage and capability.
Xún Xī appointed him as the Administrator of Chénliú,
and he alone held the area south of the Yellow River against Shí Lè,
pacifying and comforting the people with skill.
I, Kūn, appointed Qiú to act as Governor of Yǎn Province.
Later, I heard that Lord Xún appointed Lǐ Shù as Governor of Yǎn Province.
Based on general reputation and family status,
Shù cannot be mentioned in the same breath as Qiú;
as for courage and capability in handling danger,
and temporary usefulness in critical situations,
Lǐ Shù also cannot match Qiú.
However, Wáng Xuán was young,
and wanted to join in attacking Qiú.
Since Qiú had already developed a rift with Xuán,
I recalled him.
But the people and affairs within the province
were very uneasy and did not submit to Shù;
the commandery governors and the great families, both civil and military,
repeatedly sent messengers requesting a governor,
so I sent my elder brother's son, Yǎn, to replace Qiú and take charge of Yǎn Province affairs.
In the spring of last year, in the first month,
I sent him to Yè,
and by then he had beheaded Wáng Sāng and driven away Zhào Gù"
and so on.
"Now Lè occupies Xiāngguó,
pressing close to Yè City,
so I ordered Yǎn to move south.
Yǎn's current seat of administration is at Lǐnqiū,
but both Lǐ Shù and Xī Jiàn desire to contend for Yǎn Province,
some say they are employed by Lord Xún,
some say they are employed by Your Excellency.
With the great bandits not yet eliminated, they engage in warfare among themselves,
this is also a great collapse.
I have ordered Yǎn to carefully defend himself and that is all."
Note: The defeats of Wáng Sāng and Zhào Gù, and Shí Lè's attack on Yè,
all occurred in the sixth year of Yǒngjiā.
Kūn's letter also says:
"According to news from Cháng'ān,
the sovereign is the Prince of Qín."
Also, the first day of the eleventh month of the second year of Jiànxīng was Bǐngshēn,
the first day of the eleventh month of the first year was Rénshēn,
the first day of the twelfth month was Rényín,
therefore, the day Kūn sent the letter
was the first day of the twelfth month of the first year of Jiànxīng, which was Rényín.
This is a transcription error.
The officials and people of Yǎn Province did not know whom to follow.
9 The Prince of Lángyá, Ruì, appointed the former Minister of the Interior of Lújiāng, Huà Tán, as Army Consultant.
Tán had previously been in Shòuchūn under Zhōu Fù.
Ruì said to Tán:
"Why did Zhōu Zǔxuān rebel?"
Zhōu Fù,
styled Zǔxuān.
"Although Zhōu Fù is dead,
there are still outspoken gentlemen in the world.
Fù saw that the bandits were spreading,
and wanted to move the capital to alleviate the national crisis.
The ruling authorities were displeased,
raised troops to attack him,
and not long after Fù's death, Luòdū fell.
To call that rebellion,
is that not a false accusation?"
The events are recorded in the previous scroll, in the fourth and fifth years of Yǒngjiā.
"Fù held the position of a regional commander,
commanding strong troops,
yet when summoned, he did not come,
and in times of danger, he did not lend support.
He is also a criminal of the world."
Tán said:
"Indeed,
in times of danger, not lending support,
he should share the blame with the whole world,
not just Fù alone."
Many of Ruì’s assistants and subordinates avoided their duties and indulged in leisure.
The Record Affairs Army Advisor Chén Yǔn
(Record Affairs Army Advisor,
responsible for overseeing all departments,
managing their documents,
and from the senior assistants downward,
rectifying violations and errors according to the law,
in charge of all matters of supervision and investigation)
The Bái Shì Liù Tiē states: The Prefectural Registrar and the Commandery Supervisor
are equivalent to the duties of the present-day Record Affairs Army Advisor.
In my judgment, Ruì appointed Yǔn as Record Affairs Army Advisor,
while there was a separate Registrar,
as detailed in the discussion of errors.
“When Luòyáng was at peace,
court officials considered caution and reverence as vulgar,
and arrogance and insolence as elegant.
This trend spread and influenced others,
ultimately leading to the ruin of the state.
Now, the subordinates all inherit the lingering malpractices from the Western Court,
(Jiāngdōng refers to Luòdū as the Western Court.)
This is like the cart ahead has overturned, yet the cart behind still follows its path.
I request that from now on,
those who claim illness when assigned duties
all be dismissed from office.”
Ruì did not comply.
When the Three Kings executed Zhào Wáng Lún,
(see the eighty-fourth volume, the first year of Emperor Huì’s Yǒngníng era.)
Jǐhài
Since then, this practice has been followed and applied.
Yǔn submitted a memorial stating:
“In the past, when Zhào Wáng usurped the throne,
and Emperor Huì lost his position,
the Three Kings raised troops to suppress him,
thus generous rewards were given to nurture the hearts of those inclined toward righteousness.
Now, regardless of the size of achievements,
all are judged by fixed regulations,
to the extent that gold and purple adorn soldiers,
and official tallies are entrusted to the gates of servants and slaves.
This is not the way to honor titles and instruments of authority,

Yǔn came from a humble and lowly background,

10 The Grand Administrator of Wúxīng, Zhōu,
had a powerful and influential clan,
and Lángyé Wáng Ruì was quite suspicious and fearful of him.
Many of Ruì’s close associates in power
were officials from Zhōngzhōu who had lost their positions and responsibilities,
and they governed the people of Wú,
causing much resentment among them.
Zhōu felt he had lost his rightful position,
and was also looked down upon by Diāo Xié,
which deepened his shame and anger.
He secretly conspired with his associates to eliminate those in power,
and replace them with southern scholars.
The plot was exposed,
and he died of worry and indignation.
Before his death,
he said to his son, Xié:
“Those who killed me
are the northern bumpkins;
if you can avenge me,
then you are truly my son.”
11 Shí Lè attacked Lǐ Yùn at Shàngbái,
and executed him.
Wáng Jùn again appointed Bó Shèng as the Inspector of Qīng Province.
Shàngbái City
was located in Guǎngzōng County, Ānpíng.
Lǐ Yùn and Bó Shèng were both leaders of the Qǐhuó.
Fù
is pronounced fú yòu fān.
12 Wáng Jùn ordered Zǎo Sōng to command the armies and station them at the Yìshuǐ,
and summoned Duàn Jílùjuàn,
intending to join forces with him to attack Shí Lè.
However, Jílùjuàn did not come.

Jùn sent generous gifts to Tuòbá Yīlú,
and also issued a call to Mùróng Huī and others to jointly attack Jílùjuàn.
Yīlú sent the Right Worthy King Liùxiū to lead troops to join them,

Huī sent Mùróng Hàn to attack the Duàn clan,
capturing Túhé and Xīnchéng,
and advancing to Yánglè.
Yánglè County
belonged to Liáoxī Commandery.
Xián states: Yánglè
is located east of present-day Píng Province.
Hàn then remained to garrison Túhé,
fortifying at Qīngshān.
Initially,
many scholars and commoners from Zhōngguó fleeing the chaos
sought refuge with Wáng Jùn in the north.
However, Jùn was unable to provide for and comfort them,
and his governance lacked established laws,
so the scholars and commoners often left him.
The Duàn brothers focused solely on martial prowess,
and did not treat scholars with respect.
Only Mùróng Huī governed with clarity and order,
cherishing and valuing talented individuals,
so many scholars and commoners turned to him.
Huī promoted the outstanding and talented among them,
assigning positions according to their abilities.
He appointed Péi Yí from Hédōng,
Yáng Dān from Běipíng, Huáng Hóng from Lújiāng,
and Lǔ Chāng from Dài Commandery as his chief strategists.
Yóu Suì from Guǎngpíng, Péng Xiàn from Běihǎi,
Xīfāng Qián from Běipíng,
(The Hé Shì Xìng Yuàn states: Shǎohào, the Jīntiān clan,

Sòng Gāi from Píngyuán, Huángfǔ Jí from Āndìng, his younger brother Zhēn, Miào Kǎi from Lánlíng,
and Liú Bīn from Chānglí, along with Fēng Yì and Fēng Yù, managed critical affairs.
Yù
was the son of Chōu.
Pei Yi was upright and capable,
serving as the Administrator of Chānglí.
His elder brother, Pei Wu, was the Administrator of Xuāntù.
When Pei Wu died,
Pei Yi and Pei Wu's son, Pei Kai, brought his coffin back.
They passed by Mùhún Wěi.
They were traveling west from Xuāntù to return home,
and their route passed through Jíchéng.
Tù,
pronounced the same as Dū.
When they were about to leave,
(Mùhún Wěi) provided them with generous provisions and gifts for the journey.
They traveled as far as Liáoxī,
but the road was impassable.
Pei Yi wanted to turn back and join Mùhún Wěi.
Pei Kai said:
"Our hometown is to the south.
Why are we heading north?
Moreover, since we are both displaced persons,
the Duàn clan is strong,
while the Mùróng clan is weak.
Why must we leave here to join them?"
Pei Yi said:
"The Central Plains is in chaos and turmoil.
If we go there now,
it would be like leading each other into the tiger's mouth.
Furthermore, the journey is long,
how could we possibly get through?
This means that Chānglí is far from Hédōng,
and the roads are blocked,
making it impossible to get through.
Nor can we hope to get there in a matter of months or years.
This means that the world is in chaos,
and there is no time when the roads will be clear and passable.
How can we not carefully choose whom to follow?
Look at the various Duàn clan members.
Do they have any grand vision?
Moreover, can they treat men of talent as guests of the state?
Lord Mùróng cultivates virtue and practices benevolence and righteousness.
He has the ambition of a hegemon or king.
Furthermore, his state is prosperous and his people are at peace.
If we go to follow him now,
at best we can achieve merit and fame,
at worst we can protect our clan.
Why are you hesitant?"
Pei Kai then followed him.
After they arrived,
Mùhún Wěi was greatly pleased.
Yáng Dān was upright, honest, deep, and astute.
He served as the Administrator of Liáoxī.
Mùróng Hàn defeated the Duàn clan at Yánglè,
captured him,
and Mùhún Wěi treated him with courtesy and employed him.
Yóu Suì, Péng Xiàn, and Sòng Shì

Together with Huáng Hóng, they all sought refuge in Jì to avoid the turmoil,

Wáng Jùn repeatedly summoned Yóu Suì's elder brother, Yóu Chàng, with handwritten letters.
Yóu Chàng wanted to go,
but Yóu Suì said:
"Péngzǔ (Wáng Jùn) does not maintain proper punishments and administration.
Both the Huá and the Róng peoples are turning against him and rebelling.
In my estimation,
he certainly cannot last long.
Elder brother, you should wait and bide your time."
The hexagram statement for the first line (initial nine) of the Zhūn hexagram in the Yì (Book of Changes) says: Hesitant and cautious,
it is beneficial to abide in steadfastness.
Wáng Bì said: One cannot advance,
hence hesitant and cautious.
Mǎ (Róng) said: Hesitant and cautious,
means to circle around.
Dù (estimate),
pronounced Tuòluò.
"Péngzǔ is cruel and suspicious.

Yóu Suì followed his advice,

Sòng Gāi, along with Dù Qí from Píngyuán and Liú Xiáng, first relied on Wáng Jùn,

There is an old saying: The bird chooses the tree,

Shuài (lead),

Shuō (persuade),

(Gāogōulì) attacked the king of Gāogōulì, Yǐfúlì,

When subordinates are greedy,

Zhì (make/manage),
pronounced Zhízhī.
Jìn Miǎo led troops to attack Lǐ Yùn and Wáng Jiàn,

Shǎn,

whales and giant fish,

Liú Wěi was well-versed in literature and history,
