could it be the ancient Xúnyáng City?
Táo Kǎn sent General of Míngwēi Zhū Sì to rescue him,
and Tāo retreated to hold Lěngkǒu.
Shěn Yuē's Records state: Wèi established forty titles for generals,
with Míngwēi being the third.
Tāo,
is pronounced tāo.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Lěng River flows south from Mount Jiǔyí,
northward passing southwest of Lěngdào County,
then flows north into the Dūxī River,
then northwest into the Yíng River,
which is the so-called Lěngkǒu.
Yáng Zhènghéng said: Lěng
is pronounced lěng.
Upon my examination, this Lěngkǒu is very far from Wǔchāng.
Also, according to the Commentary on the Water Classic,
the river flows south of the old city of Qíchūn,
then east to Tónglíngkǒu.
Could this be it?
"Tāo will certainly march towards Wǔchāng."
So he took a shortcut back to the commandery to await him,
the shortcut
being a direct route.
Kǎn sent Zhū Sì to intercept and attack,
defeating him soundly.
Tāo fled back to Chángshā.
Zhōu Yǐ left Xúnshuǐ and went to Wáng Dūn at Yùzhāng.
Dūn detained him.
Táo Kǎn sent his Army Advisor Wáng Gòng to report the victory to Dūn.
Dūn said:
"If not for Marquis Táo,
we would have lost Jīngzhōu!"
He then recommended Kǎn as Governor of Jīngzhōu,
garrisoning at Miǎnjiāng.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Dùn River receives water from Bái Lake in Miǎnyáng,
flows southeast,
passes south of Miǎnyáng County and empties into the river,
called Dùnkǒu.
Lù Yóu said: Jiànníng Town in Jiānglíng
is probably Dùnkǒu.
Wáng Dūn appointed Táo Kǎn to Jīngzhōu,
garrisoning here.
The next year he moved to Línzhàng.
Kǎn's biography states: Initially garrisoned at Dùnkǒu,
then moved into Miǎnjiāng.
According to the Commentary on the Water Classic,
the old city of Línzhàng
was south of the Miǎn River.
Miǎnjiāng
refers to Línzhàng.
He was reappointed as Army Consultant.
21. Initially,
the Di chieftain Yáng Màosōu’s son Nándí
sent his adopted son to trade in Liángzhōu,
where he privately sold a child of a good family.
Zhāng Guāng had him flogged to death.
Nándí resented this, saying:
“When the Governor first arrived,
in the aftermath of a great famine,
the lives of the soldiers and people depended on us Di for survival.
Yet for a minor offense by a Di,
he could not grant pardon.”
When Zhāng Guāng and Yáng Hǔ attacked each other,
each sought aid from Màosōu.
Màosōu sent Nándí to rescue Guāng.
Nándí requested goods from Guāng,
but Guāng refused.
Yáng Hǔ richly bribed Nándí,
and moreover said:
“The precious goods of the displaced people
are all in Guāng’s possession,
meaning those seized and killed by Jìn Miǎo.
It would be better to attack Guāng.”
Nándí was greatly pleased.
When Guāng fought Hǔ,
he placed Zhāng Mèngcháng in the front,
with Nándí following behind.
Nándí and Hǔ attacked Mèngcháng from both sides,
crushing him utterly.
Mèngcháng and his younger brother Yuán both died.
Guāng barricaded himself in the city to defend it.
In the ninth month,
Guāng, enraged and agitated, fell ill.
His subordinates urged Guāng to retreat and hold Wèixīng.
Guāng pressed his hand to his sword and said:
“I have received a heavy responsibility from the state;
unable to punish the rebels,
now to die is like ascending to immortality.
How can one speak of retreat!”
As his voice ceased, he died.
Although Zhāng Guāng brought about the enemy invasion by trusting Jìn Miǎo,
his righteous fervor is also worthy of esteem.
Moreover, he died in battle against the Di.
The multitude recommended the Tàishǒu of Shǐpíng, Hú Zǐxù, to administer Liángzhōu.
22. Xún Fān died in Kāifēng.
Xún Fān and Fù Zhī died one after the other;
of the two traveling offices east of Shǎn,
only Xún Zǔ remained.
Textual analysis states: The Imperial Annals say
“died in Xíngyáng.”
Here we follow the biography of Fān.
23. The Hàn Zhōngshān Prince Liú Yào and Zhào Rǎn attacked Qū Yǔn at Huángbái City.
Yǔn was repeatedly defeated in battle;
an edict appointed Suǒ Lín as General-in-Chief Who Conquers the East,
to lead troops to aid Yǔn.
24. Wáng Gòng returned from Wáng Dūn’s place,
reached Jìnglíng,
and forged an order in Táo Kǎn’s name,
appointing Dù Zēng as Vanguard Commander-in-Chief,
to attack Wáng Chōng.
He beheaded him,
and all his followers surrendered.
Kǎn summoned Zēng,
but Zēng did not come.
Gòng, fearing punishment for forging the order,
then joined Zēng in counterattacking Kǎn.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Kǎn’s troops were badly defeated,
and he barely escaped with his life.
Dūn memorialized that Kǎn should serve without official rank.
Kǎn again led Zhōu Fǎng and others to advance and attack Dù Tāo,
crushing him utterly.
Dūn then petitioned to restore Kǎn’s office.
25. The Hàn Zhào Rǎn said to the Zhōngshān Prince Liú Yào:
“Qū Yǔn leads a large force outside;
Cháng’ān is empty.
It can be raided.”
Yào sent Rǎn to lead five thousand elite cavalry to raid Cháng’ān.
On the night of Gēngyín,
they entered the outer city.
The Emperor fled to the Shooting Wild Geese Tower.
Rǎn burned the Dragon’s Tail and various camps.
The Dragon’s Tail refers to
a road built along the city wall,
sloping and gradually rising higher,
the path used to ascend the battlements.
Also, the Water Classic says: In the Qín era, a black dragon
emerged from the Southern Mountains,
drank from the Wèi River,
and its path along the mountains left traces
over sixty lǐ long,
its head facing the Wèi River,
its tail reaching Fánchuān.
Hàn’s Xiāo Hé built the Wèiyāng Palace,
cutting into the Dragon’s Head Mountain to construct it.
The head was twenty zhàng high,
the tail gradually descending,
five or six zhàng high.
What is called the Dragon’s Tail
is the tail of this mountain.
At dawn on Xīnmǎo,
they withdrew and camped at Xiāoyáo Garden.
Commentary on the Water Classic: The Shěn River
receives water from the Huángzǐ Slope in Fánchuān upstream,
flows north past the west of Cháng’ān City,
and merges with the water of Kūnmíng Pond.
The Shěn River then flows northeast,
passes south of Dèng Ài’s Shrine,
and then divides east into two branches.
One branch flows east into Xiāoyáo Garden.
On Rénchén,
General Qū Jiàn led five thousand troops from Ā City to rescue Cháng’ān.
Ā City
was the Qín Epāng Palace city.
On Guǐsì,
Rǎn withdrew,
Jiàn pursued him,
and encountered Yào at Língwǔ.
Jiàn’s troops were badly defeated.
The Former Hàn Běidì Commandery had a Língwǔ County,
abolished in Later Hàn and Jìn;
by Later Wèi, Xiányáng Commandery was established,
with Chíyáng and Língwǔ counties both belonging to it.
Huángbái City is in Chíyáng.
Thus, this Língwǔ is clearly the Língwǔ of the Former Hàn Běidì Commandery and Wèi’s Xiányáng Commandery.
26. Yáng Hǔ and Yáng Nándí urgently attacked Liángzhōu.
Hú Zǐxù abandoned the city and fled.
Nándí proclaimed himself Cìshǐ.
27. The Hàn Zhōngshān Prince Liú Yào, relying on victory, made no preparations.
In the eleventh month,
Qū Yǔn led troops to raid him.
The Hàn troops were badly defeated,
and their Champion General Qiáo Zhìmíng was killed.
Yào withdrew and returned to Píngyáng.
28. Wáng Jùn, because his father’s courtesy name was Chùdào,
believed himself to correspond to
“the tall one at the road’s side”
prophecy,
and plotted to claim imperial title.
Wáng Jùn
was another Yuán Shù.
The Sīkōng’s assistant Gāo Róu earnestly remonstrated,
but Jùn killed them all.
Huò Yuán of Yānguó,
of pure and lofty will and integrity,
repeatedly declined summons to office.
Jùn asked him about claiming imperial title.
Yuán did not reply.
Jùn falsely accused Yuán of colluding with bandits,
killed him, and displayed his head.
Thereupon, scholars and commoners were shocked and resentful.
Yet Jùn grew increasingly arrogant and extravagant,
not attending to governance,
employing only harsh and petty men.
Zǎo Sōng and Zhū Shuò
were especially greedy and tyrannical.
In the northern provinces, a ballad said:
“In the office, awe-inspiring,
is Zhū Qiūbó;
ten bags, five bags,
go to Zǎo Láng.”
Zhū Qiūbó
is Zhū Shuò’s courtesy name.
Sōng was Jùn’s son-in-law,
hence called Zǎo Láng.
Those below could not endure his rule,
and many fled to join the Xiānbēi.
The clerk Hán Xián oversaw Liǔchéng.
Liǔchéng County
belonged to Liáoxī Commandery in Former Hàn,
abolished in Later Hàn and Jìn.
Oversee:
read as jiān.
He wished to admonish Jùn by this;
Jùn grew angry
and killed him.
Initially, Jùn relied solely on the Xiānbēi and Wūhuán to build his strength,
but eventually they all rebelled against him.
Additionally, locust plagues and droughts occurred year after year,
causing his military power to grow even weaker.
Shí Lè intended to launch a surprise attack against him,
but not knowing the actual situation,
he planned to send an envoy to spy on him.
His advisors suggested following the precedent set by Yáng Hù and Lù Kàng,
by sending a letter to Jùn,
intending to use the etiquette of neighboring states.
Bīn said:
"Jùn is nominally a minister of Jìn,
but in reality, he desires to overthrow Jìn and establish himself,
only worrying that heroes across the land will not follow him.
His desire to win over you, General,
is akin to Xiàng Yǔ's desire to win over Hán Xìn.
Your prestige shakes the world, General.
Now, if you use humble words and lavish gifts,
lowering yourself to serve him,
you would still fear he might not trust you,
let alone acting as an equal rival like Yáng and Lù!
To scheme against someone while letting them perceive your intentions
makes it difficult to achieve your aims."
Lè said:
"Well said!"
In the twelfth month,
Lè sent his attendants Wáng Zǐchūn and Dǒng Zhào with abundant treasures,
presenting a memorial to Jùn, saying:
"Lè is but a humble man from a minor tribe,
who encountered famine and chaos in these times,
drifting in hardship and peril,
fleeing to Jìzhōu,
where I secretly gathered people for mutual protection to save our lives.
Now the Jìn dynasty's mandate has declined,
and the Central Plains lack a ruler.
Your Highness is of noble reputation in our home region—
Lè
is from Wǔxiāng in Shàngdǎng,
while Jùn is from Tàiyuán,
hence 'home region.'
As for who should be emperor,
if not you, then who?
The reason Lè has risked his life to raise an army,
to punish the violent and chaotic,
is precisely to clear the way for Your Highness.
I humbly wish Your
Highness
to ascend the imperial throne early.
Lè will revere and support Your Highness as heaven, earth, and parents.
If Your Highness discerns Lè's humble heart,
you should also regard me as a son."
He also sent a letter to Zǎo Sōng,
bribing him heavily.
Jùn, because Duàn Jílùjuàn had recently rebelled,
and many soldiers and civilians had abandoned him,
was very pleased
to hear that Lè wished to submit to him.
He said to Zǐchūn:
"Lord Shí is a hero of the age,
holding Zhào and Wèi,
yet he wishes to pledge allegiance to me.
Can this be trusted?"
Zǐchūn said:
"General Shí's talent and strength are formidable,
truly as Your Majesty says.
However, given Your Highness's noble reputation in the Central Plains,
with prestige extending to both barbarians and Huáxià,
since ancient times, there have been Hú people who served as famous ministers and assistants,
but none who became emperor.
It is not that General Shí dislikes being emperor and thus yields to Your Highness,
but rather he recognizes that the imperial throne follows its own predetermined course,
not something obtainable by intellect or strength.
Even if seized by force,
it would surely not be endorsed by heaven and men.
Though Xiàng Yǔ was strong,
he ultimately fell to Hàn.
Comparing General Shí to Your Highness
is like comparing the moon to the sun.
Therefore, looking at past events from afar,
he submits to Your Highness.
This is precisely why General Shí's foresight far surpasses that of others.
Why should Your Highness find it strange?"
Jùn was greatly delighted,
enfeoffing Zǐchūn and Zhào as marquises,
sending an envoy to return the courtesy,
and repaying them with generous gifts.
Yóu Lún's elder brother, Yóu Tǒng,
served as Jùn's military commander,
stationed at Fànyáng.
He sent an envoy to secretly submit to Lè.
Yóu Lún held Yuànxiāng,
pretending to surrender to Lè,
but Lè had already launched a surprise attack and captured him.
Although Jùn did not punish Tǒng,
he grew even more convinced of Lè's loyalty,
with no further suspicions.
In this year,
the Left Chancellor Ruì sent his heir, Shào, to guard Guǎnglíng,
appointing the Chancellor's assistant Cài Mó as a military advisor.
Mó
was the son of Kè.
The Hàn Zhōngshān King Yào besieged the Hénán Governor Wèi Jùn at Shíliáng,
the Shíliáng stronghold,
located north of the Luò River.
Yào divided his forces to engage in battle north of the river,
defeating him.
Héběi
[north]
north of the great river,
that is, north of the Fùpíng Crossing.
Defeated,
Bǔ Mài fān.
Jùn fled at night,
but was captured and killed.
The 31st ruler, Gōng Yīlú, established Shènglè as the northern capital,
governing the old Píngchéng as the southern capital;
he also built New Píngchéng on the northern bank of Lěi Shuǐ,
and had the Right Virtuous King, Liù Xiū, stationed there,
commanding the southern region.
Shènglè County,
during the Former Hàn, belonged to Dìngxiāng Commandery,
and during the Later Hàn, it belonged to Yúnzhōng Commandery.
Píngchéng,
during the Hàn, belonged to Yànmén Commandery.
The Geographical Treatise states: Shuòzhōu in Dìngxiāng County,
was originally Hàn's Píngchéng County.
During the flourishing period of the Tuòbá Wèi,
Shuòzhōu was established at Shènglè,
and Héngzhōu at Píngchéng;
Píngchéng,
was called Dài Capital.
Since the founding ancestor relocated to Luò,
thereafter, Pòlìu-Hánbá Líng rebelled,
and the old capital became ruins.
Héngzhōu temporarily administered from Sìzhōu Xiùróng Commandery,
and Yúnzhōu temporarily administered within the Bìngzhōu boundary.
In Wèi Shòu's Geographical Records,
north of the Xínglǐng,
the records are rather brief.
During the flourishing era of the Suí,
they expelled the Tūjué to the north,
restored the former Hàn Great Wall,
and consolidated and merged the commanderies and counties established by the Later Wèi.
Shènglè was likely within the boundary of Dàlì County in Dìngxiāng Commandery,
and Píngchéng was within the boundary of Yúnnèi County in Mǎyì Commandery.
The Táng defeated the Tūjué,
and extended their reach to what Wèi and Suí once controlled: Shuòzhōu's Shànyáng County,
was the land of Hàn's Dìngxiāng and Wèi's Sāngqián;
Chányú Protectorate’s Jīnhé County,
was where the Later Wèi Dàowǔ had his capital;
Yúnzhōu's Yúnzhōng County,
was where the Later Wèi had Píngchéng as their capital.
However, from the Chányú Protectorate northeast to Shuòzhōu is three hundred fifty-seven lǐ,
and thus the distance from Shènglè to Píngchéng
can be understood from the road and distance.
Dù Yòu said: Yúnzhōng,
is now north of Mǎyì Commandery;
Píngchéng,
is today’s commandery,
at Suí's Yúnnèi County Héng'ān Town.
In the Wèi Shū's Imperial Records: Yīlú repaired old Píngchéng as the southern capital,
moving a hundred lǐ south,
and built New Píngchéng on the northern bank of Lěi Shuǐ at Huángguāduī,
which the Jìn people called Little Píngchéng.
Dù Yòu also said: Shuòzhōu’s Mǎyì Commandery,
Wèi's Píngchéng capital,
placed Huáishuò Town north of the commandery;
after relocating to Luò,
Shuòzhōu was established.
In the early Later Wèi,
Yúnzhōng was north of today's commandery over three hundred lǐ from Dìngxiāng Old City;
during Northern Qí, Shuòzhōu was established,
southwest of the old capital’s new city,
also known as Píngchéng;
later moved to Mǎyì,
which is today's commandery city.
The commandery governed Shànyáng County,
which was also the land of Hàn’s Dìngxiāng County,
with Qín’s Mǎyì City, and Wǔzhōu’s border fortress;
the Zǐ River originates here.
Sòng Bái said: The Táng Zhènwǔ Army,
was the old Chányú Protectorate,
which was Hàn’s Shènglè County in Dìngxiāng Commandery,
located on the north side of Yīn Mountain,
north of the Yellow River,
was the Shènglè of the Later Wèi capital.
After Táng pacified the Tūjué,
they established Yúnzhōng Commander Center,
which was later changed to Chányú Prefecture.
Bān Gù's Geographical Records: Right Nànpíng County, Jùnmǐ County,
Lěi Shuǐ flows south to Wúzhōng,
and enters its eastern side.
Shīgǔ said: Lěi,
pronounced as "Force Water";
also turned to "Láng Huì."
Lì Dàoyuán's Water Classic Commentary: Gēng Shuǐ joins with Bàoqiū Shuǐ,
Jùnmǐ is in the east,
far from Píngchéng,
and New Píngchéng is not on the northern bank of this Lěi Shuǐ.
According to the Wèi Shū,
Emperor Dàowǔ traveled west to Mǎyì,
to observe Lěi Shuǐ's source;
thus, Lěi Shuǐ originates from Mǎyì,
flowing northeast past the south of Píngchéng.
Lì Dàoyuán,
a person of Wèi,
his Water Classic Commentary,
should have detailed accounts of Dài Capital;
initially did not mention Píngchéng having Lěi Shuǐ,
only mentioning Shī Shuǐ passing south of Píngchéng.
Annotated: Shī Shuǐ,
originates from Gànmén Yīnguǎn County’s Shītóu Mountain,
also known as Zhì Shuǐ,
flows northeast,
out of the mountain,
passing west of Yīnguǎn County’s old city,
which was Lóufán Village.
There is also Mǎyì River Valley,
which joins Sāngqián Shuǐ and flows into Shī Shuǐ.
Shī Shuǐ flows east passing south of Píngchéng,
continues east past Guǎngníng’s Xiàluò County south,
east to Yúyáng,
entering Sì Gully.
Also examined Bān Gù's Geographical Records,
Gànmén Yīnguǎn County’s Lóufán Village’s Lěitóu Mountain,
source of Zhì Shuǐ,
flows east to Quánzhōu entering the sea.
Shīgǔ said: Lěi,
pronounced "Force" following the pronunciation of “-lèi”;
Zhì,
pronounced "Yízhī."
I suspect at the time the water originating from Lěitóu Mountain,
also had the name of Lěi water.
Shīgǔ sound followed the flat tone,
sound closely related.
It indicates that what Dàoyuán meant by Shī Shuǐ,
was Lěi Shuǐ.
Further examined Dīngdù's collection rhyme,
"Tà"
"Lěi"
"Sà"
these three characters,
annotate the same as
"Water from Gànmén,"
also possibly cited here.
Lěi,
in Lèi Piān pronounced "Lǔ Water."
Hé Zīquán Biaodiǎn Róng Zhàozǔ Niè Chōngqí Revisions
Sīmǎ Guāng
Commissioned to Edit
Later,
Xiàomǐn Emperor's Reign
Jiànxīng Second Year
(Jiǎxū, 314)
1 Spring,
First month,
Xīnwèi,
a phenomenon like the sun falling to the ground occurred;
then three suns appeared in succession,
emerging from the west and moving east.
Astronomical observation reads: On the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth day,
they appear together and contend,
leading to warfare under heaven;
it also says: When three suns appear simultaneously,
within three ten-day periods,
the feudal lords will vie for the empire.
2 Dīngchǒu,
a general amnesty was declared.
3 A meteor appeared at Colonel,
entering the Purple Enclosure,
as noted in Jìn Astronomical Records,
the six stars of Colonel,
are south of River Drum.
It fell north of Píngyáng,
transforming into flesh,
measuring thirty paces long,
and twenty-seven paces wide.
Hàn Lord Cōng was disturbed by it,
and asked his ministers.
Chén Yuándá considered it
"a sign of excessive female favor,
an omen of state downfall."
Examination of differences says: In historical records,
Yuándá and others said: "Minister fears an occurrence of three queens in the rear palace."
According to the establishment of three queens,
it was in the following year,
not yet at this time.
"It is the principle of yin and yang,
unrelated to human affairs!"
Cōng's Empress Liú was wise and virtuous,
though Cōng committed actions contrary to the way,
Liú frequently corrected him.
Jǐchǒu,
Lady Liú passed away,
posthumously titled Wǔxuān.
From then on, favored consorts competed for attention,
and the order in the rear palace was disrupted.
4 He established the positions of the Chancellor and the other six Dukes;
the seven Dukes are listed below,
ranging from Jìn Wáng Càn to Zhōngshān Wáng Yào.
The Grand Generals such as Fǔ Hàn, Dū Hù, Zhōng Jūn, Shàng Jūn, Fǔ Jūn, Zhèn, Wèi, Jīng, Qián, Hòu, Zuǒ, Yòu, Shàng, Xià Jūn, Fǔ Guó, Guàn Jūn, Lóng Xiāng, Hǔ Yá, etc.
These were filled by his sons;
he also established the Left and Right Sīlì,
each overseeing more than 200,000 households,
with one Nèishǐ appointed per 10,000 households;
the Shànyú's Left and Right Assistants,
each in charge of 100,000 settlements of the Six Yí tribes,
the Six Yí,
namely the Hú, Jié, Xiānbēi, Dī, Qiāng, and Bā Mán;
some say the Wūwán,
not the Bā Mán.
Shàn,
pronounced chán.
The Left and Right Xuǎn Cáo Shàngshū,
both in charge of official selection.
From the Sīlì downwards, these six offices,
all ranked just below the Púyè.
He appointed his son Càn as Chancellor, concurrently holding the title of Grand General, and Lù Shàngshū Shì,
and promoted him to the rank of Jìn Wáng.
Jiāngdū Wáng Yánnián was appointed Lù Shàngshū Liù Tiáo Shì,
the first appearance of this title.
Shěn Yuē's records state: During the reign of Jìn Kāngdì,
Hé Chòng's petition to decline the Lù position said:
"During the Xiánkāng period,
three Lù positions were established,
Wáng Dǎo held one,
Xún Sōng and Lù Yè each held Liù Tiáo Shì."
Then it seems there were twenty-four tiáo;
if there were only twelve tiáo,
then Xún and Lù each held six tiáo,
what did Dǎo oversee?
If Dǎo oversaw everything,
and Xún and Lù divided the responsibilities,
then it cannot be said that Dǎo held one.
Later, whenever two Lù were appointed,
it was said they each held Liù Tiáo Shì,
again suggesting there were only twelve tiáo;
these twelve tiáo,
it is unknown what they all were.
In the Jiangyou period, Zhāng Huá,
in the Jiangzuo period, Yǔ Liàng,
both were involved with the Shàngshū Qī Tiáo,
but it is also unknown what these matters were.
I note: After the Yuánjiā period of the Sòng dynasty,
Jiāngxià Wáng Yìgōng, Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn, Nánqiáo Wáng Yìxuān all held the title Lù Shàngshū Liù Tiáo Shì.
The Shěn clan served for generations in Jiangzuo,
holding high and prominent positions,
yet they did not know what these matters were,
how can later generations find evidence!
Dù Yòu said: Hé Chòng's petition to decline the Lù position stated:
"During the Xiánkāng period,
three Lù positions were established,
Wáng Dǎo held one,
Xún Sōng and Lù Yè each held Èr Tiáo Shì."
After the Jìn crossed the river,
there were the Shàngshū of Lìbù, Cíbù, Zuǒmín, Wǔbīng, and Dùzhī,
making five tiáo.
At the beginning of Jìn, there were six Cáo: Lìbù, Sāngōng, Kè Cáo, Jiàbù, Túntián, and Dùzhī,
during Tàikāng there were six Cáo: Lìbù, Diànzhōng, Wǔbīng, Tián Cáo, Dùzhī, and Zuǒmín,
likely the six tiáo.
According to Dù Yòu's words,
then the six tiáo likely refer to the six Cáo.
Shěn Yuē mistook Hé Chòng's petition
"each held Èr Tiáo"
as
"each held Liù Tiáo",
leading to this error.
Wáng Yù was appointed Tàifù,
Rèn Yǐ as Tàibǎo,
Mǎ Jǐng as Dà Sītú,
Zhū Jì as Dà Sīkōng,
Zhōngshān Wáng Yào as Dà Sīmǎ.
5 On Rénchén,
Wáng Zǐchūn and others, along with Wáng Jùn's envoy, arrived at Xiāngguó.
Shí Lè concealed his elite troops and finest armor,
displaying only weak soldiers and empty storehouses to them,
and facing north, he bowed to the envoy and received the letter.
Jùn sent Lè a zhǔwěi,
Lè pretended not to dare hold it,
hung it on the wall,
and bowed to it morning and evening,
saying:
"I cannot see Lord Wáng,
but seeing what he bestowed,
is like seeing the lord himself."
He also sent Dǒng Zhào to present a memorial to Jùn,
promising to personally go to Yōuzhōu in mid-March to offer him the imperial title;
he also sent a letter to Zǎo Sōng,
requesting the positions of Bìngzhōu Mù and Guǎngpíng Gōng.
Lè inquired about Jùn's governance from Wáng Zǐchūn,
Zǐchūn said:
"Last year, Yōuzhōu suffered a great flood,
people had no grain to eat,
the five grains did not ripen,
hence no grain to eat.
He could not provide relief,
his punishments and administration were harsh and cruel,
taxes and labor services were heavy and numerous,
loyal and worthy men were alienated internally,
the Yí and Dí tribes rebelled externally.
Everyone knows he is about to fall,
yet Jùn remains self-assured and composed,
without any fear,
and instead establishes more government offices,
appoints numerous officials,
considering himself superior even to Hàn Gāozǔ and Wèi Wǔdì."
Lè patted the table and laughed, saying:
"Wáng Péngzǔ can truly be captured."
Jùn's envoy returned to Jì,
and reported in detail
"Shí Lè's situation is weak with few troops,
and his sincerity is unwavering."
Jùn was greatly pleased,
becoming even more arrogant and negligent,
and made no further preparations.
6 Yáng Hǔ plundered officials and people of Hànzhōng and fled to Chéng,
and people of Liángzhōu, such as Zhāng Xián, raised troops to drive out Yáng Nándí.
Yáng Hǔ and Yáng Nándí attacked Hànzhōng,
the matter began in the previous volume, last year.
Xián submitted that territory to Chéng,
thus the lands of Hànjiā, Fúlíng, and Hànzhōng
Hànjiā,
originally the Qīngyī county of the Former Hàn,
belonging to Shǔ commandery,
in the second year of Yángjiā of Hàn Shùndì's reign, it was renamed Hànjiā,
and Shǔ established the separate Hànjiā commandery.
The Chéng ruler Lǐ Xióng appointed Lǐ Fèng as Liángzhōu Cìshǐ,
Rèn Huí as Níngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and Lǐ Gōng as Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Xióng was humble and fond of the worthy,
appointing people according to their talents,
ordering the Tàifù Lǐ Xiāng to nurture the people internally,
while Lǐ Fèng and others attracted and pacified externally,
his punishments and administration were lenient and simple,
and there were no prisoners left languishing in jail.
He promoted schools,
and established official historians.
As for taxes,
each adult male paid three hú of grain annually,
adult females half that,
and the sick again half of that;
household silk tax did not exceed several zhàng,
and silk floss several liǎng.
Affairs were few and labor services sparse,
the people were mostly wealthy and prosperous,
and those newly submitting were granted exemptions.
At that time, the world was in great turmoil,
yet Shǔ alone was peaceful,
with harvests repeatedly abundant,
to the extent that doors were not closed at night,
and lost items were not picked up on the roads.
Hànjiā Yí chief Wáng Chōngguī, Zhūtí Shěn Zhào, and Jiànníng Cuàn Jiāng all submitted to him.
Bā commandery once reported an emergency,
saying there were Jìn troops.
Xióng said:
"I have often worried that Lángyá was weak,
and would be destroyed by Shí Lè,
which troubled me greatly,
never expecting they could raise troops,
this makes me joyful."
However, Xióng's court lacked proper rituals and ranks,
with titles and positions granted excessively;
officials had no fixed salaries,
but took their provisions from the people;
the army had no proper organization,
and orders were not strictly enforced;
these were his shortcomings.
7 In the second month,
on Rényín,
Zhāng Guǐ was appointed Tàiwèi and Liángzhōu Mù,
and enfeoffed as Xīpíng Jùn Gōng;
Wáng Jùn was appointed Dà Sīmǎ and Dūdū of Yōu and Jì military affairs;
Xún Zǔ was appointed Sīkōng, concurrently Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè and Sīlì Xiàowèi,
handling the affairs of the provisional court;
Liú Kūn was appointed Dà Jiāngjūn and Dūdū of Bìngzhōu military affairs.
The court, considering Zhāng Guǐ old and ill,
appointed his son Shí as Deputy Cìshǐ.
Deputy Cìshǐ,
had not existed before this.
8 Shí Lè had his troops in strict readiness,
intending to launch a surprise attack against Wáng Jùn,
but he hesitated and did not set out.
Zhāng Bīn said:
"To launch a surprise attack against someone,
one must catch them unprepared.
Now the army has been on strict alert for days without moving,
is it not because you fear Liú Kūn and the Xiānbēi and Wūhuán will cause trouble for us from the rear?"
Shí Lè said:
"Yes.
What should we do about it?"
Bīn said:
"None of those three parties have wisdom and courage that match the General's.
Although the General campaigns far away,
they certainly will not dare to move.
Moreover, they do not believe the General can lead an army a thousand lǐ away to seize Yōuzhōu.
With a light force going and returning,
it will not take more than twenty days.
Even if they have such intentions,
by the time they deliberate and dispatch troops,
we will already have returned.
Furthermore, Liú Kūn and Wáng Jùn,
though both nominally serve as ministers of Jìn,
are in fact enemies.
If we send a letter to Kūn,
offering hostages to request peace,
Kūn will surely be pleased by our submission and rejoice at Jùn's demise.
In the end, he will not rescue Jùn and attack us.
In employing troops, speed is of the essence.
Do not delay."
Shí Lè said:
"What I had not grasped,
the Marquis of the Right has already grasped."
(Liǎo means
to decide.)
Thereupon, they marched by torchlight at night,
reaching Bó Rén.
(Bó Rén County,
belonged to the State of Zhào.
In Táng times, it was Yáoshān County of Xíngzhōu.)
This was because his elder brother Shí Tǒng was in Fànyáng,
and he feared military plans would be leaked.
He sent an envoy to present a letter and hostages to Liú Kūn,
confessing his own crimes,
and requesting to attack Jùn to prove his loyalty.
Kūn was greatly pleased.
He issued a proclamation to the various commanderies and prefectures,
stating
"I and Yīlú are just now planning to attack Lè.
Lè, with nowhere to flee or hide,
seeks to capture the Yōu capital to atone for his crimes.
Now I shall immediately dispatch Liù Xiū to attack Píngyáng from the south,
to eliminate the rebellious usurpers,
and force the fleeing Jié who know death is near to surrender."
(The 'rebellious usurpers'
refers to Liú Cōng;
the 'fleeing Jié',
refers to Shí Lè.
Jiàng,
read as hù jiāng fān.
Jié,
read as jū yè fān.)
"To assist the Imperial House—
this is the result of the sincere devotion and divine blessings accumulated over the years!"
Jùn and
Kūn were manipulated by Lè without realizing it.
It was fitting that they fell one after the other.
(Textual Analysis says: In the Collection of Kūn,
the proclamation begins,
"The first day of the third month, Gēngwǔ;
the fifth day, Jiǎxū."
According to this, Shí Lè captured Yōuzhōu on Rénshēn.
It seems that at Jìnyáng they did not yet know.
Wishing to finish narrating Kūn's affairs,
and then narrate Lè's affairs,
it is placed here.)
In the third month,
Lè's army reached the Yìshuǐ River.
Wáng Jùn's commander Sūn Wěi swiftly sent word to inform Jùn,
and wished to lead troops to resist them,
but Yóu Tǒng forbade it.
Jùn's officers all said:
"The Hú are greedy and untrustworthy.
They surely have a treacherous scheme.
We request to attack them."
Jùn angrily said:
"Lord Shí has come
precisely to support and honor me.
Anyone who dares speak of attacking shall be executed!"
The crowd did not dare speak again.
Jùn prepared a feast to await them.
On Rénshēn,
Lè arrived at Jì at dawn.
He shouted at the gatekeepers to open the gates;
still suspecting an ambush,
he first drove several thousand cattle and sheep,
claiming they were tribute gifts,
(meaning he intended to present the cattle and sheep to Jùn as gifts.
Shàng,
read as shí zhǎng fān.)
Only then did Jùn begin to fear,
sitting and standing restlessly.
Once Lè entered the city,
he let his troops plunder freely.
Jùn's attendants requested to resist them,
but Jùn still would not permit it.
Lè ascended his audience hall.
(The central courtyard was called the 'tīng shì',
meaning affairs were heard and lawsuits adjudicated there.
In Hàn and Jìn times it was written
'tīng shì'.
Since the Six Dynasties period, the character
was added, making it
'tīng';
both are read tā jīng fān.
A hall without walls on four sides was called a 'huáng'.)
Lè summoned Jùn's wife,
had her sit beside him,
and made Jùn stand before them.
Jùn cursed:
"Hú slave, you deceived your lord!
How could you be so vicious and rebellious!"
Lè said:
"Your position topped the highest ranks,
you held strong troops in hand,
yet you sat and watched the collapse of the imperial court,
never once sending aid.
Instead, you sought to make yourself Son of Heaven.
Is that not vicious and rebellious?
Moreover, you appointed corrupt and greedy men,
brutalized the common people,
harmed loyal and good officials,
and spread poison throughout Yān territory.
Whose crime is this!"
He sent his general Wáng Luòshēng with five hundred cavalry to escort Jùn to Xiāngguó.
Jùn threw himself into the water,
but they pulled him out and bound him,
and executed him in the marketplace of Xiāngguó.
Lè killed ten thousand elite troops under Jùn's command.
Jùn's officers vied to come to the army gate to apologize,
offering bribes and gifts in abundance.
Only the former Minister of Personnel Péi Xiàn and Attendant Gentleman Xún Chuò did not come.
Lè summoned and reprimanded them:
"Wáng Jùn was tyrannical and cruel.
I attacked and executed him.
All the others have come to congratulate and thank me.
You two alone shared his wickedness.
How will you escape execution!"
They replied:
"We, Xiàn and others, have served the Jìn court for generations,
enjoying its glory and emoluments.
Although Jùn was violent and crude,
he was still a vassal minister of Jìn.
Therefore, we followed him.
(Péi Xiàn fled to Yōuzhōu;
see the eighty-seventh scroll, the fifth year of Emperor Huái's Yǒngjiā era.)
If you, Illustrious Lord, do not cultivate virtue and righteousness,
but rely solely on power and punishment,
then our death is our due fate.
What escape is there?
We ask to be put to death."
They did not bow and left.
Lè summoned them back and apologized,
treating them with the courtesy due to guests.
Chuò was
the grandson of Xù.
Lè enumerated the crimes of Zhū Shuò and Zǎo Sōng, etc., for accepting bribes and disrupting governance,
being a scourge to Yōuzhōu.
(The events are seen in the previous scroll, last year.)
Shǔ,
read as suǒ jù fān.)
He executed them all.
(Because Shí Tǒng wished to have Fànyáng submit privately to him.)
Only Péi Xiàn and Xún Chuò had merely over a hundred bundles of books,
and about ten hú each of salt and rice.
Lè said:
"My joy lies not in gaining Yōuzhōu,
but in gaining these two gentlemen."
He appointed Xiàn as Attendant Gentleman,
and Chuò as Army Advisor.
He sent the displaced people back separately,
each to their hometowns.
Lè stayed in Jì for two days,
burned Jùn's palaces,
appointed the former Minister of Personnel, Liú Hàn of Yān, to act as Governor of Yōuzhōu,
garrisoned Jì,
established local officials, and then returned.
Sūn Wěi intercepted and attacked him,
and Lè barely escaped.
When Lè reached Xiāngguó,
he sent an envoy to present Wáng Jùn's head to Hàn as a victory trophy.
Hàn appointed Lè as Grand Commander, Commander of Military Affairs East of Shǎn,
(This 'East of Shǎn'
also takes the meaning of the division at Shǎn when appointing him.)
and added twelve commanderies to his fief.
Lè firmly declined,
accepting only two commanderies.
Liu Kun requested troops from Tuòbá Yīlú to attack the Han,
but it happened that over ten thousand households of mixed Hu tribes under Yīlú's command plotted to respond to Shí Lè,
so Yīlú executed them all,
and ultimately did not fulfill his agreement to aid Liu Kun.
Liu Kun, knowing that Shí Lè had no intention of surrendering,
became greatly fearful,
and submitted a memorial stating:
"Of the eight provinces in the northeast,
Lè has destroyed seven;
Lè entered Yè,
killing the Governor-General, the Prince of Dōngyàn, Sīmǎ Téng;
he invaded Xìndū,
killing the Inspector of Jìzhōu, Wáng Bīn;
he attacked Juànchéng,
killing the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, Yuán Fú;
he attacked Xīncài,
killing the Inspector of Yùzhōu, the Prince of Xīncài, Sīmǎ Què;
he attacked Méngchéng,
capturing the Governor-General of Qīngzhōu, Xún Xī;
he captured Shàngbái,
beheading the Inspector of Qīngzhōu, Lǐ Yùn;
he attacked Xìndū,
killing the Inspector of Jìzhōu, Wáng Xiàng;
he attacked Dìnglíng,
killing the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, Tián Huī;
he attacked Yōuzhōu,
capturing Wáng Jùn;
aside from Lǐ Yùn and Tián Huī,
who were appointed by Wáng Jùn acting under imperial authority,
thus seven have been destroyed.
The only one remaining is your servant.
Lè occupies Xiāngguó,
separated from your servant by mountains,
the mountains,
from Tàiháng and Héngshān to Yōu and Jié,
stretch continuously without break,
Xiāngguó lies east of the mountains,
Jìnyáng lies west of the mountains.
The cities and forts are terrified,
and though they harbor loyalty and indignation,
their strength does not match their wishes!"
Liu Hàn, unwilling to follow Shí Lè,
instead went over to Duàn Pǐdī,
and Pǐdī thus occupied Jìchéng.
Wáng Jùn's Attendant Gentleman Yáng Yù,
the nephew of Yáng Dān,
fled to Língzhī.
Língzhī County,
belonged to Liáoxī in the Han,
was the state of the ancient Gūzhú lord,
abolished in the Jin,
the Duàn clan occupied it as their capital.
Yīng Shào said: Líng,
pronounced líng.
Péi Sōngzhī said: Zhī,
pronounced qí'ér.
Yán Shǐgǔ said: Líng,
also pronounced lángdìng.
Dù Yòu said: Língzhī,
is present-day Lúlóng County of Běipíng Commandery.
Zhū Zuǒchē from Kuàijī, Kǒng Zuǎn from Lǔguó, and Húmǔ Yì from Tàishān fled from Jì to Chānglí,
and attached themselves to Mùróng Huì.
At this time, tens of thousands of households of displaced people from the Central States returned to Huì,
Huì established the Jìyáng Commandery for people from Jìzhōu,
according to Wèi Shōu's *Treatise on Geography*,
Jìyáng Commandery was likely established within the borders of Pínggāng County of Běipíng in the Han.
Chéngzhōu belonged to the territory of Yùzhōu,
hence it was used as the commandery name.
The *Treatise on Geography* of the Former Han states: Lín Yú County of Liáoxī,
has the Yú River,
which originates from the Báiláng River,
flows south past the west of Yíngqiū City,
where Huì established the commandery.
Bīngzhōu,
the ancient state of Táng,
Huì thus named the commandery after it.
The two commanderies of Chéngzhōu and Tángguó,
their established locations are missing.
9 Earlier,
Wáng Jùn appointed Shào Xù as the Administrator of Lèlíng,
stationed at Yàncì.
Yàncì,
originally Fùpíng County of Píngyuán Commandery in the Former Han,
renamed Yàncì by Emperor Ming of the Later Han,
in the Jin it was placed under Lèlíng,
as the administrative seat.
Dīng Dù's *Collected Rhymes*: Yàn,
pronounced yǎn.
*Jiǔyù Zhì* says: According to tradition, when Qín Shǐhuáng traveled east,
he grew weary of the aura of Jiéshí,
and lodged here,
hence the name.
Wèi Shōu said: Yàncì County of Lèlíng Commandery has Fùchéng,
where Shào Xù resided.
Xù submitted to Shí Lè,
and Lè appointed Xù's son Shào Yì as a Supervisor.
The Administrator of Bóhǎi appointed by Jùn, Liú Yìn from Dōnglái, abandoned his commandery and joined Xù,
and said to Xù:
"To achieve great merit,
one must rely on great righteousness.
You, sir,
are a loyal minister of Jin,
how can you follow the bandits and stain yourself!"
It happened that Duàn Pǐdī sent a letter inviting Xù to jointly submit to the Left Chancellor Ruì,
and Xù agreed.
His followers said:
"Now we abandon Lè and join Pǐdī,
what will happen to Yì?"
Xù wept and said:
"How can I care for my son and become a traitorous minister!"
He killed several who voiced dissent.
When Lè heard of this,
he killed Yì.
Xù sent Liú Yìn as an envoy to Jiāngdōng,
Ruì appointed Yìn as an Army Advisor,
and appointed Xù as the Administrator of Píngyuán.
Shí Lè sent troops to besiege Xù,
Pǐdī sent his younger brother Wén Yīng to rescue him,
and Lè withdrew.
10 Xiāngguó suffered a great famine,
with two shēng of grain worth one jin of silver,
and one jin of meat worth one liǎng of silver.
11 Dù Tāo's general Wáng Zhēn attacked Táo Kǎn at Línzhàng,
the *Commentary on the Water Classic* states: Línzhàng is in Zhuànyáng County of Jiāngxià,
the Miǎn River passes north of Zhuànyáng County,
then flows east past the north of the old city of Línzhàng.
Sòng Bái said: The Jin commandery of Jiāngxià had its seat at Línzhàng,
and only moved to Xiàkǒu in the first year of Yìxī.
Zhōu Fǎng came to rescue Kǎn,
attacked Tāo's troops,
and defeated them.
12 In summer,
the fifth month,
the Duke Wǔmù of Xīpíng, Zhāng Guǐ, fell ill,
and left a testament:
"The civil and military officers,
must pacify the common people,
above think of repaying the state,
below bring peace to the family."
On the jǐchǒu day,
Guǐ died;
*Examination of Discrepancies* states: The *Annals of Emperor Mǐn* records
"on the rénchén day."
Here we follow the *Extracts from the Records of Former Liáng*.
The *Extracts from the Records of Former Liáng* also says
"buried at Jiànlíng,"
likely after Zhāng Zuò usurped the title,
he posthumously honored his tomb.
13 The Han Prince of Zhōngshān, Liú Yào, and Zhào Rǎn invaded Cháng'ān.
In the sixth month,
Yào stationed at Wèi Ruì,
the *Spring and Autumn Annals* *Zuǒzhuàn* says: The Duke of Guó defeated the Róng at Wèi Ruì.
Dù Yù said: The bend of a river is called ruì;
Wáng Sù said: Ruì,
means to enter.
Lǚ Chěn said: Ruì means
the confluence of waters.
This is where the Wèi River enters the Yellow River.
Ruì,
pronounced ruì.
Suǒ Chēn led troops out to resist them.
Rǎn had a contemptuous attitude towards Chēn,
his Chief Clerk Lǔ Huī said:
"The Jin ruler and ministers,
knowing their strength is no match for ours,
will fight us to the death,
we must not underestimate them."
Rǎn said:
"With Sīmǎ Mó's strength,
I captured him like breaking rotten wood;
the event is recorded in the 87th scroll, the fifth year of Yǒngjiā of Emperor Huái.
Lā,
pronounced luòhé.
How can they soil my horse's hooves and sword's blade!"
At dawn,
he led several hundred light cavalry to meet them,
saying:
"I must capture Chēn before eating."
Chēn fought him west of the city,
west of Xīnfēng City.
Rǎn regretted, saying:
"Because I did not heed Lǔ Huī's words, I have come to this,
what face do I have to see him!"
He first ordered Huī beheaded,
Huī said:
"General, your foolish obstinacy led to defeat,
and now you resent previous advice and harm the victor,
killing the loyal and good to vent your anger,
as long as heaven and earth exist,
will you, General, be able to die in your bed!"
An edict added to Suǒ Chēn's titles: General of Agile Cavalry, Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, and Recorder of the Imperial Secretariat,
to act with imperial authority.
Yào and Rǎn, together with General Yīn Kǎi, led tens of thousands of troops toward Cháng'ān.
(Textual note: Jìn Chūnqiū records this as
"Duàn Kǎi."
Here, we follow the biography of Qū Yǔn.)
Yǔn was defeated,
gathered his troops;
at night,
he attacked Kǎi's camp,
and Kǎi was defeated and killed.
Yào then turned back to attack Hénèi Prefect Guō Mò at Huái,
deploying three encampments to surround him.
Mò ran out of food,
sent his wife and children as hostages,
and requested to purchase grain from Yào;
after the grain purchase was completed,
he again barricaded himself within the city walls and held firm.
Yào was enraged,
drowned Mò's wife and children in the river and attacked him.
Mò intended to seek refuge with Lǐ Jǔ at Xīnzhèng.
Xīnzhèng County,
during the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Hénán Commandery;
it was abolished during the Jìn dynasty,
and its location should have been within the boundaries of Xíngyáng Commandery.
Duke Huán of Zhèng, younger brother of King Xuān of Zhōu, was originally enfeoffed at Zhèng County in Jīngzhào;
his son, Duke Wǔ, established his capital between Guó and Kuài,
and it later became the state of Zhèng.
In the Zuǒ Zhuàn, Duke Zhuāng of Zhèng said,
"Our former lord established a new capital here,"
and it later became Xīnzhèng County,
to distinguish it from Zhèng in Jīngzhào.
Mò had few troops,
and did not dare to advance.
At that time, Liú Kūn sent his staff officer Zhāng Zhào leading over five hundred Xiānbēi cavalry to Cháng'ān,
but the road was blocked and impassable,
so they turned back,
passing by Jǔ's camp.
Jǔ persuaded Zhào,
to attack the Hàn troops.
The Hàn troops, upon seeing the Xiānbēi,
fled without engaging in battle,
and Mò then led his followers to join Jǔ.
The Hàn ruler Cōng summoned Yào back to station at Púbǎn.
14 In autumn,
Zhào Rǎn attacked Běidì,
and Qū Yǔn resisted him.
Rǎn was struck by a crossbow bolt and died.
15 Shí Lè began ordering the provinces and commanderies to verify the registered households,
with each household contributing two bolts of silk
and two hú of grain.
16 In winter,
the tenth month,
Zhāng Shí was appointed as Commander of Military Affairs of Liáng Province, Governor of Liáng Province, and Duke of Xīpíng.
17 In the eleventh month,
the Hàn ruler Cōng appointed the Jìn Prince Càn as Chancellor of State and Grand Chányú,
overseeing all affairs.
Càn had been talented and outstanding since youth,
but since becoming chancellor,
he became arrogant, extravagant, arbitrary, and willful,
distancing himself from the worthy and befriending flatterers,
harsh, stubborn, and rejecting remonstrance,
so the people of the state began to despise him.
(This sets the stage for Càn later being assassinated by Jìn Zhǔn.)
(Note: "Shào" is pronounced as in "shī zhào fān.")
(Note: "Yuǎn" is pronounced as in "yú yuàn fān.")
(Note: "È" is pronounced as in "wū lù fān.")
18 Zhōu Xié, following his father's dying words
(see the first year of the Jiànxīng era in the previous volume),
(Note: "Xié" is pronounced as "xié.")
plotted a rebellion;
he had Wúxīng's Registrar Xú Fù falsely claim that it was under the order of his uncle, the Assistant to the Chancellor Zhōu Zhá,
to gather followers,
in order to attack Wáng Dǎo and Diāo Xié.
Many local heroes and leaders flocked to join him,
