so I labor myself.”
Wáng Dūn appointed Dù Hóng as a general,
favoring and trusting him.
18. In the ninth month,
the Hàn ruler Liú Cōng sent the Grand Herald to bestow bows and arrows upon Shí Lè,
appointing him as Earl of Shǎndōng,
granting him authority to conduct campaigns,
appointing governors, generals, and local officials,
enfeoffing marquises,
with annual reports to be submitted.
19. The Hàn Grand Marshal Liú Yào invaded Běidì.
An edict appointed Qū Yǔn as Grand Commander and General of Swift Cavalry to resist him.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Suǒ Chēn was appointed as Imperial Secretary and Commander of the Palace City Defense.
Liú Yào advanced and captured Féngyì,
and the Grand Administrator Liáng Sù fled to Wànnián.
Qín’s Lìyáng County,
renamed Wànnián by Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
belonged to Féngyì,
and in Jìn, it belonged to Jīngzhào.
Qū Yǔn left Huángbái City,
stationed his army at Língwǔ,
the Língwǔ County of Hàn’s Běidì Commandery,
and did not dare to advance.
The Emperor repeatedly requested troops from Chancellor Sīmǎ Bǎo,
but Sīmǎ Bǎo’s attendants all said:
“When a viper bites the hand,
a strong man cuts off the wrist.
The Hànshū records
the King of Qí saying:
‘If a viper bites the hand, cut off the hand.’
It is believed that if this is not done,
the poison will spread throughout the body,
leading to death.
Bite,
pronounced shì.
Cut off,
pronounced dīngguǎn fān;
same below.
Wrist,
pronounced wūguàn fān.
We should cut off the Lǒng road and observe the changes.”
The Attendant Officer Péi Shēn said:
“Now the snake has bitten the head;
can the head be cut off?”
Sīmǎ Bǎo then appointed General Zhènjūn Hú Sōng as Acting Vanguard Commander,
waiting for all armies to assemble before advancing.
Qū Yǔn wanted to escort the Emperor to join Sīmǎ Bǎo,
but Suǒ Chēn said:
“If Sīmǎ Bǎo gains the Son of Heaven,
he will certainly pursue his own ambitions.”
So they stopped.
From then on, west of Cháng’ān,
no more tributes were sent to the court,
and officials suffered hunger and scarcity,
gathering wild grains to survive.
20. A Liángzhōu soldier, Zhāng Bīng, obtained a seal,
inscribed with the words
“Seal for the Emperor’s Use,”
and presented it to Zhāng Shí.
His subordinates all congratulated him.
Zhāng Shí said:
“This is not something a subject should keep.”
He sent an envoy to return it to Cháng’ān.
Among the various Jìn commanders and governors, only the Zhāng father and son understood the distinction between ruler and subject.
Seal,
pronounced sīshì fān.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Minister of Education Liáng Fēn proposed posthumously honoring Prince Wú Yàn.
Vice Director of the Right Suǒ Chēn and others cited Emperor Míng of Wèi's edict as grounds for deeming it impermissible;
Emperor Míng of Wèi's edict appears in scroll 71, third year of the Tàihé era.
He was given the posthumous title Xiào.
Textual analysis states: In his biography,
"Yàn's posthumous title was Jìngwáng."
Here, we follow the Annals of Emperor Mǐn.
2 The Hàn eunuchs Wáng Shěn, Xuān Huái, and Palace Attendant Guō Yī,
were all favored and wielded power.
The Hàn sovereign Cōng indulged in feasting and revelry in the rear palace,
sometimes not sobering up for three days,
or not emerging for a hundred days;
since last winter, he had not attended court,
entrusting all government affairs to Chancellor Càn,
only matters of execution or appointment requiring Shěn and others to report to him.
Shěn and others often did not report,
instead deciding matters based on their private inclinations,
so meritorious veterans sometimes went unrecognized,
while treacherous and flattering petty men could rise to the rank of two-thousand-bushel official within a few days.
Military campaigns were launched yearly,
yet generals and soldiers received no rewards of coins or silk,
while the families of the rear palace,
down to their servant boys,
were granted gifts often amounting to tens of millions.
Shěn and others' carriages, attire, and residences surpassed those of the princes,
and over thirty of their sons, nephews, and cousins served as prefects or magistrates,
all greedy and cruel, harming the people.
This refers to those of other surnames who were cousins to the sons and nephews of Shěn and others.
Shěn,
read as chí lín fān.
Prefect,
read as shì yòu fān.
Guō Yī and Jìn Zhǔn both bore grudges against the Crown Prince Yì.
Yī said to Chancellor Càn:
"Your Highness is the grandson of Emperor Guāngwén,
the sovereign's legitimate son,
all under heaven looks to you with hope,
why would you wish to yield the realm to the Crown Prince!
Moreover, I have heard that the Crown Prince and the Great General plotted to stage a rebellion during the grand feast on the third day of the third month,
once successful,
they promised to make the sovereign the Grand Emperor,
the Great General the Crown Prince,
and further promised the Guard General would become the Great Chányú.
Cōng had appointed his son Jì as Great General,
and his son Lì as Guard General,
both younger brothers of Càn.
Also, according to the chronology, Cōng appointed his son Fū as Great General,
after Fū's death,
Jì was appointed.
Both hold heavy military power,
with this, if they act,
nothing will fail.
However, these two princes covet temporary gain,
disregarding their father and elder brother;
after the deed is done,
how could the sovereign remain unharmed!
Your Highness and your brothers,
needless to say;
the Eastern Palace, the Chancellorship, the Chányú title,
would surely go to the Wǔlíng brothers,
how could they be willing to give them to others!
The Wǔlíng brothers,
likely refers to Yì's various sons.
Chancellor,
read as xī liàng fān.
Chányú,
read as chán.
You should plan against this early.
I have repeatedly spoken to the sovereign,
but the sovereign, firm in brotherly affection,
considering me a remnant of the knife and saw,
ultimately did not believe me.
I hope Your Highness will not divulge this,
but secretly memorialize the situation.
If Your Highness does not believe me,
you may summon the Great General's Attendant Gentleman Wáng Pí and the Guard Army's Major Liú Dūn,
show them favor,
promise them pardon if they confess
and inquire,
then you will surely know."
Càn agreed.
Yī secretly said to Pí and Dūn:
"The rebellious plot of the two princes,
the sovereign and the chancellor are fully aware,
are you involved?"
The two men exclaimed in alarm:
"No."
Yī said:
"This matter is already decided,
I pity you as old acquaintances,
but you will be exterminated along with your clans!"
He then sighed and shed tears.
The two men were terrified,
kowtowed and begged for mercy.
Yī said:
"I have a plan for you,
will you follow it?
When the chancellor questions you,
you just say 'Yes';
if he blames you for not reporting earlier,
you say 'I truly deserve death.
However, considering the sovereign's magnanimity and benevolence,
and Your Highness's fraternal harmony,
if my words were not believed,
I would fall into the unpredictable punishment of false accusation and slander,
hence I dared not speak.'"
Pí and Dūn agreed.
Càn summoned and questioned them,
the two men arrived at different times,
yet their statements were identical,
Càn believed it to be true.
Jìn Zhǔn further persuaded Càn:
"Your Highness should reside in the Eastern Palace yourself
(at that time, Yì resided in the Eastern Palace).
Further,
read as fú yòu fān.
So that the realm may have an early focus.
Now rumors on the streets
all say the Great General and the Guard General intend to support the Crown Prince in a revolt,
scheduled for late spring;
if the Crown Prince gains the realm,
Your Highness will have no place to stand."
Càn said:
"What should be done?"
Zhǔn said:
"If someone reports the Crown Prince's revolt,
the sovereign will surely not believe it.
You should relax the restrictions on the Eastern Palace,
allowing guests to come and go;
the Crown Prince, being fond of treating scholars well,
will certainly not mind this,
and frivolous petty men will inevitably cater to the Crown Prince's wishes and plot for him.
Then I, your humble official, will openly memorialize his crimes for Your Highness,
and Your Highness can arrest and interrogate those guests who have dealings with the Crown Prince.
Once the confessions are obtained,
then the sovereign will have no reason to disbelieve."
Càn then ordered Bǔ Chōu to withdraw troops from the Eastern Palace.
Last year, Cōng had ordered Bǔ Chōu to lead troops to guard the Eastern Palace.
The Privy Treasurer Chén Xiū and the Left Guard General Bǔ Chóng,
being upright and honest,
had long despised Shěn and others,
and even in public gatherings,
never spoke with them,
which Shěn and others deeply resented.
Palace Attendant Bǔ Gàn said to Xiū and Chóng:
"Wáng Shěn and others' power is enough to overturn heaven and earth.
Consider yourselves, in terms of closeness to the sovereign and virtue, how do you compare to Dòu Wǔ and Chén Fān?"
Meaning that Chén Fān's virtue
and Dòu Wǔ's closeness
were still overcome by eunuchs,
let alone Xiū and Chóng.
"We are over fifty,
our positions are already high,
only death remains!
To die for loyalty and righteousness
is to find our proper place;
how can we bow our heads and lower our brows to serve eunuchs!
Farewell, Lord Bǔ,
say no more!"
In the second month,
the Hàn sovereign Cōng appeared at the Shàngqiū Pavilion,
a western pavilion of the palace.
He executed them all,
all were hated by the eunuchs.
Bǔ Gàn tearfully remonstrated:
"Your Majesty is currently seeking worthies with earnestness,
yet suddenly you execute seven high ministers,
all loyal and good men of the state.
Is this not improper!
Even if Xiū and others were guilty,
Your Majesty did not hand them over to the authorities,
nor publicly revealed their crimes,
how would the realm know of them!
The edict is still in my possession,
I have not dared to announce it."
Bǔ Gàn was Palace Attendant,
edicts passed through his office,
so he retained it to remonstrate.
He then kowtowed until blood flowed.
Wáng Shěn rebuked Gàn:
"Does Palace Attendant Bǔ intend to defy the edict!"
Cōng flicked his sleeves and entered,
dismissing Gàn to commoner status.
The Grand Steward, the Prince of Héjiān, Wáng Yì,
(Textual note: In Jìn Chūnqiū,
"Yì"
is written as
"Shìtōng."
Here we follow the Zàijì.)
said, "Wáng Shěn and others have forged and manipulated imperial edicts,
deceiving and slandering the sun and moon,
flattering Your Majesty within the court,
and currying favor with the Chancellor outside,
wielding authority and power
equal to that of the sovereign.
They have fostered many treacherous factions,
spreading poison throughout the land.
Knowing that Xiū and others are loyal ministers,
who have served the state with utmost integrity,
they feared their own treacherous deeds would be exposed,
and thus skillfully framed them with false accusations.
Your Majesty, without investigation,
hastily imposed the severest punishments,
causing pain that reaches heaven and earth,
and grief and fear among the wise and foolish alike.
Now, the remnants of Jìn have not been eradicated,
Bā and Shǔ do not submit,
Shí Lè plots to seize Zhào and Wèi,
and Cáo Yì desires to rule all of Qí.
From the heart and limbs of Your Majesty,
where is there no calamity?
Yet you still allow Shěn and others to aid the chaos,
executing Wūxián,
and killing Biǎnquè.
I fear this will lead to an incurable illness."
(Mǎ Róng said: Wūxián
was a shaman of the Yīn dynasty.
Biǎnquè
was an ancient skilled physician.
The Qín physician Huǎn examined the Marquis of Jìn and said:
"The illness cannot be treated.
It lies above the gāo
and below the huāng.
It cannot be attacked,
nor reached,
and medicine cannot reach it."
Dù Yù said: Below the heart is the gāo;
huāng
is the diaphragm.
Xú said: Huāng,
pronounced huāng;
Shuōwén says: Below the heart and above the diaphragm.
Biǎn,
pronounced bǔ diǎn fān.)
It will be too late to save.
I request that Shěn and others be dismissed from their posts
and handed over to the authorities for punishment."
Liú Cōng showed the memorial to Shěn and others,
and said with a laugh:
"That boy has been led astray by Yuándá,
and has become a fool."
Shěn and others kowtowed and wept, saying:
"We are but petty men,
undeservedly recognized and promoted by Your Majesty,
allowed to serve in the inner chambers;
yet the princes and court officials hate us like enemies,
and deeply resent Your Majesty as well.
We wish to be boiled in cauldrons,
so that the court may naturally become harmonious."
Cōng said:
"Such wild talk is common,
why should you bear a grudge over it?"
Cōng asked the Chancellor Liú Càn about Shěn and others,
and Càn highly praised their loyalty and integrity.
Cōng was pleased,
and enfeoffed Shěn and others as marquises.
The Grand Steward Yì again went to the palace and submitted a memorial with extreme remonstrance.
Cōng was furious,
and tore the memorial with his own hands.
In the third month,
Yì died of anger and resentment.
Yì had always been loyal and upright,
and Chén Yuándá relied on him for support,
enabling him to remonstrate fully.
After Yì's death,
Yuándá wept bitterly for him,
saying:
" 'When men are lost,
the state is ruined and distressed.'"
(These are words from the "Zhān'ǎng" poem in the Dàyǎ section of the Shījīng.
Cuì,
pronounced qín zuì fān.)
"What use is it to live silently and cowardly?"
He returned home and committed suicide.
3 Earlier,
the King of Dài, Yīlú, favored his youngest son Bǐyán,
and wanted to make him his heir.
He sent his eldest son Liùxiū to live in Xīnpíng City,
and dismissed Liùxiū's mother.
In the first year of the Jiànxīng era,
Yīlú built Xīnpíng City.
Xīnpíng City,
known as Xīnchéng in the Táng dynasty,
was located within the boundaries of Shuòzhōu.
Shào,
pronounced shī zhào fān.
Zhǎng,
pronounced zhī liǎng fān.)
Yīlú had a horse that could travel five hundred lǐ in a day,
which he took from Liùxiū
and gave to Bǐyán.
When Liùxiū came to court,
Yīlú ordered him to bow to Bǐyán,
but Liùxiū refused.
Yīlú then seated Bǐyán in his palanquin,
(A palanquin
is not drawn by horses
but is carried by people.)
and went out on an excursion.
Liùxiū saw it from afar,
thinking it was Yīlú,
and knelt by the roadside to pay respects.
When it arrived,
it turned out to be Bǐyán.
Liùxiū, ashamed and angry, left.
Yīlú summoned him, but he did not come.
Enraged,
Yīlú led troops to attack him,
but was defeated by Liùxiū.
Yīlú disguised himself and fled among the common people,
but a lowly woman recognized him,
and he was subsequently assassinated by Liùxiū.
Tuòbá Pǔgēn had been guarding the border regions.
Hearing of the trouble, he came to aid,
attacked Liùxiū,
and destroyed him.
Pǔgēn succeeded to the throne,
but the state fell into great chaos,
with old and new factions suspicious of each other,
and successive rounds of killings.
The Left General Wèi Xióng and the General of Trust and Righteousness Jī Dàn,
who had long assisted Yīlú,
were supported by the masses.
They planned to return to Liú Kūn,
and said to the crowd:
"We hear that the old tribesmen resent the new men for their fierce combat skills."
(The old tribesmen
were the Suǒtóu tribe;
the new men
were the Jìn people and the Wūhuán.)
Hàn,
pronounced hóu gàn fān,
also pronounced xià hǎn fān.)
"What shall we do?"
The Jìn people and the Wūhuán were all alarmed and fearful,
saying:
"We will follow the two generals in life and death!"
So they, along with Liú Kūn's hostage son Zūn, led thirty thousand households of Jìn people and Wūhuán, along with one hundred thousand head of horses, cattle, and sheep, and returned to Liú Kūn.
Kūn was overjoyed,
and personally went to Píngchéng to pacify and接纳 them.
Kūn's forces thus regained strength.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Pǔgēn died.
His son had just been born,
and Pǔgēn's mother, Wéishì, established him as ruler.
(Wéishì
was the wife of Yīyǐ.)
4 Zhāng Shí issued an order:
"Any official or commoner under my jurisdiction who can point out my faults
shall be rewarded with cloth, silk, sheep, and grain."
The Assistant of the Bandit Suppression Bureau, Gāochāng's Wěi Jǐn, said:
Since the Hàn dynasty,
in the offices of the Three Excellencies, the provinces, commanderies, and kingdoms,
there have been Chiefs,
Subordinates,
and Assistants and Clerks.
The "Treatise on the Western Regions" in the Book of Hàn records,
the state of Chēshī had the Gāochāng Fort.
The Book of Táng states: The state of Gāochāng
was the former royal court of Hàn's Chēshī,
later Gāochāng was conquered,
and Xīzhōu was established.
Considering this,
then the Zhāng clan of Héxī indeed once established commanderies and counties in the Gāochāng region,
and it was not until the Later Wèi period that it became the state of Gāochāng.
Wěi,
pronunciation according to Wǔzuì.
"Now, Your Excellency governs,
handling matters regardless of their importance,
all decided by yourself.
Sometimes troops are raised or orders issued,
without the knowledge of the government offices;
government offices,
refers to the place where the staff gathers.
Cháo,
pronunciation according to Zhíyáo.
There is no way to share the blame.
Your subordinates fear your authority,
and merely accept the decisions.
In this situation,
even if you reward them with a thousand pieces of gold,
they still would not dare to speak.
I believe you should slightly reduce your personal oversight,
and for all government affairs,
consult with your subordinates,
allowing each to fully express their thoughts.
Then, select and implement them.
In that case, good advice will come naturally,
why must there be rewards!"
Shí was pleased,
and followed his advice;
he promoted Jǐn three grades in rank.
Shí sent General Wáng Gāi to lead five thousand infantry and cavalry to reinforce Cháng'ān,
and also to deliver the tribute and accounting registers from the various commanderies.
Tribute,
refers to local products;
accounting,
refers to the accounting registers.
He appointed his younger brother, Mào, as Governor of Qínzhōu.
5 Shí Lè sent Shí Hǔ to attack Liú Yǎn at Lǐnqiū,
the Governor of Yōuzhōu, Duànpídī, sent his younger brother Wényāng to rescue him;
Hǔ captured Lǐnqiū,
Yǎn fled to Wényāng's army,
Hǔ captured Yǎn's younger brother Qǐ and returned.
6 The Governor of Níngzhōu, Wáng Xùn,
was severe and harsh, fond of killing.
In the fifth month,
the Administrator of Píngyí, Léi Zhào,
in the fifth year of Emperor Huái's Yǒngjiā era,
Xùn petitioned to divide Zāngkē, Zhūtí, and Jiànníng,
and establish Píngyí Commandery,
which was the territory of the Hàn dynasty's Píngyí and Bó counties.
Bó,
pronunciation according to Mèng Kāng is Biē.
Pínglè Commandery,
verified with the Suí dynasty records,
was likely established at Qióngbù Chuān in Yuèxī Commandery,
but it is unknown who established it.
Lè,
pronunciation is Luò.
surrendered to Chéng.
7 In the sixth month,
on the first day, Dīngsì,
there was a solar eclipse.
8 In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Hàn Grand Marshal Yào besieged the Administrator of Běidì, Qū Chāng,
the Jìn dynasty's Běidì Commandery,
governed only Níyáng and Fùpíng counties.
Yào surrounded the city and set fires,
smoke rose, obscuring the sky.
He sent a double agent to deceive Yǔn, saying:
"The commandery city has already fallen,
going there is too late!"
The troops were frightened and scattered.
Yào pursued and defeated Yǔn at Pánshí Valley,
Yǔn fled back to Língwǔ,
and Yào thus captured Běidì.
Yǔn was by nature kind and generous,
lacking authority and decisiveness,
and fond of pleasing people with noble titles.
The Administrator of Xīnpíng, Zhú Huī; the Administrator of Shǐpíng, Yáng Xiàng; the Administrator of Fúfēng, Zhú Shuǎng; and the Administrator of Āndìng, Jiāo Sōng,
all held the titles of General of Conquest and General of Pacification,
wielded the imperial tally,
and were additionally appointed as Palace Attendants and Regular Attendants;
even the leaders of village strongholds,
the lesser ones were still given the title of General of the Silver Seal and Blue Ribbon;
General of Conquest and General of Pacification,
refers to the titles of the Four Conquest and Four Pacification Generals.
General of the Silver Seal and Blue Ribbon,
a general title granted with a silver seal and blue ribbon.
Shuài,
pronunciation according to Suǒlèi.
Therefore, the generals became arrogant and willful, and the soldiers were disaffected and resentful.
With Guānzhōng in danger and chaos,
Yǔn urgently sought help from Jiāo Sōng.
Sōng had always looked down on Yǔn,
and said:
"We must wait until Yǔn is in dire straits,
then we will rescue him."
Yào advanced to Jīngyáng,
and all the cities north of the Wèi River collapsed.
Jīngyáng County,
belonged to Āndìng Commandery in the Former Hàn.
The Treatise of Bān states: Jiāntóu Mountain is west of the county,
the Jīng River originates there according to the Tribute of Yǔ,
flowing northeast to Yánglíng to enter the Wèi,
passing through three commanderies,
over a distance of one thousand and sixty lǐ.
This text says Yào reached Jīngyáng,
and all cities north of the Wèi collapsed,
meaning his troops were already between Chíyáng and Yánglíng counties.
It says he was north of the Jīng River,
not at the Jīngyáng County of Āndìng.
Yào had long heard of Chōng's virtue,
and sought to capture him alive.
After seeing him,
he offered him wine, saying:
"If I obtain you,
the world will not be difficult to pacify!"
Chōng said:
"I am a general of Jìn,
and the state has suffered defeat and ruin.
I dare not seek to live.
If I receive your grace,
a swift death would be fortunate."
Yào said:
"A righteous man."
He gave him a sword,
and ordered him to commit suicide.
Liáng Wěi's wife, Lady Xīn,
was beautiful.
Yào summoned her for an audience,
intending to take her as his wife.
Qī,
pronunciation according to Rúzì.
"My husband is already dead,
it is right that I do not live alone.
Moreover, for a woman to serve two husbands,
how could Your Excellency use her!"
Yào said:
"A chaste woman."
He also allowed her to commit suicide,
and both were buried with proper rites.
9 The Hàn ruler Cōng established the former Empress Zhāng's maid, Fán, as the Upper Empress.
Besides the three empresses,
there were seven others who wore the empress's seal and ribbon.
His favored concubines wielded power,
and punishments and rewards were in disorder.
The Grand General Fū repeatedly tearfully offered earnest remonstrances.
Cōng angrily said:
"Do you want your father to die quickly?
Why do you come crying to me morning and night!"
Fū, worried and indignant,
fell ill and died.
In Hédōng and Píngyáng, there was a great locust plague,
and fifty to sixty percent of the people were displaced or starved to death.
Shí Lè sent his general Shí Yuè to lead twenty thousand cavalry to station in Bìngzhōu,
to recruit displaced people.
Two hundred thousand households of people returned to him.
Cōng sent an envoy to reprimand Lè,
but Lè did not accept the order,
secretly allying with Cáo Yí.
10 In the eighth month,
the Hàn Grand Marshal Yào pressed on Cháng'ān.
11 In the ninth month,
the Hàn ruler held a banquet for his ministers at the Guāngjí Hall,
and summoned the Grand Younger Brother Yì for an audience.
Yì's appearance was haggard,
his temples and hair graying.
He tearfully presented his apologies,
and Cōng also wept bitterly for him.
Then they drank to the fullest of joy,
and he treated him as before.
12 Jiāo Sōng, Zhú Huī, and Sòng Zhé all led troops to rescue Cháng'ān.
The Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary Huá Jí supervised the troops of the four commanderies of Jīngzhào, Féngyì, Hóngnóng, and Shàngluò,
and camped at Bàshàng.
They all feared the strength of the Hàn troops,
and did not dare advance.
The Chancellor of State Sīmǎ Bǎo dispatched Hú Sōng to lead troops to enter and provide aid.
He attacked the Hàn Grand Marshal Liú Yào at Língtái,
and defeated him.
(Sānfǔ Huángtú: King Wén of Zhōu's Língtái,
is located forty lǐ west of Cháng'ān,
twenty zhàng high,
with a circumference of one hundred and twenty paces.)
Qū Yǔn
and Suǒ Chēn
(Suǒ,
pronounced as xī gè fān)
then returned to Huáilǐ.
(Huáilǐ County,
belonged to Fúfēng in the Hàn,
and to Shǐpíng Commandery in the Jìn.)
Liú Yào attacked and captured the outer city of Cháng'ān.
Qū Yǔn and Suǒ Chēn retreated to defend the inner city to fortify themselves.
Cut off from outside,
the city suffered severe famine.
A dǒu of rice was worth two liǎng of gold.
People ate each other,
and more than half died.
Desertion and flight could not be controlled.
Only a thousand loyal troops from Liángzhōu
held firm unto death without moving.
(The Liángzhōu loyal troops
were the soldiers sent by Zhāng Guǐ and his sons.)
Qū Yǔn ground wheat bran
into porridge to supply the Emperor,
but soon it was also exhausted.
In winter,
the eleventh month,
the Emperor tearfully said to Yǔn:
"Now that we are in such dire straits,
with no external relief,
we should endure the shame and surrender,
to save the officers and people."
He then sighed and said:
"Those who have ruined my affairs
are the two lords, Qū and Suǒ!"
He sent the Palace Attendant Zōng Chǎng to deliver a surrender letter to Yào.
(Kǎo Yì says: The Emperor's Annals records
"Sòng Chǎng";
here we follow Jìn Chūnqiū.)
Suǒ Chēn sent his son to persuade Yào, saying:
"Now the food in the city is still enough to last a year.
It will not be easy to capture.
If you promise Chēn
the rank of Yìtóng and a commandery duke with ten thousand households,
I request to surrender the city."
Yào beheaded him and sent his head back,
saying:
"The army of an emperor or king
acts with righteousness.
I have led troops for fifteen years,
and have never defeated anyone by deceitful schemes.
I must exhaust military force to its utmost,
and only then take it.
Now what Suǒ Chēn says is like this.
Evil is the same under Heaven.
I have accordingly executed him.
If your troops and food are indeed not yet exhausted,
you may by all means stubbornly hold on;
if your provisions are exhausted and troops few,
you should also awaken early to the Mandate of Heaven."
On the jiǎwǔ day,
Zōng Chǎng arrived at Yào's camp.
On the yǐwèi day,
the Emperor, riding a sheep-drawn cart,
bared his upper body, held a jade disc in his mouth, and had a coffin carried out as he exited the eastern gate to surrender.
His ministers wept and wailed,
clinging to the cart and holding the Emperor's hand.
The Emperor was also overcome with grief.
The Palace Aide to the Censor-in-chief, Jí Lǎng of Féngyì, sighed and said:
"My wisdom is insufficient to devise plans,
my courage insufficient to die.
How can I bear to follow my sovereign
and serve the enemy barbarians facing north!"
He then committed suicide.
Yào burned the coffin and accepted the jade disc,
sending Zōng Chǎng to escort the Emperor back to the palace.
On the dīngyǒu day,
he moved the Emperor and the officials down to the third rank and below to his camp.
On the xīnchǒu day,
he sent them to Píngyáng.
On the rényín day,
the Hàn sovereign Liú Cōng presided at the Guāngjí Hall.
The Emperor kowtowed before him.
Qū Yǔn prostrated on the ground, weeping bitterly.
He could not rise even when helped up.
Cōng grew angry,
imprisoned him,
and Yǔn committed suicide.
Cōng appointed the Emperor as Grand Master of Splendid Happiness,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Huái'ān.
He appointed the Grand Marshal Liú Yào as Acting Commander with the Yellow Axe, Grand Governor, Commander-in-Chief of Various Military Affairs West of Shǎn, and Grand Steward,
and enfeoffed him as Prince of Qín.
He issued a great amnesty,
and changed the era name to Línjiā.
Considering Qū Yǔn's loyalty and fervor,
he posthumously awarded him the title of General of Chariots and Cavalry,
with the posthumous name Jíemǐn Marquis.
(Yǔn was indeed loyal,
but was he not behind Jí Lǎng?)
He executed Suǒ Chēn in the marketplace.
(The marketplace of Píngyáng.)
Huá Jí fled to Nánshān.
Gān Bǎo discussed this, saying: In the past, the Lofty Ancestor Emperor Xuān,
with his great talent and broad capacity,
rose in response to the times.
His nature was deep and guarded, as if having a city within,
yet he could be broad and tolerant to accommodate others.
He employed calculations and methods to manage affairs,
yet knew men well and was good at selecting and promoting them.
(It is said that those with a 'city within' their chest are mostly unable to be tolerant and forgiving;
those who rely on calculations and methods are mostly unable to employ men;
yet Emperor Xuān was able to do both.)
It is said that all under Heaven acknowledged his ability,
and none could contend with him.
(Liú Liáng said: Xiàng means law;
it is said that the Jìn's rise and establishment
began with the establishment of great laws from this point.)
The Grand Progenitor inherited the enterprise,
completely eliminating different schemes,
thereby continuing and expanding the former achievements.
(This refers to internally executing Lǐ Fēng
and Xiàhóu Xuán,
and externally pacifying Guànqiū Jiǎn, Wén Qīn, and Zhūgě Dàn.)
He thus attained the imperial position.
(Lǚ Yánjì said: Xiǎng means to assume;
huángjí means the Son of Heaven's position.)
He was frugal to ensure sufficient use,
harmonious yet not lax,
broad yet able to decide.
He covered the old domains of Táng and Yú,
and promulgated the calendar to the Eight Wastes.
(The Eight Wastes
refer to the lands beyond the eight directions,
the barbarian wilderness.)
The saying that "under Heaven there are no poor people"
(Lǚ Xiàng said: This means the common people were all wealthy.)
is also sufficient to show that the people were happy in their lives.
After Emperor Wǔ passed away,
before his tomb was dry, calamities and difficulties arose one after another.
The imperial clansmen provided no assistance like a surrounding wall;
the high ministers possessed no dignity for all to look up to.
(The Shī says: Illustrious are the high ministers,
the people all look to you.)
By evening they became Jié or Zhí;
(referring to Yáng Jùn, Wèi Guàn, Zhāng Huá, etc.)
the imperial guards were scattered outside to the four directions;
the regional lords lacked the stabilizing weight of a jūn or shí;
the passes and gates lacked the firmness of knotted grass.
(Thirty jīn make one jūn,
four jūn make one shí.
Zuǒzhuàn: Qín attacked Jìn.
Jìn's Wèi Kē defeated the Qín army,
capturing Dù Huí.
Kē dreamed of an old man knotting grass to trip Dù Huí.
Dù Huí stumbled and fell,
therefore he was captured.)
The two emperors lost their dignity.
Why?
Because the establishment of authority was faulty,
the entrustment was to those without talent,
the Four Bonds were not upheld, and there were many policies of expediency.
(Jiǎ Yì's policy said: Ritual, righteousness, integrity, and shame
are called the Four Bonds.
If the Four Bonds are not upheld,
the state will perish.)
For when the foundation is broad, it is difficult to topple;
when the roots are deep, they are hard to uproot;
when principles and order are maintained, there is no chaos;
when bonds are strong, there is no shifting.
Lǐ Zhōuhàn said: "Principles and order"
means that governance and education have proper arrangement and regulation.
"Bonds"
means firmness.
It means that if a ruler establishes a foundation of benevolence and kindness that is deep and broad,
and does not lose principles and order,
then the hearts of the people will be firmly united and cannot be shifted.
This is the way to use it.
The Zhōu dynasty, from Hòujì who loved the people,
through sixteen kings until Wǔ began to rule as sovereign.
Hòujì's son was Bùzhú,
Bùzhú's son was Jū,
Jū's son was Gōngliú,
Gōngliú's son was Qìngjié,
Qìngjié's son was Huángpú,
Huángpú's son was Chàfú,
Chàfú's son was Huǐyú,
Huǐyú's son was Gōngfēi,
Gōngfēi's son was Gāoyǔ,
Gāoyǔ's son was Yàyǔ,
Yàyǔ's son was Gōngshū Zǔlèi,
Gōngshū Zǔlèi's son was Gǔgōng Dǎnfù,
Gǔgōng Dǎnfù's son was Jìlì,
Jìlì's son was King Wén,
King Wén's son was King Wǔ,
making sixteen kings in total.
So firm was it thus.
Now, the rise of the Jìn dynasty,
its founding of the base and establishment of the foundation,
was certainly different from previous dynasties.
Moreover, at court there were few men of pure virtue,
and in the countryside there was a lack of elders who did not repeat their faults.
The Zhōu official system had village elders;
"not repeating faults"
means those who do not repeat their mistakes.
"Court"
is pronounced zhí yáo fān.
What was considered shameful and what was esteemed were misplaced.
It means that what they considered shameful was not truly shameful,
and what they esteemed was not truly worthy of esteem.
Those who engaged in discourse considered empty and unrestrained arguments as clever and looked down upon reputation and restraint,
those who conducted themselves considered unrestrained and turbid behavior as sophisticated and despised integrity and trustworthiness,
those seeking official advancement considered obtaining positions by any means as noble and scorned upright conduct,
those in office considered being aloof and empty as lofty and mocked diligence and conscientiousness.
Lǚ Yánjì said: "Being aloof and empty"
means not distinguishing right from wrong,
but merely signing documents emptily.
Fù Xián often exposed the wicked and upheld the righteous,
matters concerning Sòng and Xián are both seen in the annals of Emperor Wǔ and Emperor Huì.
"Govern"
is pronounced zhí lì fān.
Those who relied on empty talk,
and were compliant and without principle,
were all renowned throughout the land.
As for those like King Wén who was so busy he had no time to eat until sunset,
or Zhòngshān Fǔ who was diligent day and night without slacking,
they were generally ridiculed and dismissed as dust!
King Wén, from morning until midday and sunset,
had no leisure to eat,
in order to harmonize all the people.
Zhòngshān Fǔ was diligent day and night without slacking in serving his sovereign.
Evil passions rushed along the paths of greed and desire,
those selecting officials chose posts for people,
those in office chose benefits for themselves,
Lǚ Yánjì said: It means those selecting officials no longer chose worthy men for the posts,
and those in office merely pursued what was beneficial to themselves.
"Reputation"
is pronounced yú.
"For"
is pronounced yú wèi fān.
They climbed over and surpassed,
not constrained by seniority or order.
In the swirling dust of the world,
all were men rushing and competing;
though there were hundreds and thousands of officials,
there was no act of yielding to the worthy.
Zǐzhēn wrote the "Chóng Ràng" but no one heeded it;
Liú Shí,
styled Zǐzhēn;
the "Chóng Ràng Lùn" is seen in the 82nd scroll, the tenth year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ.
"Heed"
is pronounced xī jǐng fān.
Liú Sòng,
styled Zǐyǎ.
The system of nine ranks is seen in the same scroll.
They acted according to their whims,
some even defied their parents-in-law,
some killed their concubines,
both matters were initiated by Jiǎ Hòu.
Yet no one in the world criticized them.
Ritual, law, punishment, and governance,
by this time were greatly ruined.
"When a state is about to perish,
its foundation must first crumble,"
is this not what it means!
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says: When a state is about to perish,
its foundation must first crumble,
and then the branches and leaves follow.
Therefore, observing Ruǎn Jí's conduct, one realizes the cause of the collapse of ritual and education;
the matter is seen in the 78th scroll, the third year of Jǐngyuán of Emperor Yuán of Wèi.
"Conduct"
is pronounced xià mèng fān.
The matter is seen in the 79th scroll, the seventh and eighth years of Tàishǐ of Emperor Wǔ.
Reflecting on Guō Qīn's strategy, one awakens to the fact that the Róng and Dí have vulnerabilities;
the dispute over merit after pacifying Wú and Guō Qīn's memorial,
are both seen in the 81st scroll, the first year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ.
Fù Xuán and Liú Yì,
during Emperor Wǔ's time served as Sīlì,
successively investigating and impeaching,
not avoiding the noble and powerful,
thus through their words the wickedness of the hundred officials was exposed.
Fù Xián's memorial is seen in the 82nd scroll, the fourth year of Yuánkāng of Emperor Huì;
the "Qián Shén Lùn" is seen in the 83rd scroll, the ninth year of Yuánkāng.
Since it was already like this,
even if governed by a ruler of mediocre talent who merely upheld established ways,
Liú Liáng said: "Mediocre talent"
means talent that is neither worthy nor foolish;
"upholding established ways"
means a ruler who maintains peace in ordinary times.
"Govern"
is pronounced zhí zhī fān.
how much more so when our Emperor Huì ruled with his dissolute virtue!
Emperor Huái succeeded to the throne amidst disorder,
constrained by powerful ministers;
Emperor Mǐn, after fleeing and wandering,
merely held an empty title.
Since the power of the world was already lost,
unless there was a heroic talent of the age,
it could not be regained!
13 Shílè besieged the Tàishǒu of Lèpíng, Hán Jù, in the city of Diàn,
and Jù requested aid from Liú Kūn.
Kūn had newly obtained the troops of Tuòbá Yīlú,
and wished to take advantage of their sharp morale to attack Lè.
Jī Dàn and Wèi Xióng advised:
"Although these are Jìn people,
they have long been under alien rule,
and are not accustomed to Your Excellency's kindness and trustworthiness;
I fear they will be difficult to use.
It would be better to first gather the remaining grain of the Xiānbēi internally,
Tuòbá
are Xiānbēi.
"Hú"
refers to Liú and Shí.
"Raid"
is pronounced jìn jiāo fān.
focus on agriculture and rest the troops,
wait until they are submissive and moved by righteousness,
and then use them;
then no task will not succeed."
Kūn did not listen,
but mobilized all his forces,
ordering Dàn to lead twenty thousand infantry and cavalry as the vanguard,
while Kūn stationed himself at Guǎngmù,
to provide support.
Guǎngmù County,
in Hàn times belonged to Shuòfāng Commandery;
at the end of Hàn, Shuòfāng was abolished,
and Guǎngmù County was established south of Xíng,
belonging to Xīnxīng Commandery,
not the original location of Guǎngmù County.
"Lead"
is read as "shuài."
Shí Lè heard that Jī Dàn had arrived,
and was about to launch a counterattack.
Someone said:
"Dàn's troops and horses are elite and strong,
their momentum cannot be withstood.
It would be better to lead our troops away to avoid them,
dig deep trenches and build high ramparts to blunt their edge—
this is sure to be a perfectly safe strategy."
Shí Lè said:
"Although Dàn's troops are numerous,
they have come from afar and are weary,
their commands are not unified—
how can they be considered elite and strong!
Now the enemy is about to arrive,
how can we abandon our position and leave!
Once the main army moves,
how easy will it be to turn back midway!
If Dàn takes advantage of our retreat to press upon us,
we will have no time even to flee and scatter in disarray—
how then could we possibly dig deep trenches and build high ramparts!
This is the path to self-destruction."
He immediately beheaded the speaker.
He appointed Kǒng Chàng as Vanguard Commander-in-Chief,
and ordered the three armies:
"Anyone who comes out last will be beheaded!"
Shí Lè occupied a strategic position,
deployed decoy troops on the mountain,
set up two ambushes ahead,
sent out light cavalry to engage Dàn in battle,
and feigned defeat, pretending to flee.
Dàn unleashed his troops in pursuit,
and they entered the ambush.
Shí Lè attacked Dàn's army from both front and rear,
crushing them utterly,
and captured tens of thousands of sets of armor and horses.
Dàn and Xióng led over a thousand cavalry and fled to Dàijùn,
Hán Jù abandoned the city and fled,
and the entire region of Bìng was shaken with terror.
14 In the twelfth month,
on the first day, Yǐmǎo,
there was a solar eclipse.
Textual analysis notes: The Imperial Annals and the Treatise on Astronomy
both erroneously record it as
"the first day, Jiǎshēn."
The Sòng Treatise
says "the first day, Yǐmǎo,"
which matches the perpetual calendar.
We follow this here.
15 The Chief Clerk of the Minister of Works, Lǐ Hóng, surrendered Bìngzhōu to Shí Lè.
Liú Kūn was the Minister of Works,
and had appointed Hóng as his Chief Clerk.
Bìngzhōu
was then administered from Yángqū.
Not knowing what to do,
Duànpǐdī sent a messenger to invite him.
On the day Jǐwèi,
Kūn led his followers from Fēihú to flee to Jì.
Mount Héngshān lies northwest of Shàngqūyáng County in Chángshān Commandery.
There is a slope there,
called the Fēihú Pass.
Dī
is pronounced Dīngxī.
Jì
is pronounced jì.
They became very close and held each other in high esteem,
forming a marriage alliance,
and swore to be as brothers.
Shí Lè relocated the people of Yángqū and Lèpíng to Xiāngguó,
appointed officials to govern them, and then returned.
Kǒng Chàng attacked Jī Dàn at Dàijùn,
and killed him.
According to the Records of the Jin Dynasty,
Chàng attacked Dàn at Sānggān,
so this Dàijùn refers to the later Northern Wei's Dàijùn,
not the Hàn or Jìn Dàijùn.
Chàng and others attacked the rebel leaders Mǎ Yán and Féng Zhě,
but after a long time could not overcome them.
Tens of thousands of households of displaced people from Sī, Jì, Bìng, and Yǎn were in Liáoxī,
constantly inciting and recruiting each other,
and the people could not settle into their livelihoods.
Shí Lè sought counsel from the Marquis of Púyáng, Zhāng Bīn.
Bīn said:
"Yán and Zhě are not your sworn enemies to begin with,
and the displaced people all have a longing to return to their homeland.
Now if you withdraw the troops and muster the army,
select good governors and prefects to summon and pacify them,
then the bandits in Yōu and Jì can be cleared in no time,
and the displaced people of Liáoxī will lead each other to come to you."
Shí Lè then summoned Chàng and others to return,
and appointed the Magistrate of Wǔsuì, Lǐ Huí, as Protector of Yìběi,
concurrently serving as the Grand Administrator of Gāoyáng.
Wǔsuì County
belonged to the Kingdom of Héjiān in the Former Hàn,
and to the Kingdom of Ānpíng in the Later Hàn and Jìn.
Yìběi
means north of the Yì River.
Gāoyáng County
belonged to Zhuō Commandery in the Former Hàn,
to the Kingdom of Héjiān in the Later Hàn,
and in the first year of the Tàishǐ era of Emperor Wǔ, the Kingdom of Gāoyáng was separately established.
Yìng Shào said: It lies north of the Gāo River.
Many rebelled against Yán and submitted to him,
Yán, in fear, fled,
and drowned himself.
Féng Zhě led his followers and surrendered.
Huí moved to reside at Yìjīng.
Yìjīng
was built by Gōngsūn Zàn.
Shí Lè was pleased,
enfeoffed Huí as the Viscount of Yìyáng,
increased Zhāng Bīn's fief by a thousand households,
and promoted him to the rank of General of the Vanguard;
Bīn firmly declined and did not accept.
16 The Chancellor, Ruì, hearing that Cháng'ān had fallen,
led out his troops and camped in the open.
Camping in the open means
bivouacking in the wild,
with no shelter overhead.
He issued proclamations to all directions,
setting a date for a northern expedition.
Because the water transport was delayed,
he beheaded the Transport Supervisor, Clerk Chúnyú Bó.
When the executioner wiped his blade on the pillar,
the blood flowed upward against gravity,
reaching over two zhàng up the pillar before dripping down,
and all who saw it considered it an injustice.
The Chancellor's Inspector, Liú Kuí, submitted a memorial saying:
"Bó's crime did not warrant death;
I request that the Attendant Gentleman, Zhōu Yán, and others be dismissed from office."
Thereupon, the General of the Right, Wáng Dǎo, and others submitted a memorial taking the blame upon themselves,
requesting to be relieved of their duties.
Ruì said:
"Failures in governance and punishment
are all due to my own ignorance and incompetence."
He did not question anyone.
Kuí was by nature harsh and accusatory,
and many famous scholars of the time were impeached by him.
Ruì generally tolerated and pardoned them,
and as a result, all the resentment was directed at Kuí.
The General of the Southern Palace Guards, Wáng Hán,
was the elder brother of Dūn.
Because his clan was powerful and his position eminent,
he was arrogant and self-indulgent.
At one time, he requested over twenty staff assistants and local officials,
most of whom were not qualified;
Kuí impeached Hán,
drafting the indictment with extreme severity,
using harsh interpretations to establish his crimes,
and the Wáng clan deeply resented and hated him for it.
This sets the stage for Wáng Dūn's later request to execute Liú Kuí.
17 The Chancellor, Ruì, appointed Shào Xù as Governor of Jìzhōu.
Xù's son-in-law, Liú Xiá of Guǎngpíng, had gathered a following between the Huáng Hé and Jì River,
and Ruì appointed Xiá as the Interior Historian of Píngyuán.
18 Tuòbá Pǔgēn's son also died.
Tuò
is interchangeable with Tuò;
Wèi Shōu's History of the Wei originally writes it as
"Tuòbá."

Emperor Yuán of the Middle Ancestor, First Part
His personal name was Ruì,
courtesy name Jǐngwén,
great-grandson of Emperor Xuān,
grandson of Wǔ, King of Lángyé, Zhòu,
son of King Gōng, Jìn.
The posthumous naming rule says: "He who first establishes the capital of the state is called Yuán."
First Year of the Jiànwǔ Era
(Dīngchǒu, 317) In the third month of this year,
the era name was changed.
1 Spring,
first month,
Hàn troops advanced eastward to capture Hóngnóng,
and the Grand Administrator, Sòng Zhé, fled to Jiāngdōng.
Zhé was stationed at Huàyīn;
the Hàn troops advanced eastward from Cháng'ān,
so he abandoned the city and fled here.
Shǒu
is pronounced shǒu.
2 The Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, Shǐ Shū, and the Palace Censor, Wáng Chōng, fled from Cháng'ān to Liángzhōu,
claiming that the day before Emperor Mǐn went out to surrender,
he had sent Shū and others bearing an edict to bestow upon Zhāng Shí
the titles of Grand Commander-in-Chief, Governor of Liángzhōu, Palace Attendant, and Minister of Works,
authorizing him to act on imperial authority;
and furthermore said:
"We have already issued an edict for the Prince of Lángyé to temporarily assume the great position;
you must assist and support the Prince of Lángyé,
to together overcome these many difficulties."
When Shū and others arrived at Gūzāng,
Shí observed three days of mourning,
but declined the official appointments and did not accept them.
Initially,
Shí's uncle Sù served as the Governor of Xīhǎi.
Wáng Mǎng established the Xīhǎi Commandery,
but during Guāng Wǔ's restoration,
it was abandoned.
By the second year of Xiàn Dì's Xīngpíng period,
Zhāng Yǎ, Governor of Wǔwēi, requested to establish the Xīhǎi Commandery,
allocating Jiūyán county from Zhāngyè to it.
Although the name of the commandery was the same,
it was not the territory of Wáng Mǎng's Xīhǎi Commandery.
He requested to be the vanguard to provide support;
Shí, considering his age,
did not consent.
Upon hearing that Cháng'ān was undefended,
Sù died in grief and indignation.
Shí dispatched the Grand Marshal Hán Pú,
at that time held by the Zhāng clan in control of Héxī,
having officers like Grand Marshal and Chief Clerk of the Grand Marshal's Office.
Probably, the headquarters were referred to as the Grand Marshal's Office,
while the Liángzhōu office was the Lesser Marshal's office.
Pú,
is pronounced as "pí jiǎo fān."
The General of Pacifying Rong
was created by the Zhāng clan.
Shuài,
read as "lǜ,"
Qí,
pronounced as "qí jì fān."
Shěn Yuè's records note that
Wèi set up forty titles of generals,
with Exterminator of Captives ranking nineteenth.
Jìn's records state: Zhāng Mào separated the four commanderies of Wǔxīng, Jīnchéng, Xīpíng, and Āngu as Dìngzhōu.
Probably the Zhāng clan divided territories of Jīnchéng and Xīpíng to establish Āngu Commandery.
According to Āngu County,
during the Hàn, it belonged to Lǒngxī Commandery.
The Water Classic Commentary notes: Tǎo River flows eastward from Líntáo County,
then bends northward,
passing west of the old city of Āngu County,
and further north past the old city of Dǐdào County.
Dǐdào,
at the time, had established Wǔshǐ Commandery;
Āngu Commandery,
was just a county under the Hàn.
He also sent a letter to the Chancellor:
"When the royal house is in distress,
I will not hesitate to sacrifice my life.
Previously, Jiǎ Qiān was sent to observe the public and private actions,
and in the midst, he received a command,
instructing Qiān to return with his army.
The edict,
was probably from Chancellor Bǎo to Shí.
'Sent,'
pronounced as "yú jì fān."
'Received,'
pronounced as "pí yì fān."
Hú Sōng did not advance;
Qū Yǔn held five hundred pieces of gold,
seeking assistance from Sōng,
subsequently deciding to dispatch Qiān and others to advance their troops over the ridge.
From Liángzhōu, they crossed the river over to Wòyú Ridge,
reaching Dǐdào.
For loyalty unfulfilled,
his anger and pain were deep,
and he regretted it even in death.
Now, sending Pú and others again,
they will only follow your command."
Pú and his comrades ultimately could not advance and returned.
Upon reaching Nán'ān,
in Nán'ān Commandery,
governed by Míndào County.
They died,
pronounced as "zǐ xù fān."
Returned,
pronounced as "cóng xuān fān,"
also as per the character.
They held out for over a hundred days,
their supplies exhausted and arrows depleted.
Pú slaughtered oxen from the carts to feast the soldiers,
tearfully saying to them,
"Do you remember your parents?"
They said,
"We do."
"Do you remember your wives and children?"
They said,
"We do."
"Do you wish to return alive?"
They said,
"We do."
"Will you follow my orders?"
They said,
"We will."
Then they beat the drums and charged into battle,
when Zhāng Láng led Jīnchéng soldiers to join them,
attacking on both sides,
achieving a great victory,
beheading several thousand.
Before this,
there was a ballad in Cháng'ān saying:
"In the land of Qín,

In the fifth month,
on the Guǐchǒu day,
Pīdī, claiming an imperial edict, arrested Kūn,
strangled him to death,
and also killed his four sons and nephews.
Kūn's Attendant Gentleman, Lú Chén, Cuī Yuè, and others led Kūn's remaining troops to flee to Liáoxī,
relying on Duàn Mòpī,
and supported Liú Jì as their lord;
most of the officers fled to Shí Lè.
Yuè
was the great-grandson of Cuī Lín.
Cuī Lín served Wèi,
reaching the position of Minister of Works.
Hoping he could pacify Héshuò,
they did not hold mourning rites for Kūn.
Wēn Qiáo submitted a memorial
"Kūn was utterly loyal to the imperial house,
his family destroyed and himself dead,
he should be praised and compensated;"
Lú Chén and Cuī Yuè, through Mòpī's envoy,
also submitted memorials pleading Kūn's injustice.
Several years later,
they posthumously awarded Kūn the titles of Grand Commandant and Palace Attendant,
with the posthumous name Mǐn.
Thereafter, because of Kūn's death, both the Yí and Jìn people
would not submit to Pīdī.
Mòpī sent his younger brother to attack Pīdī,
Pīdī led his several thousand troops intending to flee to Shào Xù,
but Shí Lè's general, Shí Yuè, intercepted him at Yánshān.
Yánshān,
is in Gāochéng County of Bóhǎi;
Suí changed Gāochéng's name to Yánshān County.
Sòng Bái said: Yánshān is eighty lǐ southeast of the county.
Pīdī had formed an alliance with Kūn,
jointly supporting the Jìn house;
after killing Kūn,
Pīdī's power also declined,
and he was eventually captured by Shí Lè.
Pīdī returned to defend Jì again.
Mòpī declared himself Governor of Yōuzhōu.
Earlier,
Wēn Qiáo was sent by Liú Kūn to present a memorial at Jiànkāng,
his mother, Madame Cuī, firmly tried to stop him,
but Qiáo tore his robe and left.
After arriving,
he repeatedly requested to return with a reply,
but the court would not permit it.
When Kūn died,
he was appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
Qiáo heard his mother had died,
but due to the chaos, he could not rush back for the mourning and burial.
He firmly declined the appointment,
bitterly requesting to return north.
An edict said:
"For all who perform rituals,
they should make them reasonable and universally applicable.
Jīng means
'constant' or 'normative'.
The armies have not yet been able to advance to escort the imperial coffin,
how can Qiáo, as a single individual,
attend to his private difficulties
and not obey the royal command!"
Qiáo had no choice but to accept the appointment.
14 Earlier,
after Cáo Nì occupied Qīngzhōu,
he rebelled against Hàn and came to surrender.
This means he sent an envoy to Jiànkāng to present a memorial urging the Emperor to ascend the throne.
Nì,
pronunciation: yú lì fān.
His support was cut off,
so he again allied with Shí Lè,
who appointed Nì as Great General of the Eastern Provinces and Governor of Qīngzhōu,
enfeoffing him as Duke of Lángyá.
Cáo Nì wavered between the two states,
and was eventually captured.
Fù,
pronunciation: fú yòu fān.
15 In the sixth month,
on the Jiǎshēn day,
Diāo Xié was appointed President of the Imperial Secretariat,
and Xún Sōng was appointed Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Xié was by nature rigid and fierce,
often clashing with others,
he and the Palace Attendant, Liú Wěi, were both favored and trusted by the Emperor;
wishing to rectify the abuses of the time,
they often exalted the sovereign and suppressed subordinates,
opposing and suppressing the powerful families,
thus they were hated by the Wáng clan.
All harsh and petty policies
were said to have been established by Wěi and Xié.
Xié was also prone to drunkenness and insolence,
insulting and slandering the high ministers,
all who saw him glared sideways in fear.
This sets the stage for Diāo Xié's later execution.
16 On the Wùxū day,
the imperial son Xī was enfeoffed as Prince of Wǔlíng.
17. Liú Hǔ invaded the western regions of Tuòbá Yùlǜ from Shuòfāng.
Hǔ had moved to Shuòfāng;
see Volume 87, the fourth year of Emperor Huái’s Yǒngjiā era.
In the seventh month,
Yùlǜ attacked Hǔ
and routed him decisively.
Hǔ fled beyond the frontier.
His cousin Lù Gū led his tribe and surrendered to Yùlǜ.
Thereupon, Yùlǜ seized the former territory of Wūsūn in the west,
and annexed the lands west of Wùjí in the east.
The Tángshū’s “Biographies of the Northern Dí” states:
The Hēishuǐ Mòhé
dwell in the land of Sùshèn,
also called Yìlóu.
In the Yuán Wèi period, they were called Wùjí.
The Zīzhì Tōngjiàn follows Wèi Shōu’s Wèishū in recording this.
What Yùlǜ seized
was the land west of Wùjí;
he did not actually annex Wùjí itself.
The Mùróng clan of Túhé, the Duàn clan of Lìngzhī, the Yǔwén tribe, and Gāogōulí
were also not within Yùlǜ’s power to subdue.
He became powerful in the north.
18. The Hàn ruler Cōng fell ill and bedridden.
He summoned Grand Marshal Yào to serve as Chancellor,
and Shí Lè as Grand General,
both to oversee the Department of State Affairs
and receive the testamentary edict to assist the government.
Yào and Lè firmly declined.
Therefore, Yào was appointed Chancellor and concurrently Governor of Yōngzhōu,
while Lè was appointed Grand General and concurrently Governor of Yōu and Jì Provinces.
Lè declined and did not accept.
Shàngluò Prince Jǐng was made Grand Steward,
Jǐnán Prince Jì was made Grand Marshal,
Chāngguó Duke Yǐ was made Grand Preceptor,
Zhū Jì was made Grand Mentor,
Hūyán Yàn was made Grand Guardian,
all overseeing the Department of State Affairs.
Fàn Lóng acted as Director of the Department of State Affairs, with ceremonial rank equal to the Three Excellencies;
Jìn Zhǔn was made Grand Minister of Works and concurrently Colonel of the Capital Region.
They took turns deciding memorials submitted to the Department of State Affairs.
On the guǐ-hài day,
Cōng died.
On the jiǎ-zǐ day,
Crown Prince Càn ascended the throne.
Càn,
styled Shìguāng.
Lady Fán was honored as Empress Hóngdào,
Lady Wǔ as Empress Hóngdé,
Lady Wáng as Empress Hóngxiào.
He established his wife, Lady Jìn, as Empress,
and his son Yuángōng as Crown Prince.
A general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed to Hànchāng.
Cōng was buried at Xuānguāng Mausoleum,
posthumously titled Emperor Zhāowǔ,
temple name Lièzōng.
Empress Dowager Jìn and others were all under twenty years of age.
Càn often behaved improperly,
showing no further grief.
Jìn Zhǔn secretly harbored rebellious intentions.
Privately, he said to Càn:
“I have heard that the various lords intend to carry out acts like Yī and Huò,
first killing the Grand Guardian and your servant,
to let the Grand Marshal control all affairs.
Your Majesty should plan early against this!”
Càn did not heed him.
Zhǔn grew fearful.
Again, he had the two Ladies Jìn speak of it.
The two Ladies Jìn
were Cōng’s empress and Càn’s empress.
Jìn,
pronounced [AS-FED7] [AS-FBED] xīn.
Again,
pronounced fú yòu.

He arrested Grand Steward Jǐng, Grand Marshal Jì, Jì’s full younger brother Chariot and Horse General-in-Chief Prince Wú of Wú Chěng, Grand Preceptor Yǐ, and Grand Minister over the Masses Prince Qí of Qí Mài,
and killed them all.
Zhū Jì and Fàn Lóng fled to Cháng’ān.
They fled to Liú Yào.
Càn drilled troops at Shànglín,
planning to attack Shí Lè.
It seems a Shànglín Park was established at Píngyáng.
Drill,
pronounced zhí zhī.
He still garrisoned Cháng’ān.
Jìn Zhǔn was made Grand General, overseeing the Department of State Affairs.
Càn often indulged in feasts in the rear palace.
Military and state affairs
were all decided by Zhǔn.
Zhǔn forged an edict appointing his cousin Míng as Chariot and Horse General,
and Kāng as Guard General.
Zhǔn was about to stage a rebellion.
He plotted with Wáng Yán.
Yán would not comply,
and galloped off
intending to report it;
intending to report Zhǔn’s plot to Càn.
He was seized and brought back.
Zhǔn then led troops into the Guāngjí Hall,
had armored soldiers arrest Càn,
enumerated his faults and killed him,
posthumously titled Emperor Yǐn.
Men and women of the Liú clan,
regardless of age, were all beheaded at the Eastern Market.
He opened the Yǒngguāng and Xuānguāng mausoleums.
Liú Yuān’s tomb was called Yǒngguāng Mausoleum.
He burned their ancestral temples.
Zhǔn proclaimed himself Grand General, Hàn Heavenly King,
assumed imperial authority,
and established officials.
He said to Hú Sōng of Āndìng:
“Since ancient times, no Hú person has been Son of Heaven.
Now I give the imperial seal to you,
to return it to the Jìn house.”
When Luòyáng fell,
the imperial seal was moved to Píngyáng.
Go,
meaning wǎng.
Seal,
pronounced sī shì.
Zhǔn grew angry
and killed him.
He sent an envoy to inform Sīzhōu Governor Lǐ Jǔ, saying:
“Liú Yuān,
a petty villain of the Túgè,
taking advantage of the Jìn’s disorder,
falsely claimed the Mandate of Heaven,
causing the two emperors to perish in obscurity.
I have led the masses to escort the imperial coffins,
and request to report this to the Emperor.”
Jǔ swiftly sent a memorial to the Emperor.
The Emperor sent Grand Ceremonialist Hán Yìn and others to receive the coffins.
Hàn’s Director of the Department of State Affairs Běigōng Chún and others gathered Jìn people,
fortifying themselves at the Eastern Palace.
Jìn Kāng attacked and destroyed them.
Běigōng Chún surrendered to Hàn;
see Volume 87, the fifth year of Emperor Huái’s Yǒngjiā era.
Yán cursed, saying:
“You rebellious Túgè slave,
why not kill me quickly?
Place my left eye at the Xīyáng Gate,
to watch the Chancellor enter;
because Liú Yào would advance troops from the west.
To watch the Grand General enter!”
Because Shí Lè would advance troops from the east.
Chancellor Yào heard of the disorder,
and hurried from Cháng’ān.
Shí Lè led fifty thousand elite troops to attack Zhǔn,
occupying the northern plain of Xiānglíng.
Zhǔn repeatedly challenged to battle,
but Lè held his fortifications firmly to wear him down.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Yào arrived at Chìbì.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: northwest of Píshì County in Hédōng,
there is the Chìshí River.
Together with Grand Mentor Zhū Jì and others, he urged Yào to assume the imperial title.
Yào ascended the throne as emperor.
Yào,
styled Yǒngmíng,
was a clansman of Yuān.
Only Jìn Zhǔn’s entire clan was excluded from the amnesty.
The era name was changed to Guāngchū.
Zhū Jì was appointed concurrent Minister over the Masses,
Hūyán Yàn concurrent Minister of Works,
and Grand Commandant Fàn Lóng and below all resumed their former positions.
Shí Lè was made Grand Marshal and Grand General,
granted the Nine Bestowments,
with an additional ten commanderies added to his fief,
and advanced in rank to Duke of Zhào.
Lè attacked Zhǔn at Píngyáng.
Over a hundred thousand settlements of Bā and Qiāng and Jié surrendered.
Bā,
refers to the Bā Dí.
When Cáo Cāo pacified Hànzhōng,
he moved the Bā Dí to Guānzhōng.
Later, their kind multiplied,
and they were present in Hédōng and Píngyáng.
Jié,
pronounced jū yè.
The Hàn ruler Yào sent General Who Conquers the North Liú Yǎ and General Who Guards the North Liú Cè to station at Fényīn.
Fényīn County,
belonged to Hédōng Commandery in Hàn times,
abolished in Jìn.
19. In the eleventh month,
on the yǐ-mǎo day,
the sun appeared at night,
three zhàng high.
20. An edict appointed Wáng Dūn as Governor of Jīngzhōu,
and added Táo Kǎn as Commander of Jiāozhōu Military Affairs.
Dūn firmly declined the governorship,
so he was allowed to serve as Regional Inspector.
On the Gēngshēn day (the 21st),
the Emperor issued an edict ordering all the dukes, ministers, and officials to each present their views on the government's shortcomings and merits.
The Palace Aide to the Censor-in-Chief, Xióng Yuǎn, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"The Hu bandits have thrown Xià into chaos,
Kǒng Ānguó said: 'Huá' means
to throw into chaos.
Xià,
refers to Huáxià (China).
Xià,
is pronounced with the characters 'hù yǎ'.
Yet we cannot dispatch armies to advance and suppress them;
this is the first shortcoming.
Officials do not consider it a disgrace that the enemy has not yet been avenged,
but instead devote themselves to amusement, feasting, and drinking;
this is the second shortcoming.
They jest and banter to amuse each other.
They do not evaluate true virtue,
but only look at empty reputation;
they do not seek talent and ability,
but only engage in favoritism and connections;
those in office consider managing affairs as vulgar clerks' work,
upholding the law as harshness,
observing proper rituals as flattery,
being leisurely and composed as refined and lofty,
being unrestrained and dissolute as broad-minded gentlemen,
being arrogant and obstinate as simple and elegant;
this is the third shortcoming.
What the world despises
sinks into the mud and mire;
what the times praise
soars high into the clouds;
thus, the myriad affairs of state remain unregulated,
and customs become hypocritical and shallow.
The various offices of the court
consider compliance and obedience as good,
while those who dissent are disparaged;
how can there be ministers at court who engage in earnest debate,
or scholars without the desire for official salary and position?
In ancient times, when selecting officials,
they were required to present their views;
the Shùn Diǎn says: 'They presented their views.'
Kǒng Ānguó annotated: 'Fū' means
to state;
'zòu' means
to present;
each was made to state and present words on governing.
This greatly violates ancient principles.
This refers to the Xiùcái and Xiàolián being appointed as officials without examination.
The application of laws does not reach the powerful and noble,
thus talent does not suffice for practical affairs,
and wickedness goes unpunished.
If this way is not changed,
seeking to save the country from chaos,
is difficult indeed!"
Previously,
the Emperor, considering the times of turmoil and disorder,
wished to comfort and please the people's hearts.
For Xiùcái and Xiàolián from the commanderies and counties,
those who arrived were not examined,
but were all universally appointed as officials.
Xiùcái and Xiàolián,
refer to those recommended by the commanderies and counties as Xiùcái and Xiàolián.
Xiān,
is pronounced with the characters 'xī jiàn'.
"We should gradually follow the old system,
and test them with classics and policy questions."
In the early Jìn, Xiùcái and Xiàolián who passed the examinations in classics and policy,
were like Huà Tán and others.
Yún,
is pronounced with the characters 'yú lún',
also 'jū yún'.
An edict was then issued:
"For those who do not pass the examination,
the Regional Inspector and Grand Administrator shall be dismissed from office."
This intended to punish the recommending officials.
Zhòng,
is pronounced with the characters 'zhú zhòng'.
Those who had arrived,
also all pleaded illness,
so that for three years, no one came to take the examination.
The Emperor wished to specially appoint those Xiàolián who had already arrived to official posts.
The Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat, Kǒng Tǎn, submitted a memorial discussion,
stating:
"Those from nearby commanderies, fearing to implicate their lords and fathers,
all did not dare to come;
those from distant commanderies, hoping to avoid examination,
recklessly came forward.
Now if we partially grant appointments,
this would mean that those who cautiously uphold the law lose their due,
while those who seek by luck and chance gain office;
decadent customs would harm teaching,
and I fear this would begin from here.
It would be better to send them all back,
and extend the deadline for them,
allowing them to pursue studies,
then the law would be fair and the order trustworthy."
The Emperor followed this,
allowing the Xiàolián an extension until seven years before taking the examination.
Shēn,
means to extend.
He was a nephew of Yú.
On the 22nd, Jìn Zhǔn sent the Palace Attendant Bǔ Tài to deliver the imperial carriage and regalia to Shí Lè to seek peace;
Shí Lè imprisoned Bǔ Tài,
and sent him to the Hàn sovereign Liào.
Liào said to Bǔ Tài:
"In the final years of the late Emperor,
he truly violated the great moral principles.
The late Emperor,
refers to Càn;
violating moral principles,
refers to his incestuous relations with his various mothers.
That I have come to this,
his merit is great indeed.
If he had earlier welcomed the imperial carriage,
I would have entrusted all government affairs to him,
let alone sparing his life!
You, sir, shall enter the city for me,
and fully convey this meaning."
Bǔ Tài returned to Píngyáng,
but Jìn Zhǔn, considering that he had killed Liào's mother and brother,
hesitated and did not comply.
Liào's mother, Lady Hú,
was killed by Jìn Zhǔn,
his brother's name is lost in history.
Chényín,
means hesitant and indecisive.
Chén,
is pronounced with the characters 'chí lín'.
The Generals of Chariots and Cavalry on the Left and Right, Qiáo Tài and Wáng Téng, and the General of the Guards, Jìn Kāng, and others,
together killed Jìn Zhǔn,
and recommended the Imperial Secretary Ling, Jìn Míng, as their leader.
They sent Bǔ Tài to present the hereditary imperial seals of state and surrender to Hàn.
Shí Lè was greatly angered,
advanced his army to attack Jìn Míng.
Jìn Míng came out to battle,
was greatly defeated,
and then barricaded himself in the city for a firm defense.
On the Dīngchǒu day (the 23rd),
the Emperor enfeoffed the imperial prince Huàn as the Prince of Lángyé.
Huàn,
was the son of Lady Zhèng,
two years old,
and the Emperor loved him dearly.
Because his illness was severe,
he was therefore enfeoffed as a prince.
On the Jǐmǎo day,
he died.
The Emperor buried him with the rites of an adult,
prepared auspicious and inauspicious ceremonial garments,
constructed a garden tomb,
expending vast labor and resources.
The Right Regular Attendant of the Principality of Lángyé, Kuàijī's Sūn Xiāo,
Jìn records: Principalities established one Left and one Right Regular Attendant.
said: "In ancient times, during times of famine and disaster, rites were reduced;
moreover, now within the seas there is mourning and chaos,
and even following the old institutions and regulations,
we should still practice frugality.
Yet what the ritual codes do not prescribe,
why honor and adorn to such an extent!
Burying a child who died without mourning garments with the rites of an adult,
is not found in the ancient classics.
Undertaking unbeneficial matters,
exhausting already depleted resources,
expending on useless costs—
this is what makes your servant uneasy."
The Emperor did not heed him.
On the 24th, the Administrator of Péngchéng, Zhōu Fǔ, killed the Administrator of Pèi, Zhōu Mò,
and led his troops to surrender to Shí Lè.
An edict ordered the Administrator of Xiàpī, Liú Xiá, to concurrently serve as Administrator of Péngchéng,
and together with the Regional Inspector of Xúzhōu, Cài Bào, and the Grand Administrator of Tàishān, Xú Kān, to jointly attack him.
Bào,
was the great-great-grandson of Zhì.
Cài Zhì,
was a man of Hàn,
the uncle of Cài Yōng.
Kān,
is pronounced with the characters 'kǒu hán'.
On the 25th, Shí Hǔ led the troops of Yōu and Jì to join Shí Lè in attacking Píngyáng.
Jìn Míng was repeatedly defeated,
and sent an envoy to seek help from Hàn.
The Hàn sovereign Liào sent Liú Yǎ and Liú Cè to welcome him.
Jìn Míng led fifteen thousand men and women of Píngyáng to flee to Hàn.
Liào camped west at Sùyì,
Sùyì County,
belonged to the Féngyì Commandery.
He executed them all, regardless of age.
Liào welcomed the remains of his mother, Lady Hú, from Píngyáng,
and buried them at Sùyì,
naming it Yánglíng,
with the posthumous title Xuānmíng Empress Dowager.
Shí Lè burned the palaces and buildings of Píngyáng,
sent Péi Xiàn and Shí Huì to repair the two tombs, Yǒngguāng and Xuānguāng,
gathered over a hundred bodies from the Hàn sovereign Càn downwards and buried them,
established garrisons, and returned.
The governor of Liángzhōu, Lǐ Fèng, frequently achieved merits.
Chéng's ruler, Xióng's nephew Zhì, was in Jìnshòu,
and he developed a grudge against him.
Jìnshòu County belonged to Zǐtóng Prefecture.
Hé Chéngtiān said: Emperor Huì of Jìn established Jìnshòu County.
Shěn Yuē said: According to the Jìn Qǐjūzhù,
in the first year of the Tai Kang era under Emperor Wǔ,
Zǐtóng's Hànshòu was renamed Jìnshòu.
The name Hànshòu,
it is suspected was established by Shǔ;
it is said to be established by Emperor Huì,
but this is incorrect.
Xióng himself went to Fú,
sending the Grand Tutor Xiàng to attack Fèng,
and beheaded him;
appointing Lǐ Shòu as the General of the Front,
in charge of military affairs in Bāxī.

By imperial command.
Later Study Tiantai
During the reign of Zhōngzōng Yuán Huángdì in
the second year of Tàixīng
(Jǐmǎo, 319)
1 Spring,
February,
Liú Xiá and Xú Kāng attacked Zhōu Fǔ at Hánshān,
defeating and killing him.
According to Wèi Shōu's Geography,
Hánshān is located in Péngchéng County, Péngchéng Prefecture.
Kāng,
pronounced as Kuàng.
Yè's native Sū Jùn led thousands of families from his home area to build defenses for self-protection,
and many from far and near supported him.
Yè County,
belonged to Dōnglái Prefecture.
The biography of Sū Jùn states that he was from Zhǎngguǎng Yè.
According to the records,
Zhǎngguǎng Prefecture has Tǐng County,
but no Yè County.
"Leading,"
read as "commanding."
Planning to attack him,
Jùn led the masses, floated across the sea, and fled.
The Emperor appointed Jùn as the General of the Soaring Eagle,
Shěn Yuē's records: "General of the Soaring Eagle,"
during the Jiàn'ān period,
Cáo Gōng appointed Cáo Hóng.
An edict made Xiá the Prefect of Línhuái,
and Jùn the Internal Historian of Huáilíng.
In the seventh year of the Yuánkāng era under Emperor Huì,
Huáilíng Prefecture was separated from Línhuái,
this area should have been within the borders of Táng Yízhōu's Lín Yí County.
Sòng Bái says: Zhaòxìn County in Sìzhōu,
was originally Hàn Huáilíng County.
2 Shí Lè sent Zuǒ Chángshǐ Wáng Xiū to present victories to Hàn,
and Hàn's ruler Yàu sent Jiān Sītú Guō Sī to grant Lè the title of Grand Tutor,
leader of the Grand General,
advancing him to Duke of Zhào,
honoring him with special ceremonies,
with guards preceding him,
like the Cáos supporting Hàn's old practices;
appointing Wáng Xiū and his deputy Liú Mào as generals,
and granting them the titles of marquises.
Xiū's retainer Cáo Pínglè followed Xiū to Sùyì,
then stayed to serve Hàn,
reporting to Yào:
"The Grand Sīmǎ sent Xiū and others here,
when Yào first ascended the throne,
to make Lè Grand Sīmǎ,
therefore he was designated.
Internally observing the strength of the imperial forces,
waiting for his return,
and planning to ambush the royal entourage."
At the time, Hàn's soldiers were indeed exhausted,
and Yào believed him.
Thus he recalled Sī,
and executed Xiū in the marketplace.
In March,
Lè returned to Xiāngguó.
Liú Mào escaped back,
reporting the circumstances of Xiū's death.
Lè was enraged, saying:
"I served the Liú family,
going beyond the duties of a subject.
Their foundational work,
was all done by me,
now having achieved success,
they still want to plot against me.
Zhào King, Zhào Emperor,
I shall establish them myself,
what need have I for them!"
Thus, he executed Cáo Pínglè’s entire family.
This foreshadows the conflict between Liú and Shí.
3 The Emperor ordered officials to discuss the suburban sacrifice,
Shàngshū Lǐng Diāo Xié and others stated that it should wait until the return to Luò before being performed.
Sītú Xún Zǔ and others said:
"When Emperor Xiàn of Hàn moved to Xǔ,
he immediately conducted the suburban sacrifice,
according to the Fàn Shū,
in the first year of Jiàn'ān during Emperor Xiàn’s reign,
he offered sacrifice to Heaven at Anyì;
in July of that year,
he arrived at Luòyáng,
once again conducting the sacrifice to Heaven;
in August,
he moved to Xǔ,
with no recorded suburban sacrifice,
perhaps recorded in other books.
The Rites section of the Jìn Shū records Zǔ’s argument stating: when Xiàn moved to Xǔ,
the suburban altar was immediately set up.
However, the suburban sacrifice did not occur in that year of moving to Xǔ.
The Emperor agreed,
establishing a suburban altar on the Sǐ land of Jiànkāng City.
On Xīnmǎo,
