By the time they reached Liáodōng,
Bì had already been defeated,
so they went to join Mùróng Huī.
Huī appointed Péng as a participant in the military affairs of the Dragon-Charging Army.
He sent Zhèng Lín carts, oxen, grain, and silk;
but Lín did not accept any of it,
and personally farmed in the countryside.
Sòng Gāi urged Huī to report the victory to Jiāngdōng,
and Huī had Gāi draft a memorial,
which Péi Yì presented,
along with the three seals obtained, going to Jiànkāng to present them.
Gāogōulì repeatedly raided Liáodōng,
and Huī sent Mùróng Hàn and Mùróng Rén to attack them;
the Gāogōulì king Yǐfúlì came to meet them and sought an alliance,
so Hàn and Rén then returned.
18 In this year,
Pú Hóng surrendered to Zhào.
Textual analysis says: In the Thirty States and Jìn Chūnqiū,
Hóng surrendered to Liú Yào in the first year of Tàixīng.
But in the first year, Yào had not yet established his capital in Cháng'ān.
The biography of Hóng in the Jìn Shū does not give a year,
only stating
"When Yào usurped the title in Cháng'ān,
Hóng submitted to Yào,"
so it is placed in this year.
19 Túlù Lù Sōngduō raised troops in Xīnpíng and Fúfēng to support the Prince of Jìn, Sīmǎ Bǎo.
Bǎo sent his generals Yáng Màn and Wáng Lián to occupy Chéncāng,
Zhāng Yǐ and Zhōu Yōng to occupy Yīnmì,
and Sōngduō to occupy Cǎobì.
Commentary on the Water Classic: West of Lǒng Mountain,
north of Jiànglǒng City,
there is Sōngduō Chuān.
Probably Sōngduō occupied this place,
and thus it became a place name.
Cǎobì
is east of Yīnmì.
Yǐ,
Yú qǐ fān.
The Zhào ruler Yào sent his generals to attack them,
but could not overcome them;
Yào personally led troops to attack them.
1 Spring,
first month,
Yào attacked Chéncāng.
Wáng Lián died in battle,
and Yáng Màn fled to the Southern Dí.
The Dí tribes living south of Chéncāng
were the Yáng clan of Chóuchí.
Lù Sōngduō fled to Lǒngchéng;
they also captured Yīnmì.
The Prince of Jìn, Bǎo, became afraid
and moved to Sāngchéng.
Commentary on the Water Classic:
The Táo River flows northeast from Líntáo County,
passes Suǒxī City,
then goes north out of Ménxiá,
then flows northeast past the east of Sāngchéng,
then north past Āngù County.
Bǎo intended to go from Sāngchéng to Héxī.
He appointed Liú Yǎ as Grand Minister Over the Masses.
Zhāng Chūnmóu escorted Prince Bǎo of Jìn to Liángzhōu.
Zhāng Shí dispatched his general Yīn Jiàn with troops to welcome them,
claiming to provide protective escort,
but in reality to block them.
2 Duànmòbēi attacked Duànpǐdī
and defeated him.
Pǐdī said to Shào Xù:
"I am originally a barbarian,
yet I ruined my family out of admiration for righteousness.
If you do not forget our long-standing pledge,
I ask that we join forces to attack Mòbēi."
Xù agreed.
Thereupon they pursued and attacked Mòbēi together,
inflicting a major defeat upon him.
Pǐdī and his younger brother Wényāng attacked Jì.
Pǐdī fled to Shào Xù,
and Jì was taken by the Shí clan.
Jì,
pronounced jì.
At this time, both the states of Liú and Shí were named Zhào,
so historians refer to Shí Zhào as the Later Zhào to distinguish them.
Kǒng Cháng attacked eleven separate camps of Xù,
capturing them all.
In the second month,
Xù personally went out to attack Hǔ.
Hǔ had cavalry lying in ambush to cut off his retreat,
and subsequently captured Xù,
ordering him to surrender his city.
He wanted Xù to surrender Yàncì city.
Surrender,
Hùjiāng fān;
same below.
"My ambition was to repay the state,
unfortunately it has come to this.
You all must strive to serve Pǐdī as your lord,
and do not be of two minds."
Pǐdī was returning from Jì,
and before reaching Yàncì,
heard that Xù had already been lost.
The troops, frightened, scattered,
and were again intercepted by Hǔ.
Wényāng fought fiercely with several hundred of his personal guards,
and only then managed to enter the city,
joining Xù's son Jī, his elder brother's son Cún, Zhú, and others in manning the walls and holding firm in defense.
Hǔ sent Xù to Xiāngguó.
Lè, considering him loyal,
released him and treated him with courtesy,
appointing him as a Gentleman of the Masters of Writing.
He then issued an order:
"From now on, when we overcome the enemy,
and capture scholars,
they must not be summarily killed.
They must be delivered alive."
Lè treated Xù with courtesy yet ultimately killed Xù.
The reason for ordering scholars to be delivered alive
was nothing more than wanting to make them follow him.
The Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel, Liú Yìn, heard that Xù was under attack,
and said to the Emperor:
"The northern defense commands are nearly gone,
only Shào Xù remains.
If he too is destroyed by Shí Hǔ,
it will dishearten the hearts of righteous men,
and block the path for their return to allegiance.
I humbly suggest we should dispatch troops to rescue him."
Yìn
had been sent by Xù,
the matter is seen in scroll 89, the second year of Emperor Mǐn's Jiànxīng reign.
Hearing that Xù had already been lost,
he then issued an edict conferring Xù's position and duties upon his son Jī.
3 The Zhào generals Yǐn Ān, Sòng Shǐ, Sòng Shù, and Zhào Shèn, with four armies stationed in Luòyáng,
rebelled,
and surrendered to Later Zhào.
The Hàn sovereign Yào changed his state's name to Zhào,
Shí Lè proclaimed himself Prince of Zhào,
both in the previous year.
As Lè annexed Yào and finally gained the Central Plains,
therefore Later Zhào is used to distinguish them.
Ān and others rebelled again,
surrendering to the Inspector of Sīzhōu, Lǐ Jǔ.
Jǔ sent the Administrator of Yǐngchuān, Guō Mò, to lead troops into Luò.
Shí Shēng captured Sòng Shǐ's army,
and crossed the river north.
Thereupon, the people of Hénán all followed each other in submitting to Jǔ,
and Luòyáng was thus emptied.
4 In the third month,
Péi Yí arrived at Jiànkāng,
and greatly praised Mùróng Huī's might and virtue,
saying that worthy and outstanding men all served him.
The court began to regard him highly.
The court initially treated Mùróng as a border barbarian,
now, because of Yí's words, began to regard him highly.
"You are a famous minister of the central court,
you should remain in Jiāngdōng.
We will issue a separate edict to Lóngxiāng to send your family."
Yí said:
"I received the state's favor from a young age,
serving within the palace precincts.
Yí served in the Western court,
holding the positions of Vice Director of the Central Secretariat and Gentleman Attendant at the Palace Gate,
hence the statement.
Young,
Shīzhào fān.
The greatest honor of my life.
However, as the old capital has fallen,
and the imperial tombs have been desecrated,
although there are famous ministers and veteran generals,
none have been able to wash away this disgrace.
Only Mùróng Lóngxiāng has exhausted his loyalty for the royal house,
determined to eliminate the vicious rebels.
Therefore, he sent me ten thousand *lǐ* to pledge allegiance.
If I now come and do not return,
he will certainly think the court, considering him remote and backward, has abandoned him,
leaving his righteous heart isolated,
and causing him to slacken in his efforts against the bandits.
Body,
should be according to the *Zàijì* as
"slacken".
Slacken,
Jū'ài fān.
Therefore, I dare not follow personal considerations and forget public duty."
Meaning, remaining in Jiāngdōng would be following a personal plan for oneself,
returning to Jíchéng would allow assisting Huī in fighting the bandits,
which is the public duty of the realm.
Yí's heart
likely considered that Huī was someone with whom he could share achievements and fame,
and despised the Jìn sovereign and ministers for complacently enjoying peace in Jiāngtuó,
deeming them unworthy to share affairs with.
"What you say is correct."
He then sent an envoy with Yí to appoint Huī as General Who Pacifies the North and Governor of Píngzhōu.
5 In the intercalary month,
Zhōu Yǐ was appointed Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
6 Prince Bǎo of Jìn's generals Zhāng Chūn and Yáng Cì were at odds with another general, Yáng Tāo,
and urged Bǎo to execute him,
and also requested to attack Chén Ān.
Bǎo did not agree to either.
In summer,
the fifth month,
Chūn and Cì imprisoned Bǎo,
and killed him.
Bǎo's body was large and fat,
weighing eight hundred catties.
He liked to sleep,
enjoyed reading,
but was weak-willed and indecisive,
hence he met with disaster.
Bǎo had no son.
Zhāng Chūn established a son of the imperial clan, Zhān, as heir,
and titled him Grand General.
Bǎo's followers scattered,
over ten thousand fleeing to Liángzhōu.
Chén Ān submitted a memorial to the Zhào sovereign Yào,
requesting to attack Zhān and others.
Yào appointed Ān as Grand General,
to attack Zhān,
and killed him.
Zhāng Chūn fled to Fúhǎn.
Fúhǎn county,
in the Former Hàn belonged to Jīnchéng,
in the Later Hàn to Lǒngxī commandery,
Zhāng Guǐ divided it to belong to Jìnxīng commandery,
in Táng it was Hézhōu.
Fú,
pronounced fū.
He executed him before Bǎo's coffin,
and used it to sacrifice to Bǎo.
Ān buried Bǎo at Shàngguī with the rites of a Son of Heaven,
and posthumously named him Prince Yuán.
7 Yáng Jiàn campaigned against Xú Kān,
but halted his army at Xiàpī,
not daring to advance.
Cài Bào defeated Kān at Tánqiū.
Tánqiū,
located southeast of Biàn county in the state of Lǔ.
Defeat,
Bǔmài fān.
The Later Zhào Prince Lè sent his general Wáng Fúdū to rescue him,
and also had Zhāng Jìng lead troops as his rear support.
Lè made many demands,
and Fúdū was licentious and cruel,
causing Kān distress.
When Zhāng Jìng reached Dōngpíng,
Kān suspected he was coming to attack him,
so he beheaded Fúdū and over three hundred others,
and again came to request surrender.
Lè was greatly angered,
and ordered Zhāng Jìng to hold strategic positions to contain him.
Holding strategic positions to contain Kān,
wanting to prolong the situation to wear him down.
He did not accept his surrender,
and commanded Jiàn and Bào to advance and attack at the appropriate time.
Jiàn still hesitated and feared to advance.
The Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Diāo Xié, impeached and memorialized against Jiàn,
who was spared death but removed from his post,
and Cài Bào was appointed to take over command of his troops.
Wáng Dǎo, because the person he recommended was unsuitable,
requested to demote himself,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
8 In the sixth month,
Hòuzhào's Kǒng Cháng attacked Duàn Pǐdī.
Relying on his victory, he did not set up defenses.
Duàn Wényāng launched a surprise attack
and routed him completely.
9 Liú Hóng, a native of Jīngzhào, was a guest resident at Tiāntī Mountain in Liángzhōu.
Tiāntī Mountain is located
south of Gūzāng city in Wǔwēi.
Over a thousand people followed him to receive his teachings.
The attendants of Xīpíng Yuángōng Zhāng Shí all served him.
Yán Shè of the tent command and Zhào Áng of the yámén,
both fellow villagers of Liú Hóng,
were told by Liú Hóng:
"Heaven has granted me the divine seal,
signifying I should be king of Liángzhōu."
Shè and Áng believed him.
Secretly, they plotted with over ten of Zhāng Shí's attendants to assassinate Zhāng Shí
and install Liú Hóng as their lord.
Zhāng Shí's younger brother, Zhāng Mào, learned of the plot
and requested that Liú Hóng be executed.
Zhāng Shí ordered the yámén general Shǐ Chū to arrest him.
Before Chū arrived,
Shè and others, concealing blades, entered
and killed Zhāng Shí in his outer chamber.
Textual Analysis says: The Jìn Shū records
"Yán Shā, Zhào Yǎng";
and also states:
"Zhāng Shí knew of the plot,
arrested Liú Hóng and killed him."
According to the Jìn Chūnqiū,
it records
"Yán Shè, Zhào Áng";
and also, Liú Hóng died after Zhāng Shí was killed.
We now follow this.
(Liú Hóng) said:
"The Governor is already dead,
why kill me!"
Chū was furious,
cut out his tongue and imprisoned him,
had him torn apart by chariots in the Gūzāng market,
and executed several hundred of his associates.
Left Sima Yīn Yuán and others, considering Zhāng Shí's son Zhāng Jùn still young,
recommended Zhāng Mào as Governor of Liángzhōu and Duke of Xīpíng.
They granted amnesty within their territory
and appointed Zhāng Jùn as General Who Pacifies the Army.
10 On Bǐngchén,
Zhào generals Xiè Hǔ and the Commandant of Chángshuǐ Yǐn Chē plotted rebellion,
allying with Ba chieftains Jū Xú and Shè Péng, among others.
The affair was discovered,
and Hǔ and Chē were executed.
The ruler of Zhào, Liú Yào, imprisoned Xú, Péng, and over fifty others in Ēpáng,
intending to kill them.
Ēpáng
is the old foundation of the Qín dynasty's Ēpáng Palace,
also called Ē Chéng.
"A sage king employs punishments
only to execute the chief villains,
and should not kill excessively."
(Yóu Zǐyuǎn) argued this,
kowtowing until his head bled.
Liú Yào was angry,
considering him an accomplice to the rebels and imprisoned him.
He executed all of Xú, Péng, and the others,
displayed their corpses in the market for ten days,
then threw them into the water.
Thereupon, all the Ba people rebelled,
electing Ba chieftain Jū Qúzhī as their leader.
He proclaimed himself Great Qín,
changing the era name to Píngzhào.
Over 300,000 people from the Di, Qiāng, Ba, and Jié tribes in the surrounding mountains responded,
causing great chaos in Guānzhōng,
with city gates closed even during the day.
Zǐyuǎn again submitted a memorial from prison to remonstrate.
Liú Yào tore up the memorial with his own hands, saying:
"This Dàlì slave,
Dàlì
is the name of a Rong tribe;
Zǐyuǎn was likely of Rong descent.
How dare he still act like this?
Does he think death comes too late for him!"
He shouted to his attendants to kill him quickly.
Zhōngshān Wáng Liú Yǎ, Guō Sì, Zhū Jì, Hūyán Yàn, and others remonstrated:
"Zǐyuǎn is imprisoned,
facing unpredictable danger,
yet he does not forget to remonstrate.
This is the utmost loyalty.
Even if Your Majesty cannot use him,
how can you kill him!
If Zǐyuǎn is executed in the morning,
we, your ministers, should also die by evening,
to make Your Majesty's fault clear.
All under heaven will then abandon Your Majesty and leave.
With whom will Your Majesty dwell then!"
Liú Yào's anger subsided,
and he pardoned him.
Liú Yào ordered internal and external forces to be on alert,
intending to personally campaign against Qúzhī.
Zǐyuǎn again remonstrated:
"If Your Majesty truly employs my strategy,
it can be settled within a month,
and Your Majesty's royal carriage need not personally campaign."
Liú Yào said:
"Try to explain it."
Zǐyuǎn said:
"They do not have great ambitions
or seek undue aspirations,
meaning the affairs of emperors and kings
are not what common people aspire to.
They merely wish to escape death.
Your Majesty should bestow a broad and generous amnesty,
granting them a fresh start.
Regarding those implicated in the recent affair of Hǔ and Chē,
whose families, including the elderly and weak, were confiscated into the Xīguān,
release and send them all back,
allowing them to recruit each other,
and permitting them to resume their livelihoods.
Once they have a path to life,
why would they not surrender!
If among them are those who know their crimes are grave,
and who gather and refuse to disperse,
I ask to borrow five thousand of Your Majesty's weaker troops.
I will certainly behead them for Your Majesty.
Xiāo,
is an unfilial bird.
According to Shuōwén,
on the day of the winter solstice, xiāo birds are captured
and dismembered,
their heads hung on wood.
Hence, today, hanging heads is called 'xiāo shǒu'.
Wéi,
is pronounced yú wèi fān.
Xiāo,
is pronounced jiān yáo fān.
Now, the rebels fill the mountains and cover the valleys.
Mí,
means full.
Bèi,
is pronounced pí yì fān.
I fear they cannot be eliminated in a short time."
Liú Yào was greatly pleased,
issued a great amnesty that very day,
and appointed Zǐyuǎn as General of Chariots and Cavalry, Excellency with Equal Honors, Commander of Military Affairs for the Campaigns in Yōng and Qín.
Zǐyuǎn stationed his troops at Yōngchéng,
and over a hundred thousand surrendered.
Moving his army to Āndìng,
all the rebels surrendered.
Only over five thousand households of the Jū clan faction held out at Yīnmì.
He attacked them,
destroyed them,
and then led his troops to patrol Lǒngyòu.
Previously, over a hundred thousand settlements of Di and Qiāng,
relying on their strongholds, were not submissive.
Their chieftain, Xūchú Quánqú, proclaimed himself King of Qín.
Zǐyuǎn advanced and approached his fortifications.
Quánqú sent troops to resist him,
but was defeated in five consecutive battles.
Quánqú wished to surrender,
but his son Yī Yú boasted loudly to the multitude:
"In the past, even when Liú Yào came personally,
he could do nothing to us.
How much less this partial force?
Why speak of surrender!"
Leading fifty thousand elite troops,
at dawn he pressed upon the gate of Zǐyuǎn's camp.
The various generals wished to attack him,
but Zǐyuǎn said:
"Yī Yú is brave and fierce,
unmatched in the present age.
The troops he leads
are also more elite than ours.
Moreover, his father has just been defeated,
and his anger is at its peak.
His vanguard cannot be withstood.
It is better to delay,
letting his energy exhaust itself before attacking him."
So he fortified his position and did not engage.
Yī Yú grew arrogant.
Zǐyuǎn, waiting until he was unprepared,
at night,
ordered his troops to eat a morning meal in their quarters.
At dawn,
encountering a great wind and dusty darkness,
Zǐyuǎn led his entire force out to launch a surprise attack,
captured Yī Yú alive,
and took all his followers prisoner.
Quánqú was greatly frightened,
loosened his hair, cut his face, and requested surrender.
Zǐyuǎn reported to Liú Yào,
and Quánqú was appointed General Who Conquers the West and Duke of the Western Rong.
Qǐ,
means to open;
to open and present the matter to the ruler is called qǐ.
Liú Yào appointed Zǐyuǎn as Grand Minister over the Masses and Recorder of the Department of State Affairs.
Liú Yào established the Imperial Academy,
selecting 1,500 people from among the populace who were intelligent and teachable,
and chose Confucian officials to instruct them.
He constructed the Fēngmíng Observatory
and the Western Palace,
and began building the Língxiāo Terrace at Hàochí.
Sīmǎ Biāo said: Hào is located within the Shànglín Imperial Park.
Mèng Kāng said: There is a Hào Pool southwest of Cháng'ān.
Gǔ Shǐ Kǎo states: King Wǔ moved to Hào,
which is the Hào Pool at the Fēng Pavilion in Cháng'ān.
Hào is the same as Hào,
pronounced with the falling tone.
Palace Attendants Qiáo Yù and Hé Bāo submitted a memorial admonishing him,
believing:
"Duke Wén of Wèi, succeeding after a period of chaos and destruction,
practiced frugality and loved the people,
and when constructing palaces and buildings,
he did so at the appropriate time and in moderation,
thus he was able to revive the legacy of Kāngshū,
extending the state's fortune for nine hundred years.
Wèi was destroyed by the Dí people,
Duke Wén moved to reside in Chǔqiū,
wearing coarse cloth garments,
and plain silk caps,
he focused on developing resources and instructing farmers,
facilitating commerce and benefiting artisans,
only then did he begin to build cities and construct palaces,
doing so at the appropriate time and in moderation,
the common people were pleased with him,
the state became prosperous,
and Wèi was thus restored.
From when Kāngshū was first enfeoffed in Wèi,
until its destruction by Qín,
its fortune lasted over nine hundred years.
Even the petty people in the markets and streets all mocked his extravagance, saying:
'The effort spent on building one observatory
would be enough to pacify Liángzhōu!'
This means that the labor and resources used to build one observatory
would be sufficient to pacify the Zhāng clan in Héxī.
Modeling after the Qióng Terrace to build the Língxiāo Terrace,
its labor and expense
are a hundred million times that of the Fēngmíng;
if such resources were used for military campaigns,
one could simultaneously conquer Wú and Shǔ and unify Qí and Wèi!
Wú
refers to Jìn;
Shǔ
refers to Lǐ Tè;
Qí
refers to Cáo Yí;
Wèi
refers to Shí Lè.
It is four lǐ in circumference,
thirty-five zhàng deep,
with a coffin made of bronze,
adorned with gold;
such expenditure of labor and resources,
is likely beyond what the state can afford.
Qín Shǐhuáng had his tomb sealed deep into the three springs,
but before the earth was dry, it was opened and destroyed.
For details, see the memorial submitted by Liú Xiàng in the first year of the Yǒngshǐ era of Emperor Chéng of Hàn, in the thirty-first scroll.
Dry,
pronounced gān.
Tombs that are not dug up,
thus the frugal burials of sage kings,
are considerations of profound foresight.
Why does Your Majesty, in this time of restoration,
Liú Yào pacified the rebellion of the Jìn clan and established himself,
thus his ministers refer to it as a restoration.
Liú Yào issued an edict stating:
"The two Palace Attendants are earnest and possess the demeanor of the ancients,
they can be called ministers of the state;
all palace construction projects shall be halted;
the regulations for the imperial tomb,
shall fully follow the method of the Bàlíng tomb.
Enfeoff Yù as the Viscount of Ānchāng,
and Bāo as the Viscount of Píngyú,
both concurrently serving as Remonstrance Advisers;
furthermore, proclaim this throughout the land,
so that all may know that this humble court
wishes to hear of its faults."
He also abolished the Fēngshuǐ hunting park and gave it to the poor people.
The Fēng River originates from the Nánshān in Jīngzhào,
flowing northeast into the Wèi River.
Liú Yào established a hunting park on both sides of the Fēng River.
11 Zǔ Tì's general Hán Qián and the Later Zhào general Táo Bào each occupied parts of the old city of Chénchuān,
with Bào stationed at the Western Terrace,
and Qián at the Eastern Terrace,
Bào using the southern gate,
and Qián using the eastern gate,
they guarded against each other for forty days.
Zǔ Tì filled cloth sacks with soil to resemble rice,
and had over a thousand men carry them up to the terrace,
then had several men carry real rice,
resting along the road.
Bào's soldiers pursued them,
and they abandoned their loads and fled.
Bào's soldiers had long been hungry,
and upon obtaining the rice,
they believed Zǔ Tì's troops were well-supplied and well-fed,
and grew even more fearful.
First, they carried sacks of soil to transport,
this was to create suspicion for Qián;
then they had men carry rice to bait Bào's soldiers,
showing them the reality.
Zǔ Tì sent Hán Qián and another general, Féng Tiě, to ambush them at the Biàn River.
Shuǐ Jīng Zhù: The Làngdàng Canal water,
flows east from Zhōngmóu,
to Jùnyí County,
where it divides into two streams,
the southern flowing one called Shā River,
the east flowing one called Biàn River;
the Biàn River flows east into Liáng Commandery.
Bào fled overnight,
and stationed his troops at Dōngyàn City,
which was the Yàn County of the Hàn-era Dōng Commandery,
later, the Northern Wèi established Dōngyàn County,
belonging to Chénliú Commandery,
Suí changed it to Zuòchéng County,
belonging to Dōng Commandery,
Táng placed it under Huá Prefecture.
Bào's soldiers already had a fearful mindset,
and their provisions were captured by Zǔ Tì,
hence they fled overnight.
Féng Tiě occupied the two terraces,
Zǔ Tì garrisoned Yōngqiū,
Fēngqiū and Yōngqiū counties,
both belonged to Chénliú Commandery.
The Spring and Autumn Annals record,
defeating the Dí at Chángqiū,
which is within the boundaries of Fēngqiū.
Yōngqiū
was an ancient state.
Many Later Zhào garrison troops defected to Zǔ Tì,
and their territory gradually shrank.
Previously,
Zhào Gù, Shàngguān Sì, Lǐ Jǔ, and Guō Mò
were attacking each other,
Zǔ Tì sent messengers swiftly to mediate between them,
explaining the consequences of their actions,
and they all subsequently accepted Zǔ Tì's command.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
an edict was issued appointing Zǔ Tì as General Who Guards the West.
Zǔ Tì, while in the army,
shared both hardships and comforts with his officers and soldiers,
restrained himself and was generous in giving,
encouraged and supervised agriculture and sericulture,
comforted and accepted new adherents,
even those distant and lowly were treated with kindness and courtesy.
The various fortresses along the river,
which previously had hostages in Later Zhào,
were allowed to have dual allegiance,
those residing on the border between the two,
were permitted to have dual allegiance,
and were used as spies.

the Emperor stationed Liú Wěi’s army at Jīnchéng.
(Jīnchéng
was located on Púzhōu in Jiāngshèng, Dānyáng.)
The Emperor personally donned armor and inspected the troops outside the suburbs.
He appointed Gān Zhuó as Grand General Who Guards the South, Palace Attendant, and Commander of the military affairs of the two provinces of Jīng and Liáng;
Táo Kǎn was appointed concurrent Governor of Jiāng Province;
they were ordered to each lead their troops to follow behind Dūn.
When Dūn reached Shítóu,
he intended to attack Liú Wěi.
Dù Hóng said to Dūn:
“Liú Wěi has many daring soldiers;
he will not be easily defeated.
It would be better to attack Shítóu.
Zhōu Zhá is lacking in kindness,
and his troops will not fight for him.
Attacking him will surely lead to defeat;
once Zhá is defeated, Wěi will flee on his own.”
Dūn followed this advice,
appointed Hóng as vanguard,
and attacked Shítóu.
Zhá indeed opened the gates and admitted Hóng.
Dūn occupied Shítóu
and sighed, saying:
“I can no longer accomplish deeds of great virtue!”
(Dūn’s lack of loyalty to the sovereign
was evident in his words.
Fù
is pronounced Fú Yòu fān.)
“Why must it be so?
Only from now on,
let us daily forget and daily depart from it.”
(Meaning day after day,
gradually forgetting past events,
then the traces of suspicion and resentment between ruler and minister will also daily fade away.)
The emperor ordered Diāo Xié, Liú Kuí, and Dài Yuān to lead troops to attack Shítóu.
Wáng Dǎo, Zhōu Yǐ, Guō Yì, Yú Tán, and others fought out from three directions,
and the troops of Xié and others were all badly defeated.
Crown Prince Shào heard of this
and wanted to personally lead the generals and soldiers to decide the battle;
he mounted his carriage and was about to set out,
when the Palace Attendant Wēn Qiáo seized the reins and remonstrated:
"Your Highness is the heir and deputy of the state;
how can you take your own person lightly against the world!"
He drew his sword and cut the carriage yoke,
and only then did the prince stop.
Dūn held his troops and did not attend court,
allowing his soldiers to plunder.
The palace and government offices fled and scattered;
only the General of Pacifying the East, Liú Chāo, kept his troops in order and directly guarded,
along with two Palace Attendants who attended by the emperor's side.
The emperor removed his military attire,
put on court robes,
looked around and said:
"If you want my place,
you should have said so earlier!
Why must you harm the people like this!"
He also sent an envoy to say to Dūn:
"If you, sir, have not forgotten the imperial court,
and cease the troops here,
then the world can still be peacefully shared;
if not,
I shall return to Lángyá to make way for the worthy."
Diāo Xié and Liú Kuí, having been defeated,
both entered the palace
and saw the emperor on the eastern steps of the Tàijí Hall.
Steps,
meaning the palace staircase.
They wept and sobbed,
urging him to avoid disaster.
Xié said:
"Your servant should guard unto death,
and dare not have disloyalty."
The emperor said:
"Now matters are pressing;
how can we not act!"
He then ordered that horses be given to Xié and Kuí,
letting them make their own plans.
Xié was old,
unable to ride,
and had never shown kindness or discipline;
when he recruited followers,
they all abandoned him.
He traveled to Jiāngchéng,
where he was killed by someone,
and his head was sent to Dūn.
Kuí fled to Later Zhào,
where he rose to the post of Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent and died.
In the eighth year of the Xiánhé era of Emperor Chéng,
Liú Kuí followed Shí Hǔ and died in battle at Tóngguān.
Could this be the same Liú Kuí?
The emperor ordered the dukes, ministers, and all officials to go to Shítóu to see Dūn.
Dūn said to Dài Yuān:
"In the battle the other day,
did you have strength to spare?"
Yuān said:
"How could there be strength to spare in the attack?
Only that strength was insufficient!"
Dūn said:
"What does the world think of my actions now?"
Yuān said:
"Those who see the outward form call it rebellion;
those who understand the sincerity call it loyalty."
Dūn laughed and said:
"You, sir, may be called eloquent."
He also said to Zhōu Yǐ:
"Bórén,
you have failed me!"
In the first year of the Jiànxīng era of Emperor Mǐn,
Yǐ was besieged by Dù Tāo
and sought refuge with Dūn in Yùzhāng,
so Dūn considered this a favor.
"You, sir, led your army in defiance of order;
I personally led the six armies,
but could not manage the affair,
causing the royal troops to flee and be defeated—
in this I have failed you!"
On the day Xīnwèi,
a great amnesty was declared;
Dūn was appointed Chancellor, Commander of All Armies at Home and Abroad, Recorder of the Imperial Secretariat, and Governor of Jiāngzhōu,
and enfeoffed as Duke of Wǔchāng Commandery,
but he declined and did not accept.
Earlier,
when the western capital had fallen,
all sides urged the emperor to advance.
See the first year of the Jiànwǔ era in scroll ninety.
Dūn feared that the emperor, being older, would be difficult to control,
and wanted to further discuss whom to establish,
but Wáng Dǎo did not comply.
When Dūn captured Jiànkāng,
he said to Dǎo:
"Had you not followed my words,
we would nearly have been wiped out."
Dūn, because the crown prince was brave and strategic,
and admired by the court and the populace,
wanted to falsely accuse him of unfiliality and depose him.
He assembled all the officials
and asked Wēn Qiáo:
"By what virtue is the crown prince praised?"
His voice and expression were both severe.
Qiáo said:
"To probe the profound and reach the distant—
this is not something a shallow mind can measure;
viewed through ritual,
he may be called filial."
This meant that the crown prince not only had the talent to probe the profound and reach the distant,
but also fully observed the rituals of serving his parents,
thus dispelling Dūn's false accusation of unfiliality.
Dūn's plot was thus thwarted.
The Emperor summoned Zhōu Yǐ to the Guǎngshì Hall,
Guǎngshì Hall,
the name of a palace hall.
"Regarding the recent major events,
the two palaces are unharmed,
and everyone is safe.
Has the Grand General truly lived up to expectations?"
Yǐ replied:
"The two palaces are indeed as stated in Your Majesty's wise decree,
but we, your subjects, are still uncertain."
The Chief Clerk of the Protector Army, Hǎo Gǔ, and others advised Yǐ to avoid Wáng Dūn.
Yǐ succeeded Dài Yuān as General of the Protector Army,
appointing Hǎo Gǔ as Chief Clerk.
"I hold the position of a senior minister;
if the court suffers defeat and collapse,
how could I seek survival among the common folk,
or flee to foreign lands like the Hú or Yuè!"
Wáng Dūn's Army Advisor Lǚ Yī,
had once served as a Táiláng,
in the Jìn dynasty, a Shàngshū Láng was called a Táiláng.
Dài Yuān was a Shàngshū,
and disliked him.
Yī persuaded Dūn, saying:
"Zhōu Yǐ and Dài Yuān,
both enjoy high reputations,
sufficient to mislead the masses.
Their recent words
showed no trace of shame,
referring to the two men's replies to Dūn.
Zuò,
pronounced cái gè fān.
I fear there will surely be the worry of them rising again."
Dūn had long been jealous of the two men's talents,
and in his heart, he rather agreed.
Casually, he asked Wáng Dǎo:
"Zhōu and Dài,
are the hopes of the north and south,
Zhōu Yǐ,
was from Rǔnán;
Dài Yuān,
was from Guǎnglíng.
After the Jìn clan crossed south,
these two men's fame topped the era.
Cóng,
pronounced qiān róng fān.
Dǎo did not reply.
Dūn asked again:
"If not as the Three Excellencies,
should they only be made Lìng or Púyè?"
The Three Excellencies,
are the Grand Commandant, Minister over the Masses, and Minister of Works;
Lìng and Púyè,
are the Shàngshū Lìng and the Left and Right Vice Directors of the Imperial Secretariat.
Dūn said:
"If not so,
they should rightly be executed!"
Again, Dǎo did not reply.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
Dūn sent his subordinate general, Dèng Yuè from Chénjùn, to arrest Yǐ and Yuān.
Previously,
Dūn had said to Xiè Kūn:
"I intend to make Zhōu Bórén the Shàngshū Lìng,
and Dài Ruòsī the Púyè."
Dài Yuān,
styled Ruòsī.
He also asked Kūn:
"How have people's sentiments been recently?"
Kūn said:
"Your Lordship's actions,
though intended to greatly preserve the state,
the widespread talk truly does not grasp your lofty righteousness.
Meaning the masses discuss Dūn leading troops against the court,
considering it not a righteous act.
Then the sentiments would be pacified!"
Dūn angrily said:
"Are you being obtuse!
Those two are not worthy;
I have already arrested them!"
Kūn was stunned and at a loss.
Army Advisor Wáng Qiáo said:
"'With many officers, well arrayed,
King Wén's realm was greatly aided.'
From the poem 'King Wén' in the Greater Odes of the Shījīng.
Jǐ,
pronounced zǐ lǐ fān.
Dūn was greatly angered,
and wanted to execute Qiáo,
but no one dared to speak.
Kūn said:
"Your Lordship is undertaking a great endeavor,
and has not killed a single person.
If Qiáo, for offering contrary advice that offended your will,
is then used to consecrate the drums,
'What the ruler deems acceptable may have unacceptable aspects;
the minister presents the unacceptable to perfect the acceptable;
what the ruler deems unacceptable may have acceptable aspects;
the minister presents the acceptable to replace the unacceptable.'
Consecrating drums,
means killing a person and smearing their blood on drums.
Wǔ,
pronounced wǔ gù fān.
Dūn then released him,
demoting him to Chief Clerk of the Commander-in-Chief.
Demoting a Grand General's Army Advisor to Chief Clerk of the Commander-in-Chief,
sufficiently shows that Dūn's office was more powerful than other offices.
He was a distant grandson of Wáng Hún's clan.
When Yǐ was arrested,
passing by the Grand Temple on the road,
he loudly declared:
"The traitorous minister Wáng Dūn,
has overturned the state,
and unjustly killed loyal ministers;
if the spirits have power,
they should swiftly kill him!"
The arresting officer wounded his mouth with a halberd,
blood flowed down to his heels,
yet his demeanor remained composed,
and all who watched shed tears.
Together with Dài Yuān, he was killed outside the southern gate of Shítóu.
The Emperor sent the Palace Attendant Wáng Bīn to console Dūn.
Bīn had always been close to Yǐ,
so he first went to mourn Yǐ,
and then went to see Dūn.
Dūn, surprised by his sorrowful appearance,
asked about it.
Bīn said:
"I just mourned Bórén,
and could not control my emotions."
Dūn angrily said:
"Bórén brought punishment upon himself;
moreover, as an ordinary man treated you,
given Wáng Bīn's character,
Yǐ treated him as an ordinary man,
which also shows his moral judgment.
Bīn said:
"Bórén was a virtuous elder,
and a close friend of yours, elder brother;
at court, though not outspokenly forthright,
should be
Cháo,
pronounced zhí yáo fān.
yet after being pardoned, he was subjected to extreme punishment,
which is why I grieve and lament."
Then, passionately, he rebuked Dūn, saying:
"Elder brother, you raised banners and rebelled against order,
slaughtered loyal and good men,
plotted treason,
bringing disaster upon your own family!"
His words were fervent and righteous,
voice trembling with tears.
Dūn was greatly enraged,
and sternly said:
"Your madness and insubordination have reached this point!
Do you think I cannot kill you?"
At the time, Wáng Dǎo was present,
and feared for him,
urging Bīn to rise and apologize.
Bīn said:
"My foot hurts, I cannot bow;
and besides, what is there to apologize for!"
Dūn said:
"Which hurts more, your foot or your neck?"
Bīn showed no trace of fear,
and ultimately refused to bow.
Later, when Wáng Dǎo sorted through old documents in the Central Secretariat,
he saw Yǐ's memorial pleading for his life,
and holding it, he wept, saying:
"Though I did not kill Bórén,
Bórén died because of me.
I feel ashamed for the times when Dūn asked three times and I did not answer.
I have failed this good friend!"
Shěn Chōng captured Wúguó,
and killed the Internal History Zhāng Mào.
初，
Wáng Dūn heard that Gān Zhuó had raised troops,
and was greatly frightened.
Zhuó's elder brother's son Áng served as Dūn's army advisor,
and Dūn sent Áng back
to persuade Zhuó, saying:
"Your action is in accordance with a minister's duty;
I do not blame you for it.
But my family's situation is urgent,
so I had no choice but to act.
I hope you will withdraw your army to Xiāngyáng,
and we shall renew our friendship."
Although Zhuó admired loyalty and righteousness,
he was by nature suspicious and indecisive.
He stationed his army at Zhūkǒu.
The Shuǐ Jīng states: The Miǎn River flows southeast past the east of Yúndù County in Jiāngxià,
where the Xià River comes from the west to join it.
A note says: This is Zhūkǒu.
Zhū
is the same as "pig."
His army lingered there,
remaining for several ten-day periods without advancing.
After Dūn captured Jiànkāng,
he sent a court envoy with a zōuyú banner to halt Zhuó's army.
Zhū fāng,
meaning to wait for the various regional commanders to jointly send out troops.
Zōuyú,
a benevolent beast;
therefore, the zōuyú banner was used to halt the army.
Shǐ,
pronounced as shū lì fān.
Zhuó said to Áng with tears:
"What I have been worrying about
is precisely this day.
Moreover, if the Emperor remains safe and auspicious,
and the Crown Prince is unharmed,
and I am stationed upstream from Dūn,
it is not yet an immediate danger to the state.
If I were to directly occupy Wǔchāng,
Dūn, feeling pressured,
would surely seize the Son of Heaven to cut off the hopes of the realm.
It would be better to return to Xiāngyáng
and reconsider our plans later."
He then ordered the army to withdraw.
Commandant Qín Kāng and Yuè Dàoróng advised Zhuó:
"Now, if we divide our troops to cut off Péngzé,
Péngzé County,
belonging to Yùzhāng Commandery,
is where the Pénglí Lake flows into the Great River.
Dividing troops to block the mouth of Péngzé Lake
would prevent Dūn's forces above and below from communicating.
Duàn,
pronounced as dīng guǎn fān.
His troops would naturally scatter,
and he could be captured in a single battle.
You raised righteous troops but are now stopping midway;
I privately believe this is not advisable for you.
Moreover, among your subordinates,
the soldiers each seek their own advantage.
If you wish to return west,
I fear it may no longer be possible."
Zhuó did not listen.
Dàoróng wept and remonstrated day and night,
but Zhuó paid no heed;
Dàoróng died of worry and indignation.
Zhuó's nature was originally tolerant and gentle,
but he suddenly became obstinate and blocked.
This "obstinate"
means violent.
"Blocked"
means obstructed and not open.
Sāi,
pronounced as xī zé fān.
His mood was agitated,
his actions abnormal,
and those who understood knew he was about to die.
Wáng Dūn appointed Xīyáng Wáng Yàng as Grand Tutor,
promoted Wáng Dǎo to Imperial Secretary,
and made Wáng Yì the Governor of Jīngzhōu;
he changed and transferred hundreds of officials and military commanders,
demoting or dismissing them;
some appointments were changed by evening after being made in the morning,
all according to his whims.
Dūn was about to return to Wǔchāng,
and Xiè Kūn said to Dūn:
"Since you arrived in the capital,
you have claimed illness and not attended court,
so although you have achieved merit, the people's hearts are not truly won over.
Now, if you attend court to see the Son of Heaven,
and allow the ruler and ministers to clear their doubts,
then everyone will be pleased and submit."
Dūn said:
"Can you guarantee there will be no changes?"
Kūn replied:
"I recently entered the palace for an audience,
and the Emperor sat respectfully aside,
awaiting your arrival.
A ruler sits aside to await the worthy;
Kūn used this phrase.
Chí,
pronounced as zhí èr fān,
means to wait.
There will certainly be no trouble.
Mùrán,
a respectful and harmonious attitude.
I request to accompany you."
Dūn angrily said:
"Even if I kill a few hundred like you,
what harm would it do to the times!"
In the end, he did not attend court and left.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Dūn returned to Wǔchāng.
初，
Yídū Neishi Tiānmén Zhōu Jí
In the sixth year of Yǒng'ān of Sūn Hào of Wú,
Tiānmén Commandery was established from part of Wǔlíng.
Chōng County had Sōngliáng Mountain,
on the mountain was a rock,
where a crack opened several tens of zhàng wide,
its height
was such that even shooting upward with a crossbow
could not reach its top,
so it was named Tiānmén (Heaven's Gate),
and the commandery was named after it.
Sòng Bái said: Shímén County in Lǐzhōu
was where Wú established Tiānmén Commandery;
Suí abolished the commandery and made it Shímén County.
sent his elder brother's son Gāi secretly to Chángshā
to express sincerity to Chéng.
Shēn,
means to clarify;
kuǎn,
means sincerity.
Chéng sent Gāi and his assistant Shàolíng Zhōu Qí to slip out and seek help,
this is not the Shàolíng of Yǐngchuān.
In the first year of Bǎodǐng of Sūn Hào of Wú,
Shàolíng Commandery was established from the northern part of Línglíng.
Qí,
pronounced as qiū qí fān.
Jiàn,
pronounced as gǔ xiàn fān.
Yì made Qí speak to the city,
saying that the Great General had already captured Jiànkāng,
Gān Zhuó had returned to Xiāngyáng,
and external aid was logically cut off.
Meaning, judging by the circumstances,
external aid was already cut off.
Luó,
pronounced as láng zuǒ fān.
Yǔ,
pronounced as niú jù fān.
When he reached the city wall,
he shouted loudly:
"Reinforcements will arrive soon,
hold on firmly!"
Yì killed him.
Yì interrogated Gāi to death,
but he never revealed the reason,
so Zhōu Jí was spared.
Yì and others pressed their attack daily,
and Dūn also sent letters from captured court officials,
ordering Yì to shoot them into the city to show Chéng.
When those in the city learned the court could not hold,
they were all filled with regret and sorrow.
They held out for nearly a hundred days,
Liú Yì died in battle,
and the soldiers' dead and wounded lay piled on each other.
On Guǐsì,
Yì captured Chángshā,
and Chéng and others were all captured.
Yì was about to kill Yú Kuī,
and his sons and younger brothers wept before him.
Kuī said:
"All men must die;
now our entire household will become ghosts of loyalty and righteousness,
what regret is there!"
Wèi Yǐ transported Chéng and Yì Xióng to Wǔchāng in a cage cart.
All the subordinate officials fled and scattered.
Only the Registrar Huán Xióng and the Western Section Clerk Hán Jiē,
as well as the clerks of the various offices in the prefecture,
changed their clothing to serve as attendants to Chéng,
never leaving his side.
"Changed their clothing" means
they discarded their regular attire
and wore the clothing of servant boys.
"Lí"
is pronounced with the tone "lì zhì fān."
Fearing them, he killed them.
Hán Jiē and Wǔ Yán held to their resolve even more firmly.
The Inspector of Jīngzhōu, Wáng Yì, following Wáng Dūn's order,
killed Chéng along the road.
Jiē and Yán escorted Chéng's coffin to the capital,
buried him, and then departed.
When Yì Xióng reached Wǔchāng,

Wáng Dūn sent someone to show Xióng the proclamation and enumerate his crimes.
Xióng said:
"These things are indeed true.
It is only regrettable that my position was lowly and my strength weak,

To die today

Wáng Dūn was intimidated by the righteousness of his words,
released him,

Everyone congratulated him,

Soon after, Wáng Dūn sent someone to secretly kill him.
Wèi Yǐ urgently sought Dèng Qiǎn.
The villagers were all afraid for him,
but Qiǎn laughed and said:
"This is because they want to use me.
They have newly acquired the province,
and having killed many loyal and good men,
they seek me to appease public opinion."
He then went to see Yǐ.
Yǐ was pleased and said:
"You, sir,
are a Xiè Yáng of ancient times."
The Zuǒzhuàn records: The King of Chǔ besieged Sòng;
Jìn sent Xiè Yáng to Sòng,
instructing them not to surrender to Chǔ.
The people of Zhèng captured him and presented him to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ offered him great bribes,
wanting him to reverse his message,
but he refused;
after three attempts,
he pretended to agree.
They had him ascend a siege tower,
to call out to the people of Sòng and deliver his message;

The King of Chǔ was about to kill him,
and sent someone to say to him:
"You agreed to my terms and then went back on your word,

He replied:
"I received my command and set out,
prepared to die rather than fail,

My agreeing to you, my lord,
was to accomplish my mission;
to die fulfilling my mission,
is my duty and honor."
The King of Chǔ spared him and sent him back.
"Xiè"
is pronounced "hù mǎi fān."
An edict appointed Táo Kǎn as concurrent Inspector of Xiāngzhōu;
Wáng Dūn memorialized requesting Kǎn return to Guǎngzhōu,
and he was additionally appointed as a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
6 On Jiǎwǔ,
the former Zhào Empress Yáng died,
posthumously titled Xiànwén.
7 Gān Zhuó's family all urged him to guard against Wáng Dūn,
but Zhuó did not listen,
instead dispersing his troops to farm,
and whenever he heard remonstrance,
he would become angry.
The Administrator of Xiāngyáng, Zhōu Lǜ, secretly following Wáng Dūn's intention,

on Yǐhài,

Wáng Dūn appointed the Gentleman of the Palace Secretariat, Zhōu Fǔ, to supervise military affairs north of the Miǎn River,

From Nánzhèng to Xiāngyáng,
it is the course of the Miǎn River,

He was the son of Fǎng.
After Wáng Dūn achieved his ambition,
his tyranny and arrogance increased greatly.
Tribute from all quarters mostly entered his residence,
and generals, ministers, and regional governors all came from his faction.
Shùn had the Four Peaks and Twelve Pastures,

He only listened to the words of two men,

He used Zhūgě Yáo, Dèng Yuè, Zhōu Fǔ, Lǐ Héng, and Xiè Yōng as his claws and teeth.
Chōng and others were all cruel, dangerous, arrogant, and unrestrained.
They extensively built military headquarters and residences,
encroached on fields and houses,
plundered markets and roads,
and those with discernment all knew they were heading for ruin.

the seventh month,

The common people suffered famine,

He withdrew and garrisoned Héféi.
The Vice Director of the Right of the Imperial Secretariat, Jì Zhān,

It was not by imperial command,

In winter,
the tenth month,
on Jǐchǒu,
the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, the Marquis Kāng of Wǔlíng, Wáng Yì, died.

enfeoffing him as Zuǒxián Wáng,
indicating he was also of Xiōngnú descent.
Liú Yìn revealed his identity to Yùjū,
Yùjū was greatly astonished,
treated him with respect and sent him back.
Liú Yào was both sorrowful and joyful,
and said to his ministers:
"Although Yìguāng has already been made Crown Prince,
he is young, gentle, and cautious,
and I fear he may not be able to withstand the current multitude of troubles.
Yìsūn
was the former heir apparent.
(Liú Yào's Crown Prince Liú Xī, style name Yìguāng;
Liú Yìn, style name Yìsūn.)
(Nàn,
read as nàn.)
Moreover, he has experienced hardships and difficulties.
I wish to emulate King Wén of Zhōu and Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn,
to stabilize the altars of state and bring peace to Yìguāng.
What do you think?"
(King Wén of Zhōu passed over Bó Yìkǎo and established King Wǔ;
Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn passed over his eldest son Liú Jiāng and established Emperor Míng.)
"Your Majesty's plan is for the endless future of the state;
not only do we, your subjects, rely on it,
it is truly a blessing for the ancestral temples and all within the Four Seas."
Left Guānglù Dàfū Bǔ Tài and Crown Prince Tàibǎo Hán Guǎng came forward and said:
"If Your Majesty considers the removal and establishment (of the heir) to be right,
you should not further ask your ministers;
if you have doubts about it,
we would certainly be glad to hear differing opinions.
We humbly believe that deposing the Crown Prince
is wrong.
In the past, King Wén determined his successor before establishing him,
which was acceptable;
Emperor Guāngwǔ deposed his son because the mother had lost favor—
how can this be taken as a model for our sagely court!
If the heir from the Eastern Sea (i.e., Liú Xī) were maintained as successor,
he might not necessarily be inferior to Emperor Míng.
Liú Yìn's civil and military talents and strategies
are indeed supreme in the world;
however, the Crown Prince is filial, friendly, benevolent, and kind,
and is also fully capable of being a virtuous ruler in times of peace.
Moreover, the Crown Prince is
what the people and spirits rely upon;
how can it be lightly altered!
If Your Majesty truly wishes to proceed thus,
we would rather die,
and dare not accept the decree."
Liú Yào fell silent.
Liú Yìn came forward and said:
"A father's love for his sons
should be equal.
Now to depose Xī and establish me,
how dare I feel at ease!
If Your Majesty considers me somewhat capable of being driven and commanded,
could I not assist Xī in continuing the sacred enterprise!
If you must replace Xī with me,
I request to die here,
and dare not hear the command."
He then wept with sobs.
Liú Yào also could not bear to depose Liú Xī because he was born of Empress Yáng,
and thus did not depose him.
He then posthumously honored his former consort, Lady Bǔ, as Empress Yuándào.
Bǔ Tài
was Liú Yìn's maternal uncle.
Liú Yào praised his impartiality and loyalty,
appointing him as Shàng Guānglù Dàfū, Yítóng Sānsī, and concurrently Crown Prince Tàifù;
he enfeoffed Liú Yìn as Prince of Yǒng'ān,
appointing him as Shìzhōng, Wèi Dàjiāngjūn, Commander of the Imperial Guards of the Two Palaces and Various Military Affairs, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Lù Shàngshū Shì.
(The two palaces:
Liú Yào's palace and Liú Xī's palace.)
He did not use the status of heir apparent to cause Liú Xī to abandon the ordinary respect due among brothers.
18. Zhāng Mào greatly fortified the walls of Gūzāng,
and repaired the Língjūn Terrace.
(In the fourth year of Emperor Yuán's Dàxīng era,
Zhāng Mào built the Língjūn Terrace,
but stopped due to Yán Céng's remonstrance;
now he repaired it again.)
"The reason you, illustrious lord, repair the walls and build the terrace
is to learn from past calamities.
(Referring to learning from Liú Yào's attack.)
Even if you reside on a multi-layered terrace,
it will be of no benefit,
but will only cause your subordinates to doubt your loyal and trustworthy intentions,
lose the hopes of the scholars and people who rely on you,
display a shape of timidity and weakness,
and provoke the schemes of neighboring enemies.
How then will you assist the Son of Heaven,
and become hegemon among the feudal lords!
I hope you will quickly cease this project,
to rest the labor and expenses."
Zhāng Mào said:
"My late brother once lost his life to others' actions,
(Zhāng Mào's elder brother Zhāng Shí was killed by his subordinates,
events seen in the previous scroll, third year of Dàxīng.)
and I consider that calamity arose unexpectedly;
even if one had wisdom and courage, there was nothing to be done.
Kings and dukes establish defenses in dangerous places,
and brave men double their gates,
which is the way of antiquity.
(The Yìjīng says: Kings and dukes establish defenses in dangerous places to guard their states.
The Zuǒzhuàn says: Brave men double their gates,
how much more so for a state!
Chóng,
read as chóng.)
One cannot use the principles of peaceful times to demand of people in an age of hardship and difficulty."
In the end, he carried it out.
19. Wáng Dūn's nephew Wáng Yǔnzhī,
who was just at the age of wearing his hair in two topknots,
(Máo Cháng said: 'Total horns' means gathering the hair into two topknots.
Cóng,
read as cóng.)
often accompanied him.
Wáng Dūn often drank at night,
and Wáng Yǔnzhī would excuse himself, claiming drunkenness, and go to bed first.
Once, Wáng Dūn and Qián Fèng plotted rebellion,
and Wáng Yǔnzhī heard all their words.
He immediately vomited profusely where he lay,
soiling his clothes and face.
After Qián Fèng left,
Wáng Dūn indeed came with a light to look,
and seeing Wáng Yǔnzhī lying in vomit,
he no longer suspected him.
Later, when his father Wáng Shū was appointed as Tíngwèi,
Wáng Yǔnzhī requested to return and visit his father,
and fully reported Wáng Dūn and Qián Fèng's plot to Wáng Shū.
Wáng Shū and Wáng Dǎo together informed the Emperor,
who secretly made preparations.
Wáng Dūn wanted to strengthen his clan,
and weaken the imperial house.
In winter,
the eleventh month,
he transferred Wáng Hán to be Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn, Commander of Various Military Affairs in Yángzhōu Jiāngxī,
Wáng Shū to be Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ, Supervisor of Various Military Affairs in Miǎnnán, Jīngzhōu,
and Wáng Bīn to be Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
20. The ruler of Hòuzhào, Shí Lè, appointed his staff officer Fán Tǎn as Zhāngwǔ Nèishǐ.
(Zhāngwǔ County,
belonged to Bóhǎi Commandery in Hàn times;
in the first year of Emperor Wǔ's Tàishǐ era,
the separate Zhāngwǔ Principality was established;
Suí abolished Zhāngwǔ,
merging it into Héjiān Commandery;
in Táng it was Yíng Prefecture.)
He asked him.
Fán Tǎn replied frankly:
"Recently, I was plundered by Jié bandits,
and all my assets were completely lost."
Shí Lè laughed and said:
"The Jié bandits are so without principle!
I shall now compensate you."
Fán Tǎn was greatly afraid,
kowtowed, wept, and apologized.
Shí Lè bestowed upon him a carriage, horses, clothing, and three million in travel money, and sent him off.
21 This year,
the Sīsǒu of Yuèxī attacked the general Rén Huí.
The "Account of the Southwestern Barbarians" from the History of the Former Han states: From Xī northeastwards,
there were lords and chiefs numbering in the tens,
among whom the Xǐ and Zuódū were the largest.
Yán Shìgǔ notes: Xǐ and Zuódū were two states.
Xī,
is pronounced suǐ.
Xǐ,
is pronounced sī.
This Sī,
refers to the Sī people of the Han dynasty;
in Shǔ they were called Sǒu.
Jiàng (general),
is pronounced jiàng.
Rén (surname),
is pronounced rén.
22 The Neishi of Kuàijī, Zhōu Zhá,
had five marquises in his family.
Zhá was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dōngqiān County;
his elder brother Jìng's son Mào,
was Marquis of Qīngliú Pavilion;
Mào's younger brother Zàn,
was Marquis of Wǔkāng County;
Zàn's younger brother Jìn,
was Marquis of Dūxiāng;
his elder brother Xié's son Xié,
was Marquis of Wúchéng County;
making five marquises in total.
Kuài (in Kuàijī),
is pronounced guì.
No one among the gentry of Wú could compare with them;
Wáng Dūn was jealous of them.
Dūn fell ill,
and Qián Fèng urged Dūn to eliminate the Zhōu clan early,
to which Dūn agreed.
Zhōu Sōng, because of his elder brother Yǐ's death,
(the incident is recorded in the first year of Yuánchāng of Emperor Yuán's reign).
Yǐ,
is pronounced yǐ.
Dūn had no sons,
so he adopted Wáng Hán's son Yìng as his heir.
Sōng once said in public that Yìng was not fit to command troops,
which Dūn resented.
Sōng and Zhá's nephew Yán both served as Dūn's Cānjūn Zhōngláng.
At that time, the Daoist Lǐ Tuō used sorcery to deceive the masses,
and many officials and commoners believed in and served him.
Punctuated by Hé Zīquán, proofread by Wáng Chóngwǔ and Niè Chóngqí
Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by Imperial Order
Later Student Tiān Tái
Emperor Míng of Sùzōng, Part Two
Second Year of Tàiníng
(Jiǎshēn, 324)
1 Spring,
first month,
Wáng Dūn falsely accused Zhōu Sōng and Zhōu Yán of conspiring with Lǐ Tuō to commit treason,
arrested Sōng and Yán,
and executed them in the army;
he sent Cānjūn Hè Luán to Shěn Chōng in Wú,
to kill all of Zhōu Zhá's nephews;
then advanced troops to attack Kuàijī,
and Zhá died resisting the attack.
2 The Jiàngbīng Dūwèi of Later Zhào, Shí Zhān, invaded Xiàpī and Péngchéng,
capturing Dōngguǎn and Dōnghǎi,
forcing Liú Xiá to retreat and defend Sìkǒu.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Sì River flows east from Huáiyáng City past the north of Jiǎochéng,
then flows southeast into the Huái River,
which is called Sìkǒu.
Dù Yòu said: Sìkǒu,
is located within the boundaries of Sùqiān County in Línhuái Commandery.
The Sìzhōu Cìshǐ of Later Zhào, Shí Shēng, attacked the Hénán Tàishǒu of Former Zhào, Yǐn Píng, at Xīn'ān,
and killed him.
Xīn'ān County,
belonged to Hóngnóng Commandery in the Hàn dynasty,
and to Hénán Commandery in the Jìn dynasty.
Shǒu (Tàishǒu),
is pronounced shòu;
same below.
From then on, the two Zhào states became hostile,
attacking and plundering each other daily,
and the people between Hé dōng and Hóngnóng
had no means to live.
Hé dōng and Hóngnóng
were on the border between the two Zhào states.
Shí Shēng invaded Xǔ and Yǐng,
(Xǔchāng and Yǐngchuān
were originally part of the same commandery).
He attacked Guō Sòng at Yángzhái,
Sòng fought him,
and inflicted a major defeat,
forcing Shēng to retreat and defend Kāngchéng.
According to Wèi Shōu's Treatise on Geography,
Yángzhái County had a Kāngchéng.
(Later Zhào) rushed reinforcements,
attacked the Sìzhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Jǔ and Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu Guō Mò,
and defeated them both.
3 The ruler of Chéng, Lǐ Xióng,
his empress Rén had no sons,
but he had over ten sons by concubines.
Xióng established his elder brother Dàng's son Bān as crown prince,
and had Empress Rén act as his mother.
His ministers requested that he establish one of his own sons,
but Xióng said:
"My elder brother,
was the legitimate heir of the late emperor,
possessed extraordinary talent and great achievements,
and died early when his task was nearing completion,
which I have often mourned.
(Dàng's death is recorded in the second year of Tài'ān of Emperor Huì's reign, scroll 85).
(Bān) will certainly be able to carry on the legacy of our ancestors."
The Tàifù Lǐ Xiāng and Sītú Wáng Dá admonished him, saying:
"The reason why former kings always established their own sons as heirs
was to clarify the proper order and prevent usurpation.
The cases of Duke Xuān of Sòng and Yúzhài of Wú
are sufficient to illustrate this!"
The History of the Hàn states: Establishing one's own son as heir
has been the practice since ancient times.
The Gongyang Commentary states: Duke Xuān of Sòng said to Duke Mù:
"In terms of my affection for Yǔyí, it is not as great as my affection for you;
but as the master of the altars of soil and grain and the ancestral temple,
Yǔyí is not as capable as you,
so why not remain as ruler?"
After Duke Xuān died,
Duke Mù was established,
but he expelled his two sons, Duke Zhuang Féng and Zuǒshī Bó,
and gave the state to Yǔyí.
Therefore, the nobleman greatly valued maintaining proper order,
and the disaster of Sòng
was caused by Duke Xuān.
The sons of the ruler of Wú, Yè, Yúzhài, Yímèi, and Jìzǐ were born of the same mother.
Jìzǐ was young but talented,
and all his brothers loved him,
wishing to establish him as ruler.
Yè said: If we hastily give the state to Jìzǐ now,
Jìzǐ will still not accept it.
I propose we do not pass it to sons but to younger brothers,
so that the brothers take turns as ruler and eventually pass the state to Jìzǐ.
When Yímèi died,
the state should have gone to Jìzǐ,
but Jìzǐ was away on a mission.
Liáo,
was the eldest among the sons of concubines,
and he ascended the throne.
When Jìzǐ returned from his mission, he acknowledged him as ruler.
Hélǘ said:
"The reason why our late father did not pass the state to a son but to a younger brother
was entirely for Jìzǐ's sake.
If we are to follow our late father's command,
then the state should go to Jìzǐ;
if we do not follow our late father's command,
then I should be established,
so how can Liáo be the ruler!"
Thereupon, he sent Zhuānzhū to assassinate Liáo.
Zhāng Shǒujié notes: Zhài,
is pronounced zhài.
Mèi,
is pronounced mò.
Xiāng withdrew in tears, saying:
"Disorder will begin from this!"
(This sets the stage for Xióng's sons later killing Bān).
(Bān) acted in accordance with ritual and law,
and whenever Xióng had important discussions,
he always had him participate.
4 Summer,
fifth month,
on the jiǎshēn day,
Zhāng Mào fell seriously ill.
Holding the hand of his heir, Jùn, he wept and said:
"Our family has for generations been renowned for filial piety, brotherly love, loyalty, and obedience.
Now, although the empire is in great turmoil,
you must uphold these virtues,
and not let them be lost."
He also issued an order:
"My official position was not conferred by the imperial court,
but was merely assumed to accomplish tasks.
How dare I consider it an honor!
When I die,
I should be placed in the coffin wearing a plain cap,
and not buried in court robes."
That day,
he passed away.
The envoy of Emperor Mǐn, Shǐ Shū, was in Gūzāng.
After Cháng'ān fell,
Shū had nowhere to return,
so he remained in Gūzāng.
Shǐ (envoy),
is pronounced shǐ.
He had Shū appoint Jùn as Dàjiāngjūn, Liángzhōu Mù, and Duke of Xīpíng,
and grant a general amnesty within his territory.
The ruler of Former Zhào, Liú Yào, sent an envoy to posthumously honor Mào as Tàizǎi,
with the posthumous title Chéngliè Wáng;
and appointed Jùn as Shàng Dàjiāngjūn, Liángzhōu Mù, and King of Liáng.
5. Wáng Dūn was critically ill.
He forged an imperial edict appointing Wáng Yìng as General of the Martial Guards to serve as his deputy,
and appointed Wáng Hán as Grand General of Agile Cavalry, with the authority to establish a personal administrative office and the ceremonial honors equal to those of the Three Excellencies.
Qián Fèng said to Wáng Dūn:
"If something unfortunate should happen,
should we then entrust the aftermath to Yìng?"
Wáng Dūn replied:
"Extraordinary affairs
cannot be accomplished by ordinary men.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú, in his 'Difficulties with the Elders of Shǔ,' said: 'It is only when there are extraordinary men in the world that extraordinary affairs arise.'
How could he be capable of handling great matters!
After my death,
the best course would be to disband the troops and disperse the masses,
submit to the court,
and preserve our family's standing—this is the superior plan.
Retreating to Wǔchāng,
gathering troops to defend ourselves,
while continuing to offer tribute without interruption—this is the middle plan.
While I am still alive,
to lead all our forces eastward,
hoping for a stroke of luck—this is the inferior plan."
Qián Fèng said to his faction:
"The Duke's inferior plan
is actually the superior strategy."
Thereupon, he plotted with Shěn Chōng,
waiting for Wáng Dūn to die
before launching a rebellion.
With Wáng Dūn's cruelty and perversity,
combined with Shěn Chōng and Qián Fèng,
it was what is called
"the convergence of vicious virtues."
A memorial was submitted ordering that troops rotate in three shifts, with two resting.
Initially,
the Emperor personally trusted Wēn Qiáo, the Director of the Central Secretariat.
Wáng Dūn disliked him
and requested that Wēn Qiáo be appointed as his Left Military Marshal.
Wēn Qiáo then pretended to be diligent and respectful,
managing the affairs of Wáng Dūn's headquarters,
and occasionally offering secret plans to cater to Wáng Dūn's desires.
He deeply befriended Qián Fèng,
building his reputation,
often saying:
"Qián Shìyí is full of spirit and intelligence."
Wēn Qiáo had long been renowned for his discernment of talent.
Qián Fèng's courtesy name was Shìyí.
"Discernment of talent" refers to being skilled in evaluating people and recognizing talent.
To praise and embellish someone of fine quality
is called "adornment,"
like adding decorative patterns such as algae, fire, axes, and symmetrical symbols to garments.
A mirror is used to distinguish beauty from ugliness.
Therefore, those who are astute in understanding people and capable of praising and encouraging the younger generation
are said to have the reputation of "discernment of talent."
Qián Fèng deeply befriended Wēn Qiáo.
When the position of Governor of Dānyáng became vacant—
the Jìn capital was at Jiànkāng,
with the Governor of Dānyáng serving as the Capital Governor;
the Sòng, Qí, and Liáng dynasties all followed this practice.
Hóng Kuò said: In the Western Hàn, Dānyáng Commandery
was administered from Wǎnlíng,
while Dānyáng County
corresponds to present-day Jiànkāng.
In Eastern Hàn histories, it is consistently written as
"Dānyáng."
In the Western Jìn, the commandery was moved to Jiànyè,
and Emperor Yuán changed the title of Governor to Governor of Dānyáng.
The Treatise on Geography states: The mountains have many red willows,
hence the name.
Other texts recording this commandery in the Hàn and Jìn dynasties
rarely use the character with
the "wood" radical.
By the Táng dynasty's Tiānbǎo era,
Jīngkǒu was designated as Dānyáng Commandery,
and Qǔ'ē was renamed Dānyáng County,
neither of which were the original territories of the Hàn.
"The Capital Governorship is a strategic location,
you should personally select a capable person for it.
I fear the court might appoint someone
who is not entirely suitable."
Wáng Dūn agreed
and asked Wēn Qiáo:
"Who would be suitable?"
Wēn Qiáo said:
"In my humble opinion, no one is better than Qián Fèng."
Qián Fèng also recommended Wēn Qiáo,
but Wēn Qiáo feigned refusal.
Wáng Dūn did not listen.
In the sixth month,
he recommended Wēn Qiáo for the position of Governor of Dānyáng,
and also tasked him with spying on the court.
Wēn Qiáo feared that after he left, Qián Fèng might later persuade Wáng Dūn to stop him.
During Wáng Dūn's farewell banquet,
Wēn Qiáo stood up to propose toasts.
When he reached Qián Fèng,
Qián Fèng had not yet drunk.
Wēn Qiáo pretended to be drunk,
struck Qián Fèng's headscarf with his hand tablet, knocking it off,
and angrily said:
"Who does Qián Fèng think he is,
that when Wēn Tàizhēn proposes a toast, he dares not drink!"
Wēn Qiáo's courtesy name was Tàizhēn.
Both were calmed down.
As Wēn Qiáo was about to leave,
he bid farewell to Wáng Dūn,
tears streaming down his face,
exiting the gate and returning several times.
After he left,
Qián Fèng said to Wáng Dūn:
"Wēn Qiáo is very close to the court,
and deeply befriended Yǔ Liàng.
He cannot be trusted."
Wáng Dūn said:
"Tàizhēn was drunk yesterday,
and showed a little temper.
How can you slander him like this!"
When Wēn Qiáo reached Jiànkāng,
he fully informed the Emperor of Wáng Dūn's rebellious plot,
urging him to prepare in advance,
and together with Yǔ Liàng, devised a plan to attack Wáng Dūn.
When Wáng Dūn heard of this,
he angrily said:
"I have been deceived by a petty man!"
He wrote to Minister Wáng Dǎo:
"It has only been a few days since Tàizhēn left,
and he has already done such a thing!
I must recruit someone to capture him alive
and tear out his tongue myself."
Wáng Dūn controlled the court's power from afar,
but those he particularly harmed, such as Xī Jiàn and Wēn Qiáo,
ultimately could not be eliminated by his poison.
From this, it is evident that the court's order at Jiànkāng was still capable of standing on its own.
The Emperor intended to attack Wáng Dūn
and consulted Yìng Zhān, the Minister of the Imperial Household.
Yìng Zhān encouraged him to proceed,
and the Emperor's resolve was thus fixed.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
Minister Wáng Dǎo was appointed Grand Commander and Governor of Yángzhōu,
Wēn Qiáo was made Commander of the Military Affairs of the Northern Part of Dōng'ān.
Judging from the subsequent text where Yìng Zhān commanded the armies south of the bridge,
the Northern Part of Dōng'ān refers to the armies north of the Huáiqí River.
The Textual Analysis states: Wáng Dūn's biography says:
"Wáng Dūn recommended him as General Who Conquers Rebels and Commander of the Military Affairs of Shítóu;
when Emperor Míng attacked Wáng Dūn,
he was appointed General Who Guards the South, with imperial credentials."
Now, we follow Emperor Míng's Annals.
Xī Jiàn was appointed Acting General of the Guards and Commander of the Military Affairs Accompanying the Emperor,
Yǔ Liàng was made General of the Left Guard,
and Biàn Kǔn, the Minister of Personnel, was appointed Acting General of the Central Army.
Xī Jiàn believed that military titles were of no practical benefit
and firmly declined the appointment.
He requested the summoning of Sū Jùn, Governor of Línhuái, and Liú Xiá, Governor of Yǎnzhōu, to jointly attack Wáng Dūn.
Relying on righteousness is difficult,
and weakness in power leads to collapse.
With Wáng Dūn and Qián Fèng aiding each other in wickedness,
leading a large force to attack the capital,
even with the loyalty of these gentlemen,
if they had only relied on the troops within the court to resist,
it would have been a repeat of the Shítóu incident of Zhōu and Dài.
Had it not been for Xī Jiàn's proposal to summon Liú Xiá and Sū Jùn,
it would have been perilous!
The Emperor stationed himself at Zhōngtáng.
According to Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's Qí Shū, Annals of Emperor Gāo: When Guìyáng Prince Xiūfàn rebelled,
the nobles held a meeting.
The Emperor said:
"Zhōngtáng has traditionally been a place for stationing troops.
The Commander of the Army should station at Xuānyáng Gate
to coordinate the various armies."
Thus, Zhōngtáng should be located outside Xuānyáng Gate.
Minister Sītú Dǎo heard that Dūn was critically ill,
and led his sons and nephews in mourning for Dūn.
Everyone thought Dūn was truly dead,
and all felt emboldened.
Then the Imperial Secretariat issued an edict to Dūn's headquarters,
listing Dūn's crimes, stating:
"Dūn arbitrarily established his brother's son as his successor,
for there has never been a prime minister who passed on his position without the emperor's command.
Xī,
means son;
referring to making his brother Hán's son Yìng the heir.
He had no scruples;
his ambition ran wild with wickedness,
coveting the imperial throne.
Heaven does not prolong treachery,
and Dūn has perished;
Fèng inherits this villainy,
and further fans rebellion.
Now we dispatch Minister Sītú Dǎo and others with thirty thousand fierce troops,
advancing from ten routes simultaneously;
General Píngxī Suì and others with thirty thousand elite troops,
coordinating by land and water;
We personally command all armies.
To punish Fèng's crimes.
Whoever can kill Fèng and deliver his head,
will be enfeoffed as a marquis with five thousand households.
Textual analysis says: In Jìn Chūnqiū, this edict appears before Dǎo mourned for Dūn,
hence it says
'whoever can behead and deliver Dūn's head,
will be enfeoffed as a marquis with ten thousand households,
rewarded with ten thousand bolts of cloth.'
According to this edict,
'Dūn has perished,'
meaning Dūn is already dead,
so there should be no further bounty for Dūn's head.
Now we follow Dūn's biography.
No one will be questioned,
do not harbor suspicion or resentment,
lest you bring about your own destruction.
Dūn's officers and soldiers,
who followed Dūn for years,
leaving their families behind,
We deeply pity them.
