The event is seen in the previous scroll, Yuándì's first year of Yǒngchāng.
Kǔn
is pronounced kǔ běn fān.
Sītú Dǎo believed:
"In the events of previous years,
Dūn's treachery and rebellion had not yet become apparent.
From those of us with discernment and above,
all were unaware,
no different from Zhá.
Once his treachery was realized,
Zhá immediately devoted himself to the state,
and soon met his end.
The event is seen in the previous Tàiníng era, second year.
Xiāo
is pronounced jiān yáo fān.
Xī Jiàn believed:
"Zhōu and Dài died upholding their integrity,
while Zhōu Zhá let in the enemy.
Their deeds were different, yet the reward was the same.
How can this encourage or deter!
According to the Sītú's argument,
saying that in previous years, those with discernment and above were all no different from Zhá,
then Qiáo Wáng, Zhōu, and Dài should all be held accountable.
What justification is there for granting them posthumous honors!
Now that the three ministers have been praised,
then Zhá should clearly be censured."
Dǎo said:
"Zhá and Qiáo Wáng, Zhōu, and Dài,
although their perspectives differed,
all upheld the integrity of a minister."
Jiàn said:
"Dūn's rebellious plot
had been brewing for a long time, like treading on frost.
The Yì says: Treading on frost, the solid ice is coming.
Our royal armies were not vigorous.
If Dūn's earlier actions
were righteous like Duke Huán or Duke Wén,
then could our late emperor be considered a Yōu or Lì?!"
However, in the end, Dǎo's proposal was adopted,
and Zhá was posthumously granted the title of Wèiwèi.
3 The Later Zhào king Lè granted Yǔwén Qǐdéguī official rank and nobility,
ordering him to attack Mùróng Huì.
Because in the first year, Huì had detained his envoy and sent him to Jiànkāng.
Huì
is pronounced hù zuì fān.
He appointed Liáodōng Xiàng Péi Yí as the right wing,
and Mùróng Rén as the left wing.
Qǐdéguī stationed himself at Jiāoshuǐ to resist Huáng.
Jiāoshuǐ
is the same as Jiāoluò Shuǐ.
Yí
is pronounced yú lì fān.
Jiāo
is pronounced gǔ yáo fān.
Textual analysis note: The Yànshū Zhēnglǔ Rén biography records it as
"Xībá Duī".
The Later Wèishū Yǔwén Mòhuái biography records it as
"Qǐdéguī, Xībá Duī".
The Zàijì also records it as
"Guī".
The Yànshū Wǔxuān Jì records it as
"Qǐdéguī, Xībá Xióng".
Now we follow this.
They were beheaded;
taking advantage of the victory, they joined Huáng in attacking Qǐdéguī,
and routed him completely.
Qǐdéguī abandoned his army and fled.
Huáng and Rén advanced into his state's capital,
sending light cavalry to pursue Qǐdéguī.
They pursued over three hundred lǐ beyond his state before returning,
capturing all his state's precious vessels,
and livestock numbering in the millions.
The people who surrendered and submitted numbered in the tens of thousands.
4 In the third month,
Duànmòpī died,
and his younger brother Yá succeeded him.
5 On the Wùchén day,
the imperial son Yǎn was established as Crown Prince,
and a great amnesty was proclaimed.
6 The ruler of Zhào, Yào, established Empress Liú.
7 The Northern Qiāng chieftain Péngōuchú submitted to Zhào.
The Later Zhào general Shí Tuó, setting out from Yànmén, attacked him in Shàngjùn,
capturing three thousand households,
and seizing over a million head of cattle, horses, and sheep before returning.
The ruler of Zhào, Yào, sent the Prince of Zhōngshān, Yuè, to pursue him.
Yào himself encamped at Fùpíng
to provide support for Yuè.
Yuè engaged Shí Tuó in battle by the riverside,
and beheaded him.
Fùpíng County
belonged to Běidì Commandery.
Hébīn
means the banks of the great river.
The Water Classic states: The Hé River passes west of Fùpíng County.
Tuó
is pronounced tuóhé.
The Táng dynasty's Shèngzhōu Hébīn County
was located in the territory of the Suí dynasty's Yúlín County.
Dù Yòu said: Fùpíng
was originally an old Hàn county.
In the Later Hàn, Fùpíng County was moved to the area of the present-day Péngyuán Commandery;
this is the old city of Fùpíng.
According to this: Língzhōu is the territory of the Hàn dynasty's Fùpíng County.
Southwest of the present-day Jīngzhào's Fùpíng County lies the old city of Hàn Huáidé.
This Fùpíng is likely the territory of the Hàn dynasty's Huáidé County.
Yuè recovered all the captives and returned.
8 Yáng Nándí attacked Chóuchí,
and captured it.
He seized Tián Sōng,
and stood him before him.
His attendants ordered Sōng to bow.
Sōng glared and shouted at them:
"Dī dogs!
How could a Son of Heaven's regional governor bow to bandits!"
Nándí said to him:
"Zǐ Dài,
Tián Sōng,
styled Zǐ Dài.
Zhào had sent Sōng to garrison Chóuchí; see the first year of Tàiníng in the previous scroll.
Chēn,
pronounced qīrén.
You were loyal to the Liú clan;
can you not be loyal to me?"
Sōng, with a stern expression, declared loudly:
"Bandit Dī,
you are originally a slave,
how dare you speak of great enterprise!
I would rather be a ghost of Zhào,
than be your subject!"
He turned, pushed aside a man,
seized his sword,
and lunged forward to stab Nándí,
but missed.
Nándí killed him.
9 Commandant Lǔ Qián rebelled with Xǔchāng,
and surrendered to Later Zhào.
10 In summer,
the fourth month,
the Later Zhào general Shí Zhān attacked Tán Bīn, the Governor of Yǎnzhōu, at Zōushān.
The Jìn Basic Annals
writes "Bīn"
as
"Yūn".
The Collected Records writes it as
"Bīn".
Jiàng,
pronounced jíliàng.
Bīn,
pronounced bīn.
Textual analysis states: The Imperial Annals writes
"Shí Liáng",
but here we follow the Collected Records of Shí Lè.
11 The Later Zhào Western Barbarian General-in-Chief Wáng Téng killed the Governor of Bìngzhōu Cuī Kūn and the Administrator of Shàngdǎng Wáng Shèn,
and, occupying Bìngzhōu, surrendered to Zhào.
Liú Kūn had garrisoned Bìngzhōu;
in the fourth year of Emperor Mǐn's Jiànxīng reign, he was defeated by Shí Lè,
who established the Governor of Bìngzhōu to administer Shàngdǎng.
Wáng Shèn,
a man of Zhāngwǔ,
initially raised troops,
harassing Lè's commanderies of Bóhǎi and Héjiān,
but later submitted to Lè,
who had him guard Shàngdǎng.
Shèn,
is the ancient character for shèn.
12 In the fifth month,
Táo Kǎn was appointed as General-in-Chief Who Conquers the West, Commander of the military affairs of the four provinces Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, and Liáng, and Governor of Jīngzhōu.
The men and women of Jīngzhōu congratulated each other.
Kǎn was by nature intelligent, perceptive, respectful, and diligent.
All day long he would sit upright with his knees drawn together,
and the multitude of affairs in his military headquarters
he inspected and managed without omission.
Shè,
means to record,
to put in order.
He often said to people:
"The great Yǔ was a sage,
yet he treasured every inch of time.
Yù did not value a foot-long jade disk, but prized an inch of time.
Yǔ,
pronounced niújù.
One should treasure every fraction of time.
How can one merely indulge in idle wandering and drunken revelry,
living without benefit to the age,
dying without leaving a name for posterity?
This is to abandon oneself!"
If any of his staff officers or aides neglected their duties due to idle talk or games,
he would order their wine vessels and gambling implements
to be all thrown into the river.
Military officers and officials he would have flogged,
saying:
"Chūpú
is a game for shepherds and slaves!
Many men of Jìn were fond of chūpú.
They would toss five wooden dice;
the outcomes included black calf,
pheasant,
and lu;
obtaining lu meant victory.
Pū,
pronounced púbǔ.
It is not the proper speech of the former kings,
and brings no practical benefit.
A gentleman should maintain a dignified demeanor.
How can one go about with disheveled hair and bare feet,
and call himself broad-minded and unrestrained!"
When someone presented him with gifts,
he would always ask how they were obtained.
If they came from honest labor,
even if trivial, he would be pleased,
and reward them threefold in return.
Cān,
means three.
Otherwise, he would sternly reprimand and shame them.
Qiè,
means severe;
lì,
means strict.
Once, while traveling,
he saw a man holding a handful of unripe rice,
and Kǎn asked:
"What are you doing with this?"
The man said:
"I saw it along the road,
and casually took it."
Kǎn became greatly angry and said:
"You do not till the fields yourself,
yet you playfully steal others' rice!"
He seized him and had him flogged.
Therefore, the people diligently engaged in farming,
and every household had ample supplies.
Once, when building ships,
the wood shavings and bamboo scraps
Kǎn ordered to be registered and stored.
He ordered them all to be recorded and kept in custody.
Later, at the New Year's assembly,
after snow had piled up and just cleared,
the ground in front of the audience hall was still wet from the remaining snow,
so he had the wood shavings spread on the ground.
And when Huán Wēn campaigned against Shǔ,
he also used the bamboo scraps stored by Kǎn to make nails for assembling ships.
His comprehensive and meticulous management
was all of this kind.
13 Later Zhao general Shí Shēng garrisoned Luòyáng,
raiding and plundering south of the Yellow River.
Sīzhōu Governor Lǐ Jǔ and Yǐngchuān Prefect Guō Mò's armies suffered several defeats,
and were also short on food,
so they sent envoys to submit to (Former) Zhao.
The (Former) Zhao ruler Liú Yào sent Zhōngshān Prince Yuè to lead fifteen thousand troops towards Mèngjīn,
and Zhèndōng General Hūyán Mó to lead the forces of Jīng and Sī east from Xiáo and Miǎn.
At that time, Jīngzhōu still belonged to Jin,
while most of Sīzhōu's territory had fallen to Later Zhao.
Liú Yào had obtained its people who were settled in Guānzhōng,
and sent Mó to lead them eastward.
Some say: Liú Cōng made Luòyáng into Jīngzhōu,
so the so-called Jīng and Sī forces here
were all people from the Jin's Sīzhōu.
Shuài,
read as shuài;
same below.
Yuè captured the two garrisons at Mèngjīn and Shíliáng.
This Mèngjīn garrison
was likely established at Héyīn;
the Shíliáng garrison was north of Luò.
He advanced and besieged Shí Shēng at Jīnyōng.
Later Zhao's Zhōngshān Duke Shí Hǔ led forty thousand infantry and cavalry,
entering through Chénggāo Pass,
and fought Yuè west of Luò.
Yuè's troops were defeated,
he was hit by a stray arrow,
and retreated to defend Shíliáng.
Hǔ built moats and palisades encircling it,
cutting off all communication inside and out.
Yuè's troops were starving severely,
they killed and ate their horses.
Hǔ also attacked Hūyán Mó,
and beheaded him.
Yào personally led troops to rescue Yuè,
Hǔ led thirty thousand cavalry to meet him in battle.
(Former) Zhao's Qiánjūn General Liú Hēi attacked Hǔ's general Shí Cōng at Bātè Bǎn.
Shuǐjīng Zhù: The Jiàn River originates southeast of Xīn'ān County in Hénán,
flows northeast,
passes east of Hángǔ Dōngbǎn,
which is called Bātè Bǎn.
Yào encamped at Jīngǔ,
Shuǐjīng Zhù: The Jīngǔ River originates from Tàibái Yuán,
flows southeast,
passes through Jīngǔ,
then flows further southeast,
passes by the former residence of Jin's Shí Chóng,
within the boundaries of Hénán.
In the army, for no reason, great alarm arose,
soldiers fled and scattered,
so he retreated and encamped at Miǎnchí;
at night,
they were alarmed and scattered again,
and thus returned to Cháng'ān.
In the sixth month,
Hǔ captured Shíliáng,
captured Yuè and over eighty of his officers and aides,
and over three thousand Dí and Qiāng people,
all of whom were sent to Xiāngguó,
and he buried alive nine thousand of his soldiers.
He then attacked Wáng Téng in Bìngzhōu,
captured Téng,
killed him,
and buried alive over seven thousand of his soldiers.
Yào returned to Cháng'ān,
dressed in plain clothes and waited at the outskirts,
weeping,
and entered the city only after seven days,
subsequently falling ill from rage and resentment.
Guō Mò was again defeated by Shí Cōng,
abandoned his wife and children and fled south to Jiànkāng.
Lǐ Jǔ's officers and soldiers secretly plotted to defect and surrender to Later Zhao,
Jǔ was unable to suppress them,
so he also led his forces south to return,
but his men deserted along the way,
only Guō Sòng and over a hundred others followed him,
and he died at Lǔyáng.
Lǔyáng County,
belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
Thus, the lands of Sī, Yù, Xú, and Yǎn,
largely all fell to Later Zhao,
with the Huái River as the border.
14 The (Former) Zhao ruler Liú Yào appointed Yǒng'ān Prince Yìn as Grand Marshal and Grand Chanyu,
transferred his title to Nányáng Prince,
and established the Chanyu Terrace at Wèichéng.
The Left and Right Wise Kings and below,
were all filled by prominent leaders of the Hú, Jié, Xiānbēi, Dí, and Qiāng.
15 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on Xīnwèi,
appointed Shàngshū Lìng Xī Jiàn as Chēqí General, Commander of the Military Affairs of Xú, Yǎn, and Qīng Provinces, and Governor of Yǎnzhōu,
to garrison Guǎnglíng.
16 In the intercalary month,
appointed Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè Xún Sōng
as Guānglù Dàfū and Lù Shàngshū Shì,
and Shàngshū Dèng Yōu as Zuǒ Púshè.
17 Right Guard General Yú Yìn,
was the younger brother of Empress Yuánjìng,
when Yuán Dì was Prince of Lángyá,
Yú was [his consort],
upon ascending the throne,
he posthumously honored her as Empress Jìng,
and she was enshrined in the ancestral temple,
following Yuán Dì's posthumous title as Yuánjìng.
Zōng,
was the son of Rǔnán Prince Liàng.
He commanded the imperial guards,
served directly within the palace halls,
and gathered many brave warriors as his wings;
Wáng Dǎo and Yǔ Liàng both feared him,
and spoke about him quite a bit,
but the Emperor treated him even more generously,
entrusting him with
the keys to the palace gates.
Guǎn,
means jiàn;
yuè,
is the bolt,
now called the lock key.
Liàng had a memorial to submit at night,
and asked Zōng for the key;
Zōng refused to give it,
and scolded Liàng's messenger, saying:
"Is this your family's gate?!"
Liàng became even more resentful of him.
This sets the stage for Liàng later killing Zōng.
Shǐ,
read as shǐ.
(The Emperor) did not wish to see people,
and no ministers were allowed to enter.
Liàng suspected that Zōng, Yìn, and Zōng's elder brother Xīyáng Prince Yàng were plotting treason,
pushed open the door, entered, and ascended the imperial bed,
saw the Emperor in tears,
and said that Yàng and Zōng were plotting to depose the senior ministers,
seeking to become regents themselves,
and requested their dismissal;
the Emperor did not accept.
On Rénwǔ,
the Emperor summoned Grand Tutor Yàng, Minister of Education Dǎo, Shàngshū Lìng Biàn Kǔn, Chēqí General Xī Jiàn, Hùjūn General Yǔ Liàng, Lǐngjūn General Lù Yè,
According to Jin regulations,
the Lǐngjūn General ranked above the Hùjūn General;
here, Yǔ Liàng is listed before Lù Yè,
because Liàng, as a relative of the emperor, was entrusted with authority by the late emperor.
and together they received the imperial edict to assist the Crown Prince,
taking turns entering the palace to lead troops and stand guard;
also appointed Kǔn as Right General,
Liàng as Zhōngshū Lìng,
and Yè as Lù Shàngshū Shì.
Fù,
read as fù.
On Dīnghài
the imperial edict was issued;
on Wùzǐ,
the Emperor passed away.
He was twenty-seven years old.
Thus he was able to use weakness to control strength,
eliminate rebellious ministers,
and restore the great enterprise.
On Jǐchǒu,
the Crown Prince ascended the throne as Emperor,
he was five years old.
The ministers presented the imperial seal,
presenting the seal to the successor ruler.
Xǐ,
read as xǐ.
Biàn Kǔn said sternly at court:
"Is Lord Wáng truly a minister of the state?!
The late Emperor's coffin is still in place,
the successor Emperor is not yet established,
how can this be a time for a subject to claim illness?!"
Dǎo heard this,
and came in a carriage despite his illness.
A general amnesty was declared,
civil and military officials were promoted two ranks,
and Empress Yǔ was honored as Empress Dowager.
The ministers, considering the Emperor young,
petitioned the Empress Dowager to follow the precedent of Empress Héxī of Han;
meaning to hold court and issue decrees.
And she complied.
In autumn,
the ninth month,
on Guǐmǎo,
the Empress Dowager held court and issued decrees.
She appointed Minister of Education Dǎo as Lù Shàngshū Shì,
and together with Zhōngshū Lìng Yǔ Liàng and Shàngshū Lìng Biàn Kǔn, they assisted in governing the court,
but important matters were all decided by Liàng.
Xī Jiàn was additionally appointed Chēqí Dàjiāngjūn,
Lù Yè as Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū,
both with the privilege of establishing their own administrative offices.
Nándùn Prince Zōng was appointed as Piàojì General,
and Yú Yìn as Grand Minister of the Imperial Clan.
The Minister of Education, Dǎo, claimed illness and did not attend court,
but privately saw off Chī Jiàn.
Biàn Kǔn submitted a memorial,
stating, "Dǎo violates the law for personal favor,
lacking the integrity of a high minister.
I request that he be dismissed from office."
Although the matter was suppressed and not carried out,
the entire court feared him.
Kǔn was frugal, simple, honest, and incorruptible,
decisive and straightforward in judgment,
diligent and practical in his official duties.
His temperament was not broad or tolerant,
and he refused to blindly follow the prevailing trends of the time.
Therefore, he was looked down upon by many famous scholars.
To value someone is called "duō" (to esteem),
to belittle someone is called "shǎo" (to slight).
Shǎo,
pronounced as Shào.
"You are often without leisure or ease,
as if holding tiles and stones in your mouth.
Is that not exhausting?"
Kǔn replied:
"All you gentlemen consider yourselves morally grand and magnanimous,
admiring each other's elegance and refinement.
As for one who clings to vulgarity and stinginess,
if not me, then who?"
At that time, many young nobles admired Wáng Chéng and Xiè Kūn for their unrestrained and unconventional behavior.
Kǔn sternly declared in court:
"To defy ritual and harm education—
no crime is greater than this.
The collapse of the Central Dynasty
was truly due to this."
He intended to submit a memorial to investigate and prosecute them.
The Central Dynasty
refers to the Western Jìn.
To submit a memorial and investigate
means to report to the emperor
and investigate their crimes.
The matter was then dropped.
6. The Chéngrén people attacked the Sīsǒu of Yuèxī,
defeating them.
The campaign against the Sīsǒu began in the first year of Emperor Míng's Tàixīng reign, in the previous volume.
Xī,
pronounced suǐ.
7. In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Guǐchǒu day,
Guānyáng Marquis Yīng Zhàn, posthumously titled "Liè," passed away.
Guānyáng County
belonged to Línglíng Commandery,
established during the Wú period.
8. Initially,
when Wáng Dǎo assisted in governance,
he won the support of the masses through leniency and harmony.
After Yǔ Liàng came to power,
he governed by strict laws and controlled affairs,
which somewhat lost him popular support.
The Inspector of Yùzhōu, Zǔ Yuē,
believed that his reputation and seniority were no less than those of Chī and Biàn.
Reputation refers to being praised by contemporaries,
seniority refers to ranking by age.
Moreover, he hoped to be granted the authority to establish his own administrative office but failed to obtain it.
Under Jìn regulations, only the Four Expeditions and Four Garrison Great Generals could establish their own offices.
Yuē was merely a General Who Pacifies the West;
how could he hope to establish his own office?
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu.
Thus, he harbored resentment and discontent.
When the posthumous edict praised and promoted high ministers,
it did not include Yuē and Táo Kǎn.
Both suspected that Yǔ Liàng had removed their names.
To remove
means to delete.
They had rendered meritorious service to the state,
referring to the defeat of Shěn Chōng and Qián Fèng.
Sū Jùn had ten thousand elite troops,
with excellent equipment,
and the court entrusted him with the defense of the region south of the Yangtze.
However, Jùn became increasingly arrogant and overbearing,
holding the court in contempt.
He recruited fugitives and outlaws,
and his forces grew daily.
They all relied on government provisions for sustenance,
with continuous shipments of grain and supplies.
Whenever slightly dissatisfied,
he would openly voice his anger.
Liàng, already suspicious of Jùn and Yuē,
also feared Kǎn's popularity among the masses.
In the eighth month,
he appointed the Governor of Dānyáng, Wēn Qiáo, as Military Governor of Jiāngzhōu and Inspector of Jiāngzhōu,
stationed at Wǔchāng.
The Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Wáng Shū, was appointed as the Interior Minister of Kuàijī,
to expand support and reinforcements.
He also fortified Shítóu in preparation.
Liàng's fortification of Shítóu
only served to aid Sū Jùn in resisting the righteous army later.
The Governor of Dānyáng, Ruǎn Fú, seeing that the Empress Dowager was regent
and power lay with her maternal relatives,
said to his confidants:
"Now, the foundation in Jiāngdōng is still shallow,
the ruler is young,
and the times are difficult.
Yǔ Liàng is young,
and his virtue and trustworthiness are not yet established.
In my view,
turmoil is about to arise."
He then requested to be appointed as the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu.
Fú
was the son of Ruǎn Xián.
9. In winter,
the tenth month,
the emperor's younger brother, Yuè, was enfeoffed as the Prince of Wú.
10. Nándùn Prince Sī Zōng, feeling deprived of his position, harbored resentment.
Zōng had been relieved of his military guard,
hence he considered himself deprived of his position.
Yǔ Liàng wanted to execute him,
and Zōng also intended to depose those in power.
The Palace Assistant Imperial Censor, Zhōng Yǎ, impeached Zōng for plotting rebellion.
Liàng ordered the General of the Right Guard, Zhào Yìn, to arrest him.
Zōng resisted with troops,
but was killed by Yìn.
His clan was demoted to the surname Mǎ,
and his three sons—Chāo, Chāo, and Yǎn—were all reduced to commoners.
The Grand Tutor, Prince of Xīyáng, Sī Yàng, was dismissed,
demoted to the Prince of Yìyáng County.
The Chief of the Imperial Clan, Yú Yìn, was demoted to the Grand Administrator of Guìyáng.
Zōng
was a close relative of the imperial clan;
Yàng,
the former emperor's tutor and guardian.
Yàng and Zōng
were brothers.
For Zōng, it is mentioned that he was a close relative;
for Yàng, it is mentioned that he was a tutor and guardian.
For Zōng, his clan relationship is emphasized;
for Yàng, his official position is emphasized.
From then on, Liàng increasingly lost the support of both near and far.
Zōng's associate, Biàn Chǎn, fled to Sū Jùn.
Liàng ordered Jùn to hand over Chǎn,
but Jùn protected and hid him, refusing to surrender him.
When Zōng died,
the emperor was unaware of it.
After a long time,
the emperor asked Liàng:
"Where is the white-haired elder who used to be here?"
Liàng replied that he had been executed for plotting rebellion.
The emperor wept and said:
"If my uncle says someone is a traitor,
he is killed.
If someone says my uncle is a traitor,
what should be done?"
Liàng was frightened
and turned pale.
11. The Zhào general Huáng Xiù and others invaded Cuó.
Cuó County,
during the Hàn, belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
By the Jìn,
it became the seat of Shùnyáng Commandery.
Cuó,
pronounced zàn.
12. The King of Later Zhào, Lè, following Chéng Xiá's advice,
constructed palaces in Yè,
and sent his heir, Hóng, to guard Yè,
assigning him ten thousand imperial guards.
All fifty-four battalions under the command of the Chariot and Horse General were assigned to him.
The Colonel of the Rapid as Tigers Cavalry, concurrently the Libationer of the Gate Subjects, Wáng Yáng, was put in sole command of the Six Barbarian tribes to assist him.
The Duke of Zhōngshān, Shí Hǔ, considering himself highly meritorious,
had no intention of leaving Yè.
When the three terraces were repaired,
his family was relocated.
Hǔ thus harbored resentment toward Chéng Xiá.
This sets the stage for Hǔ later killing Xiá and Hóng.
On the 13th day of the 11th month,
Shí Cōng of Later Zhào attacked Shòuchūn.

(Shè
means to withdraw.)
His troops, over a hundred thousand strong,
stretched over ten miles from north to south.
When Lè saw this,
he became even more pleased.
He said to those around him:
"You may congratulate me now!"
Lè led 40,000 infantry and cavalry into Luòyáng City.
On the jǐmǎo day,
the Duke of Zhōngshān, Hǔ, led 30,000 infantry from the north of the city westward,
attacking Zhào's central army.
Shí Kān, Shí Cōng, and others each led 8,000 elite cavalry from the west of the city northward,
striking Zhào's vanguard.
A great battle took place at Xīyáng Gate.
(Xīyáng Gate
was Xuānyáng Gate of Luò City,
the first gate on the south end of the western wall;
some say: Xīyáng Gate
was the second gate, Xīmíng Gate.)
They emerged from Chānghé Gate,
attacking from both sides.
(Chānghé Gate
was the gate at the north end of the western wall of Luò City.)
In his later years, it was especially severe;
before battle,
he would drink several dǒu of wine.
The red horse he often rode would, for no reason, become cramped and stumble.
(Jú
means the feet are curled and cannot stretch;
dùn
means the head is lowered and cannot be raised.
Jú,
pronounced as jú.)
As he was about to go out,
he drank over another dǒu of wine.
Upon reaching Xīyáng Gate,
he waved his formation to level ground.
Shí Kān took advantage of this and attacked,
and the Zhào troops were utterly defeated.
Yào, drunk and dazed, retreated,
but his horse stumbled into a stone canal,
and he fell onto the ice.
He suffered over ten wounds,
three of which pierced through his body,
and he was captured by Kān.
Lè then greatly defeated the Zhào army,
beheading over 50,000.
He issued an order:
"The one we wanted to capture was a single person,
and now we have captured him.
I command the officers and soldiers to restrain their blades and halt their vigor,
leaving a path for them to surrender."
Yào saw Lè and said:
"King Shí,
do you still recall the alliance at Chóngmén?"
According to the Shuǐjīng Zhù,
Chóngmén City
was located twenty lǐ northwest of the old city of Gòng County in Hénèi.
This alliance likely took place in the fourth year of Emperor Huái's Yǒngjiā era, during the joint siege of Hénèi.
Chóng
is pronounced zhí lóng fān.
"Today's events,
Heaven has made them so;
what more is there to say!"
On yǐyǒu,
Lè withdrew his troops.
He sent General Zhēngdōng Shí Suì to lead troops and escort Yào under guard.
Suì
was Hǔ's son.
Yào's wounds were severe,
so he was transported in a horse-drawn carriage,
with physician Lǐ Yǒng accompanying him in the same carriage.
On jǐhài,
they arrived at Xiāngguó.
Yào was housed in the Yǒngfēng small city,
provided with singing girls and concubines,
and heavily guarded with soldiers surrounding him.
Liú Yuè and Liú Zhèn, along with others dressed in fine attire, were sent to see him.
Yuè had been captured; see the third year of Emperor Míng's Tàiníng era in the previous scroll.
"I thought you all had long turned to dust;
King Shí is benevolent and generous,
and has spared you until now!
I killed Shí Tuó,
see the third year of Tàiníng in the previous scroll.
Today's calamity
is simply my own fate."
They stayed for a feast throughout the day before leaving.
Lè ordered Yào to write a letter to his crown prince Xī,
instructing him to surrender quickly;
but Yào only commanded Xī and the various ministers
"to uphold and maintain the state,
and not to change their minds because of me."
Lè saw this and was displeased;
after some time,
he had Yào killed.
In this year,
Chéng-Hàn's Xiàn King Lǐ Xiāng died.
Chéng had enfeoffed Lǐ Xiāng as the King of Hàn.
Xiāng
is pronounced sī jiāng fān.
The ruler of Chéng, Lǐ Xióng, appointed Lǐ Wù as General Zhēngběi and Governor of Liángzhōu,
replacing Shòu to garrison at Jìnshòu.
In spring,
first month,
Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments Lù Yè and his younger brother, Left Deputy of the Imperial Secretariat Lù Wán, persuaded Kuāng Shù
to attach the Yuàn City to the Western Army.
All officials went there,
and they recommended Yè to oversee military affairs of the palace city.
Táo Kǎn ordered Máo Bǎo to guard the Southern City,
and Dèng Yuè to guard the Western City.
These were the Southern City and Western City of the Yuàn City.
Right Guard General Liú Chāo, Palace Attendant Zhōng Yǎ, and Jiànkāng Magistrate Guǎn Pèi plotted to escort the Emperor to join the Western Army.
The plot was exposed,
and Sū Yì sent his general Rén Ràng from Píngyuán to lead troops into the palace to arrest Chāo and Yǎ.
The Emperor held them, weeping sorrowfully, and said:
"Return my Palace Attendant and Right Guard to me!"
Ràng seized them and killed them.
Earlier,
Ràng had been unprincipled in his youth.
Grand Master of Ceremonies Huà Héng was the Grand Impartial and Just of his home province.
Huà Héng
was from Gāotáng in Píngyuán.
Shào
is pronounced shī zhào fān.
Xíng
is pronounced xià mèng fān.
Huà
is pronounced hù huà fān.
Héng
is pronounced hù dēng fān.
When Ràng became a general under Sū Jùn,
he took advantage of the situation to carry out many killings.
But whenever he saw Héng, he was always respectful,
not daring to act violently.
At the time of Zhōng and Liú's deaths,
Sū Yì wanted to kill Héng as well,
but Ràng did his utmost to protect and save him,
so Héng was spared.
Champion General Zhào Yìn sent his subordinate general Gān Miáo to attack Zǔ Yuē at Lìyáng.
On wùchén,
Yuē fled at night with several hundred attendants to Hòu Zhào.
This sets the stage for Hòu Shí Lè's killing of Zǔ Yuē.
Guàn
is pronounced gǔ wán fān.
Shuài
is read as shuài;
same below.
Sū Yì, Sū Shuò, and Hán Huǎng jointly attacked the Táichéng,
burning the Eastern Hall of the Tàijí Palace and the Imperial Library.
Máo Bǎo ascended the city wall
and shot and killed several dozen people.
Huǎng said to Bǎo:
"You are known for courage and decisiveness;
why not come out and fight?"
Bǎo replied:
"You are known as a fierce general;
why not come in and fight?"
Huǎng laughed and withdrew.
The Crown Prince of Zhào, Xī, heard that the ruler of Zhào, Yào, had been captured,
and was greatly afraid.
He plotted with the Prince of Nányáng, Yìn, to retreat west and defend Qínzhōu.
Secretary Hú Xūn said:
"Although we have lost our ruler now,
our territory is still intact,
and the officers and soldiers have not rebelled.
We should join forces to resist them;
if we cannot resist by force,
it will not be too late to flee."
Yìn was angry,
considering this to be demoralizing the troops,
and had him executed.
Then he led the officials in flight to Shàngguī.
With Liú Yìn's talent and military prowess,
he could not hold Cháng'ān to resist Shí Lè.
Once Liú Yào was captured,
Yìn's courage was broken.
Sàng
is pronounced xī làng fān.
Jǔ
is pronounced zài lǚ fān.
Guānzhōng fell into great chaos.
Generals Jiǎng Yīng and Xīn Shù held several hundred thousand troops and occupied Cháng'ān,
sending an envoy to surrender to Hòu Zhào.
Hòu Zhào sent Shí Shēng to lead the troops from Luòyáng to join them.
In the second month,
on bǐngxū,
the various armies attacked Shítóu.
Senior Clerk of Jiànwēi Téng Hán attacked Sū Yì
and defeated him heavily.
Téng Hán advanced from Senior Clerk of Qīngchē to Senior Clerk of General Jiànwēi.
They crossed the Huái to fight.
Huái
refers to the Qínhuái River.
Xiāo
is pronounced jiān yáo fān.
Hán Huǎng and others were afraid,
and led their troops to join Zhāng Jiàn at Qū'ē.
The gate was narrow and they could not get out,
trampling over each other,
with tens of thousands dying.
The Western Army captured Sū Yì
and executed him.
Téng Hán's subordinate general Cáo Jù carried the Emperor and ran to Wēn Qiáo's boat.
The ministers saw the Emperor,
kowtowed, wept, and begged for forgiveness.
They killed the Prince of Xīyáng, Yàng,
along with his two sons Bō and Chōng, grandson Sōng, and the Prince of Péngchéng, Xióng.
Yàng's allegiance to Sū Jùn is seen in the third year of Xiánhé above;
Xióng fled to Jùn is seen in the second year of the previous scroll.
They pleaded for their lives.
The Emperor said:
"These are the ones who killed my Palace Attendant and Right Guard;
they cannot be pardoned."
So they were killed.
Minister of Education Dǎo entered Shítóu,
and ordered to retrieve his former ceremonial staff.
Dǎo had been granted the ceremonial staff since the campaign against Wáng Dūn;
when he fled from Shítóu,
he had abandoned it.
"Sū Wǔ's staff was probably not like this."
Dǎo showed a look of shame.
Dǎo was ridiculed by Kǎn,
feeling ashamed of his loss of integrity.
On dīnghài
a general amnesty was declared.
When Táo Kǎn and Wēn Qiáo were suppressing Sū Jùn,
they issued a proclamation to the various regional commanders,
ordering each to lead troops to provide support.
Biàn Dūn, the Marquis of Yìyáng and Governor of Xiāng Province, held onto his troops and did not go,
nor did he supply military provisions.
He merely sent a commander with several hundred men to follow the main army.
Both the court and the populace were astonished and sighed.
They did not expect him to act this way, yet he did,
hence they were astonished;
moreover, they thought of what kind of person he had been in the past and how he now acted this way,
hence they sighed.
Táo Kǎn memorialized that Biàn Dūn had obstructed the army,
watching and waiting without coming to the aid of the state in its crisis,
and requested that he be arrested and sent to the Minister of Justice in a prison cart.
The army that came to the sovereign's aid,
with Táo Kǎn as the alliance leader;
Xiāng Province was also under Táo Kǎn's supervision,
hence Táo Kǎn memorialized for Biàn Dūn's arrest.
Obstruct,
pronunciation as in Lǚ.
Crisis,
pronunciation as in nǎi dàn.
It was appropriate to show leniency and pardon,
so Biàn Dūn was transferred to the position of General Who Pacifies the South and Governor of Guǎng Province;
he pleaded illness and did not go,
and was summoned to serve as Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments and concurrently as Minister of the Imperial Treasury.
Biàn Dūn died of worry and shame,
and was posthumously awarded his original official title,
with the additional title of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and given the posthumous name Jìng.
The rules for posthumous names state: vigilant day and night is called Jìng;
conforming to good laws and regulations is called Jìng.
How could Biàn Dūn be worthy of this!
Your subject Guāng remarks: Yǔ Liàng, as a maternal relative assisting in governance,
first initiated the calamity,
causing the state to be broken and the sovereign endangered,
while he fled to save his own life;
Biàn Dūn, holding the position of a regional commander,
with ample troops and provisions,
watched as the court was overthrown,
sitting by to observe who would win or lose;
among the crimes of a subject,
what could be greater than this!
Not only were they not properly punished according to the law,
but they were also rewarded with favor and emoluments.
The lack of governance in the Jìn court
can thus be understood.
Who bears responsibility for this,
if not Wáng Dǎo!
8 Gāomì King Hóng was transferred to become Péngchéng King.
Hóng,
was the younger brother of Xióng.
9 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Yǐwèi,
Zhǐ'ān Zhōngwǔ Duke Wēn Qiáo died,
and was buried in Yùzhāng.
The court wanted to build a large tomb for him north of the mausoleums of Emperors Yuán and Míng,
but Grand Marshal Kǎn submitted a memorial stating:
"Qiáo's loyalty was evident in this sagely age,
and his merit and righteousness moved both men and spirits.
If the deceased have consciousness,
how could they take pleasure in today's laborious and costly affairs!
I hope Your Majesty will show compassionate grace,
and halt his reburial."
An edict followed this request.
Píngnán Army Secretary Liú Yìn was appointed as Governor of Jiāng Province.
Yìn was originally Wēn Qiáo's Army Secretary.
Minister Wáng Dǎo did not agree.
Someone said to Dǎo's son Yuè:
"Now, after the great calamity,
laws and discipline are lax and neglected.
From Jiānglíng to Jiànkāng, over three thousand lǐ,
there are tens of thousands of displaced people,
scattered throughout Jiāng Province.
Jiāng Province,
is the southern bulwark of the state,
a crucial strategic location.
Yet Yìn, with his extravagant and indulgent nature,
lies idly facing this situation.
Extravagant,
means luxurious;
extravagant,
pronunciation as tài,
also pronounced dà.
There will surely be internal troubles."
Yuè said:
"This is the intention of Píngnán General Wēn."
Wēn Qiáo was Píngnán General.
10 In autumn,
the eighth month,
Zhào's Nányáng King Yǐn led tens of thousands of troops from Shàngguī towards Cháng'ān.
The various commanderies of Lǒngdōng, Wǔdū, Āndìng, Xīnpíng, Běidì, Fúfēng, and Shǐpíng—both Róng and Xià peoples—all raised troops in response.
Wèi Shōu's Treatise on Geography mentions the Lǒngdōng Commandery,
governing the three counties of Jīngyáng, Zǔlì, and Fǔyí,
likely established by Later Zhào from a division of Āndìng.
Yìng Shào said: Zǔ,
pronunciation as jū.
Master Gǔ said: Lì,
pronunciation as lài.
Xià,
pronunciation as hù yǎ.
The Zhèngguó Canal passes by Zhòngshān,
and there is a bridge over the canal,
called Zhòng Bridge,
east of Jiǔzōng Mountain.
Sòng Bái said: The city of Lǐquán County in Yōng Province,
is the Zhòng Bridge City.
Later Zhào's Zhōngshān Duke Hǔ led twenty thousand cavalry to rescue them.
In the ninth month,
Hǔ heavily defeated the Zhào army at Yìqú.
Yìqú,
was the land of the Yìqú Róng during the Warring States period,
a county in the Former Hàn,
abolished in Later Hàn and Jìn.
Hǔ pursued the victory,
with corpses lying for a thousand lǐ.
Shàngguī fell,
and Hǔ captured Zhào's Crown Prince Xī, Nányáng King Yǐn, and over three thousand of their generals, ministers, and officers,
all of whom were killed.
The Records state: From Liú Yuān to Yào,
three generations passed over twenty-seven years before destruction.
General,
pronunciation as jí liàng.
Officer,
pronunciation as hù jiào.
He also buried over five thousand Túgè from five commanderies alive in Luòyáng.
He attacked the Jímùqiě Qiāng west of the river,
and defeated them.
Túgè,
are a branch of the Xiōngnú,
the kindred of Former Zhào;
the Túgè of the five commanderies,
are the masses of the five Xiōngnú tribes.
Jímùqiě,
is the name of a Qiāng tribe.
Tú,
pronunciation as zhí yú.
Qiě,
pronunciation as zǐ yú.
Qín and Lǒng were completely pacified.
Dí King Pú Hóng and Qiāng Chief Yáo Gēzhòng both surrendered to Hǔ. Hǔ recommended Hóng as Supervisor of the Six Barbarian Military Affairs,
and Yìzhòng as Left Commander of the Six Barbarians.
He relocated one hundred and fifty thousand households of Dí and Qiāng to Sī and Jì Provinces.
11 Earlier,
the Xiānbēi of Lǒngxī, Qǐfú Shùyán, resided in Yuànchuān.
Qǐfú,
is the name of a Xiānbēi tribe,
later used as a surname.
Yuànchuān River,
originates from the Zǐchéng Southern Mountain in Yǒngshì County of Tiānshuǐ,
flows east through Zǐchéng River,
then north past the Mùshī Yuàn,
which was the location of the Hàn imperial pastures,
with Eastern and Western Yuàn Cities,
seven lǐ apart.
The Western City was where the Qǐfú resided.
Dù Yòu said: Yuànchuān,
is within the boundaries of Wǔquán County in Lán Province.
His troops and horses were strong and numerous.
When Zhào perished,
Shùyán became fearful,
and moved to Màitián.
Shùyán died,
and his son Rùdàhán succeeded him;
Rùdàhán died,
and his son Sīfán succeeded him.
Commentary on the Water Classic: Màitián Mountain,
is on the northern border of Āndìng;
northeast of the mountain,
is Màitián City,
and further north is Màitián Spring.
Rù,
pronunciation as nú wò.
Qǐfú first appears here.
The Governor of Jiāngzhōu, Liú Yìn, grew increasingly arrogant and extravagant day by day.
He devoted himself solely to trade and commerce,
amassing wealth worth millions,
indulging in excessive drinking and pleasure,
paying no heed to government affairs.
In winter,
the twelfth month,
an edict was issued summoning the Rear General Guō Mò to serve as the Right Army General.
Mò preferred being a frontier general
and was unwilling to serve in the palace guard.
He confided his feelings to Yìn.
Mò had likely been summoned after returning to Xúnyáng from pacifying Sū Jùn.
The Jìn Annals state:
According to records, during the time of Emperor Míng of Wèi, there was a Left Army;
thus, the Left Army was an official position of the Wèi.
During Emperor Wǔ's reign,
the Front Army and Right Army were also established.
In the eighth year of the Tàishǐ era,
the Rear Army was added,
making a total of four armies,
all of which were palace guard troops.
The pronunciation of "prefer" is luò.
Frontier general:
that is, Liàng's annotation;
the same applies below.
"This is not something a petty man like me can achieve."
After the Jìn dynasty,
civil and military officials often referred to themselves as "petty men,"
a practice still observed among people in the northwest today.
Mò sought financial support from Yìn,
but Yìn refused to give it.
Because of this, Mò resented Yìn.
Yìn's Chief Clerk Zhāng Mǎn and others had always looked down on Mò.
Sometimes they would appear naked in front of him,
which Mò deeply resented.
On the Là Festival day,
Yìn sent Mò pork and wine as gifts.
Mò, in the presence of the messenger, threw them into the water.
Messenger:
an envoy.
"Now the court is depleted,
officials receive no salaries,
relying solely on supplies transported from Jiāngzhōu.
Yet Yìn allows merchant caravans to block the roads,
prioritizing private interests over public duties.
I request that Yìn be dismissed from his post."
The memorial was submitted,
but Yìn did not immediately accept blame.
Instead, he defended himself.
A refugee named Gài Zhūn seized a woman to be his wife.
Those who took refuge elsewhere were called refugees.
Gài:
pronounced gǔ hé.
Zhūn:
pronounced tú kūn.
Zhūn did not comply
and said to Guō Mò:
"Governor Liú of Jiāngzhōu refuses to accept his dismissal."
This means Yìn refused to obey the order dismissing him from office.
"He is conspiring day and night with Zhāng Mǎn and others,
and they only fear Lord Guō.
They intend to eliminate you first."
Mò believed this to be true.
Leading his followers, he waited for the city gates to open at dawn and launched a surprise attack on Yìn.
Yìn's officers wanted to resist Mò,
but Mò shouted at them:
"I have received an edict to carry out a punitive expedition!
Anyone who moves will be executed along with their three clans!"
He then entered Yìn's inner chamber,
dragged Yìn down,
and beheaded him.
Afterward, he seized Yìn's aides, including Zhāng Mǎn,
falsely accused them of treason,
and executed them all.
He sent Yìn's head to the capital,
forged an imperial edict,
and proclaimed it to everyone inside and outside.
He plundered Yìn's daughters and concubines.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: "Concubine means 'to connect.'
Hearing that the other party is courteous,
one goes to seek an audience with a gentleman."
Initially, he claimed he was heading to the capital,
but then he stopped at Yìn's former headquarters.
He tried to recruit Huán Xuān, the Minister of the Interior of Qiáoguó,
but Xuān firmly refused to comply.
Huán Xuān had returned to Wēn Qiáo the previous year
and was stationed in Wǔchāng.
13 In this year,
the Hèlán tribe and other chieftains jointly established Tuòbá Yìhuái as the King of Dài.
The Hèlán tribe supported Yìhuái,
as seen in the second year of the Xiánhé era in the previous volume.
The Book of the Later Zhōu states that the ancestors of the Yǔwén clan descended from Emperor Yán.
After Emperor Yán was defeated by the Yellow Emperor,
his descendants fled to the northern wilderness.
Later, a chieftain named Pǔ Huí obtained a jade seal while hunting,
inscribed with the words
"Seal of the Emperor."
Pǔ Huí believed it was bestowed by heaven.
In their custom, the Son of Heaven was called
"Yǔwén,"
so the state was named Yǔwén,
and it became their surname.
I believe this was likely embellished by the Yǔwén clan's ministers after they rose to power in Guānxī.
Lǐ Yánshòu said: The Yǔwén tribe originated beyond the Liáodōng frontier.
Their ancestors were distant relatives of the Southern Chányú,
and for generations, they served as chieftains of the eastern tribes.
This account seems accurate.
14 The King of Hénán, Tǔyán,
was brave and valiant but highly suspicious and jealous.
A Qiāng chieftain named Jiāng Cōng stabbed him.
Tǔyán did not draw his sword.
Instead, he summoned his general Hé Gǔ Ní
and instructed him to assist his son Yèyán
in defending Báilán.
Báilán
is located southwest of Tǔyùhún.
The terrain is treacherous and remote,
inhabited by a branch of the Qiāng people.
To the northwest, it borders Lìmó Tú,
and to the south, it borders Nà'è.
Its customs and products are roughly similar to those of Dàngchāng.
Yèyán was filial and fond of learning.
He believed that according to ritual,
"the grandson of a duke may take his grandfather's personal name as his clan name."
Thus, he named his state Tǔyùhún.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn records
that Lǔ Zhòngzhòng said:
"The Son of Heaven establishes virtue,
bestowing surnames based on birth,
granting land and conferring clan names.
For feudal lords, it is based on their personal names."
Dù Yù's commentary states: The sons of feudal lords are called gōngzǐ,
the sons of gōngzǐ are called gōngsūn,
and the sons of gōngsūn take their grandfather's personal name as their clan name.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Liú Yìn's head arrived in Jiànkāng.
The Minister of Education, Dǎo, believed that Guō Mò was fierce and brave, making him difficult to control.
On the Jǐhài day,
a general amnesty was declared.
Yìn's head was displayed on the Dàháng Bridge,
and Mò was appointed as the Governor of Jiāngzhōu.
The Grand Commandant, Kǎn, heard of this
and, throwing back his sleeves, rose and said:
"This must be a fraud!"
He immediately led troops to suppress Mò.
Mò sent envoys to present female entertainers, concubines, and silk to Kǎn,
along with a forged imperial edict.
Many of Kǎn's aides advised him:
"If Mò had not received an edict,
how would he dare to do such a thing?
If you intend to advance the army,
you should wait for a response from the court."
Kǎn sternly replied:
"The state is young,
and edicts do not come from the emperor's own will.
Liú Yìn was respected by the court.
Even if he was unfit for his position,
how could he be unjustly executed?
Guō Mò relies on his bravery
and is greedy and tyrannical wherever he goes.
Taking advantage of the recent resolution of a great crisis—"
referring to the recent pacification of Sū Jùn.
Crisis:
pronounced nǎi dàn.
"He seeks to exploit the situation to act recklessly!"
He dispatched an envoy to submit a memorial explaining the situation
and wrote to Dǎo, saying:
"If Guō Mò kills a regional governor, does he immediately become the regional governor?
If he assassinates a chief minister, does he then become the chief minister?"
Dǎo then retrieved Yìn's head
and replied to Kǎn in a letter:
"Mò holds a strategic position upstream,
and with his fleet and resources,
we must tolerate and endure for now,
allowing him to keep his territory
so the court can secretly prepare.
Secretly:
meaning covertly.
Secretly prepare:
secretly ordering the armies to make ready.
Then, with swift action,
we can converge upon him."
Swift action:
meaning with great speed.
Kǎn laughed and said:
The Governor of Yùzhōu, Yù Liàng, also requested permission to suppress Mò.
An edict appointed Liàng as the Commander of the Expeditionary Forces,
leading twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to join forces with Kǎn.
The governors of Xīyáng, Dèng Yuè, and Wǔchāng, Liú Xǔ, both suspected that Huán Xuān was in league with Guō Mò.
Wáng Suí, the Western Officer of Yùzhōu, said:
"Xuān did not even submit to Zǔ Yuē,
as seen in the second year of Xiánhé in the previous volume.
Yuè and Xǔ sent Suí to Xuān to observe him.
Suí persuaded Xuān, saying:
"Although your heart is not so,
not so,
meaning not like this.
Persuade,
shū ruì fān.
Only by entrusting your worthy son to me!"
Xuān then sent his son, Róng, to accompany Suí in welcoming Táo Kǎn.
Kǎn appointed Róng as an assistant,
and recommended Xuān to be the governor of Wǔchāng.
2 In the second month,

and Xuān fought him at Nièshuǐ,
defeating him.
The Shuǐjīngzhù states: Nièshuǐ originates from Qíjí Mountain northwest of Nièyáng County,
flows southeast past Nièyáng County,
then southeast past Ānzhòng County,
then southeast to Xīnyě County,
where it enters the Yù River.
Niè,
read as niè.
Kǎn’s nephew Zhēn and the Administrator of Jìnglíng, Lǐ Yáng, attacked Xīnyě,
capturing it.
Jìng, fearing,
fled.
Xuān
then captured Xiāngyáng.
Kǎn had Xuān garrison Xiāngyáng.
Xuān won over the newly surrendered,
simplified punishments,
minimized ceremonial pomp,
encouraged agriculture and sericulture,
sometimes carrying hoes and plows in his light carriage.
Chú is
a farming tool used for standing and weeding.
Lěi,
read as lěi,
a curved wooden hand-plow.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: The lěi is made of curved wood,
six chi and six cun long,
with a base one chi and one cun long,
the central straight part three chi and three cun long,
and the curved part two chi and two cun long.
Dǐ refers to
the forward-curved part at the bottom of the lěi that connects to the sì head and holds the sì.
Sì is
made of metal or iron.
Zhèng Xuán said: The sì is
the metal part of the lěi,
five cun wide,
a farming implement,
of the zījī category.
Yáo,
read as yáo,
a small horse-drawn carriage for envoys.
Xuān,
a curved shaft.
Enclosed panels are called xuān.
He remained in Xiāngyáng for over ten years.
The Zhào attacked twice more,
but Xuān, with meager forces, held them off,
and the Zhào could not overcome him.
Contemporaries considered him second only to Zǔ Tì and Zhōu Fǎng.
The history concludes by recounting Xuān’s achievements in defending Xiāngyáng.
6. Chéng’s Grand General Shòu invaded Níngzhōu,
with his Eastern General Fèi Hēi as vanguard,
setting out from Guǎnghàn,
and Southern General Rèn Huí setting out from Yuèxī,
to divide Níngzhōu’s forces.
The Zhao general Shí Cōng and the Qiáo Commandery Administrator Péng Biāo
each sent envoys to surrender.
Cōng was then garrisoning Qiáo City.
Shǒu (守),
is glossed as shì.
Xiáng (降),
is glossed as hùjiāng.
He had adopted the surname Shí.
The imperial court sent the Protector Qiáo Qiú to lead troops to rescue them,
but before he arrived,
Cōng and others were executed by Hǔ.
6 Mùróng Huàng sent his Chief Clerk, the Bóhǎi man Wáng Jì, and others to announce the mourning.
7 In the eighth month,
the Zhao ruler Hóng appointed the Zhōngshān Prince Hǔ as Chancellor, Prince of Wèi, and Grand Chányú,
granting him the Nine Distinctions,
and making the thirteen commanderies including Wèi Commandery his principality,
overseeing all affairs.
Hǔ issued a general pardon within his territory,
established his wife, Lady Zhèng, as Queen of the Prince of Wèi;
his son Suì as Heir Apparent of Wèi,

additionally granting him the authority of Envoy with Credentials, Palace Attendant, Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs at Home and Abroad, Great General, and Manager of the Affairs of the Masters of Writing;
his second son Xuān as Envoy with Credentials, Chariot and Horse General, and Governor of Jì Province,
enfeoffed as Prince of Héjiān;
Tāo as Vanguard General and Colonel Director of the Retainers,
enfeoffed as Prince of Lè'ān;
Zūn enfeoffed as Prince of Qí,
Jiàn enfeoffed as Prince of Dài,
Bāo enfeoffed as Prince of Lèpíng;
he transferred the Prince of Píngyuán
Bīn to become Prince of Zhāngwǔ.
The old civil and military officials of Lè
were all assigned to sinecure positions;
Hǔ's own administrative staff and relatives
were all appointed to key positions in the central administration.
Hǔ resided in Yè,
his son Suì commanded all armies at home and abroad,
Xuān held Xìndū,
his administrative staff and relatives divided control of the central administration;
Hóng occupied the position of honor,
but was merely a figurehead.
Sǎn (散),
is glossed as xīdǎn.
The Master of Writing Guō Yīn was made Right Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
He renamed the Heir Apparent's palace the Chóngxùn Palace,
and the Empress Dowager Liú and those below her were all moved to reside there.
He selected the most beautiful palace women, carriages, horses, clothing, and playthings from Lè's palace,
and took them all into the Chancellor's residence.
8 Yǔwén Qǐdéguī was driven out by his eastern tribal leader Yìdòuguī,
and fled to die abroad.
Mùróng Huàng led troops to attack him,
encamping at Guǎng'ān;
Guǎng'ān,
was north of Jíchéng.
He then built the Yúyīn and Ānjìn cities and returned.
Yúyīn City,
was likely north of the Dàyú River;
Ānjìn City,
was southeast of Wēidé City.
9 The Chéng commanderies of Jiànníng and Zāngkē came to surrender,
but Lǐ Shòu attacked and recaptured them.
10 The Zhao Empress Dowager Liú said to the Prince of Péngchéng, Kǎn:
"The late emperor has just passed away,
yet the Chancellor has so quickly begun to oppress and trample us like this.
Líng (陵),
means to ride over,
to crush.
Jiè (藉),
means to tread upon.
Jiè,
is glossed as cíyè.
This likely will not last long,
what will you, Prince, do about it?"
Kǎn said:
"The old ministers of the late emperor
have all been estranged and dismissed,
military affairs are no longer under our control,
meaning Hǔ's sons all hold military authority.
Bèi (被),
is glossed as píyì.
There is nothing that can be done,
meaning the palace guards and key positions in the central administration,
are all held by Hǔ's administrative staff and relatives,
with no one to join in plotting to rectify the situation.
We should support the Prince of Nányáng, Huī, as the leader of an alliance,
Huī,
was Lè's youngest son,
then garrisoning Lǐnqiū.
Proclaim the Empress Dowager's edict to the regional inspectors, administrators, expeditionary generals, and garrison commanders,
ordering each to raise troops to punish the violent rebels,
then perhaps there is still hope of success."
Lady Liú said:
"The situation is critical!
We must act quickly."
In the ninth month,
Kǎn, in plain clothes and with light cavalry, attacked Yǎn Province,
but did not succeed,
and fled south to Qiáo City.
Chancellor Hǔ sent his general Guō Tài to pursue him,
capturing Kǎn at Chéngfù,
sending him to Xiāngguó,
where he was roasted and killed.
He summoned the Prince of Nányáng, Huī, back to Xiāngguó.
Lady Liú's plot was discovered,
Hǔ deposed and killed her,
and honored Hóng's mother, Lady Chéng, as Empress Dowager.
Kǎn was originally the son of a Tián,
having rendered much service,
the Zhao ruler Lè had adopted him as a son.
Lady Liú had courage and resourcefulness,
Lè often consulted her on military decisions,
and she assisted Lè in establishing his achievements,
possessing the style of Empress Lü,
but being even less jealous and envious.
Empress Lü was able to execute Hán Xìn and Péng Yuè,
but Lady Liú could not control Hǔ,
perhaps she was not her equal.
The Zhao Prince of Hédōng, Shēng, garrisoned Guānzhōng,
Shí Lǎng garrisoned Luòyáng.
When Liú Yìn fled west,
Shí Shēng moved from Luòyáng to garrison Cháng'ān,
and Lǎng replaced Shēng in garrisoning Luòyáng.
In the tenth month,
Shēng and Lǎng both raised troops to attack Chancellor Hǔ;
Shēng proclaimed himself Governor of Qín Province,
and sent envoys to surrender.
The Dí chieftain Pú Hóng proclaimed himself Governor of Yōng Province,
and attached himself to the west, to Zhāng Jùn.
In the fourth year of the Xiánhé era,
Hóng had surrendered to Hǔ,
now he rebelled due to the Zhao turmoil.
Shuài (帥),
is glossed as suǒlèi.
Hǔ left his Heir Apparent Suì to guard Xiāngguó,
and led 70,000 infantry and cavalry to attack Lǎng at Jīnyōng;
Jīnyōng fell,
Lǎng was captured,
had his feet cut off and was then executed;
he advanced towards Cháng'ān,
appointing the Prince of Liáng, Tǐng, as Vanguard Grand Commander.
Tǐng,
was Hǔ's son.
Shēng led a large army following behind,
encamping at Púbǎn.
Quán fought Tǐng at Tóngguān,
and routed him heavily,
Tǐng and the Chancellor's Left Chief Clerk Liú Kuí both died,
this Liú Kuí,
is presumably the one who fled from Jìn to Zhào.
Corpses lay piled for over three hundred lǐ.
The Xiānbēi secretly conspired with Hǔ,
and turned to attack Shēng.
Shēng, unaware that Tǐng had already died,
became fearful,
and fled alone on horseback to Cháng'ān.
Quán gathered the remaining troops,
retreated, and stationed them at Wèi Ruì.
Kǒng Ānguó said,
the north bank of a river is called ruì.
Dù Yù said,
the winding bend of a river is called ruì,
pronounced as rúruì.
He hid at Jītóu Mountain.
Zhāng Shǒujié said: The Kuòdìzhì states: Jītóu Mountain is twenty lǐ northeast of Shànglù County in Chéng Province,
nine hundred and sixty lǐ southwest of Cháng'ān.
Lì Dàoyuán said: It is probably another name for the Great Lǒng Mountain.
The Book of the Later Hàn records,
Wěi Xiāo sent Wáng Mèng to block the Jītóu road,
which is this one.
According to this, Yuán Province's Pínggāo County, one hundred lǐ west, also has a Jītóu Mountain,
eight hundred lǐ northwest of Cháng'ān.
Hǔ advanced his troops to attack Yīng,
and executed him.
Shēng's subordinates beheaded Shēng and surrendered;
Quán fled to Lǒngyòu.
Hǔ separately ordered his generals to garrison Qiān and Lǒng,
and sent the General Má Qiū to attack Pú Hóng.
The Fēngsútōng states,
Má,
descends from the Qí Grand Master Má Yīng.
Hǔ welcomed and appointed Hóng as General of Brilliant Might
— prior to this there was no title of General of Brilliant Might,
Shí Hǔ created it.
The Hàn had a Colonel Protector of the Qiāng,
Hǔ gave this office to Hóng,
making him supervise and protect the Dí tribes.
He advised Hǔ to relocate the powerful families of Guānzhōng and the Dí and Qiāng peoples to populate the eastern regions,
saying:
"All the Dí are under my family's command,
I will lead them to follow,
who would dare disobey!"
Hǔ agreed,
and relocated over 100,000 households of Qín and Yōng commoners and Dí and Qiāng peoples east of the passes.
He appointed Hóng as General Soaring Dragon and Commander of the Migrant People,
settling him at Fāngtóu;
this sets the stage for Fú Hóng's son Jiàn to enter Guānzhōng from Fāngtóu.
Xiāng (驤),
is glossed as sījiāng.
Fāng (枋),
is pronounced fāng.
He ordered him to lead his followers, numbering tens of thousands, to relocate and settle at Shètóu in Qīnghé.
Hǔ returned to Xiāngguó,
and a great amnesty was proclaimed.
The ruler of Zhào, Hóng, ordered Hǔ to establish a Wèi Terrace,
exactly following the precedent of King Wǔ of Wèi assisting Hàn.
11 When Mùróng Huàng first succeeded to the position,
his application of laws was severe and harsh,
causing many among the state's people to feel insecure.
The Registrar Huángfǔ Zhēn earnestly remonstrated,
but he would not listen.
Huàng's elder half-brother, the General Who Establishes Might, Hàn, and his full younger brother, the General Who Campaigns Against Caitiffs, Rén,
possessed courage and strategic ability,
had repeatedly achieved military merits,
and had won the hearts of the officers;
the youngest brother, Zhāo,
had talent and skill;
all had been favored by Wěi.
Huàng was jealous of them.
Hàn sighed and said:
"I received responsibilities from our late lord,
and dared not fail to exert my utmost effort.
Fortunately, relying on the spirit of our late lord,
wherever I went I achieved success.
This was Heaven aiding our state,
not due to human effort.
Yet people say that what I accomplish
is because my outstanding talent is difficult to control.
How can I sit still and await disaster!"
Thereupon, he and his son fled to the Duàn clan.
Duàn Liáo had long heard of his talent,
hoping to employ him,
and treated him with great affection and respect.
Rén came from Píngguō to attend the funeral.
(In the Hàn records,
Píngguō County belonged to Liáodōng Commandery;
the Jìn abolished it.
The Jìn Eastern Yi Colonel governed at Xiāngpíng.
After Cuī Bì's defeat,
Mùróng Wěi had Rén guard Liáodōng,
governing from Píngguō.)
"We have always been arrogant,
and often disrespectful towards the successor ruler.
The successor ruler is stern and severe;
even without fault one should fear him,
let alone if one has faults!"
Zhāo said:
"We are all of legitimate birth,
and have a rightful share in the state."
(Zhāo considered himself and Rén both sons of the principal wife,
and thus entitled to obtain the state.
Share,
fú wèn fān.)
"I am on the inside and am not yet suspected.
If I watch for an opportune moment,
it will not be difficult to eliminate him.
Brother, quickly raise troops and come.
I will act as your inside agent.
When the affair succeeds,
give me Liáodōng.
When a man undertakes an affair,
if he does not succeed, he dies.
I cannot imitate the General Who Establishes Might by living ignobly in a foreign land."
Rén said:
"Excellent!"
He then returned to Píngguō.
In the intercalary month,
Rén raised troops and marched west.
Someone reported the plot of Rén and Zhāo to Huàng.
Huàng did not believe it,
and sent an envoy to investigate.
Rén's troops had already reached the Huángshuǐ River.
(The Huángshuǐ River,
is the Huángshuǐ River,
located northeast of Jíchéng,
four hundred lǐ from Táng's Yíng Prefecture.
According to the historical records,
the Huángshuǐ River should be in the Hàn Liáodōng Commandery's Xiǎndú County.)
They killed the envoy
and returned to hold Píngguō.
Huàng ordered Zhāo to commit suicide.
He sent the Army Libationer Fēng Yì to pacify and soothe Liáodōng.
He appointed Gāo Xǔ as General of Broad Martiality,

leading five thousand troops along with his younger half-brothers, General Who Establishes the Military, Yòu and Zhì, General of Broad Authority, Jūn, General of Tranquil Distance, Hàn, and the Marshal of Liáodōng, Tóng Shòu, to jointly campaign against Rén.
They engaged Rén in battle north of Wènchéng.
Huàng's forces were greatly defeated,
and Yòu, Zhì, and Jūn were all captured by Rén;
Shòu had once served as Rén's Marshal,
and so surrendered to Rén.
The former Grand Minister of Agriculture Sūn Jī and others raised the city of Liáodōng to respond to Rén.
(Sūn Jī
was likely a former official who had taken refuge in Liáodōng.)
(The city of Liáodōng,
was the city of Xiāngpíng.)
They returned together with Hàn.
The Eastern Yi Colonel Fēng Chōu, the Protector of the Army Píngyuán Yǐ Yì,
(Yǐ,
is the surname;
Yì,
is the personal name.
The genealogy of surnames states: The Shang ruler Tāng's courtesy name was Tiānyǐ,
and descendants of his collateral line took this as their surname.)
Thereupon, Rén came to possess the entire territory of Liáodōng;
Duàn Liáo and the various Xiānbēi tribes all distantly responded to and supported Rén.
Huàng reflected on Huángfǔ Zhēn's words,
and appointed Zhēn as Assistant to the Governor of Píng Prefecture.
(Huàng held the post of Governor of Píng Prefecture,
and appointed Zhēn as his Assistant.)
12 In the twelfth month,
Guō Quán occupied Shàngguī,
and sent an envoy to surrender;
Jīngzhào, Xīnpíng, Fúfēng, Féngyì, and Běidì all responded to him.
13 Earlier,
Zhāng Jùn wanted to borrow a route through Chéng to send memorials to Jiànkāng.
The ruler of Chéng, Xióng, would not permit it.
Jùn then sent his Administrator of the Office of the Governor, Zhāng Chún, to declare himself a vassal to Chéng in order to borrow the route;
Xióng pretended to agree,
intending to have bandits drown him in the Eastern Gorges.
(The Three Gorges are east of Chéngdū,
hence called the Eastern Gorges.)
Chún said to Xióng:
"My humble lord sent me, his petty servant, to travel a path without footprints,
(If Shǔ did not permit Liáng people to borrow the route,
then previously there had been no footprints of Liáng people in Shǔ territory.)
because Your Majesty esteems loyalty and righteousness,
and is able to help others accomplish their good purposes.
If you wish to kill me,
you should execute me in the marketplace,
and proclaim to the multitude: 'Liáng Province has not forgotten the former virtue,
and sends an envoy to Lángyá.
(Since the restoration from Lángyá in Jiāngzuǒ,
it is referred to as such.)
Envoy,
shū lì fān.
We discovered and killed him.'
In this way,
the reputation for righteousness would spread far,
and all under heaven would stand in awe of your authority.
Now, to have bandits kill me in the river,
your awesome punishment would not be manifest,
how could that be sufficient to show all under heaven!"
Xióng was greatly startled and said:
"How could such a thing happen!"
The Colonel-Director of Retainers Jǐng Qiān
(Shǔ established the Colonel-Director of Retainers at Chéngdū.)
said, "Zhāng Chún is a stalwart man,
I request that he be detained."
Xióng said:
"How would a stalwart man be willing to stay!
However, try using your intentions to observe him."
Qiān said to Chún:
"Your body is large and stout,
the weather is hot,
you could temporarily send a subordinate official,
and stay a while to wait for cooler weather."
(Wait,
means to await.)
"My humble lord, because the imperial carriage has been displaced,
and the imperial coffins have not yet returned,
(Referring to Huái and Mǐn being covered in dust,
and ultimately meeting harm,
the imperial coffins had not returned.)
and there is no one to rescue and raise them up,
(Rescue,
means to raise up.)
the Upper Capital,
refers to Jiànkāng.)
this is not something a subordinate official can convey;
if a subordinate official could manage it,
then Chún would not have come.
Even if it were a volcano or a boiling sea,
I would still go forward,
how could I fear mere cold or heat!"
Xióng said to Chún:
"Your honorable lord's heroic name overshadows the age,
his territory is rugged and his soldiers strong.
Why does he not also proclaim himself emperor and amuse himself in his own region?"
Chún said:
"From the time of my humble lord's ancestors,
for generations they have been profoundly loyal and steadfast.
Because the shame of enmity has not yet been washed away,
they rest on their spears awaiting the dawn.
How could there be any thought of amusing themselves!"
Xióng was greatly ashamed,
and said:
"My ancestors were also originally ministers of Jìn.
Encountering the great disorder under heaven,
they fled with the people of the six commanderies to take refuge in this province,
(The event is seen in the 82nd scroll, the eighth year of the Yuánkāng era of Emperor Huì.)
Refuge,
nǎi dàn fān.
and thus have things as they are today.
If Lángyá can restore the great Jìn in the Central States,
I too should lead the multitude to assist him."
He treated Chún with rich courtesy and sent him off.
Chún ultimately delivered his mission to Jiànkāng.
The fall of Cháng'ān
is recorded in the 89th scroll, in the fourth year of Emperor Mǐn's Jiànxīng reign.
Gěng Fǎng,
a census official dispatched from Dūnhuáng,
remained in Cháng'ān and had not yet returned
when Cháng'ān fell.
Moreover, the routes through Hé and Lǒng were cut off,
so he went south into Hànzhōng,
and from Hànzhōng proceeded east down to Jiànkāng.
Dūn
is pronounced as túmén.
The court appointed Fǎng as Acting
Censor of the Imperial Library,
and conferred upon Zhāng Jùn the title of General-in-Chief Who Guards the West.
Twelve men, including Jiǎ Líng of Lǒngxī, were selected to accompany him.
To accompany
means to assist.
As the roads were impassable,
the imperial edict was entrusted to Jiǎ Líng,
who disguised himself as a merchant to deliver it.
That year,
Líng finally reached Liángzhōu,
and Jùn dispatched his subordinate commander Wáng Fēng and others to report back and express gratitude.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Zhào changed its era name to Yánxī.
2 An edict appointed Guō Quán as General Who Guards the West and Governor of Yōngzhōu.
3 The King of Qiúchí, Yáng Nándí, died.
His son Yì succeeded him,
styling himself General of the Soaring Dragons, Left Worthy King, and Duke of Xiàbiàn;
he appointed his cousin Pán, son of his uncle Jiāntóu, as Champion General, Right Worthy King, and Duke of Héchí,
and sent an envoy to declare himself a vassal.
4 In the second month,
on Dīngmǎo,

an edict was issued sending Gěng Fǎng and Wáng Fēng to bestow the seal and ribbon upon Zhāng Jùn, appointing him General-in-Chief and Commander of Military Affairs in Shǎnxi, Yōng, Qín, and Liángzhōu.
From then on, envoys were sent every year without interruption.
Qiúchí declared itself a vassal,
and the routes through Liáng and Liáng became open.
5 Mùróng Rén appointed Sima Zhái Kǎi as Colonel of the Eastern Yi,
and former Bīngzhōu Assistant Clerk Páng Jiàn as Chancellor of Liáodōng.
6 Duàn Liáo sent troops to raid Túhé,
but failed to capture it.
He then sent his brother Lán, together with Mùróng Hàn, to jointly attack Liǔchéng.
Liǔchéng County,
belonged to the Liáoxī Commandery in the Hàn dynasty,
and was abolished in the Jìn dynasty;
in the Táng dynasty, it became the seat of Yíngzhōu.
Fù
is pronounced fú yòu.
Chéngdà
means the lord of the city;
the chief of a city,
hence called chéngdà.
Ní
is the same as mud.
Liáo was furious,
sternly reprimanding Lán and the others,
ordering them to capture it at all costs.
After resting for twenty days,
they added more troops and attacked again.
The soldiers all wore double-layered armor and carried shields,
constructing scaling ladders,
scaling ladders,
also known as cloud ladders.
They attacked day and night without rest.
Cóng and Ní defended stubbornly,
inflicting over a thousand casualties,
and ultimately could not be captured.
Mùróng Huàng sent Mùróng Hàn and Sima Fēng Yì and others to jointly rescue them.
Huàng warned Hàn, saying:
"The enemy's morale is high,
do not contend with them head-on."
Hàn was brave and decisive by nature,
leading over a thousand cavalry as the vanguard,
charging straight ahead.
Fēng Yì tried to stop him,
but Hàn did not listen.
They encountered Lán at Niúwěi Valley,
Niúwěi Valley
is north of Liǔchéng.
More than half of his men were killed;
Yì reorganized the formation and fought fiercely,
thus avoiding total annihilation.
Lán wanted to pursue the victory relentlessly,
but Mùróng Hàn, fearing that this would lead to the destruction of his own state,
stopped him, saying:
"A general must prioritize caution,
assess himself and gauge the enemy,
and not act unless success is assured.
Although we have now defeated a flank of their army,
we have not yet broken their main force.
Huàng is cunning and deceitful,
fond of ambushes.
If he leads the entire army of his state to resist us,
and we are deep in enemy territory,
outnumbered and outmatched,
this would be a perilous path.
Moreover, when we received our orders,
the goal was precisely this victory;
if we disobey orders and greedily advance,
and by chance suffer defeat,
both merit and reputation will be lost.
How could we face our lord upon returning!"
Lán said:
"He is already as good as captured,
with no chance of escape.
Based on the circumstances,
Huàng is certain to be captured,
with no possibility of survival.
Now, Qiānnián is in the east.
If we advance and succeed,
I will welcome him back as the heir to the state,
and will never betray you,
causing the ancestral temple to go without sacrifices."
Qiānnián
was the childhood name of Mùróng Rén.
Hàn said:
"I have thrown myself upon your reliance,
with no intention of returning;
the survival or destruction of the state
means nothing to me!
I only wish to plan for the greater state,
and to cherish your merit and reputation together."
He then ordered his own troops to withdraw alone,
and Lán had no choice but to follow.
The historian notes that although Hàn was physically outside his state,
his heart remained with his ancestral state.
7 In the third month,
the ruler of Chéng, Lǐ Xióng, divided Níngzhōu to establish Jiāozhōu,
splitting the commanderies of Xīnggǔ, Yǒngchāng, Zāngkē, Yuèxī, and Yèláng from Níngzhōu to form Jiāozhōu.
Cuàn Shēn was appointed Governor of Jiāozhōu.
8 The Chancellor of Zhào, Shí Hǔ, sent his generals Guō Áo and Zhāngwǔ King Bīn, leading forty thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Guō Quán from the west,
encamping at Huáyīn.
In summer,
the fourth month,
the powerful clans of Shàngguī killed Quán and surrendered.
Hǔ relocated over thirty thousand households from Qínzhōu to Qīng and Bìngzhōu.
A man from Cháng'ān named Chén Liángfū fled to the Black Qiāng,
a separate branch of the Qiāng people,
including the Green Qiāng and Black Qiāng.
Zhāngwǔ King Bīn and Lè'ān King Tāo jointly attacked,
defeating him,
and Jùdà fled to Mǎlán Mountain.
Guō Áo pursued the retreating enemy,

Examination of discrepancies: Thirty Kingdoms and Jìn Chūnqiū:

and the next year changed to Jiànwǔ.”
Consider,
Thirty Kingdoms and Jìn Chūnqiū do not record Hóng changing the era name to Yánxī,
Hǔ’s establishment,
was actually in the first year of Yánxī,
hence the mistaken record of Yǒngxī,
since Hóng already used the era name Yánxī,
how could Hǔ be willing to call it Yǒngxī!
Chén Hóng states:
“Hǔ changed the fifth year of Jiànpíng to Yánxīng,
meaning Hóng did not change the era name beyond the year.”
I fear Chén Hóng’s account is mistaken.

Marriage involves Six Rites: The first is Nàcǎi (Presenting Betrothal Gifts),
meaning that before a marriage,
a matchmaker must first convey the proposal,
after which someone is sent to present the gifts of selection,
using a wild goose as the ceremonial gift,
symbolizing the mutual coming and going of yin and yang;
the second is Wènmíng (Asking for the Name),
asking for the name to divine its auspiciousness or inauspiciousness;
the third is Nàjí (Presenting the Auspicious Divination),
performing divination at the ancestral temple to obtain an auspicious omen,
and then sending someone to report the marriage arrangement;
the fourth is Nàzhēng (Presenting the Betrothal Gifts),
using dark red and light red silks,
not using a wild goose;
the fifth is Qǐngqī (Requesting the Date),
where the groom's family divines an auspicious date,
and sends someone to inform the bride's family;
the sixth is Qīnyíng (Personally Escorting the Bride),
where the groom goes to the bride's home,
drives the carriage wheel three times around,
the driver takes over,
the groom mounts his own carriage and goes ahead,
to guide the bride back home.

Liáo,

High,

1. In spring,
the first month,
on the Gēngchén day,

The courtyard torch’s oil poured down into the pan,

The Kǎoyì says: The Zàijì records
“seven people,”

Chénggōng Duàn was executed by waist-cutting.
On the Xīnsì day,
Hǔ, following the systems of Yīn and Zhōu,
proclaimed himself Great Zhào Heavenly King.
He ascended the throne at the southern suburb,
and issued a general pardon.
He established his consort, Lady Zhèng, as Heavenly King Empress.
In ancient times, when one was called king,
the consort was called queen;
when one was called emperor,
the consort was called empress;
there was no title of Heavenly King Empress.
In ancient times, for kings,
the eldest legitimate son was called heir;
during the Qín and Hàn, when one was called emperor,
the heir was called crown prince;
there was no title of Heavenly King Crown Prince.
Members of the imperial clan who were kings were demoted to county marquises.
Officials were appointed and enfeoffed according to their ranks.
2. The Director of the Imperial Academy Yuán Huái
and the Minister of Ceremonies Féng Huái,
seeing that Jiāngzuǒ was gradually stabilizing,
requested the establishment of schools.
The emperor agreed.
On the Xīnmǎo day,
the Imperial Academy was established,
and students were recruited.
However, the scholar-officials were accustomed to Lǎozǐ and Zhuāngzǐ,
and Confucianism never flourished.
Huái

Cóng,

Qí,

Jílùjuàn, Shèfùchén, Mòpī, Yá, and Liáo,

Liáo repeatedly fought with Huàng,

“ ‘Being kind to the benevolent and friendly with neighbors is the treasure of a state.’
From Zuǒzhuàn, the words of Chén Wǔfù.
We have been in-laws for generations,

4 The Crown Prince of Zhào, Suì, had always been brave and fierce,
and the King of Zhào, Hǔ, loved him dearly.
He often said to his ministers:
"The Sīmǎ family, fathers and sons, brothers, destroyed each other,
and that is why I have been able to reach this position;
so how could I have any reason to kill Ā Tiě?"
Ā Tiě
was Suì's childhood name.
Ā,
is read with the entering tone of ān.
He enjoyed dressing up beautiful concubines,
then beheading them,
washing the blood and placing the heads on a tray,
passing them around for guests to look at,
and also cooking their flesh to eat together.
The Duke of Héjiān, Xuān, and the Duke of Lè'ān, Tāo, were both favored by Hǔ,
and Suì hated them like enemies.
Hǔ was excessively indulgent in wine and women,
and his moods were unpredictable.
He had Suì review and approve matters from the Imperial Secretariat,

"Such a trivial matter,

Sometimes, if he didn't hear a report,

"Why didn't you report it!"
He would reprimand, blame, and beat him,

Suì privately said to the Palace Attendant Lǐ Yán and others:
"The Imperial Household is hard to please.
Referring to the Son of Heaven as the 'Imperial Household'
first appears here.
In the Western Hàn, the Son of Heaven was called the 'County Official,'
in the Eastern Hàn, he was called the 'State Household,'

Some say: The Five Emperors governed all under heaven as officials,

Hard to please,
chǐ zhèng fān.

Mào,
mò běi fān.

In autumn,
the seventh month,

Secretly leading over five hundred cavalry from the palace officials and military officers to drink at Lǐ Yán's separate residence,

Yán kowtowed and firmly remonstrated,

His mother, Lady Zhèng, heard of this,

Fótú Chéng said to Hǔ:

Hǔ was about to visit Suì's illness,

"I am the ruler of all under heaven,

So he ordered a trusted female secretary to go and investigate.
Suì called her forward to speak with her,
then drew his sword and struck her.
Hǔ was enraged,
arrested Lǐ Yán and others for interrogation,
and Yán fully described the situation.
Hǔ executed Yán and over thirty others.
He imprisoned Suì in the Eastern Palace,
but later pardoned him,
summoning him for an audience at the Tàiwǔ Eastern Hall;
the Shuǐjīng Zhù says: Cáo Cāo resided in Yè, building the Northern Palace,
within which was the Wénchāng Hall;
the Shí family built the Eastern and Western Tàiwǔ Halls on the site of the old hall.
See,
xián biàn fān.
After a short while, he left.

Suì went straight out,
without looking back.
Hǔ was furious,
and deposed Suì to commoner status.
That night,
he killed Suì.
Examination of discrepancies: The Yān Shū, Wénmíng Jì says:

And buried him along with twenty-six men and women in a single coffin;

1 Spring,
first month,
Yān King Mù sent Commandant Zhào Pán to Zhào,

Yōuzhōu Governor Lǐ Mèng retreated to defend Yìjīng.

leading a naval force of one hundred thousand from Piāoyú Ford;

Zhào King Hǔ advanced and stationed at Jīntái.
According to the Water Classic annotation: Jīntái is in Gù'ān County of Zhuō Commandery,

Shǒu,
read as shǒu.

Hǔ intended to attack him.

fled to Mìyún Mountain.

He took Mùróng Hàn's hand and wept, saying:

Hàn fled north to the Yǔwén clan.

Qí, Chén, and Yuè fled to Lìngzhī,

Reached Mìyún Mountain,

Zǒu,

Hǔ entered the Lìngzhī palace,

Again, I could not preserve him.

fourth month,
guǐchǒu day.

frequently executing people,
and confiscating their property and women,

Hàn King Shòu had long been noble and respected,

Cháo,
read as cháo.

Someone advised Huàng to surrender.

The Zhào troops, like ants, swarmed up the city walls from all sides—

The King of Zhào, Hǔ, sent the Cross-Liao General Cáo Fú to lead the troops of Qīng Province to garrison a sea island.

The Director of Imperial Clan Affairs does not offer honest words

He was demoted in grade and rank,

Hǔ sent the Duke of Xiāngchéng, Shèguī, and the Duke of Shàngyōng, Rìguī, to lead troops to garrison Cháng'ān.
These two Guī

Dǎo was by nature tolerant and generous,

Qín Shǐhuáng sought to keep his common people ignorant;

If one does not bow and return governance,

merely,
means just,

Bear,

He intended to raise troops together to depose Dǎo,

Nánmán Xiàowèi Táo Chēng,
Nánmán Xiàowèi,

“Lord Wáng often harbors thoughts beyond worldly affairs,

Had it not been for Xī Jiàn opposing it from without,

Yǔ Liàng’s plot
