Discord,
is pronounced gǔ xiàn fān.
He was a descendant of Sūn Chǔ.
Sūn Chǔ,
was a renowned scholar in the early Jìn.
Yet he remotely held the power of the court,
occupying the upper reaches,
commanding strong troops,

Dǎo inwardly could not be at peace,
once when the west wind raised dust,
once,
should be read as cháng.
He slowly said:
“Yuánguī’s dust sullies people!”
Dǎo appointed Jiāngxià’s Lǐ Chōng as Chéngxiàng Yuàn.
Chōng, seeing the prevailing customs favored emptiness and falsity,
wrote the Xué Zhēn.
He believed that Lǎozǐ said,
“Abolish benevolence and discard righteousness,
and the people will again be filial and compassionate,”
but does it mean that only after the ways of benevolence and righteousness are abolished

Rather, the worry is that those who genuinely practice benevolence and righteousness are few, while those who exploit them are many,
thus placing the responsibility on the sages and leaving the burden to past conventions.
Most people see the form,
but few grasp the essence,
the more they chase the traces, the more earnest they become,
the farther they stray from the root.
Therefore, he wrote the Xué Zhēn to dispel this obscurity,

“Where fame is glorified,
the Way is abandoned;
diminish what is exalted,
and elevate what is neglected.
Without benevolence, nothing can nurture things,
without righteousness, nothing can align shame,
benevolence and righteousness certainly cannot be distant,
only remove what harms benevolence and righteousness.”
8 In Hàn, Lǐ Yì’s elder cousin, Guǎnghàn Tàishǒu Qián, reported that senior ministers were plotting to depose and install.

In the eighth month,

Gōng Zhuàng submitted a sealed memorial stating:
“When Your Majesty raised troops initially,

Smear,

Great achievements were accomplished;

Meaning Shòu ascended the throne as emperor.

Some critics say that if the two provinces attach to Jìn, it will bring glory,

In the past, Gōngsūn Shù was in Shǔ,

Jīng Hán, Wáng Yuán, Tián Róng, Yán Cén,

While men of Chǔ held high positions.
Páng Tǒng, Huáng Zhōng, Dǒng Hé, Liú Bā, Mǎ Liáng and his brothers, Lǚ Yì, Liào Lì, Lǐ Yán, Yáng Yí, Wèi Yán, Jiǎng Wǎn, Fèi Yī, Dǒng Yǔn, etc.,
were all men of Chǔ.
Wú, Dèng,
refer to Wú Hàn and Dèng Ài.
How could they distinguish between guest and host!
Critics do not comprehend the foundation of stability,
merely clinging to reputation and position,
thinking that the Liú clan’s local officials served in the provinces and commanderies;
they fail to realize that was when the state perished and the sovereign changed,
how can it compare to today’s righteous uprising,
where the sovereign is honored and the ministers illustrious!
The entire state serving Jìn is a righteous uprising,
Jìn bestows favor and rank,

Fǎ Zhèng advised Liú Bèi to seize Chéngdū,

Shòu read the letter and felt inward shame,

"Wáng Dǎo is the Emperor's tutor,

Féng Huái,

Because Hán requested retirement due to age,

"Years of life lie with Heaven,

feared that his arrival was not certain;

and north to the edge of the desert,

The Commentary on the Water Classic states: East of Ānzhōu is the Wǔliè River,
its waters are formed by three tributaries merging.
The western source is called the Xīzàng Water,
flowing southwest,
and the Dōngzàng Water flows into it.
The water emerges from the eastern stream,
flows southwest out of the valley,
and merges with the Zhōngzàng Water;
the water originates from the central stream,
flows south out of the valley,
and flows south into the Dōngzàng Water.
The Dōngzàng Water then flows south and right into the Xīzàng Water.
Therefore, the river is called the Sānzàng River.
Wèi Shōu's Treatise on Geography says: In the second year of the Huángxīng era, Ānzhōu was established,
governing Mìyún and other commanderies.

Bài,
pronounced bǔ mài fān.

to garrison Xiāngyáng;

Since Lǐ Jǔ, the Inspector of Sīzhōu, retreated and stationed his troops at Lǔyáng, Sīzhōu had been temporarily administered within the boundaries of Jīngzhōu.
Now, for the first time, Sīzhōu was administered from Xiāngyáng.
Zhōu Fǎng held the post of Inspector of Liángzhōu, administering from Xiāngyáng.
Now that Sīzhōu was administered from Xiāngyáng, Liángzhōu was administered from Wèixīng.

all were granted the authority of the tally.

to lead ten thousand elite troops with Fán Jùn, the Grand Administrator of Xīyáng, to garrison Zhūchéng.

Xīyáng County belonged to Jiāngxià Commandery in Hàn times; Wèi assigned it to Yìyáng Commandery; Jìn Emperor Huì divided Yìyáng to establish the Kingdom of Xīyáng; the Eastern Jìn abolished the kingdom and made it a commandery.
Shuài is read as shuài; the same below.
He entered the Miǎn River region.
Guō Mò claimed to lead two hundred men downstream to see Liàng.
Liàng was stationed in Wǔchāng; Mò came downstream from the upper reaches to see him.
Xiāng is pronounced xiàng.
Jiàng is pronounced jiàng.
He enumerated Mò’s past and present crimes, arrested him, and executed him.
Liàng had long resented Táo Kǎn, and Mò had also slandered Liàng to Wáng Dǎo; thus, he killed him out of personal resentment.
Sù wù is pronounced sù wù.
Shǔ is pronounced shǔ.
He ordered Yǔ Yì to move and station at Bànzhōu;
Bànzhōu was within the boundaries of Jiāngzhōu. During Emperor Kāng’s time, Chǔ Póu was Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, stationed at Bànzhōu.
He advanced toward Hànzhōng.
He sent his Army Advisor, Lǐ Sōng, to attack Hàn’s Bā Commandery and Jiāngyáng.
In the summer, the fourth month, he captured Hàn’s Inspector of Jīngzhōu, Lǐ Hóng, and the Grand Administrator of Bā Commandery, Huáng Zhí, and sent them to Jiànkāng.
Hàn established Jīngzhōu in Bā Commandery.
He replaced Hóng in guarding Bā Commandery.
Yǔ Liàng submitted a memorial, stating:

“Shǔ is very weak, but the Hú are still strong. I wish to lead a large force of one hundred thousand to move and garrison Shíchéng, deploying various armies along the Jiāng and Miǎn rivers to plan an attack on Zhào.”
The Emperor referred the matter for discussion.
Chancellor Dǎo requested permission.
Grand Commandant Jiàn argued, believing that
“resources are not yet prepared; a major campaign cannot be launched.”
Court Minister Cài Mó argued, believing that

“times have their ups and downs, and the Way has its advances and retreats. If one acts rashly without considering strength and weakness, then ruin will come within a day—what achievement can there be!
For the present plan, nothing is better than nurturing our might and awaiting the right time.
The feasibility of the time depends on the strength of the Hú; the strength of the Hú depends on Shí Hǔ’s capability.
Since Shí Lè raised his cause, Hǔ often served as his claws and teeth, winning every battle, and thus pacified the Central Plains.
The territory he holds is comparable to that of the Wèi era.
After Lè’s death, Hǔ controlled the successor ruler and executed generals and ministers—referring to the killing of Shí Kān, Chéng Xiá, Xú Guāng, and other generals and ministers.

He eliminated external threats, capturing Jīnyōng in one move, capturing Shí Shēng in a second battle, executing Shí Cōng as easily as picking up something dropped, and seizing Guō Quán as easily as shaking dry leaves.

In the eighth year of the Xiánhé era, Hǔ killed Shí Cōng, captured Jīnyōng, and advanced to kill Shí Shēng; in the ninth year, he seized Guō Quán; these events are all recorded in the previous scroll.
He did not lose an inch of territory.
From this perspective, is Hǔ capable or not?
Some argue that the Hú previously attacked Xiāngyáng but could not capture it—see the first year of the Xiánkāng era in the previous scroll.
But to consider a force that wins every battle as inferior because it failed to capture one city is like an archer who hits the target a hundred times but misses once—can he be called unskilled?
Moreover, Shí Yù was a flank army, and Huán Píngběi was a frontier general—Huán Xuān was General Píngběi.
Jiàng is pronounced jiàng; the same below.
They advance when advantageous and retreat when not; it was not urgent.
Now, the General of the West, with his important garrison and renowned worthies, personally leads a large army intending to sweep across Hé’nán.
Hǔ will certainly lead the entire state’s forces to decide victory or defeat—how can this be compared to Xiāngyáng!
Now, if the General of the West wishes to engage him in battle, how does he compare to Shí Shēng?
If he wishes to defend a city, how does it compare to Jīnyōng?
If he wishes to rely on the Miǎn River, how does it compare to the Great River?
If he wishes to resist Shí Hǔ, how does he compare to Sū Jùn?
All these points should be carefully evaluated.
Shí Shēng was a fierce general with the elite troops of Guānzhōng; the General of the West’s battle would hardly be victorious!

Moreover, at that time, Luòyáng and Guānzhōng both raised troops to attack Hǔ, but now these three garrisons are instead used by him—referring to Luòyáng, Guānzhōng, and Guō Quán’s occupation of Shàngguī as three.
This is a situation of double the strength.
Shí Shēng could not withstand half, yet the General of the West wishes to face double—this is what I doubt.
Sū Jùn’s strength was inferior to Shí Hǔ’s, and the danger of the Miǎn River is inferior to the Great River.
The Great River could not defend against Sū Jùn, yet he wishes to use the Miǎn River to defend against Shí Hǔ—this is another doubt.
In the past, Zǔ Tì was in Qiáo, farming north of the city.
When the Hú came to attack, he had previously stationed troops to defend the exterior.
When the grain was about to ripen, the Hú indeed arrived.
The able-bodied men fought outside, while the old and weak harvested inside, holding many torches; in emergencies, they burned the grain and fled.
After several years like this, they ultimately could not gain advantage.
At that time, the Hú only held Héběi; compared to now, it was only one-fourth.
That is, when Zǔ Tì faced Shí Lè across the border, Lè only held the territory of Héběi; compared to the territory now held by Shí Hǔ, it was only one-fourth.
This is another doubt.
However, this only discusses the situation after the Western Expeditionary Force had already arrived,
meaning after they had reached the Central Plains.
West of Miǎn,
the water is swift and the banks are high,
boats must travel in single file against the current,
stretching for a hundred lǐ from front to rear.
This describes the narrowness and swiftness of the water,
making it impossible for boats to advance side by side in a single column.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* records: Duke Xiāng of Sòng fought the men of Chǔ at Hóng.
