all imperial parks may be abolished and given to the people without land.
Those truly poor,
the government will grant them oxen;
those with surplus strength wishing to borrow government oxen,
shall all follow the old laws of Wèi and Jìn.
Ditches and waterways
that are beneficial,
shall be repaired in due season.
Now military affairs are just rising,
merits and achievements are many,
(Merit for royal service is called xūn;
accumulated achievement is called fá.)
wait until the Central Plains are pacified and unified,
then gradually discuss further.
Artisans, merchants, and students should all be selected and reduced.
For a minister to speak to his ruler,
is most difficult,
(Guān means to report.)
Wáng Bāo's "Ode on the Sage Lord Obtaining Worthy Ministers" says: Advancing and retiring, he can report his loyalty.
One should select the good and follow it.
Wáng Xiàn and Liú Míng,
though their crimes deserved dismissal,
was also due to my lack of magnanimity,
they may all be restored to their original offices,
and still serve in remonstrance departments.
Mr. Fēng's straightforwardness,
deeply embodies the proper form of a royal minister,
(The Yì says: Royal ministers are straightforward, not for personal reasons.)
proclaim this inside and outside the court:
those wishing to state my faults,
regardless of nobility or commoner,
let there be no taboo!"
Mù was fond of literature,
often personally attending schools to lecture,
examining and testing over a thousand students,
among whom were quite a few unqualified and excessive,
hence Fēng Yù mentioned it.
4 An imperial edict summoned General of the Guards Chǔ Póu,
intending to appoint him as Inspector of Yángzhōu and Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Minister of Personnel Liú Xiá and Chief Clerk Wáng Húzhī advised Póu, saying:
"Prince of Kuàijī possesses virtuous conduct and noble reputation,
he is the Duke of Zhōu of our state.
Your Excellency should entrust the great affairs of state to him."
Póu thus firmly declined
and returned to his fief.
On the rénxū day,
Prince of Kuàijī Sīmǎ Yù was appointed as General-in-Chief Who Pacifies the Army,
with authority over the six administrative matters of the Imperial Secretariat.
Liú Cōng appointed his son Liú Càn as Chancellor,
concurrently holding the title of General-in-Chief,
and Director of the Imperial Secretariat;
Liú Yánnián was appointed Director of the Six Administrative Matters of the Imperial Secretariat.
The position of Director of the Six Administrative Matters
was subordinate to that of Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
This indicates that such an office must have existed first during the Wèi and Jìn periods,
and Cōng inherited and established it.
Commentary is also seen earlier.
Kuài,
read as "gōng wài fān."
Yù was pure, detached, and had few desires,
especially skilled in profound discourse.
He often had Liú Tán, Wáng Méng, and Hán Bó from Yǐngchuān as his conversational guests,
and also recruited Xī Chāo as his Assistant Officer of the Pacifying Army,
and Xiè Wàn as a Palace Attendant.
Chāo
was the grandson of Jiàn.
Xī Jiàn
was a renowned minister during the early southern crossing.
Assistant Officer,
read as "yǐ juàn fān."
His father Xī Yīn
was simple, silent, modest, and retiring, yet stingy with wealth,
accumulating coins to the amount of several tens of millions.
He once opened his treasury and allowed Chāo to take as he wished;
Chāo distributed and gave to relatives and old friends,
exhausting it all in one day.
History records that Xī Chāo's talents and abilities were sufficient to serve the world,
but the Jìn court could not employ him,
regretting that he was used by Huán Wēn.
Give,
read as "shì chǐ fān."
He was the younger brother of Ān,
pure, open-minded, outstanding, and transcendent,
also having fame in his time.
5 In Yān, a black dragon and a white dragon appeared at Lóngshān,
Lóngshān is east of Lóngchéng.
Appear,
read as "xián biàn fān."
They shed their horns and departed.
The King of Yān, Mùrǎng, personally offered a grand sacrifice of tàiláo,
pardoned within his territory,
and named his newly built palace Hé Lóng.
6 Marquis Sù of Dūtíng, Yǔ Yì, developed a carbuncle on his back.
The posthumous naming rule states: "Firm and capable in conquest is called Sù";
"Resolute and decisive in heart is called Sù."
Carbuncle,
read as "qiān yú fān."
He entrusted the future responsibilities;
appointed Sima Yìyáng Zhū Tāo as Commandant of the Southern Man,
with a thousand men guarding Bālíng.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the gēngwǔ day,
he died.
Yì's subordinate general Gān Zàn and others rebelled.
Gān
is a surname.
In the Zuǒzhuàn,
Sòng had a Gān Chōu.
Zàn,
read as "cáng hàn fān."
Zhū Tāo, together with Chief Clerk of the Pacifying West Jiāng Bīn,
Sima of the Establishing Military Mào Mùzhī,
Yǔ Yì appointed his son Yǔ Fāngzhī as General of the Establishing Military,
guarding Xiāngyáng,
and appointed Mùzhī as Sima.
Mùzhī was also known as Hǔshēng.
Mùzhī,
styled Xiànzǔ,
childhood name Hǔshēng,
his given name violated the taboo of Empress Wáng Jìng,
so he changed to using his style;
later, because Huán Wēn's mother's name was Xiàn,
he reverted to using his childhood name.
According to the Jìnshū biography of empresses,
Empress Āi Jìng Wáng,
her taboo name was Mùzhī.
Bīn,
was the son of Tǒng.
7 In the eighth month,
Inspector of Yùzhōu Lù Yǒng rebelled and fled to Zhào.
The King of Zhào, Shí Hǔ, had Yǒng garrison Shòuchūn.
Lù Yǒng
was a surrendered general of Sū Jùn.
8 After Yǔ Yì's death,
court discussions all held that the Yǔ family had for generations been in the western frontier,
which was comforting to popular sentiment,
and it was appropriate to follow Yì's request,
having Yǔ Àizhī succeed him in his position.
Hé Chōng said:
"Jīngchǔ,
is the western gate of the state,
with a population of a million households,
bordering the strong Hú in the north,
adjacent to the powerful Shǔ in the west,
with terrain dangerous and obstructed,
spanning ten thousand lǐ in circumference;
with the right person, the central plains can be stabilized,
without the right person, the state can be imperiled.
As Lù Kàng said, 'If it exists, Wú exists;
if it perishes, Wú perishes.'
Lù Kàng's final memorial before death,
see the tenth year of Tàishǐ of Emperor Wǔ, scroll 80.
Huán Wēn's heroic strategy surpasses others,
possessing both civil and military capabilities,
for the responsibility of the western Xià,
none surpass Wēn."
Discussants also said:
"Will Yǔ Àizhī willingly yield to Wēn?
If he resists with troops,
the shame and fear will not be slight."
Meaning they could not control Àizhī,
which would bring shame to the state,
and there were also reasons for fear.
Probably viewing Àizhī as comparable to Wáng Dūn and Sū Jùn.
"Wēn is sufficient to control him,
do not worry, gentlemen."
The Governor of Dānyáng, Liú Tán, often marveled at Wēn's talent,
yet knew he had disloyal ambitions.
He said to Prince of Kuàijī Sīmǎ Yù:
"Wēn must not be placed in a strategically advantageous location,
his rank and title should always be restrained."
He advised Yù to personally guard the upper reaches,
with himself as Army Supervisor,
but Yù did not listen;
he also requested to go himself,
which was also not heeded.
Liú Tán
was merely a conversational guest;
his words about Huán Wēn were all accurate,
showing he deeply understood Wēn's talent.
Even if Yù guarded the upper reaches,
with Tán as Sima,
it would still be insufficient to oppose Yān and Qín.
Yángzǐ said: "It is not merely knowing,
but also truly practicing;
knowing is not difficult,
acting is difficult."
Tán,
read as "tú gān fān."
On the gēngchén day,

Huán Wēn, Inspector of Xúzhōu, was appointed as General Who Pacifies the West, with authority, Commander of the military affairs of six provinces: Jīng, Sī, Yōng, Yì, Liáng, and Níng, concurrently holding the title of Commandant Who Protects the Southern Man, and Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
This laid the groundwork for Huán Wēn's autocratic control of the Jìn court.
Yōng,
read as "yú yòng fān."
Also appointed Liú Tán as Supervisor of the military affairs in Miǎnzhōng,
concurrently Governor of Yìchéng,
replacing Yǔ Fāngzhī.
Relocated Fāngzhī and Àizhī to Yùzhāng.
Huán Wēn once intended to hunt while riding in the snow,
first visiting Liú Tán.
Tán saw his attire was very formal,
and said to him:
"Old rogue, what do you intend to do with this?"
Wēn laughed and said:
"If I did not do this,
how could you sit and talk!"
Wēn's reply to Tán with these words
says it all;
Wēn also knew Tán was fully aware of his talent,
hence he spoke these words.
9 The younger brother of the Hàn ruler Shì, the Grand General Guǎng,
because Shì had no sons,
requested to be made the Crown Prince;
Shì did not permit it.
Mǎ Dāng and Xiè Sīmíng admonished him, saying:
"Your Majesty does not have many brothers;
if you further depose one,
you will become even more isolated and endangered."
They firmly requested that he be allowed.
Shì suspected they were conspiring with Guǎng,
arrested Dāng and Sīmíng and executed them,
exterminating their three clans.
The heir apparent cannot be sought;
had Mǎ Dāng and Xiè Sīmíng considered the state's interests,
they should have spoken calmly and gradually,
allowing their ruler to realize it himself;
how could they have firmly insisted on their request!
Following him to their deaths,
was fitting.
Xiè,
read as Hù Mǎi.
He demoted Guǎng to the rank of Marquis of Línqióng,
and Guǎng committed suicide.
When Sīmíng was arrested,
he sighed and said:
"The reason the state has not perished
is because there are a few of us left;
now it is in peril!"
He spoke and laughed as usual and then died.
Sīmíng was wise and resourceful,
daring to admonish and remonstrate;
Mǎ Dāng had always been popular among the people;
when they died,
the officials and commoners all mourned them.
10 In winter,
the tenth month,
the Yān King Huàng sent Mùróng Kè to attack Gāogōulí,
capturing Nánsū.
The city of Nánsū was east of Nánxiá;
when the Táng pacified Gāolì,
they established Nánsū Prefecture.
11 In the twelfth month,
Zhāng Jùn attacked Yānqí,
and it surrendered.
That year,
Jùn divided Wǔwēi and ten other commanderies to form Liáng Province.
Jùn divided Wǔwēi, Wǔxīng, Xīpíng, Zhāngyè, Jiǔquán, Jiànkāng, Xījùn, Huánghé, Jìnxīng, Xūwǔ, and Āngù, totaling eleven commanderies, to form Liáng Province.
He divided Xīngjìn and seven other commanderies to form Hé Province.
Jùn divided Xīngjìn, Jīnchéng, Wǔshǐ, Nán'ān, Yǒngjìn, Dàxià, Wǔchéng, and Hànzhōng, eight commanderies, to form Hé Province.
He divided Dūnhuáng and two other commanderies and the three garrisons of the Western Regions Protectorate to form Shā Province.
The Jìn records only mention Dūnhuáng and Jìnchāng two commanderies,
and the Western Regions Protectorate;
Zhāng Mào used the Colonel, Yùmén, and Grand Protector Army, three commanderies and three garrisons to form Shā Province,
but one commandery is not seen in the histories,
likely due to missing text.
Dūn,
read as Tú Mén.
Jùn proclaimed himself Grand Governor, Grand General, and Acting King of Liáng,
overseeing the three provinces;
he began establishing officials such as Libationer, Gentleman of the Interior, Grand Master, Retainer, and Receptionist,
their titles all imitating the imperial court
but slightly altering the names;
his carriages, attire, banners, and flags were modeled after those of a king.
12 The Zhào King Hǔ appointed the Champion General Yáo Yìzhòng as Commissioner Bearing Credentials, Grand Governor of Ten Commanderies and Six Barbarian Tribes, and Grand Champion General.
Yìzhòng was frugal, honest, and straightforward,
not cultivating an imposing demeanor,
speaking without fear or avoidance.
When Hǔ usurped the throne,
Yìzhòng sternly reprimanded him,
showing that he spoke without fear or avoidance.
Govern,
read as Zhí Zhī;
same below.
Whenever he participated in decisions,
the high ministers all feared and deferred to him.
The Left Commandant of Wǔchéng,
was the younger brother of Hǔ's favorite concubine.
Dōngwǔchéng County belonged to Qīnghé Commandery,
in the Táng it belonged to Bèi Province.
Yìzhòng was encamped at Shètou in Guǎngchuān, Qīnghé.
He harassed and disturbed his troops.
Yìzhòng arrested him and enumerated his faults, saying:
"You are a prohibitive commandant,
meaning a commandant whose duty is to prohibit wickedness and wrongdoing.
Enumerate,
read as Suǒ Jù.
I am a high minister,
what I have seen with my own eyes,
cannot be overlooked."
He ordered his attendants to execute him;
the commandant kowtowed until blood flowed,
and his attendants firmly remonstrated,
so he stopped.
13 The Yān King Huàng believed that in ancient times, when feudal lords ascended the throne,
each used their own first year,
so he began not using the Jìn era name,
calling himself the twelfth year.
From then on, Yān no longer submitted to Jìn's authority.
14 The Zhào King Hǔ sent the Eastern Expedition General Dèng Héng to lead tens of thousands of troops to station at Lè'ān,
preparing attack equipment,
planning to take Yān.
The Yān King Huàng appointed Mùróng Bà as the General Who Pacifies the Dí.
The General Who Pacifies the Dí
began with Hàn Emperor Guāngwǔ appointing Páng Méng.
Héng feared him,
and did not dare to attack.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on Bǐngyín,
a general amnesty was issued.
2 On Jǐmǎo,
the Duke Wénmù of Dūxiāng
Hé Chōng died.
Chōng had capability and vision,
in court he was stern and upright,
taking the state as his own responsibility,
those he selected and appointed were all based on merit,
not favoring relatives or old friends.
3 Initially, Fúyú resided at Lùshān.
Fúyú was over a thousand lǐ north of Xuāntú,
Lùshān likely being in that area.
Dù Yòu said: The Fúyú state had a seal,
with the inscription
"Seal of the King of Huì";
the state had an old city,
named Huì City,
likely originally the land of Huìmò.
The state was north of the Great Wall,
a thousand lǐ from Xuāntú,
bordering Gāolì to the south, Yìlóu to the east, and Xiānbēi to the west.
Among the Eastern Barbarians were the Three Hán states: one was Mǎhán,
two was Chénhán,
three was Biànhán.
Mǎhán had fifty-four states,
Bǎijì being one of them;
later it gradually grew powerful,
annexing the small states.
The state was originally over a thousand lǐ east of Liáodōng, together with Gōulí.
The Suīshū says: Bǎijì originated from Dōngmíng;
later there was one named Qiútái,
who first established the state,
gradually making it strong and prosperous.
Initially, a hundred families crossed the sea,
hence called Bǎijì.
Dù Yòu said: Bǎijì bordered Xīnluó to the south,
resisted Gāolì over a thousand lǐ to the north,
was bounded by the great sea to the west,
located south of the small sea.
They moved west, closer to Yān,
but did not set up defenses.
The Yān King Huàng sent his heir apparent Jùn to lead Generals Mùróng Jūn, Mùróng Kè, and Mùyú Gēn, with seventeen thousand cavalry, to raid Fúyú.
Jùn directed from the center,
military affairs were all entrusted to Kè.
They then captured Fúyú,
taking captive its king Xuán and over fifty thousand people of the tribe, and returned.
Huàng appointed Xuán as General Who Guards the Army,
and gave him his daughter in marriage.
4 In the second month,
on Guǐchǒu,
Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū Cài Mó was appointed to concurrently serve as Minister Over the Masses,
together with the Prince of Kuàijī, Yù, to assist in governance.
5 Chǔ Pó recommended former Guānglù Dàfū Gù Hé and former Left Director of the Secretariat of the Minister Over the Masses Yīn Hào.
In the third month,
on Bǐngzǐ,
Hé was appointed Prefect of the Masters of Writing,
and Hào was appointed General Who Establishes Might and Governor of Yáng Province.
Hé was in mourning for his mother,
and firmly declined, not taking up the post.
He said to those close to him:
"In ancient times, there were those who removed their mourning garments to serve the king,
because their talent was sufficient to manage the times;
as for someone like me,
it would only damage filial piety
and harm customs."
Those with discernment praised him.
Hào also firmly declined.
The Prince of Kuàijī, Yù, wrote to Hào, saying:
"We are facing a time of misfortune,
danger and decline have reached an extreme;
you, sir, possess deep insight and extensive knowledge,
sufficient to manage the world.
If you again deeply insist on declining and withdrawing,
merely following your original intent,
I fear that the affairs of the world will be lost from here.
Your decision to take office or not
is directly related to the rise and fall of the present time,
and the family and state are not different."
Meaning, if the state prospers, the family also prospers with it;
if the state declines, the family also declines with it.
Hào then took up the post.
6 In summer,
the fourth month,
on Jǐyǒu, the first day,
there was a solar eclipse.
7 In the fifth month,
on the bingxū day,
Zhāng Jùn, the Duke of Xīpíng and Zhōngchéng, passed away.

His officials recommended his heir, Zhòng Huá, to be appointed as Commissioner Bearing Credentials, Grand Commander, Grand Commandant, Protector Colonel of the Qiāng, Governor of Liáng Province, Duke of Xīpíng, and Acting King of Liáng;
a general amnesty was declared within his domain;
his principal mother, Lady Yán, was honored as Grand Queen Dowager,
and his own mother, Lady Mǎ, was honored as Queen Dowager.
8 In Zhào, the eunuch Yán Shēng harbored animosity towards the Imperial Secretary Zhū Guǐ.
It happened that there had been prolonged rain,
and Shēng slandered Guǐ, accusing him of failing to maintain the roads,
and also of defaming and criticizing the court's governance.
The King of Zhào, Shí Hǔ, imprisoned him.
Pú Hóng remonstrated, saying:
"Your Majesty already has palaces in Xiāngguó and Yè,
and is also constructing palaces in Cháng'ān and Luòyáng.
For what purpose are they intended!
You have made a thousand hunting chariots,
and enclosed an area of several thousand lǐ to rear birds and beasts,
seizing over a hundred thousand wives and daughters of the people to fill the rear palace.
These matters are all recorded in the previous year.
Is it truly like this!
Now, on account of the roads not being maintained,
you wish to kill an Imperial Secretary.
Your Majesty's virtuous governance is not cultivated,
and Heaven has sent down excessive rain,
which lasted for seventy days before clearing.
It has only cleared for two days;
even if there were a million ghost soldiers,
they could not remove the mud and waterlogging from the roads,
let alone men!
With governance and punishments like this,
how will you face the four seas,
how will you face future generations!
I speak of all under heaven and later ages,
who will certainly criticize and condemn these faults.
Dismantle the parks and enclosures,
release the palace women,
pardon Zhū Guǐ,
to meet the expectations of the multitude."
Although Hǔ was displeased,
he did not punish him for it,
and on account of this, he halted the construction works at Cháng'ān and Luòyáng.
However, he ultimately executed Zhū Guǐ.
He also established laws against privately discussing court affairs,
allowing officials to accuse their lords,
and slaves to accuse their masters.
From the dukes and ministers downward,
when attending court audiences, they would only exchange glances,
not daring to visit each other or converse anymore.
9 The Zhào general Wáng Zhuó attacked Zhāng Zhòng Huá,
assaulting Wǔjiē,
and captured the Protector of the Army Cáo Quán and Hú Xuān.
Zhāng Jùn had established five garrison protectorates;
Wǔjiē was one of them,
located in Lǒngxī.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: Southwest of Dídào County is the city of Wǔjiē.
According to the Jìn records,
Emperor Huì divided Lǒngxī to establish Dídào Commandery,
and also established Wǔjiē County under it.
The Governor of Liáng Province, Má Qiū,
Zhào had sent Má Qiū to attack Liáng Province,
hence he was appointed as its governor.
The Grand Administrator Zhāng Chōng requested to surrender,
causing shock and fear throughout Liáng Province.
Zhòng Huá mobilized all the troops within his domain,
and sent the General Who Subdues the South, Péi Héng, to lead them in resisting Zhào;
Héng encamped at Guǎngwǔ.
Zhāng Shí divided Língjū and Zhīyáng, two counties of Jīnchéng,
and also established Yǒngdēng County,
combining the three counties to establish Guǎngwǔ Commandery.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
The city of Guǎngwǔ is west of Zhīyáng County.
According to the Wǔdài Zhì,
Yǔnyá County of Wǔwēi Commandery,
was established by the Later Wèi,
and called Guǎngwǔ.
Liú Xù said: The Guǎngwǔ County of Táng's Lán Province
was the territory of the Hàn's Zhīyáng County.
Héng,
pronunciation hù dēng.
The Marshal of Liáng Province, Zhāng Dān, said to Zhòng Huá:
"The survival of the state depends on the military,
and the victory or defeat of the military depends on the generals.
Now, those who discuss the selection of generals
mostly recommend old veterans.
But the promotion of Hán Xìn
was not based on old virtue.
The matter of promoting Hán Xìn is recorded in the ninth scroll, in the first year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn.
Promotion is not confined to constant men;
if one's talent is suitable,
then entrust him with great affairs.
Now, with a powerful enemy at the border,
and the various generals not advancing,
the people's hearts are anxious and fearful.
The Registrar Xiè Ài,
possesses both civil and military abilities,
can be employed to resist Zhào."
Zhòng Huá summoned Ài,
and asked him about strategy;
Ài requested seven thousand troops,
vowing to defeat Zhào in response.
Zhòng Huá appointed Ài as General of the Central Resolute,
gave him five thousand infantry and cavalry,
and sent him to attack Qiū.
Ài led his troops out from Zhènwǔ,
at night two owls cried within his command tent,
Ài said:
"In liùbó, obtaining the xiāo piece means victory;
Ěryǎ Yì: The liùbó dice have the xiāo piece.
The game involves moving along unfavorable paths,
hence the xiāo is used as a dice piece.
This is an omen of defeating the enemy."
He advanced and engaged Zhào in battle,
greatly defeating them,
beheading five thousand.
Zhòng Huá enfeoffed Ài as the Earl of Fúlù.
Fúlù County,
since the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Jiǔquán Commandery.
Sòng Bái said: Fúlù County of Sù Province,
during the Zhōu and Suí dynasties was Lèhuàn County;
in the Wǔdé period it was changed to Fúlù,
taking the old Hàn name.
When Má Qiū captured Jīnchéng,
the County Magistrate of Dūnhuáng, Chē Jì, did not surrender,
but fell upon his sword and died.
County Magistrate,
refers to the Magistrate of Jīnchéng County.
Dūn,
pronunciation tú mén.
Dàxià County,
belonged to Lǒngxī Commandery in the Hàn;
Zhāng Guǐ placed it under Jìnxīng Commandery,
and later established Dàxià Commandery separately.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states:
the old city of Dàxià County,
is southwest of Fúhǎn County,
facing the Táo River to the north.
Liú Xù said: Dàxià County of Hé Province,
is an ancient county of the Hàn,
named after the Dàxià River west of the county.
He surrendered the city to Qiū,
Qiū sent Yàn with a letter to lure Sòng Jǔ, the Commandant of Wǎn Garrison of Dūnhuáng,
Jǔ said:
"As a subject,
since I have not achieved merit,
I have only the choice of dying with integrity."
He first killed his wife and children, and then cut his own throat.
Qiū said:
"They are all righteous men,"
and gathered and buried them.
10 In winter,
the Grand Guardian of Hàn, Lǐ Yì, raised troops in rebellion from Jìnshòu,
many people in Shǔ followed him,
and his followers reached tens of thousands.
The ruler of Hàn, Shì, ascended the city walls to resist the attack,
as Yì's troops were advancing and pressing upon Chéngdū.
The gate guards shot and killed him,
and his followers all dispersed.
Shì declared a general amnesty within his domain,
and changed the era name to Jiāníng.
Shì was arrogant and dissolute,
did not attend to state affairs,
mostly stayed within the palace,
rarely received dukes and ministers,
distrusted and was suspicious of old ministers,
trusted those close to him,
slander and flattery flourished together,
punishments were harsh and excessive,
causing internal and external alienation.
Previously, there were no Lǎo people in Shǔ territory,
but by this time they began to emerge from the mountains,
from Bāxī to Qiánwéi and Zǐtóng,
filling the mountains and valleys with over a hundred thousand settlements,
uncontrollable,
greatly troubling the people;
coupled with famine,
within the four borders,
it became desolate and bleak.
11 The General of Pacifying the West, Huán Wēn, was about to attack the Hàn (Cheng-Han).
His officers and aides all considered it inadvisable.
The Chancellor of Jiāngxià, Yuán Qiáo, urged him, saying:
"Now, planning and managing great affairs
certainly lies beyond the scope of ordinary understanding.
The wise man comprehends them in his own mind;
he does not necessarily wait until everyone's words are in agreement.
At present, the afflictions plaguing the empire
are only the two enemies, the Hú and Shǔ.
Although Shǔ is rugged and strong,
compared to the Hú, it is weaker.
If you intend to eliminate them,
you should start with the easier one.
Lǐ Shì is without the Way;
his ministers and people do not support him.
Moreover, he relies on his rugged and remote terrain
and does not prepare for war.
You should take ten thousand elite troops, traveling light and moving swiftly.
By the time he becomes aware of it,
we will already have passed through his strategic passes,
already have passed through his strategic passes,
meaning we will have already crossed the dangerous terrain and emerged onto level ground.
The land of Shǔ is rich and fertile;
its households and population are numerous.
The Martial Marquis Zhūgě used it to contend with the Central Plains.
Zhūgě Liàng's posthumous title was Loyal and Martial Marquis.
Xià,
read as 'hù yǎ'.
This is a great benefit for the state.
Those who discuss this fear that once the main army goes west,
the Hú will certainly harbor designs.
This seems plausible but is actually mistaken.
When the Hú hear we are campaigning ten thousand *li* away,
they will think we have heavy defenses within,
and will certainly not dare to move.
Even if they do encroach or raid,
the armies along the river are sufficient to resist and defend;
there is certainly nothing to worry about."
Wēn followed his advice.
Qiáo
was the son of Yuán Huái.
Yuán Huái appears in the 95th scroll, in the third year of the Xiánkāng era of Emperor Chéng.
Huái,
read as 'gōng huí'.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Xīnwèi,
Wēn led the Inspector of Yìzhōu, Zhōu Fǔ, and the Grand Administrator of Nánjùn, Prince Qiáo Wújì, to attack the Hàn.
He submitted a memorial and set out immediately;
he entrusted the Senior Clerk of Pacifying the West, Fàn Wāng, with the affairs of the rear,
and additionally appointed Fǔ to supervise the military affairs of the four commanderies of Liángzhōu.
The four commanderies of Liángzhōu
were Fúlíng, Bādōng, Bāxī, and Bājùn.
The court considered the roads to Shǔ dangerous and distant,
and Wēn's forces few while he was penetrating deep,
so they were all worried.
Only Liú Tán believed he would certainly conquer it.
Someone asked him the reason,
and Tán said:
"I know from gambling.
Wēn
is a skilled gambler;
if he is not certain to win, he does not act.
I only fear that after conquering Shǔ,
Wēn will ultimately monopolize control of the court."
1 In spring,
the second month,
Huán Wēn's army reached Qīngyī.
Qīngyī county belonged to the Shǔ commandery in the Hàn;
in the second year of the Yángjiā era of Emperor Shùn of the Later Hàn,
it was renamed Hànjiā;
the Shǔ (state) established it as Hànjiā commandery.
Liú Xù said: The Qīngyī River is adjacent to Qīngshén county in Méizhōu;
the Western Wèi established Qīngyī county there.
The Qīngyī River originates beyond the borders of Lúshān,
flowing northeast to Wǔyáng where it joins the (main) river.
Dù Yòu said: Jiāzhōu was the former land of Yèláng;
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn opened it up and established the Qiánwéi commandery,
with its seat at Lóngyóu county,
which was the Qīngyī Circuit of the Hàn,
located at the confluence of the Great River and the Qīngyī River.
(Lǐ Shì) sent his paternal uncle, the General of the Right Guard, Lǐ Fú; his older male cousin, the General of Pacifying the South, Lǐ Quán; the Former General, Zǎn Jiān; and others to lead troops,
advancing from Shānyáng towards Héshuǐ.
The location of Shānyáng was probably north of the Mín River,
on the southern side of Éméi Mountain.
The *Commentary on the Waterways Classic* states: The river flows southeast past Wǔyáng county of Qiánwéi,
where the Qīngyī River and the Mò River come from the southwest to join and flow into it.
The so-called Héshuǐ
must be this place.
Cóng,
read as 'cái yòng'.
Zǎn,
read as 'zǐ gǎn'.
Jiàng,
read as 'jí liàng'.
Qù,
read as 'qī yù'.
Zǎn Jiān did not follow (the planned route);
he led his troops from the northern bank of the river, crossing at Yuānyāng Qí towards Qiánwéi.
In the third month,
Wēn reached Péngmó.
Péngmó
was the Péngwáng settlement in Wǔyáng county of the Hàn's Qiánwéi commandery,
the place where Cén Péng died.
The *Commentary on the Waterways Classic* states: The river from Wǔyáng east to the Péngwáng settlement
is called the Píngmó River,
also known as the Outer River.
Píngmó is two hundred *li* from Chéngdū,
located in present-day Péngshān county of Méizhōu.
(Wēn) advanced by separate routes,
in order to divide the Hàn army's strength.
Yuán Qiáo said:
"Now we have sent an isolated army deep into a place ten thousand *li* away.
If we win, a great achievement can be established;
if we do not win, not a single living soul will remain.
We should combine our forces and unify our strength
to secure victory in one battle.
If we divide into two armies,
then the hearts of the men will not be unified.
If by chance one part is defeated—
'one part is defeated' means if the two routes advance together,
one army might be defeated by Shǔ—
it would be better to advance with the entire army,
discarding our cauldrons and pots,
carrying three days' rations,
to show we have no thought of return.
Then victory is assured."
Wēn followed him.
He left his Army Advisor, Sūn Shèng, and Zhōu Chǔ to guard the baggage train with weak troops,
while Wēn personally led the infantry straight towards Chéngdū.
Chǔ
was the son of Fǔ.
Lǐ Fú attacked Péngmó,
but Sūn Shèng and others fiercely counterattacked
and drove him off.
Wēn advanced
and encountered Lǐ Quán.
After three battles and three victories,
the Hàn troops scattered and fled back to Chéngdū.
The General of Pacifying the Army,
Lǐ Wèidū, came forward to meet Wēn and surrendered.
Zǎn Jiān reached Qiánwéi
and only then realized he and Wēn had taken different routes.
He turned back
and crossed from the Shātóu Ford.
By the time he arrived,
Wēn had already stationed his army at the Ten-*Li* Path outside Chéngdū,
and Jiān's troops collapsed on their own.
Shì brought out all his troops and fought at the Zuó Bridge outside Chéngdū.
The *Commentary on the Waterways Classic* states: West of the Wànlǐ Bridge,
the upper one is called the Yí Bridge,
also called the Zuó Bridge.
Zuó,
read as 'jí gè'.
The Army Advisor, Gōng Hù, died in battle,
and arrows reached Wēn's horse's head.
The troops were afraid
and wanted to retreat,
but the drum officer mistakenly beat the advance drum.
Beating the thunder drum to urge the troops forward is called the advance drum.
Subsequently, they greatly defeated (the enemy).
Wēn, riding the momentum of victory, drove straight to Chéngdū
and set fire to its city gates.
The Hàn people were terrified
and no longer had any will to fight.
Shì fled through the east gate at night
and reached Jiāméng.
He sent the Regular Attendant of the Palace, Wáng Yòu, to deliver a document of surrender to Wēn.
Sàn,
read as 'xī dǎn'.
Qí,
read as 'qí jì'.
"Lüèyáng Lǐ Shì kowtows, acknowledging a crime deserving death."
The Lǐ clan's ancestors had moved from Bāxī to Lüèyáng.
Wēn untied his bonds and burned his coffin,
and sent Shì and more than ten members of the imperial clan to Jiànkāng.
He appointed the Hàn's Minister of Works, Qiáo Xiànzhī, and others as his aides and officers,
promoting the worthy and commending the good,
which pleased the people of Shǔ.
2 The Governor of Rìnán, Xiàhóu Lǎn, was greedy and tyrannical,
exploiting and oppressing Hu merchants,
and additionally requisitioning timber for ships,
claiming he intended to launch a campaign.
Because of this, the various states were indignant and resentful.
The King of Línyì, Fàn Wén, attacked and captured Rìnán,
with five or six thousand officers and soldiers dying,
killed Lǎn,
and used his corpse to sacrifice to heaven;
he issued a proclamation to the Governor of Jiāozhī, Zhū Fān,
requesting to use the Héngshān north of the commandery as the boundary.
Today, the southern border of Yōngzhōu has a Héngshān,
which cuts across rivers and streams,
and our dynasty established the Héngshān Fort and horse-trading market there.
According to Liú Xù's Old Book of Tang,
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn opened up the Bǎiyuè region,
and established the Rìnán Commandery three thousand *lǐ* south of the Jiāozhǐ Commandery,
with its seat at Zhūwú.
Línyì,
was the Xiànglín County of the Hàn Dynasty's Rìnán Commandery,
located four hundred *lǐ* south of the commandery's border.
During the Later Hàn, when the Central Plains was in chaos,
a man from Xiànglín County named Ōu Lián,
killed the county magistrate,
proclaimed himself King of Línyì,
and thus established the state of Línyì.
From Yōngzhōu, crossing the sea leads to Jiāozhǐ,
and from Jiāozhǐ, three thousand *lǐ* further leads to Rìnán.
This Héngshān was naturally located at the northern border of the Rìnán Commandery,
not the present-day Héngshān in Yōngzhōu.
Fān sent the Protector-General Liú Xióng to garrison Rìnán.
3 Former Hàn officials such as the late Imperial Secretary Wáng Shì, General Zhèndōng Dèng Dìng, General Píngnán Wáng Rùn, and General Kuí Wén all raised troops in rebellion,
each commanding over ten thousand men.
Huán Wēn personally attacked Dìng,
and sent Yuán Qiáo to attack Wén,
defeating them both.
Wēn ordered the Governor of Yìzhōu, Zhōu Fǔ, to defend Péngmó,
and executed Wáng Shì and Wáng Rùn.
Wēn remained in Chéngdū for thirty days,
then marshaled his troops and returned to Jiānglíng.
The Commentary says: "Upon entering, he marshaled his troops."
Dù Yù's annotation states: "Zhèn,
means to arrange;
lǚ,
means the multitude."
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Guīyì.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Dīngsì,
Dèng Dìng, Kuí Wén, and others entered and occupied Chéngdū,
the General Zhēnglǔ Yáng Qiān abandoned Fúchéng,
and retreated to defend Déyáng.
4 The Liángzhōu Governor of Zhào, Má Qiū, attacked Fúhǎn.
The Administrator of Jìnchāng, Láng Tǎn, considered the city too large to defend easily.
Emperor Huì divided Dūnhuáng and Jiǔquán to establish Jìnchāng Commandery.
Fúhǎn County,
belonged to the Jīnchéng Commandery in the Former Hàn,
to the Lǒngxī Commandery in the Later Hàn,
and was assigned to the Jìnxīng Commandery by Zhāng Guǐ.
According to the Commentary on the Water Classic,
the Jìnchāng River is located southwest of Hàomǐn County in Huángzhōng.
Liú Xù said: Jìnchāng Commandery,
was the territory of the Hàn Dynasty's Zhì'ān County;
in the Táng Dynasty, it was Jìnchāng County,
the seat of Guāzhōu.
Fú,
is pronounced fū.
The Administrator of Wǔchéng, Zhāng Quān, said:
Wǔchéng Commandery,
was also established by the Zhāng clan.
Quān,
is pronounced chǒu yuán fān,
also qī lún fān.
"Abandoning the outer city will shake the morale of the troops,
and then the great cause will be lost."
The Commandant of Níngróng, Zhāng Qú, followed Quān's advice,
and firmly defended the main city.
The Commandant of Níngróng,
was also established by the Zhāng clan.
Láng Tǎn and Zhāng Quān likely served as administrators of their respective commanderies under Zhāng Qú in defending Fúhǎn.
Qú,
is pronounced qiú yú fān.
Cloud ladders and underground assaults,
attacked from a hundred directions;
underground assaults refer to
digging tunnels that emerge inside the city.
Qiū's forces suffered tens of thousands of casualties.
The King of Zhào, Shí Hǔ, again sent his general Liú Hún and others to lead twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to join him.
Láng Tǎn resented that his advice was not heeded,
and instructed the soldier Lǐ Jiā to secretly lead over a thousand Zhào troops to climb the wall;
Qú supervised the various generals in fierce combat,
killing over two hundred men,
and the Zhào troops then retreated.
Qú burned their siege equipment,
and Qiū retreated to defend Dàxià.
Hǔ appointed the Palace Secretary Supervisor Shí Níng as General Zhēngxī,
leading over twenty thousand troops from Bìngzhōu and Sīzhōu as reinforcements for Qiū and others.
Zhāng Chònghuá's general Sòng Qín and others led twenty thousand households to surrender to Zhào.
Chònghuá appointed Xiè Ài as Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Army Mentor General,
leading thirty thousand infantry and cavalry to advance and camp by the river.
Ài rode in a light carriage,
wearing a white cap,
and proceeded with drums beating.
Qiū saw this from afar,
and angrily said:
"Ài is a young scholar,
yet dressed in such attire,
he belittles me."
He ordered three thousand black lance dragon cavalry to charge and attack him;
Ài's left and right flanks were thrown into great confusion.
Someone urged Ài to mount a horse,
but Ài refused,
descended from the carriage,
and sat on a folding chair.
The folding chair is similar to today's folding chair.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: Today's folding chair,
originally came from the northern tribes,
but because the Sui Dynasty considered the term 'Hú' inauspicious,
it was renamed 'folding chair'.
The Zhào troops thought there was an ambush,
and, afraid, did not dare to advance.
A separate general, Zhāng Mào, led troops via a side path to cut off the Zhào army's rear,
the Zhào army retreated,
and Ài seized the momentum to press the attack,
heavily defeating them,
killing their generals Dù Xūn and Jí Yú,
capturing and beheading thirteen thousand men,
and Qiū fled alone on horseback to Dàxià.
In the fifth month,
Qiū and Shí Níng again led a force of one hundred twenty thousand men to advance and camp south of the river,
while Liú Níng and Wáng Zhuó raided the territories of Jìnxīng, Guǎngwǔ, and Wǔjiē.
Zhāng Guǐ divided the western border to establish Jìnxīng Commandery.
Qūliǔ,
is a place name,
located north of Hóngchí Ridge.
They retreated to defend Fúhǎn,
causing great alarm in Gūzāng.
Chònghuá wanted to personally go out to resist them,
but Xiè Ài firmly remonstrated.
Suǒ
Xiá said:
"The ruler is
the pillar of the state,
and must not act lightly."
Therefore, he appointed Ài as Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Commander of All Military Affairs for the Campaign, Acting General of the Guards,
and Xiá as General of the Army Rectifier,
as there was an Army Rectifier in ancient times.
The Yellow Emperor's code states,
the Rectifier is not subordinate to the general,
and if the general commits a crime, it is reported.
He was likely the law enforcer within the army.
The Zhāng clan thus used it as a title for a general.
A separate general, Yáng Kāng, defeated Liú Níng at Shāfù,
and Níng retreated to camp at Jīnchéng.
5 In the sixth month,
on the day Xīnyǒu,
a general amnesty was declared.
6 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Línyì again captured Rìnán,
killing the Protector-General Liú Xióng.
7 Kuí Wén, Dèng Dìng, and others installed the son of the former State Preceptor Fàn Chángshēng, Fàn Bēn, as emperor and supported him.
Lǐ Xióng had appointed Fàn Chángshēng as State Preceptor.
Many people of Shǔ rallied to him.
8 The King of Zhào, Shí Hǔ, again sent General Zhēngxī Sūn Fúdū and General Liú Hún to lead twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to join Má Qiū's army,
advancing swiftly across the river,
and attacked Zhāng Chònghuá's Suìchéng and Chángzuì.
Chángzuì,
is a place name,
located north of the Jīnchéng River.
Textual analysis notes: Jìn Chūnqiū records
"Shàngzuì".
Here we follow the biography of Chònghuá.
A wind blew the banners and flags pointing southeast,
and Suǒ Xiá said:
"Wind conveys commands,
now the banners point towards the enemy,
it is heaven's assistance."
The Miscellaneous Divinations of Wind, Clouds, and Weather states: When the wind does not blow sideways,
and the banners flutter and rise with the wind,
or point towards the enemy,
if the army marches all day, it will achieve merit,
a sign of victory.
Wáng Zhuó engaged Ài's vanguard in battle,
was defeated,
and fled back south of the river.
In the eighth month,
on the day Wùwǔ,
Ài advanced to attack Qiū,
heavily defeating him,
and Qiū fled back to Jīnchéng.
Hǔ heard of this,
and sighed, saying:
"With a flank army I pacified the Nine Provinces,
yet now with the strength of the Nine Provinces I am stymied at Fúhǎn.
They have capable men,
they cannot be plotted against!"
Ài returned,
and campaigned against the rebellious tribes such as Sīgǔzhēn, comprising over ten thousand settlements,
and pacified them all.
9. Zhào Wáng Hǔ controlled the territory of ten provinces,
namely Yōu, Bìng, Jì, Sī, Yù, Yǎn, Qīng, Xú, Yōng, and Qín.
The rare treasures presented by foreign states,
and the wealth stored in the treasuries,
were beyond measure;
yet he still considered it insufficient,
and excavated all the imperial tombs of previous dynasties,
taking their gold and treasures.
The Buddhist monk Wú Jìn said to Hǔ:
Yuán Hóng's Hàn Jì states: "Shāmén,"
in Hàn language means "to cease,"
meaning to cease desires and return to non-action.
"The fortune of the Hú is about to decline,
while Jìn shall be restored.
It is appropriate to impose harsh labor on the Jìn people to suppress their spirit."
Hǔ ordered the Secretary Zhāng Jǐ to conscript 160,000 men and women from the nearby commanderies,
with 100,000 carts,
to transport earth and construct the Huálín Garden and a long wall north of Yè,
spanning several tens of lǐ in length and width.
Shēn Zhōng, Shí Pú, Zhào Lǎn, and others submitted memorials stating that the celestial phenomena were disordered,
and the people were suffering and impoverished.
Hǔ was greatly angered and said:
"If the garden wall is completed by morning,
and I die by evening,
I would have no regrets."
He urged Zhāng Jǐ to have torches lit and work continued through the night;
a violent storm and heavy rain ensued,
and tens of thousands of people died.
The commanderies and kingdoms successively sent sixteen green qílín
and seven white deer.
Hǔ ordered the Director of Hunting Zhāng Hézhù to train them to pull the "zhī-gài" carriage.
According to the Jìn Zhíguān Zhì,
under the Grand Coachman there was the position of Diǎnyú Dūwèi.
The Zhào position of Sīyú
was this office.
Zhāng Hézhù
is a person's name.
The "zhī-gài"
refers to a canopy shaped like an auspicious fungus.
In the ninth month,
Hǔ ordered the Crown Prince Xuān to go out and pray for blessings at the mountains and rivers,
and to go on a hunting tour.
Xuān rode in a grand carriage,
with feather canopies and ornate covers,
and flew the banners of the Son of Heaven.
An army of 180,000 soldiers from sixteen divisions marched out from the Jīnmíng Gate.
According to the Shuǐjīng Zhù,
the city of Yè had seven gates: the southern one was called Fèngyáng Gate,
the central one Zhōngyáng Gate,
next to it Guǎngyáng Gate,
the eastern one Jiànchūn Gate,
the northern one Guǎngdé Gate,
next to it Jiù Gate,
and the western one Xīmíng Gate,
which was likely the Jīnmíng Gate.
He laughed and said:
"With my family's father and son like this,
unless heaven collapses and earth splits,
what else is there to worry about!
We only need to hold our children and play with our grandchildren,
enjoying ourselves day by day."
Wherever Xuān stayed,
he would arrange people to form a long encirclement,
each side spanning a hundred lǐ,
driving the birds and beasts,
so that by dusk they were all gathered within,
and he made the civil and military officials all kneel or stand,
forming multiple rows to guard the perimeter.
Torchlights were as bright as day,
and he ordered over a hundred strong cavalry to gallop and shoot within the enclosure.
Xuān and his concubines watched from a carriage,
continuing until all the beasts were gone.
If any beast broke through and escaped,
those responsible for guarding that section,
if they held a noble rank, would have their horses confiscated
and be made to walk for a day;
if they had no rank, they would be whipped a hundred times.
Over ten thousand soldiers died from hunger and cold,
and the three provinces and fifteen commanderies he passed through
had all their supplies and reserves completely exhausted.
Based on Tāo's subsequent expedition,
the three provinces Xuān passed through
were likely Sī, Yǎn, and Yù.
Hǔ then ordered
Tāo to follow with another expedition,
from Bìng Province to Qín and Yōng, doing the same.
Xuān was angered that Tāo was treated as his equal,
and grew even more jealous of him.
The eunuch Zhào Shēng was favored by Xuān,
but not by Tāo,
and subtly urged Xuān to eliminate him,
thus beginning the plot to kill Tāo.
10. Zhào Má Qiū again attacked Zhāng Chónghuá's general Zhāng Mào,
and defeated him.
According to the Zàijì,
Mào was stationed at Héxiá at the time.
Defeated,
Bǔ Mài fān.
The Protector of Fúhǎn, Lǐ Kuí, led seven thousand troops to surrender to Zhào,
and south of the Yellow River,
the Dí and Qiāng tribes all submitted to Zhào.
11. In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Yǐchǒu day,
the Court Gentleman-in-Attendance Yú Guī was sent to Liáng Province,

to confer upon Zhāng Chónghuá the titles of Palace Attendant, Grand Commander, Commander of the Military Affairs of Lǒngyòu and Guānzhōng, Great General, Governor of Liáng Province, and Duke of Xīpíng.
When Guī arrived at Gūzāng,
Chónghuá wished to proclaim himself King of Liáng,
and was unwilling to accept the edict.
He had his confidant Shěn Měng privately say to Guī:
"Our lord's family has for generations been loyal ministers of Jìn.
'Yìshì'
means successive generations.
Why is it, then,
that the court enfeoffed Mùróng Huàng as King of Yān,
while our lord is only made a Great General?
How can this encourage loyalty and worthiness!
You, the illustrious envoy, should issue a dispatch to Héyòu,
and together urge our provincial lord to become King of Liáng.
Guī, as a Court Gentleman-in-Attending,
because of his mission,
is called 'míngtái'.
'Dispatch'
means to issue an official document.
If it benefits the state,
you may take the initiative."
Guī replied:
"You are mistaken!
In ancient times,
ministers of various states commonly addressed each other as 'my lord'.
The Yílǐ Zhù states: 'Zǐ'
is an honorable title for a man.
Saying 'my lord'
is a term of intimacy.
No noble rank is higher than that of 'Shànggōng';
during the Three Dynasties' enfeeffment system,
the ranks of nobility were five,
namely Duke, Marquis, Earl, Viscount, and Baron;
the 'Shànggōng' held the nine-fold mandate to act as a feudal lord.
Wú and Chǔ first presumptuously claimed the title of King,
and the other feudal lords did not condemn them,
because they were treated as barbarians;
if Qí or Lǔ had called themselves kings,
would the other feudal lords not have attacked them from all sides!
Hàn Gāozǔ enfeoffed Hán Xìn and Péng Yuè as kings,
but soon had them executed,
which was an expedient measure for the time,
not a mark of great favor.
The Sage Emperor, considering your lord's loyalty and worthiness,
has thus enfeoffed him as a 'Shànggōng',
and appointed him as a regional overlord.
His favor and honor have reached the utmost;
how can the Xiānbēi barbarians compare!
Moreover, I have heard that
achievements vary in scale,
and rewards vary in weight.
Now, if your lord were to become king immediately upon succeeding his father,
meaning Chónghuá has just succeeded his father's position,
without having rendered any service to Jìn and seeking to become king,
then when he pacifies the Hú and Jié in the east,
restores the imperial tombs and temples,
and welcomes the Son of Heaven back to Luòyáng,
what higher reward could be given to him then?"
Chónghuá then desisted.
12. The Dí king of Wǔdū, Yáng Chū, sent an envoy to pledge allegiance.
An edict appointed Chū as Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Campaigning South General, Governor of Yōng Province, and Duke of Chóuchí.
13. In the twelfth month,
the Inspiring Might Protector Xiāo Jìngwén killed the Campaigning Against Caitiffs General Yáng Qiān,
attacked Fúchéng,
captured it,
and proclaimed himself Governor of Yì Province;
he then seized Bāxī,
connecting with Hànzhōng.
Inspiring Might Protector
was a Jìn official title.
Xiāo Jìngwén, because Jìn had newly annexed Shǔ,
and there was also the rebellion of Fàn Bēn,
thus also took advantage to rebel.
Fú,
pronounced fú.
Punctuated by Zhèng Tiāntǐng, reviewed by Wáng Chóngwǔ and Niè Chóngqí.
Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial order.
Later student from Tiāntāi.
Xiàozōng Mù Huángdì, Part One, Lower Section.
Fourth year of Yǒnghé
(Wùshēn, 348 CE)
1. In summer,
the fourth month,
Línyì invaded Jiǔzhēn.
Having already twice defeated Rìnán,
they advanced to invade Jiǔzhēn.
Jiǔzhēn commandery
corresponds to Táng's Ài Prefecture.
2. Zhào Qín Gōng Tāo was favored by King Hǔ of Zhào,
and he wished to establish him as heir.
However, because Crown Prince Xuān was the elder,
he hesitated and could not decide.
Once, Xuān had offended the king's will,
and Hǔ angrily said:
"I regret not having established Tāo!"
From then on, Tāo became even more arrogant.
He built a hall in the Grand Commandant's residence,
naming it the Xuānguāng Hall,
with a beam nine zhàng long.
When Xuān saw it,
he was greatly enraged.
He beheaded the craftsman,
cut the beam, and left—
because it violated his name.
Tāo then increased it to ten zhàng.
When Xuān heard of this,
he said to his trusted followers Yáng Bēi,
Móu Chéng, and Zhào Shēng:
"That vicious and arrogant wretch dares to act like this!
If you can kill him,
I will enter the Western Palace.
(Hǔ resided in the Western Palace.)
When Tāo dies,
the ruler is sure to attend the funeral.
I will then carry out the great affair,
and nothing will fail to succeed."
(Zuǒzhuàn: Pān Chóng said to Chǔ Shāngchén:
"Can you carry out the great affair?"
Dù Yù's commentary states: The great affair
refers to regicide.)
In autumn,
the eighth month,
Tāo held a banquet with his subordinates at night in the Dōngmíng Observatory.
(Shuǐjīng Zhù: The Shí family established the Dōngmíng Observatory on the eastern wall of Yè.)
Buddhist jīngshè
are Buddhist temples.
They are places where monks concentrate on cultivation and practice,
hence called jīngshè.
Shìwù Jìyuán states: Emperor Míng of Hàn established a jīngshè outside the Dōngdū Gate
to house Shè Móténg and Zhú Fǎlán.)
The ladder was narrow and long,
and people climbed it like macaques,
hence it was called the macaque ladder.
He left his knife and arrows there and departed.
The next morning,
Xuān reported it.
Hǔ was grief-stricken and shocked, falling into a faint,
and only revived after a long while.
He was about to go out to attend the funeral,
but Minister of Works Lǐ Nóng admonished:
"The person who harmed Duke Qín is unknown,
and the culprit is in the capital.
Your Majesty's carriage should not lightly go out."
Hǔ then stopped
and, with strict military guard, held mourning in the Tàiwǔ Hall.
Xuān went to attend Tāo's funeral,
but did not weep.
He merely uttered
"hēhē,"
had them lift the shroud to view the corpse,
then laughed loudly and left.
(A large coverlet is called a qīn.)
He intended to implicate him with a crime.
Hǔ suspected Xuān of killing Tāo.
He wanted to summon him,
but feared he would not enter.
So he falsely claimed that his mother, Empress Dù, was grief-stricken and critically ill.
Xuān, not suspecting he was under suspicion,
entered the palace to attend court,
and was thus detained.
Shǐ Kē of Jiànxīng knew of the plot
and reported it.
(Wèi Tǔdì Jì states: Jiànxīng Commandery administered Yáng'ē County;
Yáng'ē County
belonged to Shàngdǎng Commandery in Hàn times.
Wèi Shōu's records state: Mùróng Yǒng divided Shàngdǎng to establish Jiànxīng Commandery.
Thus, this place was not the Jiànxīng Commandery established by the Shí Zhào.
Shuǐjīng Zhù states: Tián Róng said that Zhào established Jiànxīng Commandery within Guǎngzōng City,
which is correct.)
They all fled;
Zhào Shēng was captured,
interrogated,
and fully confessed.
Hǔ's grief and rage grew even more intense.
He imprisoned Xuān in the Mat Storehouse.
(The Mat Storehouse
was a place for storing mats.)
He took the knife and arrows that killed Tāo and licked the blood,
wailing so loudly it shook the palace halls.
Fótú Chéng said:
"Xuān and Tāo are both Your Majesty's sons.
Now, to kill Xuān for Tāo
is to double the calamity.
If Your Majesty can show mercy and forgiveness,
your fortune and longevity will still be long.
If you insist on executing him,
Xuān will become a comet sweeping down to destroy the Yè palace."
Hǔ did not listen.
He piled firewood north of Yè,
erected a post on it,
and placed a pulley at the top of the post.
A rope was threaded through it.
(The pulley is a wooden lùlú.)
He sent Xuān beneath it,
and had Tāo's favored eunuchs Hǎo Zhì and Liú Bà pull out his hair,
extract his tongue,
and drag him up the ladder.
Hǎo Zhì threaded a rope through his jaw
and hoisted him up with the pulley.
Liú Bà severed his hands and feet,
gouged out his eyes, and ruptured his intestines,
just like Tāo's wounds.
Then they set fire from all sides,
and smoke and flames reached the sky.
Hǔ, along with several thousand people from the Zhaoyi down, ascended the Central Terrace to watch.
(The Central Terrace
is the middle of the Three Terraces,
namely the Copper Sparrow Terrace.)
They took the ashes and placed them at the intersections of the various gates.
(Intersections
are crossways;
one vertical and one horizontal form a crossway.)
Xuān's youngest son was only a few years old,
and Hǔ had always loved him.
He held him and wept,
wanting to pardon him,
but his ministers would not allow it.
They took him from his embrace and killed him.
The child clutched Hǔ's clothes and screamed,
until the belt snapped,
and Hǔ fell ill because of this.
He also deposed his empress, Dù, to commoner status.
He executed over three hundred people from his four guard commanders down,
and fifty eunuchs,
all torn apart by chariots and dismembered joint by joint,
and thrown into the Zhāng River.
(The Eastern Palace had left, right, front, and rear four guard commanders.
Shuài
is pronounced suǒ lǜ fān.
Dismemberment
means severing the four limbs;
joint-by-joint dismemberment
means dismembering every bone joint by joint.)
Over a hundred thousand guards of the Eastern Palace were exiled to garrison Liángzhōu.
(Zhào had not yet obtained Liángzhōu;
they established Liángzhōu in Jīnchéng,
exiling them to garrison the borders of Liángzhōu.)
This sets the stage for the rebellion of the Gāolì troops below.
Zhào Lǎn said to Hǔ:
"There will be a change in the palace;
you should prepare for it."
After Xuān killed Tāo,
Hǔ suspected that he knew but did not report it,
and also executed him.
The history states that Zhào Lǎn practiced divination in a suspicious and violent court, bringing disaster upon himself.
Xiān
is pronounced xī jiàn fān.
3. The court discussed the merits of pacifying Shǔ,
and wanted to enfeoff Huán Wēn with the Yùzhāng Commandery.
Left Assistant of the Secretariat Xún Ruí said:
"If Wēn pacifies Hé and Luò again,
what will we reward him with then?"
So they instead appointed Wēn as General Who Conquers the West and granted him the privilege of establishing a personal administration with the same honors as the Three Excellencies,
enfeoffing him as Duke of Línhè Commandery.
They appointed Prince Qiáo Wújì as General of the Vanguard;
Yuán Qiáo as General Who Soars Like a Dragon,
enfeoffing him as Earl of Xiāngxī.
Ruí
was the son of Sōng.
(Xún Sōng
was the brother of Xún Fān.
During the disaster of Yǒngjiā,
they jointly established a mobile secretariat in Mì.
At the beginning of the Jiànxīng era,
he also once governed Wǎn.)
After Wēn destroyed Shǔ,
his prestige and fame greatly increased,
and the court feared him.
Prince Yù of Kuàijī, because the Governor of Yángzhōu, Yīn Hào, had great fame
and was admired and respected by both court and commoners,
drew him close as a trusted confidant,
letting him participate in and oversee court authority,
intending to use him to oppose Wēn.
From then on, he and Wēn gradually became suspicious and estranged.
This sets the stage for Wēn deposing Hào and coercing the court.
Cháo
is pronounced zhí yáo fān.
Kuài
is pronounced gōng wài fān.
Hào, considering that the Northern Expedition Chief Clerk Xún Xiàn and former Jiangzhou Governor Wáng Xīzhī
had long enjoyed fine reputations,
promoted Xiàn to be the Administrator of Wú Commandery.
Among the commanderies and principalities south of the Yangtze,
Wú was considered the foremost.
He intended to use them as his wings.
Xiàn was
the younger brother of Rúi;
Xīzhī was
the nephew of Dǎo.
Xīzhī believed that only when internal and external affairs were harmonious
could the state be secure,
and he advised Hào
not to create a rift with Wēn;
Hào did not listen.
4 The King of Yān, Huàng, fell ill.
He summoned his heir apparent, Jùn, and entrusted him, saying:
"Now the Central Plains are not yet pacified,
and we must rely on worthy and outstanding men to manage worldly affairs.
Kè possesses both wisdom and courage,
and his talent is sufficient to bear heavy responsibilities.
You must entrust him,
to fulfill my ambition!"
He also said:
"Yáng Shìqiū's conduct is lofty and pure,
loyal, capable, steadfast, and firm.
Yáng Wù,
courtesy name Shìqiū.
Conduct,
read as xià mèng fān.
You must treat him well!"
In the ninth month,
on the day Bǐngshēn,
he passed away.
He was fifty-two years old.
5 The King of Zhào, Hǔ, deliberated on establishing a crown prince.
Grand Commandant Zhāng Jǔ said:
"Duke Yān, Bīn, possesses military strategy,
Duke Péngchéng, Zūn, possesses civil virtue.
It is up to Your Majesty to choose."
Hǔ said:
"Your words precisely align with my thoughts."
The Róngzhāo General Zhāng Chái said:
The Zǎijì states: Hǔ established the Left and Right Róngzhāo and Yàowǔ Generals,
whose positions were above the Left and Right Guards.
"Duke Yān's mother was of low status,
and he has also previously committed offenses;
referring to his intention to kill Zhāng Hèdù,
the matter is recorded in the ninety-sixth scroll, in the sixth year of Emperor Chéng's Xiánkāng era.
Zūn and Suì shared the same mother.
The deposition of Lady Zhèng is recorded in the ninety-fifth scroll, in the third year of the Xiánkāng era.
I fear there may be subtle resentment,
Your Majesty should consider this carefully!"
Earlier,
when Hǔ captured Shàngguī,
see the ninety-fourth scroll, the fourth year of Emperor Chéng's Xiánhé era.
there was a woman of exceptional beauty,
whom he took for Hǔ.
Hǔ favored her,
and she gave birth to Duke Qí, Shì.
Chái, considering Hǔ old and ill,
wished to establish Shì as heir,
hoping that Lady Liú would become Empress Dowager,
so that he himself could serve as regent.
He then advised Hǔ, saying:
"Your Majesty has twice established crown princes,
and their mothers were all from entertainer or lowly backgrounds,
hence disasters and chaos followed one after another.
Now you should choose one whose mother is noble and whose son is filial to establish."
Hǔ said:
"Do not speak further,
I know where the crown prince should be."
Hǔ again discussed with his close ministers in the Eastern Hall.
Hǔ said:
"I wish to cleanse my intestines with three hu of pure ashes.
Why do I only sire wicked sons,
who, upon reaching twenty, always wish to kill their father!
Now Shì is just ten years old.
By the time he is twenty,
I will already be old."
He then settled the matter with Zhāng Jǔ and Lǐ Nóng,
ordering the dukes and ministers to submit memorials requesting the establishment of Shì as crown prince.
The Grand Minister of Agriculture Cáo Mò refused to sign his name.
Hǔ sent Zhāng Chái to ask the reason.
Mò kowtowed and said:
"The state is a weighty vessel;
it is not appropriate to establish a minor.
Therefore, I dare not sign."
Hǔ said:
"Mò
is a loyal minister,
but he does not understand my intent.
Zhāng Jǔ and Lǐ Nóng understand my intent.
They can be ordered to explain it to him."
Subsequently, Shì was established as crown prince,
and Lady Liú was made empress.
Hǔ and his sons harmed each other,
deposing the elder and establishing the younger.
Heaven would lend its hand to Rǎn Mǐn to exterminate their kind.
6 In winter,
the eleventh month,
on the day Jiǎchén,
the King of Yān, Wénmíng, was buried.
Huàng was posthumously titled Wénmíng.
Jùn,
courtesy name Xuānyīng,
was the second son of Huàng.
He sent an envoy to Jiànkāng to announce the mourning.
He appointed his younger brother Jiāo as Left Worthy King,
and Left Chief Clerk Yáng Wù as Chief of the Gentlemen of the Palace.
7 In the twelfth month,
Left General of the Palace Gentlemen, concurrently Minister over the Masses, and Recorder of the Imperial Secretariat Cài Mó was appointed Palace Attendant and Minister over the Masses.
Mó submitted a memorial firmly declining,
saying to those close to him:
"If I were to become Minister over the Masses,
I would be ridiculed by later generations.
In righteousness, I dare not accept."
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Xīnwèi, the first day of the month,
a great amnesty was declared.
2 The King of Zhào, Hǔ, ascended the imperial throne.
Hǔ had ascended the position of Heavenly King in the third year of Emperor Chéng's Xiánkāng era,
and now he ascended the imperial throne.
He changed the era name to Tàiníng;
all his sons were advanced in rank to kings.
The former Eastern Palace "Mighty Warriors" and others, over ten thousand men, were exiled to garrison Liáng Province.
Shí Xuān had selected many strong men to guard the Eastern Palace,
calling them "Mighty Warriors,"
and appointed commanders to lead them.
They were from Yōng County in Fúfēng.
Yōng,
read as yòng fān;
same below.
He also ordered the Governor of Yōng Province, Zhāng Mào, to escort them.
Mào seized all their horses,
forcing them to walk and push deer-carts,
transporting provisions to the garrison post.
The Mighty Warriors Commander from Dìngyáng, Liáng Dú,
Dìngyáng County,
belonged to Shàng Commandery in the Hàn,
abolished in the Jìn.
Later, during the Tài'ān era of the Later Wèi, Dìngyáng Commandery was established;
in the Táng, it became Línzhēn County of Yán Province.
plotted to rebel and return east.
The multitude, hearing this,
all leaped and clapped, shouting loudly.
Leaping,
means jumping.
Clapping,
means striking hands together.
Shouting,
read as huǒ gù fān.
He led his multitude to attack and capture Xiàbiàn.
The General Pacifying the West, Liú Níng, attacked them from Āndìng,
but was defeated by Dú.
The Mighty Warriors were all strong and skilled archers,
each worth more than ten men.
Although they lacked armor and weapons,
they seized axes from the people,
fitted them with ten-foot handles,
and fought like spirits.
Handle,
means axe haft.
The garrison soldiers all followed them,
attacking and capturing commanderies and counties,
killing chief officials and officials of two thousand piculs rank,
advancing eastward unimpeded.
By the time they reached Cháng'ān,
their multitude had reached one hundred thousand.
The King of Lèpíng, Bāo, exhausted his elite troops to resist them,
but was defeated in one battle.
Dú then exited east through Tóng Pass,
advancing towards Luòyáng.
The Lord of Zhào, Hǔ, appointed Lǐ Nóng as Grand Commander and Acting Grand General,
commanding the Guard Army General Zhāng Hèdù and others, with one hundred thousand infantry and cavalry, to suppress them.
They fought at Xīn'ān.
Xīn'ān County,
belonged to Hóngnóng Commandery in the Hàn,
and from the Jìn onward, belonged to Hénán Commandery.
Cavalry,
read as qí jì fān;
same below.
They fought at Luòyáng,
and were again defeated,
retreating to fortify at Chénggāo.
The rebels then plundered eastward through the various commanderies of Xìngyáng and Chénliú.
In the second year of Emperor Wǔ’s Tàishǐ era,
Xìngyáng Commandery was established by partitioning Hénán.
The King of Yān, Shí Bīn, was appointed Grand Commander-in-Chief,
overseeing all military affairs both within and outside the court,
and leading Champion General-in-Chief Yáo Yìzhòng, Chariot and Cavalry General Pú Hóng, and others to suppress them.
Yìzhòng led his troops, over eight thousand men, to Yè,
traveling from Làtóu to Yè.
To lead (將),
is pronounced jiàng.
Shí Hǔ was ill,
and did not see him,
but had him escorted to the Office of the General of the Central Army.
The Office of the General of the Central Army
was where the General of the Central Army conducted affairs.
Yìzhòng was angry,
refused to eat,
and said:
"The sovereign summoned me to attack the rebels;
he should grant me strategies face to face.
Did I come for food?
Moreover, if the sovereign does not see me,
how can I know whether he is alive or dead?"
Hǔ, despite his severe illness, received him.
Yìzhòng reproached Hǔ, saying:
"Is it because your son died
that you are grieving,
and thus have fallen ill?
When your son was young, you did not choose good men to teach him,
leading him to rebel;
since he rebelled and was executed,
why grieve further?
Moreover, you have been ill for a long time,
and the son you established is young,"
referring to Crown Prince Shì.
"The realm is bound to fall into chaos;
you should worry about this first,
not about the rebels!
The rebels, in desperate straits and longing to return home,
have gathered to become bandits;
wherever they pass, they commit atrocities,
but what can they achieve?
This old Qiāng will finish them off for you in one stroke!"
To finish (了),
means to decide.
He addressed everyone, regardless of rank, as "you,"
yet Hǔ did not reprimand him for it.
On the spot, he was granted the authority of Commissioner Bearing Credentials,
General-in-Chief Who Conquers the West,
and was bestowed with armor and horses.
Yìzhòng said:
"Do you think this old Qiāng is capable of crushing the rebels?"
He then donned his armor, mounted his horse in the courtyard,
spurred his horse southward,
and left without taking his leave.
He then joined Bīn and others in attacking the rebels at Xìngyáng,
where they inflicted a major defeat,
beheaded the rebel leader, and returned,
suppressing the remaining factions
until they were completely eradicated.
Hǔ granted Yìzhòng the privilege of wearing his sword and shoes in the palace,
and of not hastening his steps when entering court.
He was further enfeoffed as Duke of Xīpíng Commandery.
Pú Hóng was appointed General of Chariots

and Cavalry, General-in-Chief, granted the right to establish a personal administrative office with honors equal to the Three Excellencies, Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in Yōng and Qín Provinces, and Governor of Yōng Province,
and was enfeoffed as Duke of Lüèyáng Commandery.
3 Mǎ Xù of Shǐpíng gathered troops,
proclaiming himself a general.
Dù Yòu states: Hàn’s Pínglíng
was renamed Shǐpíng by Jìn,
and had the old city of Mǎ Wéi.
He executed over three thousand households.
4 In summer,
during the fourth month,
Zhōu Fǔ, Governor of Yì Province, and Zhū Tāo, General of Soaring Dragons, attacked Fàn Bēn,
beheading him,
and pacifying Yì Province.
Fàn Bēn’s rebellion began in the third year of the previous scroll.
Soaring (驤),
is pronounced xiāng.
5 An edict was issued dispatching the Court Gentleman for Ceremonials Chén Shěn to Yān,

to appoint Mùróng Jùn as Commissioner Bearing Credentials, Palace Attendant, Grand Commander-in-Chief, Commander-in-Chief of military affairs north of the Yellow River, Governor of Yōu and Píng Provinces,
General-in-Chief, Great Chányú, and King of Yān.
6 Huán Wēn dispatched Téng Jùn, Commander of Supervising Guards, to lead troops from Jiāo and Guǎng to attack King Wén of Línyì at Lúróng,
but was defeated by Wén,
retreating to Jiǔzhēn.
7 On the yǐmǎo day,
King Hǔ of Zhào was gravely ill.
He appointed Péngchéng King Shí Zūn as General-in-Chief,
to guard the region west of the passes;
Yān King Shí Bīn as Chancellor,
overseeing the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat;
and Zhāng Chái as General-in-Chief of Garrison Defense, General of the Central Army, and Minister of Personnel.
Liú Cōng established sixteen General-in-Chiefs,
with Garrison Defense being one of them.
Shí Hǔ established the General of Garrison Defense,
ranking above the General of Chariots and Cavalry;
now appointing Zhāng Chái as General-in-Chief of Garrison Defense
was to elevate his title.
The General of the Central Army held military authority,
while the Minister of Personnel managed official appointments;
thus, both civil and military powers were entrusted to Chái.
Empress Liú despised Bīn’s role in assisting governance,
fearing it would be unfavorable to the crown prince,
and conspired with Zhāng Chái to remove him.
Bīn was then in Xiāngguó.
They sent a messenger to deceitfully tell Bīn:
"The sovereign’s illness is gradually improving; if Your Highness wishes to hunt,
you may stay a while."
Bīn, who was fond of hunting and indulged in drink,
thus remained to hunt
and indulged in wine.
Lady Liú and Chái then forged an edict accusing Bīn of lacking loyalty and filial piety,
dismissing him from office and ordering him to return to his residence,
and dispatched Chái’s younger brother, Xióng, with five hundred Dragon Soaring guards to guard him.
This was the same stratagem Shí Hǔ had used to confine Shí Hóng;
Zhāng Chái followed and employed it—
was it not taught by Hǔ?
Shí Bīn was also a mediocre man;
with his sovereign and father critically ill,
he was summoned to receive the testament and assist governance.
Even if Hǔ’s illness had slightly improved,
he should have traveled day and night;
yet he indulged in wine and hunting—
his lack of wisdom was such!
Even if he had gained power,
his younger brothers would have wrested it from him.
Zhāng Jǔ claimed he had military prowess,
but that was baseless!
On the yǐchǒu day,
Zūn arrived from Yōu Province to Yè.
He was ordered to receive his appointment at the court hall,
was allocated thirty thousand imperial guards, and sent off,
departing in tears.
That day,
Hǔ’s illness slightly improved,
and he asked:
"Has Zūn arrived yet?"
His attendants replied:
"He left long ago."
Hǔ said:
"I regret not seeing him!"
Hǔ approached the western pavilion,
the western pavilion of the Tàiwǔ Hall.
Hǔ asked:
"What do you seek?"
They all said:
"The sacred body is unwell;
we should order the King of Yān to enter and guard the palace,
and command the troops."
Some said:
"We beg to establish him as crown prince."
Hǔ said:
"Is the King of Yān not inside?
Summon him here!"
His attendants said:
"The king is ill from drink
and cannot enter."
Hǔ said:
"Quickly prepare a carriage to fetch him;
I shall entrust him with the imperial seal."
Yet no one acted.
The attendants all sided with Empress Liú and her son,
thus no one acted.
Seal (璽),
is pronounced xǐ.
Ribbon (綬),
is pronounced shòu.
Confused (惛),
means bewildered and forgetful.
Dizzy (眩),
means blurred vision.
They killed Bīn, hoping to unify the people’s hearts,
unaware that there were already those urging Shí Zūn to ascend the throne.
On the wùchén day,
Lady Liú again forged an edict appointing Chái as Grand Guardian, Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs within and outside the court,
overseeing the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat,
following the precedent of Huò Guāng.
Palace Attendant Xú Tǒng sighed:
"Chaos is about to erupt;
I shall not be involved in it."
He drank poison and died.
On the jǐsì day,
Hǔ passed away.
Crown Prince Shì ascended the throne,
honoring Lady Liú as Empress Dowager.
Lady Liú assumed regency and issued decrees,
appointing Zhāng Chái as Chancellor.
Chái declined the appointment,
requesting instead that Péngchéng King Zūn and Yìyáng King Jiàn be appointed as Left and Right Chancellors,
to appease their hearts.
Lady Liú complied.
Chái plotted with Grand Commandant Zhāng Jǔ to kill Grand Minister of Works Lǐ Nóng.
Jǔ had always been on good terms with Nóng,
and secretly informed him;
Nóng fled to Guǎngzōng,
leading tens of thousands of households of Qǐhuó to defend Shàngbái.
Qǐhuó
were the remaining followers of Lǐ Yùn and Tián Huī,
who since the Yǒngjiā era
had been garrisoned at Shàngbái.
The term "shuài"
is read as "shuài";
the same applies below.
Chái appointed Zhāng Lí as General-in-Chief Who Guards the Army,
overseeing all military affairs inside and outside the capital,
making him his deputy.
Prince Péngchéng Shí Zūn arrived at Hénèi,
where he heard of the mourning.
Yáo Yìzhòng, Pú Hóng, Liú Níng, and General Who Pacifies the Caitiffs Shí Mǐn, General of the Martial Guards Wáng Luán, and others, returning from their campaign against Liáng Dú,
met Zūn at Lǐchéng.
According to the Continued Records of the Hàn,
Pínggāo County in Hénèi had a Lǐchéng.
The Records of the Grand Historian states
that Lǐ Tóng of Hándān repelled the Qín army,
and Zhào enfeoffed his father as Marquis Lǐ,
which refers to this city.
"Your Highness is both elder and worthy,
and the late emperor also intended for Your Highness to be his heir;
this refers to Shí Hǔ's intention to follow Zhāng Jǔ's advice.
The term "shuō"
is pronounced as "shuō, shū ruì fān."
The term "zhǎng"
is pronounced as "zhī liǎng fān."
But you were misled by Zhāng Chái.
Now, a female ruler presides over the court,
treacherous ministers hold power,
the standoff at Shàngbái remains unresolved,
the capital's guards are empty and weak,
if Your Highness proclaims Zhāng Chái's crimes
and marches forth to punish him,
who would not open the gates, turn their weapons, and welcome Your Highness!"
Zūn followed this advice.
Zūn
raised troops from Lǐchéng,
and turned back toward Yè.
Governor of Luò Province Liú Guó led the forces of Luòyáng to join him.
When the proclamation reached Yè,

The position of Palace General was established in the early Jìn dynasty;

The rank of Guānwài Hóu was established by Wèi Wǔwáng Cáo Cāo in the twentieth year of the Jiàn'ān era of Hàn Xiàndì,
which is the so-called titular marquis.
I note that during the Qín and Hàn dynasties, marquises with fiefs had territories and estates;
Guānnèi Hóu had no territories or estates,
but held a position at court.
Those without official posts resided in the capital,
hence they were called Guānnèi Hóu.
Many marquises with fiefs who went to their territories were located outside the passes.
Later, Cáo Cāo established the rank of Guānwài Hóu below that of Guānnèi Hóu,
which was not in line with the original intent of the Qín and Hàn noble ranks.
Moreover, he further inscribed names to distinguish good and evil in order to suppress them,
causing widespread resentment and anger.

rose up in Chíyáng,
Liú Zhēn and Xiàhóu Xiǎn rose up in Hù,
Qiáo Bǐng rose up in Yōng,
Húyáng Chì rose up in Sīzhú,
and Hūyán Dú rose up in Bàchéng.
Chíyáng County,
belonged to Féngyì in the Hàn dynasty,
to Fúfēng in the Jìn dynasty,
and became Yúnyáng County in the Táng dynasty,
under Jīngzhào.
Hù County,
belonged to Fúfēng in the Hàn dynasty,
to Shǐpíng Commandery in the Jìn dynasty,
and under Jīngzhào in the Táng dynasty.
Yōng County,
belonged to Fúfēng in the Hàn dynasty,
was renamed Tiānxīng County in the Táng dynasty,
and became the seat of Fèngxiáng Prefecture.
Bàlíng County,
belonged to Jīngzhào in the Hàn dynasty,
and was renamed Bàchéng in the Jìn dynasty.
"Qiáo Bǐng"
is recorded as
"Qiáo Jǐng" in the historical records,
to avoid a Táng dynasty taboo.
"Kǒng Chí"
is recorded as
"Kǒng Tè".
Hù,
is pronounced hù.
Yōng,
is pronounced yòng.
They each sent envoys to request troops.
11. The state of Qin appointed the Left Deputy Yú Zūn as Minister of Works.
12. In the ninth month,
the Qin Chancellor Xióng led 20,000 troops back to Cháng'ān,
and sent Prince Jīng of Píngchāng to pacify Shàngluò.
He established a Jīng Province in Fēngyáng Chuān.
Shàngluò County,
belonged to Hóngnóng Commandery under the Western Hàn capital,
and to Jīngzhào in the Eastern Hàn;
in the second year of the Tàishǐ era of Emperor Wǔ (266 AD),
Shàngluò Commandery was separately established.
Fēngyáng Chuān was within the commandery's boundaries.
According to the Supplementary Records of the Hàn Dynasty,
Xī County in Nányáng Commandery had a Fēngyáng city.
In the second year of the Tài'ān era of the Later Wèi (456 AD),
Fēngyáng County was established.
The place mentioned in the Zuǒ Zhuàn
"the Minister of War arose in Fēng and Xī"
refers to this area.
Liú Xù said: The Táng dynasty's Fēngyáng County in Shāng Prefecture,
was the territory of Shāng County in the Hàn dynasty.
The Jìn dynasty separated Shāng County to establish Fēngyáng County,
named after Fēngyáng Chuān.
Xióng, along with Prince Fǎ of Qīnghé and Fú Fēi, separately campaigned against Kǒng Chí and others.
13. Yáo Xiāng was stationed in Lìyáng.
Considering that Yān and Qín were currently strong,
he had no intention of launching a northern expedition.
Instead, he extensively established military agricultural colonies along both sides of the Huái River,
and trained and disciplined his officers and soldiers.
Yīn Hào was in Shòuchūn,
and resented Xiāng's growing strength.
He imprisoned Xiāng's younger brothers,
and repeatedly sent assassins to kill him,
but the assassins all revealed the truth to Xiāng.
General Ānběi Wèi Tǒng died.
Wèi Tǒng had surrendered,
as seen in the seventh year above.
Hào secretly sent Jǐng to lead 5,000 troops to attack him.
Xiāng killed Jǐng,
and absorbed his troops.
Hào disliked him even more.
He had General Lóngxiāng Liú Qǐ guard Qiáo,
and relocated Xiāng to Lítái in Liáng Principality.
According to Sīmǎ Biāo's Records of Commanderies and States,
Suīyáng County had a Lúmén Pavilion.
Inside the city was a high tower,
very elegant and spacious,
towering majestically and standing alone,
rising loftily and uniquely,
called the Lí Tower.
Dù Yù said: Lúmén
was the southern gate of the Sòng city.
The Continued Record of Campaigns says: The winding path resembles a gourd ladle (lí),
hence it was called the Lí Tower.
Lí,
is pronounced according to its character;
if according to the explanation in the Record of Campaigns,
it is pronounced luógē.
Wèi Jǐng's sons and brothers frequently traveled to and from Shòuchūn,
making Xiāng increasingly suspicious and fearful.
He sent his staff officer Quán Yì as an envoy to Hào.
Hào said:
"I and General Yáo Píngběi both serve as ministers of the sovereign,
sharing both joy and sorrow.
Yet General Píngběi often acts arbitrarily on his own authority,
greatly violating the principle of mutual dependence like cheek and jawbone.
How can this be what is expected!"
The Zuǒ Zhuàn says: The cheek and jawbone depend on each other.
Dù Yù's commentary notes: The cheek (fǔ)
is the jowl;
the jawbone (chē)
is the tooth-bearing bone.
Chē,
is pronounced chǐ shē.
"General Píngběi possesses peerless heroic bearing,
commands tens of thousands of troops,
and came from afar to submit to the Jìn court
because the court upholds the Way,
and the chief ministers are wise and enlightened.
Now, General, you lightly believe slanderous and malicious words,
creating a rift with General Píngběi.
In my humble opinion, the origin of suspicion and estrangement
lies here, not there."
Hào said:
"General Píngběi's nature is bold and unrestrained,
freely deciding life and death,
and he even allowed his underlings to plunder my horses.
Is this the proper conduct
of a royal minister?"
Yì replied:
"General Píngběi submitted to the sacred court,
how would he recklessly kill the innocent!
As for wicked and lawless men,
they are also intolerable under the king's law.
What harm is there in killing them!"
Hào said:
"Then what about plundering the horses?"
Yì said:
