"General, you believed General Píngběi was formidable and martial, difficult to control,
and would eventually campaign against him.
Therefore, he took the horses intending to defend himself."
Hào laughed and said:
"Why would it come to that!"
Quán Yì's words
had touched upon Hào's true intentions,
hence his laugh.
The historian remarks that Hào was incapable of pacifying and controlling new adherents.
Initially,
Hào had secretly sent people to entice Liáng Ān and Léi Ruò'ér,
urging them to kill the Qin ruler Jiàn,
promising them authority over the region west of the passes.
Ruò'ér pretended to agree,
and requested troops for support.
When Hào heard that Zhāng Yù had rebelled,
and that Jiàn's nephew, General Fǔguó Fú Huángméi, had fled west from Luòyáng,
he thought Ān and others' plan had succeeded.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Hào personally led 70,000 troops from Shòuchūn on a northern expedition,
intending to advance and occupy Luòyáng,
and restore the imperial tombs.
The Minister of Personnel Wáng Biāozhī sent a memorandum to the Prince of Kuàijī, Yù,
stating that:
"Ruò'ér and others might be deceitful,
Hào should not advance lightly."
Yù did not listen.
Even if Liáng and Léi had indeed accepted Hào's instigation and killed Jiàn,
Hào would still have been unable to cross the passes and Shǎn to capture Cháng'ān.
His desire to take advantage of Fú Huángméi's departure to occupy Luòyáng
was merely to achieve merit by restoring the imperial tombs.
Yù, however, believed he could truly achieve merit,
and did not heed Wáng Biāozhī's words.
No wonder Huán Wēn was able to use this to depose Hào and control Yù.
Hào appointed Yáo Xiāng as the vanguard.
Xiāng led his troops northward,
and anticipating Hào's approach,
feigned a night retreat with his troops,
secretly setting an ambush to intercept him.
Hào, upon hearing this, pursued Xiāng to Shānsāng;
Shānsāng County,
belonged to the Pèi Commandery in the Former Hàn,
to the Rǔnán Commandery in the Later Hàn,
and to the Qiáo Commandery in the Jìn.
Regarding Shānsāng,
during the military conflicts of the Six Dynasties,
it was part of the Guōyáng region,
and in the Táng, it became part of Méngchéng County in Bó Prefecture.
Hào suffered a major defeat,
abandoned his baggage and supplies,
and fled to defend Qiáochéng.
Xiāng captured and beheaded over ten thousand men,
seized all their supplies and weapons,
left his elder brother Yì to guard Shānsāng,
and Xiāng returned to Huáinán.
The Prince of Kuaìjī, Yù, said to Wáng Biāozhī:
"Your words never miss the mark,
not even Zhāng or Chén could surpass you!"
Zhāng and Chén
refer to Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng.
14 Zhāng Chónghuá, the Duke Jìngliè of Xīpíng, fell ill.
His son, Yàolíng, was only ten years old,
and was established as heir,
with a general pardon issued throughout his domain.
Chónghuá's elder half-brother, the Marquis of Chángníng, Zuò,
possessed courage, strength, and administrative talent.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: Forty lǐ northwest of Xīpíng in Jīnchéng is the Chángníng Pavilion.
The Jìn court's Xīpíng Commandery had a Chángníng County.
He formed a sworn brotherhood with Chónghuá's favored ministers, Zhào Cháng and Wèi Jī.
Wèi
is a surname.
The Zuǒzhuàn mentions the Zhèng minister Wèi Zhǐ.
Bì,
pronounced bēi,
also pronounced bó jì.
Chónghuá said:
"I intend to make Zuò like the Duke of Zhōu,
to assist my young son.
What kind of talk is this!"
The difficulty of entrusting an orphan has always been great,
let alone for Zhāng Chónghuá!
Xiè Ài, due to his achievements at Fūhǎn
(events seen in scroll 97, third year of Yǒnghé),
Fū,
pronounced fū.
was resented by those around him,
who slandered Ài,
leading to his appointment as Prefect of Jiǔquán.
Ài submitted a memorial stating:
"Favorites are wielding power,
and the ducal house is in danger.
I beg to be allowed to enter and serve."
He also said
"The Marquis of Chángníng, Zuò, and Zhào Cháng and others are about to rebel,
and they should all be expelled."
In the eleventh month,
on the day Jǐwèi,
Chónghuá's illness worsened,
and he issued a handwritten order summoning Ài to serve as General of the Guards,
overseeing all military affairs,
to assist in governance;
Zuò, Cháng, and others concealed it and did not announce it.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
Chónghuá died,
and the heir, Yàolíng, succeeded him,
styled as Grand Marshal, Governor of Liáng Province, and Duke of Xīpíng.
Zhào Cháng and others forged Chónghuá's final decree,
appointing the Marquis of Chángníng, Zuò, as Commander of All Military Affairs and General Who Pacifies the Army,
to assist in governance.
The history records the disorder of the Zhāng clan.
15 Yīn Hào sent his generals Liú Qǐ and Wáng Bīnzhī to attack Yáo Yì at Shānsāng.
Yáo Xiāng, coming from Huáinán, attacked them,
and Qǐ and Bīnzhī were both defeated and killed.
Qǐ
was the grandson of Liú Yú.
16 At the end of the Zhào,
Zhū Tū of Lèlíng, Dù Néng of Píngyuán, Dīng Ráo of Qīnghé,
and Sūn Yuán of Yángpíng each held troops and occupied cities and towns.
By now, they all surrendered to Yān;
the Yān ruler, Jùn, appointed Tū as Governor of Qīng Province,
Néng as Prefect of Píngyuán,
Ráo as General Who Establishes Integrity,
and Yuán as Governor of Yǎn Province,
each remaining to pacify their camps.
17 The Qín Chancellor, Xióng, captured Chíyáng,
and beheaded Kǒng Chí.
In the twelfth month,
Prince Fǎ of Qīnghé and Fú Fēi captured Hù,
and beheaded Liú Zhēn and Xiàhóu Xiǎn.
18 Yáo Xiāng crossed the Huái River,
and encamped at Xūyí,
recruiting and plundering refugees,
until his forces reached seventy thousand.
He appointed local officials,
and encouraged agriculture and sericulture;
Yáo Xiāng's actions were merely this,
yet the Jìn people were already alarmed and fearful of him,
something that must have been secretly laughed at by crafty heroes.
He also submitted a statement of apology.
An edict appointed Xiè Shàng as Commander of Military Affairs in Jiāngxī and Huáinán, and Governor of Yù Province,
to guard Lìyáng.
Because Shàng had won Xiāng's favor,
he was used both to recruit and appease him,
and to guard against him.
19 The Senior Clerk of the Right of Liáng, Zhào Cháng, and others proposed,
believing that
"the times are troubled and not yet pacified,
an elder ruler should be established.
Yàolíng is young and immature,
we request to establish the Marquis of Chángníng, Zuò."
Zhāng Zuò had previously gained the favor of Chónghuá's mother, Lady Mǎ,
and Lady Mǎ agreed,
so they deposed Zhāng Yàolíng as the Marquis of Liángníng,
and established Zuò as Grand Commander, Grand General, Governor of Liáng Province, and Duke of Liáng.
Once Zuò achieved his ambition,
he indulged in debauchery and cruelty,
killing Chónghuá's consort, Lady Péi, and Xiè Ài.
Debauchery:
having relations with his lord's mother;
cruelty:
killing Lady Péi and Xiè Ài.
These two acts alone,
his other debaucheries and cruelties were but further poison.
20 The Yān generals, the Guard General Kè, the Pacifying Army General Jūn, and the Left General Biāo
repeatedly recommended that the Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gate, Bà, possessed talent to command the age,
and should be entrusted with great responsibilities.
This year,
the Yān ruler, Jùn, appointed Bà as Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, General Who Pacifies the East, and Governor of Northern Jì Province,
to guard Chángshān.
The Governor of Jì Province guarded Xìndū,
now establishing Northern Jì Province at Chángshān.
1 Spring,
first month,
Zhāng Zuò proclaimed himself King of Liáng,
changing the forty-second year of Jiànxīng to the first year of Hépíng;
the Zhāng clan of Héxī,
loyal to the Jìn court,
had upheld the Jiànxīng reign title for over forty years.
Zhāng Zuò, cruel and debauched,
changed the reign title and usurped imperial prerogatives,
something his ancestors would not have recognized.
He made his son Tàihé Crown Prince;
enfeoffed his younger brother Tiānxī as Marquis of Chángníng,
and his son Tíngjiān as Marquis of Jiànkāng.
The Jiànkāng Commandery,
likely established by the Zhāng clan,
was divided by Zhāng Mào to belong to Liáng Province.
He established all officials,
performed suburban sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
and used the ritual music of the Son of Heaven.
The Secretary, Mǎ Jí, earnestly remonstrated,
and was dismissed from office.
The Gentleman of the Interior, Dīng Qí, again remonstrated, saying:
"Since our Duke Wǔ,
(Zhāng Guī was posthumously titled Duke Wǔ).
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu.
we have embraced loyalty and practiced humility for over fifty years,
practicing humility,
meaning we have never established a state and proclaimed ourselves kings.
In the first year of Yǒngníng of Emperor Huì,
Zhāng Guī governed the Liáng territory,
up to now, fifty-four years.
We have resisted the enemies of the entire world,
troops have been raised year after year,
yet the people have not complained of weariness.
Your Highness's merit and virtue are not higher than those of our former lord,
yet you hastily plan to change the mandate,
I do not see how this can be done.
The reason why the officers and people obey orders,
and distant regions turn to us,
is because we are able to serve the Jìn court.
Now, if you exalt yourself,
then both internal and external will become disaffected,
how can we use a corner of land to resist the powerful enemies of the world!"
Zuò was greatly angered,
and beheaded him at the palace gate.
Since ancient times, those who have killed remonstrating ministers
have never avoided ruin.
He ordered Wáng Bà, the Inspector of Jìzhōu, to move his administrative seat to Xìndū.
The previous year, Bà had governed Chángshān.
Mùróng Huàng, the Prince of Yān, considered Bà's talent extraordinary,
hence he named him Bà (meaning "Overlord"),
intending to make him his heir apparent;
his ministers remonstrated and he stopped,
yet the favor and treatment Bà received still surpassed that of the heir apparent.
Because of this, Mùróng Jùn hated him,
and because Bà had once fallen from a horse and broken his teeth,
he changed his name to Qūe;
soon, because this name corresponded to a prophecy,
he changed it again to Chuí;
he was promoted to Palace Attendant,
put in charge of the affairs of the temporary capital,
and transferred to garrison Lóngchéng.
Chuí greatly won over the hearts of the people in the northeast,
making Jùn hate him even more,
and he was summoned back again.
Although Jùn was jealous of Chuí,
in the end, it was Chuí who restored the Yān dynasty's fortune.
What Heaven has established,
can it be cast aside!
11 In the fifth month,
refugees from Jiāngxī, Guō Chǎng and others,
captured Liú Shì, the Administrator of Chénliú,
and surrendered to Yáo Xiāng.
After the Jìn crossed south,
the commandery of Chénliú was administratively attached to the territory of Chángyuán County in Qiáo Commandery.
According to the "Records of the Carrying,"
Liú Shì was at that time in Tángyì.
He appointed Zhōu Mǐn, the Minister of Personnel, as General of the Central Army,
stationed at Zhōngtáng,
and Xiè Shàng, the Inspector of Yùzhōu, returned from Lìyáng to guard the capital,
securing the river defenses.
12 Wáng Zhuó captured Chéncāng,
killing Máo Nán, the Administrator of Fúfēng for Qín.
13 Wáng Měng of Běihǎi,
was fond of learning from a young age,
unconventional and having great ambitions,
disdaining trivial matters,
and people all looked down on him.
Měng was carefree and content,
living in seclusion at Huàyīn.
The Biography of Wáng Měng states: Měng,
was from Jù County in Běihǎi,
his family resided in Wèi Commandery,
Xú Tǒng summoned him but he did not respond,
and subsequently he went into seclusion at Huàyīn Mountain.
Huàyīn County,
during the Former Hàn belonged to Jīngzhào,
during the Later Hàn and Jìn belonged to Hóngnóng Commandery.
Tì,
is pronounced tì.
Huà,
is pronounced huà.
He wore coarse clothing to visit him,
picking off lice while discussing the affairs of the world,
hè,
woolen cloth.
Shī,
is pronounced shī.
Wēn found him remarkable,
and asked:
"I have received the Son of Heaven's command,
leading a crack force of a hundred thousand to rid the common people of the cruel bandits,
yet not a single hero from Sānqín has come to join me,
why is that?"
Měng said:
"You, sir, have not hesitated to travel several thousand lǐ,
penetrating deep into enemy territory,
yet now Cháng'ān is within a stone's throw and you do not cross the Bà River,
the common people do not know your true intentions,
that is why they have not come."
Wēn fell silent, having nothing to reply,
and after a while said:
"In Jiāngdōng, there is no one to compare with you!"
Měng had evidently pointed out Wēn's true thoughts,
believing that Wēn's campaign against Qín,
was merely to use military achievements to overawe Jiāngdōng,
not truly having the heart to punish the guilty and comfort the people,
and recover lost territory;
otherwise,
why would he not cross the Bà River,
and directly attack Cháng'ān?
This is why Wēn had nothing to say in reply.
However, in my observation of Huán Wēn's military campaigns,
when attacking Qín he reached Bàshàng,
when attacking Yān he reached Fāngtóu,
in both cases he advanced with the momentum of victory,
pressing close to their capitals,
yet then he became cautious and waited,
ultimately leading to defeat.
It seems Wēn,
was a cunning and ambitious man,
advancing with victorious troops,
pressing close to the enemy capital,
hoping they would be overawed by his might from afar,
leading to internal collapse and mutiny.
Pressing close to the capital but the enemy having no internal mutiny,
he therefore became cautious and waited;
his true situation revealed and his momentum exhausted,
the enemy took advantage of this,
hence leading to defeat.
As Sū Zǐyóu said, when wisdom encounters wisdom,
then that wisdom is insufficient to rely upon, this is it.
Wēn engaged in battle with the Qín Chancellor Fú Xióng and others at Báilùyuán,
Wēn's troops fared poorly,
with over ten thousand dead.
Initially,
Wēn had pointed to the Qín wheat as provisions,
but afterwards the Qín people harvested all the wheat,
clearing the fields in preparation for him,
and Wēn's army ran short of food.
In the sixth month,
on Dīngchǒu,
he relocated over three thousand households from Guānzhōng and returned.
He appointed Wáng Měng as High Official Supervisor and Protector,
his position being Supervisor and Protector,
with the addition of "High Official."
Between Wèi and Jìn,
all those holding regional military commands,
their subordinate generals had the title Supervisor and Protector,
and later the High Official Supervisor and Protector was also established.
When Wáng Dūn garrisoned Wǔchāng,
there was a High Official Supervisor and Protector Miào Tǎn.
Měng declined and did not take up the post.
Měng was unwilling to follow Wēn,
did Wēn not wish to kill him then!
It seems Wēn's army was already defeated,
hastily retreating,
and had no time to kill him.
Hūyán Dú led ten thousand troops to follow Wēn back.
The Qín Crown Prince Fú Chǎng and others pursued and attacked Wēn,
by the time they reached Tóngguān,
Wēn's army had been repeatedly defeated,
with losses and deaths numbering in the tens of thousands.
When Wēn was stationed at Bàshàng,
Xuē Zhēn, the Administrator of Shùnyáng, urged Wēn to advance directly and press Cháng'ān;
Emperor Chéng changed Shùnyáng to Nánxiāng Commandery,
but later restored the old name.
Zhēn led a separate force and crossed alone,
achieving some gains.
When Wēn retreated,
he then returned,
speaking openly among the troops,
boasting of his own bravery and blaming Wēn for his caution;
Wēn had him killed.
14 The Qín Chancellor Fú Xióng attacked Sīmǎ Xūn and Wáng Zhuó at Chéncāng,
Xūn from Nǚwābǎo joined Zhuó in attacking Chéncāng.
Zhuó fled to Lüèyáng.
15 Qín appointed Zhào Jù, a Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments, as Inspector of Luòyáng,
to garrison Yíyáng.
16 Fú Xióng, the Reverent Martial King of Dōnghǎi for Qín, attacked Qiáo Bǐng at Yōng;
on Bǐngshēn,
he died.
The Qín ruler Fú Jiàn wept for him until he vomited blood,
saying:
"Does Heaven not wish for me to pacify the four seas!
Why does it take my Yuáncái away so quickly?"
Fú Xióng,
styled Yuáncái.
His funeral rites followed the precedent of Ānpíng, the Dedicated King of Jìn.
Xióng, as a founding meritorious minister,
held power equal to the ruler,
yet was humble, respectful, broadly benevolent,
and observed the laws and regulations,
therefore Jiàn valued him highly,
often saying:
"Yuáncái,
is my Duke of Zhōu."
His son Jiān inherited his title.
Jiān inherited the title Prince of Dōnghǎi.
From a young age he had ambition and judgment,
was widely learned and capable in many things,
associated with heroes and outstanding men,
Lǚ Pólóu, Qiáng Wāng, and Liáng Pínglǎo of Lüèyáng were all on good terms with him.
The affairs of Fú Jiān begin here.
17 Mùróng Gōu, the Administrator of Lèlíng for Yān,
was the son of Mùróng Hàn,
Mùróng Hàn had achievements in defeating Gāogōulí and destroying Yǔwén.
Gōu, relying on being a member of the imperial clan,
often bullied and insulted Tūfā Sī.
Sī could not contain his anger,
in autumn,
the seventh month,
he attacked Gōu,
killed him,
and fled south to Duàn Kān.
This sets the stage for the later Yān ruler's execution of Sī.
On the Renwu day,
Fu Jiàn appointed the Grand Marshal, the Prince of Wǔdū, Fu Ān, to command all military affairs, both internal and external.
After Fú Xióng died,
Jiàn had appointed Fú Jīng to command all military affairs;
after Jīng was executed for treason,
Ān was appointed in his place.
On the Jiǎshēn day,

Jiàn summoned the Grand Preceptor Yú Zūn, the Chancellor Léi Ruò'ér, the Grand Tutor Máo Guì, the Minister of Works Wáng Duò, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat Liáng Lèng, the Left Executive of the Imperial Secretariat Liáng Ān, the Right Executive of the Imperial Secretariat Duàn Chún, the Minister of Personnel Xīn Láo, and others to receive his final edict to assist in governance.
Jiàn said to the Crown Prince, Shēng:
"If the chieftains of the Six Barbarian tribes or the powerful ministers
do not obey your commands,
you should gradually eliminate them."
This laid the groundwork for Fú Shēng's cruel execution of ministers.
Chieftain,
pronounced as cí yóu.
Commander,
pronounced as suǒ lèi.
Your subject, Guāng, comments: Ministers entrusted with a ruler's final mandate
are meant to assist and guide the successor,
serving as his wings.
To serve as his wings yet teach him to cut them off—
how can he avoid perishing!
If you know they are not loyal,
then simply do not appoint them;
having entrusted them with great authority,
and then to suspect them—
rarely does this not lead to chaos.
On the Yǐyǒu day,
Jiàn died;
he was thirty-nine years old.
His temple name was Gāozǔ.
On the Bǐngxū day,
the Crown Prince Shēng ascended the throne.
Fú Shēng,
styled Chángshēng,
was the third son of Jiàn.
He changed the era name to Shòuguāng.
A minister memorialized:
"To change the era name before the mourning year is over
is contrary to ritual."
According to ancient ritual,
when a ruler dies,
the heir apparent ascends the throne,
and only after the mourning year passes is a new era name proclaimed.
After thoroughly investigating who proposed this,
they found it was the Right Executive of the Imperial Secretariat Duàn Chún,
and had him executed.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Minister of Personnel Zhōu Mǐn was appointed as Left Executive of the Imperial Secretariat.
Someone reported to the Prince of Kuàijī, Sīmǎ Yù:
"In the residence of the Prince of Wǔlíng, weapons and equipment are being extensively prepared,
suggesting plans for an extraordinary event."
This refers to the Prince of Wǔlíng, Sīmǎ Xī.
Sīmǎ Biāozhī said:
"The Prince of Wǔlíng's ambitions
are fully satisfied by galloping and hunting;
I sincerely hope to calm such talk,
to settle differing opinions,
and not to speak of this again!"
Yù approved of this.
This laid the groundwork for the Prince of Wǔlíng ultimately suffering disaster over this, which Biāozhī could not prevent.
Again,
pronounced as fú yòu.
The Qín ruler Shēng honored his mother, Lady Qiáng, as Empress Dowager,
and established Lady Liáng as Empress.
Lady Liáng
was the daughter of Liáng Ān.
He appointed his favored minister, the Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent's household, Nán'ān's Zhào Sháo, as Right Executive of the Imperial Secretariat.
According to the "Continued Hàn Records": The Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent's household, two persons,
their rank is comparable to that of a General of the Gentlemen of the Household.
Favored,
pronounced as bēi yì,
also as bó jì.
The Editorial Director Dǒng Róng was appointed as a Minister of the Imperial Secretariat.
The Liáng ruler Zuǒ was licentious, cruel, and without virtue,
causing resentment and anger among both high and low.
Zuǒ hated the strength of the Governor of Hé Province, Zhāng Guàn.
Zhāng Jùn established Hé Province,
governing from Fúhǎn.
Hate,
pronounced as wū lù.
He sent Guàn to suppress rebellious Hú tribes,
and also dispatched his generals Yì Chuāi and Zhāng Líng to lead thirteen thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Guàn.
A man from Zhāngyè, Wáng Luán, who understood divination,
said to Zuǒ:
"This army that has set out
will certainly not return,
and the state of Liáng will be in danger;"
and he also listed three instances of Zuǒ's lack of virtue.
Zuǒ was greatly angered,
considered Luán's words seditious,
and had him executed as a warning.
Luán said at his execution:
"After I die,
the army will be defeated abroad,
and the King will die within—
this is certain!"
Zuǒ exterminated his clan.
When Guàn heard of this,
he beheaded the messenger,
raised troops to attack Zuǒ,
issued a proclamation to the provinces and commanderies,
deposing Zuǒ,
reducing him to the rank of Marquis and returning him to his residence,
and reinstating the Marquis of Liángníng, Zhāng Yàolíng.
The deposition of Yàolíng is recorded in the previous year's scroll.
Guàn defeated them.
Chuāi and others fled back alone on horseback,
with Guàn's army in pursuit,
causing terror in Gūzāng.
The Valiant Cavalry General, Dūnhuáng's Sòng Hún's elder brother Xiū,
had a grudge against Zuǒ,
and feared disaster.
In the eighth month,
Hún and his younger brother Chéng fled west,
gathering over ten thousand men to support Guàn,
and marched back toward Gūzāng.
Zuǒ sent Yáng Qiūhú to take Yàolíng to the Eastern Park,
broke his back, and killed him.
Take,
pronounced as rú zì.
Break,
pronounced as lú hé.
He was posthumously titled Duke Āi.
The Qín ruler Shēng enfeoffed the Grand General of the Guards, Huáng Méi, as the Prince of Guǎngpíng,
and the Former General Fēi as the Prince of Xīnxīng,
both of whom he had long favored.
He summoned the Grand Marshal, the Prince of Wǔdū, Fu Ān, to concurrently serve as Grand Commandant.
When Jiàn was near death,
he had appointed Ān to command all military affairs, both internal and external,
but he was still in Púbǎn;
now Shēng summoned him.
He was stationed at Púbǎn;
the Prince of Wèi, Fú Sōu, was appointed as General Who Guards the East and Governor of Yù Province,
stationed at Shǎnchéng.
The Director of the Central Secretariat, Hú Wén, and the Head of the Central Secretariat, Wáng Yú, said to Shēng:
"Recently, a comet has appeared near Dàjiǎo,
and Mars has entered the Eastern Well constellation.
Dàjiǎo
is the Emperor's seat;
the Eastern Well
corresponds to the region of Qín;
according to the "Treatise on Astronomy": Dàjiǎo is located between Shètí.
Dàjiǎo
is the seat of the Heavenly King.
The Eastern Well
consists of eight stars.
The Eastern Well and Yǔguǐ constellations
correspond to the regions of Qín and Yōng Province.
Recently,
pronounced as pí zhì.
Comet,
pronounced as pú nèi.
Seat,
pronounced as cú wò.
Correspond,
pronounced as fú wèn.
This portends a great mourning for the state,
and the execution of high ministers;
we hope Your Majesty cultivates virtue to avert this!"
Shēng said:
"The Empress and I jointly face the realm—
she can correspond to the great mourning.
The Grand Tutor Máo, the Chariot and Horse General Liáng, and the Executive of the Imperial Secretariat Liáng received the final mandate to assist in governance—
they can correspond to the high ministers."
In the ninth month,
Shēng had Empress Liáng, Máo Guì, Liáng Lèng, and Liáng Ān executed.
Guì
was the Empress's maternal uncle.
The Right Executive of the Imperial Secretariat, Zhào Sháo, and the Central Protector of the Army, Zhào Huì,
were both younger cousins of the Governor of Luò Province, Zhào Jù.
Zhào Jù was stationed at Yíyáng;
this is recorded in the previous year's scroll.
Cousin,
pronounced as cái yòng.
They then appointed Jù as Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Jù firmly declined due to illness,
and said to Sháo and Huì:
"You no longer care for your ancestors,
and wish to bring about the extermination of our clan!
What crime did Máo and Liáng commit,
that they were executed?
What merit do I have,
that I should replace them?
You may do as you please,
but I shall die!"
He then died of grief.
14. Liáng: Sòng Hùn stationed his army at Wǔshǐ Great Marsh.
Zhāng Jùn divided the Dīdào County,
establishing Wǔshǐ Commandery.
Sòng Hùn fled westward,
and if he raised troops, he certainly would not head east toward Dīdào.
The Water Classic states: Dūyě Marsh is northeast of Wǔwēi County.
The annotation says: It is three hundred lǐ north of Gūzāng City.
Dūyě is the Zhūyě mentioned in the Tribute of Yǔ.
Its waters flow from the Gūzāng Wǔshǐ Marsh,
which is west of Gūzāng.
In the intercalary month,
Hùn’s army reached Gūzāng.
The King of Liáng, Zuǒ, arrested Zhāng Guàn’s younger brother Jū and his son Sōng,
intending to kill them.
Jū and Sōng, hearing of this,
recruited several hundred men from the market,
proclaiming loudly:
"Zhāng Zuǒ is without virtue.
Our elder brother’s great army has already reached the east of the city.
Anyone who dares raise a hand will have his three clans exterminated!"
They then opened the western gate to admit Hùn’s troops.
The General of the Central Army, Zhào Cháng, and others, fearing punishment—
Zhào Cháng
was the one who had requested establishing Zuǒ—
therefore feared punishment—
established Liáng Wǔ Hóu Xuánjìng as ruler.
Yì Chuāi and others led troops into the palace,
arrested Cháng and the others,
and killed them.
Zuǒ, grasping his sword in the palace hall,
shouted loudly,
berating his attendants to fight fiercely.
Zuǒ had long lost the hearts of the masses,
and no one was willing to fight for him.
He was thus killed by the soldiers.
Hùn and others displayed his head on a pole,
announcing it to the court and the public,
exposed his corpse by the roadside,
and throughout the city, all hailed "Long live!"
They buried him with the rites of a commoner
and also killed his two sons.
Hùn and Jū elevated Xuánjìng to Grand General, Governor of Liáng Province, and Duke of Xīpíng.
"Elevated"
is read as "shí zhǎng fān."
They resumed using the forty-third year of the Jiànxīng reign.
Zhāng Zuǒ had changed the Jiànxīng reign title,
as seen in the previous year of the previous scroll.
Zhāng Guàn arrived at Gūzāng,
supported Xuánjìng as King of Liáng,

and appointed himself as Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Commander of All Military Affairs Within and Without, Prefect of the Masters of Writing, Governor of Liáng Province, and Duke of Zhāngyè Commandery,
with Sòng Hùn as Vice Director of the Masters of Writing.
Lǐ Yǎn of Lǒngxī occupied the commandery,
not accepting Guàn’s orders,
using the reign title of Jiāngdōng,
using the Yǒnghé reign title.
This sets the stage for Lǐ Yǎn’s later submission to Qín.
Before he arrived,
Wèi Chēn of Xīpíng also occupied the commandery and rebelled.
Bà’s troops were defeated,
and he fled back.
Guàn sent his younger brother Jū to attack Chēn,
defeating him.
Mǎ Jī, the Grand Administrator of Jiǔquán, raised troops in response to Chēn.
Guàn sent his Marshal Zhāng Yáo and Wáng Guó to attack and behead him.
15. In winter,
the tenth month,
Xiè Shàng, Governor of Yù Province, was appointed to oversee the three provinces of Bìng, Jì, and Yōu.
At that time, Jiāngzuǒ had established the four provinces of Qīng, Jì, Bìng, and Yōu north of the river as émigré provinces.
At the beginning of the southern crossing,
Zǔ Tì, as Governor of Yù Province, governed from Qiáo City.
In the first year of Yǒngchāng,
Zǔ Yuè retreated and stationed at Shòuchūn.
In the fourth year of Emperor Chéng’s Xiánhé reign,
Yǔ Liàng, as Governor of Yù Province, governed from Wúhú.
In the fourth year of Xiánkāng,
Máo Bǎo, as Governor of Yù Province, governed from Zhū City.
In the sixth year,
Yǔ Yì, as Governor of Yù Province, governed from Wúhú.
In the first year of Yǒnghé,
Zhào Yìn, as Governor of Yù Province, governed from Niúzhǔ.
In the second year,
Shàng, as Governor of Yù Province, governed from Wúhú.
Now advancing to Shòuchūn,
all were western bulwarks of Jiànkāng.
For advancing and seizing, they stationed at Shòuchūn;
for defending the river, they were mostly at the two places of Lìyáng and Wúhú.
16. Zhènběi General Duàn Kān wrote a letter to the Yān ruler Jùn,
asserting the protocol of maternal cousins.
Jùn
was born of the Duàn clan,
so Kān asserted the protocol of maternal cousins with him.
Kān
is read as "kǔ hán fān";
same below.
Jùn was angered.
In the eleventh month,
he appointed Tàiyuán Prince Kè as Grand Commander and Fǔjūn General,
with Yáng Wù as his deputy,
to attack Kān.
17. Qín appointed Xīn Láo as Prefect of the Masters of Writing,
Zhào Sháo as Left Vice Director,
the Master of Writing Dǒng Róng as Right Vice Director,
and Central Protector of the Army Zhào Huì as Colonel Director of the Retainers.
18. In the twelfth month,
King Zhāo of Gāogōulì sent an envoy to Yān to offer hostages and tribute,
requesting the return of his mother.
The Yān ruler Jùn agreed,
sending Palace General Diāo Kān to escort Zhāo’s mother, Lady Zhōu, back to his country.
He appointed Zhāo as Grand General Who Conquers the East and Governor of Yíng Province,
enfeoffing him as Duke of Lèlàng,
remaining King as before.
He remained King of Gāogōulì as before.
19. Féng Yāng of Shàngdǎng expelled the Yān Grand Administrator Duàn Gāng,
occupying Ānmín City.
Wèi Shōu’s Treatise on Geography states: The Yān Grand Administrator of Shàngdǎng governed from Ānmín City.
Ānmín City is in Xiāngyuán County.
It was likely built during the Yǒngjiā period,
when Liú Kūn sent Zhāng Yǐ to construct it
to pacify the people of Shàngdǎng,
hence the name.
He sent an envoy to surrender.
20. The Qín Chancellor Léi Ruò'ér was by nature upright and outspoken.
Seeing Zhào Sháo and Dǒng Róng corrupting the government,
he often spoke openly at court,
and whenever he saw them, he gnashed his teeth.
Sháo and Róng slandered him to the Qín ruler Shēng.
Shēng killed Ruò'ér along with his nine sons and twenty-seven grandsons.
Thereupon, the various Qiāng tribes became disaffected.
Léi Ruò'ér
was a Qiāng chieftain of Nán'ān.
Dying without crime,
the various Qiāng tribes thus became disaffected.
Although Shēng was in the mourning hut,
he indulged in travel and drinking as usual,
bending bows and baring blades,
to receive his court officials.
Hammers, pincers, saws, and chisels—
tools that could harm people—
were fully prepared around him.
Not long after ascending the throne,
from the empress and high officials down to servants and slaves,
he killed over five hundred people in total.
Severing shins, breaking ribs, sawing necks, and disemboweling fetuses—
such acts were frequent.
21. The Yān ruler Jùn, considering Duàn Kān currently strong,
said to Tàiyuán Prince Kè:
"If Kān sends troops to block the river,
and you cannot cross,
you may directly take Lǚ Hù and return."
Lǚ Hù was then occupying Yěwáng.
Prepare boats and oars to observe Kān’s intentions.
Kān’s younger brother Pí,
brave and resourceful,
said to Kān:
"Mùróng Kè excels at using troops,
and with his numerous forces,
if we allow him to cross the river,
and he advances to the city walls,
I fear that even if we beg to surrender,
it may not be granted.
I ask you, elder brother, to hold firm in defense,
while I lead elite troops to resist him at the river.
If we are fortunate and win the battle,
you, elder brother, can lead the main force to follow up,
and we will surely achieve great merit.
If we are not victorious,
it would be better to surrender early,
still not losing the chance to be a Marquis of a Thousand Households."
Kān did not listen.
Pí persistently pleaded without end.
Kān became angry
and killed him.
1 In spring,
the first month,
the King of Tàiyuán of Yān, Mù Kè, led his troops across the river.
Before reaching Guǎnggù by over a hundred lǐ,
Duàn Kān led thirty thousand men to meet him in battle.
On Bǐngshēn,
Kè heavily defeated Kān at the Zī River.
According to the Zǎijì,
Kè defeated Kān south of the Jì River.
Now it says before reaching Guǎnggù by over a hundred lǐ,
it was likely that they met in battle upon reaching the Zī River.
The Shuǐ Jīng states,
the Zhuó River passes west of Guǎnggù City,
flows east to Guǎngráo,
enters Jùdiàn,
and then northwards joins the Zī River.
The Right Chief Clerk Yuán Fàn and others were beheaded.
The King's Companion of Qí, Pìlǘ Yù, was wounded.
Duàn Kān proclaimed himself King of Qí,
hence he established the office of King's Companion.
Yù,
read as yū wù.
Wound,
read as chū liáng.
He sent someone to search for him,
but Yù had already died.
Several thousand soldiers surrendered.
Kān escaped,
returned to the city and held fast,
Kè advanced and besieged it.
2 The Qín Minister of Works Wáng Duò was by nature stern and unyielding.
The Right Deputy Director Dǒng Róng and the Palace Attendant Qiáng Guó both rose through flattery and favor.
Duò hated them like enemies.
Every time at court audience,
Róng never spoke with him.
The sentence ends with "every time at court."
Court,
read as zhí yáo.
Audience,
read as rú zì.
"Lord Dǒng is incomparably noble and favored,
you should slightly lower your attitude and receive him."
Duò said:
"What kind of chicken or dog is Dǒng Lóng?"
Lóng,
was Dǒng Róng's childhood name.
There happened to be a celestial anomaly.
Róng and Qiáng Guó spoke to the Qín ruler Shēng, saying:
"Now the heavenly reprimand is very severe,
it should be answered with a high minister."
Shēng said:
"The high ministers are only the Grand Marshal and the Minister of Works."
Róng
said:
"The Grand Marshal is the state's close relative,
he cannot be killed."
The Grand Marshal refers to the Prince of Wǔdū, Ān,
Shēng's uncle.
As he was about to be executed,
Róng said to him:
"Do you still dare to compare Dǒng Lóng to chickens and dogs today?"
Duò glared and shouted at him.
The Governor of Luò Prefecture Dù Yù,
was Duò's nephew.
The Left Deputy Director Zhào Sháo hated him,
slandered him to Shēng,
claiming he was disloyal to Jìn, and had him killed.
On Rénxū,
Shēng feasted his ministers at the Tàijí Hall,
appointing the Secretary General Xīn Láo as the wine supervisor.
When the wine was flowing freely,
Shēng angrily said:
"Why aren't you forcing people to drink, and there are still those sitting!"
He drew his bow and shot Láo,
killing him.
The ministers were terrified,
none dared not get drunk,
collapsing and losing their caps,
then Shēng was pleased.
3 The Xiōngnú chieftain Liú Wùhuán died,
his younger brother Ètóu succeeded him,
intending to defect to Dài.
In the second month,
the King of Dài, Shíyìjiān, led troops westward, patrolling to the river.
Ètóu feared,
and requested to surrender.
4 The King of Tàiyuán of Yān, Mù Kè, pacified the various cities of Duàn Kān.
Kè besieged Guǎnggù but had not yet captured it,
so he first pacified the various cities within its jurisdiction.
On Jǐchǒu
the Inspector of Xú Province appointed by Kān, the Duke of Yángdū Wáng Téng, led his followers to surrender.
Kè ordered Téng to return to his former post and garrison Yángdū.
Duàn Kān established Xú Province in Lángyá's Yángdū County.
Dù Yòu said: The old city of Hàn's Yángdū County is south of Yíshuǐ County in Yí Prefecture.
5 The Qin generalissimo of the Eastern Expedition, Prince of Jin, Fú Liǔ, sent his aides Yán Fù and Liáng Shū as envoys to Liáng,
bearing a letter to persuade Liáng King Zhāng Xuánjìng.
Fù and Shū arrived at Gūzāng,
where Zhāng Guàn met them and said:
"I
am a subject of Jin;
subjects do not engage in external relations,
why have you two gentlemen come to disgrace me?"
Fù and Shū replied:
"The Prince of Jin and you, sir, are neighboring vassals,
though mountains and rivers separate us,
the winds and roads connect us for meetings.
Qin has sent Fú Liǔ to garrison Púbǎn,
which is not adjacent to Liángzhōu,
hence we speak of winds and roads connecting us for meetings.
Why do you find this strange!"
Guàn said:
"I have served Jin with utmost loyalty,
for six generations now.
Guī, Shí, Mào, Jùn, Chónghuá, Yàolíng, and Zuò make seven generations,
but now you speak of six generations,
excluding Zuò from the count.
This would be to defy the will of our former lords above,
and to ruin the integrity of our officials and people below,
how can this be done!"
Fù and Shū said:
"The Jin house has declined,
having lost the Mandate of Heaven,
indeed for a long time now;
therefore, the two kings of Liáng submitted to the two Zhào states in the north,
simply knowing the opportunity.
Zhāng Mào submitted to the Former Zhào,
Zhāng Jùn submitted to the Later Zhào.
If the King of Liáng wishes to proclaim himself emperor west of the Yellow River,
he is no match for Qin;
if he wishes to serve a greater power as a lesser one,
then why not abandon Jin and serve Qin,
to preserve fortune and emolument forever!"
Guàn said:
"The Central States are fond of breaking promises,
previously, as soon as the Shì family's envoys had just returned,
their barbarian cavalry had already arrived,
I dare not trust them."
Fù and Shū said:
"Since ancient times, emperors and kings in the Central States,
their governance and transformation have each been different,
Zhào was treacherous and deceitful,
Qin is sincere and righteous,
how can they be treated as all the same!
A level is used to even out bushels and pecks,
treating them all the same,
means making no distinction between high and low.
Our late emperor campaigned against and captured them,
capturing Zhāng Xiān, see the 98th scroll, sixth year,
he never captured Yáng Chū,
Fù and Shū merely said this.
He honored them with ranks and salaries,
certainly not comparable to the Shì family."
Guàn said:
"If it is as you say,
Qin's might and virtue are unmatched,
why not first take Jiāngnán,
then the whole world would belong to Qin,
why would the Eastern Expedition trouble to send orders here!"
Fù and Shū said:
"Jiāngnán has the custom of tattooing the body,
the ancient custom of the Jīngmán,
cutting hair and tattooing the body to avoid harm from dragons.
Fù and Shū use this to disparage them.
At that time, the cultured and civilized,
were all in Jiāngnán,
and it is where the legitimate calendar resides.
Fù and Shū bark at Yáo and criticize Yóu,
knowing each serves his own lord only!
Transformation flourishes, submission comes later.
Zhèng Xuán said: Wū,
means to kill.
The Yì says: Gāozōng attacked Guǐfāng,
and conquered it in three years.
Commentators of the time consider Jīng and Chǔ to be light and fierce,
the way of killing leads to early rebellion,
transformation flourishing leads to later submission,
therefore Fù and Shū also use this to disparage Jiāngnán.
Héyòu can be won over by righteousness,
hence we sent envoys first to express great goodwill.
If you, sir, do not understand the Mandate of Heaven,
then Jiāngnán may extend its life for a few years,
but Héyòu may no longer be your land."
Guàn said:
"I straddle and control three provinces,
the three provinces refer to Liáng, Hé, and Shā,
which Zhāng Mào and Zhāng Jùn divided and established.
To the west, encompassing the Cōnglíng Mountains,
to the east, reaching the great river,
we have more than enough to attack others,
let alone for self-defense,
what do we fear from Qin!"
Fù and Shū said:
"How does the strength of your province's mountains and rivers
compare to Xiáo and Hán?
The abundance of your people and goods,
how does it compare to Qín and Yōng?
Dù Hóng and Zhāng Jǔ,
relying on the Zhào family's established resources,
with strong soldiers and abundant wealth,
had the ambition to envelop Guānzhōng and sweep across the four seas,
yet when our late emperor's army pointed westward,
they melted like ice and scattered like clouds,
within ten days to a month,
they found their masters changed without realizing it.
See the 98th scroll, sixth year.
If our emperor now rises in majestic anger,
with a million bowstrings under his control,
and marches westward with drums beating,
I wonder how your province will respond?"
Guàn laughed and said:
"This matter should be decided by the king,
it is not for me to resolve."
Liǎo,
means to resolve.
"Though the King of Liáng is wise and intelligent from youth,
he is still in his tender years;
you, sir, hold a position like Yī and Huò,
the safety and danger of the state,
depend on your single move."
Guàn became afraid,
and on Xuánjìng's order sent an envoy to submit to Qin as a vassal,
Qin accordingly granted Xuánjìng the official titles and ranks he claimed.
6 General Liú Dù attacked the Qin governor of Qīngzhōu, Wáng Lǎng, at Lúshì;
Lúshì County,
in the Hàn dynasty belonged to Hóngnóng Commandery,
in the Jin dynasty belonged to Shàngluò Commandery,
in the Táng dynasty belonged to Guó Prefecture.
He attacked the Qin governor of Yōuzhōu, Qiáng Zhé, at the Péi family fortress.
During the Yǒngjiā disturbances,
the Péi clan gathered their whole family, occupied a strategic location, and built a fortress to defend themselves,
later generations thus established a garrison there,
hence the fortress still bears the Péi name,
located within Hé dōng's borders.
Cháng,
read as zhǎng.
The general of the Establishment of Standards, Dèng Qiāng, resisted Chángqīng.
Before Fēi arrived, Dù retreated.
Qiāng fought Chángqīng,
defeated him soundly,
capturing Chángqīng and over two thousand armored heads.
7 Huán Wēn requested to move the capital to Luòyáng,
to repair the imperial tombs,
submitting over ten memorials;
he was not permitted.
He was appointed grand commander of expeditions,
overseeing military affairs of Sī and Jì provinces,
to campaign against Yáo Xiāng.
8 In the third month,
the Qin ruler Shēng conscripted the people of the three auxiliary regions to build the Wèi River bridge,
the grand master of the palace with golden seal and purple ribbon, Chéng Gōng, remonstrated,
considering it harmful to agriculture;
Shēng had him killed.
9 In summer,
the fourth month,
a great wind struck Cháng'ān,
tearing off roofs and uprooting trees.
The wind swept away roof tiles,
lifting eaves and rafters, tearing off roofs.
Some claimed bandits had arrived,
the palace gates were closed in daytime,
for five days before it stopped.
The Qin ruler Shēng interrogated those who reported bandits,
cut out their hearts.
The grand master of the palace of illustrious happiness, Qiáng Píng, remonstrated:
"Heaven sends down calamities and anomalies,
Your Majesty should cherish the people and serve the spirits,
relax punishments and honor virtue to respond to them,
then they can be stopped."
Mǐ,
means to stop.
He had his skull chiseled open and killed him.
The general of the guards, Prince of Guǎngpíng Huángméi, the former general Prince of Xīnxīng Fēi, and the general of the establishment of standards Dèng Qiāng,
because Píng
was the empress dowager's brother,
kowtowed and firmly remonstrated;
Shēng did not listen,
sent Huángméi out as governor of Zuǒ Féngyì, Fēi as governor of Yòu Fúfēng, and Qiáng as acting governor of Xiányáng.
In the Former Hàn, Fúfēng's Wèichéng County,
was the Qin Xiányáng,
abolished in Later Hàn and Jin.
Wèi Shōu's Treatise on Geography: Xiányáng Commandery governed Shí'ān County,
which was the Hàn Wèichéng,
renamed by Shì Lè.
This commandery was likely established by the Jìhú after Yǒngjiā.
Therefore, he did not kill them.
In the fifth month,
Empress Dowager Qiáng died of worry and resentment,
posthumously titled Míngdé.
10 Yáo Xiāng attacked Zhōu Chéng at Luòyáng from Xǔchāng.
Zhōu Chéng had seized Luòyáng by surprise,
see the tenth year of the previous scroll.
16. The Qin ruler Shēng ate many dates at night,
and in the morning fell ill.
He summoned the Grand Physician-in-Chief Chéng Yán
to diagnose him.
Yán said:
"Your Majesty has no other ailment,
you simply ate too many dates."
Shēng angrily said:
"You are no sage,
how could you know I ate dates!"
He then had him executed.
17. The Yan Grand Marshal Kě besieged Duàn Kān in Guǎnggù.
His generals urged him to attack swiftly,
but Kě said:
"In the use of military force,
there are situations where it is appropriate to proceed slowly,
and others where it is appropriate to act swiftly;
this cannot be overlooked.
If the enemy and we are evenly matched in strength,
and they have strong external support,
fearing the danger of being attacked from both front and rear,
then the attack must not be delayed.
But if we are strong and they are weak,
with no external aid,
and we have sufficient strength to control them,
we should contain and watch over them,
waiting for them to collapse.
The Art of War speaks of 'encircling with ten times the force, attacking with five times the force,'
precisely referring to this situation.
Master Sūn said: The method of using troops,
with ten times the force, encircle them;
with five times the force, attack them.
(They) had not yet become disheartened;
the battle of Jìnán,
was the battle of Zīshuǐ.
Calling it Jìnán
is based on speaking of the Jì River as the great boundary between north and south.
But Kān employed it without proper strategy,
thus bringing about his defeat.
Now, relying on the formidable defenses of a strong city,
with high and low united in effort,
if we exhaust our elite troops in attacking it,
we could probably capture it in a matter of days,
but many of our soldiers would certainly be killed.
Since engaging in affairs in the Central Plains,
our troops have not rested even briefly.
'Zàn'
is the same as 'temporary.'
At night, we forget to sleep;
how can we lightly treat their deaths!
The essential point is to capture it,
we need not seek rapid achievement of merit!"
The generals all said:
"This is beyond our reach."
When the army heard this,
everyone was moved and pleased.
Thereupon, they built high walls and deep moats to maintain the siege.
People of Qí competed to transport grain to supply the Yān army.
Kān defended the city and held out,
the paths for gathering firewood were cut off,
and people in the city resorted to cannibalism.
Kān led all his troops out to fight,
but Kě defeated them within the encirclement.
At that time, they had built a long siege wall outside,
hence the battle took place within the encirclement.
They were stationed at the various gates of Guǎnggù city.
'Jì'
is pronounced 'qíjì'.
He barely managed to get back in,
the remaining troops were all lost.
Thereupon, morale in the city plummeted,
and no one had firm resolve.
In the eleventh month,
on Bǐngzǐ day,
Kān, with hands bound behind his back, came out and surrendered,
and also apprehended Zhū Tū and sent him to Jì.
Kě pacified and settled the new people,
completely pacifying the Qí region,
and relocated over 3,000 households of Xiānbēi, Hú, and Jié to Jì.
The Yān king Jùn subjected Zhū Tū to the Five Punishments.
Zhū Tū had killed Mùróng Gōu and fled to Kān,
see the tenth year of the previous scroll.
Kě left Mùróng Chén to guard Guǎnggù,
appointed the Left Assistant of the Imperial Secretariat Jū Yīn as the Governor of Dōnglái,
and the Governor of Zhāngwǔ, Xiānyú Liàng, as the Governor of Qí Commandery,
then returned.
Yīn
was the son of Péng.
Péng was at that time the Grand Prolonged Autumn of Yān.
He sent a letter admonishing Yīn, saying:
"Wáng Mí and Cáo Nì
surely have descendants;
you must skillfully summon and pacify them,
do not pursue old grievances,
thereby prolonging the source of disorder!"
Yīn sought them out,
and found Mí's nephew Lì and Nì's grandson Yán in the mountains.
He requested to meet with them,
and formed a deep bond of friendship.
Péng further sent an envoy to present them with carriages, horses, and clothing.
The commandery's people thereby became greatly harmonious.
Jū Péng returned to Yān from Dōnglái,
see the second year of Yuándì's Tàixīng era, scroll ninety-one.
Xún Xiàn heard that Kān had already been defeated,
withdrew and returned to Xiàpī,
leaving General Zhūgě Yōu and the Governor of Gāopíng, Liú Zhuāng, to lead three thousand men to guard Lángyá,
and the Army Advisor, Dài Duàn of Qiáoguó, and others to lead two thousand men to guard Tàishān.
Yáng Zhènghéng said: 'Duàn'
is pronounced 'dùn'.
Biànchéng
is Jùnyí City.
I believe
'Biàn'
should be
'Biàn'.
It is the city of Biàn County in the State of Lǔ.
Liú Xù said: Sìshuǐ County of Yǎnzhōu
is the ancient city of Biàn County.
18. An edict was issued sending the concurrent Minister of Works and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Chē Guàn and others, bearing the imperial tally, to Luòyáng,
to repair the five imperial mausoleums.
The mausoleum of Emperor Xuān is at Shǒuyáng Mountain in Héyīn;
Emperor Jǐng's mausoleum is called Jùnpíng,
Emperor Wén's mausoleum is called Chóngyáng,
Emperor Wǔ's mausoleum is called Jùnyáng,
and Emperor Huì's mausoleum is called Tàiyáng.
'Sǎn'
is pronounced 'xǐdǎn'.
'Jì'
is pronounced 'qíjì'.
'Chē'
is pronounced 'chǐshē'.
On Gēngxū day,
the Emperor and all the officials wore mourning garments of coarse hemp,
and observed mourning in the Tàijí Hall for three days.
'Sī'
is cloth of fifteen sheng,
with half the threads removed.
'Lín'
is pronounced 'lìzhèn'.
19. The Governor of Sīzhōu, Xiè Shàng, due to illness, did not proceed,
and Wáng Húzhī, the Governor of Dānyáng, replaced him.
Húzhī
was the son of Yì.
Wáng Yì,
was a cousin of Wáng Dūn,
see the third year of Mǐndì's Jiànxīng era, scroll eighty-nine.
'Yì'
is pronounced 'yángzhì',
also 'yìzhí'.
20. That year,
the Duke of Chóuchí, Yáng Guó, was killed by his uncle Jùn, who then established himself;
(the court) appointed Jùn as Duke of Chóuchí.
Guó's son Ān fled to Qín.
Later, Qín employed Yáng Ān to capture Chóuchí.
Could this be Guó's son?
First year of Shēngpíng era
(Dīngsì year, 357)
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the first day of the month, Rénxū,
the Emperor assumed the cap of manhood;
the Empress Dowager issued an edict returning governance to him,
proclaimed a great amnesty,
changed the era name,
and the Empress Dowager moved to reside in the Chóngdé Palace.
2. The Yān ruler Jùn summoned the Governor of Yōuzhōu, Yǐ Yì, to serve as Grand Master of the Palace of Splendid Happiness.
Yì and his wife rode together in a deer-drawn cart;
his son Zhāng followed with several tens of cavalry,
his clothing and ornaments extremely splendid,
to welcome them on the road.
Yì was greatly angered,
shut himself in the cart and did not speak to him.
Upon reaching the city,
he severely reprimanded him.
'Upon reaching the city'
means upon reaching Jì City.
In the eighth year of Yǒnghé era,
the Yān king made his capital at Jì,
established a branch secretariat at Lóngchéng,
and appointed Yǐ Yì to oversee its affairs.
It seems he served as Governor of Yōuzhōu, stationed at Lóngchéng.
'Jì'
is pronounced 'qíjì'.
Yì constantly worried he would bring ruin,
yet Zhāng was further promoted and appointed,
serving successively as Director of the Central Secretariat and Palace Aide to the Censor-in-Chief.
Yì then sighed and said:
"In my youth, I cultivated myself,
restrained myself and upheld the Way,
and barely managed to avoid offense.
Zhāng does not govern his conduct with restraint,
indulges exclusively in extravagance and license,
yet he holds even more pure and eminent positions.
This is not only Zhāng's shameful fortune,
it truly reflects the decline of the times."
3 In the second month, on the guǐchǒu day,
the ruler of Yān, Mùróng Jùn,
established his son, the Prince of Zhōngshān, Mùróng Wěi, as Crown Prince.
A general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed to Guāngshòu.
4 The planet Venus entered the Eastern Well constellation.
The officials of Qín memorialized:
"Venus is a star of punishment.
The Eastern Well is the division corresponding to Qín.
There will certainly be violent soldiers rising in the capital."
The ruler of Qín, Fú Shēng, said:
"Venus entering the Well
is simply because it is thirsty.
What is there to be surprised about!"
5 Yáo Xiāng planned to seize Guānzhōng.
In summer,
the fourth month,
he advanced from Běiqū and stationed his troops at Xìngchéng.
Běiqū County
belonged to Hédōng Commandery in the Hàn dynasty,
and to Píngyáng Commandery in the Jìn dynasty.
Shī Gǔ says: Qū
is pronounced jū wù fān.
It was the residence of Prince Yíwú of Jìn.
According to Bān Zhì,
the Húkǒu Mountain mentioned in the Yǔ Gòng is southeast of Běiqū County.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: Běiqū is ten lǐ west of the Yellow River,
and Mèngmén Mountain is on the river.
Yáo Xiāng likely crossed the river from Běiqū and stationed his troops at Xìngchéng.
The Wǔdài Zhì states: Chāngníng County in Fénzhōu has Húkǒu Mountain.
Sòng Bái says: Jíxiāng County in Cízhōu
was Běiqū County in Hàn times;
the old city twenty-one lǐ north of the present county
was the Hàn administrative seat.
According to Wèi Shōu's Treatise on Geography,
Chéngchéng County had Xìngchéng.
Shī Gǔ says: Chéngchéng
was Zhēng County of Féngyì in Hàn times.
Zhēng
is pronounced chéng.
According to the Zǎijì,
Xìngchéng was north of Mǎlán Mountain.
Dù Yòu says: Yáo Chàng established Xìngchéng Garrison,
located seven lǐ west of present-day Fángzhōu.
Fūchéng
was the later Táng dynasty's Fūchéng County in Fángzhōu;
the Later Wèi established Fūchéng County,
which Suí changed to Fūchéng.
The General Who Spreads Martial Might
was likely an appointment by the Zhào Shí clan.
Yáo Lán
was Yáo Xiāng's elder cousin;
Yáo Yìshēng
was Yáo Xiāng's elder brother.
Over fifty thousand households of Qiāng, Hú, and Qín people submitted to him.
The Qín general Fú Fēilóng attacked Yáo Lán
and captured him.
Yáo Xiāng led his troops forward and occupied Huángluò.

The ruler of Qín, Fú Shēng, sent the Grand General of the Guards, the Prince of Guǎngpíng Fú Huángméi; the General Who Pacifies the North, Fú Dào; the General of the Soaring Dragon, the Prince of Dōnghǎi Fú Jiān;
and the General Who Establishes Integrity, Dèng Qiāng
(During the Hàn and Wèi period, the General of the Central Army Who Establishes Integrity was established,
later it became a general's title.)
Yáo Xiāng fortified his position and did not engage in battle.
Dèng Qiāng said to Fú Huángméi:
"Yáo Xiāng was defeated by Huán Wēn and Zhāng Píng,
and his morale is lost.
However, his nature is fierce and stubborn.
If we beat drums, shout, and raise banners,
pressing directly against his camp,
he will certainly become angry and come out.
Then we can capture him in one battle."
In the fifth month,
Dèng Qiāng led three thousand cavalry to press against the gate of his camp and deployed his forces.
Yáo Xiāng was enraged
and came out with all his troops to fight.
Dèng Qiāng feigned defeat and fled.
Yáo Xiāng pursued him to Sānyuán.
Sānyuán was within the boundaries of Chíyáng County of Féngyì in Hàn times.
Sòng Bái says: Fú Jiān established the Sānyuán Protectorate north of Jiéniè.
Later Zhōu established Sānyuán County.
Fú Huángméi and others arrived with the main force.
Yáo Xiāng's troops were utterly defeated.
The fine horse Yáo Xiāng rode was called Líméi Guā.
The horse fell,
and Qín soldiers captured and beheaded him.
His younger brother, Yáo Chàng, led his followers and surrendered.
Yáo Xiāng had been carrying the coffin of his father, Yáo Yìzhòng, in the army.
The ruler of Qín, Fú Shēng, buried Yáo Yìzhòng with the rites of a prince at Gūpán.
Gūpán
was within the boundaries of Jì County in Tiānshuǐ.
Fú Huángméi and others returned to Cháng'ān.
Fú Shēng did not reward them
and repeatedly insulted Fú Huángméi in front of the multitude.
Fú Huángméi was furious
and plotted to assassinate Fú Shēng.
The plot was discovered,
and he was executed.
The affair implicated princes, dukes, and relatives,
and many were put to death.
6 On the wùyín day,

the ruler of Yān, Mùróng Jùn, sent the General Who Pacifies the Army, Mùróng Chuí; the General of the Central Army, Mùróng Qián; and the General Who Protects the Army, Píng Xī, leading eighty thousand infantry and cavalry to attack the Chìlè north of the frontier.
The New Táng History says: The Chìlè,
their ancestors were the Xiōngnú.
During the Yuán Wèi period, they were called the Gāochē tribe.
Later, the name was corrupted to
"Tiělè".
The fifteen kinds of Tiělè in the Táng dynasty were these.
The Zǎijì records it as
"Dīnglíng Chìqín
[lè]". They were utterly defeated,
over a hundred thousand were captured or killed,
130,000 horses were captured,
and hundreds of millions of cattle and sheep were taken.
7 The Xiōngnú Chányú, Hèlàitóu, led his tribe of thirty-five thousand people and surrendered to Yān.
Since the Eastern Hàn,
the Xiōngnú who entered and settled within the frontier comprised nineteen tribes in total,
Hèlài being one of them.
Chán
is pronounced chán.
In Hàn times, Dài Commandery had Píngshū County,
and Bóhǎi had Dōngpíngshū County.
Dōngpíngshū
belonged to Héjiān Principality in Later Hàn,
and to Zhāngwǔ Principality in Jìn.
The Píngshū of Dài Commandery
never changed its affiliation;
it is recorded as Dài Commandery to distinguish it from the Píngshū of Zhāngwǔ.
The Píngshū of Dài Commandery
should have been in the northern region of present-day Táng's Yù.
Chǔ
is pronounced chāng lǚ fān.
8 The ruler of Qín, Fú Shēng, dreamed that a big fish ate pú plants.
The Fú clan
originally came from the Pú family,
hence he considered the dream of a fish eating pú as an omen.
"The great fish of the Eastern Sea transforms into a dragon;
the males all become kings, the females become dukes."
Fú Shēng then executed the Grand Tutor, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, and Duke of Guǎngníng, Yú Zūn, along with his seven sons and ten grandsons.
The Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Niú Yí, fearing disaster,
requested to be appointed to Jīngzhōu.
The Qín Jīngzhōu administration was at Fēngyáng Chuān.
He was appointed General of the Central Army.
When summoned for an audience,
Fú Shēng teased him, saying:
"Oxen are by nature slow and steady,
good at pulling the yoke shafts.
Yuán
refers to the shafts.
The part in front of the shaft is called the yoke,
placed on the ox's neck.
È
is pronounced è.
They can pull loads of a hundred shí."
Niú Yí said:
"Although I have pulled large carts,
I have not yet traversed steep cliffs.
I wish to try a heavy load,
then my merit will be known."
Fú Shēng laughed and said:
"How eager you are!
Do you find the load too light?
I shall give you the ducal title of Yú."
Niú Yí was terrified,
returned home, and committed suicide.
Róng was fond of literature,
exceptionally clear and discerning,
able to recite what he heard,
and never forgot what he saw;
his strength could match a hundred men,
skilled in riding, archery, and spear fighting,
he had a fine reputation from a young age;
Jiān loved and valued him,
often discussing state affairs with him.
Róng managed both internal and external affairs,
punishments and governance were well-ordered,
he recommended talents and promoted those who had been overlooked,
his contributions were many and great.
Hóng,
meaning great.
In governing the people and deciding legal cases,
all were second to Róng.
History says that even though Jiān had such a brother and son, it did not save him from defeat and ruin,
showing that when Heaven abandons someone,
it is not something human power can support.
Zhì,
pronounced zhí.
Duàn,
pronounced dīng luàn.
Wēi,
was the maternal cousin of Empress Dowager Xún,
and had long been friendly with Prince Wěi Xióng,
Shēng repeatedly wanted to kill Jiān,
but he was saved thanks to Wēi's rescue efforts.
Wēi enjoyed favor with Empress Dowager Xún,
and Jiān served him like a father.
Wēi knew of Wáng Měng's worth,
and often urged Jiān to entrust state affairs to him;
Jiān said to Měng:
"Lord Lǐ knows you,
just as Bào Shūyá knew Guǎn Zhòng."
Guǎn Zhòng in his youth associated with Bào Shūyá,
Bào Shū knew his worth,
and treated him well.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"When I was first in hardship,
I traded with Bào Shū,
and when dividing the profits, I took more for myself,
Bào Shū did not consider me greedy,
knowing I was poor.
I once planned matters for Bào Shū,
but it led to greater hardship,
Bào Shū did not consider me foolish,
knowing that the times could be favorable or unfavorable.
I served three times and was dismissed three times,
Bào Shū did not consider me incompetent,
knowing I had not met with opportunity.
I fought three battles and fled three times,
Bào Shū did not consider me cowardly,
knowing I had an elderly mother.
When Prince Jiǔ failed,
Zhào Hū died for him,
I was imprisoned and suffered disgrace,
Bào Shū did not consider me shameless,
knowing I was not ashamed of minor matters but ashamed that my achievements and fame were not known throughout the world.
Those who gave me life are my parents,
but the one who knows me is Master Bào."
9 The Yān ruler Jùn killed Duàn Kān,
burying alive over three thousand of his followers.
10 In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Qín Grand General and Governor of Jìzhōu, Zhāng Píng, sent an envoy to request surrender,
and was appointed Governor of Bìngzhōu.
11 In the eighth month,
on Dīngwèi day,
Empress Hé was established.
The empress was
the daughter of the former Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Hé Zhǔn of Lújiāng.
Sàn,
pronounced xī dǎn.
Qí,
pronounced qí jì.
In the second year of the Xiánkāng era of Emperor Chéng,
Empress Dù was established.
12 The Qín ruler Jiān appointed Quán Yì as Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gates,
Quán Yì served Qín,
long holding important positions,
but eventually defected to the Yáo clan.
Considering that he was trusted and employed by Fú Jiān,
although he did not sing the songs of Yuè like Zhuāng Xì,
he certainly harbored it in his heart.
He and Wáng Měng jointly managed confidential matters.
In the ninth month,
the titles of Grand Preceptor Yú Zūn and others were posthumously restored,
they were reburied with proper rites,
and their surviving descendants were all promoted according to their abilities.
13 Zhāng Píng held the territories of Xīnxīng, Yànmén, Xīhé, Tàiyuán, Shàngdǎng, and Shàngjùn,
with over three hundred fortifications,
and over a hundred thousand households of both non-Hàn and Hàn people.
The fortifications
were likely built by local magnates for self-protection
during times of chaos and separation.
The Shí clan employed Zhāng Píng for Bìngzhōu,
so he was able to hold these lands,
and govern these people.
Xià,
pronounced hù yǎ.
He intended to make Yān and Qín his enemy states.
After the Shí clan's defeat,
Píng submitted to both Yān and Qín,
but now, relying on his strength,
he intended to make Yān and Qín his enemy states.
In the tenth month,
Píng invaded and plundered Qín territory,
Píng probably took advantage of Qín's internal troubles,
but who knew this would lead to his defeat and ruin!
He was additionally appointed Governor of Bìngzhōu,
and stationed at Púbǎn to defend against him.
14 In the eleventh month,
on Guǐyǒu day,
the Yān ruler Jùn moved the capital from Jì to Yè.
15 The Qín Empress Dowager Xún was touring the Xuānmíng Terrace,
when she saw the gate of the residence of the Duke of Dōnghǎi, Fǎ, crowded with carriages and horses,
and feared he would ultimately be detrimental to the Qín ruler Jiān,
so she plotted with Lǐ Wēi to have Fǎ executed.
Jiān bid farewell to Fǎ in the Eastern Hall,
weeping bitterly and vomiting blood;
he was posthumously titled Duke Xiàn'āi,
and his son Yáng was enfeoffed as Duke of Dōnghǎi,
and Fū as Duke of Qīnghé.
This sets the stage for Yáng's later plot for revenge.
16 In the twelfth month,
on Yǐsì day,
the Yān ruler Jùn entered the Yè palace,
and issued a general pardon.
He also rebuilt the Bronze Bird Terrace.
Wèi Wǔ established his state at Yè,
and built the Bronze Bird Terrace,
the Shí clan expanded and repaired it,
but it was destroyed in the turmoil of war,
so Mùróng, having made Yè his capital, rebuilt it,
restoring it to its former state.
17 Tài Cháng Wáng Biāozhī was appointed Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
18 The Qín ruler Jiān, while inspecting the Imperial Secretariat,
found the documents and records in disorder,
dismissed Left Assistant Chéng Zhuó from his post,
and replaced him with Wáng Měng.
Jiān promoted exceptional talents,
restored neglected duties,
encouraged agriculture and sericulture,
relieved the impoverished,
honored the various spirits,
established schools,
commended integrity and righteousness,
and continued lines that had died out;
the people of Qín were greatly pleased.
History states that Fú Jiān was able to employ Wáng Měng to govern Qín.
Xiào,
pronounced hù jiào.
1 In spring,
the first month,
the Minister of Education Yù kowtowed and returned the reins of government;
the Emperor did not permit it.
2 Earlier,
Féng Yāng, after surrendering with Shàngdǎng,
see above, the eleventh year of the Yǒnghé era.
also submitted to Yān,
but later rebelled against Yān again.
In the second month,
the Yān Minister of Education, the King of Shàngyōng, Píng, attacked him,
but could not subdue him.
3. The King of Qín, Fú Jiān, personally led an army to campaign against Zhāng Píng.
He appointed Dèng Qiāng as the Vanguard Commander and Protector,
leading five thousand cavalry,
and stationed his army at the banks of the Fén River;
this refers to the area along the Fén River.
The character 帥 here
is read as 率 (meaning "to lead").
The character 騎
is pronounced qí (meaning "cavalry").
Zhāng Chī was exceptionally strong and agile,
capable of dragging an ox backward while walking;
no matter the height of a city wall,
he could leap over it.
He and Dèng Qiāng confronted each other for over ten days,
with neither able to gain the upper hand.
In the third month,
Fú Jiān arrived at Tóngbì,
a place between the Huáng Hé and Fén River called Tóngchuān.
Its inhabitants, encountering turmoil,
built a fortified wall (bì) for self-defense,
hence the name Tóngbì (Copper Wall).
Zhāng Chī, riding alone on his horse and shouting loudly,
charged into and out of the Qín battle formation four or five times.
Fú Jiān offered a reward for anyone who could capture him alive.
The Soaring Hawk General Lǚ Guāng stabbed Zhāng Chī,
hitting him,
and Dèng Qiāng captured Zhāng Chī and presented him.
Zhāng Píng's forces then completely collapsed.
Zhāng Píng, in fear,
requested to surrender.
Fú Jiān appointed Zhāng Píng as General of the Right,
and made Zhāng Chī a General of the Household Rapid as Tigers.
Zhāng Chī
originally had the surname Gōng.
According to surname records: the surname Gōng
originated from Lǚ Shūgōng.
Fú Jiān treated him with great favor and closeness,
often keeping him by his side.
The people of Qín considered both Dèng Qiāng and Zhāng Chī to be match for ten thousand men.
Lǚ Guāng
was the son of Pó Lóu.
Fú Jiān relocated over three thousand households from Zhāng Píng's territory to Cháng'ān.
4. On the jiǎxū day,
the ruler of Yān, Mùróng Jùn, sent the General of the Guards Mùyú Gēn to lead troops to assist the Minister over the Masses Mùróng Píng in attacking Féng Yāng.
Gēn wanted to attack urgently,
but Píng said:
"Yāng's fortifications are strong,
it is better to proceed slowly."
Gēn said:
"That is not so.
Your Excellency has been at the city walls for a month,
yet has not engaged in battle.
The rebels think the state's strength is only this much,
so they have solidified their unity,
hoping for a slim chance.
This means Yāng harbors a wishful hope that he might possibly defend the city.
Now is precisely the time when our momentum is rising,
the rebel forces are fearful,
and all have thoughts of desertion.
Their plans are not yet settled;
if we attack them now,
there is nothing we cannot overcome."
He then launched a fierce attack.
Yāng and his followers indeed became suspicious and jealous of each other.
Yāng fled to Yěwáng to rely on Lǚ Hù,
and his followers all surrendered.
5. In summer,
the fourth month,
the King of Qín, Fú Jiān, went to Yōng,
to perform sacrifices at the Five Altars;
in the sixth month,
he went to Hédōng,
to sacrifice to the Earth God.
He followed Hàn dynasty rituals.
The character 雍
is pronounced yōng.
The character 畤
is pronounced zhǐ.
6. In autumn,
the eighth month,
the Governor of Yùzhōu, Xiè Yì, died.
Yì
was the elder brother of Xiè Ān.
The Minister over the Masses Sīmǎ Yù appointed the General Who Establishes Might Huán Yún as his replacement.
Yún
was the younger brother of Huán Wēn.
[Sīmǎ Yù] consulted the Imperial Secretary Wáng Biāozhī,
who said:
"Yún is not without talent,
but Wēn already holds the upper reaches [of the Yangtze],
controlling half the empire.
If his younger brother is again placed in the western frontier;
the Eastern Jìn's Yùzhōu was stationed west of the Yangtze,
while Jiànkāng was east of the river,
hence Yùzhōu was considered the western frontier.
The character 復 here
is pronounced fù (meaning "again").
The character 處
is pronounced chǔ (meaning "to be placed");
the same applies below.
This is not appropriate for establishing deep roots and firm stability.
A person's capability cannot be pre-measured,
but we should only ensure he does not become an adversary to Your Highness."
Yù nodded and said:
"What you say is correct."
On the rénshēn day,
he appointed the Administrator of Wúxīng, Xiè Wàn, as General of the Western Headquarters,
Supervisor of the military affairs of the four provinces Sī, Yù, Jì, and Bìng, and Governor of Yùzhōu.
The areas governed by Sī, Yù, Jì, and Bìng
were all relocated commanderies.
The character 監
is pronounced jiān (meaning "to supervise").
Wáng Xīzhī wrote a letter to Huán Wēn, saying:
"Xiè Wàn's talent and standing are refined and perceptive,
meaning his abilities are sufficient for managing the world's affairs,
and among his contemporaries he is considered insightful.
He is truly an outstanding figure of the younger generation;
but now to have him stoop to govern a devastated frontier region,
is nearly to misuse his talent and assign him an unsuitable task."
This means the soldiers and people of the border commanderies are all survivors of war and devastation,
exhausted and not yet recovered, rough and difficult to manage,
requiring someone to stoop and gently pacify them;
now Wàn is not the right talent for this, so using him
constitutes misusing talent.
The character 務
means "task" or "affair";
with Wàn's talent, he is suited for the court,
but to place him in a remote border area,
is to assign him an unsuitable task.
The character 處
is pronounced chǔ.
The character 近
is pronounced jìn.
"With your lofty and unconcerned demeanor,
to stoop and involve yourself in trivial military details,
is truly hard to bear.
This refers to his pride and disdain for the minor tasks of military life.
One should simply adapt one's actions to the circumstances.
I hope you will always share joys and hardships with the lowliest soldiers,
then all will be perfect."
Wàn was unable to follow this advice.
The Governor of Xúzhōu and Yǎnzhōu, Xún Xiàn, fell ill,
and appointed the Palace Assistant Secretary Xī Tán as his
Army Supervisor.
Tán
was the son of Xī Jiàn.
7. In the ninth month,
on the gēngchén day,
the King of Qín, Fú Jiān, returned to Cháng'ān,
and appointed the Grand Commandant Fú Hóu as Prefect of the Masters of Writing.
This refers to the Duke of Yǒng'ān, Fú Hóu.
At this time, Qín suffered a great drought;
Jiān reduced his meals and ceased music,
ordering everyone from the empress down to forgo fine silks;
Yán Shīgǔ's commentary states: Wán sù
refers to what is now called juàn (silk).
The character 去
is pronounced qù (meaning "to remove").
Both the court and commoners shared in this austerity,
halting military campaigns to nurture the people;
thus the drought did not become a disaster.
Wáng Měng became increasingly favored and wielded power daily.
Many of the imperial clan, relatives, meritorious officials, and old guards resented him.
The Specially Advanced, Marquis of Gūzāng, Fán Shì,
originally a powerful Dí chieftain,
who assisted the ruler of Qín, Fú Jiàn, in pacifying Guānzhōng,
said to Měng:
"Did we plow the fields,
for you to eat the harvest?"
Měng said:
"Not only did I make you plow them,
I will also make you cook the meal!"
Shì became furious and said:
"I will surely hang your head on the Cháng'ān city gate;
otherwise,
I will not live in this world!"
Měng reported this to Jiān,
who said:
"We must kill this old Dí,
and only then can the hundred officials be disciplined."
It happened that Shì came in to discuss matters,
and argued with Měng before Jiān.
Shì tried to rise and strike Měng;
Jiān, enraged,
had him executed.
From then on, when the various ministers saw Měng, they all held their breath.
Holding one's breath
means not daring to breathe.
One inhalation and exhalation constitutes a breath.
The character 屏
is pronounced bǐng.
8 When Zhào fell,
its generals Zhāng Píng, Lǐ Lì, and Gāo Chāng all sent envoys to surrender to Yān.
Later they surrendered to Jìn,
then surrendered to Qín,
each receiving noble ranks and positions,
wishing to remain neutral to secure themselves.
Lǐ Lì and Gāo Chāng initially surrendered to Jìn,
Zhāng Píng surrendered to Qín,
in the seventh year of the Yǒnghé era.
In the eighth year,
Lì and Chāng surrendered to Qín,
and that same year they surrendered to Yān together with Zhāng Píng.
After Fú Shēng's death,
Zhāng Píng surrendered to Jìn again,
each receiving noble ranks and positions.
Jiàng,
read as liàng.
Shǐ,
read as shǐ.
Xiáng,
read as xiáng.
The Minister of Works, Yáng Wù, attacked Gāo Chāng at Dōngyàn,
and Prince Lè'ān, Zāng, attacked Lǐ Lì at Pú.
Yáng Wù attacked Chāng's deputy general at Líyáng,
but failed to capture it.
Lì fled to Xíngyáng,
and his troops all surrendered.
Over a hundred fortifications in Bìngzhōu surrendered to Yān,
and Jùn appointed Yuè Wǎn, the Vice Director of the Right, as Governor of Bìngzhōu to pacify them.
Zhūgé Xiāng, the General Who Conquers the West appointed by Píng, and others led 138 fortifications to surrender to Yān,
and Jùn restored all their official positions and ranks.
Píng led three thousand troops to flee to Píngyáng,
and again requested to surrender to Yān.
9 In winter,
the tenth month,
the Grand Administrator of Tàishān, Zhūgé Yōu, attacked the Dōng Commandery of Yān,
entering Wǔyáng.
In the Later Hàn, the Dōng Commandery was governed from Dōngwǔyáng.
In the second year of the Xiánkāng era of Emperor Wǔ,
he enfeoffed his son Yǔn,
and because
"Dōng"
could not be used as a state name,
and the Dōng Commandery had the county of Púyáng,
it was renamed the State of Púyáng.
When Yǔn was transferred to be enfeoffed in Huáinán,
it reverted to being called Dōng Commandery.
When the Prince of Zhào, Lún, usurped the throne,
he demoted the Grandson Heir, Zāng, to Prince of Púyáng,
and the Dōng Commandery was then named Púyáng.
Here,
it seems Yān restored the name Dōng Commandery.
According to the Jìn Records: Wǔyáng County was part of Yángpíng Commandery.
Liú Xù said: Cháochéng County of Wèi Prefecture,
was the territory of Suí's Wǔyáng County,
renamed in the seventh year of the Tiānbǎo era.
Yōu was defeated and fled,
returning to Tàishān.
Kè then crossed the Yellow River,
seizing territory south of the river,
and appointed local officials.
10 The Yān ruler Jùn wanted to manage affairs with Qín and Jìn,
and in the twelfth month,
ordered the provinces and commanderies to verify the actual number of adult males,
jiào shí,
means to check and verify the actual numbers.
Xiàn,
read as xiàn.
All others were to be conscripted as soldiers,
intending to have an infantry force of 1.5 million men,
planning to assemble them in Luòyáng in the coming spring.
Liú Guì of Wǔyì submitted a memorial,
strongly stating
"the people are impoverished and exhausted,
and this conscription is unlawful,
as the law does not allow leaving only one male per household while conscripting all others as soldiers."
Jùn approved of this,
and thus changed the order to conscript one out of every three or five men,
extending the deadline,
to assemble in Yè by the following winter.
At that time, Yān's levies and conscriptions were frequent and numerous,
with various government offices each sending envoys,
causing congestion on the roads,
and the commanderies and counties suffered greatly.
The Grand Commandant and concurrently Director of the Central Secretariat, Fēng Yì, requested
"from now on, unless it is a critical military emergency,
no envoys should be dispatched;
all other tax collections and conscriptions should be the responsibility of the provinces and commanderies,
and all supervising officials dispatched by the various offices to the regions
should all be recalled."
Shè,
means to collect,
to recall.
11 The Yān Grand Administrator of Tàishān, Jiǎ Jiān, garrisoned Shānchí.
Shānchí,
was the Chí County of the Former Hàn,
part of Tàishān Commandery,
renamed Shānchí in the Later Hàn.
Chí,
read as chí.
Jiān commanded only a little over seven hundred men,
while Xiàn's forces were ten times larger than Jiān's.
Jiān was about to go out to battle,
and his generals all said:
"Our numbers are few,
it would be better to hold firm in defense."
Jiān said:
"Holding firm in defense will not save us either,
it is better to fight."
So he went out to battle,
leading his troops personally,
killing over a thousand of Xiàn's soldiers,
then returned to the city.
Xiàn attacked him,
and Jiān sighed, saying:
"Since I came of age,
I have aspired to achieve merit and fame,
yet I have often encountered desperate situations,
is this not fate!
I wanted to break their momentum,
to make Xiàn fear and retreat.
Now Xiàn attacks me,
my plans are exhausted.
It is better to maintain my integrity and die."
Then he said to his officers and soldiers:
"Now we are in dire straits,
with no plans left,
you all may leave,
I will stay and die."
The officers and soldiers all wept and said:
"If you, Prefect, do not leave,
we will all die together."
So they helped Jiān onto his horse,
but Jiān said:
"If I wanted to escape,
I would certainly not send you away.
Now I will fight a decisive battle for you all,
but if the situation becomes untenable,
you should quickly leave,
and do not look back for me!"
Then he opened the gates and charged straight out.
Xiàn's troops surrounded them from all sides,
Jiān reined his horse on the bridge,
shooting left and right,
and all his arrows hit their mark, felling the enemy.
Xiàn's troops were numerous,
and they went under the moat to chop at the bridge,
causing Jiān and his horse to fall together,
and he was captured alive,
thus Shānchí was taken.
Xiàn said to Jiān:
"Your father and grandfather served as officials of Jìn for generations,
why do you betray your roots and not surrender?"
Jiān replied:
"Jìn itself abandoned the Central Plains,
it is not I who rebelled.
Jiān's words here,
would shame many of the generals and ministers south of the Yangtze.
When strong, one entrusts one's life.
Once having served a master,
how can one change one's integrity!
I cultivated myself and established my own standing,
meaning from the time I studied under a teacher,
I was determined to establish myself.
Master Zhū said: Xiū,
is dried meat.
Ten strips make one bundle.
In ancient times, when studying under a teacher, one always presented a bundle of dried meat as a gift.
I have never changed my aspirations.
Jiān did not surrender to Yān,
see the seventh year of Yǒnghé in scroll 98.
Xiàn again reproached him,
and Jiān angrily said:
"You brat,
you treat your elder like a child!"
Calling himself "your elder,"
disrespecting Xiàn and treating him like a child.
