Saying "treat,"
means as if driving children.
They placed him in the rain;
after several days,
Jiān died of indignation and resentment.
The Yān Governor of Qīngzhōu, Mùróng Chén, sent Sima Yuèmíng to rescue Tàishān,
and Xiàn's troops were heavily defeated,
allowing Yān to retake Shānchí.
The Yān ruler Jùn appointed Jiǎ Jiān's son, Huó, as Grand Administrator of Rènchéng.
Xún Xiàn became critically ill,
and was recalled to court.
Xī Tán was appointed General of the Northern Headquarters, Commander of the military affairs of the five provinces Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, Jì, and Yōu,
of these five provinces,
only Xúzhōu had actual territory.
Xī,
read as xī.
Tán,
read as tán.
and stationed at Xiàpī.
7. The Governor of Liángzhōu, Zhāng Guàn,
was suspicious, jealous, harsh, and cruel,
basing rewards and punishments solely on his personal likes and dislikes.
The Gentleman of the Interior, Yīn Xún, remonstrated with him.
Guàn said:
"A tiger, three days after its birth,
can eat meat on its own,
it does not need to be taught by anyone."
Consequently, the people's hearts were not attached to him.
The General Who Supports the State, Sòng Hùn,
was by nature loyal and upright.
Guàn feared him
and wanted to kill Hùn and his younger brother Chéng,
thereby deposing the Prince of Liáng, Xuán Jìng, and taking his place.
He mustered tens of thousands of troops
and assembled them at Gūzāng.
Hùn learned of this
and, together with Chéng, led over forty cavalrymen including the brave warrior Yáng Hé in a sudden raid into the Southern City.
(Wáng Yǐn's Jìn Shū states: The city of Liángzhōu has the shape of a dragon,
hence it is called the Reclining Dragon City.
It is seven lǐ from north to south,
and two lǐ from east to west,
originally built by the Xiōngnú.
Later, the Zhāng clan resided there for generations,
and added four more cities,
each with walls one thousand paces long,
making five cities together with the old one.
Also, according to the biography of Zhāng Jùn: Jùn built five palaces south of Gūzāng,
each side corresponding to the color of its direction,
and he resided in them according to the seasons.
Thus, the Southern City was where the Zhāng clan resided.)
(Shuài,
read as "lead."
Jì,
read with the tone qí jì.)
"Zhāng Guàn is plotting rebellion,
by order of the Empress Dowager, he is to be executed."
Soon, their numbers reached two thousand.
Guàn led his troops out to fight,
but Hùn attacked and defeated him.
Guàn's subordinate Xuán Lú stabbed Hùn,
but could not pierce his armor.
(Xuán
is a surname.
Fēngsú Tōng: In ancient times, there was the state of Xuándū among the feudal lords.
Lú,
read as líng rú.
Cì,
read as qī yì;
same below.)
Guàn's troops all surrendered.
Guàn and his younger brother Jū both committed suicide,
and Hùn exterminated their clan.
Xuán Jìng appointed Hùn as Commissioner Bearing Credentials, Commander of All Military Affairs Within and Without, General of Agile Cavalry, and Marquis of Jiǔquán Commandery,
to replace Guàn in assisting the government.
Hùn then requested Xuán Jìng to abandon the title of Prince of Liáng.
(Zhāng Zuò first assumed the title of Prince of Liáng,
see scroll 99, the tenth year of Yǒnghé.
Zhāng Guàn supported Xuán Jìng as Prince of Liáng,
see above, the eleventh year.)
(Qù,
read as qiǎng lǚ.)
Hùn said to Xuán Lú:
"You stabbed me,
fortunately without injury.
Now that I am assisting the government,
are you afraid?"
Lú said:
"I received Guàn's favor,
I only regret that my stab at Your Excellency was not deep enough,
secretly, I have no fear!"
Hùn considered him righteous,
and appointed him as a trusted aide.
8. Gāo Chāng was unable to resist Yān,
and in autumn,
the seventh month,
fled from Báimǎ to Xíngyáng.
9. The Prince of Qín, Fú Jiān, returned from Hédōng,
and appointed the General of Agile Cavalry, Dèng Qiāng, as Imperial Censor.
In the eighth month,
he appointed the Neishi of Xiányáng, Wáng Měng, as Palace Attendant and Director of the Central Secretariat,
concurrently serving as Governor of the Capital District.
The Specially Advanced and Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, Qiáng Dé,
was the younger brother of the Empress Dowager.
(Empress Dowager Qiáng
was the consort of the ruler of Qín, Fú Jiàn.)
He was powerful and tyrannical,
plundering people's wealth, goods, and children,
causing suffering to the common people.
Měng, upon taking office, arrested Dé.
Before the memorial could be reported,
he had already displayed the corpse in the marketplace.
Jiān hastily sent an envoy to pardon him,
but it was too late.
Together with Dèng Qiāng, sharing the same purpose,
they hated evil and investigated cases,
without any顾忌,
Within a few dozen days,
over twenty powerful magnates and noble relatives
were either executed or dismissed from office and punished.
The court was shocked and trembled,
wicked and crafty people held their breath,
and lost items were not picked up on the road.
Jiān sighed and said:
"Only now do I begin to understand that there is law in the world!"
10. The Grand Administrator of Tàishān, Zhūgě Yōu, led twenty thousand troops by water and land to attack Yān,
entering from Shímén,
and encamping at Hézhǔ.
The Prince of Shàngyōng of Yān, Mùróng Píng, and the Grand Administrator of Chánglè, Fù Yán, led fifty thousand infantry and cavalry to fight Yōu at Dōng'ē,
and Yōu's troops were greatly defeated.
In winter,
the tenth month,
an edict ordered Xiè Wàn to station his army at Xiàcài and Xī Tán to station his army at Gāopíng to attack Yān.
Wàn was arrogant and haughty, looking down on others,
only considering himself lofty through whistling and chanting,
and never comforting his troops.
His elder brother Ān was deeply worried about this,
and said to Wàn:
"You are the commander-in-chief,
you should frequently receive and converse with the various generals to please their hearts.
How can someone as arrogant and unrestrained as you accomplish anything!"
Wàn then summoned the various generals,
but said nothing at all,
simply pointing his rúyì to the four directions and saying:
"All the generals are strong soldiers."
The generals hated him even more.
(Rúyì,
an iron rúyì.
Zuò,
read as cú wò.)
(Generally, those who rise from the ranks
忌讳 being called soldiers or privates;
once they become generals,
to be called privates
is why they hated him even more.)
Then, from the team leaders down,
he personally visited everyone without exception,
forming close relationships and entrusting them with tasks.
Soon after, Wàn led his troops into the Wō and Yǐng river regions to reinforce Luòyáng.
(The Wō River flows to Shānsāng and enters the Huái,
the Yǐng River flows to Xiàcài and enters the Huái.
Xiè Shàng's troops
entered the area between the Wō and Yǐng from Xiàcài.)
Wàn, thinking the Yān troops were very strong,
and that Tán had retreated,
immediately led his troops back,
and the army then panicked and collapsed.
(Advancing an army is easy,
retreating an army is difficult.
Therefore, a good commander, when wanting to retreat,
must first extensively plan strategies before leading the retreat,
not only to guard against the enemy's pursuit and interception,
but also to prevent his own troops from panicking and collapsing.)
The soldiers wanted to take advantage of his defeat to plot against him,
but refrained because of Ān.
After returning,
an edict demoted Wàn to commoner status,
and reduced Tán's title to General Who Establishes Military Might.
Consequently, cities such as Xǔchāng, Yǐngchuān, Qiáo, and Pèi successively fell to Yān.
11. The Prince of Qín, Fú Jiān, appointed Wáng Měng as Minister of Personnel,
and soon promoted him to Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent.
In the eleventh month,
he became Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
retaining his other positions as before.
12. In the twelfth month,
the son of the Prince of Wǔlíng, Sīma Xī, named Bīn, was enfeoffed as Prince of Liáng.
13. There was a great drought.
14. On the Xīnyǒu day,
the ruler of Yān, Mùróng Jùn, fell seriously ill.
He said to the Grand Marshal, the Prince of Tàiyuán, Mùróng Kè:
"My illness will certainly not improve.
Now, the two sides are not yet pacified,
(the two sides
refer to Jìn and Qín.)
the state faces many difficulties.
I wish to follow the example of Duke Xuān of Sòng,
and entrust the state to you.
What do you think?"
Kè said:
"Although the Crown Prince is young,
he is a ruler capable of overcoming cruelty and achieving good governance.
What kind of person am I,
that I dare to interfere with the legitimate succession!"
Jùn angrily said:
"Between brothers,
how can there be empty flattery!"
Kè said:
"If Your Majesty considers me capable of bearing the responsibility for the world,
how could I be unable to assist a young ruler!"
Jùn happily said:
"If you can be a Duke of Zhōu,
what more do I have to worry about!
Lǐ Jī is pure, upright, loyal, and bright,
treat him well."
He summoned the Prince of Wú, Mùróng Chuí, back to Yè.
(Summoned back from Liáodōng.)
15. The Qín king Jiān appointed Wáng Měng as Assistant General of the State and Colonel Director of Retainers,
stationed in the capital to guard the palace,
while retaining his previous posts as Vice Director of the Left, Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent, Palace Attendant, Palace Secretary, and in charge of official selection.
Měng submitted a memorial declining and yielding,
and recommended in his place the Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary, Duke of Yángpíng, Róng, and the Cavalier Attendant of the Household of the Palace Attendants, Rén Zhì of Xīhé.
Cavalier Attendant of the Household of the Palace Attendants:
This refers to a Grand Master of the Palace with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon serving as a Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary.
"Cavalier"
is pronounced sàn,
with the tone of dǎn.
"Attendant"
is pronounced jì,
with the tone of qí jì.
"Rén"
is pronounced as Rén.
Jiān did not permit it,
and instead appointed Róng as Palace Attendant, Palace Secretary Supervisor, and Vice Director of the Left,
and appointed Rén Zhì as Grand Master of the Palace with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon, in charge of the Household of the Heir Apparent.
The "Jìn Shū" Treatise on Officials states: The Household of the Heir Apparent
is in charge of punishments and prisons, grain and goods, and food and drink,
its duties comparable to those of the Minister of Agriculture and the Privy Treasurer.
According to the Hàn system: The Imperial Secretariat had thirty-six Assistant Directors.
A Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat initially came from the Three Bureaus to the Imperial Secretariat,
and after a probationary period was called a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat.
After one year, he was called a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat,
and after three years, an Assistant Director.
The "Jìn Shū" Treatise on Officials states: The duties of the Household of the Heir Appendant are comparable to those of a Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary and the Palace Secretary Supervisor.
"Zhū Tóng"
should be
"Zhū Róng".
Within a year, he was promoted five times:
Měng was promoted from Assistant Director of the Left of the Imperial Secretariat to Administrator of Xiányáng;
then to Palace Attendant and Palace Secretary;
in charge of the Capital District;
then to Minister of Personnel;
soon after to Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent,
and to Vice Director of the Left;
up to now, a total of five promotions.
There were people who slandered him,
and Jiān would punish them,
so from then on, none of the officials dared to speak again.
He appointed Vice Director of the Left Lǐ Wēi to concurrently command the Palace Guard;
Vice Director of the Right Liáng Pínglǎo as Commissioner Bearing Credentials, Commander of Various Military Affairs of the Northern Frontier, Great General Who Guards the North,
to garrison west of Shuòfāng;
and the Army Advisor to the Chancellor, Jiǎ Yōng, as Protector of Yúnzhōng,
to garrison south of Yúnzhōng.
16. The troops levied by Yān from the commanderies and principalities all assembled at the city of Yè.
Levied last year,
they now all assembled.

Compiled by Sīmǎ Guāng
by Imperial Command
Later Scholar from Tiāntái
The Lower Part of the Chronicle of Emperor Mù of the Xiào Zōng
The Fourth Year of Shēngpíng (Gēngshēn, 360)
1. In spring,
the first month, on the day Guǐsì,
the Yān ruler Jùn held a grand review at Yè,
intending to have the Grand Marshal Kè and the Minister of Works Yáng Wù lead them on an invasion;
but he happened to fall critically ill,
so he summoned Kè, Wù, the Minister over the Masses Píng, the General of the Central Army Mùyú Gēn, and others to receive the posthumous edict to assist in governance.
On the day Jiǎwǔ,
he died.
He was forty-two years old.
On the day Wùzǐ,
the heir apparent Wěi ascended the imperial throne.
Wěi,
styled Jǐngmào,
was the third son of Jùn.
According to the perpetual calendar,
the first month of this year
began on the day Jiǎxū.
Now Jùn died on Jiǎwǔ,
so Wùzǐ is before Jiǎwǔ.
The accession to the throne was probably on Wùxū.
A great amnesty was declared,

2. The Qín king Jiān divided the Capital Province to establish the Yōng Province,
appointing the Duke of Hénán, Shuāng, as Commander of Various Military Affairs of the Three Provinces of Yōng, Hé, and Liáng, Great General Who Conquers the West, and Governor of Yōng Province,

and stationing him at Āndìng.
The Hé and Liáng Provinces were not Qín territory.
The actual territory under Shuāng's command

This sets the stage for Shuāng's rebellion from Āndìng.
3. The Duke of Chóuchí, Yáng Jùn, died,

"Court"

Yáng Wù was appointed Grand Guardian,
Mùyú Gēn was appointed Grand Preceptor,

Gēn was by nature stubborn and unyielding.
Yán Shìgǔ said: "Stubborn" means straightforward and unyielding.
"Unyielding"
is pronounced qiáng,
with the tone of qí liǎng.
Since the time of Huàng,
Gēn had repeatedly achieved military merits.
His actions were arrogant and haughty.
At that time, Empress Dowager Kězúhún was quite involved in external affairs,
and Gēn wanted to start a rebellion,
so he said to Kè:
"Now the ruler is young,
and the mother empress interferes in governance.
Your Highness should guard against unexpected changes,
and think of ways to protect yourself.
Moreover, it was Your Highness's merit that stabilized the empire.
When the elder brother dies, the younger brother succeeds;
this is an established rule from ancient to modern times.
This is the Yīn law,
not the Zhōu law.
You should depose the ruler to be a prince,
and Your Highness should ascend to the honored position yourself,

Kè said:
"Are you drunk, sir?
How perverse your words are!
I and you received the late emperor's posthumous edict;

Gēn, ashamed, apologized and withdrew.
Kè told the Prince of Wú, Chuí, about this,

Kè said:
"Now we have just suffered a great loss,

The two neighbors
refer to Jìn and Qín.
"I fear it would violate the expectations of those near and far,

The Supervisor of the Palace Library, Huángfǔ Zhēn, said to Kè:
"Gēn is fundamentally a mediocre and lowly fellow,
who received excessive favor from the late emperor,
and was brought in to participate in the deathbed mandate.
But a petty man has no understanding;

his arrogance and recalcitrance have increased daily,
and he will cause disaster and chaos.
Your Excellency now occupies the position of the Duke of Zhōu;
you should deeply plan for the state,

Kè did not listen.
Gēn also said to Empress Dowager Kězúhún and the Yān ruler Wěi:

I request to lead the imperial guards to execute them."
Empress Dowager Kězúhún was about to agree,

"These two lords

They certainly would not do such a thing;

So they stopped.
Gēn also missed and longed for the eastern lands.

"Now the empire is desolate,

When Kè heard this,

A great amnesty was declared.
After executing Gēn and his wife, children, and faction,

The execution and extermination were widespread,

The Grand Tutor Kè behaved as usual,

Someone advised him that he should strengthen his own security,

"People's hearts are just now fearful;

Why should we alarm and disturb ourselves again?
Although Kè held overall authority,

7 Xiè Ān had a great reputation from a young age,
repeatedly summoned to office,
but he did not accept;
he lived in Kuàijī,
enjoying himself with landscapes and literature.
Although a commoner,
people of the time expected him to become a high official,

"If Ānshí does not come out,

Xiè Ān,

The people of Jiāngdōng first placed their hopes on Yīn Hào,
but Hào failed to meet expectations,
then they hoped for Xiè Ān,
and Ān ultimately was able to assist the Jìn court.
Commentators of the time,
all praised Ān and criticized Hào.
I say that under a great reputation,
reality is hard to match.
The reason Hào failed,
was precisely because he shared fame with Huán Wēn,
his heart envied Wēn;
also, encountering the chaos of the Shí clan,
he thought he could achieve merit,
but failed due to recklessness.
Xiè Ān, during Huán Wēn's monopolization of power,
and having served as his subordinate,
learned from Hào's mistakes,
guarded against Wēn and prepared accordingly;
after Wēn's death, facing the strength of Qín,
he diligently planned for self-preservation,
always maintaining caution,

Historians say he could suppress emotions and remain composed,
known from the broken clog tooth and the white rooster dream.
Dōngshān,

Minister of Education Yù heard of this,

Yàn's Yuèxī led troops to seize the various cities in Hénán,
capturing them all.
12 The Qín King Jiān ordered each ducal state to establish three ministers.
The Jìn system: A princely state established the Chamberlain for the Palace Garrison, the Commandant of the Capital, and the Grand Minister of Agriculture as the three ministers;
Qín followed this system.
Only the Chamberlain for the Palace Garrison was established for each.
Wealthy merchants like Zhào Duō and others had carriages and clothing that exceeded regulations and were extravagant.
The various dukes vied to appoint them as ministers;
the Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, Āndìng's Chéng Xiàn,
requested they be punished.
Jiān then issued an edict stating:
"Originally, I intended for the various dukes to select eminent scholars,
yet instead it has become so corrupt and excessive!
Let the relevant officials investigate and examine,
and for those who summoned inappropriate persons,
all shall be demoted in rank to marquis.
From now on, state officials shall all be entrusted to the Ministry of Personnel for selection.
The Ministry of Personnel,
refers to the Minister of Personnel.
They may not ride in carriages or on horseback;
within a hundred lǐ of the capital,
artisans, merchants, servants, and slaves
may not wear gold, silver, brocade, or embroidery.
Offenders shall be executed in the marketplace."
Thereupon, the Dukes of Píngyáng, Píngchāng, Jiǔjiāng, Chénliú, and Ānlè were all demoted in rank to marquis.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on Gēngshēn,
the Empress, née Wáng, passed away.
2. Liú Wèichén again rebelled against Dài.
(Liú Wèichén had previously submitted to Dài;
see the fifth year of Shēngpíng above.)
(Fù,
fú yòu fān.)
(Dài) attacked and drove him away.
Shíyìjiān was by nature tolerant and generous.
The Gentleman of the Palace, Xǔ Qiān, stole two bolts of silk.
Shíyìjiān knew about it but concealed it.
According to the *History of the Northern Dynasties*,
the customs of the Dài state did not include silk fabrics,
and Qiān stole them;
his crime was unpardonable.
Yet Shíyìjiān was able to tolerate him,
so the historian uses this to illustrate one aspect of his tolerance and generosity.
"I cannot bear to see Qiān's face.
If Qiān, out of shame, commits suicide,
it would be as if I killed a scholar over property."
Once, when attacking western rebels,
a stray arrow struck his eye.
Later, the archer was captured.
His ministers wanted to slice him to pieces.
Shíyìjiān said:
"He was merely fighting for his lord.
What crime is that!"
He then released him.
3. The Grand Marshal, Wēn, moved his garrison to Gūshú.
(Wēn again moved east from Zhěqí to garrison Gūshú.)
On the yǐwèi day,
he appointed his younger brother, General of the Right, Huò, to supervise the military affairs of Yìchéng in Jīngzhōu and Yángzhōu, and Jīngzhào in Yōngzhōu,
and to concurrently serve as Governor of Jīngzhōu.
(The Yìchéng Commandery was established in Xiāngyáng.
Xiāngyáng Commandery belonged to Jīngzhōu,
but Yìchéng Commandery administered Píng'ē and Xiàcài in Huáinán, Yángzhōu.
It seems that earlier, Huán Xuān first retreated to Huáinán with Zǔ Yuē,
and later garrisoned Xiāngyáng.
Táo Kǎn used his Huáinán troops to establish the Yìchéng Commandery in Gǔchéng.
It seems there were people from Yángzhōu, and so Yángzhōu émigré counties were established in Gǔchéng.
Gǔchéng
was within the jurisdiction of Jīngzhōu.
Hence, it was called Yìchéng of Jīngzhōu and Yángzhōu.
Calling it Yìchéng
means it was formed by the Yìchéng Army,
and thus the commandery was named after it.
Later people added
the character
"chéng"
with the radical "tǔ"
beside it, losing the original intent behind establishing the commandery.
Jīngzhào Commandery belonged to Yōngzhōu,
and at that time, it was also established as an émigré commandery in Xiāngyáng.)
(Yōng,
yú yòng fān.)
Earlier,
Chōng was appointed Inspector of Jiāngzhōu,
concurrently serving as Grand Administrator of Xīyáng and Qiáo Commanderies.
Now, he was additionally appointed to supervise Xià and Suí Commanderies in Jīngzhōu, and Rǔnán, Xīyáng, Xīncài, and Yǐngchuān Commanderies in Yùzhōu,
totaling six commanderies,
making eight commanderies together with Xúnyáng, where he was garrisoned.
(Jiān,
gōng xián fān.)
*Textual Analysis* says: The Basic Annals of the Emperor states:
"Chōng held the title of Colonel of the Southern Man."
(In the Jiangdong regime, only Jīngzhōu had a Colonel of the Southern Man.
Chōng's biography also does not mention it.
It seems the Annals mistakenly repeated it from Huán Huò's record.
I do not adopt it here.)
The Minister over the Masses, Yù, heard that Chén Yòu had abandoned Luòyáng.
He met with the Grand Marshal, Wēn, at Lièzhōu.
(Now, there is Liè Mountain in the river at Gūshú;
this is the place.)
On the bǐngshēn day,
the Emperor passed away in the Western Hall,
at the age of twenty-five.
(The Western Hall
was the Western Hall of the Tàijí Palace.
The Tàijí Palace in Jiànkāng had Eastern and Western Halls.
The Eastern Hall was for receiving ministers,
the Western Hall was a place for rest.)
The Emperor had no heir.
On the dīngyǒu day,
the Empress Dowager issued an edict ordering the Prince of Lángyá, Yì, to succeed to the throne.
(Yì
should be written as Yì.)
On that day,
he ascended the throne as Emperor,
and a general amnesty was declared.
4. Qín declared a general amnesty,
and changed the era name to Jiànyuán.
5. The Grand Minister over the Masses of Yān, Kè, and the Prince of Wú, Chuí, jointly attacked Luòyáng.
Kè said to his generals:
"You gentlemen often complained that I did not attack.
Now, Luòyáng's walls are high, but its troops are weak.
It is easy to capture.
Do not be fearful and slack off!"
They then attacked it.
In the third month,
they captured it,
and captured the General Who Inspires Martial Might, Shěn Jìn.
Jìn's spirit and expression remained unperturbed.
Kè intended to pardon him.
The General of the Central Army, Mùyú Qián, said:
"Although Jìn is an extraordinary man,
judging by his aspirations and bearing,
he will never serve another.
If we pardon him now,
he will surely become a future trouble."
They then killed him.
Kè expanded his territory to Xiáo and Miǎn.
(Xiáo
is Xiáo Valley;
Miǎn
is Miǎnchí.)
(Miǎn,
mí yǎn fān.)
The King of Qín, Jiān, personally led troops to garrison Shǎnchéng to guard against him.
Yān appointed the General of the Gentlemen of the Left, Mùróng Zhù, as Governor of Luòzhōu,
to garrison Jīnyōng.

The Prince of Wú, Chuí, was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of ten provinces: Jīng, Yáng, Luò, Xú, Yǎn, Yù, Yōng, Yì, Liáng, and Qín; Grand General Who Conquers the South; and Governor of Jīngzhōu.
He was allotted ten thousand troops
and garrisoned Lǔyáng.
The Grand Minister over the Masses, Kè, returned to Yè.
He said to his subordinates:
"Previously, when I pacified Guǎnggù,
I could not save Pìlǘ Wèi;
(see the twelfth year of Emperor Mù's Yǒnghé era in the previous scroll.)
now I have caused Shěn Jìn to be killed.
Although neither was my original intention,
as the commander-in-chief,
I am truly ashamed before the world."
The court commended Jìn's loyalty,
and posthumously awarded him the title of Grand Administrator of Dōngyáng.
Your servant, Guāng, says: Shěn Jìn can be called a capable son!
Ashamed of his father's evil,
he sought death to wash it away,
transforming a clan of treacherous rebels into a family of loyalty and righteousness.
The *Book of Changes* says:
"Dealing with the father's troubles,
he uses praise."
(This is the line of the fifth six in the hexagram Gǔ of the *Book of Changes*.
The *Image* says: Dealing with the father, he uses praise,
continuing with virtue.)
"You should cover the faults of your predecessors,
with loyalty and filial piety."
(See the *Book of Documents*.)
6. The Grand Minister over the Masses, Kè, as a general,
did not rely on authority and severity,
but exclusively used kindness and trust.
In caring for his soldiers, he focused on the major points,
not issuing harsh orders,
so that everyone could feel at ease.
Ordinarily, the camp was relaxed and permissive,
as if it could be violated.
However, the guard and precautions were strict and meticulous.
When the enemy arrived, none could approach,
so he never suffered defeat.
7. On the rénshēn day,
Emperor Āi and Empress Jìng were buried at Ānpíng Líng.
(Empress Wáng
was posthumously named Jìng.
The *History of Jin* writes
"Jìng".)
8. In summer,
the fourth month,
on the rénwǔ day,
the Grand Commandant of Yān, the Duke of Wǔpíng, Fēng Yì, passed away.
(According to the rules of posthumous names: "Upright heart and great magnanimity is called Kuāng.")
The Palace Attendant and Grand Master of Splendid Happiness, Huángfǔ Zhēn, was appointed Minister of Works,
concurrently overseeing the Palace Secretariat.
Yáng Wù served four reigns,
(the four reigns of Mùróng Huì, Huàng, Jùn, and Wěi).
(Cháo,
zhí yáo fān.)
Everyone from the Grand Minister over the Masses, Kè, downwards paid their respects to him.
Yet Wù remained humble, respectful, cautious, and sincere,
even more so than in his youth.
He strictly disciplined his sons and grandsons.
Although they wore the red and purple robes of high officials,
none dared to violate his rules and standards.
(Fēng Yì served Yān,
also serving four reigns.
His contributions and labors exceeded those of Yáng Wù,
and the nobility and prominence of his descendants also surpassed the Yáng clan.
Could it be that Fēng Yì's humble virtue was inferior to Wù's?
Or perhaps the historians recorded this based on the Yáng clan's family biography,
while the Fēng clan's records are lacking and unmentioned.)
(Shào,
shī zhào fān.)
9 In the sixth month, on the
Wùzǐ day,
Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Jiànchéng Xiānggōng Zhōu Fǔ passed away.
According to the rules of posthumous naming: "Xiāng" is conferred for achieving merit through service.
In the third year of Emperor Mù's Yǒnghé era,
Huán Wēn pacified Shǔ,
and left Fǔ to garrison it.
Up to this point, it had been only nineteen years.
Before Jìn had obtained Shǔ,
the position of Yìzhōu Cìshǐ was established in Bādōng.
Fǔ had already been appointed Cìshǐ earlier;
after Wēn conquered Shǔ,
Fǔ remained as Yìzhōu Cìshǐ,
garrisoning Péngmó.
The statement that he was in Yìzhōu for over thirty years
is because the historical record combines the years he garrisoned Bādōng and Péngmó.
An edict ordered his son, the Tàishǒu of Qiánwéi, Zhōu Chǔ, to replace him.
10 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Jǐyǒu day,
Huìjī Wáng Sīmǎ Yù was transferred back to being Lángyé Wáng.
Emperor Yuán had appointed Yù as Lángyé Wáng
to continue the sacrifices for Prince Gōng.
In the first year of Emperor Chéng's Xiánhé era,
Yù's birth mother, Lady Zhèng, passed away.
Yù, in mourning and longing, requested to observe mourning rites,
and was again transferred and enfeoffed as Huìjī Wáng.
After this,
Emperor Kāng, Emperor Āi, and the current emperor
all succeeded to the throne from the position of Lángyé Wáng.
Huì
is pronounced like "gōngwài fān."
11 On the Rénzǐ day,
Lady Yǔ was established as Empress.
The Empress
was the daughter of Yǔ Bīng.
12 On the Jiǎshēn day,
Sīmǎ Yù's son, Chāngmíng, was established as Huìjī Wáng;
Yù firmly declined,
and still referred to himself as Huìjī Wáng.
13 The Xiōngnú Right Virtuous King Cáo Gǔ and Left Virtuous King Liú Wèichén both rebelled against Qín.
Gǔ led twenty thousand troops to raid Xìngchéng.
The Qín king Fú Jiān personally led an army to attack him,
and ordered Grand General Wèi Lǐ Wēi and Left Púyè Wáng Měng to assist the Crown Prince Hóng in guarding Cháng'ān.
In the eighth month,
Jiān attacked Gǔ,
defeated him,
and beheaded Gǔ's younger brother, Huó.
Gǔ requested to surrender,
and over six thousand households of prominent families were relocated to Cháng'ān.
Jiànjié General Dèng Qiāng attacked Wèichén,
capturing him at Mùgēn Mountain.
Mùgēn Mountain is in Shuòfāng.
In the ninth month,
Jiān went to Shuòfāng,
to inspect and pacify the various Hú tribes.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Zhēngběi General and Huáinán Gōng Fú Yòu led the troops of Xìngchéng to take advantage of the emptiness and raid Cháng'ān.
Lǐ Wēi attacked and beheaded him.
Yòu
was also a younger brother of the Qín ruler Fú Shēng.
14 The Xiānbēi Tūfā Chuíjīn passed away,
at the age of one hundred and ten.
His son, Sīfùjiān, succeeded him in leading his people.
Chuíjīn
was the grandson of Shùjīnéng's cousin, Wùwán.
Shùjīnéng caused chaos in Liángzhōu,
as recorded in the annals of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn.
Cóng
is pronounced like "cái yòng fān."
15 Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Sīmǎ Xūn
governed with cruel tyranny.
If the Zhìzhōng, Biéjià, or prominent local magnates of the province
spoke words that displeased him,
he would immediately behead them in their seats,
or personally shoot them to death.
He often harbored ambitions to seize Shǔ,
but feared Zhōu Fǔ,
and did not dare to act.
After Fǔ passed away,
Xūn then raised troops in rebellion;
Biéjià Yōng Duān and Xīróng Sīmǎ Kuí Cuì earnestly remonstrated,
Xīróng Sīmǎ
is a subordinate official of the Xīróng Xiàowèi.
Yōng
is pronounced like "yú yòng fān."
Kuí
is pronounced like "wǔ zuì fān."
He proclaimed himself Governor of Liáng and Yì Provinces and Chéngdū Wáng.
In the eleventh month,
Xūn led troops into Jiàngé,
attacking Fú.
Xīyí Xiàowèi Guànqiū Wěi abandoned the city and fled.
Jìn initially established the Xīyí Xiàowèi,
stationed at Wènshān.
Now it was likely stationed at Fúchéng.
Fú
is pronounced like "fú."
On the Yǐmǎo day,
he besieged Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Zhōu Chǔ in Chéngdū.
Grand Marshal Huán Wēn recommended Yīngyáng General and Jiāngxià Xiàng Yìyáng Zhū Xù as Zhēngtǎo Dūhù to rescue him.
16 The Qín king Fú Jiān returned to Cháng'ān,
appointed Lǐ Wēi as Tàiwèi,
and added the title of Shìzhōng.
He enfeoffed Cáo Gǔ as Yànmén Gōng,
and Liú Wèichén as Xiàyáng Gōng,
each allowing them to govern their own tribes.
17 In the twelfth month,
on the Wùxū day,
Shàngshū Wáng Biāozhī was appointed as Púyè.
Hǎixī Gōng Shàng
His personal name was Yì,
courtesy name Yánlíng,
the younger brother of the same mother as Emperor Āi;
in the eighth year of the Xiánkāng era,
he was enfeoffed as Dōnghǎi Wáng;
in the fifth year of Emperor Mù's Shēngpíng era,
he was re-enfeoffed as Lángyé Wáng;
after ascending the throne,
Huán Wēn deposed him to Hǎixī Gōng.
First year of Tàihé era (Bǐngyín, 366)
1 In spring,
the third month,
Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Huán Huò sent Dūhù Huán Pí to attack Nánzhèng,
to campaign against Sīmǎ Xūn.
2 Yān Tàizǎi and Grand Marshal Mù Kè,
Tàifù and Sītú Píng,
bowed their heads and returned governance,
presenting their seals and ribbons,
requesting to return to their residences;
the Yān ruler Mù Wěi did not permit it.
3 In summer,
the fifth month,
on the Wùyín day,
Empress Yǔ passed away.
4 Zhū Xù and Zhōu Chǔ attacked Sīmǎ Xūn,
defeated him,
captured Xūn and his associates,
and sent them to Grand Marshal Huán Wēn;
Wēn executed them all,
and sent their heads to Jiànkāng.
5 Dài Wáng Tuòbá Shíyìjiān sent Left Chief Clerk Yān Fèng to present tribute to Qín.
6 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Guǐyǒu day,
Empress Xiào was buried at Jìngpíng Líng.
Empress Yǔ
was given the posthumous title Xiào.
7 Qín Fǔguó General Wáng Měng, Qián General Yáng Ān, Yángwǔ General Yáo Cháng, and others led twenty thousand troops to raid Jīngzhōu,
attacking Nánxiāng Commandery;
Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Huán Huò came to its rescue,
and in the eighth month,
stationed his army at Xīnyě.
The Qín troops plundered over ten thousand households from Ānyáng and then withdrew.
Ānyáng County,
belonged to Hànzhōng Commandery in Hàn times.
Wèi established Wèixīng Commandery,
and Ānyáng belonged to it;
it was abolished in Jìn times.
Qín attacked Nánxiāng and then retreated;
how could they penetrate deep into mountainous terrain
to plunder the people of Ānyáng?
The Zǎijì records it as
"Hànyáng,"
meaning north of the Hàn River.
It should be correct to follow the Zǎijì.
8 In the ninth month,
on the Jiǎwǔ day,
a special pardon was granted for Liáng and Yì Provinces.
After Sīmǎ Xūn was initially pacified,
his branch followers and those coerced into following were pardoned.
9 In winter,
the tenth month,
Sītú Yù was additionally appointed as Chéngxiàng and Lù Shàngshūshì,
allowed to enter court without hurrying,
praised and saluted without being named,
and to wear his sword and shoes when ascending the palace hall.
10 Zhāng Tiānxī sent an envoy to the Qín border,
to announce the severance of relations with Qín.
Liáng had relations with Qín,
as seen in the previous volume, in the twelfth year of Emperor Mù's Yǒnghé era.
Shǐ
is pronounced like "shū lì fān."
11 Yān Fǔjūn General and Xiàpī Wáng Lì raided Yǎnzhōu,
capturing several commanderies including Lǔ and Gāopíng,
established administrators and magistrates, and then returned.
12. Initially,
Lǒngxī's Lǐ Yǎn surrendered his commandery to Qín,
but later re-established contact with Zhāng Tiānxī.
Lǐ Yǎn held Lǒngxī,
the matter beginning in the eleventh year of Yǒnghé in the previous scroll.
Surrendered,
read as "jiàng".
Re-established,
read as "fù".
The Qiāng leader Liǎn Qí rebelled against Qín with four thousand households from Lüèyáng,
and pledged allegiance to Yǎn;
the Zǎijì records it as
"Liǎn Qí".
The Biography of Zhāng Tiānxī records it as
"Lián Qí".
Liǎn,
is a Qiāng surname.
He severed relations with Qín and Liáng.
13. Nányáng's military supervisor Zhào Yì, holding Wǎnchéng, surrendered to Yān,
while the grand administrator Huán Dàn fled to defend Xīnyě;
the Yān people sent the Central General of the South Zhào Pán from Lǔyáng to garrison Wǎn.
14. The Inspector of Xú and Yǎn, Yǔ Xī,
due to his relation to the imperial consort clan,
saw his brothers become noble and prominent,
which Grand Marshal Huán Wēn resented.
1. In spring,
the first month,
Yǔ Xī was charged with failing to rescue Lǔ and Gāopíng,
and was dismissed from office.
An examination of discrepancies states: The Annals of Emperor Mù,
in this month,
states that Xī committed a crime,
and fled to the sea.
According to his main biography,
after the deposition of Hǎixī,
Xī fled to Hǎilíng,
at this time he was merely dismissed from office.
2. In the second month,
Yān's General of Pacifying the Army, the Prince of Xiàpī, Mùróng Lì, and General Who Guards the North, the Prince of Yídū, Mùróng Huán, attacked the Chìlè.

3. Qín's General of Assisting the State Wáng Měng, the grand administrator of Lǒngxī Jiāng Héng, the grand administrator of Nán'ān from Nán'ān, Shào Qiāng, and General Who Spreads Martial Might Yáo Cháng, among others, led seventeen thousand troops to suppress Liǎn Qí.
In the third month,
Zhāng Tiānxī sent his former general Yáng Yù towards Jīnchéng,
and General Who Conquers the East Cháng Jù towards Zuǒnán,
Zhāng Guǐ established Zuǒnán County,
belonging to Jìnxīng Commandery.
Kàn Yǐn's Shísānzhōuzhì states: West of Shíchéng one hundred and forty lǐ,
there is Zuǒnán City,
the Hé River passes south of it,
called the Zuǒnán Crossing.
Yù,
pronounced "yù".
The Jìnshū Treatise on Geography,
Báitǔ County belongs to Jīnchéng Commandery.
Shísānzhōuzhì: West of Zuǒnán Crossing sixty lǐ is Báitǔ City,
the city is north of the Great River,
serving as a crossing point along the river.
Cāngsōng County,
since Hàn times belonged to Wǔwēi Commandery,
later, Liáng's Lǚ Guāng changed it to Chāngsōng County.
General,
read as "jiàng".
Liǎn Qí's tribe originally belonged to Yáo Yìzhòng,
hearing that Yáo Cháng had arrived,
they all surrendered;
Wáng Měng then captured Lüèyáng,
and Liǎn Qí fled to Báimǎ.
Báimǎ,
is the land of the Báimǎ Dí in Wǔdū.
4. In summer,
the fourth month,
Yān's Mùróng Chén raided Jìnglíng,
but the grand administrator Luó Chóng repelled him.
5. Zhāng Tiānxī attacked Lǐ Yǎn's two commanderies of Dàxià and Wǔshǐ,
and captured them.
Sòng Bái states: In the eighteenth year of Zhāng Jùn,
he divided Wǔshǐ, Xīngjìn, and Guǎngwǔ to establish Dàxià Commandery;
in Táng times it was Dàxià County,
belonging to Hézhōu.
Zhāng Jùn established Wǔshǐ Commandery with Dídào County,
present-day Xīzhōu is that area.
Xià,
read as "xià".
Tiānxī advanced and encamped at Zuǒnán.
Yǎn, fearing,
retreated to defend Fúhǎn,
and sent his nephew Lǐ Chún to Qín to apologize for his crime,
and also request rescue.
The Qín king Fú Jiān sent former general Yáng Ān and General Who Establishes Authority Wáng Fǔ with twenty thousand cavalry,
to join Wáng Měng to rescue Yǎn.
Měng sent Shào Qiāng to pursue Liǎn Qí,
Wáng Fǔ to guard Héhé,
and Jiāng Héng to guard Báishí.
Báishí County,
in Former Hàn belonged to Jīnchéng Commandery,
in Later Hàn belonged to Lǒngxī Commandery.
Xián states: Báishí Mountain is in present-day Lánzhōu.
Sòng Bái states: Fènglín County in Hézhōu,
originally the land of Hàn's Báishí County,
in the eighth year of Zhāng Jùn,
was changed to Yǒnggù County.
Tiānxī sent Yáng Yù to engage in battle east of Fúhǎn,
but Měng heavily defeated him,
capturing and beheading seventeen thousand,
and faced Tiānxī in a standoff below the city.
Below Fúhǎn city.
Sent him.
Měng sent a letter to Tiānxī stating:
"I have received an edict to rescue Yǎn,
not to engage Liángzhōu in battle,
now we should deepen our walls and heighten our ramparts,
to await later edicts.
Prolonging this day after day,
I fear both sides will be exhausted,
which is not a good plan.
Both sides,
meaning Qín and Liáng.
I shall take Yǎn east,
and you, General, move your people west and return,
would that not be acceptable!"
Tiānxī said to his generals:
"Měng's letter is thus;
I originally came to punish rebellion,
not to battle Qín."
Thereupon he led his troops back.
Lǐ Yǎn had still not admitted the Qín army,
Wáng Měng, wearing plain clothes and riding in a carriage,
with several tens of followers,
requested to meet with Yǎn.
Yǎn opened the gates and invited him in,
before he could prepare,
soldiers and officers followed in,
and thus seized Yǎn.
He appointed General Who Establishes Loyalty Péng Yuè as General Who Pacifies the West and Inspector of Liángzhōu,
to garrison Fúhǎn.
General Who Establishes Loyalty,
was a position created by Fú Qín.
When Zhāng Tiānxī returned west,
Lǐ Yǎn's general Hè Chún advised Yǎn:
"With your divine martial prowess,
and officers and soldiers fierce and brave,
why submit to others!
Wáng Měng's isolated army came from afar,
his soldiers are weary and exhausted,
and since he came at our request for rescue,
he surely is unprepared,
if we take advantage of their weariness to attack,
we can achieve our aim."
Yǎn said:
"To seek rescue from others to avoid calamity,
then once the calamity is avoided to attack them,
what would the world say of me!
It is better to firmly defend and wear them out,
they will retreat on their own."
Měng reproached Yǎn for not coming out to welcome him,
Yǎn told him of Hè Chún's plan;
Měng beheaded Chún,
and took Yǎn back.
Arriving at Cháng'ān,
Jiān appointed Yǎn as Superintendent of the Imperial Household,
and bestowed the title of Marquis Guī'ān.
6. Yān's Prince of Tàiyuán, Huán, Mùróng Kè, said to the Yān ruler Mùróng Wěi:
The interpretation of the posthumous title "Huán": Opening territory and subduing distant lands is called "Huán".
"The Prince of Wú, Mùróng Chuí,
has talent as a general and minister ten times greater than mine,
the late emperor, due to order of age,
thus I preceded him.
After my death,
I hope Your Majesty will entrust the entire state to the Prince of Wú."
In the fifth month,
on the Rénchén day,
Kè became critically ill,
Wěi personally visited him,
asking about later matters.
Kè said:
"I have heard that repaying kindness is no greater than recommending the worthy,
the worthy, even if among builders,
can still be made minister,
meaning the Yīn king Gāozōng raised Fù Yuè from among builders,
and appointed him minister.
The Prince of Wú is endowed with both civil and martial abilities,
second only to Guǎn and Xiāo,
meaning his talent is second to Guǎn Zhòng and Xiāo Hé.
The state can be secure;
if not,
Qín and Jìn will surely have designs to spy and covet."
He finished speaking and died.
When King Fú Jiān of Qín heard of Mùróng Kè's death,
he secretly harbored plans to plot against Yān,
and wanted to assess whether it was feasible.
He ordered Cáo Gǔ of the Xiōngnú to send an envoy to Yān to pay tribute.
Cáo Gǔ
was the Right Virtuous King of the Xiōngnú,
who had surrendered to Qín the previous year.
Cháo (朝) is pronounced zhāo.
Guō Biàn served as his deputy.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn established the Western Róng Colonel at Cháng'ān,
and Qín likely followed this practice;
the Registrar
was one of his subordinates.
Textual Analysis: In the eighth year of Yān's Jiànxī era,
Huángfǔ Zhēn was Grand Commandant.
The Yān History, Basic Annals, and Huángfǔ Zhēn's biography
all place Guō Biàn's arrival in Yān
after Huángfǔ Zhēn became Grand Commandant.
The Jìn Chūnqiū places it in the eighth month of the tenth year of Jiànxī.
I fear both are incorrect,
so I have appended it here under Cáo Gǔ's surrender to Qín.
Tiǎn was a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
Huángfǔ Zhēn,
originally from Āndìng,
served in Yān.
Cóng (從) is pronounced cái yòng fān.
Sàn (散) is pronounced xī dǎn fān.
Jì (騎) is pronounced qí jì fān.
[Guō Biàn] visited the various high ministers in succession,
and said to Huángfǔ Zhēn:
"I was originally a man of Qín,
but my family was executed by Qín,
so I entrusted my life to King Cáo.
Your esteemed elder brother, the Regular Attendant, and the Fèn and Fù brothers have long been acquainted with me."
Huángfǔ Zhēn angrily said:
"A minister should have no friendships beyond the borders.
How can such words involve me!
You seem like a treacherous person.
Could it be that you are making false claims based on some connection?"
He reported this to Mùróng Wěi,
requesting a thorough investigation;
but the Grand Tutor, Mùróng Píng, did not permit it.
When Biàn returned,
he said to Fú Jiān:
"The Yān court administration lacks order and discipline,
and can indeed be plotted against.
The only one who can discern opportunities and recognize changes
is Huángfǔ Zhēn."
Fú Jiān said:
"With the masses of six provinces,
(The six provinces: Yōu, Bìng, Jì, Sī, Yǎn, and Yù.)
Cáo Gǔ soon died.
Qín divided his tribe into two parts,
having his two sons separately command them,
calling them the Eastern and Western Cáo.
Fú Jiān divided Gǔ's tribe:
the more than 20,000 households west of Èrchéng
were placed under the command of Gǔ's eldest son, Xǐ;
the more than 20,000 households east of Èrchéng
were placed under the command of Gǔ's younger son, Yín.
7. Jīng Province Governor Huán Huò and Jìnglíng Administrator Luó Chóng attacked Wǎn,
capturing it;
Zhào Yì fled,
and Zhào Pán retreated to Lǔyáng.
Huò pursued and attacked Pán at Zhìchéng,
capturing him.
Zhì County,
since the Hàn dynasty, has belonged to Nányáng Commandery.
Its location should be within the boundaries of Táng's Dèng Province Xiàngchéng County.
The New Táng History Treatise states: Eighty lǐ north of Xiàngchéng County is the Lǔyáng Pass.
8. In autumn,
the seventh month,
Yān's Xiàpī King Mùróng Lì and others defeated the Chìlè,
capturing tens of thousands of horses and cattle.
Previously,
when Lì's troops passed through Dài territory,
they trampled their millet fields;
King Shǐyìjiān of Dài was angered.
Yān's General Who Pacifies the North, Wǔqiáng Duke Yǐ, garrisoned Yúnzhōng with Yōu Province troops.
In the eighth month,
Shǐyìjiān attacked Yúnzhōng.
Yǐ abandoned the city and fled.
Yǐ (埿)
is the same as ní (泥).
9. In the ninth month,
[Jìn] appointed Kuàijī Administrator Xī Yīn as Commander of the various military affairs of Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, Yōu, and Yáng Provinces and Jìnlíng, and Governor of Xú and Yǎn Provinces,
stationing him at Jīngkǒu.
10. When Qín's Duke of Huáinán, Fú Yòu, rebelled,
General Who Conquers the East, Shepherd of Bìng Province, Duke of Jìn, Fú Liǔ,
and General Who Conquers the West, Governor of Qín Province, Duke of Zhào, Fú Shuāng,
were both involved in the conspiracy.
King Fú Jiān of Qín, because Shuāng
was his full younger brother, his closest kin,
and Liǔ
was Fú Jiàn's beloved son,
concealed the matter and did not inquire into it.
Liǔ and Shuāng again conspired with General Who Guards the East, Governor of Luò Province, Duke of Wèi, Fú Sōu,
and General Who Pacifies the West, Governor of Yōng Province, Duke of Yān, Fú Wǔ, to start a rebellion.
The Registrar of the General Who Guards the East, Yáo Tiào of Nán'ān,
admonished:
"My lord, with the closeness of a Zhōu or Shào,
entrusted with a regional command,
when the state faces difficulty,
you should exert all efforts to eliminate it.
How much more so when you yourselves are creating the difficulty!"
Sōu did not listen.
When Fú Jiān heard of this,
he summoned Liǔ and the others to Cháng'ān.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Liǔ occupied Púbǎn,
Shuāng occupied Shàngguī,
Sōu occupied Shǎnchéng,
and Wǔ occupied Āndìng,
all raising troops in rebellion.
This was exactly as Wáng Měng had predicted.
[Fú Jiān] said: "I have treated you gentlemen
with the utmost kindness.
Why must you rebel!
I now cease the summons.
You should disband your troops,
each settle in your positions,
everything as before."
He had each bite a pear as a pledge.
They all refused to comply.
Pear flesh is crisp and easy to bite into,
metaphorically meaning that when relatives rebel,
the state's strength becomes fragile,
and it will be taken advantage of by enemies.
Therefore, he bit the pear and gave it to the envoy,
bestowing it upon Liǔ and the others as a pledge.
Shǐ (使)
is pronounced shū lì fān.
Niè (齧)
is pronounced yú jié fān.
11. King Shǐyìjiān of Dài attacked Liú Wèichén.
The river ice had not yet frozen solid.
Shǐyìjiān ordered reeds to be tied around floating ice.
Soon the ice solidified.
From Dài, he attacked Shuòfāng,
crossing the great river to the west.
The crossing was called the Jūnzǐ Ford.
Gēng (緪)
is pronounced jū dēng fān.
Then they scattered reeds upon it.
The ice and grass intertwined,
forming something like a floating bridge.
The Dài troops crossed upon it.
Wèichén had not expected troops to arrive so suddenly.
He fled west with his clan.
Shǐyìjiān captured about sixty or seventy percent of his tribe and returned.
Wèichén fled to Qín.
King Fú Jiān of Qín sent Wèichén back to Shuòfāng,
dispatching troops to garrison there.
12. In the twelfth month,
on the jiǎzǐ day,
Yān's Grand Commandant, Duke Jìng of Jiànníng, Yáng Wù, died.
The rules for posthumous names state: Conforming to good laws and regulations is called Jìng;
being vigilant day and night is called Jìng.
Grand Master of Imperial Entertainment Lǐ Hóng became Minister of Works.
1. In spring,
the first month,
King Fú Jiān of Qín dispatched Rear General Yáng Chéngshì and Left General Máo Sōng to separately attack Shàngguī and Āndìng.
Assistant General Wáng Měng and General of the Standard Dèng Qiāng attacked Púbǎn.
Former General Yáng Ān and General of Ferocious Might Zhāng Cì attacked Shǎnchéng.
Fú Jiān ordered the armies at Pú and Shǎn to camp thirty lǐ from the cities,
fortifying their positions and not engaging in battle,
waiting until Qín and Yōng were pacified,
and then combining forces to capture them.
2. Initially,
the Grand Tutor of Yān, Mùróng Kè, was ill.
Considering that the ruler of Yān, Mùróng Wěi, was young and weak,
and political power was not in his own hands,
while the Grand Tutor Mùróng Píng was full of suspicion and jealousy,
he feared that the appointment of the Grand Marshal might not be given to a suitable person.
He said to Mùróng Wěi's elder brother, the Prince of Lè'ān, Mùróng Zāng:
"Now, to the south, there is the remnant Jìn,
and to the west, there is the powerful Qín.
These two states have long harbored ambitions to advance and seize territory,
but they are merely waiting for us to show a weakness.
The rise and fall of a state
depends on its chief ministers.
The Grand Marshal commands the six armies;
it cannot be entrusted to an unsuitable person.
After my death,
in terms of closeness of relation,
it should fall to you and Chōng.
Although both of you are talented, intelligent, and quick-witted,
you are still young
and cannot yet bear the burden of many difficulties.
The Prince of Wú, Mùróng Chuí, is endowed with heroic and outstanding qualities by nature,
and his wisdom and strategies surpass his generation.
If you two can yield the position of Grand Marshal and confer it upon him,
he will certainly be able to unify the four seas.
As for external enemies,
they are not worth fearing.
Be careful not to covet gain and forget harm,
nor to disregard the interests of the state."
"Coveting gain and forgetting harm" means
that the gain lies in obtaining military power,
and coveting the appointment as Grand Marshal,
while forgetting the harm of losing the state and ruining the family.
When Mùróng Kè died,
Mùróng Píng did not follow his advice.
In the second month,
he appointed the General of Chariots and Cavalry, the Prince of Zhōngshān, Mùróng Chōng, as Grand Marshal.
Mùróng Chōng
was Mùróng Wěi's younger brother.
He appointed the Inspector of Jīng Province, the Prince of Wú, Mùróng Chuí, as Palace Attendant, General of Chariots and Cavalry, and granted him the same honors as the Three Excellencies.
This laid the groundwork for the rift between Mùróng Píng and Mùróng Chuí.
(Note on pronunciation: "Chariot" is pronounced qí, with the tone jì.)
(Note on pronunciation: "Cavalry" is pronounced qí, with the tone jì.)
3. The Duke of Wèi of Qín, Fú Sōu, surrendered the city of Shǎnchéng to Yān,
requesting troops to respond and support him.
The people of Qín were greatly alarmed,
and heavily garrisoned troops to defend Huàyīn.
Huàyīn County lies to the west of Shǎnchéng,
possessing the strategic pass of Tóngguān.
(Note on pronunciation: "Surrender" is pronounced xiáng, with the tone hù jiāng.)
(Note on pronunciation: "Surrender" is pronounced xiáng, with the tone hù jiāng.)
(Note on pronunciation: "Huà" is pronounced huà, with the tone hù huà.)
(Note on pronunciation: "Huà" is pronounced huà, with the tone hù huà.)
The Governor of Wèi Commandery of Yān, the Prince of Fànyáng, Mùróng Dé,
(Yān's capital was at Yè,
so the Administrator of Wèi Commandery was titled Governor of Wèi.)
believed:
"Our late emperor responded to Heaven's will and received the Mandate,
with the ambition to pacify the world.
Your Majesty has succeeded to the throne,
and should continue and complete this task.
Now, the Fú clan is torn by internal strife among its own flesh and blood,
and the state is divided into five parts.
(Púbǎn, Shǎnchéng, Shàngguī, Āndìng, and Cháng'ān make five.)
One after another, they seek each other out;
this is Heaven granting Qín to Yān.
If Heaven gives it and you do not take it,
you will instead suffer calamity.
The affairs of Wú and Yuè
are sufficient to illustrate this.
(From the *Guóyǔ*: Fàn Lǐ of Yuè said: 'In the past, Heaven granted Yuè to Wú,
but Wú did not dare to take it.
Now Heaven grants Wú to Yuè;
how dare Yuè oppose Heaven?')
Let the Prince of Wú, Mùróng Chuí, lead the troops of Xǔ and Luò to swiftly relieve the siege on Fú Sōu,
while the Grand Tutor leads the elite troops of the capital as the rear support for the two armies.
Issue proclamations to the Three Adjuncts,
making clear to them the consequences of fortune and misfortune,
and openly set rewards for achievements.
They will certainly respond like grass bending to the wind.
The time for unification
lies right here!"
At that time, many in Yān requested to rescue Shǎnchéng
and thereby seize Guānzhōng.
The Grand Tutor Mùróng Píng said:
"Qín
is a great state.
Although it now faces difficulties,
it is not easy to conquer.
Although our court is enlightened,
it is not like the late emperor.
(The people of Yān refer to their ruler as 'the court.')
Nor am I comparable to the Grand Tutor.
It is enough if we can close the passes and protect our borders.
Pacifying Qín is not our affair."
The Duke of Wèi, Fú Sōu, sent a letter to the Prince of Wú, Mùróng Chuí, and Huángfǔ Zhēn, saying:
"Fú Jiān and Wáng Měng
are both outstanding men of their generation.
They have long plotted to bring disaster upon Yān.
If we do not seize this opportunity to take them now,
I fear that in the future, the ruler and ministers of Yān will have the regret of Yǒngdōng!"
(From the *Zuǒzhuàn*: When Wú invaded Yuè,
the ruler of Yuè took refuge in Kuàijī,
and sent an envoy to sue for peace with Wú,
which the ruler of Wú agreed to.
Wǔ Zǐxū advised against it,
but he was not heeded.
Later, Yuè invaded Wú
and requested that the ruler of Wú reside in Yǒngdōng.
The ruler of Wú said:
'I am old,
and cannot serve Your Majesty.
I regret not heeding Zǐxū's words,
which has brought me to this plight!'
Then he hanged himself.
Jiǎ Kuí said: Yǒngdōng is a remote area of Yuè,
east of the Yǒng River.
East of the Yǒng River.
Sǎoyǐn says: The present Mào County is the location.
(Note on pronunciation: "Yǒng" is pronounced yǒng, with the tone yú lǒng.)
(Note on pronunciation: "Yǒng" is pronounced yǒng, with the tone yú lǒng.)
"At present, those who will bring disaster upon others are certainly in Qín.
Our sovereign is still young,
and judging by the Grand Tutor's insight and judgment,
how can he be a match for Fú Jiān and Wáng Měng?"
Huángfǔ Zhēn said:
"Indeed,
although I know this,
what can I do if my words are not heeded?"
4. In the third month,
on the first day, Dīngsì,
there was a solar eclipse.
5. On the Guǐhài day,
a general amnesty was declared.
6. In Qín, Yáng Chéngshì was defeated by Gǒu Xīng, a general under the Duke of Zhào, Fú Shuāng.
Máo Sōng was also defeated by the Duke of Yān, Fú Wǔ,
and fled back.

The King of Qín, Fú Jiān, again sent the General of the Palace Guard, Wáng Jiàn, the General of Níngshuò, Lǚ Guāng, the General Féngyì Guō Jiāng, and Zhái Nù, among others, to lead thirty thousand troops to attack them.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Fú Shuāng and Fú Wǔ, riding on their victory, advanced to Yúméi,
with Gǒu Xīng as the vanguard.
Wáng Jiàn wished to engage quickly,
but Lǚ Guāng said:
"Gǒu Xīng has just achieved success;
his morale is at its peak.
We should be cautious and wait.
When his provisions run out, he will certainly retreat.
When he retreats, we attack him;
there is no way we will not succeed!"
After twenty days, Gǒu Xīng retreated.
Lǚ Guāng said:
"Gǒu Xīng can be attacked now."
So they pursued him;
Gǒu Xīng was defeated,
and they then attacked Fú Shuāng and Fú Wǔ,
routing them completely.
They beheaded and captured fifteen thousand men.
Fú Wǔ abandoned Āndìng
and fled with Fú Shuāng to Shàngguī.
Wáng Jiàn and others advanced to attack them.
The Duke of Jìn, Fú Liǔ, repeatedly came out to challenge,
but Wáng Měng did not respond.
Fú Liǔ thought Wáng Měng feared him.
In the fifth month,
he left his heir, Fú Liáng, to guard Púbǎn,
and led twenty thousand troops westward toward Cháng'ān.
When he was about a hundred *lǐ* from Púbǎn,
Dèng Qiāng led seven thousand elite cavalry in a night attack
and defeated him.
Fú Liǔ led his army back,
but Wáng Měng intercepted and attacked him,
capturing all his troops.
Fú Liǔ entered the city with several hundred cavalry,
and Wáng Měng and Dèng Qiāng attacked it.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Wáng Jiàn and others captured Shàngguī,
beheaded Fú Shuāng and Fú Wǔ,
but spared their wives and children.
He appointed the General of the Left Guard, Fú Yǎ, as Inspector of Qín Province.
In the eighth month,
he appointed the Duke of Chánglè, Fú Pī, as Inspector of Yōng Province.
In the ninth month,
Wáng Měng and others captured Púbǎn,
beheading the Duke of Jìn, Fú Liǔ, along with his wife and children.
Wáng Měng stationed troops at Púbǎn
and sent Dèng Qiāng to join Wáng Jiàn and others in attacking Shǎnchéng.
7. The princes and nobles of Yān occupied many commoners as dependents,
so that the state's registered households
were fewer than those of private families,
the granaries and treasuries were empty,
and resources were insufficient.
Yuè Wǎn, the Left Executive Assistant to the Minister of Works and Duke of Guǎngxìn, said:
"Now the three powers stand like a tripod,
(the three powers
refer to Yān, Jìn, and Qín).
Yet our state's laws and governance are not established,
the powerful and noble act wantonly and oppressively,
causing the people's households to be exhausted,
with no one to deliver supplies,
officials lacking their regular salaries,
soldiers deprived of rations,
and the government having to lend grain and silk to support itself;
this must not be heard by neighboring enemies,
and moreover, it is not the way to govern.
All dependent households should be abolished,
and they should all be returned to the commanderies and counties."
The ruler of Yān, Mùróng Wěi, followed this advice,
appointing Wǎn to take sole charge of the matter.
He exposed hidden wrongdoings,
and no one dared conceal anything.
Over two hundred thousand households were removed (from private registers),
causing resentment and anger throughout the court.
Wǎn had been ill beforehand,
but he exerted himself to rectify and examine the household registers,
and his illness grew severe.
In winter,
the eleventh month,
he died.
8. In the twelfth month,
the Qín general Wáng Měng and others captured Shǎnchéng,
capturing the Duke of Wèi, Fú Sōu,
and sent him to Cháng'ān.
The Qín ruler Fú Jiān asked him why he rebelled,
and he replied:
"Your subject originally had no rebellious intent,
but because my brothers repeatedly plotted rebellion and disorder,
I feared being implicated and killed,
so I plotted rebellion."
Jiān wept and said:
"You have always been a decent man,
I knew it was not your heart;
moreover, Gāozǔ cannot be without descendants."
(Fú Jiàn's temple name was Gāozǔ).
He pardoned his seven sons,
having the eldest inherit the title of Duke of Wèi,
and enfeoffing the remaining sons as dukes of counties,
to continue the lines of the Prince of Yuè, Lì, and his other brothers who had no heirs.
(Fú Shēng was demoted to Prince of Yuè,
and given the posthumous name Lì).
"Sōu and Shuāng both rebelled,
why is Shuāng alone not allowed to have heirs?"
(Someone asked).
Jiān said:
"The empire
is the empire of Gāozǔ,
Gāozǔ's sons cannot be without descendants.
As for Zhòngqí,
he disregarded the Empress Dowager,
and plotted to endanger the ancestral temple.
(Fú Shuāng,
courtesy name Zhòngqí).
He cannot be treated with partiality!"
He appointed Fú Yì, Duke of Fànyáng, as General-in-Chief Who Conquers the East and Governor of Bìng Province,
to guard Púbǎn;
Dèng Qiāng as General Who Establishes Might and Governor of Luò Province,
to guard Shǎnchéng.
He promoted Yáo Tiào to be Grand Administrator of Jí Commandery.
9. Special honors were conferred upon Grand Marshal Huán Wēn,
placing his rank above that of the feudal princes.
10. That year,
Yáng Shì, Duke of Chóuchí, was appointed Governor of Qín Province,
and his younger brother Yáng Tǒng was appointed Grand Administrator of Wǔdū.
Shì also declared himself a subject of Qín,
and Qín appointed Shì as Governor of Nán Qín Province.
Wáng Chóngwǔ punctuated; Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí reviewed.
Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial order.
Later Student Tiān Tāi
Hǎixī Gōng, Part Two
The fourth year of Tàihé (Jǐsì, 369)
1. In spring,
the third month,

Grand Marshal Huán Wēn requested to launch a campaign against Yān together with Xī Yīn, Governor of Xú and Yǎn Provinces, Huán Chōng, Governor of Jiāng Province, and Yuán Zhēn, Governor of Yù Province, among others.
Initially,
Yīn was in the Northern Administration,
(the Jìn capital was Jiànkāng,
with Jīngkǒu as the Northern Administration,
Lìyáng as the Western Administration,
and Gūshú as the Southern Region).
"Jīngkǒu's wine is drinkable,
its troops are usable."
(The statement that Jīngkǒu's troops were usable
was likely due to the natural advantages of its mountains, rivers, and climate,
surely it was not only after Xiè Xuán used them that the enemy came to fear them!)
But Yīn was oblivious to the situation,
and sent a letter to Wēn,
wishing to jointly support the royal house,
and requesting to lead his own troops to the north of the Huáng Hé.
Yīn's son, Xī Chāo, was Wēn's Army Advisor.
He took the letter, looked at it,
and tore it to pieces;
then he forged another letter in Yīn's name,
stating that he himself was not a talented commander,
unfit for military affairs,
old and ill,
and begging for a quiet post to support himself,
urging Wēn to concurrently take command of his troops.
Wēn was greatly pleased upon receiving the letter,
and immediately transferred Yīn to be General of the Guards and Imperial Secretary of Kuàijī.
Wēn himself took on the positions of Governor of Xú and Yǎn Provinces.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Gēngxū day,
Wēn led fifty thousand infantry and cavalry from Gūshú.
2. On the Jiǎzǐ day,
the Yān ruler Mùróng Wěi established Empress Kězúhún,
the daughter of his maternal uncle, the Minister of Works and Duke of Yùzhāng, Kězúhún Yì.
3. Grand Marshal Wēn launched an expedition against Yān from Yǎnzhōu.
Xī Chāo said:
"The route is long,
and the Biàn River is shallow.
In the aftermath of military turmoil,
the Biàn River has silted up,
and no one has ever dredged it,
hence it is shallow.
Biàn,
pronounced with the initial 'p' and the rhyme 'iàn'.
Wēn did not heed this.
In the sixth month,
on the Xīnchǒu day,
Wēn reached Jīnxiāng.
Jīnxiāng County,
belonged to Shānyáng Commandery in the Later Hàn,
to Gāopíng Commandery in the Jìn,
to Jìyīn Commandery in the Suí,
to Yǎnzhōu in the Táng,
and to Jìzhōu in our Sòng dynasty,
the county is located ninety lǐ southeast of the prefecture.
The waterway was cut off,
so Wēn ordered Champion General Máo Hǔshēng to dig a three-hundred-lǐ canal through Jùyě,
diverting the Wèn River to join the Qīng River.
According to Bān Gù's "Treatise on Geography,"
the Wèn River originates southwest of Láiwú County in Tàishān,
and flows into the Jì River.
The "Commentary on the Water Classic" states: The Jì River flows northeast into Jùyě,
and its old course further northeast joins the Hóng River on the right;
the Hóng River originates from Xuēxùnzhǔ in Jùyě,
called Huán Gōng's Channel,
from here the Jì River flows north.
Dù Yòu said: The Jì River,
because the channel dried up at the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign and no longer crossed the Yellow River,
now within the boundaries of Dōngpíng, Jǐnán, Zīchuān, and Běihǎi, there is a river flowing into the sea,
called the Qīng River,
which is actually the combined flow of the Hé Marsh and the Wèn River,
also called the Jì River,
likely retaining the old name,
but it is not the original Jì River.
Wèn,
pronounced 'wèn'.
He was the son of Bǎo.
Máo Bǎo had contributed to the suppression of Sū Jùn.
The commentary is also seen earlier.
Boats stretched for several hundred lǐ.
Xī Chāo said:
"The Qīng River enters the Yellow River,
making transportation difficult.
From the Qīng River into the Yellow River,
it is all against the current,
and the route is circuitous and long,
hence it is said to be difficult for transportation.
The supply route is again cut off,
relying on the enemy for provisions,
yet nothing can be obtained,
this is a perilous path.
It would be better to mobilize all available troops and head straight for Yèchéng.
They fear your prestige and reputation,
and will surely flee in panic at the news,
retreating north to Liáo and Jié.
If they dare to come out and fight,
then the matter can be decided in one battle.
If they wish to fortify Yè and defend it,
then in the midst of this hot summer,
it will be difficult for them to accomplish much,
with the common people scattered in the fields,
all becoming government property,
the area south of the Yì River will surely come with arms bound to beg for orders.
But I fear that you, wise sir, consider this plan too rash and risky,
with victory or defeat uncertain,
and if you wish to prioritize caution,
then nothing is better than stationing troops at the Yellow River and Jì River,
controlling and utilizing water transport,
waiting until supplies and reserves are fully prepared,
and then advancing next summer;
although this seems slow and delayed,
shē,
means distant.
To abandon these two strategies and lead the army northward,
advancing without swift resolution,
retreat will surely lead to error and shortage.
Qiān,
means error or discrepancy.
Fá,
means exhaustion or depletion.
This refers to grain transport.
As it gradually approaches autumn and winter,
the water will become even more sluggish and obstructed.
Moreover, the northern regions turn cold early,
and few among the three armies have fur or coarse garments,
I fear that by then the worries will not be limited to just lack of food."
Wēn again did not heed.
Xī Chāo's strategic planning,
how could it be matched by ordinary people?
No wonder Huán Wēn valued him.
He valued him but did not follow his plan because,
heading straight for Yèchéng,
deciding victory or defeat in one battle,
was something Wēn did not dare;
stationing troops at the Yellow River and Jì River to wait until the next year,
allowing Yān to prepare,
was also something Wēn would not do.
Wēn sent Jianwei General Tán Xuán to attack Húlù,
and captured it.
Húlù County,
in the Former Hàn was called Húlíng,
belonging to Shānyáng Commandery,
Emperor Zhāng changed the name to Húlù;
in the Jìn it was divided and belonged to Gāopíng Commandery.
Xián said: The old city of Húlù is southeast of present-day Fāngyǔ County in Yǎnzhōu.
The Yān ruler Wěi appointed Xiàpī King Lì as Grand Governor of Expeditionary Operations,
leading twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to engage in battle at Huángxū.
The "Commentary on the Water Classic" states: Xiǎohuáng County in Chénliú has a Huáng Township.
Dù Yù said: East of Wàihuáng County is Huángchéng,
after military turmoil,
the city became mounds and ruins,
hence called Huángxū.
Shuài,
read as 'lǜ'.
Qí,
pronounced with the initial 'q' and the rhyme 'í'.
He fled back alone on horseback.
Gāopíng Grand Administrator Xú Fān surrendered the entire commandery.
The vanguard Dèng Xiá and Zhū Xù defeated the Yān general Fù Yán at Línzhǔ.
The "Commentary on the Water Classic" states: The Huá River flows east past the north of Fěichéng,
which is Běilín Pavilion.
In the Spring and Autumn period, the feudal lords met at Fěilín to rescue Zhèng,
and encountered at Běilín.
According to this, the old city of Línxiāng is north of Xīnzhèng;
there is also Báiyànbēi,
northeast of Chángshè,
and southwest of Línxiāng.
Bài,
pronounced with the initial 'b' and the rhyme 'ài'.
Zāng could not resist,
so he sent Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Lǐ Fèng to seek help from Qín.
Sàn,
pronounced with the initial 's' and the rhyme 'àn'.
Qí,
pronounced with the initial 'q' and the rhyme 'í'.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Wēn stationed at Wǔyáng.
This is Dōngwǔyáng,
belonging to Dōng Commandery in the Hàn,
to Yángpíng Commandery in the Wèi and Jìn,
in the Táng renamed Cháochéng County, belonging to Wèizhōu.
Wēn reached Fāngtóu.
Wěi and Grand Tutor Píng were greatly frightened,
and planned to flee to Hélóng.
King of Wú Chuí said:
"I request to attack them;
if we are not victorious,
it will not be too late to flee."
Wěi then appointed Chuí to replace Lè'ān King Zāng as Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Grand Governor of Southern Campaigns,
leading General of Conquering the South Fànyáng King Dé and others with fifty thousand troops to resist Wēn.
Chuí memorialized that Left Chief Clerk of the Minister of Education Shēn Yìn, Gentleman of the Yellow Gate Fēng Fú, and Court Gentleman Xìluó Téng all joined the army.
Xìluó Téng,
was likely a foreigner,
taking his tribe as his surname,
as recorded in the "Treatise on Officials and Clans" of the Wèi History,
such as the Chìluó and Rúluó clans among the various surnames that entered during the Shényuán period.
He was the son of Zhōng;
Fú,
was the son of Fàng.
Shēn Zhōng appears in scroll 95, the ninth year of Xiánhé of Emperor Chéng.
Fēng Fàng appears in scroll 99, the seventh year of Yǒnghé of Emperor Mù.
Mùróng Wěi again dispatched the Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary Lè Sōng to request rescue from Qín,
promising to cede the territory west of Hǔláo as a bribe.
The Qín king Fú Jiāng summoned his ministers to deliberate in the Eastern Hall.
They all said:
"In the past, Huán Wēn attacked us,
reaching Bàshàng.
See the tenth year of the Yǒnghé era in the 99th volume.
Now Wēn attacks Yān;
why should we rescue them?
Moreover, Yān does not acknowledge us as their suzerain;
why should we rescue them!"
Wáng Měng secretly advised Jiāng, saying:
"Although Yān is powerful,
Mùróng Píng is no match for Wēn.
If Wēn conquers the lands east of the mountains,
advances and stations troops at Luòyì,
gathers the soldiers of Yōu and Jì,
draws upon the grain supplies of Bìng and Yù,
and displays his military might at Xiáo and Miǎn,
then Your Majesty's great enterprise will be lost.
Now it would be better to join forces with Yān to repel Wēn.
Once Wēn retreats,
Yān will also be weakened.
Then we can take advantage of their exhaustion to seize them.
Would that not be excellent?"
Wáng Měng's strategy for capturing Lǐ Yǎn
also originated from this.
In the eighth month,
they dispatched General Xún Chí and the Governor of Luò Prefecture, Dèng Qiāng, leading twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to rescue Yān.
They set out from Luòyáng,
and the army reached Yǐngchuān.
Yǐngchuān Commandery
had its seat at Xǔchāng.
Wáng Měng was appointed as the Imperial Secretary.
The Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent, Fēng Fú, asked Shēn Yìn:
"Wēn's forces are strong and his troops disciplined;
he advances directly along the river.
Now our great army merely lingers on the high banks,
with weapons not yet crossing,
and I see no principle for achieving victory and annihilation.
How will matters turn out?"
Yìn replied:
"Judging by Wēn's present momentum,
it seems he could accomplish something.
However, in my view,
he will certainly not succeed.
Why is that?
The Jìn court is weak and declining.
Wēn monopolizes power in his state,
and the court officials of Jìn do not necessarily all share his heart.
Therefore, Wēn's success
is not what the multitude desires.
They are sure to create discord and obstruction to ruin his affairs.
'Guāi' means
'different.'
'Zǔ' means
'to block.'
'Bài' is pronounced
'bǔ mài fān.'
Wēn is arrogant and relies on his numbers,
yet timid in adapting to changing circumstances.
With a large force penetrating deep,
encountering an opportune moment to exploit,
he instead idles in the midstream,
not advancing to seize advantage,
hoping to prolong the situation,
sitting back to achieve complete victory.
Wēn's strategy is precisely like this;
Shēn Yìn assessed him accurately.
Once his true situation is revealed and his momentum exhausted,
he will certainly be defeated without fighting,
such is the natural course of events."
Wēn attacked Qín but did not cross the Bà River;
he attacked Yān but hesitated at Fāngtóu.
Everyone blamed him for not advancing.
Knowing both the enemy and oneself,
Wēn perhaps only realized this when facing the enemy.
Although Wēn's wisdom was insufficient to suppress violence and secure achievements,
he was still far superior to the common multitude.
'Qiān'
refers to the failure of grain transport to arrive on schedule.
'Xuán'
means 'cut off.'
'Xiàn' is pronounced
'xián biàn fān.'
Wēn used the Yān defector Duàn Sī as a guide.
Xīluó Téng engaged Wēn in battle
and captured Sī alive.
Wēn sent the former Zhào general Lǐ Shù to raid Zhào and Wèi.
Téng, together with the Leader of the Palace Guard, Rǎngān Jīn, attacked and killed him.
Rǎngān
is also a foreign surname,
like Xīluó.
Initially,
Wēn ordered the Governor of Yù Prefecture, Yuán Zhēn, to attack Qiáo and Liáng,
and to open the Shímén to facilitate water transport.
Zhēn captured Qiáo and Liáng but could not open Shímén.
Qiáo and Liáng refer to
Qiáo Commandery and the State of Liáng.
In the ninth month,
the Yān Prince of Fànyáng, Mùróng Dé, led ten thousand cavalry, and the Palace Censor Liú Dāng led five thousand cavalry to station at Shímén.
The Governor of Yù Prefecture, Lǐ Guī, led five thousand provincial troops to cut off Wēn's grain supply route.
The Yān Governor of Yù Prefecture administered from Xǔchāng.
'Duàn' is pronounced
'dīng guǎn fān.'
He was the son of Liú Pèi.
Liú Pèi was a general under Mùróng Huàng,
repelled Shí Hǔ,
attacked Yǔwén,
and achieved merit in all.
When they encountered the Jìn troops,
Mùróng Zhòu said:
"The Jìn men are swift and impetuous,
timid in engaging the enemy,
but bold in pursuing retreating forces.
We should set bait to lure them."
He then sent two hundred cavalry to provoke battle,
dividing the remaining cavalry into three ambushes.
The challengers fled before engaging.
The Jìn troops pursued them,
and Zhòu led the ambushers to attack.
The Jìn troops suffered heavy casualties.
Wēn suffered several defeats in battle,
his grain reserves were again exhausted,
and he heard that the Qín troops were about to arrive.
On the bǐngshēn day,
he burned his boats,
abandoned the baggage, armor, and weapons,
and fled back by land.
He appointed Máo Hǔshēng to oversee the military affairs of Dōngyàn and three other commanderies,
concurrently serving as the Grand Administrator of Dōngyàn.
Shěn Yuē said: Dōngyàn Commandery
was established by Jìn from part of Púyáng.
I note that Shí Hǔ assigned Dōngyàn Commandery to Luò Prefecture,
so this commandery was likely established when Zǔ Tì was in Yù Prefecture.
'Yàn' is pronounced
'yú xián fān.'
Wēn traveled from Dōngyàn to Cāngyuán,
digging wells to drink,
as the Biàn River and Jì waterway both flow from north to south.
Fearing the pursuing troops might poison the upstream water,
he dug wells to drink.
The various Yān generals vied to pursue him.
The Prince of Wú, Mùróng Chuí, said:
"No.
In his initial retreat, Wēn is alarmed and fearful,
and will certainly set up strict precautions,
selecting elite troops as a rear guard.
Attacking him may not achieve our aim.
It is better to delay.
He, fortunate that we have not arrived,
will certainly march day and night at full speed.
Wait until his troops are exhausted and their morale low,
then attack him.
There will be nothing we cannot overcome."
He then led eight thousand cavalry, following slowly behind.
Wēn indeed advanced by forced marches.
After several days,
Chuí told his generals:
"Wēn can be attacked now."
They then pursued urgently
and caught up with Wēn at Xiāngyì.
Xiāngyì County
had belonged to Chénliú Commandery since Hàn times.
They attacked Wēn together with Chuí,
inflicting a major defeat,
beheading thirty thousand.
Qín's Xún Chí intercepted and attacked Wēn at Qiáo,
again defeating him,
with casualties again numbering in the tens of thousands.
Sūn Yuánsuì occupied Wǔyáng to resist Yān.
The Yān General of the Left Guard, Mèng Gāo, campaigned against and captured him.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Jǐsì,
Grand Marshal Wēn gathered his scattered troops
and stationed them at Shānyáng.
Liú Xù said: Shānyáng
was the territory of Shèyáng County in the Hàn dynasty;
the Jìn dynasty established Shānyáng Commandery,
which was changed to Shānyáng County,
and in the Táng dynasty it became the seat of Chǔ Prefecture.
He then blamed Yuán Zhēn for the defeat,
citing the failure to open the Shímén pass and the interruption of grain transport as Zhēn’s crimes.
He also dismissed Champion General Dèng Xiá from his post.
Zhēn, believing that Wēn had falsely accused him,
refused to accept this,
and submitted a memorial detailing Wēn’s crimes;
the court did not respond.
Zhēn then occupied Shòuchūn and rebelled, surrendering to Yān,
and also requested aid;
he also sent envoys to Qín.
Wēn appointed Máo Hǔshēng as the acting Governor of Huáinán,
to guard Lìyáng.
The Governor of Huáinán was originally stationed at Shòuchūn,
but since Shòuchūn had rebelled,
Hǔshēng was appointed to govern Huáinán and guard Lìyáng.
Lìyáng was originally a county under Huáinán,
and with Hǔshēng guarding it,
it served externally to defend against Shòuchūn,
and internally to protect Jiāngnán.
4 Since Yān and Qín had established friendly relations,
envoys frequently traveled between them.
The Yān Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary
Hǎo Guǐ and the Palace Attendant Huángmén Shìláng Liáng Chēn successively went to Qín.
Guǐ was previously acquainted with Wáng Měng,
and Měng received him with the courtesy of an old friend,
inquiring about affairs in the east.
Guǐ, seeing that Yān’s governance was in disarray while Qín was well-ordered,
secretly wished to align himself with Měng,
and revealed much of the truth.
When Chēn arrived at Cháng’ān,
the Qín King Jiān was hunting at Wànnián.
Wànnián,
formerly Lìyáng of Qín,
was renamed by Emperor Gāo of Hàn,
belonging to Féngyì Commandery,
and in the Jìn dynasty, it was under Jīngzhào.
Chēn said:
"When Qín envoys come to Yān,
the ruler and ministers of Yān dress in court attire and prepare the proper rituals,
sweep and clean the palace courtyards,
and only then dare to receive them.
Now the Qín king wishes to meet me in the wilds;
this envoy dares not accept such a command!"
The Qín Secretary Láng Xīn Jìn said to Chēn:
"When a guest enters another’s territory,
it is up to the host to decide how to receive him;
how can you, sir, dictate the rituals!
Moreover, the Son of Heaven is called the imperial carriage,
and wherever he goes is called the temporary residence;
how can there be a fixed dwelling!
Furthermore,
the Spring and Autumn Annals also record the ritual of an unplanned meeting,
as in the Spring and Autumn Annals: In the fourth year of Duke Yǐn,
the Duke and the Duke of Sòng met at Qīng.
The Gōngyáng Commentary says: What is a meeting?
It is an unplanned encounter.
Dù Yù said: A meeting is
a hastily arranged appointment,
where both states simplify their rituals,
as if meeting by chance on the road.
Chēn said:
"The Jìn dynasty lost its guiding principles,
and the divine mandate shifted to those with virtue.
The divine mandate,
is akin to what Bān Biāo in his 'Wáng Mìng Lùn' called the mandate of the spirits.
Both received the clear mandate.
Yet Huán Wēn acted recklessly,
encroaching upon our royal domain.
The Zuǒzhuàn says: 'Invading and damaging the royal domain.'
Dù Yù’s commentary states: Domain,
refers to the laws and institutions of governance.
I believe this 'domain'
refers to territorial boundaries,
as in the Zuǒzhuàn
'the king gave him the domain of Wǔgōng'
meaning domain.
Given the circumstances, we could not stand alone,
so the ruler of Qín shared our concern for the troubles of the time,
and sought to establish friendly alliances.
The ruler and ministers of the eastern court,
gazing westward with necks outstretched,
ashamed of their own weakness,
viewed their neighbor’s troubles with concern.
'Weakness'
means lack of strength.
'Court,'
pronounced zhāo;
