the same below.
They treated you with increased respect.
Now that the powerful enemy has retreated,
and diplomatic exchanges have just begun,
it is proper to uphold rituals and deepen righteousness to solidify the friendship between our two states;
if you neglect and slight the envoy,
you belittle Yān.
Is this the way to cultivate good relations!
The Son of Heaven regards all within the four seas as his home,
hence when traveling he is called the imperial carriage,
and when stationary, the temporary residence.
Now the realm is divided,
as Zōu Yǎn said: Within China there is the Divine Land of the Red County,
and within the Divine Land of the Red County there are nine provinces,
which are the nine provinces ordered by Yǔ;
beyond them are lesser seas encircling them.
The term 'realm within the seas'
likely originates from this.
How can one speak of the imperial carriage and temporary residence now!
According to ritual,
an unplanned meeting is called an encounter;
it is conducted out of necessity and expediency,
with simplified rituals.
How can it be compared to the leisurely rituals of ordinary times!
An envoy traveling alone
may indeed be at a disadvantage before the host;
but if rituals are not observed,
I dare not comply."
Jiān then set up a temporary palace for him,
with all officials in attendance,
and only then received the guest,
following the rituals of a Yān court audience.
After the audience,
Jiān held a private banquet for him,
imitating the ancient ritual of a private audience.
He asked, "Who are the famous ministers of the eastern court?"
Chēn replied:
"The Grand Tutor, Prince of Shàngyōng, Píng,
virtuous and closely related by kinship,
brilliantly assists the royal house;
the General of Chariots and Cavalry, Prince of Wú, Chuí,
whose heroic strategies are unmatched in the world,
repels enemies and defends against insults;
the others have advanced either through civil service
or military merit,
all are competent in their posts,
and there are no talents left unused in the countryside."
Chēn’s cousin Yì served as a Secretary Láng in Qín,
and Jiān had him act as the Reception Official,
lodging Chēn at Yì’s residence.
The Hàn dynasty had the office of Reception Official,
later changed to Grand Herald.
Here, he was temporarily appointed as the Reception Official.
'Lodge,'
pronounced guàn;
the same below for 'fruit lodge.'
Chēn said: "In the past, when Zhūgě Jǐn was sent by Wú to Shǔ,
he only met Zhūgě Liàng in official court settings,
and never privately,
even though Jǐn and Liàng were brothers.
'For,'
pronounced wèi.
Now, to have me lodge in a private residence,
I dare not accept."
Thus, he did not end up lodging there.
Yì came several times to the guesthouse,
staying and resting with Chēn,
occasionally asking about affairs in the eastern state.
Chēn said:
"Now our two states are divided and rule separately,
and we brothers both enjoy honor and favor,
but in our hearts,
our loyalties lie with our respective states.
If I were to speak of the virtues of the eastern state,
it might not be what the western state wishes to hear;
Yān is east of the pass,
Qín is west of the pass,
thus divided,
so Yān is called the eastern state,
and Qín the western state.
Moreover, it is not for an envoy to discuss such matters.
Why, brother, do you ask!"
Jiān had the Crown Prince meet Chēn.
The Qín officials wanted Chēn to bow to the Crown Prince,
and first hinted to him:
"The ruler of a neighboring state
is like one’s own ruler;
how is the heir of a neighboring state
any different!"
Chēn said:
"The son of the Son of Heaven is treated as a Yuánshì (lowest rank of nobility),
to allow him to rise from humble to noble.
The Book of Rites, 'Jiāo Tè Shēng,' says: The eldest son of the Son of Heaven
is a Shì (gentleman),
for no one in the world is born noble.
How much more so for a minister of another state!
If there is no pure reverence,
then rituals involve mutual exchange;
how could I forget to be respectful,
but I fear that lowering myself would be troublesome."
Meaning he should return the bow.
Wáng Měng advised Fú Jiān to detain Liú Chēn,
but Jiān did not agree.

5. The ruler of Yān, Mùróng Wěi, sent the Grand Herald Wēn Tǒng to appoint Yuán Zhēn as Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs in Huáinán, General-in-Chief Who Conquers the South, and Governor of Yángzhōu,
and enfeoffed him as Duke of Xuānchéng.
Tǒng died before crossing the Huái River.
6. The Prince of Wú, Mùróng Chuí, returned to Yè from Xiāngyì,
and his prestige and fame grew even greater,
causing the Grand Tutor Mùróng Píng to become increasingly jealous of him.
Chuí submitted a memorial
stating, "The officers and soldiers I recruited have forgotten themselves and achieved merit;
General Sūn Gài and others charged at the enemy's vanguard and broke their formations,
achieving merit."
(End of sentence.)
"Charged,"
meaning to strike,
directly striking the enemy's vanguard.
Píng suppressed all of this and did not act upon it.
Chuí repeatedly spoke about it,
and argued with Píng at court,
causing their resentment and rift to deepen.
The Empress Dowager Kězúhún shì had always disliked Chuí,
as seen in the events of the first year of Shēngpíng of Emperor Mù (Volume 100).
"Disliked,"
pronounced wù lù fān.
She conspired with Píng to kill him.
Mùróng Kǎi, the son of the Grand Steward Mùróng Kè, and Chuí's maternal uncle Lán Jiàn learned of this
and informed Chuí, saying:
"Strike first to gain the upper hand.
The Art of War says: 'Strike first to gain the upper hand,
those who strike later are controlled by others.'
After that, there is nothing they can do."
Chuí said:
"For flesh and blood to harm each other and be the first to cause chaos in the state—
I would rather die
than do such a thing."
Shortly after,
the two informed him again,
saying:
"The inner court's decision has been made."
"Inner court's decision"
refers to the intention of Empress Dowager Kězúhún.
Chuí said:
"If it is truly irreconcilable,
I would rather avoid it by leaving the court.
There is nothing else to discuss."
Chuí was inwardly worried
but did not dare to tell his sons.
His eldest son, Lìng, asked him:
"Father, lately you seem to have a worried expression.
(Lìng addressed his father as 'Father.')
'Lately,'
pronounced pí zhì fān.
Is it because the Grand Tutor envies the worthy,
and your achievements are high and your reputation great,
making you increasingly suspected and resented?"
Chuí said:
"Yes.
I exhausted my strength and risked my life to defeat a powerful enemy,
originally intending to preserve the family and the state.
Who would have thought that after achieving success,
I would instead find myself with nowhere to turn?
Since you understand my heart,
what plan do you have for me?"
Lìng said:
"The ruler is weak and dim-witted,
entrusting everything to the Grand Tutor.
Once disaster strikes,
it will be swifter than a triggered crossbow.
'Trigger,'
refers to the crossbow's mechanism.
It is like drawing a crossbow;
unexpectedly, the mechanism fires first,
startling people,
hence 'triggered crossbow.'
Without abandoning great righteousness,
the best course is to flee to Lóngchéng,
humbly apologize and admit fault,
and wait for the ruler to understand.
Like the Duke of Zhōu residing in the east,
perhaps he will be moved to realization and allow your return.
This would be the greatest fortune.
The Book of Documents states: King Wǔ fell ill,
and the Duke of Zhōu offered prayers to Tài Wáng, Wáng Jì, and King Wén,
requesting to take the king's place.
After King Wǔ passed away,
Guǎn Shū and his younger brothers spread rumors, saying:
'The Duke will harm the young king.'
The Duke of Zhōu campaigned eastward against them.
The Duke of Zhōu resided in the east for two years,
and the guilty were captured.
He then composed a poem to present to the king,
titled 'Chī Xiāo.'
The king still did not dare to blame the Duke.
Heaven sent great thunder, lightning, and wind.
The king opened the metal-bound coffer,
found the Duke of Zhōu's prayer to take King Wǔ's place,
and, holding the document, wept,
welcoming the Duke of Zhōu back.
'Perhaps,'
pronounced jū xī fān.
Then, pacify Yān and Dài internally,
and win over the various barbarian tribes externally.
Guard the strategic pass of Féirú to protect yourself—
this would be the next best option."
The strategic pass of Féirú
is the Lúlóng Pass.
"Excellent!"
In the eleventh month,
on the first day, Xīnhài,
Chuí requested to go hunting at Dàlù.
The Continued Records of the Hàn states: Jùlù,
formerly Dàlù,
had the Dàlù Marsh,
also known as the Guǎng'ē Marsh.
He intended to head to Lóngchéng.
Upon reaching Hándān,
his youngest son, Lín,
whom Chuí had never favored,
fled back to report the situation.
Many of Chuí's attendants deserted and rebelled.
The Grand Tutor Píng informed the ruler of Yān, Mùróng Wěi,
who sent the Duke of Xīpíng, Mùróng Qiáng, to lead elite cavalry in pursuit.
They caught up at Fànyáng.
The eldest son, Lìng, covered the rear,
and Qiáng did not dare to press the attack.
As dusk fell,
Lìng said to Chuí:
"Originally, we intended to protect the Eastern Capital to ensure our safety.
Since Yān had its capital at Yè,
Lóngchéng was called the Eastern Capital.
But our plans have not been properly arranged.
The ruler of Qín is currently recruiting heroes and talented individuals.
It would be better to go and submit to him."
Chuí said:
"Given today's circumstances,
where else can we go but this?"
They then dispersed their cavalry and erased their tracks,
skirting the southern mountains to return to Yè,
and hid at the Xiǎnyuán Mausoleum of Zhào.
The Xiǎnyuán Mausoleum
was the empty burial site of Shí Hǔ, the ruler of Zhào.
To resist was impossible,
to flee offered no path,
and they did not know what to do.
Just then, the hawks of the hunters all flew away,
and the pursuing cavalry dispersed.
Chuí then killed a white horse to sacrifice to Heaven
and swore an oath with his followers.
The eldest son, Lìng, said to Chuí:
"The Grand Tutor envies the worthy and resents the capable.
Since he began plotting against you,
people have become increasingly resentful.
(Referring to the plot to kill Chuí.)
No one knows your whereabouts,
and they long for you like an infant longing for its mother.
Both barbarians and Chinese feel the same.
If we follow the people's hearts,
attack while they are unprepared,
seizing power will be as easy as pointing at one's palm.
After the matter is settled,
reform the abuses, select the capable,
greatly rectify the court's governance,
assist the ruler,
bring peace to the state and preserve the family—
this would be the greatest achievement.
The opportunity today
truly must not be missed.
I ask for a few cavalrymen—
that will be enough to accomplish it."
Chuí said:
"If we follow your plan,
success would indeed bring great fortune,
but if we fail, how could we ever regret it enough?
It is better to flee west—
that would ensure absolute safety."
His son Mǎnú secretly planned to flee back,
so Chuí killed him and continued on.
Upon reaching Héyáng,
they were detained by the ferry official,
so they killed him and crossed the river.

From Luòyáng, they fled to Qín together with Lady Duàn, the eldest son Lìng, Lìng's younger brothers Bǎo, Nóng, and Lóng, his elder brother's son Kǎi, his maternal uncle Lán Jiàn, and the Gentleman of the Palace Guard Gāo Bì,
leaving Kězúhún shì in Yè.
Lady Duàn
was Chuí's former younger sister.
Kězúhún
was the younger sister of Empress Dowager Kězúhún,
as detailed in the second year of Shēngpíng of Emperor Mù (Volume 100).
Gāo Bì
was a minister of Chuí's state.
The Yìquán Garrison,
also known as the Yìquán Fortress defended by Wèi Gāi,
was located southwest of Yíyáng County,
on the northern plateau of the Luò River.
Wénxiāng was in Hú County, Hóngnóng.
"Wén,"
pronounced mín.
Initially,
when King Fú Jiān of Qín heard of Grand Tutor Mùróng Kè's death,
he secretly harbored ambitions to plot against Yān,
but feared Mùróng Chuí's formidable reputation,
and dared not act.
Upon hearing of Chuí's arrival,
he was overjoyed,
went out to the suburbs to welcome him,
took his hand and said:
"When Heaven produces worthy and outstanding men,
they must join together to achieve great deeds;
this is the natural order of things.
I shall certainly join with you, my lord, to pacify the realm,
announce our success at Mount Tài,
and then return you to your native state,
enfeoffing you as hereditary lord of Yōuzhōu,
so that your departure from your state does not forfeit a son's filial duty,
and your return to me does not lose a subject's loyalty to his sovereign.
Would this not be splendid!"
Chuí thanked him, saying:
"A minister in exile,
to escape punishment is fortune enough;
the glory of my native state
is something I dare not hope for!"
Jiān also admired the talents of the heir, Lìng, and of Mùróng Kǎi,
treating them both with great courtesy,
bestowing lavish rewards worth tens of thousands,
and whenever they came for audience,
he would gaze upon them intently.
The officials and commoners of Guānzhōng had long heard of the fame of Chuí and his sons,
and all looked up to and admired them.
Wáng Měng said to Jiān:
"Mùróng Chuí and his sons
are like dragons and tigers,
creatures that cannot be tamed.
To tame
means to subdue,
to follow,
to obey.
To rear fierce beasts,
making them docile, familiar, and obedient to human will is called taming.
Tame,
pronounced in detail as xún.
Once they are grown, they cannot be controlled again;
it would be better to eliminate them early."
Jiān said:
"I am just gathering heroes to pacify the realm;
why should I kill them!
Moreover, when they first came,
I already received them with sincere trust;
even a common man does not go back on his word,
how much less a sovereign of ten thousand chariots!"
He then appointed Chuí as Champion General,
enfeoffed him as Marquis of Bīntú,
and appointed Kǎi as Crossbow General.
Mùróng Dé, Prince of Fànyáng, who served as Governor of Wèi Commandery in Yān, had always been on good terms with Chuí,
and along with Chariot and Horse Attendant Gentleman Gāo Tài,
both were implicated and dismissed from office.
When Chuí was Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry in Yān,
he appointed Tài as Attendant Gentleman.
"Now that Prince Wú has fled,
rumors are rampant abroad,
as Yán Shīgǔ said: 'Rampant'
means numerous and disorderly.
This can roughly dispel slander."
Mùróng Píng said:
"Who is suitable?"
Shào said:
"Gāo Tài is the leading candidate."
He then appointed Tài as Gentleman of the Masters of Writing.
Tài
was a nephew of Gāo Zhān;
Gāo Zhān appears in the 91st scroll, second year of Yuándì's Tàixīng reign.
Nephew,
pronounced cóng, with the meaning of usefulness.
He was the son
of Yìn.
Qín detained Liáng Chēn for over a month,
then sent him back.
Chēn traveled day and night to return,
where a day's journey
refers to the distance between postal stations.
It means a traveler covers two stations in one day's journey;
if one covers four stations in a day's journey,
that is traveling day and night.
Prince Wú, Chuí, had already fled to Qín.
Chēn said to Grand Tutor Píng:
"The people of Qín daily review their troops,
and are gathering much grain east of Shǎn;
from my observation,
the peace cannot last long.
Now Prince Wú has also gone and submitted to them,
Qín surely has designs to spy on Yān;
we should prepare early."
Píng said:
"Would Qín accept a traitorous minister and ruin the good relations between our states!"
Chēn said:
"Now our two states divide and occupy the Central Plains,
and each has always harbored ambitions to swallow the other;
when Huán Wēn invaded,
they came to our aid by stratagem,
not out of love for Yān;
if Yān shows a crack,
how could they forget their original ambition!"
The schemes of Fú Jiān and Wáng Měng
were indeed already discerned by Liáng Chēn.
"What kind of man is the ruler of Qín?"
Chēn said:
"Perceptive and decisive."
Asked about Wáng Měng,
he said:
"His reputation is not undeserved."
Píng did not agree with any of this.
Chēn also reported this to the ruler of Yān, Mùróng Wěi,
but Wěi also did not believe it.
He reported it to Huángfǔ Zhēn,
who was deeply concerned,
and submitted a memorial stating:
"Although Fú Jiān frequently sends envoys with inquiries,
in truth he has designs to spy on our superior state;
he is not one who admires and delights in virtue and righteousness,
nor does he remember long-standing agreements.
Previously, when he sent troops to the Luò River area,
referring to when Xún Chí and Dèng Qiāng came to Yān's aid.
The perilousness, ease, strengths, and weaknesses of our state,
he has learned them all.
Now Prince Wú, Chuí, has also gone to join him,
becoming his chief strategist;
the disaster of Wǔ Yuán
cannot be left unprepared for.
Wǔ Yuán left Chǔ and fled to Wú,
borrowing Wú's troops to attack Chǔ and enter Yǐng,
as recorded in the Zuǒzhuàn.
Yuán,
pronounced yún.
We should all select generals and increase troops,
to guard against what has not yet occurred."
The subsequent route of Qín's campaign against Yān
indeed turned out as Zhēn had predicted.
Dù Yòu said: Lùzhōu's Shàngdǎng County,
was Húguān County in Hàn times.
Píng said:
"The state of Qín is small and weak in strength,
and relies on us for support;
moreover, Fú Jiān perhaps follows the good way,
meaning although Fú Jiān may not purely use the good way in dealing with neighbors,
he perhaps approximates it.
Perhaps,
pronounced jī, with the meaning of hope.
To sever the good relations between our two states;
we should not lightly alarm ourselves and stir up hostile intentions."
In the end, they made no preparations.
Qín sent Gentleman of the Yellow Gate Shí Yuè as an envoy to Yān,
and Grand Tutor Píng displayed extravagance to him,
wishing to boast of Yān's wealth and prosperity.
Gāo Tài and Grand Tutor's Army Advisor Liú Jìng of Héjiān said to Píng:
"Yuè's words are boastful and his gaze distant;
he is not seeking good relations,
but rather looking for cracks.
We should display our troops to show him,
to thwart his schemes.
Now instead we show him extravagance,
which will only make him despise us more."
Píng did not listen.
Tài then pleaded illness and retired.
6 Both Yān and Qín sent troops to aid Yuán Jǐn.
The Grand Marshal Wēn dispatched the Protector-in-Chief Zhú Yáo and others to resist them.
The Yān troops arrived first.
Yáo and others fought them at Wǔqiū,
and defeated them.
Wǔqiū,
is Qiūtóu.
When King Wén pacified Zhūgě Dàn,
he changed its name to Wǔqiū,
to commemorate the military achievement.
Dù Yòu said: Qiūtóu is Shěnqiū County in Yǐngzhōu.
Emperor Huì divided Rǔnán,
and established the Nándùn Commandery.
Nánchéng,
refers to the southern city of Shòuchūn.
He was the younger cousin of Wēn.
7 The Qín King Jiān again dispatched Wáng Měng to supervise the Campaign-South General Yáng Ān and ten other commanders, leading an army of sixty thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Yān.
8 Mùróng Lìng, judging that he would ultimately not escape punishment,
secretly plotted to raise troops.
In Shāchéng, there were several thousand soldiers serving penal garrison duty.
Lìng treated them all with great kindness.
In the fifth month,
on the day Gēngwǔ,
Lìng killed the Commandant Mèng Guī.
The city's Grand Officer Shè Guī, fearing for himself,
requested to prove his loyalty.
The Surname Register states: Shè,
is a surname.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn records that in Jìn there was a Grand Officer named Shè Tuó.
Guī,
is pronounced Jūwéi.
Lìng took him and placed him among his close attendants.
He then led the penal garrison troops east to attack Wēidé City.
Wēidé City,
was the city where Yǔwén Shèyègān resided.
The Yān King Huǎng renamed it Wēidé City.
Occupying the city, he made deployments,
and sent people to summon the various garrisons east and west,
and they all responded in unison.
The Garrison-East General, the Bóhǎi Prince Liàng, was stationed at Lóngchéng.
Lìng planned to attack him.
His younger brother Lín reported this to Liàng,
and Liàng closed the city gates to defend it.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
Shè Guī, taking advantage of his duty serving as a guard, attacked Lìng.
Lìng had taken Shè Guī and placed him among his close attendants,
hence he was able to attack him while serving guard duty.
Lìng's followers all scattered.
Shè Guī pursued Lìng to the Xuělí Marsh,
captured and killed him,
then went to Lóngchéng to report to Liàng.
Liàng executed Shè Guī,
collected Lìng's corpse and buried it.
9 In the sixth month,
on the day Yǐmǎo,
the Qín King Jiān escorted Wáng Měng to Bàshàng,
and said:
"Now I entrust you with the responsibility for the region east of the passes.
You should first capture Húguān,
and pacify Shàngdǎng.
Wèi Shōu said: Qín established Shàngdǎng Commandery,
with its seat at Húguān City.
The Former Hàn had its seat at Zhǎngzǐ City.
Dǒng Zhuó made Húguān City the seat.
The Mùróng clan made Ānmín City the seat,
and later moved it to Húguān City.
This is the so-called 'a sudden clap of thunder leaves no time to cover the ears.'
A saying from the Huáinánzǐ.
Following you, I will dispatch troops swiftly,
'xīng fā' means to set out while the stars are still out.
This explains 'xīng fā'.
Advancing by both land and water,
you need not worry about me arriving later."
Měng said:
"Your servant, relying on Your Majesty's awesome might,
and implementing the established strategy,
will sweep away the remnant Hú barbarians,
like the wind scattering leaves.
I hope it will not be necessary for the imperial carriage to personally brave the dust and fog.
I only ask that you swiftly order the relevant officials to arrange a place for the Xiānbēi."
This means to prepare lodgings in advance,
to await their arrival.
10 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the first day of the month, Guǐyǒu,
there was a solar eclipse.
11 The Qín commander Wáng Měng attacked Húguān,
and Yáng Ān attacked Jìnyáng.
In the eighth month,
the Yān ruler Wěi ordered the Grand Tutor, the Shàngyōng Prince Píng, to lead the elite troops from inside and outside, totaling three hundred thousand, to resist Qín.
The Textual Analysis notes: The Zàijì says
"four hundred thousand",
but here we follow the Jìn Chūnqiū.
He summoned the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Lǐ Fèng,
'sàn'
is pronounced sěidǎn.
'qí'
is pronounced qíjì;
the same below.
and asked: "How numerous are the Qín troops?
Now that our great army has been dispatched,
will Qín dare to fight?"
Fèng replied:
"The Qín state is small and its soldiers weak,
they are no match for the royal army.
Jǐnglüè is of ordinary talent,
and again cannot compare to the Grand Tutor.
There is no cause for worry."
Wáng Měng,
courtesy name Jǐnglüè.
"Victory or defeat lies in strategy,
not in numbers.
Qín has come from afar to invade,
how could they not be willing to fight!
Moreover, we should use strategy to seek victory,
how can we merely hope they will not fight and leave it at that!"
Wěi was displeased.
Wáng Měng captured Húguān,
and seized the Shàngdǎng Grand Administrator, the Nán'ān Prince Yuè.
The commanderies and counties he passed through
all submitted upon hearing of his approach.
The people of Yān were greatly shaken.
The Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, Fēng Fú, asked the Minister Over the Masses's Chief Clerk, Shēn Yǐn:
"How will things turn out?"
Yǐn sighed and said:
"Yè is sure to fall.
We will now become captives of Qín.
However, Yuè obtained the Year Star's favor, yet Wú attacked it,
and in the end suffered disaster from it.
The Zuǒ Zhuàn: In the thirty-second year of Duke Zhāo,
Wú attacked Yuè.
Shǐ Mò said:
'Before forty years have passed,
Yuè will possess Wú!
Yuè has obtained the Year Star, yet Wú attacks it,
it is sure to suffer misfortune.'
Dù Yù's commentary states: That year, the Year Star was in Xīngjì.
Xīngjì
is the division corresponding to Wú and Yuè.
Where the Year Star resides,
that state has good fortune.
Wú initiated military action,
therefore it conversely suffered calamity.
'Zú',
is pronounced zǐxù.
The virtue and good fortune lie with Yān,
also meaning the Year Star is in Yān's division.
This is what Fú Jián later referred to
when he said, 'In the past when I destroyed Yān,
I also transgressed against the Year Star and was victorious.'
This is it.
But Yān's re-establishment
will not take more than one cycle of twelve years."
This sets the stage for the Later Yān's revival.
'Fù',
is pronounced fúyòu,
or also as the original character.
12 The Grand Marshal Wēn, leading twenty thousand troops from Guǎnglíng, went to attack Yuán Jǐn.
He appointed the Xiāngchéng Grand Administrator Liú Bō as the Interior Historian of Huáinán,
and had him lead five thousand men to garrison Shítóu.
Bō
was the grandson of Kuí.
At the end of Emperor Yuán's reign,
Liú Kuí, to avoid the trouble caused by Wáng Dūn,
fled north to Later Zhào.
'Shuài',
is read as 'lǜ'.
'Jiàng',
is pronounced jíliàng;
the same below.
On the day Guǐchǒu,
Wēn defeated Jǐn at Shòuchūn,
and then besieged him.
The Yān Left Guard General Mèng Gāo led cavalry to rescue Jǐn.
When they reached the north of the Huái River,
before crossing,
it happened that Qín was attacking Yān,
and Yān recalled Gāo back.
13 In Guǎnghàn, the sorcerer-rebel Lǐ Hóng,
falsely claiming to be the son of the Hàn Guīyì Marquis Shì,
gathered a crowd of over ten thousand people,
proclaimed himself Sage King,
and adopted the reign title Fènghuáng.
A man from Lǒngxī, Lǐ Gāo,
falsely claimed to be the son of the Chéng ruler Xióng,
attacked and captured Fúchéng,
and drove out the Liángzhōu Governor Yáng Liàng.
In the ninth month,
the Yìzhōu Governor Zhōu Chǔ sent his son Qióng to attack Gāo,
and also had Qióng's son, the Zǐtóng Grand Administrator Xiāo, attack Hóng.
Both were pacified.
In the 14th year, Qín Yáng'ān attacked Jìnyáng.
Jìnyáng had many soldiers and ample provisions,
and it was not captured for a long time.
Wáng Měng left the Garrison Cavalry Commandant Gǒu Cháng to defend Húguān.
"Gǒu Cháng"
likely should be
"Gǒu Cháng."
They dug tunnels,
and sent the Tiger-Tooth General Zhāng Hào to lead several hundred strong warriors to secretly enter the city.
They shouted loudly and broke through the gates,
letting the Qín troops in.
On the Xīnsì day,
Měng and Ān entered Jìnyáng,
capturing the Yān Bīng Province Governor, the Prince of Dōnghǎi, Mùróng Zhuāng.
The Grand Tutor, Mùróng Píng, feared Měng and did not dare advance,
instead stationing his troops at Lùchuān.
According to the Commentary on the Water Classic: Lùchuān is north of Lù County in Shàngdǎng.
Kàn Yīn said: Lùshuǐ
is the Zhāngshuǐ.
It irrigates Jìzhōu.
In the tenth month,
on the Xīnhài day,
Měng left General Wǔdū Máo Dāng to defend Jìnyáng,
advanced his troops to Lùchuān,
and confronted Mùróng Píng.
On the Rénxū day,
Měng sent General Xú Chéng to spy on the Yān army's situation and key points.
The situation refers to
what is visible externally;
the key points refer to
what lies within.
Observing the situation
is insufficient to determine victory or defeat;
observing the key points
allows the decisive moment of victory or defeat to be determined.
To spy,
pronounce as chōu lián fān,
or chōu yàn fān.
He returned at dusk,
and Měng was furious,
intending to execute him.
Dèng Qiāng pleaded for him, saying:
"Now the enemy is numerous and we are few,
and we will fight tomorrow morning;
Dù Yù said: 'Tomorrow morning'
means at dawn.
'Míng,'
pronounce as qù jí fān.
'Morning,'
pronounce as usual.
He is a senior general,
you should spare him for now."
Měng said:
"If I do not kill Chéng,
military law will not be upheld."
Qiāng firmly pleaded:
"Chéng
is the commander of my commandery,
Chéng likely served as the Grand Administrator of Qiāng's home commandery.
'Commander,'
pronounce as jí liàng fān;
the same below.
Qiāng is willing to fight alongside Chéng to atone for his offense."
'Fight,'
means to exert effort in a decisive battle.
Qiāng became angry,
returned to camp,
beat the drums and marshaled his troops,
intending to attack Měng.
Měng asked the reason,
and Qiāng said:
"I received an edict to attack distant enemies;
now there are nearby enemies,
killing each other,
and I wish to eliminate them first!"
Měng saw that Qiāng was righteous and brave,
and sent someone to tell him:
"General, stop,
I will pardon him now."
Once Chéng was spared,
Qiāng went to Měng to apologize.
Měng took his hand and said:
"I was testing you, General.
Since you are like this even for your commandery commander,
how much more for the state?
I will no longer worry about the enemy!"
Grand Tutor Píng believed that Měng's army was deep in enemy territory and isolated,
and intended to wear them down through a protracted war.
Píng was greedy and petty,
monopolizing the mountains and springs,
and selling firewood and water.
The mountains are
where firewood is gathered;
the springs are
where water is drawn.
By monopolizing the mountains and springs,
he prevented the soldiers from gathering firewood or drawing water,
and sold firewood and water for profit.
Jiǎ Gōngyàn said: A high mound is called a hill,
a large mound is called a ridge.
The soldiers had no will to fight.
When Měng heard this,
he laughed and said:
"Mùróng Píng is truly a slave!
Even if he had millions of troops, they would not be fearsome,
let alone hundreds of thousands!
I will surely defeat him this time."
He then sent the Guerrilla General Guō Qìng to lead five thousand cavalry,
who took a hidden path at night to emerge behind Píng's camp,
burning Píng's supplies.
The fire was visible in Yè.
The Yān ruler Mùróng Wěi was afraid,
and sent the Palace Attendant Lán Yī to reprimand Píng, saying:
"You, Prince,
are the son of Gāozǔ.
Mùróng Huī's temple name was Gāozǔ.
Why do you not care for the soldiers but instead monopolize and sell firewood and water,
focusing solely on profiteering!
The wealth stored in the treasury,
I share with you, Prince.
Why worry about poverty!
If the enemy advances,
and our state and family perish,
where will you, Prince, keep your money and silk!"
He then ordered all the money and silk to be distributed to the soldiers.
Lì Dàoyuán said: Píng sold water to the soldiers,
charging one bolt of silk
for two dàn of water.
Píng was greatly afraid,
and sent an envoy to request battle with Měng.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
Měng arrayed his troops at Wèiyuán and made a vow.
Note: The Wèishuǐ does not originate from Lù County.
The Commentary on the Water Classic mentions the Nièshuǐ, which originates from Mount Fùzèng west of Lù County.
Perhaps
the character "Wèi"
is an error for
"Niè"
Also, according to Sīmǎ Guāng's Jīgǔ Lù,
it records Wáng Měng defeating Píng at Qīngyuán.
Dù Yù said: North of Wénxǐ County in Hédōng is Qīngyuán.
This place is also far from Lùchuān,
so I will leave this as a doubt for those who know.
Dù Yòu's Tōngdiǎn records it as
"Lùyuán."
'Array,'
read as 'zhèn';
the same below.
"Wáng Jǐnglüè has received great favor from the state,
holding both internal and external responsibilities.
Now, with all of you, I have advanced deep into enemy territory.
We must exert our utmost and fight to the death,
advancing without retreating,
to achieve great merit together,
and repay the state.
To receive titles in the court of an enlightened ruler,
and raise cups in our parents' homes,
is that not splendid!"
'To receive titles in the court of an enlightened ruler'
means to receive rewards at court for meritorious service.
'To raise cups in our parents' homes'
means to return after receiving rewards,
and toast to our parents' longevity.
'Court,'
pronounce as zhí yáo fān.
They smashed their cauldrons and abandoned their provisions,
shouting loudly as they charged forward.
Wang Měng gazed upon the vast numbers of Yān troops,
and said to Dèng Qiāng:
"The matter today,
cannot be accomplished without you, General, to defeat this formidable enemy.
The turning point between success and failure
lies in this single action.
General, exert your utmost!"
Qiāng replied:
"If you can grant me the position of Director of the Capital Region,
then you, sir, need not worry."
Měng said:
"That is not within my authority."
He would certainly arrange for him to be Administrator of Āndìng Commandery and a Marquis of Ten Thousand Households.
The Qín Inspector of Yōng Province governed Āndìng.
Āndìng was a major commandery within Qín territory.
"Arrange" is pronounced chǔ,
chāng lǚ fān.
Shortly after, the armies engaged.
Měng summoned Qiāng,
but Qiāng remained in bed and did not respond.
Měng galloped to him and promised him the position.
Qiāng then drank heavily in his tent,
and together with Zhāng Hào, Xú Chéng, and others, mounted their horses, brandished their spears,
and charged towards the Yān battle formation.
They charged in and out four times,
as if no one else was around,
killing and wounding several hundred.
By midday,
the Yān army was utterly defeated,
with over fifty thousand captured or slain.
Pursuing the victory,
they killed or forced the surrender of another hundred thousand or more.
Mùróng Píng fled alone on horseback back to Yè.
Cuī Hóng said: Dèng Qiāng requested a commandery from his general to bend the law,
this was favoritism;
leading troops intending to attack Wáng Měng,
this was disrespect for superiors;
before battle, preemptively seeking the Directorship of the Capital Region,
this was extorting the ruler;
possessing these three faults,
whose crime could be greater!
Yet Měng was able to tolerate his shortcomings,
and utilize his strengths,
like taming a fierce tiger,
or driving a headstrong horse,
to achieve great success.
The Book of Songs says:
"When gathering the turnip and the radish,
do not reject them for their roots."
These are the words of the "Valley Wind" poem.
Master Máo said: Fēng,
is the turnip;
fěi,
is the radish;
"lower part",
refers to the root and stem.
Master Zhèng said: These two vegetables,
are types like the turnip and the fú,
both tops and roots can be eaten.
However, their roots sometimes are good,
sometimes bad;
those who gather them,
cannot discard the leaves just because the roots are bad at that time.
Lù Jī's "Explanations of Plants and Trees" says: Fēng,
is the turnip.
Fěi,
is the xī vegetable.
Guō Pú said: Fēng,
is the sōng vegetable.
South of the river there is sōng,
north of the river there is the turnip,
similar but different.
Fěi,
is the radish,
also called earth melon.
The xī vegetable resembles the turnip,
its flowers are purple-red,
and it is edible.
Fú,
has large leaves,
white flowers,
roots like fingers,
white in color and edible.
Fú,
is pronounced fāng liù fān.
The Qín army drove eastward in a long advance,
from Lùchuān eastward to attack Yè.
On the day Dīngmǎo
they besieged Yè.
Měng submitted a memorial stating:
"On the day Jiǎzǐ,
I utterly annihilated the vile horde.
This means the victory was achieved on the day Jiǎzǐ,
an event similar to King Wǔ of Zhōu conquering Zhòu.
"Annihilate" is pronounced xiān,
xī lián fān.
I have made the officials and commoners of the six provinces
unaware of the change of ruler.
Unless they obstinately persist in error and defy orders,
they will suffer no harm whatsoever."
The Qín King Fú Jiān replied to him:
"You, General, completed the campaign without exceeding the season,
three months constitute a season.
Your merit surpasses that of the ancients.
I now personally lead the six armies,
swiftly as stars and lightning.
The Book of Songs says: 'By starlight, early I drive.'
This means setting out early by carriage while stars are still visible.
"Swift as lightning"
speaks of its speed.
"Lead"
is read as shuài.
Wait until I arrive,
and then we will capture it."
Before Měng arrived,
around Yè, plunder and robbery were openly rampant.
When Měng arrived,
near and far became peaceful and orderly.
His orders were strict and clear,
and the army committed no private offenses,
meaning the soldiers did not dare to privately harm the people of Yè.
The people of Yān each pursued their livelihoods in peace,
and said to one another:
"We never imagined we would see the Prince of Tàiyuán again today!"
Wáng Měng, hearing this,
sighed and said:
"Mùróng Xuángōng is truly an extraordinary man!
He can be called a legacy of ancient benevolent love!"
Mùróng Kè,
courtesy name Xuángōng,
was enfeoffed as Prince of Tàiyuán.
In the eleventh month,
the Qín King Fú Jiān left Lǐ Wēi to assist the Crown Prince in guarding Cháng'ān,
while the Duke of Yángpíng, Fú Róng, garrisoned Luòyáng.
He personally led a crack force of one hundred thousand to Yè,
reaching Ānyáng in seven days.
The Jìn Records state: Ānyáng County belonged to Wèi Commandery.
Wèi Shōu's Records say: In the first year of Tiānpíng,
Dàngyīn and Ānyáng were merged into Yè.
Also, in the Northern Xiūwǔ County of Jí Commandery, there was an Ānyáng city.
Fú Hóng and his sons had previously stationed at Fāngtóu.
Some of the old elders were still alive,
and hearing of Jiān's arrival,
welcomed him at Ānyáng,
so he feasted them.
Jiān said:
"In the past, Zhōu Yàfū did not welcome Emperor Wén of Hàn,
see scroll fifteen, the sixth year of Emperor Wén of Hàn's later reign.
Why was that?"
Měng said:
"Yàfū slighted his sovereign to seek fame.
I privately hold him in low regard.
Moreover, I, relying on Your Majesty's awesome might,
am attacking a nearly defeated foe.
It is like fish in a cauldron,
what is there to worry about!
The Supervisor of the State is young,
the Crown Prince guarding [the capital] is called Supervisor of the State.
"Supervise"
is pronounced gōng xián fān.
If something unexpected occurs,
what regret would there be!
Has Your Majesty forgotten my words at Bàshàng?"
Initially,
the Yān Prince of Yìdū, Mùróng Huán, led over ten thousand troops and camped at Shātíng.
Dù Yù said: Yuánchéng County in Yángpíng had Shātíng.
Hearing of Píng's defeat,
he led his troops to camp at Nèihuáng.
Nèihuáng County, since the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Wèi Commandery.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
Huán led five thousand Xiānbēi and fled to Lóngchéng.
On the day Wùyín,
the Yān Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Yú Wèi led over five hundred hostages from Fúyú, Gāogōulí, and Shàngdǎng,
and at night,
opened the northern gate of Yè to admit the Qín troops.

The Yān ruler Mùróng Wěi, together with the Prince of Shàngyōng Mùróng Píng, the Prince of Lè'ān Mùróng Zāng, the Prince of Dìngxiāng Mùróng Yuān, the General of the Left Guard Mèng Gāo, and the Palace General Ài Lǎng, fled to Lóngchéng.
The "Register of Surnames": The surname Ài,
in the "Spring and Autumn Annals of Master Yàn", Qí had a senior official Ài Kǒng.
The "General Customs" mentions Páng Jiǎn's mother, née Ài.
On the day Xīnsì,
the Qín King Fú Jiān entered the palace at Yè.
Mùróng Chuí met with the dukes, ministers, and senior officials of Yān, as well as his former colleagues and subordinates,
showing a displeased expression.
Gāo Bì said to Chuí:
"Your Highness relies on the accumulated resources of your ancestors,
and possesses the extraordinary strategy of a heroic talent.
Though you have encountered hardship and adversity,
and have taken refuge in a foreign state,
now, even though your family and state have collapsed,
who knows if this is not the beginning of a rising fortune!
In my humble opinion, you should treat the old subjects of the state
with the magnanimity of rivers and seas,
and find ways to comfort and win their hearts,
in order to lay the foundation for rebuilding the state
and achieve the great accomplishment of piling up earth to form a mountain.
This saying is like building a mountain:
starting from covering one basket of earth to advancing and completing the work of piling it nine rèn high.
Kuì (簣)
is pronounced qiú wèi fān,
meaning a basket for earth.
Eight chǐ is called one rèn.
I privately believe that Your Highness should not act otherwise!"
Gāo Bì had previously followed Chuí in fleeing to Qín,
hence he dared to offer this advice.
Wéi (為)
is pronounced yú wèi fān.
Chuí followed his advice.
When the Yān ruler Mùróng Wěi left Yè,
he still had over a thousand cavalry guards.
After leaving the city,
they all scattered,
leaving only a dozen or so riders accompanying him.
The Qín ruler Fú Jiān sent the游击将军 Guō Qìng to pursue him.
The road was difficult,
and Mèng Gāo supported and attended to Wěi,
protecting and escorting the two princes.
The two princes
refer to Prince Lè'ān Mùróng Zāng and Prince Dìngxiāng Mùróng Yuān.
Moreover, they encountered bandits along the way,
fighting their way forward.
After several days,
they reached Fúlù,
and rested by a grave mound.
Jiě xī (解息)
means to unsaddle the horses and rest.
Zhǒng (冢)
is pronounced zhī lǒng fān.
They all carried bows and arrows.
Mèng Gāo held a sword and fought,
killing and wounding several people.
Gāo exhausted his strength,
meaning he was utterly fatigued.
Then he charged forward and grabbed one bandit,
slammed him to the ground,
and shouted loudly:
"This man is at his end!"
The remaining bandits shot Gāo from the side,
killing him.
Ài Lǎng saw Gāo fighting alone,
turned back and rushed at the bandits,
and died together with him.
Wěi lost his horse and fled on foot.
Guō Qìng caught up with him at Gāoyáng.
His subordinate general Jù Wǔ was about to bind him.
According to the genealogy of surnames: Jù
is a surname.
"Who are you, a lowly person,
to dare bind the Son of Heaven!"
Wǔ said:
"I have received an edict to pursue a rebel,
what Son of Heaven!"
He captured him and presented him to the Qín ruler Fú Jiān.
Jiān questioned him about not surrendering but fleeing.
Wěi replied:
"When a fox dies, its head points toward its den;
I wished to return and die at the graves of my ancestors."
The ancestors of the Mùróng clan were all buried in Chānglí.
Jiān ordered him to return to the palace,
and lead his civil and military officials out to surrender.
In the eighth year of the Yǒnghé era of Jìn Emperor Mùdì,
the Yān ruler Mùróng Jùn changed the reign title and declared himself emperor.
He passed the throne to his son Wěi.
Altogether, it lasted nineteen years before its fall.
Shuài (帥)
is read as shuài.
Jiān ordered him to be buried with generous rites,
and appointed his son as a Langzhōng.
Guō Qìng advanced to Lóngchéng.
The Grand Tutor Mùróng Píng fled to Gāogōulí.
Gāogōulí captured Píng
and sent him to Qín.
Prince Yídū Mùróng Huán killed the General Who Guards the East, Prince Bóhǎi Mùróng Liàng,
and took over his troops,
fleeing to Liáodōng.
The Administrator of Liáodōng, Hán Chóu,
had already surrendered to Qín earlier.
When Huán arrived,
he could not enter,
so he attacked,
but failed to capture it.
Guō Qìng sent General Zhū Yí to attack him.
Huán abandoned his troops and fled alone.
Yí captured and killed him.
The various regional governors, administrators, and chieftains of the Six Barbarians all surrendered to Qín.
In total, they obtained 157 commanderies,
2,460,000 households,
and a population of 9,990,000.
He distributed the palace women and treasures of Yān among the officers and soldiers.
He issued an edict of general amnesty, saying:
"I, with my meager virtue,
have unworthily received the glorious mandate.
I have been unable to embrace the distant with virtue,
and gently subdue the four directions.
The four directions are: the southeast,
the southwest,
the northeast,
and the northwest.
I have harmed these people.
Although it is the fault of the common people,
it is also my crime.
Let there be a great amnesty throughout the land,
and let us make a fresh start together."
Earlier,
when Liáng Chēn was sent as an envoy to Qín,
he took Shìniǎn Xún Chún as his deputy.
The office of Shìniǎn
was likely a close attendant position established by Yān.
Chēn did not inform Chún beforehand;
Chún resented this,
and upon returning, said to the Yān ruler Wěi:
"Chēn in Cháng'ān
was very close and friendly with Wáng Měng,
and I suspect he had treacherous plans."
Chēn also repeatedly praised the virtues of the Qín ruler Fú Jiān and Wáng Měng,
and said that Qín would raise an army,
so they should prepare for it.
Later, Qín indeed attacked Yān,
just as Chēn had said.
Wěi then suspected that Chēn knew the situation.
After Mùróng Píng was defeated,
he arrested Chēn and imprisoned him.
When the Qín ruler Fú Jiān entered Yè, he released him,
and appointed him as a Zhōngshū Zhùzuò Láng.
Qín likely followed the system of early Jìn,
merging the Imperial Library into the Zhōngshū Department.
Jiān said to him:
"You previously said that Prince Shàngyōng and Prince Wú were both extraordinary talents fit to be generals and ministers.
Why were they unable to devise plans,
and instead brought about the destruction of their own state?"
Chēn replied:
"The rise and fall of states is determined by Heaven's Mandate;
how could two men change it!"
Jiān said:
"You were unable to perceive the subtle signs and act accordingly,
vainly praising Yān's virtues.
Loyal but failing to protect yourself,
instead bringing disaster upon yourself—
can this be called wise?"
Chēn replied:
"I have heard that 'the subtle signs are the minute movements
that foretell
good or ill fortune.'
These are words from the Great Commentary of the Yì.
Jī (幾)
is pronounced jū xī fān.
Xiàn (見)
is pronounced xián biàn fān.
This is truly beyond my ability.
However, for a minister, nothing is more important than loyalty;
for a son, nothing is more important than filial piety.
Unless one has a heart of utmost sincerity,
one cannot maintain loyalty and filial piety from beginning to end.
Therefore, the resolute men of ancient times
did not change in the face of danger,
did not avoid death when they saw it,
but sacrificed themselves for their ruler and parents.
Those who know the subtle signs
understand safety and danger in their hearts,
choose for themselves whether to stay or leave,
with no regard for their family and state.
Even if I had known,
I still could not have borne to act that way,
let alone when it was beyond my perception!"
Liáng Chēn was loyal to the cause he served.
The Qín ruler Fú Jiān was unable to honor and employ him.
Those with discernment could see from this that the Qín dynasty's fortune would not last long.
Jiān heard of Yuè Wǎn's loyalty.
The events concerning Yuè Wǎn are recorded in the tenth scroll, third year.
He appointed his son as a Langzhōng.

Jian appointed Wáng Měng as Commissioner Bearing Credentials, Commander of Military Affairs of the Six Guāndōng Provinces, General of Chariots and Cavalry, Excellency with Equal Honor to the Three Ministers, and Governor of Jìzhōu,
stationing him at Yè,
and promoted him to the rank of Marquis of Qīnghé Commandery,
bestowing upon him all the possessions from Mùróng Píng's mansion.
He granted Yáng Ān the rank of Marquis of Bópíng County; appointed Dèng Qiāng as Commissioner
Bearing Credentials, General Who Conquers Caitiffs, and Grand Administrator of Āndìng,
granting him the rank of Marquis of Zhēndìng Commandery;
Guō Qìng was appointed as Commissioner Bearing Credentials, Commander of Military Affairs of Yōuzhōu, and Governor of Yōuzhōu,
stationed at Jì,
and granted the rank of Marquis of Xiāngchéng.
Granting rank means
bestowing the marquis rank upon them,
not granting them a state or land.
Another interpretation:
previously they had not been granted ranks,
and now they were first bestowed.
Jian appointed Wéi Zhōng of Jīngzhào as Grand Administrator of Wèi Commandery,
and Péng Bào as Grand Administrator of Yángpíng;
Yān's capital was at Yè,
so the Grand Administrator of Wèi Commandery served as the Capital Governor.
Yángpíng
was an auxiliary commandery,
therefore Jian appointed men of Qín to guard both.
All were appointed according to the old system.
Completely changing the governors, grand administrators, magistrates, and chiefs of the provinces and counties
would both startle public perception
and cause discord between the sentiments of the old and new people,
therefore all followed the old system.
He sent them, along with the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Wéi Rú of Jīngzhào, to serve as Embroidered Uniform Commissioners,
touring the Guāndōng provinces and commanderies,
observing and examining customs,
encouraging and supervising agriculture and sericulture,
relieving and aiding the impoverished and distressed,
collecting and burying the dead,
commending and honoring virtuous conduct,
and altering or abolishing any Yān policies
that were inconvenient for the people.
Both Yān and Qín men were employed as Embroidered Uniform Commissioners.
Employing Yān men
was because they were familiar with Guāndōng customs;
employing Qín men
was to have them proclaim Jian's virtuous intentions.
Xíng,
read as xià Mèng fān.
In the twelfth month,
the Qín king Jiān relocated Mùróng Wěi, the Yān empress, princes, dukes, officials, and over forty thousand households of Xiānbēi to Cháng'ān.
This sets the stage for the later Xiānbēi taking advantage of chaos to attack Qín.
Wáng Měng submitted a memorial requesting to retain Liáng Chēn as Registrar,
concurrently overseeing the Records Office Supervisor.
Jìn system: the establishments of the various dukes had one Registrar and one Records Office Supervisor each.
Now Měng had Chēn hold both concurrently.
Měng, while feasting and conversing with his subordinates, mentioned the Yān court envoys,
saying:
"People's minds differ: previously, Lord Liáng, upon reaching Cháng'ān,
exclusively praised his own court;
Lord Lè only spoke of Huán Wēn's formidable army;
Lord Hǎo subtly mentioned the state's shortcomings."
Referring to Liáng Chēn, Lè Sōng, and Hǎo Guǐ.
"His own court" and "the state's shortcomings"
both refer to Yān.
Cháo,
read as zhí yáo fān.
Shǐ,
read as shū lì fān.
"Now all three are ministers of this state,"
this state refers to Qín.
Měng said:
"Lord Hǎo knew the subtle signs first."
Dàn said:
"Then, My Lord, you are rewarding Dīng Gong while executing Jì Bù."
Meaning his way of employing ministers
differed from that of Emperor Gāo of Hàn.
The Qín king Jiān traveled from Yè to Fāngtóu,
feasted the elders,
changed Fāngtóu's name to Yǒngchāng,
and exempted it from taxes for life.
On the jiǎyín day,
he arrived at Cháng'ān,
enfeoffed Mùróng Wěi as Marquis of Xīnxīng;
appointed former Yān minister Mùróng Píng as Imperial Secretary,
Huángfǔ Zhēn as Commandant of Imperial Chariots,
Lǐ Hóng as Commandant of Imperial Escort,
all granted court audience privileges;
these three men
were the Three Excellencies of Yān.
Fēng Héng was appointed as Gentleman of the Masters of Writing,
Mùróng Dé as Grand Administrator of Zhāngyè,
setting the stage for Dé's nephew Chāo remaining in Zhāngyè and later joining the Yáo clan.
Xīluó Téng was appointed as Gentleman of the Three Bureaus;
Hàn had Gentlemen of the Five Offices Bureau, Left Bureau, and Right Bureau,
hence called Gentlemen of the Three Bureaus.
Old system: gentlemen aged fifty and above
belonged to the Five Offices Bureau,
the next were divided between the Left and Right Bureaus;
Qín thus used Gentleman of the Three Bureaus as an official title.
Héng
was the son of Yù.
When Mùróng Huàng rose to power,
Fēng Yù became prominent for his loyal admonitions.
The former Yān Grand Astrologer Huáng Hóng sighed:
"Yān will certainly be restored,
and it will be through the Prince of Wú!
I regret that I am old,
and will not live to see it!"
When the Mùróng clan first rose,
Huáng Hóng submitted to them.
And when Jùn seized the Central Plains,
Huáng Hóng supported his decision: Hóng was one who understood fate.
"The Mandate of Heaven lies with Yān,"
meaning the Year Star was in Yān's division.
"In fifteen years,
Qín will certainly be possessed by Yān again."
Mùróng Huán's son Fèng,
aged eleven,
secretly harbored a desire for revenge,
and Xiānbēi and Dīnglíng men of spirit and capability all devoted themselves to befriending him.
This sets the stage for the later Mùróng Fèng and the Dīnglíng raising troops to attack Qín.
"A child should make himself known through talent and reputation;
do not imitate your father who did not recognize the Mandate of Heaven!"
Fèng sternly said:
"Our former king wished to establish loyalty but did not succeed;
this was the integrity of a minister;
Your Lordship's words,
are they the principle of encouraging and guiding future generations?"
Yì changed expression and apologized to him,
and said to the Qín king Jiān:
"Mùróng Fèng is passionate and has talent and capability;
but he has the wild ambition of a wolf cub,
I fear he will ultimately not be usable by others."
Zuǒzhuàn: Chǔ's Lingyǐn Zǐwén said:
"A wolf cub has a wild heart."
The history records that Yān's ministers and sons were not those who would long remain subordinates.
16 Qín abolished Yōngzhōu.
Qín had established Yōngzhōu at Āndìng,
now abolished Yōngzhōu and incorporated it into the Colonel Director of the Retainers.
17 This year,
the Duke of Chóuchí Yáng Shì died,
his son Zuǎn succeeded him,
and began to break with Qín.
His paternal uncle, the Grand Administrator of Wǔdū Yáng Tǒng, contended with him for the state,
raising troops to attack each other.
This sets the stage for Qín attacking Chóuchí.
Wáng Chóngwǔ punctuation; Róng Zhàozǔ, Niè Chóngqí proofread
Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial order
Later Student Tiān Tái
Emperor Tàizōng Jiǎnwén
personal name Yù,
courtesy name Dàowàn,
was the youngest son of Emperor Yuán;
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Lángyá,
later transferred and enfeoffed as Prince of Kuàijī.
When Hǎixī ascended the throne,
the Lángyá line had no heir,
so he was again transferred and enfeoffed as Prince of Lángyá,
but he firmly declined;
therefore, although enfeoffed as Prince of Lángyá, he did not relinquish the title of Prince of Kuàijī.
Interpretation of the posthumous title: "Unwavering in virtue is called Jiǎn;
extensively learned in the Way and its virtue is called Wén."
First year of Xián'ān (xīnwèi, 371)
In the eleventh month of this year,
Hǎixī was deposed,
the Emperor ascended the throne,
and began the new era name Xián'ān.
The Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government is arranged by year,
therefore it uses the new era name to connect them.
1 Spring,
first month,
Yuán Jǐn and Zhū Fǔ sought aid from Qín,
the Qín king Jiān appointed Jǐn as Governor of Yángzhōu,
Fǔ as Governor of Jiāozhōu,
and sent the General of the Martial Guard, the King of Wǔdū Jiān, and the Former General Zhāng Háo to lead twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to rescue them.
The Grand Marshal Wēn sent the Grand Administrator of Huáinán Huán Yī, the Grand Administrator of Nándùn Huán Shíqián, and others to attack Jiān and Háo at Shíqiáo,
according to Huán Wēn's biography,
Shíqiáo was north of the Féi River.
Shǒu,
read as shì yòu fān.
The Qín troops retreated and stationed at Shènchéng.
Shèn County,
belonged to Rǔnán Commandery in Hàn times,
in Jìn times it was divided and belonged to Rǔyīn Commandery.
The Shèn County of Táng's Lúzhōu
was the Shèn County of the Southern Liáng Commandery during the Liáng and Wèi period,
the territory of the Qūnqiú County of Jiǔjiāng in Hàn times,
not this Shènchéng.
He was the son of Xuān.
Huán Xuān assisted Zǔ Tì in resisting Zǔ Yuē,
defended Xiāngyáng,
and both had achievements.
On the dīnghài day
Wēn captured Shòuchūn, captured Jǐn and Fǔ,
and along with their clans sent them to Jiànkāng,
where they were executed.
The king of Tǔyùhún, Pìxī, heard that Yáng Zuǎn had been defeated.
In the fifth month,
he sent an envoy to present a thousand horses and five hundred catties of gold and silver to Qín.
Tǔ,
follows the entering tone of tūn.
Yù,
pronounced yù.
Pìxī
was the son of Yèyán,
Yèyán appears in the ninety-fourth volume, the fourth year of Emperor Chéng's Xiánhé era.
Qiáng,
pronounced qí liáng.
He lacked authority and decisiveness,
and his three younger brothers acted arbitrarily and unrestrainedly,
causing distress among the people.
The Chief Clerk Zhōng Èdì,
a powerful Qiāng chieftain from Xīqiáng,
said to the Marshal Qǐ Sùyún:
"The three younger brothers are running rampant,
their power surpassing that of the king,
nearly bringing the state to ruin.
We two hold positions as chief ministers,
Chief Clerk and Marshal,
the principal officials of the administration.
Tomorrow is the full moon,
the sun moves slowly,
completing one circuit of the heavens in a year;
the moon moves swiftly,
completing one circuit of the heavens in a month and meeting with the sun.
The meeting of the sun and moon
is called conjunction.
After conjunction,
the moon again moves ahead of the sun,
until the fifteenth day,
when the sun and moon face each other,
called the full moon.
Jié,
pronounced qù jí.
I intend to take action against them.
The king's attendants are all our Qiāng sons,
with a single glance,
they can be captured immediately."
Sùyún requested to first inform the king,
but Èdì said:
"The king is benevolent but indecisive,
informing him will certainly not lead to compliance;
if by any chance the matter is leaked,
we will be wiped out.
The matter has already been spoken,
how can we change midway!"
So they seized the three brothers in their seats,
and killed them.
Pìxī was shocked and terrified,
throwing himself under the bed,
Èdì and Sùyún hurried over to support him, saying:
"Your servant dreamed last night that the late king commanded me, saying: 'The three younger brothers are about to rebel,
they must be dealt with.'
That is why they were executed."
From then on, Pìxī fell ill and became confused,
when a person lacks clarity of mind,
it is called confusion.
"I have brought disaster upon my own brothers,
how can I face them underground!
Matters of state, great and small,
I entrust to you to manage,
my remaining years and frail life,
are merely sustained by food."
He then died of sorrow.
Shìlián succeeded him,
he did not drink alcohol or go hunting for seven years,
military and state affairs,
he entrusted to his generals and aides.
Zhōng Èdì admonished him,
believing that a ruler should enjoy himself,
and establish authority and spread virtue.
Shìlián wept and said:
"Since the time of my ancestors,
benevolence, filial piety, loyalty, and forgiveness have been passed down.
The late king, grieving that brotherly love did not last,
died in sorrow and indignation.
Although I have inherited the enterprise,
I am but an empty shell,
music, women, and hunting pleasures,
how could they bring me peace!
The establishment of authority and virtue,
should be left to the future."
The death of Pìxī,
and the succession of Shìlián,
these events did not all occur in this year.
The Zīzhì Tōngjiàn, because Pìxī presented tribute to Qín,
thus recorded them together,
to show that Pìxī and his son were by nature benevolent and filial,

Moreover, with Xī Chāo's power and influence being such,
after Huán Wēn died,
Chāo was able to die peacefully in his home,
likely because he used his wisdom to avoid disaster.
Wéi,
pronounced yú wèi fān.
In the 21st year, Qín appointed the Governor of Hé Province, Lǐ Biàn, to concurrently serve as Grand Administrator of Xīngjìn,
and returned him to garrison Fúhǎn.
Xīngjìn and Fúhǎn
were both established as commaneries by the Zhāng clan of Héxī.
Xīngjìn should also be near the Fúhǎn area.
[The Governor of Hé Province] moved his seat of administration from Tiānshuǐ to Jīnchéng.
[The Governor of Liáng Province] was greatly afraid,

hence his fear.
He sacrificed the three sacrificial animals,
led his officials and subordinates,
and made a covenant from afar with the Three Dukes of Jìn.
He sent the Gentleman of the Bureau of Affairs, Hán Bó, to present a memorial delivering the covenant text,

He wanted Jìn to raise troops to attack Shǔ and then meet at Shàngguī.
In this year,
the Governor of Yì Province of Qín, Wáng Tǒng, attacked the Xiānbēi chieftain Qǐfú Sīfán of Lǒngxī at Dùjiān Mountain.
Sīfán led thirty thousand cavalry to resist Tǒng at Yuànchuān.
Tǒng secretly attacked Dùjiān Mountain.
The Qǐfú clan first moved south from north of the desert and camped at Gāopíngchuān,
then moved southwest from Gāopíng to Màitián Mountain,

The Commentary on the Water Classic states: Yuànchuān is within the boundaries of Yǒngshì County in Tiānshuǐ.
Dù Yòu said: It is within the boundaries of Wǔquán County in Lán Province.
Judging from the later appointment of Qǐfú Tǔléi as Protector of Yǒngshì,

His troops, hearing that their wives and children had already surrendered to Qín,

Sīfán, having nowhere to go,

The King of Qín, Fú Jiān, appointed Sīfán as Southern Chányú,

Yǒngshì,
a Hàn county,

This established a Protectorate based on the name of the Hàn county.
This sets the stage for the later rebellion of the Xiānbēi under Qǐfú Bùtuí against Qín.
The ministers were hesitant and doubtful,

Some said:
"We must await the Grand Marshal's decision."
The Minister of Works, Wáng Biàozhī, sternly said:
"When the Son of Heaven passes away,

How can the Grand Marshal have any objection!
If we consult him first,

The court's decision was thus settled.
The Crown Prince ascended the throne as emperor,

The Empress Dowager Chóngdé issued an order.
Empress Dowager Chǔ, the Kāngxiàn Empress, had already returned governance to Emperor Mù,

During the reigns of Emperor Āi and the Duke of Hǎixī,
she once again assumed regency and issued decrees.
After the Duke of Hǎixī was deposed,

As the emperor was in mourning,

The matter was already being implemented,

"This is an extraordinary and major affair.
The Grand Marshal will certainly firmly decline,

I dare not accept this order,

The matter was thus not carried out.
This incident marks the beginning of returning imperial edicts sealed.
Wēn had hoped that Emperor Jiǎnwén would abdicate the throne to him on his deathbed,

As his expectations were not met,

He wrote to his younger brother Chōng, saying:

Wēn suspected that Wáng Tǎnzhī and Xiè Ān were behind this,

An edict ordered Xiè Ān to summon Wēn to assist in governance;

The Head of the Secretariat

The Metropolitan Governor

All matters, great and small, are involved.
Even with the virtue of Yī, Lǚ, Xiāo, and Dèng,

I am unworthy,

Měng was resolute, clear, and strict,

He dismissed and demoted incompetent officials,

He encouraged agriculture and sericulture,
trained the army,

As a result, the state became wealthy and the military strong,
winning every battle,

Jiān instructed the Crown Prince Hóng and the Duke of Chánglè, Pī, among others, saying:

The Duke of Yángpíng, Róng, was in Jìzhōu,

'Administrative staff'
refers to officials who manage various affairs.
The Genealogy of Surnames states: The surname Fáng originated from Dānzhū,
whom Shùn enfeoffed as the Marquis of Fángyi.
His son, Líng, took his father's fief as his surname.
He managed the records office.
Róng was young,
and in governance, he favored novelty,
valuing strict scrutiny.
Shēn Shào repeatedly admonished and corrected him,
guiding him toward leniency and harmony.
Although Róng respected him,
he did not fully follow his advice.
Later, Shào was sent out to serve as the Grand Administrator of Jǐběi.
Róng frequently had his faults reported,
and was reprimanded several times.
He then regretted not following Shào's advice.
Róng once sat... (text unclear) and established a school, for which he was impeached by the authorities.
He sent his Registrar, Lǐ Zuǎn, to Cháng'ān to plead his case.
Zuǎn was anxious and fearful,

Róng asked Shēn Shào:
"Who can be sent?"
Shào said:
"Gāo Tài, a Secretary in the Yān court,
is clear in argument and courageous and wise.
He can be sent."
Previously, both Chancellor Měng and Róng had repeatedly summoned Tài,
but Tài did not respond.
At this time,
Róng said to Tài:
"A gentleman helps others in urgent need;
you cannot decline again!"
Tài then accepted the mission.
Arriving in Cháng'ān,
Měng saw him
and laughed, saying:
"Gāo Zǐbó has only come now—
how late it is!"
Gāo Tài,
courtesy name Zǐbó.
"A criminal comes to face punishment;
why ask about lateness or speed!"
Měng said:
"What do you mean?"
Tài said:
"In the past, Duke Xī of Lǔ was praised for establishing the Pàn Palace.
The Odes of Lǔ, 'Pàn Water,'
praises Duke Xī for being able to build the Pàn Palace.
The Records of the Grand Historian states: King Xuān of Qí delighted in scholars of literature and rhetoric.
Scholars such as Zōu Yǎn, Chúnyú Kūn, Tián Pián, Shèn Dào, Jiē Zǐ, and Huán Yuān, seventy-six in total,
were all granted residences,
and the scholars at Jìxià numbered in the hundreds and thousands.
Liú Xiàng's Bié Lù states: Qí had the Jì Gate,
a city gate.
Scholars of rhetoric
would gather at Jìxià.
Yú Xǐ said: Qí had Mount Jì,
and established lodges below it to host wandering scholars.
Following the examples of Qí and Lǔ,
I have not heard of an imperial edict praising such deeds,
but instead, the authorities are troubled to investigate and impeach.
Your Excellency assists the sacred court,
yet your rewards and punishments are like this.
How can your subordinate officials escape blame!"
Měng said:
"This is my fault."
The matter was thus resolved.
Měng then sighed and said:
"How could Gāo Zǐbó be merely a subordinate official for Yángpíng!"
He spoke of this to the Qín King, Jiān.
Jiān summoned Tài for an audience,
was pleased with him,

Tài replied:
"The fundamental of governance lies in obtaining the right people;
obtaining the right people lies in careful selection;
careful selection lies in verifying the truth.
There has never been a case where officials are the right people and the state is not well-governed."
Jiān said:
"Your words are concise, yet the principle is profound."
He appointed Tài as a Secretary in the Imperial Secretariat.
Tài firmly requested to return to his province,
meaning to return to Jìzhōu.

the late Lady Wáng, Princess of Kuàijī, was posthumously honored as Empress Shùn.

Kuài,

the tenth month,

Sorcerer,

Led,

same below.

Precautions,

preparation.
Again,

courtesy name Chāngmíng,

First year of Níngkāng (guǐyǒu, 373)

first month,

new moon,

Trembled,

Zuǒzhuàn: Chǔ's Shěn Yǐnxū said: The Son of Heaven guards the four barbarians,

seventh month,
jǐhài day,

Hóng showed it to Wáng Biāozhī.

Again,
pronounced fú yòu.
Wēn's

Observing how Huán Wēn treated Ān and Tǎnzhī like this,

Wen, considering his heir Xi to be lacking in talent,

"Shào"

(Huán Shíxiù) was Huò's son.
