The Qín king Fú Jiān sent the General Who Smashes the Caitiffs, Lǚ Guāng, to attack and annihilate them.
The General Who Smashes the Caitiffs
was likely an office established by the Fú Qín.
In the fourth month,
on the Wùshēn day,
Wéi Zhōng captured Wèixīng.
Jí Yì drew his sword intending to kill himself,
but his attendants seized the sword.
Just then, the Qín men arrived,
captured him,
and Jí Yì refused to speak or eat until he died.
The Qín king Fú Jiān sighed and said:
"Zhōu Mèngwēi did not yield before,
Dīng Yànyuǎn kept himself pure afterward,
and Jí Zǔchōng sealed his lips and died.
How many loyal ministers does the Jìn house have!"
Zhōu Xiāo,
styled Mèngwēi;
Dīng Mù,
styled Yànyuǎn;
Jí Yì, styled Zǔchōng.
When they returned,
they obtained Jí Yì's final handwritten note.
An edict posthumously awarded him the title of Governor of Yìzhōu.
7 Qín generals Máo Dāng and Wáng Xiǎn led twenty thousand troops from Xiāngyáng eastward to join Jù Nán and Péng Chāo in attacking Huáinán.
In the fifth month,
on the Yǐchǒu day,
Nán and Chāo captured Xūyí,
capturing Máo Zǎozhī, the Internal Historian of Gāomì.
Gāomì
was an émigré commandery;
Máo Zǎozhī served as Internal Historian,
garrisoning Xūyí.
Zǎo,
read as zǐ hào.
The Jìn established émigré provinces of Yōu, Jì, Qīng, and Bìng north of the river at Sān'ā,
which is the area of present-day Bǎoyìng Army.
The court was greatly alarmed,
establishing garrisons along the river,
and sent the General Who Conquers Caitiffs, Xiè Shí, to lead a naval force and station at Túzhōng.
Shí
was the younger brother of Ān.
The Right Guard General Máo Ānzhī and others led forty thousand troops to station at Tángyì.
Qín generals Máo Dāng and Máo Shèng led twenty thousand cavalry to attack Tángyì,
and Máo Ānzhī and others were alarmed and routed.
The Governor of Yǎnzhōu, Xiè Xuán, came from Guǎnglíng to rescue Sān'ā.
On the Bǐngzǐ day,
Nán and Chāo were defeated in battle,
retreating to defend Xūyí.
In the sixth month,
on the Wùzǐ day,
Xuán and Tián Luò led fifty thousand troops to attack Xūyí,
and Nán and Chāo were again defeated,
retreating to station at Huáiyīn.
Xuán sent Hé Qiān and others to lead the naval force upstream with the tide.
At night,
they burned the Huái Bridge.
The Qín had built a bridge across the Huái River to move troops.
Upstream,
read as shí zhǎng.
Nán and Chāo retreated to station north of the Huái.
Xuán, together with Hé Qiān, Dài Tuàn, and Tián Luò, pursued them,
fighting at Jūnchuān.
Present-day Xūyí County has Jūn Mountain six li to the north.
This likely refers to the river of Jūn Mountain.
Nán and Chāo fled north,
barely escaping with their lives.
Xiè Xuán returned to Guǎnglíng,
and an edict promoted him to the title of Champion General,
additionally appointing him as Governor of Xúzhōu.
When the Qín king Fú Jiān heard this,
he was furious.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Péng Chāo was arrested in a cage cart and sent to the Court of Justice,
and he committed suicide.
Jù Nán was demoted to commoner status.
Máo Dāng was appointed as Governor of Xúzhōu,
garrisoning Péngchéng;
Máo Shèng was appointed as Governor of Yǎnzhōu,
garrisoning Húlù.
The Continued Hàn Records state: Húlù,
formerly Húlíng,
renamed by Emperor Zhāng.
The Former Hàn Records say: Wáng Mǎng changed it to Húlù.
Now, regarding Húlù County,
it belonged to Shānyáng Commandery in Hàn times,
and in Jìn times it was divided and belonged to the Principality of Gāopíng.
Wèi Shōu's Treatise on Geography states: Gāopíng County has the city of Húlíng.
It should be within the boundaries of Rènchéng County, Táng's Yǎnzhōu.
Garrisoning Xiàpī.
Xiè Ān served as chancellor,
and the Qín people repeatedly invaded,
with border troops suffering defeats.
Ān
always pacified matters with harmony and calm.
In his governance,
he focused on the major principles,
not concerning himself with minor details.
People at the time compared Ān to Wáng Dǎo,
and said his refinement surpassed him.
8 In the eighth month,
on the Dīnghài day,
the Left General Wáng Yùn was appointed as Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Shortly after,
he was transferred to be Governor of Dānyáng.
Yùn, considering himself a relative by marriage to the imperial family,
Yùn
was the father of the empress.
persistently requested an outside post,
and was again appointed as Commander of Military Affairs of the Five Commanderies East of the Zhè River and Internal Historian of Kuàijī.
Yùn had previously commanded Xúzhōu,
and now commanded eastern Zhè.
Again,
read as fú yòu.
Kuài,
read as gōng wài.
9 That year,
there was a great famine in Qín.
1 In spring,
the first month,
the Qín king Fú Jiān again appointed the Duke of Běihǎi, Fú Zhòng, as Great General Who Guards the North,
garrisoning Jì.
Fú Zhòng plotted rebellion yet was not executed,
and was again entrusted with a regional command.
It was fitting that he and his brother Fú Luò rebelled.
Again,
read as fú yòu.
In the second month,
a military training hall was built at Wèichéng.
In the first year of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn,
Xiányáng was renamed Xīnchéng;
in the third year of Yuándǐng of Emperor Wǔ,
it was renamed Wèichéng;
it was abolished in Later Hàn and Jìn times;
Shí Lè established Shí'ān County,
and the Fú Qín again called it Wèichéng.
The Director of the Palace Library, Zhū Róng, remonstrated:
"Your Majesty campaigns east and west,
invincible wherever you go.
Of the lands within the Four Seas,
you have gained eight-tenths.
Although Jiāngnán is not yet subdued,
it is hardly worth mentioning.
It is appropriate to gradually reduce military affairs
and increase the cultivation of civil virtue.
Yet now you begin establishing schools
to teach people the techniques of combat.
This is hardly the way to gradually achieve peace and prosperity.
Tame,
means to follow,
meaning to achieve peace and prosperity from this.
Why worry that they are not practiced in warfare,
and instead have them receive instruction from scholars?
This is not the way to strengthen their will and spirit.
This brings no real benefit and damages your reputation.
I beg Your Majesty to consider this!"
Fú Jiān then stopped.

6. The Qin ruler Fú Jiān summoned the Duke of Yángpíng, Fú Róng, to serve as Palace Attendant, Director of the Central Secretariat, Commander of the Capital and Regional Forces, General of Chariots and Cavalry, Colonel-Director of Retainers, and Recorder of the Imperial Secretariat.

He appointed the General Who Pacifies the South and Acting Imperial Secretary, the Duke of Chánglè, Fú Pī, as Commander of the Armies East of the Passes, General Who Conquers the East, and Governor of Jì Province.
Fú Jiān, because the various Dí tribes had become numerous and prosperous,
in autumn,
the seventh month,
divided 150,000 households from the Dí of Sānyuán, Jiǔzōng, Wǔdū, Qiān, and Yōng.
(Mount Jiǔzōng
lies within the boundaries of Yúnyáng County, Féngyì Commandery of the Han.
In the Táng, it was in Lǐquán County.
Zōng,
pronounced zū hóng fān.
Qiān,
pronounced kǔ jiān fān.
Yōng,
pronounced yú yòng fān.)
He dispersed them to reside in the frontier commands,
like the feudal lords of antiquity.
The Duke of Chánglè, Fú Pī, was given command of 3,000 Dí households.
He appointed the Dí chieftain from Chóuchí, Commandant of the Archers Who Raise the Alarm, Yáng Yīng, as Left Marshal of the Army That Conquers the East,
and the Dí chieftain from Jiǔzōng, Commandant of the Chang River, Qí Wǔ, as Right Marshal,
each commanding 1,500 households,
to be hereditary ministers of the Duke of Chánglè.
(In ancient times, when feudal states were established,
the appointed ministers all held their offices hereditarily.
Fú Jiān divided the imperial clansmen and dispersed them to reside in the frontier commands,
each appointing hereditary ministers from their own tribes.
Lè,
pronounced yīn luò.
Chieftain,
pronounced cí yóu fān.
Yuán,
is a Dí surname.
Later, they followed Emperor Wǔ of Sòng south and submitted,
subsequently becoming a family of generals for generations.)
Shēn Shào served as his Assistant.
Yáng Yīng
was the elder brother of Fú Pī's wife;
Qí Wǔ
was Yáng Yīng's father-in-law.
In the eighth month,
he divided Yōu Province to establish Píng Province.
(The Jìn Shū states: According to this, Píng Province
was within the domain of Jì Province according to the Tribute of Yǔ,
during the Zhōu it was within the boundaries of Yōu Province,
and during the Hàn it belonged to Běipíng Commandery.
At the end of the Later Hàn,
Gōngsūn Dù styled himself Governor of Píng Province.
When his grandson Wényì was destroyed by Wèi,
Píng Province was consequently established,
governing five commanderies: Liáodōng, Chānglí, Xuāntú, and Dàifāng.
Later, it was merged back into Yōu Province.
When Fú Qín destroyed Yān,
it again divided Yōu Province to establish Píng Province.
Gōngsūn Yuān,
styled Wényì;
the Táng, to avoid the taboo of Emperor Gāozǔ's name,
referred to him by his style.)
Its seat was at Lóngchéng.
The Director of the Central Secretariat, Liáng Dǎng, was made Governor of Yōu Province,
with his seat at Jìchéng.
General Who Pacifies the Army, Máo Xīng, was made Commander of the Armies of Hé and Qín Provinces and Governor of Hé Province,
with his seat at Fúhǎn.
Commandant of the Chang River, Wáng Téng, was made Governor of Bìng Province,
with his seat at Jìnyáng.
Hé and Bìng Provinces were each allocated 3,000 Dí households.
Máo Xīng and Wáng Téng were both related by marriage to the Fú clan,
and were highly esteemed among the Dí.
The Duke of Píngyuán, Fú Huī, was made Commander of the Armies of Yù, Luò, Jīng, Nán Yǎn, Dōng Yù, and Yáng Provinces, General Who Guards the East, and Governor of Yù Province,
with his seat at Luòyáng.
(The Qín Governor of Yǎn Province was stationed at Cāngyuán,
and the Nán Yǎn Province seat was at Húlù.
Furthermore,
Qín initially stationed the Governor of Yù Province at Xǔchāng.
After destroying Yān,
it stationed the Governor of Yù Province at Luòyáng,
and established Dōng Yù Province at Xǔchāng.
"Yáng"
should be
"Yáng".
According to the Treatise on Geography in the Hòu Wèi Shū: In the first year of Tiānpíng,
Yáng Province was first established at Yíyáng.
Fú Jiān appointed Wáng Xiǎn as Governor of Yáng Province,
garrisoning Xiàpī,
which was precisely under Fú Huī's command.
Fú Qín initially stationed the Governor of Luò Province at Shǎnchéng,
and the Governor of Jīng Province at Fēngyáng.
After capturing Xiāngyáng,
it was made the seat of Jīng Province,
and the seat of Luò Province was moved to Fēngyáng.
Fēngyáng
was the territory of Shàngluò County in the Hàn.
Sòng Bái states: Fēngyáng
was the territory of Shāng County in the Hàn.
In the third year of Tàishǐ of Jìn, Fēngyáng County was separately established,
located in the Fēngyáng River valley.)
It was allocated 3,200 Dí households.
Fú Jiān escorted Fú Pī as far as Bàshàng.
The various Dí people, parting from their fathers and elder brothers,
all wailed bitterly,
their grief moving passersby.
Zhào Zhěng, taking advantage of attending a banquet,
took up a qín and sang:
(Xiàng Ānshí's Jiā Shuō states: Fúxī made the qín,
three chi, six cun, and six fen long,
symbolizing the three hundred and sixty-six days;
six cun wide,
symbolizing the six directions.
Its markings:
the upper part is called the "pool",
the lower part is called the "cave".
The pool,
symbolizes level water.
Broad in front and narrow behind,
symbolizes the noble and the humble.
Round above and square below,
follows heaven and earth.
Five strings,
represent the officials.
The large string,
represents the ruler,
broad, harmonious, and gentle.
The small strings,
represent the ministers,
pure, incorruptible, and not disorderly.
King Wén added three strings,
to unite the grace between ruler and ministers.
Yuán,
pronounced yú yuán fān.
Dù Yòu states: The Shì Běn says: The qín
was created by Shénnóng.
The Qín Cāo says: Fúxī made the qín,
to cultivate one's person and regulate one's nature,
returning to one's natural innocence.
The Bái Hǔ Tōng says: Qín
means to restrain;
to restrain from evil,
to rectify the human heart.
The Guǎng Yǎ says: King Wén and King Wǔ added two strings,
to unite the grace between ruler and ministers.
Yáng Xióng's Qín Qīng Yīng says: Shùn played the five strings and the world was transformed,
Yáo added two strings to unite the grace between ruler and ministers.)
"Ā dé zhī,
ā dé zhī,
the uncle of the shrike is Chóu Suī,
(Ěr Yǎ: Jú,
is the bóláo.
Guō Pú states: The bóláo resembles the xiáhé but is larger,
it cannot soar when flying,
only raising and lowering its wings.
The Guǎng Yǎ states: Bóláo,
also called bóláo,
also called bózhào.
Chóu Suī,
it is not known what this is.)
You send the tribesmen far away and keep the Xiānbēi,
(This refers to dispersing the various Dí and keeping the Mùróng.)
Zhǒng,
pronounced zhāng yǒng fān.)
Fú Jiān laughed but did not accept it.
7. In the ninth month,
on Guǐwèi day,
the Empress, née Wáng, passed away.
8. In winter,
the tenth month,
the Grand Administrator of Jiǔzhēn, Lǐ Xùn, occupied Jiāo Province and rebelled.
9. The Qin ruler Fú Jiān appointed the Left Palace Guard General, Yáng Bì, as Governor of Qín Province;
the Imperial Secretary, Zhào Qiān, as Governor of Luò Province;
and the Commandant of Nánbā, Jiāng Yǔ, as Governor of Níng Province.
(Fú Qín established the Commandant of Nánbā in the southern region.)
10. In the eleventh month,
on Yǐyǒu day,
the Empress Dìng was buried at the Lóngpíng Mausoleum.
11. In the twelfth month,
Qín appointed the Left General, Dū Guì, as Governor of Jīng Province,
with his seat at Péngchéng.
(Dū Guì was stationed at Xiāngyáng.
Péngchéng is an error.)
12. Dōng Yù Province was established,
with Máo Dàng appointed as its Governor,
stationed at Xǔchāng.
13. This year,
the Qin ruler Fú Jiān sent the Grand Administrator of Gāomì, Máo Zǎozhī, and over two hundred others to return and submit.
(Máo Zǎozhī was captured;
see the fourth year above.)
1 In spring,
the first month,
the Emperor began to revere the Buddhist Dharma.
He established a vihāra within the palace halls.
The *Book of the Later Han*, Biography of Jiāng Gōng, states: "He went to the jīnglú to seek an audience with the recluse."
The commentary of Lǐ Xián states: "Jīnglú
is the same as jīngshè.
It likely takes its meaning from the idea of concentrating and diligently studying one's profession.
Nowadays, the places where Confucian scholars and Buddhist monks pursue their studies
are both called jīngshè."
The Left Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Wáng Yǎ, submitted a memorial admonishing against this,
but the Emperor did not comply.
Yǎ
was the great-grandson of Sù.
Wáng Sù served under the Cáo Wèi,
and was renowned for his classical scholarship.
Emperor Wǔ
was Sù's grandson by his daughter.
2 On Dīngyǒu day,
Xiè Shí, the Imperial Secretary, was appointed as Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
3 In the second month,
sixty-two states from the Eastern Yi and the Western Regions presented tribute to Qín.
4 In summer,
the sixth month,
on the Gēngzǐ day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
5 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Jiǎwǔ day,
the Governor of Jiāozhǐ, Dù Yuàn, executed Lǐ Xùn,
and Jiāozhōu was pacified.
6 In winter,
the tenth month,
the former Prince of Wǔlíng, Sīmǎ Xī, died in Xīn'ān.
Xī had been exiled to Xīn'ān,
as seen in the first year of the Xián'ān era of Emperor Jiǎnwén in the previous scroll.
He commanded his son Zūn to be his heir.
7 In the eleventh month,
on the Jǐhài day,
the former Governor of Kuàijī, Xī Yīn, was appointed as Minister of Works;
Yīn firmly declined and did not take up the post.
8 Dū Guì, the Governor of Jīngzhōu for Qín, sent his Marshal Yán Zhèn and Central Army Adjutant Wú Zhòng to lead twenty thousand troops to raid Jìnglíng.
Jìnglíng
was a marquisate.
Under the Former Hàn, it belonged to Jiāngxià Commandery;
Emperor Huì established the separate Jìnglíng Commandery.
Shímín
was the younger brother of Shíqián.
In the twelfth month,
on the Jiǎchén day,
Shíqián launched a surprise attack on Zhèn and Zhòng,
routing them decisively.
Zhèn and Zhòng retreated and defended Guǎnchéng.
Shíqián advanced and attacked them.
On the Guǐhài day,
he captured Guǎnchéng.
According to the *Records of the States*,
Shíqián defeated Zhèn and Zhòng in a surprise attack at the Ào River,
after which Zhèn and Zhòng retreated to defend Guǎnchéng.
Also, according to the *Classic of Waterways*,
the Miǎn River passes by the old city wall of Jùn County to the south,
then flows east,
where the Ào River joins it.
The Ào River flows southwest into the Miǎn,
and the place is indeed called Àokǒu.
The Miǎn River then flows south past the west of Shíchéng;
the city used the mountains for its fortifications,
and it was the seat of the Jìn Jìnglíng Commandery.
Based on this examination,
Guǎnchéng should have been north of the Ào River.
Seven thousand heads were taken,
and ten thousand captives were seized.
An edict enfeoffed Huán Chōng's son Qiān as Marquis of Yíyáng.
Huán Shíqián was appointed to concurrently serve as Governor of Hédōng.
Shěn Yuē states: In the third year of the Xiánkāng era of Emperor Chéng,
General Chéngxī, Yǔ Liàng, established the Southern Hédōng Commandery using refugee households from Sīzhōu,
and placed it under Jīngzhōu.
The *Treatise of the Five Dynasties* states: Sōngzī County of Nán Commandery
was where the Eastern Jin established Hédōng Commandery.
9 This year,
there was a great famine east of the Yangtze.
1 The Grand Minister of Agriculture of Qín, the Duke of Dōnghǎi, Yáng, and the Extraordinary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Wáng Pí,
The *Jìn Treatise on Official Posts* states: There were four Cavalier Attendants-in-Ordinary.
They were established together with the Regular Cavalier Attendants at the beginning of the Wèi;
the Extraordinary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary
was established by Emperor Wǔ of Jìn.
Sàn
is pronounced sǎndǎn fān.
Qí
is pronounced qíjì fān.
Their plot was discovered,
and they were arrested and handed over to the Commandant of Justice.
Yáng
was the son of Fǎ;
Pí
was the son of Měng.
The Qín King Jiān questioned them about their rebellion.
Yáng said:
"My father, the Duke Āi, died not for any crime."
Fǎ's death is seen in the first year of the Shēngpíng era of Emperor Mù, scroll one hundred.
Jiān wept and said:
"The death of the Duke Āi
was not a matter for which I was responsible.
Do you not know this?"
Wáng Pí said:
"My father was Chancellor,
with meritorious service in assisting the founding of the state,
yet I cannot escape poverty and low status.
Therefore, I sought wealth and honor."
Jiān said:
"The Chancellor, on his deathbed, entrusted you
with ten pairs of oxen as capital for managing fields.
He never sought an official post for you.
There is none who knows a son like his father.
How clear-sighted he was!"
Zhōu Xiāo said:
"Generations of my family have received the grace of Jìn.
In life, I am a subject of Jìn;
in death, I shall be a ghost of Jìn.
What more is there to ask?"
Previously,
Xiāo had repeatedly plotted rebellion.
Those around Jiān all requested that he be executed.
Jiān said:
"Mèng Wēi is a man of staunch integrity.
Holding to his principles like this,
how could he fear death?
Killing him would only serve to complete his fame!"
He pardoned them all,
and did not execute them.
He exiled Yáng to the Gāochāng Commandery of Liángzhōu.
Consulting the various Jìn treatises,
the Zhāng clan of Héxī never established a Gāochāng Commandery.
When Fú Jiān pacified Héxī,
he appointed Yáng Gàn of Gāochāng as Governor of Gāochāng.
It is suspected that the Zhāng clan established this commandery,
and the Fú clan continued it.
Gāochāng
is the place of the Gāochāng Garrison of the Later Section of Chēshī in Hàn times.
Commentary is also seen later.
Xiāo died in Shuòfāng.
Yáng possessed courage and strength surpassing others.
Soon after, he was again exiled to Shànshàn.
By the end of the Jiànyuán era,
the state of Qín fell into great disorder.
In the nineteenth year of Jiànyuán,
Jiān attacked Jìn and was defeated,
and Qín subsequently fell into chaos.
In the twentieth year,
Jiān died.
This was the eighteenth year of Jiànyuán.
Fù
is pronounced fúyòu fān.
Shàn
is pronounced shàngshàn fān.
The King of Shànshàn killed him.
The historian concludes the matter here.
2 The Qín King Jiān moved the bronze camels, bronze horses, feiliana, and stone statues from Yè to Cháng'ān.
These were what Shí Hǔ had placed in Yè.
3 In summer,
the fourth month,
Jiān appointed the Governor of Fúfēng, Wáng Yǒng, as Governor of Yōuzhōu.
Below "Jiān"
there should be
the character "yǐ"
He was the elder brother of Pí.
Pí was vicious and treacherous, without virtue,
while Yǒng was pure, cultivated, and fond of learning.
Therefore, Jiān employed him.
He appointed the Duke of Yángpíng, Róng, as Minister over the Masses;
Róng firmly declined and did not accept.
Jiān was then planning to attack Jìn,
so he appointed Róng as General-in-Chief Who Conquers the South, with the rank of Excellency with Special Powers.
4 In the fifth month,
locusts appeared in Yōuzhōu,
covering an area a thousand li in breadth and length.
The Qín King Jiān sent the Regular Cavalier Attendant Liú Lán of Péngchéng to mobilize the people of Yōu, Jì, Qīng, and Bìng to catch and eliminate them.
5 In autumn,
the eighth month,
on the Guǐmǎo day,
a general amnesty was declared.
6 The Qín King Jiān appointed the Grand Master of Remonstrance, Péi Yuánlüè, as Governor of the two commanderies of Bāxī and Zǐtóng,
ordering him to secretly prepare a naval force.
He intended to follow the old stratagem of Wáng Jùn,
to sail down the river eastward and attack Jìn.
7 In the ninth month,
Mí Tián, the king of the Former Cheshi, and Xiūmìtuó, the king of Shànshàn,
came to the court of Qin,
requesting to serve as guides
to attack those in the Western Regions who were not submissive,
and to establish a Protector-General according to the Han system to govern them.
The King of Qin, Fú Jiān, appointed the Valiant Cavalry General Lǚ Guāng as Commissioner Bearing Credentials, Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs for the Campaign Against the Western Regions,
along with the River-Crossing General Jiāng Fēi,
(The title "River-Crossing General"
was established by Prince Wén of Jin
and conferred upon Luó Xiàn.)
Dù Jìn and Kāng Shèng held positions equivalent to generals,
but did not have formal general titles.
With five thousand armored cavalry,
they were to attack the Western Regions.
The Duke of Yángpíng, Fú Róng, remonstrated, saying:
"The Western Regions are desolate and distant.
Their people cannot be made to serve,
and their land cannot be cultivated for food.
When Emperor Wu of Han campaigned there,
the gains did not compensate for the losses.
(This refers to Emperor Wu of Han's campaigns
which
heavily defeated Lóulán and Gūshī,
and established agricultural colonies in Cheshi.)
Now to weary our army thousands of miles away,
merely to follow in the mistaken footsteps of the Han dynasty,
is something I privately regret."
(Fú Jiān) did not listen.
8 Huán Chōng sent the General Who Spreads Awe, Zhū Chuò, to attack Dū Guì, the Qin Governor of Jīng Province, at Xiāngyáng.
He burned and trampled the military agricultural colonies north of the Miǎn River,
plundered six hundred households, and returned.
9 In winter,
the tenth month,
the King of Qin, Fú Jiān, assembled his ministers in the Tàijí Hall
and deliberated, saying:
"Since I inherited the enterprise,
nearly thirty years have passed.
(Fú Jiān established himself in the first year of Shēngpíng,
and by now it was twenty-six years in total.)
Considering the length of time,
I fear not reaching a proper end,
yet still hope to do so.
(But then he desired to exhaust the people to satisfy his ambition,
so his downfall was fitting.)
The four quarters are largely pacified,
only the southeastern corner
remains untouched by royal transformation.
Now, roughly calculating our troops,
we can muster nine hundred and seventy thousand.
I intend to personally lead them to attack it.
What do you think?"
The Director of the Palace Library, Zhū Róng, said:
"Your Majesty is respectfully carrying out Heaven's punishment.
There will certainly be a campaign but no battle.
If the Jin ruler does not come with a jade tablet in his mouth to surrender at the army gate,
then he will flee to die by river or sea.
Your Majesty will return the gentlemen and commoners of the Central States
to restore them to their mulberry and catalpa trees (i.e., their ancestral homes).
(This refers to the descendants who crossed south to avoid chaos at the end of the Yǒngjiā period.)
Then you may report completion at Dàizōng."
(Dù Yòu said: Dàizōng
is the Eastern Peak.
Specifically, Mount Tài is called Dàizōng
because it is located in the northeast,
situated between the directions yín and chǒu,
the place where the myriad things end and begin,
the site where yin and yang hand over and take over,
the ancestor of all mountains.
Therefore it is called Dàizōng.)
Fú Jiān happily said:
"This is my ambition."
The Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Quán Yì, said:
"In the past, when Zhòu was without the Way,
the three humane men were still at court,
and King Wu of Zhou still turned his army back.
(The Analects: Wēizǐ left him,
Jīzǐ became his slave,
Bǐgān remonstrated and died.
Confucius said:
'The Yin had three humane men.')
The Records of the Grand Historian: In the ninth year of King Wu's reign,
he reviewed troops in the east, reaching Méngjīn.
Eight hundred lords gathered without prior arrangement,
all saying:
'Zhòu can be attacked.'
King Wu said:
'It is not yet possible,'
and then withdrew his army.
After two years,
Zhòu's tyranny and cruelty increased greatly.
He killed Prince Bǐgān,
imprisoned Jīzǐ,
and Wēizǐ fled to Zhou.
King Wu announced to the lords:
'The Yin have grave crimes,
they cannot be left unpunished!'
And so he destroyed them.)
(朝, pronounced zhāo.)
(直遙翻。)
(猶為, pronounced yóu wèi.)
(于偽翻。)
Now Jin has no great wickedness.
Xiè Ān
and Huán Chōng are both outstanding men south of the river.
Ruler and ministers are harmonious,
inner and outer are of one mind.
In my view,
they cannot be plotted against!"
Fú Jiān remained silent for a long time,
then said:
"Let each of you gentlemen state your views."
The Commandant of the Left Guard of the Heir Apparent, Shí Yuè, said:
"This year, the Year Star and the Saturn Star guard the Dipper.
The virtue and blessings are in Wu.
(The Year Star
is Jupiter.
The Guarding Star,
is Saturn.
The Dipper, Ox, and Maiden constellations
correspond to the divisions of Wu, Yuè, and Yáng Province.)
There will certainly be heavenly calamity.
Moreover, they rely on the natural barrier of the Long River,
and the people serve them.
It is probably not advisable to attack them!"
Fú Jiān said:
"In the past, when King Wu attacked Zhòu,
he went against the Year Star and defied the divination.
(Xúnzi said: When King Wu executed Zhòu,
he faced east and confronted the Grand Year Star.
Yáng Liàng's commentary says: Confronting
means going against the Grand Year Star.
Shizi says: When King Wu attacked Zhòu,
Yú Xīn remonstrated, saying:
'The Year Star is in the north,
you cannot campaign northward.'
King Wu did not listen.
The Records of the Grand Historian, Hereditary House of Qí: When King Wu was about to attack Zhòu,
he divined with a turtle shell.
The omen was inauspicious,
wind and rain suddenly arrived violently,
and all the dukes were terrified.
Only Tàigōng insisted strongly,
urging King Wu,
and King Wu then proceeded.)
(The outcome) is not easily knowable.
Fūchāi and Sūn Hào both protected themselves relying on rivers and lakes,
yet could not avoid destruction.
Now with the multitude of troops I have,
if we threw our whips into the river,
it would be enough to dam its flow.
What natural barrier is sufficient to rely on then!"
(Shí Yuè) replied:
"The rulers of those three states were all licentious, cruel, and without the Way.
(The rulers of the three states
refer to Zhòu, Fūchāi, and Sūn Hào.)
(Conquering them was) as easy as picking up something dropped.
Now Jin, though lacking in virtue,
has committed no great crime.
I wish Your Majesty would for now halt the troops and accumulate grain,
and wait for their lapse."
Thereupon, the ministers each spoke of advantages and disadvantages,
and for a long time no decision was reached.
Fú Jiān said:
"This is what is called building a house by the roadside,
which can never be completed.
(The Book of Songs says: Like building a house by consulting with passersby on the road,
therefore it does not reach completion.)
All the ministers withdrew,
leaving only Yángpíng Gōng Fú Róng,
to whom he said:
"Since ancient times, those who decide great matters
have been no more than one or two ministers.
Now the multitude of opinions is chaotic,
only confusing people's minds.
I shall decide this with you."
Fú Róng replied:
"Now there are three difficulties in attacking Jìn: Heaven's will is not favorable,
first;
the state of Jìn has no internal strife,
second;
our troops are weary from frequent battles,
and the people have a fear of the enemy,
third.
The ministers who say Jìn cannot be attacked
are all loyal ministers.
I hope Your Majesty will heed them."
Fú Jiān changed countenance and said:
"If even you are like this,
what hope have I left!
I have a million strong soldiers,
supplies and weapons piled like mountains;
though I may not be an exemplary ruler,
I am not foolish and incompetent either.
'Liè' means
weak.
To strike a state on the verge of collapse,
why worry about not conquering it?
How can we leave these remaining bandits
to become a lasting worry for the state!"
Hàn and Wèi ministers had a saying: Relying on the state's great size,
boasting of the multitude of its people,
and seeking to display might before the enemy
is called an arrogant army.
An arrogant army perishes.
Does this not describe Fú Jiān!
'Fù'
is pronounced fú yòu fān;
the following 'fù liú' is the same.
"That Jìn cannot be destroyed
is abundantly clear.
Now to toil the army in a great campaign,
I fear there will be no certain success.
Moreover, what I worry about
does not stop here.
Your Majesty nurtures and favors the Xiānbēi, Qiāng, and Jié,
spreading them throughout the capital region.
These are all our deep enemies.
The Crown Prince alone, with only tens of thousands of weak troops, guards the capital.
I fear unforeseen changes may arise in our very heart and bosom,
which would be irremediable.
My stubborn folly
is truly not worth adopting;
but Wáng Jǐnglüè was an outstanding hero of his time.
Your Majesty often compared him to Zhūgě Wǔhóu.
Zhūgě Liàng's posthumous title was Wǔhóu.
See the third year of Níngkāng in the previous scroll.
At this time, many court officials offered remonstrance.
Fú Jiān said:
"With me attacking Jìn,
comparing the strength and weakness of the situation,
it is like a swift wind sweeping away autumn leaves.
Yet both inside and outside the court, all say it cannot be done.
This is truly what I do not understand!"
Crown Prince Fú Hóng said:
"This year's celestial alignment favors Wú's region,
and moreover the ruler of Jìn is without fault. If the great campaign is not victorious,
I fear our prestige will be damaged abroad,
and our resources and strength exhausted internally.
This is why all below doubt it!"
Fú Jiān said:
"In the past when I destroyed Yān,
I also acted against the celestial alignment and was victorious.
Heaven's will is truly hard to know.
When Qín destroyed the six states,
were the rulers of the six states all tyrannical and cruel?"
Champion General, Capital Governor Mùróng Chuí
'Champion'
means Champion General.
The Jìn Shū Zǎijì records,
generally writing the general's title without attaching 'general';
the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn follows this.
'Guàn'
is pronounced gǔ wàn fān.
"The weak are annexed by the strong,
the small are annexed by the large.
This is the natural principle and trend,
not hard to understand.
With Your Majesty's divine martiality responding to the times,
might extending beyond the seas,
a million tiger-like troops,
Hán and Bái filling the court—
Hán and Bái
refer to Hán Xìn and Bái Qǐ.
It means Qín has many fine generals.
That Jìn alone defies the royal command—
how can we leave it to be passed on to our descendants!
The Shī says:
'Planners are many,
therefore nothing is accomplished.'
These are words from the Shī, Xiǎomín.
Why must we broadly consult the court multitude!
When Jìn Wǔ conquered Wú,
he relied only on two or three ministers like Zhāng and Dù.
If he had followed the words of the court multitude,
how could he have achieved the merit of unification!"
This refers to Zhāng Huá and Dù Yù.
The event is seen in scroll 80, the fifth year of Xiánníng of Wǔ Dì.
'Cháo'
is pronounced zhí yáo fān.
"The one who will settle the world with me
is you alone."
He bestowed five hundred bolts of silk.
Fú Jiān was determined to seize Jiāngdōng,
unable to sleep until dawn.
Yángpíng Gōng Fú Róng remonstrated:
"'Knowing contentment avoids disgrace,
knowing when to stop avoids danger.'
Words from the Lǎozǐ, Dàodéjīng, Lìjiè Piān.
There has never been one who did not perish.
Moreover, our state is originally of the Róngdí.
The legitimate calendar surely does not belong to others.
'Huì'
means essentially,
meaning that essentially the legitimate calendar of the Central Plains is transmitted,
not belonging to the barbarians.
However, the Central Plains' legitimate line,
Heaven's will surely will not sever it."
Fú Jiān said:
"The succession of emperors and kings,
how can it be constant?
It lies only where virtue resides!
Was Liú Shàn not a descendant of Hàn?
Yet he was ultimately destroyed by Wèi.
The reason you are not like me
is precisely because you suffer from not understanding adaptability!"
Fú Jiān had long trusted and respected the Buddhist monk Dào'ān.
Dào'ān was in Xiāngyáng.
When Fú Jiān captured Xiāngyáng,
he had him carried in a carriage to him.
In the eleventh month,
Fú Jiān and Dào'ān rode together in a carriage to tour the eastern park.
Fú Jiān said:
"I shall travel south with you to Wú and Yuè,
sail upon the Cháng Jiāng,
and face the vast sea.
Would that not be joyful!"
Dào'ān said:
"Your Majesty responds to Heaven and rules the world,
residing in the central land and controlling the four directions.
This is sufficient to compare gloriously with Yáo and Shùn.
Why must you comb the wind and bathe in rain,
managing distant regions!
Moreover, the southeast is low and damp,
pestilential qi easily gathers.
Yú Shùn traveled there and did not return,
the Great Yǔ went there and did not come back.
Yú Shùn made an imperial tour to the south,
and died in the wilderness of Cāngwú.
Yǔ made an imperial tour to the east,
and reached Kuàijī, where he died."
Fú Jiān said:
"Heaven gives birth to the multitude and establishes a ruler for them,
to shepherd them.
How dare I fear toil,
leaving that one region alone without receiving grace!
If it must be as you say,
then the ancient emperors and kings all had no campaigns!"
Dào'ān said:
"If it is truly unavoidable,
Your Majesty should station yourself at Luòyáng,
send envoys with a letter ahead,
and have the generals lead the six armies behind.
They will surely bow their heads and become your subjects.
There is no need to personally cross the Jiāng and Huái."
Fú Jiān did not listen.
The favored Lady Zhāng advised Jiān:
"I have heard that heaven and earth give birth to the myriad things,
and the sage kings govern the world,
all by following their natural course and complying with it.
Therefore, no endeavor fails to succeed.
Thus, the Yellow Emperor yoked oxen and rode horses,
because it suited their nature;
meaning that by following the nature of oxen and horses,
they could pull heavy loads and travel far.
He contained the nine marshes,
because it suited their configuration;
meaning that by following the high and low terrain,
he could cleanse the sources and embank the marshes.
He followed the seasons;
by sowing and planting in accordance with the heavenly seasons,
the hundred grains would ripen.
He followed the hearts of the people;
by employing troops in accordance with the people's hearts,
the world would submit.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
Without following these principles, one will fail.
Now, everyone at court and among the common people says that Jìn cannot be attacked.
Your Majesty alone is determined to carry it out.
I do not know what principle Your Majesty is following.
The Book of Documents says: 'Heaven's seeing and hearing come from our people's seeing and hearing.'
These are the words from the Counsels of Gāo Yáo.
How much more so for humans!
I have also heard that when a king sends out his army,
he must observe the way of heaven above,
and comply with the people's hearts below.
Now, the people's hearts are already not in favor.
Let us examine the way of heaven.
A proverb says: 'When chickens crow at night, it is unfavorable for marching an army;
when dogs gather and howl, palaces and houses will become empty;
when weapons move and horses startle,
the army will be defeated and not return.'
Since autumn and winter,
many chickens have crowed at night,
dogs have gathered and howled mournfully,
stable horses have often been startled,
and weapons in the armory have moved on their own, making sounds.
These are all inauspicious signs for sending out an army."
Jiān said:
"Matters of the army and campaigns
are not something a woman should interfere with!"
Jiān's youngest son, the Duke of Zhōngshān, Shēn, was most favored.
He also advised:
"I have heard that the rise and fall of a state
depends on the employment or dismissal of worthy men.
Now, Yángpíng Gōng
is the chief strategist of the state,
yet Your Majesty opposes him.
Jìn has Xiè Ān and Huán Chōng,
yet Your Majesty attacks them.
I am privately perplexed by this!"
Jiān said:
"Great affairs of the world—
how could a child understand them!"
10. In Qín, Liú Lán was sent to combat locusts,
but through autumn and winter, he could not eliminate them.
In the twelfth month,
the responsible officials petitioned to summon Lán to the Court of Judicial Review.
The King of Qín, Jiān, said:
"Disasters descend from heaven;
they are not something human strength can remove.
This is due to my failures in governance.
What crime has Lán committed?"
That year,
Qín had a great harvest.
The best fields yielded seventy dàn per mǔ,
and the poorest yielded thirty dàn.
Locusts did not go beyond the borders of Yōuzhōu,
and did not eat hemp or beans.
The best fields yielded one hundred dàn per mǔ,
and the poorest yielded fifty dàn.
When things go against the norm, it is an omen.
Locusts causing disasters is an old story.
Locusts being born but not eating the five grains
is a great omen.
Farmers toil in the fields and exert strength in cultivation,
until the autumn harvest.
Since ancient times,
there has never been a principle of harvesting one hundred dàn or seventy dàn per mǔ.
And harvesting fifty dàn or thirty dàn per mǔ
has also never been heard of.
If it were truly so,
would it not also be a great anomaly?
If it were not so,
then the prefectures and counties were colluding to deceive and flatter to mislead the emperor,
which is also a great inauspicious sign.
It was fitting that Qín perished!
Wáng Chóngwǔ punctuated; Róng Zhàozǔ and Niè Chóngqí reviewed.
Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command.
Later student from Tiāntāi
Xiàozōng Xiàowǔ Huángdì, first part, lower section
Eighth year of Tàiyuán (Guǐwèi, 383)
1. Spring,
first month,
Qín's Lǚ Guāng set out from Cháng'ān,
with the King of Shànshàn, Xiūmìtuó, and the King of Chēshī Qiánbù, Mítián, as guides.
2. Third month,
dīngsì day,
a great amnesty was declared.
3. Summer,
fifth month,
Huán Chōng led a host of one hundred thousand to attack Qín,
attacking Xiāngyáng;
he sent the Former General Liú Bō and others to attack the various cities north of the Miǎn River;
the Assistant General Yáng Liàng attacked Shǔ,
capturing five cities,
and advanced to attack Fúchéng;
the Soaring Hawk General Guō Quán attacked Wǔdāng.
Sixth month,
Chōng's separate generals attacked Wànsuì and Zhùyáng,
capturing them.
Wànsuì,
the name of a city,
was likely near Zhùyáng.
Zhùyáng County,
in the Hàn dynasty belonged to Nányáng Commandery,
in Jìn belonged to Shùnyáng Commandery;
it was the state of the Earl of Gǔ in the Spring and Autumn period;
in the Táng dynasty, it was Gǔchéng County of Xiāngzhōu.
Shī Gǔ said: Zhù,
pronounced zhú.
Guān,
therefore wán fān.
Qí,
qí jì fān.
The Rear General Zhāng Cì and the Infantry Commandant Yáo Cháng relieved Fúchéng;
Ruì stationed his army at Xīnyě,
Chuí stationed his army at Dèngchéng.
Dèngchéng County,
belonged to Xiāngyáng Commandery,
likely established in the Jìn dynasty.
Autumn,
seventh month,
Guō Quán and the Champion General Huán Shíqián defeated Zhāng Chóng at Wǔdāng,
plundering two thousand households and returning.
The Duke of Jùlù, Ruì, sent Mùróng Chuí as the vanguard,
advancing to the Miǎn River.
Chuí ordered the soldiers at night to each hold ten torches,
tied to tree branches,
illuminating several tens of lǐ.
Chōng became fearful,
retreated, and returned to Shàngmíng.
Chōng garrisoned Shàngmíng; see the second year of the previous volume.
Yáng Liàng led his troops back.
Chōng petitioned for his elder brother's son, Shí Mín, to be appointed as the Administrator of Xiāngchéng,
and to garrison Xiàkǒu.
Chōng himself requested to be appointed as the Governor of Jiāngzhōu;
an edict granted it.
4 The King of Qín, Fú Jiān, issued an edict for a massive invasion.
From every ten adult males among the people, one soldier was conscripted.
Sons from respectable families under the age of twenty,
who were talented and brave,
were all appointed as Yǔlín Guards.
He also said:
"I appoint Sīmǎ Chāngmíng as the Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
Xiè Ān as the Minister of Personnel,
and Huán Chōng as Palace Attendant.
The return of our forces is not far off.
This means, judging by the situation,
the time to conquer Jìn
is close at hand,
and the return of our army is imminent.
'Return'
is pronounced like 'xuán,'
but can also be read as usual.
Over thirty thousand cavalrymen from respectable families arrived,
and Zhào Shèngzhī, the Registrar of Qínzhōu,
was appointed as the Commander of the Youth Army.
The title 'Commander' as an official position
originated here.
'Shào'
is pronounced as in 'shī zhào fān.'
The same applies below.
The court officials all opposed Fú Jiān's campaign,
but only Mùróng Chuí, Yáo Chāng, and the sons from respectable families encouraged it.
The Duke of Yángpíng, Fú Róng, said to Fú Jiān:
"The Xiānbēi and Qiāng barbarians
are our enemies.
Mùróng Chuí
is a Xiānbēi;
Yáo Chāng
is a Qiāng.
Their states were both destroyed by Qín.
Although they claim to submit,
they are actually enemies.
How can we follow
the strategies they propose!
The youths from respectable families are all sons of wealthy families,
unfamiliar with military affairs.
They merely flatter and cater to Your Majesty's wishes.
'Cater'
means to align with.
To undertake such a major campaign lightly,
I fear not only will we fail to achieve success,
but there will also be future troubles.
Regret will be too late!"
Fú Jiān did not listen.
In the eighth month,
on the day Wùwǔ,
Fú Jiān sent the Duke of Yángpíng, Fú Róng, to command the vanguard of 250,000 infantry and cavalry, including Zhāng Cì and Mùróng Chuí.
He appointed Yáo Chāng, the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, as General of Soaring Dragons, overseeing military affairs in Yìzhōu and Liángzhōu.
Fú Jiān said to Yáo Chāng:
"In the past, I established my enterprise as General of Soaring Dragons.
Fú Jiān, as General of Soaring Dragons, killed Fú Shēng
and obtained the state of Qín.
'Soaring'
is pronounced as 'sī jiāng fān.'
You must strive hard!"
General of the Left Dòu Chōng said:
"A king should not speak in jest.
This is an ominous sign!"
Fú Jiān fell silent.
Mùróng Kǎi and Mùróng Shào said to Mùróng Chuí:
"The ruler has become excessively arrogant and conceited.
Uncle, the task of restoring our dynasty
lies in this campaign!"
Mùróng Chuí said:
"Indeed.
Without you,
who could accomplish it with me!"
By this point,
Mùróng Chuí knew Fú Jiān would surely be defeated,
and only then did he speak openly with his nephews.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
Fú Jiān departed from Cháng'ān,
with over 600,000 soldiers
and 270,000 cavalry.
Banners and drums stretched as far as the eye could see,
covering a thousand lǐ from front to rear.
In the ninth month,
Fú Jiān reached Xiàngchéng,
while troops from Liángzhōu had just arrived at Xiányáng,
troops from Shǔ and Hàn were descending along the river,
and troops from Yōuzhōu and Jìzhōu had reached Péngchéng.
From east to west, the forces spanned ten thousand lǐ,
advancing simultaneously by land and water,
with tens of thousands of supply vessels.
The Duke of Yángpíng, Fú Róng, and others led 300,000 troops
and arrived first at Yǐngkǒu.
This is where the Yǐng River flows into the Huái River.
The Geographical Records state: The Yǐng River originates from Yángqián Mountain in Yángchéng County,
flowing east to Xiàcài, where it enters the Huái River.
An edict appointed Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat Xiè Shí as General Who Conquers Barbarians and Grand Commander of the Expeditionary Force,
and Xiè Xuán, Inspector of Xúzhōu and Yǎnzhōu, as Vanguard Commander,
joining Assistant General of the State Xiè Yǎn and General of the Western Section Huán Yī, leading a total of 80,000 troops to resist the enemy.
General of Soaring Dragons Hú Bīn was sent with 5,000 naval troops to reinforce Shòuyáng.
Xiè Yǎn
was the son of Xiè Ān.
At this time, the Qín forces were formidable,
and the capital was in a state of panic.
Xiè Xuán entered
and asked Xiè Ān for a strategy.
Xiè Ān remained calm and composed.
'Calm'
means tranquil,
even.
This means he was as composed as on ordinary days.
"Separate orders have already been issued."
After that, he fell silent.
Xiè Xuán did not dare to speak further,
so he had Zhāng Xuán make another request.
Xiè Ān then ordered his carriage and went out to his mountain villa for an excursion,
gathering all his relatives and friends.
He played a game of wéiqí with Xiè Xuán, wagering the villa.
Xiè Ān's wéiqí skills were usually inferior to Xiè Xuán's,
but on that day,
Xiè Xuán was fearful,
and even as an equal opponent, he could not win.
'Equal opponent'
means placing stones to compete for advantage,
with strategies evenly matched.
Xiè Xuán's mind was not on the game,
so he could not defeat Xiè Ān.
They did not return until nightfall.
Huán Chōng was deeply concerned about the security of the capital,
and sent 3,000 elite troops to guard the capital.
Xiè Ān firmly refused them,
saying:
"The court's arrangements have already been decided,
and there is no shortage of troops or equipment.
The western border should retain them for defense."
Huán Chōng sighed to his subordinates:
The assistants in the various regional offices are called subordinates.
"Xiè Ānshí has the capacity for governance at court,
but he is unfamiliar with military strategy.
Now, with a formidable enemy approaching,
he is leisurely engaging in conversation,
sending inexperienced youths to resist them.
Their forces are few and weak.
The outcome of the empire's affairs is already clear.
We will soon be wearing barbarian garments!"
5 Lángyé Prince Dàozǐ was appointed to oversee the six departments of the Imperial Secretariat.
The position of overseeing the six departments of the Imperial Secretariat
began with Liú Cōng.
6 In winter,
in the tenth month,
the Qín general Yángpíng Gōng Fú Róng and others attacked Shòuyáng;
on Guǐyǒu day,
they captured it,
and captured the Pínglǔ General Xú Yuánxǐ and others.
Fú Róng appointed his staff officer, Guō Bāo from Hénán, as the Tàishǒu of Huáinán.
The Huáinán commandery was originally administered from Shòuyáng,
and after Qín obtained it,
they appointed Guō Bāo as its Tàishǒu.
Dù Yù said: Southeast of Yúndù county in Jiāngxià commandery was the city of Yún.
Yún,
yú fēn fān.
They retreated to defend Xiáshí.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: The Huái River flows east past the north of Shòuchūn county,
and to the right is the Héféi River;
it then flows north through a mountain gorge,
which is called Xiáshí,
where two fortresses were built on the mountains on opposite banks,
to guard the strategic crossing.
Dù Yòu said: Xiáshí
is present-day Xiàcài county in Rǔyīn commandery.
The Qín general Wèi Jiāngjūn Liáng Chéng and others led fifty thousand troops to station at Luòjiàn,
building a barrier on the Huái River to block the eastern forces.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: The Luòjiàn receives water from the Sǐmǎ Táng,
flows north past Qínxū,
and empties into the Huái River,
which is called Luòkǒu.
Shuài,
read as shuài;
same below.
They feared Liáng Chéng and did not dare advance.
Hú Bīn’s provisions were exhausted,
and he secretly sent a messenger to report to Xiè Shí and others, saying:
“Now the enemy is strong and our provisions are exhausted,
I fear we may not see the main army again!”
The Qín men captured the messenger,
and sent him to Yángpíng Gōng Fú Róng.
Fú Róng swiftly sent a messenger to report to the Qín king Fú Jiān, saying:
“The enemy is few and easy to capture,
but I fear they may escape,
so we should quickly advance upon them!”
Fú Jiān then left the main army at Xiàngchéng,
and led eight thousand light cavalry,
traveling day and night to join Fú Róng at Shòuyáng.
He sent the Shàngshū Zhū Xù to persuade Xiè Shí and others,
believing that:
“The disparity in strength is great,
so it would be better to surrender quickly.”
In the third year,
Fú Jiān captured Zhū Xù at Xiāngyáng,
and appointed him as Dùzhī Shàngshū.
Shuō,
shū ruì fān.
Xiáng,
hù jiāng fān.
“If all of Qín’s million troops arrive,
it will truly be difficult to oppose them.
Now, while their various armies have not yet assembled,
we should quickly attack them;
if we defeat their vanguard,
then their morale will be broken,
and we can then defeat them.”
Xiè Shí heard that Fú Jiān was at Shòuyáng,
and was greatly afraid,
wanting to avoid battle to wear down the Qín army.
Xiè Yǎn urged Xiè Shí to follow Zhū Xù’s advice.
In the eleventh month,
Xiè Xuán sent the Guǎnglíng Xiàng Liú Láozhī to lead five thousand elite troops toward Luòjiàn.
When they were still ten lǐ away,
Liáng Chéng blocked the stream and formed a battle array to await them.
Liú Láozhī advanced directly and crossed the water,
attacked Liáng Chéng,
and heavily defeated him,
beheading Liáng Chéng and the Yìyáng Tàishǒu Wáng Yǒng;
Cáo Wèi divided Xīyáng and Qíchūn,
and established Yìyáng commandery;
Qín had not yet gained control of that territory,
and Wáng Yǒng only held the title of Tàishǒu.
Yìyáng,
in the Táng dynasty was the territory of the three prefectures of Guāng, Qí, and Huáng.
The Qín infantry and cavalry collapsed,
and they rushed toward the Huái River,
with fifteen thousand soldiers dying,
and they captured the Qín Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Xiǎn and others,
seizing all their weapons and military supplies.
Thereupon, the various armies of Xiè Shí and others
advanced by water and land in succession.
The Qín king Fú Jiān and Yángpíng Gōng Fú Róng ascended the walls of Shòuyáng to observe them,
and saw that the Jìn troops were arrayed in strict formation,
and also saw the grass and trees on Bāgōng Mountain, all of which they thought were Jìn soldiers.
Bāgōng Mountain is located four lǐ north of present-day Shòuchūn county.
Legend has it that Hàn Huáinán King Ān was fond of immortals,
when suddenly eight old men, all with white hair and beards,
came to his gate seeking an audience.
The gatekeeper said:
“Our king seeks long life,
and now you gentlemen have no method to halt aging,
so I dare not announce you.”
The eight old men all transformed into youths.
Thus a temple was built on the mountain.
Some say that those now receiving sacrifices on this mountain
are actually Zuǒ Wú, Zhū Jiāo, Wǔ Bèi, Léi Bèi, and the other eight,
all retainers of the Huáinán King,
but the world mistakes the eight old men for immortals,
which is an error.
“These are also formidable enemies,
how can they be called weak!”
Crestfallen, he began to show a fearful expression.
The Qín troops pressed close to the Féi River and formed their battle array,
and the Jìn troops could not cross.
Xiè Xuán sent a messenger to say to Yángpíng Gōng Fú Róng:
“You have advanced deep with your army isolated,
and have deployed your array close to the water,
this is a strategy for prolonging the conflict,
not one seeking a quick battle.
If you shift your array slightly back,
to allow the Jìn troops to cross,
and decide victory or defeat,
would that not be good!”
The various Qín generals all said:
“We are many and they are few,
it would be better to block them,
and prevent them from coming ashore,
to ensure complete safety.”
Fú Jiān said:
“Just lead the troops to retreat slightly,
let them cross halfway,
and then I will use iron cavalry to press upon and kill them,
and there will be no chance of not winning!”
Fú Róng also thought this was right,
and so waved his troops to retreat.
The Qín troops then retreated,
and could not be stopped again.
When two arrays face each other,
the side that retreats first is defeated,
this is the constant principle of warfare.
Fù,
fú yòu fān.
Fú Róng galloped through the array,
wanting to lead those retreating,
but his horse fell,
and he was killed by Jìn soldiers,
and the Qín troops then collapsed.
Xiè Xuán and others took advantage of the victory to pursue and attack,
reaching Qīnggāng;
Qīnggāng is thirty lǐ from present-day Shòuchūn county.
Those who died by trampling each other
covered the fields and choked the streams.
This means the defeated troops trampled each other,
and died piled upon one another.
Jiè,
cí yè fān.
Sāi,
xī zé fān.
They all thought the Jìn troops were about to arrive,
and dared not rest day or night,
traveling through grass and sleeping in the open.
Traveling through grass means
walking through grass,
not daring to take the mountain paths;
sleeping in the open means
camping in the wild,
not daring to enter people’s homes;
all because they feared the pursuing troops.
Seven or eight out of ten died.
Initially,
when the Qín troops retreated slightly,
Zhū Xù, who was behind the array, shouted:
“The Qín troops are defeated!”
The multitude then fled in great disorder.
Zhū Xù thereupon, together with Zhāng Tiānxí and Xú Yuánxǐ, all came over to our side.
They captured the mica carriage that the Qín king Fú Jiān rode in.
They recaptured Shòuyáng,
and captured its Huáinán Tàishǒu Guō Bāo.
Jìn recaptured Shòuyáng,
so the Tàishǒu appointed by Qín was captured.
Fú Jiān was hit by a stray arrow,
and fled alone on horseback to the north of the Huái River.
He was extremely hungry,
and a commoner offered him a pot of cooked rice and a pig leg.
Fú Jiān ate it,
and bestowed ten bolts of silk,
and ten catties of silk floss.
The man declined, saying:
“Your Majesty grew weary of peace and pleasure,
and brought this danger and hardship upon yourself.
I am Your Majesty’s subject,
and Your Majesty is my lord,
how can a subject feeding his lord seek reward!”
He turned and left without looking back.
Fú Jiān said to Lady Zhāng:
“What face do I have now to govern the empire!”
Tears streamed down his face.
At this time,
all the armies were routed,
only the thirty thousand troops led by Mùróng Chuí remained intact.
Chuí had separately attacked Yúnchéng,
and did not participate in the Battle of Féishuǐ.
Moreover, he maintained strict military discipline,
therefore, while all other armies were routed, Chuí's army alone remained intact.
The character "jiàng" (將) is pronounced with the falling tone, as in "liàng" (亮).
The heir apparent, Bǎo, said to Chuí:
"Our family and state have been overthrown.
The Mandate of Heaven and the hearts of the people all belong to Your Majesty.
It is only that the time and fortune have not yet arrived,
therefore we have concealed our traces and hidden ourselves.
Now the ruler of Qín has been defeated in battle,
and has entrusted himself to us.
This is Heaven providing us with an opportunity to restore the Yān dynasty.
This moment must not be lost.
I hope you will not, for the sake of slight personal favor and sentiment, forget the importance of the altars of state!"
"Slight personal favor and sentiment" refers to Fú Jiān's generous treatment of Chuí and his sons.
"Your words are correct.
However, he has entrusted his life to me with sincere devotion.
How can I harm him!
If Heaven has indeed abandoned him,
there is no need to worry that he will not perish.
It is better to protect him in his peril to repay his kindness,
and gradually await his internal conflicts to plot against him.
This way, we neither betray our original intentions,
and moreover can righteously take possession of the world."
These words of Mùróng Chuí
still show the bearing of a ruler.
"When Qín was strong, it annexed Yān.
Now that Qín is weak, we plot against it.
This is to avenge our shame,
not to betray our original intentions.
Why should you, Elder Brother, not seize this opportunity,
and instead release tens of thousands of troops to hand them over to others?"
Chuí said:
"In the past, I was not tolerated by the Grand Tutor,
and had nowhere to place myself.
I fled to Qín to escape death.
See the fourth year of the Tàihé era of Duke Hǎixī, in scroll one hundred and two.
I received the utmost kindness and courtesy.
Later, I was again betrayed by Wáng Měng,
and had no way to clear myself.
The ruler of Qín alone was able to vindicate me.
See the fifth year of Tàihé.
If the fortune of the Dí people is indeed exhausted,
I should gather and pacify the lands east of the passes,
to restore our ancestral enterprise.
The lands west of the passes will certainly not be ours."
The Acting Army Advisor Zhào Qiū said:
"Your Excellency is destined to revive and restore the Yān dynasty,
as recorded in the prophetic charts and texts.
Now the heavenly timing has arrived,
what more are you waiting for!
If you kill the ruler of Qín,
occupy Yèdū and march westward with drums beating,
then the Three Qín regions will also no longer belong to the Fú clan!"
Many of Chuí's relatives and partisans urged him to kill Fú Jiān.
Chuí did not follow any of them,
and instead handed over all his troops to Jiān.
The General Who Pacifies the South, Mùróng Wěi, was stationed at Yúnchéng.
Hearing of Jiān's defeat,
he abandoned his troops and fled.
When he reached Xíngyáng,
Mùróng Dé again urged Wěi to raise troops to restore the Yān dynasty.
Wěi did not comply.
Xiè Ān received the courier's report,
and learned that the Qín army had been defeated.
At the time, he was playing Go with a guest.
He took the letter and placed it on the bed,
showing not the slightest sign of joy.
"Shè" (攝) means to take or collect.
The guest asked him about it.
He slowly replied:
"The youngsters have finally defeated the enemy."
After the game ended,
he returned inside.
While crossing the threshold,
he did not notice that the teeth of his clogs had broken.
This describes his extreme joy.
The historian's words indicate that Ān suppressed his emotions to maintain composure.
A minister finds joy in bringing peace to the altars of state.
A great enemy pressed upon the border.
They were defeated in a single battle.
How could he not be joyful!
The breaking of his clog teeth
is also not something to criticize Ān for.
On the day Dīnghài,
Xiè Shí and others returned to Jiànkāng.
They obtained Qín's court musicians,
who were able to perform the old music.
Thereupon, the ancestral temples for the first time were equipped with music of metal and stone instruments.
During the chaos of the Yǒngjiā era,
musicians and musical instruments were all lost to Liú and Shí.
When Jiāngzuǒ was first established,
the ancestral temples had neither proper ceremonial music nor musicians.
The offices of the Grand Music Master and the Drum and Wind Instrument Master were abolished.
After this, they somewhat obtained music for sacrificial hymns and banquet performances,
but it was still incomplete.
At the end of the Tàiníng era,
Emperor Míng again consulted Ruǎn Fú and others to augment it.
During the Xiánhé era,
Emperor Chéng then re-established the office of the Grand Music Master,
gathered surviving musicians,
but still did not have metal and stone instruments.
When Mùróng Jùn pacified Rǎn Mǐn,
amidst the warfare,
quite a few musicians from Yè came over.
When Xiè Shàng garrisoned Shòuyáng,
he collected musicians to prepare for the Grand Music,
and also made stone chimes.
Ceremonial music then began to be somewhat complete.
When Wáng Měng pacified Yè,
the music obtained by the Mùróng clan
again entered the region west of the passes.
Now, having defeated Fú Jiān,
they captured his musicians such as Yáng Shǔ,
who were well-versed in the old music.
Thereupon, metal and stone instruments were finally complete.
On the day Yǐwèi,
Zhāng Tiānxì was appointed as a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
The character "sàn" (散) is pronounced with the falling-rising tone, as in "sǐ dǎn" (悉亶).
The character "qí" (騎) is pronounced with the falling tone, as in "qí jì" (奇寄).
7. The Qín king, Fú Jiān, gathered his scattered forces.
By the time he reached Luòyáng,
he had over a hundred thousand troops.
The officials, ceremonial objects, and military appearance were roughly restored.
Mùróng Nóng said to Mùróng Chuí:
"The Honored One does not force others into peril,
Honored One,
refers to his father, Chuí.
Mùróng Lìng also called Chuí 'Honored One',
likely a common form of address between father and son.
Nóng has heard the secret record say: 'Yān's revival should be at Héyáng.'
Picking fruit before it is ripe versus after it falls naturally,
differs by no more than ten days or so,
yet the difficulty and ease, the beauty and ugliness,
are vastly different!"
Chuí in his heart approved of his words.
Traveling to Miǎnchí,
he said to Jiān:
"The people of the northern borderlands,
hearing of the imperial army's setback,
are lightly inciting each other.
I request to take the imperial edict to pacify, console, and settle them,
and on the way, pay a visit to the ancestral tombs and temples."
Chuí wished to take this journey to visit his grandfather's and father's tombs and temples.
Quán Yì advised:
"The state's army has recently been defeated,
all quarters harbor thoughts of disloyalty.
We should summon and gather the famous generals,
stationing them in the capital,
to solidify the root and foundation,
and pacify the branches and leaves.
Chuí's courage and strategy surpass others,
for generations he was a powerful figure in the eastern Xià region.
Recently he came here to avoid disaster,
but his ambition surely is not merely to become a champion general!
He is like a raised eagle:
when hungry it clings to a person,
but whenever it hears the wind and gale rise,
it always harbors the ambition to soar to the clouds.
We should precisely tighten its leash and cage,
Biāo,
is a whirling wind.
The commentary says: A swift wind rising from below upwards is called biāo,
pronounced bēi yáo fān.
Tāo,
tā dāo fān;
a silk rope,
used to tether an eagle.
How can we let it do as it pleases!"
Jiān said:
"Your words are correct.
However, I have already promised him.
Even a common man does not go back on his word,
Kǒng Ānguó said: To 'eat one's words' means,
to consume one's words entirely,
false and insincere.
If the Mandate of Heaven has its declines and revivals,
it certainly cannot be changed by human intelligence or strength."
Yì said:
"Your Majesty values minor trustworthiness and disregards the altars of state.
I foresee his departure and not his return.
The chaos east of the passes,
will begin from this."
Jiān did not listen.
He sent generals Lǐ Mán, Mǐn Liàng, and Yǐn Gù
to lead three thousand troops to escort Chuí.
He also sent the Valiant Cavalry General Shí Yuè to lead three thousand elite soldiers to garrison Yè,
the Swift Cavalry General Zhāng Cì to lead five thousand Imperial Forest Guards to garrison Bīngzhōu,
and the Garrison Army General Máo Dāng to lead four thousand troops to garrison Luòyáng.
Quán Yì secretly dispatched strong men to intercept Chuí at the empty granary south of the Hé Bridge.
Chuí grew suspicious,
and from Liángmǎ Tái, he made a raft of bundled reeds to cross.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: In Báimǎ County of Dōngjùn, there is a Liángchéng,
the Hé River passes north of it;
there is a Divine Horse Pavilion,
about twenty lǐ west of the Báimǎ Ferry.
It is solidly built with layered structures,
two hundred paces from north to south,
and about fifty paces from east to west.
Now, considering that the Divine Horse Pavilion is in Dōngjùn,
and Báimǎ is directly opposite the Líyáng bank,
how could Chuí bypass Xíng and Luò to reach this point to cross the river!
This Liángmǎ Tái must be west of the Fùpíng Jīn Bridge.
Liángmǎ Tái,
got its name because people of old bathed horses in the river islets here.
After bathing,
they drove the horses to higher ground to cool off,
hence the name.
Mounting his own horse,
he headed with his servant towards the Hé Bridge.
Diǎnjūn,
likely an official of the princely state,
appointed when Chuí was Prince of Wú in Yān.
Tóng yī,
yú jì fān.
Qù,
qī yù fān.
They galloped together and escaped.
In the twelfth month,
the Qín king Jiān reached Cháng'ān.
He mourned Yángpíng Gōng and then entered,
posthumously honoring him as Duke Āi.
He issued a great amnesty,
and exempted the families of those who died in service from taxes.
8 On Gēngwǔ,
a great amnesty was issued.
Xiè Shí was appointed as President of the Imperial Secretariat.
Xiè Xuán was promoted to the title of Former General;
he firmly declined and did not accept.
9 Xiè Ān's son-in-law Wáng Guóbǎo,
was the son of Wáng Tǎnzhī.
Ān disliked his character,
often suppressing him and not employing him,
appointing him only as a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat.
Guóbǎo, considering himself from a prestigious clan,
believed that by precedent one should only serve in the Bureau of Personnel,
not in other bureaus.
Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat:
under the Jìn system, there were thirty-five bureaus,
with twenty-three gentlemen appointed,
overseeing each other in turn.
By the time of Jiāngzuǒ,
the ten bureaus of Direct Affairs, Right People, Military Colonies, Chariots, Separate Troops, Capital Troops, Cavalry, Left and Right Gentlemen, and Transport were gone.
After the reigns of Kāng and Mù,
the two bureaus of Yu and Two Thousand Shí were also gone,

leaving only the eighteen bureaus: Palace, Sacrificial, Personnel, Ceremonial, Three Excellencies, Comparative, Treasury, Granaries, Finance, Capital Officials, Left People, Construction, Waterways, Reception, Carriages and Cavalry, Storehouses, Central Troops, and Outer Troops.
Later, the bureaus of Reception, Construction, and Waterways were abolished,
leaving fifteen bureaus,
with the Bureau of Personnel being the most prestigious selection.
Because of this, he resented Ān.
Guóbǎo's paternal cousin was married to the Prince of Kuàijī, Dàozǐ.
The Emperor and Dàozǐ were both fond of wine,
associating intimately with flatterers and sycophants.
Guóbǎo then slandered Ān to Dàozǐ,
making him sow discord between Ān and the Emperor.
Ān's achievements and fame were already great,
and those of treacherous and ambitious nature seeking advancement,
often disparaged and belittled Ān.
The Emperor thus gradually grew distant and suspicious of him.
10 Initially, the prohibition on alcohol was lifted.
During the Jiàn'ān era of Hàn,
Duke Cáo strictly prohibited alcohol.
Five shí per person.
In the fifth year of Xiánhé,
Emperor Chéng began measuring the people's fields,
taking one-tenth,
at a rate of three shēng of rice per mǔ.
When Emperor Āi ascended the throne,
he reduced the land tax,
to two shēng per mǔ.
In the second year of Tàiyuán,
the Emperor abolished the system of measuring fields to collect rent,
and from the dukes and princes down,
levied a tax of three hú per person,
exempting only those currently in service.
By this year,
the rice tax was increased again,
to five shí per person.
11 Qín's Lǚ Guāng traveled over three hundred lǐ of shifting sands.
Starting from Yùmén,
he crossed the shifting sands,
traveled west to Shànshàn,
then north to Chēshī.
Also,
the state of Qiěmò is west of Shànshàn.
Northwest of that state,
there are shifting sands several hundred lǐ wide.
In summer, there are hot winds,
a hazard for travelers.
When the wind arrives,
only old camels know in advance,
immediately snorting and gathering to stand,
burying their mouths and noses in the sand.
People often use this as a sign,
and also immediately cover their noses and mouths with felt.
The wind is swift,
passing completely in a moment.
If one does not take precautions,
it will certainly lead to danger and death.
Sāng Qīn said: The shifting sands are located northwest of Jūyán County in Zhāngyè.
Dù Yòu said: The shifting sands are in Shāzhōu,
eighty lǐ west of Dūnhuáng Commandery.
Lì Dàoyuán said: The Ruò River enters the shifting sands.
Shifting sands,
flow along with the water.
It is also said to originate from Zhōng Mountain,
flowing west to the extreme Yānzī Mountain,
north of Xīhǎi Commandery;
the shifting sands also pass by Fúzhǔ,
traverse the state of Hèshì,
then pass east of Niǎoshān Mountain in Cháoyún State,
west past Kūn Mountain,
and emerge southwest from Guòyíng Mountain.
The Classic of the Great Wilderness says: Beyond the southwestern sea,
the shifting sands emerge.
[derivation]
Only the King of Qiūcí, Bóchún, resisted him,
fortifying the city and defending it stubbornly.
Guāng advanced his army and attacked it.
12. When King Fú Jiān of Qín invaded,
he appointed Qǐfú Guórén as Front General,
leading the vanguard cavalry.
It happened that Guórén's uncle Bùtuí rebelled in Lǒngxī,
so Jiān sent Guórén back to suppress him.
Guórén
had succeeded Sīfán in garrisoning Yǒngshì,
see the first year in the previous scroll.
He was greatly pleased,
and welcomed Guórén on the road.
Guórén set out wine,
and declared loudly:
"The Fú clan exhausts the people and indulges in warfare,
they are nearly doomed to perish.
I shall join with you all to establish an enterprise of our own."
After Jiān's defeat,
Guórén then coerced the various tribes,
attacking and annexing those who did not submit,
until his followers numbered over a hundred thousand.
13. Mùróng Chuí arrived at Ānyáng,
Ānyáng is southwest of Yèchéng.
Fú Pī heard that Chuí was coming from the north,
and suspected he intended to cause trouble,
yet he personally went to welcome him.
Zhào Qiū urged Chuí to seize Pī during the meeting,
and then occupy Yè to raise troops;
Chuí did not agree.
Pī plotted to attack Chuí,
but Attendant Gentleman Jiāng Ràng of Tiānshuǐ advised:
According to Jìn regulations,
a princely kingdom had two Attendant Gentlemen.
"Chuí's signs of rebellion are not yet evident,
yet if you, Illustrious Lord, rashly kill him,
it would not be in accordance with the duty of a subject;
it would be better to treat him with the courtesy due to a distinguished guest,
guard him closely with troops,
secretly report the situation,
and await an imperial decree before planning further."
Pī followed this advice,
and lodged Chuí west of Yè.
Chuí secretly plotted with former officials of Yān to restore the Yān dynasty.
It happened that the Dīnglíng Zhái Bīn raised troops in rebellion against Qín.
The Dīnglíng tribe
originally resided in Zhōngshān.
When Fú Jiān destroyed Yān,
he relocated them to Xīn'ān.
Bīn served Qín as a Gentleman of the Army of the Guards.
Bīn
is pronounced bīn.
King Fú Jiān of Qín sent a dispatch ordering Chuí to lead troops to suppress him.
Shí Yuè said to Pī:
"The royal army has recently been defeated,
the people's hearts are not yet settled,
those bearing guilt who have fled and hidden,
many long for disorder.
Thus, with the Dīnglíng's first call,
within ten days,
their numbers have already reached several thousand—
this is proof.
Mùróng Chuí,
a longstanding figure of prestige in Yān,
has the intention to revive the old enterprise.
Now if we further supply him with troops,
this is adding wings to a tiger."
Pī said:
"Having Chuí in Yè is like having a tiger sleeping on one's mat or a dragon in one's pond;
I constantly fear a sudden change close at hand.
Now sending him far away to the outside,
is that not better!
Moreover, Zhái Bīn is fierce and rebellious,
he certainly will not submit to Chuí.
Let the two tigers fight to the death,
and we can control them afterward—
this is the strategy of Biàn Zhuāngzǐ."
He then gave Chuí two thousand weak soldiers and worn-out armor and weapons,
and also sent General of Broad Martial Might Fú Fēilóng to lead a thousand Dī cavalry as Chuí's deputy.
He secretly instructed Fēilóng:
"Chuí is the commander of the three armies,
you are the general who will plot against Chuí.
Go forth,
and exert yourself!"
Prince Chéngdū Yǐng sent Hé Yǎn to plot against Wáng Jùn;
Yīn Hào sent Wèi Jǐng to plot against Yáo Xiāng;
Fú Pī sent Fú Fēilóng to plot against Mùróng Chuí—
their wisdom and strategy were insufficient to succeed,
their failures followed the same track.
Shuài (to lead)
is pronounced suǒ lèi fān.
Jiàng (general)
is pronounced jí liàng fān.
Chuí requested to enter Yè city to pay respects at the ancestral temple.
Yān's capital was Yè,
hence its ancestral temple was in Yè city.
He then secretly changed his attire and entered;
a station officer tried to stop him,
Chuí became angry,
killed the officer, burned the station, and left.
Shí Yuè said to Pī:
"Chuí dares to lightly insult a regional command,
killing an officer and burning a station—
his rebellious intent is already revealed.
We can use this to eliminate him."
Pī said:
"During the defeat at Huáinán,
Chuí protected and escorted the imperial carriage—
this merit cannot be forgotten."
Yuè said:
"Chuí was not even loyal to Yān,
how could he be completely loyal to us!
If we do not seize him now,
he will certainly be a future calamity."
Pī did not listen.
Yuè withdrew,
and told others:
"The lord and his father are fond of practicing petty benevolence,
disregarding the grand strategy.
In the end, they will be captured by others."
Pī and his father later indeed met the fate Yuè predicted.
Hào (fond of)
is pronounced hū dào fān.
Chuí left Mùróng Nóng, Mùróng Kǎi, and Mùróng Shào in Yè.
When he reached Tāngchí in Ānyáng,
Mǐn Liàng and Lǐ Pí came from Yè,
