mobilizing troops from Yànmén, Shànggǔ, and Dàijùn,
and stationing them at Fánzhì.
Mùyú Jù's son Wén and Mùyú Qián's son Cháng,
(Mùyú Jù appears in scroll 98, 6th year of the Yǒnghé era of Mùdì.)
(Mùyú Qián appears in scroll 101, 3rd year of the Xīngníng era of Āidì.)
Jù,
pronounced as gōu.
Knowing that the troops from the three commanderies were unwilling to campaign far away,
they therefore started a rebellion,
attacking Kùrén at night,
killing him,
stealing his fine horses,
and fleeing to Yān.
Gōngsūn Xī's troops, hearing of the disorder, disbanded on their own,
and Xī fled to Zhái Zhēn.
Kùrén's younger brother Tóujuàn took over leadership of Kùrén's troops.
48 Qín's Chánglè Gōng Pī sent Guāng Zuò and his参军 (cānjūn) Féng Fú to summon the Agile Cavalry General Zhāng Háo and the Governor of Bìngzhōu Wáng Téng from Jìnyáng for his own rescue;
Háo and Téng, due to their small numbers, were unable to go.
Qín considered Dèng Qiāng and Zhāng Háo to be match for ten thousand men.
At this time, Dèng Qiāng was already dead,
and Zhāng Háo ultimately could not save Qín from its fall.
This shows that those with mere courage but no strategy
contribute nothing to the outcome of success or failure.
Háo,
pronounced as qī lì fān.
(Pī) consulted with his aides.
His司马 (sīmǎ) Yáng Yīng requested to submit to Jìn on his own,
but Pī did not consent.
Meanwhile, Xiè Xuán had sent the Dragon Steed General Liú Láozhī and others to occupy Qiāo'áo,
the city of Qiāo'áo,
the seat of Jǐběi Commandery,
was a strategic location along the river.
Qiāo,
pronounced as qiū jiāo fān.
'Áo,
pronounced as niú jiāo fān.
Yáng Zhènghéng said: Qiāo,
pronounced as kǒu láo fān.
Dù Yòu said: Qiāo,
pronounced as kǒu jiāo fān.
'Áo,
pronounced as áo.
Shěn Yuē said: Jìn Huìdì separated Chénliú to form the Jìyáng principality.
Huátái,
was Hàn's Báimǎ,
and Táng's Huá Prefecture.
After Sòng's southern crossing,
they sent Fàn Chéngdà as an envoy north,
by which time the Yellow River had shifted southward,
and Huá Prefecture and Báimǎ County were both north of the river,
the ancient Huá Prefecture had already sunk into the river.
Shèngshuǐ was southwest of Jùn Prefecture,
accumulated water like a lake;
facing Jùn Prefecture city,
was Líyáng Mountain.
Jì,
pronounced as zǐ lǐ fān.
Héběi,
refers to the north bank of Huátái.
Liú Xí attacked and seized it by night,
driving them off,
and thus captured Líyáng.
Pī became fearful,
and sent his cousin Jiù and his参军 (cānjūn) Jiāo Kuí to request aid from Xuán,
sending a letter stating
"We wish to borrow a route to seek provisions,
and proceed west to aid the national crisis.
Once the relief forces have made contact,
we will hand over Yè to you.
If the western route is blocked,
and Cháng'ān falls,
we request to lead our troops to defend Yè city."
Kuí and his参军 (cānjūn) Jiāng Ràng secretly said to Yīng:
"Now that we are defeated and in such a state,
with Cháng'ān cut off,
survival is uncertain.
To humble ourselves and plead sincerely for provisions and aid,
we still fear we may not receive it;
yet His Lordship's arrogant spirit remains undiminished,
still setting up two alternatives,
so the endeavor is bound to fail.
We should properly write a memorial,
promising that when the royal army arrives,
we will personally submit and return south;
if he does not agree,
we can bind him by force and hand him over."
Yīng believed he had the power to control Pī himself,
(Yáng Yīng,
was Pī's elder brother,
hence he believed he had the power to control Pī.)
49 Xiè Xuán sent Téng Tiánzhī, the Grand Administrator of Jìnlíng, to cross the river and defend Líyáng.
Tiánzhī
was the great-grandson of Xiū.
Téng Xiū was a general of Wú,
and when Sūn Hào perished,
Xiū submitted to Jìn.
Xuán was additionally appointed Commander of the military affairs of the seven provinces: Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, Sī, Jì, Yōu, and Bìng.
50 When the Later Qín king Cháng heard that Mùróng Chōng was attacking Cháng'ān,
he assembled his aides to discuss whether to advance or halt,
they all said:
"Your Majesty should first take Cháng'ān,
establish a foundation,
and then plan for the four directions."
Cháng said:
"Not so.
The Yān people have raised troops because their masses have a desire to return home.
If they achieve their aim,
they certainly will not remain long in Guānzhōng.
I should move and station troops north of the ridges,
(Lǐngběi,
means north of Jiǔzōng,
encompassing all the areas of Xīnpíng, Běidì, and Āndì.)
to wait for Qín's fall and Yān's departure,
and then take it effortlessly."
He then left his eldest son Xīng to guard Běidì,
sent the General Who Pacifies the North Yáo Mù to guard Tóngguānchuān,
and personally led his troops to attack Xīnpíng.
初，
新平人殺其郡將，
秦王堅缺其城角以恥之，
石虎之末，
清河崔悅為新平相，
為郡人所殺。
悅子液仕堅，
為尚書郎，
自表父仇，
不同天地，
請還冀州。
堅愍之，
禁錮新平人，
缺其城角以恥之。
將，
即亮翻。
民望，
郡之賢豪，
為一郡所宗嚮者。
及後秦王萇至新平，
新平太守南安苟輔欲降之，
苟輔，
氐也，
秦之外戚。
降，
戶江翻；
下同。
「昔田單以一城存齊。
傑等皆新平人。
太康地志曰：汶山郡，
漢武帝立；
孝宣地節三年，
合蜀郡；
劉蜀又立郡。
蓮，
音輦。
汶，
讀曰岷。
田單事見四卷周赧王三十六年。
猶連城過百，
柰何遽為叛臣乎！ 」
輔喜曰：
「此吾志也；
但恐久而無救，
郡人橫被無辜。
諸君能爾，
吾豈顧生哉！ 」
於是憑城固守。
後秦為土山地道，
輔亦於內為之，
或戰地下，
或戰山上，
後秦之衆死者萬餘人。
輔詐降以誘萇，
萇將入城，
覺之而返；
輔伏兵邀擊，
幾獲之，
又殺萬餘人。
51隴西處士王嘉，
隱居倒虎山，
水經註：倒虎山在新豐縣南。
處，
昌呂翻。
能知未然；
秦人神之。
秦王堅、後秦王萇及慕容沖皆遣使迎之。
十一月，
嘉入長安，
衆聞之，
以為堅有福，
故聖人助之，
三輔堡壁及四山氐、羌歸堅者四萬餘人。
堅置嘉及沙門道安於外殿，
動靜咨之。
52燕慕容農自信都西擊丁零翟遼於魯口，
破之。
遼退屯無極，
農屯藳城以逼之。
無極縣，
漢屬中山，
晉省；
後魏復置無極縣，
唐末為祁州治所。
藳城縣，
前漢屬真定，
後漢屬鉅鹿，
晉省。
今所屯蓋故縣城也。
唐復置藳城縣，
屬恆州。
真之從兄也。
53鮮卑在長安城中者猶千餘人，
慕容紹之兄肅，
與慕容暐陰謀結鮮卑為亂。
十二月，
暐白堅，
以其子新昏，
請堅幸其家，
置酒，
欲伏兵殺之。
堅許之，
會天大雨，
不果往。
事覺，
堅召暐及肅，
肅曰：
「事必洩矣，
入則俱死。
今城內已嚴，
已嚴者，
謂鮮卑之衆也。
既得出門，
大衆便集。
暐不從，
遂俱入。
堅曰：
「吾相待何如，
而起此意？ 」
暐飾辭以對。
肅曰：
「家國事重，
何論意氣！ 」
意氣，
謂堅相待之厚。
乃殺暐及其宗族，
城內鮮卑無少長、男女，
皆殺之。
燕王垂幼子柔，
養於宦者宋牙家為牙子，
故得不坐，
與太子寶之子盛乘間得出，
奔慕容沖。
為後慕容盛等自長子歸燕張本。
間，
古莧翻。
54燕慕容麟、慕容農合兵襲翟遼，
大破之，
遼單騎奔翟真。
55燕王垂以秦長樂公丕猶據鄴不去，
乃更引兵圍鄴，
開其西走之路。
垂志在得鄴，
故開其走路，
所謂圍城為之缺也。
玄欲徵丕任子，
然後出兵；
逵固陳丕款誠，
幷述楊膺之意，
玄乃遣劉牢之、滕恬之等帥衆二萬救鄴。
丕告飢，
玄水陸運米二千斛以饋之。
56秦梁州刺史潘猛棄漢中，
奔長安。
梁州之地，
自此復歸于晉。
王崇武標點容肇祖聶崇岐覆校
司馬光
奉敕編集
後 學 天 台
烈宗孝武皇帝中之上
太元十年(乙酉 、三八五)
正月，
秦王堅朝饗㣥臣。
時長安饑，
人相食，
諸將歸，
吐肉以飼妻子。
2 慕容沖即皇帝位于阿房，
是為西燕。
沖有自得之志，
賞罰任情。
慕容盛年十三，
謂慕容柔曰：
「夫十人之長，
亦須才過九人，
然後得安。
今中山王才不逮人，
功未有成，
而驕汰已甚，
殆難濟乎！ 」
沖在前燕時封中山王。
汰，
侈也，
溢也。
史言慕容盛幼而有識略，
所以能自奮而有國。
盛、柔歸沖，
見上卷上年。
3 後秦王萇留諸將攻新平，
自引兵擊安定，
擒秦安西將軍勃海公珍，
嶺北諸城悉降之。
On the Jiǎyǐn day (4th),
the Qín king Fú Jiān fought with the ruler of Western Yān, Mùróng Chōng, at Chóubānqú,
and inflicted a major defeat upon him.
Mùróng Chuí had revived in Shāndōng,
while Chōng had declared his title in Guānzhōng,
therefore it is recorded as Western Yān to distinguish them.
On the Yǐmǎo day
they fought at Quèsāng,
and again defeated him.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
they fought at Báiqú.
Báiqú
is the canal dug by Lord Bái in the Hàn dynasty.
The Western Yān troops surrounded the Qín king Fú Jiān.
The Palace General Dèng Mài fought fiercely and repelled them,
allowing Jiān to escape.
On the Rénshēn day,
Chōng sent his Chief Secretary Gāo Gài to launch a night attack on Cháng'ān,
entering its southern city.
The Left General Dòu Chōng, former Forbidden Army General Lǐ Biàn, and others attacked and defeated them,
beheading eight hundred,
and dividing and eating their corpses.
On the Yǐhài day,
Gāo Gài led troops to attack the various fortifications north of the Wèi River.
The Crown Prince Fú Hóng fought him at Chéng'èr Bì.
Chéng'èr
was likely a person's name;
Guānzhōng was in great chaos,
and people built fortifications to protect themselves,
hence it became a place name.
Thirty thousand were beheaded.
5. The Yān Prince of Dàifāng, Mùróng Zuǒ, together with the Pacifying North General Píng Guī, jointly attacked Jī.
Wáng Yǒng's troops were repeatedly defeated.
In the second month,
Yǒng sent Sòng Chǎng to burn the palaces of Hélóng and Jī City,
and led thirty thousand followers to flee to Húguān;
Zuǒ and others entered Jī.
6. Mùróng Nóng led troops to join Mùróng Lín at Zhōngshān,
and together they attacked Zhái Zhēn.
Lín and Nóng first led several thousand cavalry to Chéngyíng,
to observe the situation.
Zhái Zhēn saw them,
deployed his troops, and came out.
The various generals wished to retreat,
but Nóng said:
"The Dīnglíng are not without strength and courage,
but Zhái Zhēn is cowardly.
Now select the elite,
aim for where Zhēn is and charge him.
When Zhēn flees,
his followers will certainly scatter.
Then block the gate and press them,
and we can kill them all."
He sent the Valiant Cavalry General Mùróng Guó to lead over a hundred cavalry to charge them.
Zhēn fled,
and his followers fought for the gate,
trampling each other,
with more than half dying.
They then captured the outer wall of Chéngyíng.
7. On the Guǐwèi day,
the Qín king Fú Jiān fought with the ruler of Western Yān, Mùróng Chōng, west of the city,
meaning west of Cháng'ān city.
They pursued the fleeing enemy to Āchéng.
Āchéng,
was the Āfáng Palace city,
Chōng's lair.
Jiān feared being ambushed by Chōng,
and led his troops back.
The lord of ten thousand chariots
certainly must not take risks seeking luck;
yet Qín's defeats were such,
riding the victorious spirit of the generals to seek a chance of success,
was possible;
leading the troops back,
why?
Huán (return),
read as Xuān.
8. On the Yǐyǒu day,
the Qín Governor of Yìzhōu, Wáng Guǎng, appointed the Shǔ man, Administrator of Jiāngyáng Lǐ Pī, as Governor of Yìzhōu,
to guard Chéngdū.
Shěn Yuē said: Jiāngyáng Commandery,
was established by Liú Zhāng dividing Qiánwéi.
Shǒu (guard),
read as Shìyòu.
On the Jǐchǒu day,
Guǎng led his forces back to Lǒngxī,
with over thirty thousand Shǔ people following him.
9. Liú Láozhī arrived at Fāngtóu.
Yáng Yīng and Jiāng Ràng's plot was exposed,
(Yīng and Ràng's plot seen in the previous year's volume).
Láozhī heard of it,
and hesitated to advance.
10. The Qín Duke of Mourning for Píngyuán, Fú Huī, was repeatedly defeated by the ruler of Western Yān, Mùróng Chōng.
The Qín king Fú Jiān reproached him, saying:
"You,
are my talented son,
commanding a great host to fight the little white slave brat,
yet repeatedly defeated,
what use is it to be alive!"
In the third month,
Huī, in anger and resentment, committed suicide.
The former Forbidden Army General Lǐ Biàn and the Director of Waterways, Péng Hézhèng of Lǒngxī, fearing Cháng'ān could not be held,
gathered people from the western provinces.
Jìn Shū Treatise on Officials: Director of Waterways,
subordinate to the Minister of Agriculture.
Shěn Yuē's Treatise: Director of Waterways,
in charge of boats and transportation.
Lǐ Biàn,
was the son of Lǐ Yǎn,
also from Lǒngxī.
Jiān summoned them,
but they did not come.
(This sets the stage for later when Jiān attacks the leek garden).
Jiǔ (leek),
read as Jǔyǒu.
11. The ruler of Western Yān, Mùróng Chōng, attacked the Qín Duke of Mourning for Gāoyáng, Fú Fāng, at Líshān,
and killed him.
(Fú Fāng was garrisoning Líshān, seen in the seventh month of the previous year's volume).
He appointed Fāng's son, Fú Qiān, as Administrator of Féngyì,
and sent him to gather the people of the Sānfǔ region.
The fort commander of Féngyì, Shào Ānmín, and others reproached Qiān, saying:
"You are from a distinguished clan of Yōngzhōu,
with seven chancellors and five dukes.
The distinguished clans of Yōngzhōu
were descendants of Zhōng and Gài Wéixián.
Yōng,
read as Yúyòng.
To act with them in disloyalty and unrighteousness,
what face do you have to walk in the world!"
Qiān reported this to Zhōng,
and Zhōng committed suicide.
Qiān came fleeing.
The Qín Left General Xún Chí and Right General Jù Shízǐ fought with the ruler of Western Yān, Mùróng Chōng, at Líshān,
and were defeated.
The Western Yān general Mùróng Yǒng beheaded Xún Chí,
and Jù Shízǐ fled to Yè.
Yǒng,
was the grandson of Mùróng Yùn, brother of Mùróng Huī;
Shízǐ,
was the brother of Jù Nán.
(Jù Nán seen in the third year of Tàiyuán, volume 104).
Huī,
read as Hùzuì.
They inflicted a great defeat,
capturing over ten thousand Xiānbēi and returning,
burying them all alive.
Dìng,
was the grandson of Fónú.
Běishǐ says: Dìng,
was the son of Fónú;
Fónú,
was the son of Sòngnú.
12. Zhèng Xiè of Xíngyáng surrendered with his commandery.
13. The Yān king Mùróng Chuí attacked Yè,
but could not capture it for a long time.
He intended to go north to Jìzhōu,
so he ordered the General Who Pacifies the Army, Mùróng Lín, to garrison Xìndū,
and the Prince of Lèlàng, Mùróng Wēn, to garrison Zhōngshān,
and summoned the General of Agile Cavalry, Mùróng Nóng, back to Yè.
Upon hearing this, people near and far
thought Yān was not thriving,
and many considered leaving or staying.
Nóng arrived at Gāoyì,
(Gāoyì was originally Hào County;
Hàn Emperor Guāngwǔ ascended the throne here,
and changed it to Gāoyì,
belonging to Chángshān;
Jìn Treatise places it in Zhào State).
He overstayed and did not return.
Chief Clerk Zhāng Pān said to Nóng:
"Liú Suì and the staff officers under him,
(staff officers under him, meaning those close at hand),
I request to turn the army back and punish them."
Nóng did not respond,
but ordered the preparation of provisional appointments,
appointing Suì as Administrator of Gāoyáng.
For staff officers whose families were north of Zhào,
he provisionally appointed and sent them back.
(North of Zhào, meaning north of Zhào State.
Provisional appointment means temporarily appointing them to office with provisional tablets,
without yet reporting to the Yān king Mùróng Chuí).
Over twenty chief clerks
withdrew and said to Pān:
"Your view is greatly mistaken.
How can we now devour each other!
Wait until we return north,
Suì and the others will certainly welcome us by the roadside.
You just watch."
(This sets the stage for later when Suì and others welcome Nóng).
Lèlàng Prince Wēn was in Zhōngshān,
his military strength was very weak,
the Dīnglíng tribes were scattered everywhere,
occupying various cities separately;
Wēn said to his generals:
"With our troops,
we are insufficient for attacking,
but we have more than enough for defending.
The Piàoqí and Fǔjūn armies,
with their forces connected from front to rear,
will eventually destroy the rebels,
so we should just gather provisions and sharpen our weapons to await the right moment."
Thereupon, he comforted the old and recruited the new,
encouraged farming and sericulture,
the people who came to submit followed one after another,
the commanderies and counties, as well as the fortresses, competed in sending military provisions,
and the granaries and storehouses were filled to overflowing.
Zhái Zhēn attacked Zhōngshān at night,
Wēn defeated him,
and from then on he did not dare to come again.
Wēn then dispatched ten thousand troops to transport provisions to supply Chuí,
and also built palaces and halls in Zhōngshān.
He intended to welcome Chuí to establish his capital in Zhōngshān.
Liú Láozhī attacked Liú Fǔ, the Tàishǒu of Líyáng of Yān, at Sūn Jiù's stockade,
Sūn Jiù,
was a person's name,
who had probably set up a stockade within the boundaries of Líyáng,
and Liú Fǔ was stationed there.
He personally led troops to rescue him.
When the Qín Chánglè Duke Pī heard of this,
he dispatched troops to take advantage of the emptiness and attacked the Yān camp at night,
but Nóng defeated him.
Liú Láozhī engaged Chuí in battle,
but was unsuccessful,
retreated and stationed his troops at Líyáng,
and Chuí returned to Yè again.
14 Lǚ Guāng, because Qiūcí was rich and pleasant,
wanted to stay and reside there.
The Tiānzhú monk Jiūmóluóshí said to Guāng:
"This is an ominous and doomed place,
not worth staying in;
according to historical records,
Jiūmóluó,
is the surname;
Shí,
is his given name.
On the way back, there is naturally a blessed land where you can reside."
Jiūmóluóshí knew divination,
and knew that Lǚ Guāng would certainly obtain the land of Liángzhōu and occupy it.
They discussed whether to advance or retreat,
and everyone wanted to return.
So they loaded more than twenty thousand camels with foreign treasures and curios,
and drove more than ten thousand fine horses back.
15 In summer,
the fourth month,
Liú Láozhī advanced his troops to Yè,
the Yān King Chuí engaged him in battle but was defeated,
so he lifted the siege,
retreated and stationed his troops at Xīnchéng,
on the yǐmǎo day,
he fled north from Xīnchéng.
Láozhī did not inform the Qín Chánglè Duke Pī,
but immediately led his troops in pursuit.
When Pī heard of this,
he dispatched troops to follow and advance.
On the gēngshēn day,
Láozhī caught up with Chuí at Dǒngtángyuān.
Chuí said:
"Qín and Jìn are like tiles joined together,
relying on each other to appear strong,
'tiles joined together,'
means their situation is not firmly glued,
if you touch and move them,
one tile falls and breaks,
then all the tiles will come apart.
The character 'dài' [待],
should be
'shì' [恃].
Now looking at the character 'dài,'
the meaning is also understandable.
If one fails, they will all collapse,
they are not of one mind.
Now the two armies are following one after the other,
their situation is not yet united,
we should attack them quickly."
Láozhī's army hurriedly advanced two hundred lǐ,
reaching Wǔqiáozé,
Wǔqiáozé,
is north of Línzhāng County.
According to military strategy,
one who advances a hundred lǐ for gain will cause the supreme general to stumble;
let alone two hundred lǐ!
Chuí intercepted and attacked,
greatly defeated him,
beheading several thousand;
Láozhī fled alone on horseback,
and when the Qín reinforcements arrived,
he managed to escape.
The Yān Guànjūn General Yídū King Fèng
in every battle fought without regard for his own safety,
in total, large and small, two hundred and fifty-seven battles,
he never failed to achieve merit.
Chuí admonished him, saying:
"Now the great enterprise has just been accomplished,
you should first take care of yourself!"
He made him the deputy of the Chēqì General Dé to curb his sharpness.
Because Dé was steady and prudent.
In Yè, the famine was severe,

Ní,
is the same as ní.
He divided his territory to establish Wǔchéng and eleven other commanderies.
The Zǎijì states: Established Wǔchéng, Wǔyáng, Āngù, Wǔshǐ, Hànyáng, Tiānshuǐ, Lüèyáng, Qiángchuān, Gānsōng, Kuāngpéng, Báimǎ, and Yuànchuān, twelve commanderies.
Shuǐjīng Zhù: Yuànchuān River flows from the Zǐchéng Southern Mountains of Yǒngshì County,
passes north by the Pastoral Enclosure,
the site of the old Hàn pastoral enclosure,
there are eastern and western Yuàn cities,
the distance between the two cities is seven lǐ;
the western city is where Qǐfú established his capital.
39 The Qín Minister of Works, Duke of Wèichāng Cuàn, fled from Guānzhōng to Jìnyáng;
the Qín sovereign Pī appointed Cuàn as Grand Commandant,
and enfeoffed him as Prince of Dōnghǎi.
40 Winter,
tenth month,
the Western Yān sovereign Chōng sent the Minister of Works Gāo Gài to lead a force of fifty thousand to attack the Later Qín,
they fought south of Xīnpíng,
Gài was greatly defeated,
and surrendered to the Later Qín.
Initially,
Gài had adopted Yáng Dìng as a son,
and when Gài was defeated,
Dìng fled to Lǒngyòu,
and again gathered his old followers.
41 Fú Dìng, Fú Shào, Fú Mó, and Fú Liàng heard that the Qín sovereign Pī had ascended the throne,
and all sent envoys from Héběi to apologize for their crimes;
Dìng, Shào, Mó, and Liàng had surrendered to Yān,
see the previous year in the previous scroll.
Originally Xīnpíng Dí,
they firmly held Bólíng,
resisting Yān for Qín.
Eleventh month,
Pī appointed Dìng as Governor of Jì Province,
Dìng as Governor of Jì Province,
Shào as Military Governor of Jì Province,
Mó as Governor of Yōu Province,
Liàng as Military Governor of Yōu and Píng Provinces,
and all advanced their noble ranks to Commandery Duke.
The Left General Dòu Chōng occupied Zīchuān,
Zīchuān,
is Bàchuān;
the Bà River,
in ancient times was called the Zī River.
When Duke Mù of Qín became hegemon,
he changed the name of the Zī River to Bà River to display his hegemonic achievement.
Now called Zīchuān,
following the ancient name.

Together with the Governor of Qín Province Wáng Tǒng, the Governor of Hé Province Máo Xìng, the Governor of Yì Province Wáng Guǎng, the Governor of Nán Qín Province Yáng Bì, and the Guard General Yáng Dìng, all sent envoys from Lǒngyòu to invite Pī
to jointly attack the Later Qín.
Pī appointed Dìng as Governor of Yōng Province,
Chōng as Governor of Liáng Province,
additionally appointed Tǒng as General-in-Chief Guarding the West,
Xìng as General of Chariots and Cavalry,
Bì as General-in-Chief Conquering the South,
all with the privilege of establishing a personal administrative staff,
additionally appointed Guǎng as General Pacifying the West,
and all advanced their positions to Provincial Governor.
Yáng Dìng soon moved his administrative seat to Lìchéng,
and established a storehouse at Bǎiqǐng,
Bǎiqǐng,
since Yáng Màosōu,
had been defended as a stronghold.
He sent an envoy to declare himself a vassal;
an edict was issued granting him the title he claimed.
Afterwards, he also took the lands of Tiānshuǐ and Lüèyáng,
and proclaimed himself Governor of Qín Province and Prince of Lǒngxī.
42 Cài Kuāng of Yìmù occupied the city and rebelled against Yān,
Yìmù County,
since the Hàn had belonged to Qīnghé Commandery,
until the Suì when it was abolished,
and incorporated into Ānlè County of Dé Prefecture.
The Administrator of Tàishān, Rén Tài, secretly led troops to rescue Kuāng,
arriving eight lǐ south of Kuāng's fortifications,
when the Yān men then became aware of them.
The various generals, because Kuāng had not yet been subdued and an external enemy had suddenly arrived,
were very concerned.
Lóng said:
"Kuāng relies on external rescue,
therefore he does not surrender promptly.
Now I estimate Tài's troops are no more than several thousand men.
Before they have joined forces,
attack them.
If Tài is defeated,
Kuāng will surrender on his own."
They then abandoned Kuāng and attacked Tài,
greatly defeating him,
beheading more than a thousand.
Kuāng then surrendered,
the Yān King Chuí killed him,
and moreover massacred his fortifications.
43 Mùróng Nóng arrived at Lóngchéng,
having passed through Yēwēng Pass and Fánchéng,
to reach Lóngchéng.
His generals all said:
"Your Highness's arrival,
took a very swift route,
yet now that you are here, you linger long without advancing.
Why is this?"
Nóng replied:
"The reason I came swiftly
was because I feared Yú Yán would cross the mountains to plunder and rob,
harassing the good people.
This mountain
refers to Báiláng Mountain.
Plunder,
Chǔ Jiāo's annotation.
He deceived and lured the starving youths,
gathering like crows into a mob,
lacking any discipline;
I have already seized them by the throat,
and in time they will scatter,
unable to accomplish anything.
Now the fields here are ripe and abundant,
if we leave without harvesting them,
it would merely waste and deplete them.
We should wait until the harvest is completed,
then go and behead him,
which will not take more than ten days."
Shortly after,
Nóng led thirty thousand infantry and cavalry to Língzhī,
causing Yán's followers to tremble in fear,
and gradually they crossed the city walls to surrender to Nóng.
Yán, with no options left, came out and surrendered,
and Nóng executed him;
he then advanced to attack Gāogōulí,
recovering the two commanderies of Liáodōng and Xuántú.
(After Hǎo Jǐng's defeat,
Gāogōulí had captured Liáodōng and Xuántú.)
Tú,
Tóngdū's annotation.
He submitted a memorial requesting the repair of the imperial tombs and temples.
(Before Mùróng Huàng, all the Yān rulers were buried in Liáoxī,
hence the tombs and temples were located there.)
The King of Yān, Chuí, appointed Nóng as Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Commander of Military Affairs of Yōu and Píng Provinces and the Northern Barbarians, and Governor of Yōu Province,
to garrison Lóngchéng.
He transferred the Governor of Píng Province, the Prince of Dàifāng, Zuǒ, to garrison Píngguō.
Nóng then established laws and regulations,
governing with leniency and simplicity,
clarifying criminal cases,
reducing taxes and corvée labor,
encouraging agriculture and sericulture,
making the residents wealthy and prosperous,
with tens of thousands of displaced people from all directions arriving before and after.
Previously, many displaced people from Yōu and Jì had entered Gāogōulí,
so Nóng appointed Piāoqí Simǎ Fànyáng Páng Yuān as the Grand Administrator of Liáodōng,
to recruit and pacify them.
44 Mùróng Lín attacked Wáng Yǎn at Bólíng.
The city's grain was exhausted and arrows were spent,
when the Merit Official Zhāng Yī climbed over the city wall and went out,
gathering a crowd to support Lín.
Yǎn addressed him from the city wall, reproaching him:
"You are a subject of Qín,
and I am your lord.
You raise troops to support the rebels,
calling yourself 'righteous troops,'
how can name and reality be so contradictory?
The ancients sought loyal ministers from the households of filial sons,
(as stated by Wéi Biāo of the Later Hàn).
You have abandoned and disregarded this,
what do I have to do with you!
Now people may take your momentary achievements as acceptable,
but how can they forget your disloyal and unfilial deeds?
I never expected that in the land of rites and righteousness of the Central Plains,
there would be someone like you!"
In the twelfth month,
Lín captured Bólíng,
seized Yǎn and Fú Jiàn,
and executed them.
The Grand Administrator of Chānglí, Sòng Chǎng, led the forces of the Wūhuán and Suǒtóu to rescue Yǎn,
but arrived too late and returned.
The Qín ruler Pī appointed Chǎng as Governor of Píng Province.
(Chǎng was at the time following Wáng Yǒng at Húguān.)
45 The Yān ruler Chuí traveled north to Zhōngshān,
and said to his generals:
"The Prince of Lèlàng has gathered the displaced,
filled the granaries,
supplied military provisions externally,
and constructed palaces internally.
Even the achievements of Xiāo Hé—
how could they surpass this!"
(The achievements of the Prince of Lèlàng, Wēn, are detailed above.)
(When Hàn Gāozǔ was confronting Xiàng Yǔ,
Xiāo Hé pacified Guānzhōng,
serving as the foundation.)
On Bǐngshēn,
Chuí finally established the capital at Zhōngshān.
(Dù Yòu said: The Later Yān capital was at Zhōngshān,
present-day Tángchāng County of Bólíng Commandery.)
46 Qín's Fú Dìng held Xìndū and resisted Yān.
The King of Yān, Chuí, appointed his cousin, the Prince of Běidì, Jīng, as Governor of Jì Province,
to lead troops to attack him.
47 Tuòbá Guī's great-great-uncle Hèluó, along with his brother Jiàn and the leaders of various tribes, jointly requested Hè Nè to support Guī as their ruler.
1 In spring,
the first month,
on Wùshēn,
Tuòbá Guī held a grand assembly at Niúchuān.
(From Wǔzhōu Pass west to Niúchuān,
north of Niúchuān,
is all desert.)
According to the Wèi Annals,
when Kūduō came to invade,
Guī sought troops from Yān,
traveled from Nǔshān to Niúchuān,
camped at Yánshuǐ,
and went south from Dàigǔ to join the Yān forces.
Also according to the Commentary on the Water Classic,
Yánshuǐ flows south of Chángchuān City,
so Chángchuān is Niúchuān.
According to the Bǎn Zhì,
Yánshuǐ originates outside Qiěrú Pass in Dài Commandery,
so Niúchuān should also be outside Qiěrú Pass.)
Also,
when Emperor Míngyuán conducted a great hunt at Niúchuān,
he ascended Fǔshān.
(Kuòdìzhì: Fǔshān is three lǐ north of Huáiróng County in Guī Province.)
(The "qiě" in Qiěrú
is pronounced zǐrú fān.)
Guī
was the legitimate grandson of Shíyìjiān,
the son of the heir Shí.
The Tuòbá clan thus rose to prominence.
He appointed Chángsūn Sōng as the Southern Tribal Leader,
and Shūsūn Pǔluò as the Northern Tribal Leader,
dividing the governance of the people.
(The Wèishū states: In the early Wèi, when they migrated south from the northern wilderness,
they established four tribal leaders,
who sat in the royal court,
adjudicated disputes,
used verbal agreements,
carved notches to record events,
had no prisons or interrogation methods,
and all criminals were judged and punished on the spot.)
Govern,
Zhízhī fān;
the same below.)
Xǔ Qiān was appointed as Right Simǎ,
and Guǎngníng Wáng Jiàn, the Xiānbei Hé Bá, Shūsūn Jiàn, and Yǔ Yuè were appointed as Outer Court Leaders.
(The Wèishū Official Clan Records: Tuòbá Lín designated the descendants of his paternal uncles as the Yǐzhān clan,
later changed to the Shūsūn clan.)
Court,
Zhíyáo fān.
They were all responsible for palace guard duties and participating in military and state planning;
Chángsūn Dàoshēng, Hè Pí, and others attended to him left and right,
issuing and receiving orders.
(Wáng Jiàn married the daughter of the King of Dài, Shíyìjiān;
Yuè
was Hé Chén's younger brother;
Dàoshēng
was Sōng's nephew.)
(Yǔ Hé Chén escorted Guī's mother, Lady Hè, to flee to Guī,
and Chángsūn Sōng led his tribal followers to submit to Guī,
events both recorded above.)
From,
Cáiyòng fān.
2 The King of Yān, Chuí, ascended the throne as emperor.
(Chuí's courtesy name was Dàomíng,
the fifth son of the Yān ruler Huàng.)
3 The Later Qín king, Cháng, went to Āndìng.
4 Nán'ān's Mì Yí
(Mì
is a surname.
The Hànshū Table of Meritorious Officials lists the Marquis of Dài, Mì Péng.
At that time, the Mì clan was a powerful family in Nán'ān.)
led five thousand troops to counterattack Guórén,
but was severely defeated.
Yí fled back to Nán'ān.
5 After Xiānyú Qǐ killed Zhái Zhēn,
(Zhái Zhēn was killed,
see the fourth month of the previous year.)
the Grand Administrator of Líyáng, Téng Tiánzhī, greatly trusted and favored him.
Tiánzhī enjoyed hunting,
but did not care for his soldiers,
while Liáo secretly practiced deceitful kindness to win the people's hearts.
When Tiánzhī went south to attack Lùmíng City,
(Líyáng is north of the river,
Lùmíng City is south of the river.)
(Lì Dàoyuán said: According to the Bamboo Annals,
in the thirteenth year of King Huìchéng of Liáng,
he captured Zhènglù,
which is this city.
Now within the city there is a platform,
still called Lùmíng Platform,
also called Lùmíng City.)
Tiánzhī fled east to Juànchéng,
Liáo pursued and captured him,
and thus occupied Líyáng.
The Governor of Yù Province, Zhù Xù, sent Generals Qín Yīng and Tóng Bīn, along with the various commanderies of Huái and Sì, to jointly suppress him.
13. The ruler of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, posthumously honored his mother, Lady Lán, as Empress Wénzhāo.
He intended to remove the late Empress Duàn, who held the temple name Wénmíng,
so that Lady Lán could be enshrined alongside Tàizǔ.
Empress Duàn
was the principal wife of Mùróng Huàng, the Prince of Yān.
Lady Lán
was a concubine of Huàng.
Huàng's temple name was Tàizǔ,
and his posthumous name was Emperor Wénmíng.
The court officials all considered this appropriate.
They complied with Chuí's wishes.
"Yáo's mother was a consort of Emperor Kù,
ranked third,
and did not use her noble status to overshadow Jiāngyuán.
The *Records of Emperors and Kings* states: Emperor Kù had four consorts: the primary consort was a woman from the Yǒutái clan named Jiāngyuán,
who gave birth to Hòujì;
the second was a woman from the Yǒusōng clan named Jiǎndí,
who gave birth to Xiè;
the third was a woman from the Chénfēng clan named Qìngdū,
who gave birth to Fàngxūn;
the fourth was a woman from the Jūzī clan named Chángyì,
who gave birth to Zhì.
Kù
is pronounced kù wò fān.
They prioritized utmost impartiality;
Empress Wénzhāo should have a separate temple established for her."
Chuí was angered
and pressured them.
Xiáng and Mì said:
"What Your Majesty wishes to do,
there is no need to consult your ministers.
We, your ministers, adhere to the classics and uphold the rites,
and dare not have conflicting views."
Chuí then ceased consulting the Confucian scholars.
He ultimately removed Empress Duàn
and replaced her with Lady Lán.
He also held Empress Kězúhún, who held the temple name Jǐngzhāo, responsible for the collapse of the state,
and posthumously deposed her.
He honored Consort Duàn of Lièzǔ as Empress Jǐngdé
and enshrined her alongside Lièzǔ.
Lady Kězúhún
was the principal wife of Mùróng Jùn, the Prince of Yān.
The incident of the state's collapse is recorded in scroll 102,
in the fourth year of the Tàihé era of the Duke of Hǎixī.
Lady Duàn
was a concubine of Jùn.
Jùn's temple name was Lièzǔ,
and his posthumous name was Emperor Jǐngzhāo.
Cuī Hóng remarked: Duke Huán of Qí commanded the feudal lords not to make concubines their principal wives.
Mencius said: At the Kuíqiū assembly of Duke Huán of Qí,
the first command was:
"Punish the unfilial,
do not lightly change the designated heir,
and do not make a concubine the principal wife."
Even then, a concubine could not replace a principal wife,
let alone a son replacing his own mother!
What the *Spring and Autumn Annals* refers to as "the mother becoming noble through the son"
means that after the principal wife has passed away,
the mother who was a concubine may be honored as the lesser lord.
The *Gōngyáng Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals* states: Duke Huán was young but noble,
while Duke Yǐn was older but of lower status.
Duke Yǐn was older and virtuous,
and the great ministers supported Duke Yǐn and established him.
The establishment of Duke Yǐn
was for the sake of establishing Duke Huán.
Since Duke Yǐn was older and virtuous,
why was it inappropriate to establish him?
The establishment of the heir apparent is based on seniority, not virtue;
the establishment of a son is based on nobility, not seniority.
Why was Duke Huán noble?
Because his mother was noble.
If the mother is noble,
then why is the son noble?
The son is noble because of the mother,
and the mother is noble because of the son.
The *Zuǒ Commentary* states: Duke Huì of Lǔ's principal wife was Méngzǐ.
After Méngzǐ passed away,
Shēngzǐ succeeded her as consort,
and gave birth to Duke Yǐn.
Duke Wǔ of Sòng gave birth to Zhòngzǐ,
who became the wife of the ruler of Lǔ,
and gave birth to Duke Huán.
After Duke Huì passed away,
Duke Yǐn was established and served him.
Thus, Chéngfēng could never be enshrined alongside Duke Zhuāng.
The wife of Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ was Lady Jiāng.
Chéngfēng
was a concubine of Duke Zhuāng
and the mother of Duke Xī.
Lady Jiāng had an affair with Gòng Zhòng,
assassinated Duke Mǐn, and attempted to establish Gòng Zhòng,
but failed.
She then fled to Zhū,
and Duke Huán of Qí had her killed.
After Duke Xī was established,
he requested her remains
and buried her with the rites of a principal wife.
Ministers and sons will inevitably learn and imitate such actions,
just as form and sound correspond to shadow and echo.
Bǎo's forced killing of his mother
is recorded later in scroll 108, in the twenty-first year of the Tàiyuán era.
The abdications of Yáo and Shùn
still led to the disasters of Zhī and Kuài,
as recorded in scroll 2, in the fifth year of King Shènjìng of Zhōu.
In the past, Wén Jiāng offended Duke Huán,
yet the *Spring and Autumn Annals* did not depose her.
The wife of Duke Huán of Lǔ was Wén Jiāng.
She had an affair with Duke Xiāng of Qí.
Duke Huán reprimanded her.
The wife informed Duke Xiāng,
and Duke Xiāng subsequently killed Duke Huán.
In the twenty-first year of Duke Zhuāng's reign,
the *Spring and Autumn Annals* records the death of Lady Jiāng, wife of the ruler;
in the twenty-second year, it records the burial of our lesser lord Wén Jiāng.
This shows she was not deposed.
However, the rites for the lesser lord were completed.
Chuí deposed her out of personal resentment.
Personal resentment
refers to the slander that led to the killing of Chuí's wife, Lady Duàn,
and the slander that caused Chuí to be exiled to Qín.
All of this was contrary to the rites.
14. Liú Xiǎn fled south from Shànwú to Mǎyì,
fearing pressure from Dài,
and also apprehensive about settling old grievances.
Núzhēn had an elder brother named Jiān,
who previously resided with the Hèlán tribe.
Núzhēn spoke to the King of Dài, Tuòbá Guī,
requesting to summon Jiān and cede his own tribe to him.
Guī agreed.
After Jiān took command of the tribe,
he sent his younger brother, Qùjīn, to present gold and horses to Hè Nè.
Hè Rǎngān said to Qùjīn:
"I have treated you and your brother generously.
Now that you command the tribe,
you should come and follow me."
Qùjīn agreed.
Núzhēn angrily said:
"From the time of my grandfather and father,
our family has been loyal ministers of Dài for generations.
That is why I ceded the tribe to you,
wishing to act righteously.
Now, you behave without principle,
plotting to betray the state.
Where is the righteousness in that!"
He then killed Jiān and Qùjīn.
When Rǎngān heard of this,
he led troops to attack Núzhēn.
Núzhēn fled to Dài.
Guī sent an envoy to reprimand Rǎngān,
and Rǎngān then ceased.
From then on, a rift developed between Guī and the Hèlán tribe.
Envoy,
is pronounced shū lì fān.
15. The Western Yān's Vice Director
Mùróng Héng and Minister Mùróng Yǒng attacked Duàn Suí,
and killed him.
They established Yí, son of the Prince of Yídū, as the King of Yān.
Yí was likely the son of Mùróng Huán, the Prince of Yídū of Yān.
Yí
is pronounced yú qǐ fān.
They led over 400,000 men and women of the Xiānbēi people away from Cháng'ān and headed east.
In the fifth year of the Tàihé era of the Duke of Hǎixī,
Qín relocated the Xiānbēi to Cháng'ān.
By this time, only seventeen years had passed,
yet their population had multiplied to such an extent.
The incident of Āshǐnà Jiéshèlǜ during Táng Tàizōng's reign,
was also fortunate to have occurred early.
Led,
is read as shuài.
They killed him at Línjìn.
Héng was furious,
abandoned Tāo, and left.
Yǒng and the General of the Martial Guards, Diāo Yún, led troops to attack Tāo.
Tāo was defeated
and fled to Héng's camp.
Héng established Yáo, son of the Western Yān ruler Mùróng Chōng, as emperor,
changing the era name to Jiànpíng.
Chōng was posthumously named Emperor Wēi.
The masses all abandoned Yáo and fled to Yǒng.
Yǒng captured Yáo,
killed him,
and established Zhōng, son of Mùróng Hóng, as emperor,
changing the era name to Jiànwǔ.
Zhōng appointed Yǒng as Grand Commandant,
acting as Minister of the Imperial Secretariat,
and enfeoffed him as Duke of Hédōng.
Yǒng administered the law with leniency and fairness,
and the Xiānbēi were content.
Upon reaching Wénxǐ,
they heard that the ruler of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, had already assumed the imperial title.
They dared not advance further
and built the city of Yānxī to settle in.
This sets the stage for Mùróng Chuí's destruction of Western Yān.
16. After the Xianbei moved eastward,
Chang’an was left empty and undefended.
Former Róngyáng
Gāolíng’s Zhào Gǔ and others recruited Hǎo Nú, the leader of the Lúshuǐ Hú from Xìngchéng, along with four thousand households, and entered Chang’an.
All areas north of the Wei River responded to them,
and they appointed Zhào Gǔ as Chancellor.
Wáng Lín of Fúfēng had several thousand followers,
and he held Mǎwéi for defense.
Mount Mǎwéi is located west of Xiányáng County,
over a hundred lǐ from the city of Chang’an.
Dù Yòu said: Jīngzhào’s Jīnchéng County has the old city of Mǎwéi.
Sūn Jǐng’ān’s Zhēngtú Jì states: Mǎwéi was built,
but it is unknown which generation built it.
Jīnchéng,
was called Quǎnqiū during the Zhōu dynasty,
Fèiqiū during the Qín dynasty,
and Huáilǐ during the Hàn dynasty.
Lín,
is pronounced lí zhēn.
Wéi,
is pronounced wú huí.
In summer,
the fourth month,
Later Qín King Yáo Cháng attacked from Āndìng,
and Wáng Lín fled to Hànzhōng.
Yáo Cháng advanced with a large force,
and Hǎo Nú, fearing,
requested to surrender.
He was appointed as General Who Guards the North and Grand Governor of the Six Valleys.
The southern mountains of Chang’an have six valleys.
17. On Guǐsì,
Lù Nà, the Deputy Director of the Imperial Secretariat, was appointed as Left Deputy Director,
and Prince Tián of Qiáo was appointed as Right Deputy Director.
The Jìn Shū states: Left and Right Deputy Directors are not always both appointed,
sometimes only the Deputy Director of the Imperial Secretariat is appointed.
He was the son of Lù Wán.
Lù Wán,
appears in the ninety-fourth volume, in the fourth year of Emperor Chéng’s Xiánhé era.
18. Máo Xìng attacked Wáng Guǎng,
defeating him.
Wáng Guǎng fled to Qín Province;
the Xīanbēi leader Pǐlán of Lǒngxī captured Wáng Guǎng and sent him to Later Qín.
Máo Xìng then wanted to attack Wáng Tǒng in Shàngguī,
but the various Dí in Fúhàn were weary and resentful of military affairs.
The various Dí,
were likely those whom King Jiān of Qín had Máo Xìng lead to garrison Fúhàn.
Fù,
is pronounced fú yòu.
Fú,
is pronounced fū.
They recommended Wèi Píng as Governor of Hé Province,
because Wèi Píng’s clan was strong,
hence they recommended him.
19. King Mùróng Chuí of Yān enfeoffed his son Mùróng Nóng as Prince of Liáoxī,
Mùróng Lín as Prince of Zhào,
and Mùróng Lóng as Prince of Gāoyáng.
20. King Tuòbá Guī of Dài initially changed his title to King of Wèi.
From this point, the Tuòbá clan’s state was named Wèi.
21. Zhāng Dàyù advanced from Yángwù and stationed west of the city of Gūzāng,
while Wáng Mù and Xīyú, son of Tūfǎ Sīfùjiān, led thirty thousand troops and stationed south of the city.
Lǚ Guāng launched an attack,
heavily defeating them,
and beheaded over twenty thousand, including Xīyú.
22. Qín issued a general amnesty,
appointing Wèi Píng as General Who Pacifies the Army and Governor of Hé Province,
and Lǚ Guāng as Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry and Governor of Liáng Province.
However, the envoys were all intercepted by Later Qín,
and could not reach their destinations.
At that time, King Fú Pī of Qín was in Jìnyáng,
and Later Qín blocked the route,
so the two garrisons could not be reached.
23. King Mùróng Chuí of Yān appointed Mùróng Dé, Prince of Fànyáng, as Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
Mùróng Kǎi, Prince of Tàiyuán, as Left Deputy Director,
and Mùróng Wēn, Prince of Lèlàng, as Colonel of the Capital Region.
Mùróng Wēn had defended Zhōngshān,
with achievements in constructing palaces and establishing the capital,
and thus was appointed as Colonel of the Capital Region.
Lèlàng,
is pronounced luò láng.
24. Later Qín King Yáo Cháng ascended the throne as emperor in Chang’an.
Yáo Cháng, styled Jǐngmào,
was the twenty-fourth son of Yáo Yìzhòng.
He changed the era name to Jiànchū,
and named the state Great Qín.
He posthumously honored his father Yáo Yìzhòng as Emperor Jǐngyuán,
and established his wife, Lady Shé, as empress.
According to the Lèipiān, Shé,
is pronounced yǐ zhě,
a surname of the northern tribes.
The Xìngpǔ states: Yáo Cháng’s empress was of the Shé clan,
from Nán’ān.
Shé,
is pronounced shí zhē,
also pronounced tā.
He established the hundred officials.
Yáo Cháng feasted with his ministers,
and when the wine was flowing freely,
he said:
“All of you gentlemen once faced north as subjects of the Qín court alongside me,
but now suddenly we are ruler and ministers.
Does this not bring shame?”
Zhào Qiān said:
“Heaven is not ashamed to have Your Majesty as its son,
so how could we be ashamed to be your ministers!”
Yáo Cháng laughed heartily.
25. King Tuòbá Guī of Wèi went east to Língshí.
Língshí,
is a place name,
located east of Shènglè.
His generals requested to pursue him,
but Tuòbá Guī said:
“Hóu Chén and others have served for generations,
and even if they have committed offenses, we should bear with them.
Now, the state is newly established,
and people’s sentiments are not yet unified.
It is natural for the foolish to waver,
advancing and retreating,
meaning they are inconsistent in their loyalty and rebellion.
The history records that Tuòbá Guī could recognize the times and adapt to pacify those with wavering loyalties.
26. In the sixth month,
on Gēngyín,
former General Who Supports the State Yáng Liàng was appointed as Governor of Yōng Province,
to guard the imperial tombs.
The emperor established Yōng Province in Xiāngyáng;
now he sent Yáng Liàng to hold the title of Governor of Yōng Province,
and garrison Luò.
Yōng,
is pronounced yú yòng.
Xiàzhī.
The Xìngpǔ states: In the Zuǒzhuàn, the state of Qí had the Yàn clan,
who served as senior officials for generations.
The two counties of Hú and Shǎn,
both belonged to Hóngnóng.
Shǎn,
is pronounced shì rǎn.
27. Diāo Yún and others of Western Yān killed the ruler of Western Yān, Mùróng Zhōng,

and recommended Mùróng Yǒng as Commissioner Bearing Credentials, Grand Governor of All Military Affairs Within and Without, Grand General, Great Chányú, Governor of Yōng, Qín, Liáng, and Liáng Provinces, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, and Prince of Hédōng,
declaring himself a vassal to Yān.
He declared himself a vassal to King Mùróng Chuí of Yān.
Shǐ,
is pronounced shū lì.
Yōng,
is pronounced yú yòng.

28. King Mùróng Chuí of Yān sent Mùróng Kǎi, Prince of Tàiyuán; Mùróng Lín, Prince of Zhào; Mùróng Shào, Prince of Chénliú; and Mùróng Zhòu, Prince of Zhāngwǔ to attack Fú Dìng, Fú Shào, Fú Mó, and Fú Liàng of Qín.
Last year,
Fú Dìng and others had betrayed Yān and sided with Qín.
They explained the consequences of fortune and misfortune,
and Fú Dìng and others all surrendered.
Mùróng Chuí enfeoffed Fú Dìng and others as marquises,
saying:
“To repay the virtue of the King of Qín.”
29. King Fú Pī of Qín appointed Wáng Yǒng, Grand Governor of All Military Affairs Within and Without, Minister Over the Masses, and Director of the Imperial Secretariat, as Left Chancellor;
Fú Zuǎn, Grand Commandant and Prince of Dōnghǎi, as Grand Marshal;
Zhāng Chì, Minister of Works, as Grand Commandant;
Xú Yì of Xiányáng, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, as Minister of Works;
and Wáng Téng, Colonel of the Capital Region, as Grand General of Agile Cavalry and Specially Advanced.
Wáng Yǒng issued a proclamation to all dukes, marquises, governors, commandants, fortress commanders, and local magnates,
calling on them to jointly attack Yáo Cháng and Mùróng Chuí,
ordering each to lead their troops
and assemble with the imperial carriage in Línjìn in the first ten days of the tenth month.

As a result, Jiāng Yán of Tiānshuǐ, Kòu Míng of Féngyì, Wáng Zhāo of Hédōng, Zhāng Yàn of Xīnpíng, Dù Mǐn of Jīngzhào, Mǎ Lǎng of Fúfēng, and Wáng Mǐn, General Who Establishes Loyalty and Commandant of Pastures of Gāopíng in Fúfēng,
General Who Establishes Loyalty,
was likely an office created by the Fú clan.
Gāopíng County,
belonged to the Āndìng Commandery during the Hàn dynasty,
abolished during the Jìn dynasty,
and used by Former Zhào’s Liú Yào as the seat of Shuò Province.
Qín established the Commandant of Pastures in that area.
Each had tens of thousands of followers,
and sent envoys to Qín.
Fú Pī appointed them all as generals and commandery governors,
enfeoffing them as marquises.
Champion General Dèng Jǐng led five thousand troops and occupied Péngchí,
coordinating with Dòu Chōng as front and rear,
to attack Later Qín.
“Péngchí,”
likely should be
“Biāochí.”
Biāochí is west of Chang’an,
as mentioned in the Shījīng,
“Biāochí flows north.”
Dòu Chōng occupied Zīchuān,
southeast of Chang’an,
allowing them to coordinate as front and rear.
Also, according to the New Tángshū Geography Treatise,
Níng Province has Péngchí,
but it is far from Zīchuān.
Dèng Jǐng,
was the son of Dèng Qiāng.
Dèng Qiāng,
was a famous general of Qín.
30. Later Qín King Yáo Cháng relocated over five thousand households from Āndìng to Chang’an.
In the autumn of the 31st year,
in the seventh month,
Jīn Xī, the Administrator of Píngliáng of Qín, and Mòyígān, the Commandant of Āndìng, fought against Yáo Fāngchéng, the Left General of Hòu Qín, at Sūnqiū Valley.
Sūnqiū Valley should be located in Āndìng.
The ruler of Hòu Qín, Cháng, appointed his younger brother, the General Who Conquers Caitiffs, Xù, as Colonel-Director of Retainers,
to guard Cháng'ān;
he personally led troops to Āndìng
to attack Xī and others,
and inflicted a major defeat on them.
Jīn Xī was originally of the Dōnghú stock;
Qín referred to the Xiānbēi stock residing in Liáojié as Dōnghú.
Stock,
Zhāng Yǒng's annotation.
He was the chieftain of the Duōlán tribe of the Xiānbēi.
In the 32nd year, the various Dí of Fúhǎn,
considering Wèi Píng old and feeble,
and difficult to achieve success with,
discussed deposing him,
but feared the strength of his clan,
and for several days could not reach a decision.
The Dí Dàn Qīng said to the various generals:
"Major matters should be settled promptly,
otherwise,
changes will arise.
Gentlemen, please just invite Duke Wèi to a gathering,
and observe what I do."
During the grand banquet on the Qīxī festival,
Qīng drew his sword and stepped forward, saying:
"Now the world is in great chaos,
we share both joy and sorrow,
and without a worthy ruler we cannot accomplish great deeds.
Duke Wèi is old,
he should return to his original position to make way for the worthy.
Wèi Píng,
originally a subordinate general of Máo Xìng.
Although a distant relative of the royal house,
his ambition and strategy are outstanding and wise,
I request that we together establish him,
to respond to the imperial carriage.
Wishing to respond to the proclamation of Wáng Yǒng and go to the Qín ruler Pī.
If there are differing opinions, speak now."
Then he brandished his sword and rolled up his sleeves,
intending to behead those with differing views.
The multitude all followed him,
none dared to look up.
Thereupon they recommended Dēng as Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers,
Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Lǒngyòu, General Who Pacifies the Army, Governor of Yōng and Hé Provinces, and Duke of Lüèyáng,
leading a force of fifty thousand,
eastward down Lǒng,
attacking Nán'ān,
capturing it,
and sending a swift messenger to request orders from Qín.
Dēng,
was a clansman of the Qín ruler Pī.
Fú Dēng's affairs begin here.
Commissioner,
Shū Lì's annotation.
Yōng,
Yú Yòng's annotation.
Lead,
read as command;
same below.
In the 33rd year, Mì Yí and Mòhóu Tìjuàn led their people, over thirty thousand households, to surrender to Qǐfú Guórén,
Guórén appointed Yí as Governor of Dōng Qín Province,
and Tìjuàn as Governor of Liáng Province.
Mòhóu,
a compound surname of barbarians.
Surrender,
Hù Jiāng's annotation;
same below.
On the Jǐyǒu day,
the King of Wèi, Guī, returned to Shènglè,
returning from Língshí.
After more than ten days,
he again fled to Liú Xiǎn;
Guī had his grandson Bèijīn take command of his people in his stead.
Liú Xiǎn's younger brother Fèiní led his people to surrender to Wèi.
In the eighth month,
the ruler of Yān, Chuí, left the heir apparent Bǎo to guard Zhōngshān,
appointing the King of Zhào, Lín, as Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs,
to administer the remaining administration.
On the Gēngwǔ day,
he personally led Fànyáng King Dé and others south to seize territory,
sending Gāoyáng King Lóng east to subdue Píngyuán.
The Dīnglíng Xiānyú Qǐ held Qūyáng West Mountain,
Qūyáng County,
belonged to Chángshān Commandery.
He came out to camp at Wàngdū,
Wàngdū County,
belonged to Zhōngshān Commandery.
Commentary on the Water Classic: Yáo was enfeoffed at Táng,
Yáo Mountain is to the northeast,
Yáo's mother Qìngdū Mountain is to the south,
ascending Yáo Mountain one sees Dū Mountain,
hence Wàngdū County is named thus.
The King of Zhào, Lín, personally went out to attack him,
the various generals all said:
"Your Highness empties the town for a distant campaign,
if by chance you return without success,
it will damage your prestige and dignity,
it would be better to send the various generals to attack him."
Lín said:
"Qǐ, hearing that the imperial carriage is outside,
has nothing to fear or忌讳,
and will certainly not make preparations,
he can be taken in one move,
it is not worth worrying about."
Then he announced he was going to Lǔkǒu,
at night,
turned back towards Qǐ,
by dawn,
reached his camp,
launched a surprise attack,
and captured him.
In the 36th year, Zhái Liáo invaded Qiáo,
Zhū Xù attacked and drove him away.
In the 37th year, the Qín ruler Pī appointed Fú Dēng as Grand General Who Conquers the West, Palace Attendant with Equal Honors, and King of Nán'ān,
Commissioner, Provincial Governor, Commander-in-Chief,
all according to what he had claimed and were granted to him.
He also appointed Xú Yì as Right Chancellor.
Leaving Wáng Téng to guard Jìnyáng,
and Vice Director of the Right Yáng Fǔ to defend Húguān,
he led a force of forty thousand,
advanced and stationed at Píngyáng.
Initially,
the younger brother of the Hòu Qín ruler Cháng, Shuòdé, commanded his Qiang tribe residing in Lǒngshàng,
hearing that Cháng had raised troops,
proclaimed himself General Who Conquers the West,
and gathered a multitude at Jìchéng to respond to him;
appointing his elder brother's grandson Xiáng as General Who Pacifies Distant Lands,
occupying Lǒngchéng,
and his cousin's grandson Xùn as General Who Pacifies the West,
occupying Chìtíng in Nán'ān,
the various Yáo were originally Chìtíng Qiang.
Cháng led troops from Āndìng to join Shuòdé in attacking Tǒng,
the Tūgè of Tiānshuǐ and the Qiang and Hú of Lüèyáng who responded numbered over twenty thousand households.
The Qín Administrator of Lüèyáng, Wáng Pí, surrendered to them.
Initially,
when Qín destroyed Dài,
they moved the younger son of the King of Dài, Shíyìjiān, Kūduō to Cháng'ān,
the event is seen in the 104th scroll, the first year of Tàiyuán.
Kū,
Kǔ Gǔ's annotation.
Duō,
Dāng Mò's annotation.
Yǒng appointed Kūduō as Administrator of Xīnxīng.
Liú Xiǎn sent his younger brother Kàngní to welcome Kūduō,
with troops following him,
pressing on the southern borders of Wèi,
causing unrest among the various tribes.
Yú Huán and others around the King of Wèi, Guī, plotted with tribesmen to seize Guī to respond to Kūduō,
the Banner General, the Dàirén Mò Tí and others also secretly communicated with Kūduō.
Wèi's official clan records;
in the first year of Dàowǔ's Dēngguó era,
six Banner Generals were established,
commanding the three corps of guards on duty in the forbidden palace,
all under the command of those from Palace Attendants down to Cavalier Attendants and above.
During Tuòbá Jiéfén's time,
among the various surnames of the remaining tribes that entered,
there was the Mònálóu clan,
later becoming the Mò clan.
Banner,
Zhí Jiāng's annotation.
Guī executed Huán and five others,
but pardoned Mò Tí and the seven clans without questioning them.
Setting the stage for Guī later killing Mò Tí.
He crossed north over Yīn Mountain,
again relying on the Hèlán tribe,
and sent the Outer Court Dàrén of Liáodōng, Ān Tóng, to seek help from Yān,
Genealogy of Surnames: The prince of Ānxī entered service,
thus becoming a Hàn person.
Common Customs,
Hàn had Ān Chéng who was a commandery administrator.
Records of Lú Mountain mention Ān Gāo, prince of the Ānxī state.
Court,
Zhí Yáo's annotation.
In the ninth month,
Wáng Tǒng surrendered Qín Province to Hòu Qín.
The ruler of Hòu Qín, Cháng, appointed Yáo Shuòdé as Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Lǒngyòu, and Governor of Qín Province,
to guard Shàngguī.
In the 41st year, Lǚ Guāng received the bad news of the Qín ruler Jiān's death,
the entire army wore mourning white,
and posthumously honored him as Emperor Wénzhāo.
In winter,
the tenth month,
a great amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed to Dà'ān.
The Jìn Shū Zǎijì records it as
"Tài'ān."
42. Mùróng Yǒng of Western Yān sent an envoy to Qín ruler Fú Pī requesting passage eastward to return home.
Pī refused,
and fought Yǒng at Xiānglíng.
Xiānglíng County,
belonged to Hédōng Commandery during the Hàn,
and to Píngyáng Commandery during the Jìn.
Left Chancellor Wáng Yǒng and Guard General Jù Shízǐ both died.
Earlier,
Dōnghǎi Prince Fú Zì came from Cháng'ān;
last year,
Zì fled to Pī.
Pī was wary of him,
and after being defeated,
feared being killed by Zì.
He led several thousand cavalry south to flee to Dōngyuán.
Dōngyuán County,
was renamed Zhēndìng by the Hàn;
this Dōngyuán was within the boundaries of Xīn'ān County in Hénán.
Sòng Bái said: Wángwū County in Hénán Prefecture,
was the location of Yuán County in Hédōng Commandery during the Hàn.
Also,
Yuán County in Jiàng Prefecture,
originally a county name in Hédōng Commandery,
its location is where Zhōu and Shào divided Shǎn.
Also said: Hénán Prefecture,
was Hénán Commandery during the Hàn,
administered Luòyáng;
Later Hàn capital Luòyáng,
Hénán belonged to the Sīlì Xiàowèi.
Wèi Chénliú Prince Cáo Huàn combined Hénán and four other commanderies to establish Sīzhōu,
Liú Cōng made it Jīngzhōu,
Shí Hǔ made it Luòzhōu,
Fú Jiān made it Yùzhōu;
when Sòng Wǔ entered Luò,
he re-established Dōngyuán and Xīyuán counties,
and still placed Sīzhōu at Hǔláo.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
Jì,
read as jì.
General Yángwēi Féng Gāi intercepted him from Shǎn,
killed Pī,
captured his crown prince Níng and Chánglè Prince Shòu,
and sent them to Jiànkāng.
An edict pardoned them from execution,
and handed them over to Fú Hóng.
Fú Hóng came last year,
and was settled in Jiāngzhōu.
The remaining princes, dukes, and officials all fell to Yǒng.
Yǒng then advanced and occupied Chángzǐ,
ascended the imperial throne,
and changed the era name to Zhōngxīng.
He intended to make the Qín empress Yáng his senior consort,
but Yáng drew a sword and stabbed Yǒng,
and was killed by Yǒng.
43. On Jiǎshēn,
Duke Hǎixī Sīmǎ Yì died in Wú.
He was forty-five years old.
44. The Yān eunuch Wú Shēn occupied Qīnghé and rebelled.
Yān ruler Mùróng Chuí attacked him,
but did not overcome him.
45. Later Qín ruler Yáo Chǎng returned to Āndìng.
He returned to Āndìng from Shàngguī.
46. Qín Nán'ān Prince Fú Dēng, having captured Nán'ān,
had over thirty thousand households of Yí and Xià peoples submit to him.
He then attacked Yáo Shuòdé at Qínzhōu,
and Later Qín ruler Yáo Chǎng personally went to rescue him.
Dēng fought Chǎng at Húnú Fù,
Húnú Fù is west of Shàngguī.
Over twenty thousand heads were cut off,
General Dàn Qīng shot Chǎng,
hitting him.
Chǎng was severely wounded,
fled and defended Shàngguī,
and Yáo Shuòdé replaced him in commanding the troops.
47. Before Yān Zhào Prince Mùróng Lín's army reached Wèi,
Tuòbá Kūduō gradually advanced and pressured Wèi ruler Tuòbá Guī,
and Hè Rǎngān invaded northern Wèi to respond to him.
The Wèi forces were alarmed and disturbed,
and northern tribal leader Shūsūn Pǔluò fled to Liú Wèichén.
When Lín heard this,
he hastily sent Ān Tóng and others back.
The Wèi people, knowing the Yān army was nearby,
felt somewhat reassured.
Kūduō advanced and stationed at Gāoliǔ.
Gāoliǔ County,
belonged to Dài Commandery during the Hàn,
and was abolished during the Jìn.
Lì Dàoyuán said: Gāoliǔ is within Dài,
its mountains are layered peaks and stacked ridges,
clouds rise high like rosy clouds,
the mountains stretch faintly eastward beyond the Liáo frontier.
Kūduō was greatly defeated,
fled to Liú Wèichén,
and Wèichén killed him.
Guī gathered all his followers,
and appointed the Dài man Kùdí Gān as northern tribal leader.
The Wèishū Official Clan Records: Among the southern tribes,
there was the Kùdí clan,
later changed to Dí clan.
Liú Wèichén resided in Shuòfāng,
with abundant troops and horses.
Later Qín ruler Yáo Chǎng appointed Wèichén as Grand General, Grand Chányú, Héxī King, and Yōuzhōu Governor.
Western Yān ruler Mùróng Yǒng appointed Wèichén as Grand General and Shuòzhōu Governor.
48. In the eleventh month,
Qín Minister Kòu Yí escorted Bóhǎi Prince Fú Yì and Jìběi Prince Fú Chǎng from Xìngchéng to flee to Nán'ān.
Nán'ān Prince Fú Dēng held a funeral and observed mourning,
posthumously naming Qín ruler Fú Pī as Emperor Āipíng.
Dēng proposed establishing Yì as ruler,
but the crowd said:
"Although Bóhǎi Prince is the son of the late emperor,
he is still young,
and cannot endure many hardships.
Now three enemies are watching covetously,
the three enemies,
refer to Yáo Chǎng, Mùróng Chuí, and Mùróng Yǒng.
Only you, Great King, can handle this."
Dēng then built an altar east of Lǒng,
and ascended the imperial throne.
Dēng,
courtesy name Wéngāo,
was a clansman descendant of Fú Jiān.
He changed the era name to Tàichū,
and established officials.
49. Mùróng Róu, Mùróng Shèng, and Shèng's younger brother Huì were all in Chángzǐ.
In the ninth year of Tàiyuán,
Róu and others escaped from Cháng'ān,
and fled to Mùróng Chōng;
after Chōng died,
they followed Yǒng eastward.
"Our sovereign has already restored Yōu and Jì,
our sovereign,
refers to Yān ruler Mùróng Chuí.
East,
refers to Yān ruler Mùróng Chuí;
west,
refers to Yān ruler Mùróng Yǒng.
Whether wise or foolish,
we will all be unable to avoid disaster,
it is better to return east in time,
and not sit waiting to be slaughtered!"
So they fled together and returned to Yān.
Over a year later,
Western Yān ruler Mùróng Yǒng executed all descendants of Yān ruler Mùróng Jùn and Yān ruler Mùróng Chuí,
leaving none, male or female.
The history remarks on Mùróng Shèng's wisdom.
50. Zhāng Dàyù entered Líntáo from Xījùn,
plundered over five thousand households,
and occupied and defended Jùchéng.
Jùchéng is within Líntáo's boundaries.
51. In the twelfth month,

Lǚ Guāng proclaimed himself Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Palace Attendant, Grand Commander of Internal and External Forces, Commander of Military Affairs in Lǒngyòu and Héxī, Grand General, Liángzhōu Governor, and Duke of Jiǔquán.
52. Qín ruler Fú Dēng established the spirit tablet of Ancestor Shìzǔ in the army,
Qín ruler Fú Jiān's temple name was Shìzǔ.
A carriage with screens on all four sides is called a zīpíng.
Píng,
read as pián.
He guarded it with three hundred Tiger Guards,
and whatever he wished to do,
he would first report to the tablet and then act.
Leading fifty thousand troops,
he attacked Later Qín eastward.
The officers and soldiers all engraved "death"
and "rest"
on their spears and armor;
móu,
helmet.
kǎi,
armor.
móu,
pronounced móu.
Meaning they wished to take revenge, and would only rest upon death.
Yáng Zhènghéng said: According to the Zìlín: móu,
ancient form of the character for spear.
Knowing the thickness of the armor,
distributing it from within,
thus each man fought for himself,
and they were invincible wherever they went.
Earlier,
when Cháng'ān was about to fall,
referring to when Fú Jiān was besieged by Mùróng Chōng.
they built fortifications to defend themselves;
later they accepted Later Qín official titles.
Later Qín ruler Yáo Chǎng buried Qín ruler Fú Jiān with royal rites between the two fortifications.
When Dēng arrived,
Sōng and Kōng surrendered with their troops.
Dēng appointed Sōng as Yōngzhōu Governor,
Kōng as Jīngzhào Governor,
and reburied Jiān with imperial rites.
On the 53rd day, Yǐyǒu,
the ruler of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, attacked Wú Shēn's fortifications,
captured them,
and Shēn fled alone on horseback.
Wú Shēn was then occupying Qīnghé and had rebelled against Yān.
Liáochéng County,
during the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Dōng Commandery,
and during the Jìn dynasty, belonged to Píngyuán Commandery.
Wēn Xiáng, the former Crown Prince's Assistant of Yān, came to surrender,
and was appointed as the Grand Administrator of Jìběi,
stationed at Dōng'ē.
Dōng'ē County,
during the Hàn dynasty, belonged to Dōng Commandery,
and during the Jìn dynasty, belonged to Jìběi Commandery.
For "洗" (xiǎn),
the pronunciation is according to "悉薦翻" (xī jiàn fān).
For "濟" (Jì),
the pronunciation is according to "子禮翻" (zǐ lǐ fān).
Xiáng sent his cousin Wēn Pān to guard the southern bank of the Yellow River,
and his son Wēn Kǎi to guard Qiāo'áo to resist them.
On the 54th day, the ruler of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, appointed the King of Wèi, Tuòbá Guī, as the Western Chányú,
and enfeoffed him as the King of Shànggǔ;
Guī did not accept.
Guī's refusal of Yān's enfeoffment
indicates that his ambitions are not small.
For "單" (chán),
the pronunciation is "音蟬" (yīn chán).
