Emperor Lièzōng Xiàowǔ, Middle Part Two
The twelfth year of Tàiyuán (Dīnghài, 387)
1 In spring,
the first month,
on the day Yǐsì,
Zhū Xù was appointed as the Inspector of Qīng and Yǎn provinces,
replacing Xiè Xuán to garrison Péngchéng;
Xù requested to garrison Huáiyīn instead,
and this was approved.
Xù requested to garrison Huáiyīn
because Yān was strong at the time,
and was certain to advance and seize the region south of the Yellow River.
Péngchéng was far from Jiànkāng,
making it difficult to receive reinforcements and support, hence the request.
This was to give Xuán a more secure interior region.
For "會" (guì),
the pronunciation is "工外翻" (gōng wài fān).
2 On the day Dīngwèi,
a general amnesty was declared.
3 The ruler of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, reviewed his troops by the Yellow River,
Wéi Zhāo said: "觀" (guàn) means to display,
to show,
deploying troops to demonstrate might and power.
For "觀" (guàn),
the pronunciation is "古玩翻" (gǔ wán fān).
"Wēn Xiáng and his followers,
are all pale-faced Confucian scholars,
a disorderly mob gathered together,
relying solely on the long river for their defense;
if our great army crosses the river,
they will surely tremble at the sight of our banners and collapse,
without even engaging in battle."
Chuí followed this advice.
On the day Wùwǔ,
he sent General Zhènběi Lán Hàn and General Hùjūn Píng Yòu to cross the river forty lǐ west of Qiāo'áo,
and Lóng deployed the main force on the northern bank.
Wēn Pān and Wēn Kǎi indeed fled toward the city,
likely toward Dōng'ē city.
For "趣" (qū),
the pronunciation is "七喻翻" (qī yù fān).
They were heavily defeated.
Xiáng fled by night with his wife and children to Péngchéng,
and his followers, over thirty thousand households, all surrendered to Yān.
Chuí appointed the King of Tàiyuán, Mùróng Kǎi, as the Inspector of Yǎn province,
to garrison Dōng'ē.
Initially,
when Chuí was in Cháng'ān,
the King of Qín, Fú Jiān, once held his hand and spoke with him,
the Attendant Officer Guāng Zuò said to Jiān:
"Does Your Majesty somewhat suspect Mùróng Chuí?
Chuí is not one to remain under others for long."
Jiān informed Chuí of this.
When the ruler of Qín, Fú Pī, fled from Yè to Jìnyáng,
as seen in the tenth year of the previous scroll.
Zuò followed Fú Pī in Yè,
as seen in the ninth year of the previous scroll.
He was the son of Fēng Yì.
Fēng Yì served Yān,
when Yān rose in Chānglí,
Yì contributed greatly.
See the ninth year of scroll one hundred and five.
An edict appointed Zuò and others as Grand Administrators of various commanderies in Héběi,
all stationed in Jìběi and Púyáng,
Jìběi and Púyáng,
two commanderies.
For "濟" (Jì),
the pronunciation is "子禮翻" (zǐ lǐ fān).
For "濮" (Pú),
the pronunciation is "博木翻" (bó mù fān).
Shī Gǔ said: This means to loosely control and attach them.
They all went to the Yān army and surrendered.
Chuí pardoned them,
treating and安抚 them as before.
When Chuí saw Guāng Zuò,
tears streamed down, soaking his lapels,
and he said:
"The King of Qín treated me deeply,
and I served him to the fullest;
but because of the suspicions and jealousy of the two lords,
the two lords,
referring to Chánglè Duke Pī and Píngyuán Duke Huī.
As seen in the ninth year of scroll one hundred and five.
I could not sleep at midnight."
Zuò also wept bitterly.
Chuí bestowed gold and silk upon Zuò,
but Zuò firmly declined,
Chuí said:
"Do you still suspect me?"
Zuò said:
"In the past, I only knew to be loyal to whom I served,
never expecting Your Majesty to still remember it until now,
how dare I escape death!"
Chuí said:
"This is your loyalty,
exactly what I seek,
my earlier words were just in jest."
Using Confucius's words.
He appointed him as a Regular Palace Attendant.
Guāng Zuò,
was a eunuch of Qín,
hence he was given this position.
4 Zhái Liáo sent his son Zhái Zhāo to raid Chén and Yǐng,
Zhū Xù sent General Qín Yīng to attack and drive them away.
5 The ruler of Qín, Fú Dēng, established Máo Shì as empress,
and the King of Bóhǎi, Fú Yì, as Crown Prince.
The empress,
was the daughter of Máo Xìng.
He sent an envoy to appoint the King of Dōnghǎi, Fú Zuǎn, as Commissioner with Extraordinary Powers, Commander of All Military Affairs, Grand Preceptor, and concurrently Grand Marshal,
enfeoffing him as the Prince of Lǔ;
Zuǎn's younger brother, Fú Shīnú, as General Fǔjūn and Governor of Bìng province,
enfeoffed as the Duke of Shuòfāng.
Zuǎn angrily said to the envoy:
"The King of Bóhǎi is the former emperor's son,
why did Nán'ān not establish him and instead establish himself?"
Chief Clerk Wáng Lǚ admonished:
"Nán'ān has already been established,
and there is no reason to change midway;
now the enemy invaders are not yet destroyed,
we cannot have enmity within the imperial clan."
Zuǎn then accepted the appointment.
Subsequently, the Lúshuǐ Hú Péng Pèigǔ, the Tūgè Dǒng Chéng and Zhāng Lóngshì, and the Xīnpíng Qiāng Léi Èdì all submitted to Zuǎn,
giving him over a hundred thousand followers.
Because Dēng and Zuǎn joined forces,
their influence gradually grew,
hence they came to submit to him.
For "屠" (Tū),
the pronunciation is "直於翻" (zhí yú fān).
6 The ruler of Later Qín, Yáo Cháng, relocated thirty thousand households of powerful families from Qín province to Āndìng.
Last year, Cháng relocated people from Āndìng to populate Cháng'ān,
and now he relocates powerful families from Qín province to populate Āndìng.
It seems Cháng started his uprising with Āndìng as his base,
and desired to make Cháng'ān his capital,
hence he relocated people in stages according to distance.
7 Initially, Qí Shè of Āncì County gathered a crowd of over eight thousand households and occupied Xīnzhà,
surrendering to Yān.
Āncì County
belonged to Bóhǎi in the Former Hàn,
to Guǎngyáng Principality in the Later Hàn,
and to Yān Principality in Jìn.
Xīnzhà was likely within the boundaries of Wèi Commandery.
To surrender,
hù jiāng fān.
Later, he rebelled again,
allying with Zhāng Yuàn.
Yuàn personally led over ten thousand men to advance and station at Wèngkǒu in Zhù'ē.
Zhù'ē County
belonged to Píngyuán Commandery in Hàn,
and to Jǐnán Commandery in Jìn.
Yuàn advanced from Tàishān and stationed there.
Liú Xù said: Yǔchéng County of Qí Prefecture,
was Zhù'ē County in Hàn.
In the first year of Tiānbǎo,
it was renamed.
Sòng Bái said: Zhù'ē,
like Dōng'ē,
was the ancient Zhù State, descendants of the Yellow Emperor.
According to ancient Dōng'ē,
Qí was Dōng'ē,
Hàn was Zhù'ē County.
The old city was two lǐ northeast of present-day Fēngqí County;
Táng changed it to Yǔchéng.
Again,
fú yòu fān.
To lead,
dú yuē shuài.
Wèng,
wū gòng fān.
Together, they responded to Shè.
Gāoyáng Prince Lóng said to Chuí:
"Xīnzhà is solid and strong,
attacking it would not be easy to capture quickly.
If we keep our troops stationed under its walls for long,
Zhāng Yuàn, leading the displaced people,
might ally with Dīnglíng in the west.
Dīnglíng,
refers to Zhái Liáo.
To lead,
dú yuē shuài.
Although Yuàn's troops are many,
they are all newly attached,
and not yet capable of fierce combat.
Taking advantage of their arrival,
we should strike them first.
Yuàn and his son rely on their bravery,
and will certainly not avoid battle.
They can be captured in one battle.
Once Yuàn is defeated,
Shè will not be able to survive on his own."
Chuí followed his advice.
In the second month,
he sent Fànyáng Prince Dé, Chénliú Prince Shào, and General of Dragon-Steeds Zhāng Chóng
to lead twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to join Lóng in attacking Yuàn.
The army reached Dǒuchéng,
over twenty lǐ from Wèngkǒu,
and dismounted to rest.
Yuàn led his troops in a sudden attack,
startling the Yān men into panic.
Dé's troops retreated and fled,
but Lóng held his troops steady.
Yuàn's son Guī charged out to assault the formation,
and Lóng sent his attendant Wáng Mò to counterattack,
beheading him.
Lóng slowly advanced to battle,
and Yuàn's troops then retreated.
Dé retreated over a lǐ,
then reorganized his troops,
returned, and joined Lóng,
saying to Lóng:
"The enemy's morale is at its peak,
we should delay for now."
Lóng said:
"Yuàn took advantage of our unpreparedness,
and should have achieved a great victory;
but our soldiers, all separated by the river crossing,
under pressing circumstances,
each thinks of fighting on his own.
This means the troops are separated by the river crossing,
with strong enemies ahead,
retreat means drowning,
so they think of it and each fights for himself.
Now that the enemy has not gained advantage,
their morale is exhausted and their momentum weakened.
They all have thoughts of advancing or retreating,
and cannot fight together vigorously.
We should attack them quickly."
Dé said:
"I will follow whatever you decide."
They then advanced,
fought at Wèngkǒu,
and greatly defeated them,
beheading seven thousand eight hundred;
Yuàn escaped and defended Sānbùkǒu.
The Yān army advanced to Lìchéng.
Lìchéng County had belonged to Jǐnán Commandery since Hàn times.
Chuí appointed Chénliú Prince Shào as Governor of Qīng Province,
to guard Lìchéng.
Dé and others returned with their troops,
and Dōng Luán of Xīnzhà captured Shè and sent him over.
It indeed turned out as Mùróng Lóng had predicted.
Tángyùn: Dōng,
is a surname.
The rest were all pardoned.
8 In the third month,
Qín ruler Dēng appointed Dòu Chōng as Governor of Nán Qín Province,
Yáng Dìng as Governor of Yì Province,
Yáng Bì as Minister of Works and Governor of Liáng Province,
and Qǐfú Guórén as Grand General, Great Chányú, and Prince of Yuànchuān.
Dù Yòu said: Yuànchuān is in Wǔquán County of Lán Prefecture,
near the Great and Small Yú Valleys.
I say Dù Yòu spoke from his own opinion.
Chán,
yīn chán.
9 Wáng Mǐn of Shànggǔ in Yān killed Grand Administrator Fēng Jí,
and Xǔ Qiān of Dài Commandery expelled Grand Administrator Jiǎ Rùn,
each attaching their commanderies to Liú Xiǎn.
This sets the stage for Yān to attack Liú Xiǎn.
10 Yān's Lèlàng Prince Wēn was appointed Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs.
Under "Yān"
there should be
the character "yǐ"
Lèlàng,
yīn luò láng.
11 In summer,
the fourth month,
on Wùchén,
the Emperor's mother Lǐ Shì was honored as Empress Dowager,
with ceremonial attire like that of an Empress Dowager.
12 Later Qín's General Who Conquers the West Yáo Shuòdé, pressured by Yáng Dìng,
retreated to defend Jīngyáng.
Jīngyáng County,
belonged to Āndìng Commandery in the Former Hàn,
was abolished in the Later Hàn and Jìn,
and in Qín belonged to Lǒngdōng Commandery.
Dù Yòu said: Hàn's Jīngyáng County is the old Jīngyáng city within the boundaries of present-day Píngliàng Commandery.
They fought at Jīngyáng,
and Shuòdé was greatly defeated.
Later Qín ruler Cháng came from Yīnmì to rescue him,
and Zuǎn retreated to station at Fūlù.
Yīnmì County,
belonged to Āndìng Commandery,
was the Mì State in the Yīn era.
Fūlù,
is Táng's Fāng Prefecture Fūchéng County,
which is that place.
13 Yān ruler Chuí returned from Qiáo'áo to Zhōngshān,
and Mùróng Róu, Mùróng Shèng, and Mùróng Huì came from Zhǎngzǐ.
Róu and others had fled from Zhǎngzǐ last year,
and now reached Zhōngshān.
On Gēngzǐ,
Chuí held a great amnesty for them.
Joyful that his descendants were safe and had returned east,
he therefore held a widespread amnesty for them.
For,
yú wèi fān.
"How are the sentiments of the people in Zhǎngzǐ,
can it be taken?"
Shèng said:
"The western army is in turmoil,
the people have thoughts of returning east.
Your Majesty should only cultivate benevolent governance and wait for it.
If the great army approaches,
they will certainly cast aside their weapons and come,
like filial sons returning to a loving father."
Chuí was pleased.
On Guǐwèi,
he enfeoffed Róu as Prince of Yángpíng,
Shèng as Duke of Chánglè,
and Huì as Duke of Qīnghé.
14 Zhái Chàng, a man from Gāopíng, captured the Grand Administrator Xú Hǎnyuǎn and
surrendered the commandery to Zhái Liáo.
The ruler of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, said to his generals:
"Liáo, with the forces of a single city,
shifts allegiance between three states."
The three states
refer to Jìn, Yān, and Western Yān.
In the fifth month,
he appointed Zhāngwǔ Prince Mùróng Zhòu as Supervisor of Military Affairs Inside and Outside,
to assist the Crown Prince Bǎo in guarding Zhōngshān;
Chuí personally led the generals south to attack Liáo,
appointing Tàiyuán Prince Mùróng Kǎi as Vanguard Commander-in-Chief.
Liáo's troops were all men from Yān and Zhào;
upon hearing of Kǎi's arrival,
they all said:
"The son of the Prince of Tàiyuán
is like our father and mother!"
Kǎi's father, Mùróng Kè, had served as Chancellor of Yān,
and the people of Yān and Zhào cherished his memory,
hence this statement.
Liáo, fearing this,
sent an envoy to request surrender;
Chuí appointed Liáo as Governor of Xúzhōu,
enfeoffing him as Duke of Hénán.
He proceeded to Líyáng,
accepted the surrender, and then returned.
Jiǎ Bào, a man from Jǐngxíng,
Jǐngxíng County belonged to Chángshān Commandery.
Xíng,
pronounced xíng.
launched a night attack on Zhōngshān,
breaching its outer walls.
Zhāngwǔ Prince Mùróng Zhòu led a surprise force to attack from outside,
while Crown Prince Bǎo raised a clamor from within,
and they joined in a combined assault,
crushing the enemy,
capturing all their troops.
Only Jiǎ Bào escaped alone on horseback and got away.
15 Liú Xiǎn's territory was vast and his soldiers strong,
making him powerful in the north.
At that time, discord arose among his brothers.
The Chief Clerk of Wèi, Zhāng Gǔn, said to the Prince of Wèi, Tuòbá Guī:
"Xiǎn's ambition is to annex others;
if we do not take advantage of his internal collapse to seize him now,
Núzhēn and Fèiní have surrendered to us one after another,
hence this statement.
However, I cannot overcome him alone;
I request that we join with Yān to attack him together."
Guī agreed
and again sent Ān Tóng to request troops from Yān.
Last year, Wèi had sent Ān Tóng to request troops from Yān to defeat Kūduō,
hence the term "again" here.
Again,
pronounced fú yòu fān.
16 An edict was issued summoning the recluse Dài Kuí from Kuàijī,
but Kuí repeatedly declined and did not go;
the commandery and county authorities persistently urged and pressured him without cease,
so Kuí fled and hid in Wú.
Xiè Xuán submitted a memorial stating:
"Kuí seeks to follow his own will;
the Analects say: 'He retires from the world to follow his own will.'
He will suffer the hardships of wind and frost.
Since Your Majesty already loves and values him,
you should also allow his person and reputation to be preserved intact.
I request that the summons be rescinded."
The Emperor approved.
Xuán was the Neishi of Kuàijī,
hence he submitted the memorial on Kuí's behalf.
He was the elder brother of Dài Suì.
Dài Suì appears in the fourth year of the 104th scroll.
17 The ruler of Qín, Fú Dēng, appointed his elder brother Fú Tóngchéng as Minister over the Masses and Acting Prefect of the Masters of Writing,
enfeoffing him as Prince of Yǐngchuān;
his younger brother Fú Guǎng as Palace Assistant Imperial Clerk,
enfeoffing him as Prince of Ānchéng;
and his son Fú Chóng as Left Deputy of the Masters of Writing,
enfeoffing him as Prince of Dōngpíng.
18 The ruler of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, returned from Líyáng to Zhōngshān.
19 Wú Shēn killed the Grand Administrator of Qīnghé in Yān, Dīng Guó;
Wáng Zǔ, a man from Zhāngwǔ, killed the Grand Administrator Bái Qīn;
and Zhāng Shēn, a man from Bóhǎi, occupied Gāochéng and rebelled.
Gāochéng County belonged to Bóhǎi Commandery.
Xián states: The old city of Gāochéng
is south of present-day Yánshān County in Cāngzhōu.
20 Yuànchuān Prince Qīfú Guórén led thirty thousand cavalry to attack the three tribes of the Xiānbēi chieftains Mìguì, Yùgǒu, and Tílún at Liùquán.
Mìguì led one tribe,
Yùgǒu led one tribe,
and Tílún led one tribe.
Liùquán is in Gāopíng.
Shuài,
pronounced shuài.
Qí,
pronounced jì.
In the seventh month,
he fought Mòyígān and Jīn Xī at Kěhúnchuān.
According to the Zǎijì,
Guórén attacked the three tribes,
and Mòyígān and Jīn Xī joined forces to attack Guórén,
hence they met in battle at Kěhúnchuān.
The location should be northeast of Yǒngshì County in Tiānshuǐ.
All three tribes surrendered.
21 The ruler of Qín, Fú Dēng, encamped at Wǎtíng.
The ruler of Later Qín, Yáo Cháng, attacked Péng Pèigǔ's fort,
captured it,
and Pèigǔ fled to Xìngchéng.
Péng Pèigǔ
was a Lúshuǐ Hú,
who had established a fort in Èr County.
Dù Yòu states: Xìngchéng is west of Fāngzhōu.
He appointed the Crown Prince Yáo Xīng to guard Cháng'ān.
22 The Prince of Zhào of Yān, Mùróng Lín, campaigned against Wáng Mǐn in Shànggǔ,
and executed him.
23 Liú Wèichén presented horses to Yān,
but Liú Xiǎn plundered them.
The ruler of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, was angered
and sent Tàiyuán Prince Mùróng Kǎi with troops to assist Prince of Zhào Mùróng Lín in attacking Xiǎn,
crushing him decisively.
Xiǎn fled to the western mountains of Mǎyì.
The Prince of Wèi, Tuòbá Guī, led troops to join Lín in attacking Xiǎn at Mízé.
According to the Wèishū Dìjì,
Mízé is south of Mǎyì.
Xiǎn fled to Western Yān,
and Lín gathered all his tribesmen,
seizing horses, cattle, and sheep numbering in the tens of millions.
With Liú Xiǎn destroyed, the Tuòbá clan grew strong.
For those planning for the Mùróng clan,
nothing would be better than to allow both to benefit and coexist,
so as to avoid the calamity of the state's destruction in the future.
24 Lǚ Guāng's generals Péng Huǎng and Xú Jiǒng attacked Zhāng Dàyù at Líntáo,
defeating him.
Zhāng Dàyù had fled to Líntáo,
see the previous year in the previous scroll.
Táo,
pronounced tǔ dāo fān.
Wáng Mù fled to Jiànkāng.
In the eighth month,
a man from Guǎngwǔ captured Dàyù and sent him to Gūzāng,
where he was executed.
Mù attacked and occupied Jiǔquán,
proclaiming himself Grand General and Governor of Liángzhōu.
25 On the Xīnsì day,
the Emperor's son Dézōng was established as Crown Prince,
and a general amnesty was declared.
26 The ruler of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, established Liú Xiǎn's younger brother Kění as Prince of Wūhuán,
to pacify his people,
and relocated over eight thousand households to Zhōngshān.
27 The Grand Administrator of Féngyì of Qín, Lán Dú, led twenty thousand troops from Pínyáng into Héníng.
Pínyáng County
was established by Duke Lì of Qín,
and since Hàn times has belonged to Féngyì.
Yīng Shào states: It is on the north bank of the Pín River.
According to the Zǎijì,
Héníng is southeast of Xìngchéng, north of the mountains.
Shuài,
pronounced shuài.
Dú's younger brother Shīnú urged Dú to claim the imperial title,
but Dú refused;
Shīnú killed Dú and replaced him,
so Dú broke with Shīnú.
The ruler of Western Yān, Mùróng Yǒng, attacked Dú,
and Dú
requested aid from Later Qín.
The ruler of Later Qín, Yáo Cháng, wished to rescue him personally.
The Prefect of the Masters of Writing Yáo Mín and the Left Deputy Yǐn Wěi said:
"Fú Dēng is nearby at Wǎtíng,
and will take advantage of our rear being empty to attack."
Cháng said:
"Fú Dēng's forces are numerous,
and cannot be subdued in a short time;
Dēng is slow and cautious, lacking decisiveness,
and certainly will not lightly lead his army deep into our territory.
Within two months,
I will surely defeat the enemy and return;
even if Dēng arrives by then,
he will be unable to accomplish anything."
In the ninth month,
Cháng encamped at Níyuán.
The Hànshū Dìlǐzhì states
that Běidì Commandery had Níyáng County.
Yīng Shào's commentary states: The Ní River emerges from the northern barbarian lands of Yùzhì.
He was greatly defeated,
and fled to the Xiānbēi.
Later Qín gathered all his troops,
and Tūgè leaders like Dǒng Chéng all surrendered.
With the defeat of the Fú Dú brothers,
Fú Dēng's situation became isolated.
Tū,
pronounced zhí yú fān.
28 The ruler of Qín, Fú Dēng, advanced and occupied Húkōng Fort,
a fort built by the Commandant of the Garrison Cavalry of Qín, Hú Kōng,
located within the boundaries of Xīnpíng.
29 In winter,
the tenth month,
Zhái Liáo rebelled against Yān once more,
sending troops to join Wáng Zǔ and Zhāng Shēn in raiding and plundering Qīnghé and Píngyuán.
30. Later Qin ruler Yáo Cháng advanced to attack Western Yan ruler Mùróng Yǒng west of the Yellow River.
"Western Yan King"
should be
"Western Yan ruler."
This refers to the area from Lóngmén to Huàyīn,
west of the Yellow River.
Lán Dú again deployed troops to resist and defend,
Cháng attacked him;
in the twelfth month,
captured Dú,
and then proceeded to Xìngchéng.
31. Later Qin's Yáo Fāngchéng attacked the fortress of Qín's Yōng Province governor Xú Sōng,
captured it,
seized Sōng and enumerated his crimes.
Sōng cursed, saying:
"Your Yáo Cháng's crimes deserve ten thousand deaths.
Fú Huángméi wanted to execute him,
but the late emperor stopped it.
This refers to the time when Yáo Xiāng was defeated in the first year of Mùdì's Shēngpíng era.
He received the utmost favor and honor.
Yet he was even less grateful than dogs or horses that recognize the kindness of their caretakers,
personally committing great treason.
This refers to killing Qín ruler Fú Jiān at the Xìnpíng Buddhist temple.
Why not kill me quickly!"
Fāngchéng became angry,
executed Sōng three times.
The three executions mean:
cutting off his feet,
cutting off his waist,
and cutting off his neck.
He rewarded the army with Sōng's wife and children.
Later Qin ruler Yáo Cháng dug up the corpse of Qín ruler Fú Jiān,
whipped it countless times,
stripped off its clothes leaving it naked,
laid it on thorns,
dug a pit and buried it.
Jiān was buried between the fortresses of Xú Sōng and Hú Kōng.
Since Xú Sōng's fortress had already fallen,
Yáo Cháng was able to dig up the grave and whip the corpse to vent his anger.
Luǒ (倮),
pronunciation: lǎng guǒ fān.
Jiàn (薦),
means to lay upon.
32. Liáng Province suffered a great famine,
one dǒu of rice cost five hundred coins,
people ate each other,
more than half died.
33. Lǚ Guāng's Xīpíng commandery governor Kāng Níng proclaimed himself King of the Xiōngnú,
killed Huánghé commandery governor Qiáng Xǐ and rebelled.
Xīpíng commandery,
established at the end of the Eastern Hàn,
partitioned from Jīnchéng,
corresponds to the Táng dynasty's Shànzhōu,
that is its location.
Huánghé commandery,
established by the Héxī Zhāng clan,
likely also within the boundaries of Shànzhōu.
Qiáng (強),
pronunciation: qí liǎng fān.
In the east, he allied with Kāng Níng,
in the west, he communicated with Wáng Mù.
Guāng wanted to personally attack Huǎng,
his generals all said:
"Now Kāng Níng is in the south,

If Huǎng and Mù are not yet eliminated,

we will be in a difficult position,
the situation will surely be extremely dangerous."
Guāng said:
"It is indeed as you say.
However, if I do not go now,
I am just sitting and waiting for them to come.
If the three bandits join forces,
the three bandits refer to
Kāng Níng, Péng Huǎng, and Wáng Mù.
then the areas outside the city will all be lost to us,
and the great enterprise will be finished.
Now Huǎng has just rebelled,
his ties with Níng and Mù are not yet close,

capturing him should be relatively easy."
He then personally led thirty thousand cavalry,

and upon arrival,
attacked for twenty days,
captured the city,
and executed Huǎng.
Initially,

"Now the people are about to become barbarians,

He then, together with his commandery fellow Suǒ Gǔ, raised troops in response to Mù,

Mù appointed Yǔ as Left Director of the Grand Secretariat and Army Counselor General,

Later, Mù listened to slanderous words,
led troops to attack Gǔ,
Yǔ remonstrated but was not heeded,

"I will not see you again!"
He returned, pulled the covers over his face,

Lǚ Guāng, hearing of this, said:
"The two rebels are attacking each other,
this means they will be captured.
We must not fear the hardship of repeated battles and miss the opportunity for lasting peace.
'One effort for lasting peace,'
there is an ancient saying for this."
He defeated them.

Xīng (騂),
pronunciation: sī róng fān.
Lǚ Guāng had newly acquired Héxī,
with partisans rebelling internally,
and enemies attacking externally.
Although he won battle after battle,
his foundation was not solid,
and he was likely insufficient to bequeath to his descendants.

read as zhī liǎng.
Thirteen is considered a half laborer.
The tasks assigned are no longer those for children,
does this not harm natural principles and burden the people!
I propose that twenty be considered a full laborer,
sixteen a half laborer,
then people will not die prematurely,
and will grow and multiply."
The Emperor adopted many of his suggestions.
While in Yùzhāng,
Nìng dispatched fifteen advisory officers to subordinate cities,
Yùzhāng administered sixteen counties: Nánchāng, Hǎihūn, Xīngàn, Jiànchéng, Wàngcài, Yǒngxiū, Jiànchāng, Wúpíng, Yùzhāng, Péngzé, Ài, Kānglè, Fēngchéng, Xīnchāng, Yífēng, and Zhōnglíng.
One county was near the city walls,
the remaining fifteen counties each sent one advisory officer.
Xià,
read as xiá jià.
Together with officials on leave,
they inquired about the strengths and faults of the local officials.
Xú Miǎo wrote to Nìng saying:
"Your judgments are fair and wise,
and affairs are handled without delay,
then officials are cautious about their faults
fù,
meaning crimes.
If officials fear punishment,
they will be careful in every matter.
Duàn,
read as dīng luàn.
Rén tīng,
that is, mín tīng.
The historians of the Jìn Shū avoided Táng Tàizōng's taboo,
changing mín to
"rén",
and the Zīzhì Tōngjiàn followed this.
How can they embellish their wandering reputations!
Not only is it insufficient to bring benefit,
it truly provides the means for exploitation;
cán yú,
meaning those sent out feed off and plunder the people.
Zhèng Xuán said: East of Zhào and Wèi,
shí and shí are pronounced the same.
Shí,
means "this" or "is".
The Shī says:
"He built walls and moats,
he measured fields and registered them."
"Shí"
should be written as
"shí".
It says that the ancestors of the Marquis of Hán were weak,
and the states they received were mostly extinguished.
Now restoring the old duties,
continuing the extinct lines,
therefore he built this city,
repaired these moats and wells,
pastured these fields,
collected these taxes,
making them as before.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: Whenever shí is used,
it affirms something that already exists.
Here, it is just describing actions, not affirming them,
so it is changed to shí,
interpreted as "is".
East of Zhào and Wèi,
shí and shí are pronounced the same,
Zhèng verified this based on contemporary usage.
In the sixth year of Duke Huán in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
"The Duke of Zhōu shí came."
Because the sounds were the same,
the characters could vary.
In my opinion, Xú Miǎo's interpretation of shí as "is"
also makes sense in meaning.
How much more so for those who make many reports!
Since ancient times,
those who wish to be the ruler's eyes and ears,
are invariably petty men,
all first use minor loyalty to achieve great disloyalty,
first rely on minor trustworthiness to achieve great untrustworthiness,
thereby causing slander and flattery to flourish together,
good and evil to be inverted,
should we not be wary of this!
You should carefully select administrators,
the commandery uses its assistants as administrators.
Each bureau should have good clerks to handle documents,
shè,
means to oversee,
to organize.
Àn,
means to rely on.
Wén àn,
refers to the bureau documents kept for reference.
Then integrity and ability,
will be clear from the affairs;
you need only judge with an impartial mind,
what need is there for eyes and ears!
In the past, Empress Mǎ, the Virtuous, never looked to her attendants to speak,
Emperor Hàn Míngdì's Empress Mǎ was posthumously titled Empress Virtuous.
How much more should a great man not be able to avoid this!"
On the 21st day of the 12th month,
the Later Qin ruler Yáo Chàng sent his Eastern Gate General Rén Pén
(Eastern Gate General:
Yáo Chàng had him guard the eastern gate of Āndìng.)
(Rén:
pronounced like Rén.)
(Pén:
same as "盆",
pronounced Púbēn fān.)
to pretend to open the gate and let (Fú Dēng) in.
Dēng was about to follow this plan,
but his Campaigning East General Léi Èdì, who was leading troops outside,
(jiàng:
jí liàng fān.)
galloped on horseback to see Dēng,
saying:
"Yáo Chàng is full of deceit,
he cannot be trusted!"
Dēng then stopped.
When Chàng heard that Èdì had gone to see Dēng,
he said to his generals:
"If this Qiāng sees Dēng,
our plan will not succeed!"
Dēng, because Èdì's courage and strategy surpassed others,
secretly feared him.
Èdì became afraid,
and surrendered to Later Qin.
Chàng appointed Èdì as General Who Guards the Army.
22. The (Former) Qin appointed Prince Ānchéng (Fú) Guǎng as Minister over the Masses.
The 15th year (Gēngyín, 390)
1. Spring,
first month,
on Yǐhài,
Duke Xiàojìng of Qiáo, Tián, passed away.
2. The Western Yàn ruler Mùróng Yǒng led troops towards Luòyáng.
Zhǔ Xù crossed the river north from Héyīn,
and attacked and defeated him.
Xù pursued him to the Báishuǐ River.
(The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: The Báishuǐ River originates west of the old city of Gāodū County in Shàngdǎng,
flowing east past Tiānjǐng Pass.)
The place Xù reached
was 160 lǐ from Zhǎngzǐ.
As Zhái Liáo was plotting to advance on Luòyáng,
Xù then led his troops back,
attacked and drove him away;
he left the Soaring Hawk General Zhǔ Dǎng to garrison Shímén,
had his son Zhǔ Lüè supervise and protect Luòyáng,
with Army Advisor Zhào Fān assisting him,
and he himself returned to Xiāngyáng.
3. Sīmǎ Dàozǐ, the Prince of Lángyá, relying on favor, became arrogant and unrestrained; when attending feasts he would get heavily drunk,
sometimes lacking proper ritual respect.
The Emperor increasingly could not bear it,
and wanted to select someone of contemporary reputation for a frontier command to secretly check Dàozǐ.
He asked Wáng Yǎ, the Director of the Crown Prince's Guards of the Left:
"I wish to employ Wáng Gōng and Yīn Zhòngkān, what do you think?"
Yǎ said:
"Wáng Gōng's demeanor and spirit are aloof and noble,
his will and character upright and stern;
Zhòngkān is meticulous in minor conduct,
and is renowned for literary refinement and righteousness.
However, both are severe, narrow-minded, and self-opinionated,
and moreover, their practical abilities and strategic insight are not extensive;
if entrusted with a regional command,
when the empire is without incident,
they would be sufficient to maintain their duties,
but if incidents occur,
they will certainly become the steps to disorder!"
The Emperor did not listen.
(This sets the stage for the later military actions of Wáng and Yīn.)
(He was the son of Wáng Yùn;
Wáng Yùn
was the Empress's father.)
(He was the grandson of Yīn Róng.)
(Yīn Róng appears in the 96th scroll, in the 5th year of the Xiánkāng era of Emperor Chéng.)
On Xīnsì,
he appointed Secretariat Director Wáng Gōng as Commander of the military affairs of the five provinces Qīng, Yǎn, Yōu, Bìng, and Jì, and Governor of Yǎn and Qīng,
stationing him at Jīngkǒu.
4. Third month,
on Wùchén,
a general amnesty was issued.
5. The Later Qin ruler Yáo Chàng attacked the Former Qin Administrator of Fúfēng, Qí Yìnán, at Xīnluó Fortress,
capturing it.
Yìnán fled.
The Former Qin ruler Fú Dēng attacked the Later Qin Administrator of Tiānshuǐ, Zhāng Yèshēng, at Lǒngdōng.
(Lǒngdōng:
the area of Jīngyáng County in Āndìng.)
Dēng then withdrew.
6. Summer,
the Former Qin's General Who Guards the East, Wèi Jiēfēi, proclaimed himself the Soaring Heavenly King.
(The Jìn Shū Zǎijì writes
"Wèi Hèfēi".
In the first year of the Tàiyuán era,
Qin sent the Court General Wèi Héfēi to attack the Dí and Qiāng;
presumably this is the same person.)
The General Who Guards the Army, Léi Èdì, rebelled and responded to him,
attacking the General Who Guards the East, Yáo Hàndé, at Lǐrùn.
(Lǐrùn:
a place name,
south of Xíngwàng.
Lǐ Yánshòu said: East of Féngyì there is Lǐrùn Garrison.
According to the Wèi Shū, Biographies of the Imperial Clan,
Prince Āndìng of the Yuán clan, Xiè, in a memorial upon being appointed Governor of Huá Province, said:
"I humbly note that the provincial seat is at Lǐrùn Fortress.
Although it is the old territory of Shǎoliáng,
the granted lands of Jìn and Ruì,
however, as the Hu and Yi tribes have submitted internally,
it has become a settlement of Rong tribesmen.
I request to move to the old city of Féngyì.")
His ministers all said:
"Your Majesty does not worry about Fú Dēng who is sixty lǐ away,
(At that time, Dēng was heading for Cháng'ān,
occupying the Qiānhù stronghold at Xīnfēng.)
why is this?"
Chàng said:
"Dēng cannot be swiftly destroyed,
and our city also cannot be swiftly taken by Dēng.
Èdì's wisdom and strategy are extraordinary;
if he links up with Jiēfēi in the south,
and allies with Dǒng Chéng in the east,
(Dǒng Chéng
was of the Túgè tribe,
at that time occupying Běidì.)
then the area northeast of Cháng'ān will not be ours."
He then secretly led 1,600 elite troops to go there.
Jiēfēi and Èdì had tens of thousands of followers,
with Dí and Hu tribesmen joining them continuously.
Every time Chàng saw an army arrive,
he was pleased.
His ministers found this strange and asked him,
Chàng said:
"Jiēfēi and others incite and lure those of the same evil intent;
their kind is very numerous.
Even if I defeat their chief leaders,
the remaining factions will not be easy to pacify quickly;
now they gather like crows,
and I can take them while riding the momentum of victory,
finishing them off in one stroke."
(This is the same stratagem Cáo Cāo used against Mǎ Chāo and Hán Suì.)
(Jiēfēi and Èdì) attacked with all their forces;
Chàng firmly held his fortifications and did not engage,
showing weakness,
while secretly sending his son, the General of the Central Army, Yáo Chóng, to lead several hundred cavalry to come out behind them.
Jiēfēi's troops were thrown into disorder.
Chàng sent the General Who Pacifies Distant Lands, Wáng Chāo, and others to unleash their troops to attack,
beheading Jiēfēi and over ten thousand of his officers and men.
Èdì requested to surrender,
and Chàng treated him as before.
Èdì said to others:
"I considered myself outstanding in wisdom and courage for my time,
yet every time I encounter Old Man Yáo I am thwarted.
This is surely my lot!"
Chàng ordered Yáo Dāngchéng, at the site of their camp,
to plant a wooden stake in each fence hole to mark their battle achievements.
(They dug holes in the ground,
erected wooden stakes to make a fence,
hence there were fence holes.)
When asked about it,
Dāngchéng said:
"The camp ground is too small,
I have already expanded it."
Chàng said:
"Since I tied up my hair and came of age,
fighting with others,
I have never had such a swift victory,
using a thousand-some troops to defeat a host of thirty thousand.
The camp ground being small is what makes it remarkable;
how could larger be considered superior!"
7. The Tǔyùhún ruler Shìlián sent an envoy to offer tribute to the Prince of Jīnchéng, Qīfú Gānguī.
Gānguī appointed Shìlián as Governor of Shā Province and Prince of Báilán.

(Zhāng Mào of Héxī made the three commanderies of Dūnhuáng, Jìnchāng, and the Western Regions Protectorate, Colonel, and the Jade Gate Grand Army Protector, and their three encampments, into Shā Province;
Tǔyùhún did not yet possess this territory.)
(Lǐ Yánshòu said: This is because within the Tǔyùhún territory there is yellow sand,
extending for several hundred lǐ in circumference,
where no grass or trees grow,
hence it was called Shā Province.)
(Shǐ:
shū lì fān.)
(Xiàn:
xián biàn fān.)
8. On Bǐngyín,
the Prince of Wèi, Tuòbá Guī, met the Prince of Zhào of Yān, Mùróng Lín, at Yìxīn Mountain.
(Yìxīn Mountain is north of Niúchuān,
where the Hèlán tribe resided.
According to the Běi Shǐ,
crossing the Yīn Mountains to the north,
one reaches the Hèlán tribe.)
He defeated him,
and both the Hétūlín and Héxī tribes surrendered to Wèi.
(This shows that Yān cleared the way for Wèi.)
(Xiáng:
hù jiāng fān.)
9 In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Guō Zhì from Féngyì raised troops in Guǎngxiāng to respond to the state of Qín.
In the Wèi Shōu Dìxíngzhì,
it is recorded that Zhèng County had Guǎngxiāngyuán.
Zhèng County at that time belonged to Jīngzhào.
"Yáo Chǎng is cruel and oppressive,
his poison extends to both spirits and men.
Our generation has long enjoyed the benevolence of the late emperor, who was like Yáo and Shùn.
The late emperor
refers to the Qín ruler Jiān.
Chángbó
is Shìzhōng.
Nàyán
is Shàngshū.
Rather than living in shame,
it is better to die upholding the Way."
Thereupon, the fortresses in the Sānfǔ region all responded to him;
only Xún Yào from Zhèng County
gathered several thousand followers and submitted to the Later Qín.
Qín appointed Zhì as the Tàishǒu of Féngyì.
Later Qín appointed Yào as the Cìshǐ of Yùzhōu.
Xún Yào later wavered between the two sides,
was killed by Later Qín,
as will be seen later.
10 Liú Wèichén sent his son Zhílìdī to attack the Hèlán tribe.
Hè Nè was in dire straits,
and requested to surrender to Wèi.
On the bǐngzǐ day,
the Wèi king Guī led troops to rescue him,
and Zhílìdī retreated.
Guī relocated Nè's tribe,
settling them in the eastern region.
11 In the eighth month,
Liú Láozhī attacked Zhái Zhāo at Juànchéng,
Zhāo fled north of the Yellow River;
he also defeated Zhái Liáo at Huátái,
and Zhāng Yuàn came to surrender.
Zhái Liáo and Zhāng Yuàn's rebellion
is recorded in the eleventh year of the previous scroll.
Flee,
pronunciation zòu.
Defeat,
pronunciation bǔmài fān.
Juàn,
pronunciation juàn.
12 In the ninth month,
Wú Zhù from Běipíng gathered over a thousand followers,
established the monk Fǎ Cháng as the Son of Heaven,
captured Běipíng Commandery,
then advanced to raid Guǎngdū,
and entered Báilángchéng.
Báiláng County,
during the Former Hàn belonged to Yòuběipíng Commandery,
and was abolished during the Later Hàn and Jìn.
The Wèi Shōu Dìxíngzhì records: In the eighth year of Zhēnjūn of Later Wèi,
Jiàndé Commandery was established,
with its seat at Báilángchéng,
and Guǎngdū County belonged to it.
During the Yān period, it likely belonged to Běipíng Commandery.
The commandery and county officials all gathered there,
and when the masses heard that Zhù had rebelled,
they requested Lóng to return to the city,
and to send a large army to suppress him.
Lóng said:
"Now the common people are peacefully settled,
and the people have no thought of rebellion.
Zhù and his ilk use deceitful schemes to delude the foolish,
enticing and coercing them to gather,
but they are incapable of achieving anything."
Thereupon, he stayed to complete the burial,
and sent the Tàishǒu of Guǎngpíng and the Lìng of Guǎngdū to return first.
"Guǎngpíng"
should be
"Běipíng".
When Zhù's followers heard this,
they all dispersed,
were pursued and captured,
and executed.
13 Appointed Shìzhōng Wáng Guóbǎo as Zhōngshūlìng,
and shortly after, concurrently Zhōnglǐngjūn.
This was Dàozǐ's decision.
14 On the dīngwèi day,
appointed Wújùn Tàishǒu Wáng Xún as Shàngshū Yòupúyè.
15 Tǔyùhún Shìlián died,
and his son Shìpí succeeded him.
Shìpí, because his father and grandfather were kind and benevolent,
and were invaded and bullied by neighboring states,
Tǔyùhún Pìxī and Shìlián were kind and benevolent,
as recorded in the first year of Xián'ān of Emperor Jiǎnwén, scroll 103.
desired to achieve great deeds.
In winter,
the tenth month,
the Jīnchéng king Qiānguī sent an envoy to appoint Shìpí as Shāzhōu Mù and Báilán King;
Shìpí did not accept.
This sets the stage for the later campaign of Qǐfú Qiānguī against Tǔyùhún.
16 In the twelfth month,
Guō Zhì and Xún Yào fought east of Zhèng,
Zhì was defeated,
and fled to Luòyáng.
East of Zhèng
means east of Zhèng County.
17 Yuèzhì Jiégūī occupied Píngxiāng,
and rebelled against the Jīnchéng king Qiānguī.
In the twelfth year,
Yuèzhì Jiégūī submitted to the Qǐfú clan.
Sixteenth Year (Xīnmǎo, 391)
1 In spring,
the first month,
Yān established a mobile administration at Jì,
and added to Chánglè Gōng Shèng the duty of Lù Xíngtái Shàngshū Shì.
2 The Jīnchéng king Qiānguī attacked Yuèzhì Jiégūī;
Jiégūī surrendered,
and Qiānguī gave him a female relative in marriage.
3 Hè Rǎngān plotted to kill his elder brother Nè,
Nè learned of it,
and raised troops to attack him.
The Wèi king Guī informed Yān,
requesting to serve as a guide to suppress them.
In the second month,
on the jiǎxū day,
the Yān ruler Chuí sent the Zhào king Lín to lead troops to attack Nè,
and Zhènběi Jiāngjūn Lán Hàn led troops from Lóngchéng to attack Rǎngān.
Hè Rǎngān's tribe,
likely resided in the eastern part of the Hèlán tribe's territory,
hence Yān used troops from Lóngchéng to attack him.
Lead,
pronunciation jíliàng fān.
Lead,
read as shuài.
4 In the third month,
the Qín ruler Dēng advanced from Yōng to attack the Later Qín Āndōng Jiāngjūn Jīn Róng at Fànshìbǎo,
and captured it;
then crossed the Wèi River,
attacked the Jīngzhào Tàishǒu Wéi Fàn at Duànshìbǎo,
but did not capture it;
he then advanced and occupied Qūláo.
Qūláo is northeast of Dù County.
5 In summer,
the fourth month,
Yān's Lán Hàn defeated Hè Rǎngān at Niúdū.
Dū,
means a gathering place,
its location should be at Niúchuān,
where the barbarians herd and graze,
and gather here,
hence the name.
6 Xún Yào had ten thousand followers,
and secretly summoned the Qín ruler Dēng,
promising to act as an insider;
Dēng advanced from Qūláo towards Fánchuān,
Fánchuān,
likely refers to the Fánchuān of Dùlíng County.
In the fifth month,
the Later Qín ruler Chǎng led troops to meet him in battle,
Dēng attacked and defeated him,
killing his Right General Wú Zhōng.
Chǎng gathered his troops and fought again,
Yáo Shuòdé said:
"Your Majesty is usually cautious about engaging lightly in battle,
often preferring to use strategy to achieve victory,
now that the battle is lost, why do you press forward to confront the enemy again?"
Chǎng said:
"Dēng's use of troops is slow and hesitant,
and he does not understand the actual situation.
Now he advances lightly with his troops,
and occupies a position far to our east,
the location of Mǎtóuyuán is likely east of Cháng'ān.
A skilled commander,
observes the enemy's movements and discerns their true situation,
and thus is able to achieve victory.
Therefore, before they can join forces,
I must strike swiftly to disrupt their plans."
Thereupon he advanced to battle,
and inflicted a major defeat on them.
Dēng retreated and encamped at Méi.
7 The Qín Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ Qiáng Jīnchuí occupied Xīnpíng,
and surrendered to Later Qín,
sending his son Kuí as a hostage.
The Later Qín ruler Chǎng, with several hundred cavalry, entered Jīnchuí's camp.
His subordinates advised against it,
Chǎng said:
"Jīnchuí has already left Qín,
and Fú Dēng also desires to plot against me,
where else can he turn to?
Moreover, he has just come to submit sincerely,
we should treat him with sincerity to win him over,
how can we treat him with distrust and suspicion again!"
Later, some Dí people wanted to seize Chǎng,
but Jīnchuí did not agree.
Qiáng Jīnchuí,
was of the Dí ethnicity,
and a relative of the Qín ruling house.
Yáo Chǎng treated him with sincerity,
in order to divide Fú Dēng's faction.
8 In the sixth month,
on the jiǎchén day,
Yān’s Zhào Wáng, Mùróng Lín, defeated Hè Nè at Chìchéng,
capturing him.
The Shuǐ Jīng states: “The Hé River flows south from Zhēnlíng County in Yúnzhōng, passing east of Chìchéng,
then further south passes west of Tóngguò County in Dìngxiāng.”
Also, the Wèi Shū, Annals of Emperors, records:
In the third year of Dēngguó,
[the emperor] visited Eastern Chìchéng.
In the eighth year of Tàicháng of Emperor Míngyuán,
the Great Wall was built south of Chángchuān,
starting from Chìchéng,
extending west to Wǔyuán,
stretching over two thousand lǐ.
The Yān ruler, Mùróng Chuí, ordered Lín to return Hè Nè’s tribe,
and relocated Rǎngān to Zhōngshān.
Lín returned
and said to Chuí:
“I observe Tuòbá Guī’s actions;
he will ultimately become a threat to the state.
It would be better to summon him back to court,
and have his younger brother oversee state affairs.”
Chuí did not heed this.
Shè means
to record,
to gather.
Mùróng Lín, treacherous and deceitful,
knew that Tuòbá Guī would ultimately be uncontrollable,
yet Mùróng Chuí did not follow his advice.
Heaven was about to enable Guī to destroy Yān;
even with Chuí’s wisdom,
he did not perceive it at all.
Jiān:
pronounced jiān.
9 The Western Yān ruler, Mùróng Yǒng, invaded Hénán,
but Tàishǒu Yáng Quánqī repelled him.
10 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the rénshēn day,
the Yān ruler, Mùróng Chuí, went to Fànyáng.
Fànyáng County
belonged to Zhuō Commandery in the Hàn dynasty;
Emperor Wén of Wèi changed Zhuō Commandery to Fànyáng Commandery.
11 The Wèi king, Tuòbá Guī, sent his younger brother, Gū, to present tribute to Yān.
The Yān ruler, Mùróng Chuí, was aged,
and his sons and nephews were in charge of affairs.
They detained Gū to demand fine horses.
The Wèi king, Tuòbá Guī, did not give them,
and thus broke off relations with Yān;
this laid the groundwork for conflict between Yān and Wèi.
Gū escaped to return,
but the Yān crown prince, Bǎo, pursued and captured him.
Chuí treated him as before.
12 The Qín ruler, Yáo Dēng, attacked Xīnpíng,
but the Later Qín ruler, Yáo Cháng, came to its rescue,
and Dēng withdrew.
13 The Qín Piàojì General, Mòyígān,
sent his two sons as hostages to the Jīnchéng king, Qīan Guī,
requesting a joint attack on the Xiānbēi chieftain Dàdōu.
Qián Guī and Mòyígān attacked Dàdōu at Míngchán Fortress,
capturing it.
According to the Zǎijì,
Dàdōu was then occupying Ānyáng City.
Ānyáng City was within the boundaries of Lǒngchéng County of Táng’s Qín Prefecture;
Míngchán Fortress was likely also in that area.
Qián Guī gathered his tribe’s people and returned,
returning Mòyígān’s two sons.
Mòyígān soon rebelled,
joining Liú Wèichén in the east.
In the eighth month,
Qián Guī led ten thousand cavalry to attack Mòyígān.
Mòyígān fled to Tālóu City.
Tālóu City was in Gāopíng.
In the sixth year of Zhēnguān of Táng Tàizōng,
Yuán Prefecture was established with surrendered Tūjué households,
governing Tālóu City in Pínggāo;
Emperor Gāozōng established Tālóu County,
later abolished and incorporated into the territory of Xiāoguān County of Yuán Prefecture.
Zhōngmù.
14 In the ninth month,
on the guǐwèi day,
Shàngshū Yòu Púshè Wáng Xún was appointed Zuǒ Púshè,
and Tàizǐ Zhānshì Xiè Yǎn was appointed Yòu Púshè.
Tàixué Bóshì Fàn Hóngzhī argued that Yīn Hào should be granted posthumous honors and a posthumous title,
and in doing so recounted Huán Wēn’s acts of disloyalty.
At that time, the Huán clan was still powerful.
Wáng Xún
was a former subordinate of Wēn,
having previously served as Wēn’s Zhǔbù.
He had a loyal and steadfast character;
he demoted Hóngzhī to Yúháng County Magistrate.
Yúháng County
belonged to Kuàijī Commandery in the Hàn dynasty.

Those skilled at controlling the enemy

Gǒu Yào vacillated between Fú and Yáo,

He was like a festering sore on the Yáo clan's flank.
If Cháng had summoned him,

If Cháng were in Cháng'ān,

Cháng went out to lure him,

The two Qín states were at war,

The Yáo clan's flank sore was thus removed.
Is this not achieving success by adapting to circumstances?
Cháng defeated Dēng east of Āndìng City.

"I am inferior to my late elder brother in four aspects: He was eight chǐ five cùn tall,

is the name of a mixed barbarian tribe.
Xiǎnqīn County,
was established by Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn,
and belonged to Hànyáng Commandery.
In Jìn, Xiǎnqīn was changed to Xiǎnxīn,
and Hànyáng was restored as Tiānshuǐ Commandery.
According to the records of Yáo Xīng in the Jìn Shū,
"Quán Qiānchéng"
is written as
"Quán Gānchéng,"
a powerful clan from Lüèyáng.
19 Lǐ Liáo of Qīnghé submitted a memorial requesting an imperial order for Yǎnzhōu to repair the Temple of Confucius,
The Temple of Confucius is in Lǔ.
Lǔ Commandery,
during the Former Hàn, belonged to Xúzhōu;
during the Later Hàn and Jìn, it belonged to Yùzhōu;
it was only after the Jiāngbiǎo period that it was assigned to Yǎnzhōu.
He also proposed establishing schools,
to gather and teach scholars,
saying:
"There are matters that seem distant but are actually urgent."
This shí is the same as the shí meaning real or actual, as opposed to false or empty.
The memorial was not acted upon.
1 In spring,
the first month,
the Yān Prince of Yángpíng, Róu, passed away.
2 Quán Qiānchéng, pressured by Qín,
surrendered to the King of Jīnchéng, Gān Guī,
who appointed him as the Governor of Dōng Qínzhōu, Grand Commander of the Xiūguān, and Duke of Xiǎnqīn.
3 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the gēngzǐ day,
the Yān ruler Chuí conferred upon the Crown Prince Bǎo the title of Great Chányú;
he appointed the Prince of Āndìng, Wěi of the Kùnùguān clan, as Grand Commandant;
the Prince of Fànyáng, Dé, as Minister over the Masses;
the Prince of Tàiyuán, Kǎi, as Minister of Works;
and the Prince of Chénliú, Shào, as Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs.
In the fifth month,
he enfeoffed his son Xī as the Prince of Héjiān,
Lǎng as the Prince of Bóhǎi,
and Jiàn as the Prince of Bólíng.
4 The Qín Right Chancellor Dòu Chōng was arrogant about his talent and looked down on others,
looking down on others means
belittling them and placing himself above them.
The Qín ruler Dēng did not approve.
In the sixth month,
Chōng proclaimed himself the King of Qín,
and changed the era name to Yuánguāng.
5 The King of Jīnchéng, Gān Guī, established his son Chìpán as Crown Prince.
Chìpán was brave, strategic, clear-sighted, and decisive,
surpassing his father.
6 In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Qín ruler Dēng attacked Dòu Chōng at Yěrén Fort,
and Chōng sought help from Later Qín.
Yǐn Wěi said to the Later Qín ruler Cháng:
"The Crown Prince's reputation for benevolence and generosity
is well-known far and wide,
but his heroic and strategic abilities are not yet evident.
I request that he be sent to attack Fú Dēng to demonstrate them."
Cháng agreed.
Crown Prince Xīng led troops to attack Húkōng Fort,
and Dēng lifted the siege against Chōng to go and meet him.
Xīng then took advantage of the situation to attack Píngliáng,
returning with great spoils.
After Fú Dēng's defeat at Dàjiè,
he made Píngliáng his base.
7 The Wèi ruler Guī, because Tàixīfú of Xuēgān did not hand over Liú Bóbó,
as seen in the events of the sixteenth year of the previous scroll,
attacked his city,
slaughtered its inhabitants,
and Tàixīfú fled to Qín.
8 The Dí chieftain Yáng Fúsōng rebelled,
and fled to Later Qín.
Yáng Quánqī and Zhào Mù pursued him.
In the ninth month,
on the bǐngxū day,
they defeated Fúsōng at Tóngguān.
The Later Qín general Yáo Chóng came to Fúsōng's aid,
defeated the Jìn troops,
and Zhào Mù died.
9 In winter,
the tenth month,
the Later Qín ruler Cháng became seriously ill,
and returned to Cháng'ān.
10. The ruler of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, deliberated on attacking Western Yān.
All his generals said:
"Mùróng Yǒng has given us no opening.
We have campaigned year after year,
and our soldiers are weary and exhausted.
It is not feasible."
The Prince of Fànyáng, Mùróng Dé, said:
"Yǒng is not only a branch of our royal house,
but has also presumptuously assumed the title and position of ruler,
confusing the people's sight and hearing.
He should be eliminated first,
to unify the people's hearts.
Although the soldiers are weary,
how can we stop now?"
Chuí said:
"The Minister over the Masses' opinion is exactly the same as mine.
I am growing old,
but even tapping the wisdom left in the bottom of my bag,
it is enough to capture him.
I will ultimately not leave this villain to burden our descendants."
Chuí did not wish to leave Mùróng Yǒng to burden his descendants,
but did not know that Tuòbá Guī was already watching from north of Dài.
Therefore, those who possess states and families
do not rely on having no enemy states or external troubles,
but rely on having the means by which they transmit the state and inherit the family being sufficient to deal with them.
Lěi,
pronounced lì ruì fān.
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu fān.
In the eleventh month,
Chuí mobilized 70,000 infantry and cavalry from Zhōngshān,
sending the General Who Guards the West, the Prince of Dānyáng, Mùróng Zàn,
"Zàn"
should be
"Zàn".
to attack Mùróng Yǒng, the Duke of Wǔxiāng of Western Yān, at Jìnyáng.
General Who Conquers the East, Píng Guī, attacked General Who Guards the East, Duàn Píng, at Shātíng.
Shātíng is southwest of Yè.
Yǒng,
was Yǒng's younger brother.
In the twelfth month,
Chuí reached Yè.
11. On the jǐhài day,
the ruler of Later Qín, Yáo Cháng, summoned the Grand Commandant Yáo Mín, the Attendant Gentleman Yáo Wěi, Yáo Huàng, General Yáo Dàmù, and the Imperial Secretary Dí Bózhī into the palace,
to receive his testamentary decree to assist in government.
Cháng said to the heir apparent, Yáo Xīng:
"If there are those who slander these gentlemen,
be careful not to accept it.
You should treat your kin with kindness,
receive ministers with ritual,
handle affairs with trustworthiness,
and encounter the people with benevolence.
If you do not lose these four,
I will have no worries."
The instructions Yáo Cháng gave to his son
surpassed those of Fú Jiàn.
Cháng said:
"Now the great enterprise is near completion,
and Xīng's talent and wisdom are sufficient to manage it.
What more is there to ask!"
On the gēngzǐ day,
Cháng died.
He was sixty-four years old.
He appointed his paternal uncle Yáo Xù to guard Āndìng,
Yáo Shuòdé to guard Yīnmì,
and his younger brother Yáo Chóng to guard Cháng'ān.
Someone said to Shuòdé:
"Your prestige and reputation have always been great,
and your troops are the strongest.
Now, at this time of generational change,
you will certainly be suspected by the court.
It would be better to flee to Qín Province for now."
Shuòdé originally raised troops in Lǒngshàng,
occupying Jìchéng.
Shuòdé said:
"The heir apparent's will and measure are broad and enlightened.
There certainly will be no other concerns.
Now Fú Dēng is not yet destroyed, yet if kin attack each other,
it is bringing about our own destruction.
I would rather die;
I will ultimately not do it."
Thereupon he went to see Xīng,
and Xīng treated him with exceptional courtesy and sent him off.
Xīng proclaimed himself Grand General,
appointed Yáo Wěi as Chief Clerk,
Dí Bózhī as Marshal,
and led the multitude to attack Qín.
1. In spring,
the ruler of Qín, Fú Dēng, heard that the ruler of Later Qín, Yáo Cháng, had died.
He joyfully said:
"Yáo Xīng is a mere child.
I will break a rod and flog him."
Thereupon he issued a great amnesty,
and led all his forces eastward.
Those who underestimate the enemy are defeated.
This explains why Fú Dēng did not perish in Yáo Cháng's time, but perished when Yáo Xīng had just ascended.
The heir apparent Fú Chóng guarded the Húkōng Fortress.
He sent an envoy to appoint the Prince of Jīnchéng, Qīfū Gānguī, as Left Minister, Prince of Hénán, and Governor of the five provinces of Qín, Liáng, Yì, Liáng, and Shā,
and granted him the Nine Bestowments.
2. Earlier,
Tūfǎ Sīfùjiān died,
and his son Wūgū succeeded him.
Wūgū was heroic, courageous, and had great ambition.
He plotted with the great general Fēntuó to seize Liáng Province.
He wanted to annex Lǚ Guāng.
Jiàng,
pronounced jí liàng fān.
"If you, my lord, certainly wish to obtain Liáng Province,
you should first devote effort to agriculture and discuss military affairs,
treat the talented and worthy with ritual,
and cultivate government and punishments.
Only then will it be possible."
Wūgū followed this.
The Prince of Sānhé, Lǚ Guāng, sent an envoy to appoint Wūgū as Champion General-in-Chief and Grand Commander of the Xiānbēi West of the River.
Wūgū consulted with his subordinates about this, saying:
"Should we accept it?"
All said:
"Our soldiers and horses are numerous.
Why should we be subordinate to others!"
Shízhēn Ruòliú did not answer.
Wūgū said:
"Are you, sir, afraid of Lǚ Guāng?"
Shízhēn Ruòliú said:
"Our foundation is not yet solid,
and in size we are not his match.
If Guāng were to fight us to the death,
how would we handle it?
It would be better to accept it to make him arrogant,
and wait for an opening to act.
Then there is nothing we cannot overcome."
Wūgū then accepted it.
Fēntuó and Shízhēn Ruòliú
were both men capable of carefully assessing what was appropriate and responding to affairs.
The history records why Tūfǎ Wūgū rose.
Fēn and Shízhēn
are probably both barbarian surnames.
3. In the second month,
the ruler of Qín, Fú Dēng, attacked the two fortresses of the Túgè, Yáo Nú and Bó Pú,
and captured them.
These two fortresses
are east of the Húkōng Fortress.
Tú,
pronounced zhí yú fān.
4. The ruler of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, left the Duke of Qīnghé, Mùróng Huì, to guard Yè.
He mobilized troops from Sī, Jì, Qīng, and Yǎn provinces,
sending the Prince of Tàiyuán, Mùróng Kǎi, out through the Fǔkǒu Pass,
and the Prince of Liáoxī, Mùróng Nóng, out through the Húguān Pass.
Chuí himself went out from Shātíng to attack Western Yān.
"Tíng"
should be
"tíng";
its location is southwest of Yè.
Each army took up its encampment.
They deployed troops in separate positions to confuse the enemy,
making them not know where to prepare.
Qū,
pronounced qī yù fān;
same below.
They arrayed troops and defended along separate routes,
gathering grain at Táibì.
The Water Classic Commentary states: North of Lù County faces the old Táibì.
The Zhāng River emerges to its south,
originally established by the Viscount of Lù.
In Wèi Shōu's Treatise on Geography,
in Yìlíng County of Xiāngyuán Commandery,
which was Lù County in Hàn and Jìn times,
there is Táibì.
At that time, among the ministers of Western Yān there were two Yìdòuguīs,
hence this one is called the lesser Yìdòuguī.
Cóng,
pronounced cái yòng fān.
10. The Qin ruler Dēng sent his son, the Prince of Rǔyīn, Zōng, as a hostage to the King of Hénán, Qiángūi, to request aid.
He advanced Qiángūi's title to King of Liáng,
and took Qiángūi's younger sister as the Queen of the King of Liáng.
Qiángūi sent the former Army General Qǐfú Yìzhōu and others to lead ten thousand cavalry to rescue him.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Dēng led his troops out to meet Qiángūi's army.
The Later Qin ruler Xīng went from Āndìng to Jīngyáng,
and fought Dēng south of the mountains,
that is, south of Mǎmáo Mountain.
He killed him.
Dēng was fifty-two years old.
[Xīng] sent [the people] back to agriculture;
he relocated thirty thousand households from Yīnmì to Cháng'ān,
and bestowed the Lady Lǐ, [Dēng's] queen, upon Yáo Huǎng.
Yìzhōu and others, hearing of this,
led their troops back.
The character 還 (huán),
is pronounced according to the Xuán annotation,
and also according to its usual reading.
[Xīng] then assumed the imperial throne,
changing the era name to Yánchū;
he posthumously honored Dēng as Emperor Gāo,
and his temple name was Tàizōng.
11. The Later Qin generals, the Pacifying-the-South General Qiáng Xī and the Pacifying-Distant-Regions General Qiáng Duō, rebelled,
and supported Dòu Chōng as their leader.
The Later Qin ruler Xīng personally led a campaign against them,
his army reaching Wǔgōng.
Duō's elder brother's son, Liánguó, killed Duō and surrendered.
Xī fled to Qínzhōu,
and Chōng fled to Qiānchuān,
Qiānchuān being the territory of Qiān County in Fúfēng Commandery.
The character 汧 (qiān),
is pronounced according to the Kǔjiān annotation.
12. The King of Sānhé, Guāng, appointed his son Fù as Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs West of Yùmén and Grand Protector of the Western Regions,
stationing him at Gāochāng;
he ordered the sons and younger brothers of his high officials to accompany him.
13. In the eighth month,
on the day Jǐsì,
[the emperor] honored the Empress Dowager, Lady Lǐ, as Grand Empress Dowager,
and she resided in the Chóngxùn Palace.
14. The Western Yān ruler Yǒng, in dire straits,
sent his son, the Duke of Chángshān, Hóng, and others to seek aid from the Governor of Yōngzhōu, Xī Huī,
and also presented a jade seal.
Huī memorialized:
"If Chuí annexes Yǒng,
the trouble will become even greater.
It would be better to let both survive,
so we can seize the opportunity for both to perish."
The Emperor considered this correct,
and issued an edict ordering the Governors of Qīngzhōu and Yǎnzhōu, Wáng Gōng, and the Governor of Yùzhōu, Yǔ Kǎi, to rescue him.
Kǎi
was the grandson of Liàng.
The Yǔ clan was exterminated by Huán Wēn,
and Kǎi, moreover, was unable to revive it,
and from then on it declined.
[Yǒng] also sent his heir apparent, Liàng, to come as a hostage.
Píng Guī pursued Liàng and caught up with him at Gāodū,
capturing him.
Gāodū County belonged to Shàngdǎng Commandery.
In Suí times it was Dānchuān County of Zézhōu,
and in Táng times it was Jìnchéng County.
The Wèi ruler Guī sent the Duke of Chénliú, Qián, and General Yǔ Yuè to lead fifty thousand cavalry east across the [Yellow] River,
and stationed them at Xiùróng to rescue [Yǒng].
This was Northern Xiùróng,
located within the boundaries of the Hàn dynasty's Dìngxiāng Commandery.
Later, the Wèi established Xiùróng Commandery and Xiùróng County there.
They also established a Xiùróng Protectorate Army sixty *li* northwest of the Fén River,
and relocated the Hú people of Northern Xiùróng to live there.
This was Southern Xiùróng.
Liú Xù said: Xiùróng County of Xīnzhōu
was the territory of Fényáng County in Hàn times.
In Suí times, it was moved from the old Xiùróng city to this place,
and consequently renamed.
The character 帥 (shuài),
is read as 率 (lǜ).
The character 騎 (qí),
is pronounced according to the Qíjì annotation.
[Qián] was the son of Gégēn.
Gégēn appears in the first year of the 104th scroll.
The character 紇 (hé),
is pronounced according to the Hùgǔ annotation.
Dàyìdòuguī's subordinate general Fá Qín and others opened the gates and let the Yān troops in.
The men of Yān captured Yǒng,
and beheaded him,
also beheading over thirty of his high ministers and senior generals such as Diāo Yún and Dàyìdòuguī.

They obtained the eight commanderies and over seventy thousand households that Yǒng had ruled, as well as a great quantity of Qín imperial carriages, clothing and utensils, musicians and entertainers, and precious treasures.
The Yān ruler Chuí appointed the Prince of Dānyáng, Zàn, as Governor of Bìngzhōu,
stationing him at Jìnyáng;
and the Prince of Yídū, Fèng, as Governor of Yōngzhōu,
stationing him at Zhǎngzǐ.
Yǒng's Ministers of Works, the Chānglí man Qū Zūn,

Minister Yángpíng Wáng Dé, Director of the Palace Library, the Zhōngshān man Lǐ Xiān, Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent, the Bóhǎi man Fēng Zé, Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, the Tàishān man Húmǔ Liàng, Gentleman of the Central Secretariat Zhāng Téng, and Gentleman of the Ministry of Works, the Duke of Yànjùn, Gōngsūn Biǎo, were all promoted and appointed according to their talents.
Lǐ Xiān and Gōngsūn Biǎo
later both served Wèi,
reaching high and prominent positions.
In the ninth month,
Chuí went from Zhǎngzǐ to Yè.
15. In winter,
the tenth month,
the Qín ruler Chóng was driven out by the King of Liáng, Qiángūi,
and fled to the King of Lǒngxī, Yáng Dìng.
Dìng left the Army Minister Shào Qiáng to guard Qínzhōu,
and personally led twenty thousand troops together with Chóng to attack Qiángūi.
Qiángūi sent the Governor of Liángzhōu, Kēdàn, the Governor of Qínzhōu, Yìzhōu, and the General for Establishing Righteousness, Jiégūi, to lead thirty thousand cavalry to resist them.
Kēdàn, Yìzhōu, and Jiégūi were all of the Qǐfú clan.
The Governors of Liáng and Qínzhōu
were appointed by Qiángūi,
but he did not actually possess those territories.
"Kēdàn"
is written as
"Kēdān" in the *Jìnshū* Basic Annals.
The character 帥 (shuài),
is read as 率 (lǜ);
same below.
They were defeated at Píngzhōu.
The Basic Annals writes it as
"Píngchuān",
which should be followed.
Kēdàn's Army Minister Zhái Wěn, brandishing his sword angrily, said:
"Our sovereign, with his heroic and martial prowess, founded this state,
and wherever he went, he was invincible,
his might shaking Qín and Shǔ.
You, General, hold the post of Commander-in-Chief as a member of the imperial clan.
You should exhaust your strength and devote your life to assisting the state.
Now, although our Qínzhōu army has been defeated,
the other two armies are still intact.
How can you retreat in fear at the mere sight of the enemy,
and what face will you have to see our sovereign!
Although I, Wěn, hold no important post,
can I not, on my own authority, behead you, General!"
Kēdàn apologized, saying:
"Previously, I did not know how the morale of the troops was.
If they are truly like this,
how dare I begrudge death!"
Then he led the cavalry forward to attack.
Yìzhōu and Jiégūi also marshaled their troops and followed him.
They heavily defeated Dìng's army,
killing Dìng and Chóng,
and beheading seventeen thousand men.
In the seventh year of the Yǒnghé era of Emperor Mù,
the Qín ruler Jiàn changed the era name and assumed the throne.
Through six rulers,
after forty-two years, it perished.
The Qǐfú clan finally obtained Qínzhōu.
Dìng had no sons.
The son of his paternal uncle Fógǒu, Shèng,
had previously guarded Qiúchí,
and proclaimed himself General Who Conquers the West, Governor of Qínzhōu, and Duke of Qiúchí.
He posthumously honored Dìng as King Wǔ;
and still sent envoys to declare himself a vassal.
The Qín heir apparent, Xuān, fled to Shèng.
[Shèng] divided
the Dí and Qiāng into twenty Protectorate Army units,
each serving as garrison posts,
and did not establish commanderies and counties.
16. The Yān ruler Chuí made an eastern tour of Yángpíng and Píngyuán,
and ordered the Prince of Liáoxī, Nóng, to cross the [Yellow] River,
and together with the Pacifying-the-South General Yǐn Guó, to seize territory in Qīngzhōu and Yǎnzhōu.
Nóng attacked Lǐnqiū,
and Guó attacked Yángchéng,
capturing them both.
The Grand Administrator of Dōngpíng, Wéi Jiǎn, died in battle.
The various commanderies of Gāopíng, Tàishān, and Lángyá all abandoned their cities and fled in collapse.
Nóng advanced his army to Línhǎi,
meaning adjacent to the Eastern Sea.
17. The Rúrán leader Hèduōhàn abandoned his father,
and together with Shèlún led his followers west.
The Rúrán surrendered to Wèi;
see the sixteenth year of the previous scroll.
The character 汗 (hàn),
is pronounced hán.
The character 崙 (lún),
is pronounced according to the Lúkūn annotation.
[Shèlún] caught up with him at the Bánà Mountain in Shàngjùn,
and beheaded Hèduōhàn.
Shèlún gathered his remaining followers, several hundred men,
and fled to Hóubá.
Hóubá settled them in his southern border region.
Shèlún attacked Hóubá,
and killed him;
Hóubá's sons, Qǐbá and Wúxié, all fled to Wèi.
Shèlún plundered the various tribes west of Wǔyuán,
and fled north across the desert.
From then on, the Rúrán became a problem for Wèi.
According to the Basic Annals,
Shèlún is considered a Western [River] Xiānbēi,
so the Rúrán were also of Xiānbēi stock.
On the 18th day of the 11th month,
the King of Liáoxī of Yān, Mùróng Nóng, defeated Pìlǘ Hún at Lóngshuǐ.
Guō Yuánshēng's "Shùzhēng Jì" states: Féng Mountain is located twenty lǐ south of Guǎnggù.
Yángshuǐ flows past its northern side and runs northeast,
commonly known as Shígōu Shuǐ.
It originates from the north of Wěisù Mountain,
and flows east into Jùyáng Shuǐ,
where it is called Shígōu Kǒu.
However, the lower reaches of this waterway sometimes become blocked and sometimes flow freely.
During the spring and summer when the water rises,
the river flows continuously without interruption,
and it is also sometimes called Lóngquán Shuǐ.
(Defeat: pronounced bǔ mài fān.)
In the 12th month,
the ruler of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, summoned Nóng and others to return.
On the 19th day,
the ruler of Qín, Yáo Xīng, sent an envoy to establish friendly relations with Yān,
and also sent Mín, the son of Crown Prince Bǎo, to Yān.
Yān enfeoffed Mín as the Duke of Hédōng.
On the 20th day,
the King of Liáng, Qǐfú Gānguī, proclaimed himself King of Qín
and issued a general pardon.
From this point onward,
the histories distinguish him as the Western Qín.
In the spring,
in the 1st month,
the ruler of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, sent the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Féng Zé to return the diplomatic visit to Qín.
He then went hunting from Píngyuán through Guǎngchuān, Bóhǎi, and Chánglè before returning.
(Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn established Xìndū Commandery.
In the 2nd year of Emperor Jǐng's reign,
it became the Kingdom of Guǎngchuān.
Emperor Míng renamed it Lèchéng.
Emperor Ān changed it to Ānpíng.
In Jìn, it was changed to Chánglè Commandery,
and a separate Guǎngchuān Commandery was established.
Lè is pronounced luò.)
The King of Western Qín, Qǐfú Gānguī, appointed his Crown Prince Chìpán to concurrently hold the office of President of the Imperial Secretariat.
Left Chief Clerk Biān Ruì was made Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
and Right Chief Clerk Mì Yí was made Right Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
He established offices following the precedents of Wèi Wǔ and Jìn Wén,
but still styled himself Grand Chányú and Great General.
Biān Ruì and others continued to hold their former positions as assistants in the headquarters.
Tàixīfú of Xuègàn fled from Cháng'ān back north of the mountains.
(North of the mountains refers to north of the Jiǔzōng Mountains.
In the 18th year,
Tàixīfú fled to Qín.)
In the 2nd month,
on the jiǎyín day,
the President of the Imperial Secretariat, Lù Nà, died.
In the 3rd month,
on the gēngchén day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
The Crown Prince moved out to the Eastern Palace,
and the Governor of Dānyáng, Wáng Yǎ, was appointed Junior Tutor.
At that time, the Prince of Kuàijī, Sīmǎ Dàozǐ, monopolized power and was extravagant and unrestrained.
His favorite, Zhào Yá, was originally an entertainer,
and Rǔ Qiānqiū was originally a constable who captured thieves in Qiántáng.
(The county of Qiántáng belonged to Kuàijī Commandery in the Former Hàn,
and to Wú Commandery in the Later Hàn.
The "Qiántáng Jì" states: The Commandery's Administrative Clerk Huá Xìn proposed building this dike to guard against seawater.
When construction began,
he offered one thousand cash to anyone who could deliver one hú of earth.
Within a month,
people came in great numbers.
When the dike was not yet completed, he stopped paying,
so those carrying earth and stones all dumped their loads and left.
The dike was thus completed,
hence the name Qiántáng [Money Dike].
Yáng Zhènghéng said: Rǔ is pronounced rú,
also ér jù fān;
there has long been this surname in the Zhè region.)
Dàozǐ appointed Yá as the Grand Administrator of Wèi Commandery,
and Qiānqiū as a Consultant Colonel of the Cavalry.
Yá built an eastern mansion for Dàozǐ,
constructing artificial hills and digging ponds,
at an enormous cost.
The Emperor once visited the mansion
and said to Dàozǐ:
"Having hills within the mansion
is very good;
however, the ornamentation is excessive."
Dàozǐ had no reply.
After the Emperor left,
Dàozǐ said to Yá:
"If the Emperor knew the hills were man-made,
you would certainly die!"
Yá said:
"With Your Highness here,
how dare I die!"
The construction became even more extravagant.
Qiānqiū sold offices and wielded power,
amassing wealth amounting to hundreds of millions.
The Magistrate of Bópíng, Wénrén Shì of Wúxīng, submitted a memorial reporting this.
(The county of Bópíng belonged to Dōng Commandery in Hàn,
and to Píngyuán Commandery in Jìn;
south of the Yangtze, it was attached to Wèi Commandery,
both being established as émigré commanderies.)
However, pressured by the Empress Dowager,
the Emperor could not bear to depose Dàozǐ.
Instead, he promoted men of reputation and his own favorites—Wáng Gōng, Xī Huī, Yīn Zhòngkān, Wáng Xún, and Wáng Yǎ—
placing them in important internal and external positions to guard against Dàozǐ.
Dàozǐ, in turn, enlisted Wáng Guóbǎo and Guóbǎo's cousin, the Neishi of Lángyé, Xù, as his confidants.
Thus, factions competed and arose,
and the former affection and harmony no longer existed.
The Empress Dowager often mediated between them.
The Gentleman of the Central Secretariat, Xú Miǎo, spoke earnestly to the Emperor:
"Even Emperor Wén of Hàn, an enlightened ruler,
regretted his actions against the King of Huáinán;
Emperor Shìzǔ [of Jìn], wise and perceptive,
felt ashamed before the Prince of Qí.
(The Huáinán affair is recorded in scroll 14, the 6th year of Emperor Wén of Hàn.
The Prince of Qí affair is recorded in scroll 81, the 4th year of Tàikāng of Emperor Wǔ.)
This truly shows deep caution.
Although the Prince of Kuàijī has the flaw of indulgence and impropriety,
you should be magnanimous and tolerant,
to dispel the divisive discussions.
Externally, it is for the state's plans;
internally, it comforts the Empress Dowager's heart."
The Emperor accepted his advice
and continued to entrust Dàozǐ as before.
Earlier,
after Yáng Dìng's death,
Jiāng Rǔ of Tiānshuǐ attacked and occupied Shàngguī.
In the summer,
in the 4th month,
the King of Western Qín, Qǐfú Gānguī, sent Qǐfú Yìzhōu with six thousand cavalry to attack him.
The Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Biān Ruì, and the Minister of Revenue, Wáng Sōngshòu, said:
"Yìzhōu, having won many victories, has become arrogant.
He should not be solely entrusted;
he will certainly underestimate the enemy and suffer defeat."
Gānguī said:
"Yìzhōu is brave and fierce;
none of the other generals compare to him.
We should assign capable assistants to support him."
He then appointed General Who Pacifies the North, Wéi Qián, as Chief Clerk,
and General of the Left Guard, Wùhé, as Army Major.
(Wù is a surname.
In ancient times, there was Wù Guāng.)
Dàhán Ridge is west of Shàngguī.
Yìzhōu allowed the officers and soldiers to roam, hunt, and drink freely,
issuing an order:
"Anyone who dares to speak of military affairs will be executed!"
Qián and others remonstrated, but he would not listen.
Rǔ launched a counterattack
and routed them decisively.
The King of Wèi, Tuòbá Guī, rebelled against Yān,
invading and threatening the various tribes attached to the border.
In the 5th month,
on the jiǎxū day,
the ruler of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, sent Crown Prince Bǎo, the King of Liáoxī, Mùróng Nóng, and the King of Zhào, Mùróng Lín, leading eighty thousand troops,
to attack Wèi from Wǔyuán.
The King of Fànyáng, Mùróng Dé, and the King of Chénliú, Mùróng Shào, separately led eighteen thousand infantry and cavalry as the rear force.
The Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Gāo Hú remonstrated:
"Wèi and Yān have been intermarrying for generations.
The King of Dài, Tuòbá Shíyìjiān, married twice from the Mùróng clan,
but both died early.
In the 1st year of Lónghé of Emperor Āi,
Shíyìjiān took a daughter from Yān,
and Yān also gave a daughter to him in marriage.
Yān truly preserved him.
(The events are recorded in scroll 106, year 11, and scroll 107, year 12.)
(Difficult: pronounced nǎi dàn fān.)
Friendly relations have long been established.
Recently, because horses were not obtained, his younger brother was detained.
(The event is recorded in the previous scroll, year 16.)
(Good: pronounced hū dào fān;
the same below.)
How can we suddenly raise troops to attack him!
Tuòbá Shèguī is deep, courageous, and resourceful.
(Xiāo Zǐxiǎn said: Guī,
styled Shèguī.)
(Deep: pronounced chí lín fān.)
His soldiers are elite and his horses strong;
he is not easy to underestimate.
The Crown Prince is young,
determined and sharp in spirit.
Now entrusting him with sole command,
he will certainly belittle Wèi and take it lightly.
If things do not go as desired,
it will damage our prestige and undermine our weight.
I hope Your Majesty will consider this deeply!"
His words were rather impassioned and blunt.
Chuí became angry
and dismissed Hú from office.
Hú was the son of Tài.
During the time of Former Yān,
when Chuí was General of Chariots and Cavalry,
he appointed Tài as a Gentleman of the Headquarters.
9 In the sixth month,
on the guǐchǒu day,
the Prince of Tàiyuán of Yān, Yuánwáng Kǎi, passed away.
10 The Western Qín king, Qiánguī, moved to Xīchéng.
This was the western city of Yuànchuān.
11 In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Prince of Sānhé, Guāng, led a force of one hundred thousand to attack Western Qín.
Western Qín's Left Assistant Mì Guìzhōu and Left Guard General Mòzhě Gǔdī
(Mì took the state as his surname.
According to the Surname Genealogy: In Hàn times, there was a Secretary Mì Zhōng.
Based on the following text of the Comprehensive Mirror,
it appears that Mìguì was used as the surname.
Mòzhě
is a foreign compound surname.)
offered their son Chìbó as a hostage.
Guāng then withdrew his troops and returned.
Qiánguī regretted this,
and executed Zhōu and Gǔdī.
12 Wèi's Zhāng Gǔn, hearing that the Yān army was approaching,
said to the Wèi king, Guī:
"Yān, emboldened by their victories at Huátái and Zhǎngzǐ,
(the Huátái affair is seen in the seventeenth year above;
the Zhǎngzǐ affair is seen last year.)
(Niǔ,
is the same as niǔ.
Dù Yù said: Niǔ
means being accustomed to.)
has a contemptuous view of us.
We should feign weakness to make them arrogant,
and then we can defeat them."
Guī followed this advice,
moving all the tribes and their livestock
westward across the river for over a thousand lǐ to avoid them.
The Yān army reached Wǔyuán,
subjugating over thirty thousand households of Wèi's separate tribes,
and collecting over a million hú of millet fields.
They established Hēichéng.
(Hēichéng is north of the river in Wǔyuán.
According to the Wèi Shū, Imperial Annals: In the fifth year of Dēngguó,
Liú Wèichén sent his son Zhílìdī out of the Gǔyáng Pass,
invading as far as Hēichéng.
This can be known from that.)
The Water Classic states: The river water from Xīnqínzhōng bends and flows south,
passing south of counties such as Wǔyuán, Xī'ānyáng, Chéngyí, Yíliáng, Línwò, and Gǔyáng.
Guī sent Right Sima Xǔ Qiān to Qín to request troops.
13 Tūfǎ Wūgū attacked the Yǐfú, Zhéjué, and other tribes,
defeating and subjugating them all.
He built the fortress of Liánchuān and made it his capital.
(The Yǐfú and Zhéjué tribes
were both west of the Tūfǎ clan.
Liánchuān is in Huángzhōng.)
(Jiàng,
read as hù jiāng fān.)
Shào, fond of unusual strategies,
hearing that Wūgū was at Liánchuān,
abandoned his family to follow him.
Wūgū joyfully said:
"With Zhào Shēng,
my great undertaking will succeed!"
He appointed him as Left Sima.
The Prince of Sānhé, Guāng, enfeoffed Wūgū as Duke of Guǎngwǔ Commandery.
14 A long star appeared from Xūnǚ
reaching Kūxīng.
(The Astronomical Treatise states: Xūnǚ consists of four stars.
Xū
is a term for low-ranking concubines,
the humblest of women's duties.
Dǒu, Niú, and Nǚ
correspond to the division of Yángzhōu.
Xū has two stars, Wēi has three stars,
both governing death and mourning.
Kūqì and Fénmù,
four stars,
belong below Wēi,
governing death, mourning, weeping, and graves.)
(Xiàn,
read as xián biàn fān.)
In the Huálín Garden, he raised a cup and toasted it, saying:
(The Jìn capital Jiànkāng
imitated Luòdū,
building the Huálín Garden.)
read as wū lù fān.)
"Long star,
I offer you a cup of wine;
since ancient times, has there ever been an emperor who lived ten thousand years?"
15 In the eighth month,
the Wèi king Guī trained troops south of the river;
in the ninth month,
he advanced his army to the river's edge.
The Yān crown prince Bǎo arrayed his troops preparing to cross,
when a sudden storm arose,
blowing several dozen of his ships to the southern bank.
Wèi captured over three hundred of his armored soldiers,
but released and sent them all back.
When Bǎo departed from Zhōngshān,
the Yān ruler Chuí was already ill.
After reaching Wǔyuán,
Guī had men intercept the road to Zhōngshān,
watching for his messengers,
and captured them all.
(Sì,
read as xiāng lì fān.
Shǐ,
read as shū lì fān.)
Guī had the captured messengers stand by the river and tell them:
"Your father has already died;
why not return early?"
Bǎo and others grew worried and fearful,
and the soldiers were alarmed and shaken.
Guī had Duke Chénliú, Qián, lead fifty thousand cavalry to station east of the river,
and Duke Dōngpíng, Yí, lead one hundred thousand cavalry to station north of the river.
