(The river water from Jīnchéng passes through the boundaries of Wǔwēi, Tiānshuǐ, Āndìng, and Běidì commanderies,
generally flowing northeast,
reaching the boundary of Shuòfāng's Wòyě County,
where it bends and flows southeast.
Qián stationed east of the river,
Yí stationed north of the river,
both in the river bend area,
not having crossed the river.)
(The History of the Northern Dynasties states: Yí occupied Shuòfāng.)
(Jiàng,
read as jí liàng fān;
same below.)
Zūn
was the son of Shòujiū.
(Shòujiū appears in the first year of the one hundred and fourth volume.)
The Yān diviner Jìn Ān said to Crown Prince Bǎo:
"The celestial timing is unfavorable;
Yān will surely suffer a great defeat.
Leaving quickly may allow escape."
Bǎo did not listen.
Ān withdrew
and told others:
"We will all be left as corpses in the wilds,
unable to return!"
Yān and Wèi faced each other for several ten-day periods.
The King of Zhào, Lín, and Mùyú Sōng, believing that Chuí had truly died,
plotted a rebellion,
intending to install Lín as ruler.
The affair was exposed,
and Sōng and others were executed.
Bǎo, Lín, and others grew suspicious among themselves.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the xīnwèi day,
they burned their boats and fled at night.
At that time, the river ice had not yet formed,
and Bǎo believed the Wèi troops certainly could not cross,
so he set no scouts.
In the eleventh month,
on the jǐmǎo day,
a sudden storm
caused the ice to congeal.
The Wèi king Guī led his troops across the river,
left the heavy baggage behind,
and selected over twenty thousand elite cavalry to pursue them urgently.
The Yan army arrived at Canhebei.
A great wind arose,
and a black mass like a dike
came from behind the army,
looming over and covering the troops.
The monk Zhī Tánměng
(Regarding "Zhī,"
it is Tánměng's secular surname.
Tán,
pronounced as "tán.")
said, "The wind is fierce and swift—
a sign that the Wei troops are about to arrive.
We should send soldiers to defend against them."
Mùróng Bǎo, believing the Wei army was already far away,
laughed and did not respond.
Tánměng persistently pleaded without ceasing,
and Mùróng Lín angrily said:
"With His Highness's divine might
and the strength of our troops,
we are more than enough to sweep across the desert.
How dare those barbarians come from afar!
In the eighteenth year of the Tàiyuán era,
Mùróng Lín already knew that Tuòbá Guī would surely become a threat to Yan.
Yet now he underestimates them like this—
could it be that his heart harbors doubts and he wishes to ruin Bǎo's army?
Later, Bǎo could not hold Zhōngshān, and Lín could not stand on his own either,
both ending in chaos, that is all.
Suǒ,
pronounced as "suǒ."
He should be executed as a warning!"
Tánměng wept and said:
"The Fú clan, with a million-strong army,
was defeated at Huáinán—
precisely because they relied on their numbers, underestimated the enemy,
and did not believe in the Way of Heaven!"
The event is recorded in volumes 104, 5, years 7 and 8.
Bǎo then sent Lín to lead thirty thousand cavalry to position behind the army as a precaution against unexpected events.
Lín considered Tánměng's words absurd,
and allowed his cavalry to roam and hunt,
refusing to make preparations.
Bǎo sent cavalry scouts to reconnoiter the Wei troops.
The scouts rode for over ten *lǐ*,
then unsaddled and slept.
The Wei army marched day and night,
and on the day *yǐyǒu*,
at dusk,
they reached the west of Canhebei.
The Yan army was east of the slope,
encamped by the water south of Pányáng Mountain.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* records: The Kěbùní River originates from a mountain sixty *lǐ* southeast of Wòyáng County in Yànmén,
flows northwest into the Wò River,
merges and flows east,
passing south of Cānhé County.
They covered and surrounded the Yan army,
with soldiers gagging themselves and binding their horses' mouths to advance stealthily.
On the day *bǐngxū*,
as the sun rose,
the Wei army ascended the mountain,
looking down upon the Yan camp;
the Yan army was about to move eastward,
(meaning to march east.)
The soldiers were greatly startled and thrown into chaos.
Guī unleashed his troops to attack them,
and the Yan soldiers fled toward the water,
men and horses trampling over one another,
with tens of thousands crushed or drowned to death.
The Duke of Lüèyáng, Tuòbá Zūn, led troops to intercept them from the front,
and forty to fifty thousand Yan soldiers
simultaneously laid down their weapons, surrendered, and were captured.
Those who managed to escape numbered no more than a few thousand,
and Crown Prince Bǎo and others barely escaped alone on horseback.
They killed the Yan Right Deputy Minister, the Mourning King of Chénliú, Mùróng Shào,
and captured alive the King of Lǔyáng, Mùróng Wōnú,
the King of Guìlín, Mùróng Dàochéng, the Duke of Jìyīn, Yǐn Guó, and several thousand civil and military officials and officers.
Weapons, armor, grain, and goods were captured in immense quantities.
Dàochéng
was a younger cousin of Mùróng Chuí.

The King of Wei, Tuòbá Guī, selected capable and useful Yan ministers—the Governor of Dàijùn, Jiǎ Rùn of Guǎngchuān; his cousin, the Chief Clerk of the Cavalry General and Governor of Chānglí, Jiǎ Yí; the Grand Historian, Cháo
Chóng, and others—and kept them.
As for the rest, he intended to provide them all with clothing and provisions and send them back,
to win over the hearts of the people in the Central Plains.
The Central Tribal Chief, Wáng Jiàn, said:
"The Yan forces are strong and numerous,
and now they have come with their entire nation's strength.
We are fortunate to have achieved a great victory.
It would be better to kill them all,
so that their state will be emptied,
making it easier to seize.
Moreover, to capture the enemy and then release them—
surely that cannot be right!"
So they buried them all alive.
In the twelfth month,
Guī returned to Shènglè in Yúnzhōng.
The *Zīzhì Tōngjiàn*, in the fifth year of Emperor Huì's Yuánkāng era,
records Shènglè as the old city of Dìngxiāng,
while here it records Shènglè as part of Yúnzhōng;
this is because over generations, commanderies and counties were abolished, moved, and changed irregularly.
In the Former Hàn, Chénglè County belonged to Dìngxiāng,
while in the Later Hàn, Chénglè County belonged to Yúnzhōng.
The earlier record of Shènglè in Dìngxiāng
refers to the old city of the Former Hàn;
this record of Shènglè in Yúnzhōng
refers to the old city of the Later Hàn.
The Yan Crown Prince Bǎo, shamed by the defeat at Canhe,
requested to attack Wei again.
The Minister of Education, Mùróng Dé, said to the Yan ruler, Mùróng Chuí:
"The barbarians, due to their victory at Canhe,
hold the Crown Prince in contempt.
We should use Your Majesty's divine strategy to subdue them,
otherwise,
they will become a future calamity."
Chuí then appointed the Duke of Qīnghé, Mùróng Huì, to oversee affairs at the留守台,
and appointed him Governor of Yōuzhōu,
replacing the King of Gāoyáng, Mùróng Lóng, in guarding Lóngchéng;
he appointed the King of Yángchéng, Lán Hàn, as General of the Northern Central Guard,
replacing the Duke of Chánglè, Mùróng Shèng, in guarding Jì;
he ordered Lóng and Shèng to lead all their elite troops back to Zhōngshān,
planning a major campaign against Wei the following year.
16 In this year,
the Qín ruler, Yáo Xīng, enfeoffed his uncle, Yáo Xù, as Prince of Jìn,
Yáo Shuòdé as Prince of Lǒngxī,
his younger brother, Yáo Chóng, as Duke of Qí,
and Yáo Xiǎn as Duke of Chángshān.
1 In spring,
the first month,
the Yan King of Gāoyáng, Mùróng Lóng, led the armored troops from Lóngchéng into Zhōngshān.
The army's appearance was elite and orderly,
and the morale of the Yan people slightly revived.
The Hàn people have a saying:
"The might of victory
boosts morale a hundredfold;
the soldiers of a defeated army
never again stand straight in their lifetime."
This refers to such a situation.
2 The Xiūguān leader, Quán Wànshì, led his followers to surrender to Western Qín.
The previous year,
Qǐfú Gānguī declared himself King of Qín,
hence called Western Qín to distinguish it from Yáo Qín.
Shuài,
read as "shuài."
Xiáng,
pronounced as "xiáng."
3 The Yan ruler, Mùróng Chuí, sent the General Who Conquers the East, Píng Guī, to mobilize troops in Jìzhōu.
In the second month,
Guī rebelled at Lǔkǒu with troops from the three commanderies of Bólíng, Wǔyì, and Chánglè,
and his nephew, the Governor of Jìzhōu, Píng Xǐ, advised against it,
but he did not listen.
Guī's younger brother, the Magistrate of Hǎiyáng, Píng Hàn, also raised troops in Liáoxī to respond to him.
Hǎiyáng County has belonged to Liáoxī Commandery since the Hàn dynasty.
The Píng Guī brothers rebelled because the Yan army was defeated.
(Thus they rebelled.)
Sōng was defeated and died.
Chuí personally led troops to attack Guī,
and upon reaching Lǔkǒu,
Guī abandoned his followers,
and fled across the river with his wife, children, Píng Xǐ, and several dozen others.
Chuí then withdrew his troops and returned.
Hàn led his troops toward Lóngchéng,
and the Duke of Qīnghé, Mùróng Huì, sent the Duke of Dōngyáng, Mùróng Gēn, and others to attack Hàn,
defeating him.
Hàn fled to the south of the mountains.
(South of the Báiláng, Xúwú, and other mountains.)
4 In the third month, on the Gēngzǐ day,
the ruler of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, left Fànyáng Prince Mùróng Dé to guard Zhōngshān,
and led his troops out in secret.
They crossed Qīng Lǐng,
passed through Tiānmén.
Qīng Lǐng is likely Guǎngchāng Lǐng,
located south of Guǎngchāng County in Dài Commandery,
which is the so-called Wǔhuí Road.
To its south, layered cliffs pierce the sky;
the steepness of the piled rocks,
with sheer cliffs rising straight up,
is likely Tiānmén.
Emerging where Wèi did not expect,
they headed straight for Yúnzhōng.
The Wèi Duke of Chénliú, Tuòbá Qián, commanded over thirty thousand tribal households garrisoning Píngchéng.
When Chuí reached Liè Lǐng—
Liè Lǐng
is northeast of Xiàwū Mountain;
when Wèi's capital was at Píngchéng,
they often hunted here—
at this time,
the Yān troops, having recently been defeated,
all feared Wèi.
Only the soldiers from Lóngchéng were brave, sharp, and vied to be first.
Qián had never made defensive preparations.
In the intercalary month, on the Yǐmǎo day,
the Yān army reached Píngchéng.
Only then did Qián become aware of them.
Leading his subordinates out to battle,
he was defeated and died.
The Yān army gathered all his tribes.
The King of Wèi, Tuòbá Guī, was shocked and terrified, wanting to flee.
The various tribes, hearing of Qián's death,
all became disloyal.
Guī did not know where to go.
Qián's bravery likely surpassed all north of the frontier.
Once he was defeated and died,
therefore the various tribes all became disloyal.
However, Heaven was about to destroy Yān;
Chuí subsequently perished.
This certainly was not something human strength could achieve.
"Shuài" is read as "lǜ."
"Bù" is pronounced pǔ bù fān.
When Chuí passed by Cānhé Pō,
seeing piled bones like mountains,
he performed sacrifices for them.
The soldiers all wailed bitterly,
their voices shaking the mountains and valleys.
Chuí, ashamed and indignant, vomited blood.
From this, illness arose.
He advanced riding in a horse-drawn carriage,
and halted thirty lǐ northwest of Píngchéng.
The Crown Prince Bǎo and others, hearing of this,
all led their troops back.
Defectors from the Yān army ran to report to Wèi, saying:
"Chuí is already dead;
his corpse is in the army carriage."
The King of Wèi, Tuòbá Guī, wanted to pursue them,
but hearing that Píngchéng had already fallen,
he led his troops back to Yīnshān.
There is a saying among Wèi people:
"The dead Zhūgě makes the living Zhòngdǎ flee."
Tuòbá Guī, hearing of Mùróng Chuí's death, dared not advance;
this is also similar.
Chuí remained at Píngchéng for ten days.
His illness turned critical.
He then built Yànchāng City and returned.
The Water Classic states: Yànchāng City is forty lǐ north of Píngchéng.
In the fourth month, on the Guǐwèi day,
he died at Jǔyáng in Shànggǔ.
Xián states: The old city of Jǔyáng County
is east of present-day Guī Prefecture.
"Jǔ" is pronounced zǔ.
Chuí was seventy-one years old.
On the Bǐngshēn day,
they reached Zhōngshān.
On the Wùxū day,
the funeral was held.
He was posthumously titled Emperor Chéngwǔ,
and his temple name was Shìzǔ.
On the Rényín day,
Crown Prince Bǎo ascended the throne.
Bǎo,
styled Dàoyòu,
was Chuí's fourth son.
He changed the era name to Yǒngkāng.
5 In the fifth month, on the Xīnhài day,
he appointed Fànyáng Prince Mùróng Dé as Commander of Military Affairs of the Six Provinces of Jì, Yǎn, Qīng, Xú, Jīng, and Yù, Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Governor of Jì Province,
to guard Yè.
He appointed Liáoxī Prince Mùróng Nóng as Commander of Military Affairs of the Six Provinces of Bìng, Yōng, Yì, Liáng, Qín, and Liáng, and Governor of Bìng Province,
to guard Jìnyáng.
He also appointed Prince of Āndìng Kùnùguān Wěi as Grand Tutor,
and Prince of Fúyú Wèi as Grand Mentor.
Wèi
was a prince of Fúyú.
When the King of Yān, Mùróng Huàng, defeated Fúyú, he obtained him.
When Yān perished,
he entered Qín.
When Qín was in chaos,
he returned to Yān.
The ruler of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, enfeoffed him as Prince of Fúyú.
On the Jiǎyín day,
he appointed Zhào Prince Mùróng Lín to concurrently hold the position of Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
Gāoyáng Prince Mùróng Lóng to concurrently hold the position of Right Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
Duke of Chánglè Mùróng Shèng as Colonel of the Capital Region,
and Yídū Prince Mùróng Fèng as Governor of Jì Province.
5 On the Yǐmǎo day,
he appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Péngchéng's Liú Gāi as Governor of Xú Province,
to guard Juànchéng.
6 On the Jiǎzǐ day,
he appointed Duke of Wàngcài Xiè Yǎn as Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
Wàngcài County belonged to Yùzhāng Commandery.
Shěn Yuē states: In the Zhōngpíng era of Hàn Emperor Líng,
people from Shàngcài in Rǔnán were divided and relocated to this city,
establishing a county named Shàngcài.
In the first year of Tàikāng of Jìn Emperor Wǔ,
it was renamed.
Sòng Bái states: Because the people of Shàngcài longed for their native land,
it was called Wàngcài.

7 Initially, the King of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, first had sons Lìng and Bǎo with the former Duchess Duàn. Later, he had sons Lǎng and Jiàn with the later Duchess Duàn, and he loved the sons by his various consorts: Lín, Nóng, Lóng, Róu, and Xī.
When Bǎo first became crown prince,
he had a fine reputation.
Later, he became dissolute and negligent,
causing disappointment both inside and outside the court.
The later Duchess Duàn once said to Chuí:

(The King of Yān, Mùróng Chuí, first married a woman of the Duàn clan. Due to the slander of Empress Kězúhún, she died. After he ascended the throne, he posthumously honored her as empress. He then took another woman of the Duàn clan as empress, so the histories record her as the later Duchess Duàn to distinguish her.)

"The crown prince, encountering a time of peace, is sufficient to be a ruler who maintains achievements. Now the state's situation is difficult; I fear he is not a talent to save the age. The two princes of Liáoxī and Gāoyáng are Your Majesty's worthy sons. You should choose one and entrust him with the great enterprise. Zhào Prince Lín is treacherous, deceitful, stubborn, and willful. In the future, he will certainly be a calamity for the state. You should plan against him early."
Bǎo served Chuí's attendants well,
and the attendants often praised him.
Therefore, Chuí considered him worthy.
He said to Duchess Duàn:
"Do you want me to become like Duke Xiàn of Jìn!"
(Duke Xiàn of Jìn believed the slander of Lady Lí and killed Crown Prince Shēnshēng.)
She told her younger brother, Fànyáng Prince Mùróng Dé:

"The crown prince lacks talent, as all under heaven know. I spoke for the sake of the altars of state, yet the ruler compares me to Lady Lí. How bitter this is! I observe that the crown prince will certainly ruin the altars of state. Fànyáng Prince has extraordinary capacity. If the Yān mandate is not yet exhausted, it lies with the Prince!"
Bǎo and Lín heard this and resented her.
On the Yǐchǒu day,
Bǎo sent Lín to tell Duchess Duàn:
"You often said the ruler could not preserve the great enterprise. Now, can he or not? You should end your own life early to preserve the Duàn clan!"
Duchess Duàn angrily said:
"You brothers do not find it difficult to force your mother to death; how could you preserve the ancestral enterprise! Do I cherish life? I only think the state will perish soon."
Then she committed suicide.
Bǎo proposed that because Duchess Duàn plotted to depose the legitimate heir, she lacked the way of a mother-empress and should not be given a full funeral.
All the ministers agreed.
The Director of the Central Secretariat, Suī Suìyáng, declared in court:

"There is no principle for a son to deny funeral rites to his mother. Empress Yán of Hàn Ānsī personally deposed Emperor Shùn. (The event is seen in the fiftieth scroll, third year of Yánguāng of Hàn Emperor Ān.) How much more so when the words of the former empress are ambiguous, and their truth or falsehood is unknown!"
Then a full funeral was held.
8 In the sixth month, on
Guǐyǒu,
King Guī of Wèi sent General Wáng Jiàn and others to attack Liú Kàngní, the Grand Administrator of Guǎngníng of Yān,
and beheaded him.
Guǎngníng County,
during the Hàn Dynasty, belonged to Shànggǔ Commandery.
During the Tàikāng era of Jìn,
Guǎngníng Commandery was established separately.
Kàng,
read as kǔ làng.
Xiáng, the Duke of Kāifēng and Grand Administrator of Shànggǔ of Yān, abandoned his commandery and fled.
Xiáng
was the great-grandson of Huǎng.
9 On Dīnghài,
Empress Dowager Hè of Wèi passed away.
She was the mother of King Guī of Wèi.
10 The ruler of Yān, Bǎo, fixed the old registers of the scholar-official clans,
distinguishing between the pure and the impure,
reviewed and examined the household registrations,
abolished the households under military camp protection and patronage,
and placed them all under the commanderies and counties.
The households under military camp protection and patronage
were those taken under the protection of various armies to serve as private troops.
This began to create disaffection.
This matter, if implemented,
might not necessarily be wrong;
but at the beginning of Mùróng Bǎo's reign,
the state army had just been defeated,
and there was also a great mourning period,
with many among the people harboring rebellious intentions,
so it was not appropriate to implement it hastily.
The Great Learning says: "Things have their roots and branches,
affairs have their beginnings and ends.
Knowing what comes first and what comes last,
then one is close to the Way."
11 The King of Sānhé, Lǚ Guāng, assumed the title of Heavenly King,
with the state name Dà Liáng,
proclaimed a general amnesty,
and changed the era name to Lóngfēi.
Lǚ Guāng,
styled Shìmíng,
was a Dí from Lüèyáng.
His father, Pó Lóu,
was an assistant to Fú Jiān.
He appointed his heir, Shào, as Crown Prince,
and enfeoffed twenty of his sons and brothers as dukes and marquises.
He appointed the Director of the Central Secretariat, Wáng Xiáng, as Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
and the Gentleman of Writings, Duàn Yè, and four others as Directors of the Imperial Secretariat.
Guāng sent an envoy to appoint Tūfǎ Wūgū as General-in-Chief Who Conquers the South, Governor of Yìzhōu, and Left Worthy King.
Wūgū said to the envoy:
"The sons of King Lǚ are greedy and licentious.
Among Guāng's sons recorded in history,
are Zuǎn, Hóng, Shào, and Fù.
Guāng's nephew, Shí Cōng, slandered and killed Dù Jìn.
The other two should be examined.
How can I go against the hearts of the people
and accept an unjust title!
I shall undertake the affairs of an emperor."
He then kept the ceremonial music and feather insignia,
thanked the envoy, and sent him away.
12 Píng Guī gathered his remaining followers and occupied Gāotáng.
Gāotáng County,
since the Hàn Dynasty, belonged to Píngyuán Commandery.
The people of the eastern region,
who had long cherished Lóng's kindness,
lined the roads to welcome and await him.
They lined the roads in succession.
Shǔ,
read as zhī yù.
In the seventh month,
Lóng advanced his army to the river,
and Guī abandoned Gāotáng and fled.
Lóng sent the General Who Establishes Might, Mùróng Jìn, and others to cross the river and pursue him,
and beheaded Guī in Jìběi.
Píng Xǐ fled to Péngchéng.
13 He took the daughter of the late Director of the Central Secretariat, Wáng Xiànzhī, as the Crown Prince's consort.
Xiànzhī
was the son of Xīzhī.
Xīzhī
was the nephew of Wáng Dǎo.
14 The ministers of Wèi urged King Guī of Wèi to assume the imperial title.
Guī began to use the banners of the Son of Heaven,
with guards clearing the way when he went out and returning,
and changed the era name to Huángshǐ.
Guī,
the legitimate grandson of Shíyìjiān,
son of Shí,
details are in the first year of the 104th volume.
From Fú Jiān's defeat at Huái and Féi,
to this time, fourteen years had passed.
Between the passes and the rivers,
the chieftains of the Róng and Dí,
rose and fell in succession.
The people of Jìn looked upon this
with indifference, not concerning themselves with it.
Tuòbá Guī rose, and the situation of North and South was determined.
Once the situation of North and South was determined,
eventually the South was annexed by the North.
Alas!
After the Suí Dynasty,
those whose names were renowned in their times,
ten out of six or seven were descendants from north of the passes.
Distinguishing between clans and lineages,
what benefit does it truly bring!
Guī approved of this.
The King of Liáoxī of Yān, Nóng, led all his private troops, numbering tens of thousands of households, to Bìngzhōu.
Bìngzhōu had long lacked stored provisions,
and that year there was an early frost,
so the people could not supply them with food.
He also sent various army protectors to separately supervise the various Hú tribes,
causing both the Han people and the tribes to resent him,
and they secretly summoned the Wèi army.
In the eighth month,
on Jǐhài,
King Guī of Wèi launched a major campaign against Yān.
An army without internal support and a sure plan for victory
should not launch a major campaign.
He marched south from Mǎyì,
crossed Jūzhù,
with banners stretching over two thousand lǐ,
advancing with drums beating.
General of the Left, Lǐ Lì of Yànmén, led fifty thousand cavalry as the vanguard.
Separately, he sent General Fēng Zhēn and others to take the eastern route from Jūndū,
to attack Yān's Yōuzhōu.
The Wèishū Official Clan Records: During the time of Tuòbá Jiéfén,
among the various surnames of the remaining tribes that entered were the Shìbēn clan,
later changed to the Fēng clan.
Jūndū County,
during the Former Hàn, belonged to Shànggǔ Commandery,
during the Later Hàn, belonged to Guǎngyáng Commandery,
during Jìn, belonged to the State of Yān.
There was the Jūndū Pass.
Xián said: Present-day Chāngpíng County of Yōuzhōu has Mount Jūndū,
to the northwest.
15 The General-in-Chief Who Conquers the North, Governor of Yōu and Píng Provinces, and Duke of Qīnghé of Yān, Huì, had a low-born mother but was the eldest son.
He was heroic, talented, and skilled.
The ruler of Yān, Chuí, loved him.
When Bǎo campaigned against Wèi,
Chuí ordered Huì to act as regent of the Eastern Palace and oversee administration,
treating him with the same courtesy as the Crown Prince.
"Oversee administration"
means overseeing the administration of court affairs.
He ordered Huì to guard Lóngchéng,
entrusting him with the affairs of the northeast.
The officials and assistants of his princely establishment
were all selected from among the talented and prestigious of the time.
When Chuí was critically ill,
he left instructions ordering Bǎo to make Huì his successor.
But Bǎo loved his younger son, the Duke of Púyáng, Cè,
and his mind was not on Huì.
The Duke of Chánglè, Shèng, was the same age as Huì,
and felt ashamed to be beneath him.
So he and the King of Zhào, Lín, together urged Bǎo to establish Cè,
and Bǎo followed their advice.
On Yǐhài,
he established Lady Duàn as Empress,
Cè as Crown Prince,
and both Huì and Shèng were promoted in rank to kings.
Cè was eleven years old,
and had always been foolish and weak.
When Huì heard this,
he felt resentful and indignant.
In the ninth month,
Zhāngwǔ King Zhòu escorted the remains of the ruler of Yān, Chuí, and the late Empress Duàn of Chéng'āi for burial at the Xuānpíng Mausoleum in Lóngchéng.
The late Empress of Chéng'āi
was the Lady Duàn, Bǎo's stepmother, whom Bǎo had killed.
Lóng had returned from Lóngchéng to Zhōngshān the previous year,
and Huì actually replaced him,
so he ordered the return of his private troops and assistants.
Many private troops were not sent back.
Zhòu was older and of higher seniority,
but Huì bullied and humiliated him in every matter,
and those who saw this all knew he had different intentions.
This sets the stage for the mutual plotting between Bǎo and Huì, father and son.
16 On Wùwǔ,
the Wèi army reached Yángqǔ.
Yángqǔ County, since the Hàn Dynasty, belonged to Tàiyuán Commandery.
Sòng Bái said: The old city of Yángqǔ County
was forty-five lǐ north of Tàiyuán County,
where it was moved at the end of the Later Hàn.
Emperor Wén of Suí changed it to Yángzhí,
and later changed it again to Fényáng County.
They approached Jìnyáng,
and sent cavalry to circle the city, shouting loudly, then left.
The King of Liáoxī of Yān, Nóng, went out to fight,
was badly defeated,
and fled back to Jìnyáng.
Sima Mùyú Sōng closed the gates and refused him entry.
Previously, there was a Mùyú Sōng who plotted to support the King of Zhào, Lín, in a rebellion and was executed.
This is another person.
The General of the Central Guard of Wèi, Zhǎngsūn Féi, pursued him.
The General of the Central Guard
was a position established by Wèi,
similar to the Central Guard General of Wèi and Jìn.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
He captured Nóng's wife and children.
The Yān army was completely wiped out.
Nóng was wounded,
and escaped back to Zhōngshān alone with three horsemen.
Bǎo sent a man to request from the King of Wei, Guī,
wanting to have his younger brother Gū returned.
(The matter of Gū being detained in Yān is recorded in the 107th scroll, the 16th year of the Xiàowǔ Tàiyuán era.)
West of Chángshān,
is the territory of Bīngzhōu.
Afterwards, Bǎo regretted it.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
Guī went to Lúnú.
(The Wèishū Dìxíngzhì states: The administrative seat of Zhōngshān Commandery is Lúnú.)
Lì Dàoyuán said: In the northwest corner of Lúnú city,
there is water,
deep and stagnant,
stretching one hundred paces from north to south,
and over a hundred paces from east to west;
the water’s color is pitch black, called “lú,”
and its stagnant nature is called “nú,”
hence the city derived its name from this.
On the day Xīnhài,
he again besieged Zhōngshān.
(Dù Yòu said: The Later Yān capital was Zhōngshān,
which is present-day Tángchāng County in Bólíng Commandery.
Tángchāng was originally the Hàn dynasty’s Kǔxíng County,
changed to Hànchāng by Emperor Zhāng,
changed to Wèichāng by Cáo Wèi,
changed to Suíchāng by Suí,
and changed to Tángchāng during the Táng dynasty’s Wǔdé era.)
Fù,
fú yòu fān.
“Now we sit and guard this impoverished city,
ultimately facing exhaustion and ruin.
We, your subjects, wish to go out once and fight joyfully;
the soldiers are all willing to fight to the death,
which is what is meant by fighting joyfully.
Lè,
yīn luò.
This is to sit and bring about our own defeat.
Moreover, we have endured the siege for a long time,
with no other extraordinary changes,
merely hoping that over time the enemy bandits will retreat on their own.
The current situation, both internal and external,
shows a vast disparity in strength,
and it is clear they will certainly not retreat on their own.
We should follow the masses and make a decisive stand.”
Bǎo agreed.
Lóng withdrew and marshaled his troops,
summoning his various aides and saying to them:
“The imperial majesty is not振作,
and enemy bandits insult us from within,
a shared shame for subjects and sons,
duty demands no regard for life.
If we are fortunate now to defeat the enemy,
returning safely would of course be good;
but if we meet misfortune,
it will still allow our resolve and integrity to be displayed.
Should any of you go north and see my mother,
convey this sentiment to her for me!”
(When Lóng initially garrisoned Lóngchéng,
he went north together with his mother;
when Chuí summoned Lóng to attack Wèi,
his mother remained in Lóngchéng.)
Wèi,
yú wèi fān.
He went to the gate and awaited orders.
Lín again firmly stopped Bǎo,
and the masses were greatly indignant.
Lóng returned in tears.
That night,
Lín used troops to coerce the Left Guard General, the Prince of Běidì, Jīng,
ordering him to lead the imperial guards to assassinate Bǎo.
Jīng refused on grounds of righteousness,
Lín became angry,
killed Jīng,
fled to the Western Mountains,
and relied on the remaining Dīnglíng people.
(Two hundred li northwest of Zhōngshān is Lángshān;
from Lángshān westward,
south connecting to Chángshān,
the mountains and valleys are deep and treacherous.
At the end of the Hàn, Zhāng Yàn of the Hēishān, and during the Five Dynasties, the brothers Sūn Fāngjiǎn, all relied on and held that area.
The remaining Dīnglíng people
were part of Dí Zhēn’s faction,
defeated by Yān,
retreated and gathered in the Western Mountains.
The Western Mountains
are the western mountains of Qūyáng.)
Bǎo did not know where Lín had gone.
Zhī,
wǎng yě.
Fearing Lín would seize Huì’s army,
and first occupy Lóngchéng,
he then summoned Lóng and the Cavalry General-in-Chief Nóng,
planning to leave Zhōngshān,
and flee to safeguard Lóngchéng.
Lóng said:
“The late emperor toiled through wind and rain to achieve the restoration enterprise,
yet not a full year after his passing, the realm has fallen into great ruin—
how can this not be called a betrayal!
Now with external enemies strong and internal troubles arising again,
flesh and blood estranged,
the common people suspicious and fearful,
we truly cannot resist the enemy.
Moving north to the old capital
is indeed the appropriate course of action.
However, Lóngchuān is narrow in territory and poor in people—
(Lóngchuān refers to the Hé Lóng area.)
and again we hope morning and night for great achievements—
this is certainly impossible.
If we practice frugality and cherish the people,
devote ourselves to agriculture and train soldiers,
within a few years,
both public and private sectors will be abundant,
and in the regions between Zhào and Wèi,
the people, weary and suffering from enemy violence,
will remember Yān’s virtue.
Perhaps then we can turn our banners back,
and recover our former enterprise.
If we cannot achieve that,
then relying on natural defenses to fortify ourselves,
we can still leisurely nurture our strength.”
Bǎo said:
“Your words are entirely reasonable,
I will fully follow your advice.”
(Lóng’s strategy was indeed sound,
but what could be done about fate!
Military strategists turn defeat into success—
Lóng’s wisdom was insufficient to reach this.
Had Bǎo consistently followed Lóng’s advice from start to finish,
he might still have avoided Lán Hàn’s calamity.)
Liáodōng’s Gāo Fǔ,
skilled in divination,
had long been trusted and valued by Lóng.
He privately said to Lóng:
“If Your Highness goes north,
you will ultimately not reach your destination,
nor will you be able to see the Grand Empress Dowager.
If you let the sovereign go alone,
and Your Highness secretly remain here,
you are sure to achieve great merit.”
Lóng said:
“The state faces great calamity,
the sovereign is in distress,
and moreover my elderly mother is in the north.
If I can die with my head facing north,
I will have no regrets.
What kind of talk is this!”
He then summoned all his subordinates,
asking whether they would leave or stay.
Only Sima Lǔ Gōng and Army Advisor Chéng Jí were willing to follow,
the rest all wished to stay.
Lóng allowed them all their choice.
Nóng’s general Gǔ Huìguī persuaded Nóng, saying:
“The people in the city
are all relatives of those killed by Guī at Cānhé.
Fathers, brothers, and sons weep tears of blood and are eager,
wishing to fight Wèi but suppressed by the Guard Army.
(Mùróng Lín was the Guard General-in-Chief,
hence referred to as the Guard Army.)
They all say: ‘If we could get one person of the Mùróng clan to support and establish him,
and fight Wèi with him,
we would die without regret.’
If Your Highness fortunately remains here,
fulfilling the hopes of the masses,
repelling the Wèi army,
pacifying the capital region,
and welcoming back the imperial carriage,
you would still not fail to be a loyal subject.”
Nóng wanted to kill Guī but valued his talent and strength,
and said to him:
“If I must live hoping for this,
I would rather go to my death!”
(Both Nóng and Lóng were reputed to be wise and strategic,
yet their views were like this.
Heaven was abandoning Yān,
so the wise lost their wisdom.)
On the day Rénzǐ,
at night,
Bǎo, Crown Prince Cè, the Prince of Liáoxī Nóng, the Prince of Gāoyáng Lóng, the Prince of Chánglè Shèng, and over ten thousand cavalry went out to join Huì’s army.
The Prince of Héjiān Xī, the Prince of Bóhǎi Lǎng, and the Prince of Bólíng Jiàn were all young,
unable to leave the city.
Lóng returned to fetch them,
personally preparing the carriage and horses,
and they all escaped.
The Yān general Wáng
Shěn and others surrendered to Wèi.
The Prince of Lèlàng Huì, the Secretariat Gentleman Hán Fàn, the Vice Director Duàn Hóng, the Grand Astrologer Liú Qǐ, and others led three hundred artisans and performers to flee to Yè.
Those around him advised Mùróng Bǎo to kill Mùróng Huì.
The Palace Censor, Qiúní Guī, heard of this,
and reported to Huì, saying:
"What Your Highness relies upon is your father,
but your father has already changed his intentions;
what you lean on is your troops,
but your troops have already slipped from your grasp;
where do you intend to find a place for yourself!
It would be better to execute the two Princes,
depose the Crown Prince,
and have Your Highness take up residence in the Eastern Palace yourself,
concurrently holding the responsibilities of general and minister,
in order to restore and rectify the state,
this is the best strategy."
Huì hesitated and did not consent.
Bǎo said to Mùróng Nóng and Mùróng Lóng:
"Judging by Dàotōng's (Mùróng Huì's courtesy name) aspirations and inclinations,
he will certainly rebel without a doubt,
we should eliminate him early."
Nóng and Lóng said:
"Now the enemy invades and insults us from within,
the Central Plains are in turmoil,
the peril facing the state
is like a pile of eggs.
Huì has pacified and guarded the old capital,
and came from afar to aid the nation in its crisis,
the weight of his prestige and fame
is sufficient to shake our neighbors on all sides.
To hastily kill him before his rebellious intentions have become manifest
would not only injure the affection between father and son,
but we fear it would also greatly damage your prestige and authority."
Bǎo said:
"Huì's rebellious intent is already formed,
you gentlemen are kind and forgiving,
and cannot bear to kill him early,
but I fear that once he stages a revolt,
he will certainly first harm his uncles,
and then reach me,
when that time comes, do not regret and blame yourselves!"
When Huì heard this,
he became even more afraid.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the day Guǐyǒu,
Bǎo was staying overnight at Huángyú Valley in Guǎngdū.
(The *Wèi Shū: Treatise on Geography* states: Guǎngdū County
belonged to Jiàndé Commandery,
located within the boundaries of Báiláng County of Běipíng in Han times,
and was abolished and merged into Liǔchéng County of Liáoxī during Sui.)
(Huì) divided his forces and launched a surprise attack on Nóng and Lóng,
killing Lóng in his tent;
Nóng was severely wounded,
captured Qiúní Guī,
and fled into the mountains.
Huì, because Qiúní Guī had been captured,
realized the affair would ultimately be exposed,
so that night he went to see Bǎo and said:
"Nóng and Lóng plotted rebellion,
I have already eliminated them."
Bǎo wanted to punish Huì,
but pretended with kind words to reassure him, saying:
"I have long suspected these two Princes,
it is very good that you eliminated them."
On the day Jiǎxū,
at dawn,
Huì had his guard of honor stand in strict formation,
and then led the way.
Huì wanted to abandon Lóng's coffin,
but Yú Chóng tearfully and firmly pleaded,
so he allowed it to be carried along with the army.
Nóng came out
and surrendered himself,
Bǎo rebuked him, saying:
"Why have you betrayed yourself?"
Bǎo pretended to reprimand Nóng while hinting at his previous words.
After traveling over ten *li*,
Bǎo looked back and summoned his close ministers to eat,
and also to discuss Nóng's crime.
As Huì took his seat,
Bǎo signaled with his eyes to the General of the Guard Army, Mùyú Téng, ordering him to behead Huì,
but he only wounded his head,
and failed to kill him.
Huì ran to join his troops,
and led his soldiers to attack Bǎo.
Bǎo led several hundred cavalry and galloped two hundred *li*,
by late afternoon,
he reached Lóngchéng.
Huì sent cavalry in pursuit as far as Shíchéng,
but they did not catch up.
(Shíchéng County
belonged to Běipíng Commandery in Han times,
to Jiàndé Commandery in Later Wei,
and was merged into Liǔchéng County during Sui.)
On the day Yǐhài,
Huì sent Qiúní Guī to attack Lóngchéng,
Bǎo dispatched troops at night to launch a surprise attack,
and defeated them.
Huì sent an envoy requesting the execution of the sycophantic ministers around Bǎo,
and also asked to be made Crown Prince;
Bǎo did not consent.
Huì gathered up all the imperial carriages, utensils, and garments,
distributed the women of the rear palace among his generals and commanders,
appointed and established the various officials,
proclaimed himself Crown Prince and Recorder of the Department of State Affairs,
and led his troops towards Lóngchéng,
using the pretext of punishing Mùyú Téng;
on the day Bǐngzǐ,
he halted his troops beneath the city walls.
Bǎo ascended the west gate tower,
Huì, mounted on his horse, spoke to Bǎo from a distance,
and Bǎo reproached and reprimanded him.
Huì ordered his soldiers to shout loudly towards Bǎo to display his might,
the officers and soldiers within the city were all enraged,
and towards evening they came out to fight,
inflicting a major defeat on him.
Huì's troops suffered over half casualties,
and fled back to their camp.
The Palace Attendant Gentleman Gāo Yún led over a hundred daring warriors at night to launch a surprise attack on Huì's army.
(When Bǎo was Crown Prince,
Yún, because of his martial skills, served in the Eastern Palace,
and was appointed Palace Attendant Gentleman.)
Huì fled with a dozen or so cavalry to Zhōngshān,
where the Duke of Kāifēng, Mùróng Xiáng, killed him.
Bǎo killed Huì's mother and his three sons.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
Bǎo issued a great amnesty,
all those who had conspired with Huì
had their crimes pardoned,
and were restored to their former positions;
he rewarded according to merit,
appointing generals and enfeoffing marquises for several hundred men.
The Prince of Liáoxī, Mùróng Nóng, had his skull broken and his brain exposed,
Bǎo personally bandaged his wound,
and he barely survived.
He appointed Nóng as Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs,
and soon after appointed him as Minister of Works and concurrently Director of the Department of State Affairs.
Yú Chóng came out and surrendered himself,
Bǎo praised his loyalty,
appointed him as General of the Central Resolute,
and put him in charge of the palace guard.
He posthumously honored the Prince of Gāoyáng, Mùróng Lóng, as Minister over the Masses,
and bestowed upon him the posthumous title "Kāng".
Bǎo appointed Gāo Yún as General Who Establishes Might,
enfeoffed him as Duke of Xīyáng,
and adopted him as his son.
Yún
was a collateral relative of the Gāogōulì,
(the Gāogōulì themselves claimed to be descendants of Gāoyángshì,
hence they took Gāo as their surname.
*Gōu*
is pronounced as written,
also pronounced *jū*.
*Lì*
is pronounced *lì*, with the *zhī* tone.)
He had been relocated to Qīngshān,
(the defeat of Gāogōulì is seen in scroll 97, the eighth year of the Xiánkāng era of Emperor Chéng.)
(Qīngshān
is the Qīngshān in Túhé County of Liáoxī.)
Yún was deep, steady, and taciturn,
and people at the time did not understand him,
only the General of the Central Guard, Féng Bá of Chánglè
(Wèi Shōu said: Emperor Gāo of Han established Xìndū Commandery,
in the second year of Emperor Jǐng,
it became the Kingdom of Guǎngchuān,
Emperor Míng renamed it the Kingdom of Lèchéng,
Emperor Ān changed it to the Kingdom of Ānpíng,
and Jìn changed it to Chánglè Commandery.
Checking the Jìn records,
there is Ānpíng but not Chánglè,
it is unknown when the name was changed.
*Lè*
is pronounced *luò*.)
became friends with him.
(The affairs of Gāo Yún and Féng Bá begin to appear here,
laying the groundwork for their later acquisition of Yān.)
(Féng Bá) served the ruler of Western Yān, Mùróng Yǒng, as a general,
after Yǒng's defeat,
he relocated to Hélóng.
10 The Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs Wáng Guóbǎo and the General Who Establishes Might Wáng Xù attached themselves to the Prince of Kuàijī, Sīmǎ Dàozǐ,
accepting bribes and indulging in extreme luxury,
knowing no bounds.
They hated Wáng Gōng and Yīn Zhòngkān,
and urged Dàozǐ to reduce their military authority;
inside and outside the court, there was great unrest and anxiety.
Gōng and others each repaired their armor and drilled their troops,
and submitted memorials requesting a northern expedition;
Dàozǐ was suspicious of them,
and an edict was issued stating that the height of summer would hinder agriculture,
ordering them all to stand down from alert.
Wáng Gōng dispatched an envoy to conspire with Yīn Zhòngkān to campaign against Wáng Guóbǎo and others.
Huán Xuán, dissatisfied with his official career,
wished to borrow Yīn Zhòngkān's military strength to create chaos.
Huán Xuán was dissatisfied with his official career;
this matter is recorded in the seventeenth year of the Xiàowǔ Emperor's Tàiyuán era.
"Guóbǎo and you gentlemen have long been adversaries,
the matter begins in the fifteenth year of the Xiàowǔ Emperor's Tàiyuán era, scroll one hundred and seven.
Duì,
means enemy.
Shuō,
is pronounced shuì, with the Ruì tone;
the same below.
Now that he holds great power,
and collaborates with Wáng Xù,
his manipulations and changes,
all go as he wishes;
Xiàobó occupies the position of the emperor's maternal uncle,
so he certainly does not dare to harm him.
Wáng Gōng's courtesy name is Xiàobó;
he was the brother of the Xiàowǔ Emperor's Empress Wáng.
Chāo holds a frontier command,
and public sentiment considers you, sir, as someone who, though thoughtful,
is not a talent for governing a province.
Also seen in the fifteenth year of Tàiyuán.
Sī,
is pronounced xiàng lì.
Appointing Yīn Jì as Governor of Jīngzhōu,
the Colonel of the Southern Barbarians could, by seniority, become Governor of Jīngzhōu,
hence the statement.
Jì,
is pronounced jì.
Zhòngkān said:
"I have long been worried about this,
what plan should we adopt?"
Xuán said:
"Xiàobó deeply detests evil,
you should secretly make a pact with him,
raising troops from Jìnyáng to eliminate the wicked ones by the ruler's side.
The Spring and Autumn Annals' Gōngyáng Commentary says: Zhào Yǎng raised troops from Jìnyáng,
to eliminate the wicked ones by the ruler's side.
Jiānglíng is in the west,
Jīngkǒu is in the east,
hence it is said to act simultaneously from east and west.
I am willing to lead the heroes of Jīng and Chǔ,
bearing arms to lead the vanguard;
this would be a meritorious achievement like those of Huán and Wén."
Zhòngkān inwardly agreed with this,
so he externally allied with the Governor of Yōngzhōu, Xī Huī,
and internally conspired with his elder cousin, the Colonel of the Southern Barbarians, Yīn Jì, and the Chancellor of Nánjùn, Jiāng Jì of Chénliú.
Jì said:
"As subjects, each should abide by their duties and roles;
matters of right and wrong in the court,
how can those in frontier posts control them!
As for the affair of Jìnyáng,
I dare not participate."
Zhòngkān firmly urged him,
Jì angrily said:
"In advancing, I dare not agree;
in retreating, I dare not dissent."
Jì also strongly argued that it was not feasible.
Jì, fearing that Jì would meet with disaster,
mediated to reconcile them on the spot.
Jì said:
"How could a true man be threatened with death!
Jiāng Zhòngyuán is sixty years old,
only lacking a place to die!"
Jiāng Jì,
courtesy name Zhòngyuán.
He was replaced by Yáng Quánqī.
When the court heard of this,
it summoned Jì to serve as Imperial Censor.
Jì then claimed to be suffering from the effects of the cold-food powder,
and resigned his position.
Many people of Jìn took the cold-food powder,
its toxicity could flare up and sometimes cause death.
Now, the "Thousand Gold Prescriptions" contain several formulas.
Sǎn,
is pronounced xǐ dǎn.
He said to Jì:
"Elder brother's illness is truly worrying."
Jì said:
"My illness at most means my own death,
but your illness will bring about the extermination of your clan.
You should deeply cherish yourself,
do not worry about me!"
Xī Huī also refused to comply.
Zhòngkān hesitated, unable to decide,
when an envoy from Wáng Gōng arrived,
Zhòngkān agreed to it,
and Gōng was greatly pleased.
On the jiǎxū day,
Gōng submitted a memorial listing Guóbǎo's crimes,
and raised troops to campaign against him.
Initially,
the Xiàowǔ Emperor entrusted Wáng Xún with responsibilities,
but when the emperor died suddenly,
he did not receive a final edict of entrustment.
Xún, once losing power,
remained silent and passive.
Xún mò means,
following routine without uttering a word.
On the dīngchǒu day,
Wáng Gōng's memorial arrived,
and the palace and capital were placed under martial law.
Sīmǎ Dàozǐ asked Xún:
"The two frontier governors are rebelling,
did you know about it?"
Xún said:
"Gains and losses in court governance,
Xún does not participate in;
how could I know
that Wáng and Yīn would create trouble!"
Wáng Guóbǎo was terrified,
not knowing what to do.
He dispatched several hundred men to garrison Zhúlǐ.
Zhúlǐ,
is present-day Zhúxiǎo Town in Jiànkāng Prefecture,
located about thirty lǐ northeast of the temporary palace city.
They all dispersed and returned.
Wáng Xù advised Guóbǎo to forge an order from the Prince-Chancellor to summon Wáng Xún and Chē Yìn and kill them,
to eliminate prominent figures of the time,
and then, relying on the ruler and chancellor, to raise troops to campaign against the two frontier governors.
Guóbǎo agreed.
When Xún and Yìn arrived,
Guóbǎo did not dare to harm them,
and instead asked Xún for advice.
Xún said:
"Wáng and Yīn have no deep-seated enmity with you,
what they contend for is merely power and profit."
Guóbǎo said:
"Are you going to treat me like Cáo Shuǎng?"
Meaning Xún was like Jiǎng Jì persuading Cáo Shuǎng to relinquish power,
but Sīmǎ Yì ultimately exterminated his clan.
This matter is recorded in scroll seventy-five, the first year of the Shàolíng Lìgōng's Jiāpíng era of Wèi.
"What kind of talk is this!
How could you have Shuǎng's crimes,
and is Wáng Xiàobó comparable to Xuāndì?"
He also asked Yìn for advice.
Yìn said:
"In the past, Duke Huán besieged Shòuyáng,
and it took a long time to capture it.
See scroll one hundred two, the fifth year of Hǎixīgōng's Tàihé era, and scroll one hundred three, the first year of Jiǎnwéndì's Xián'ān era.
Gōng will certainly defend the city.
If Jīngkǒu is not taken and troops from the upper reaches suddenly arrive,
how will you, sir, deal with it?"
Guóbǎo became even more frightened,
and so submitted a memorial resigning his post,
proceeding to the palace gate to await punishment;
but soon regretted it,
falsely claiming an edict had restored him to his original office.
Dàozǐ was dim-witted and weak,
wishing to seek temporary appeasement.
Gū,
means for the time being.
Xī,
means to stop.
Gūxī,
means to stop for the time being.
He dispatched the Consultative Army Advisor of the Swfit Cavalry, Prince Qiáo Wáng Shàngzhī, to arrest Guóbǎo and hand him over to the Court of Judicial Review.
Hóng Jǐngbó said: The Consultative Army Advisor,
was first established in the Eastern Jìn,
derived from the Army Consultant Libationer.
His position was above that of other army advisors.
Piào,
is pronounced pǐ miào.
Qí,
is pronounced qí jì.
He was the son of Wáng Tián.
On the jiǎshēn day,
Guóbǎo was ordered to commit suicide,
Xù was executed in the marketplace,
an envoy was sent to Gōng,
deeply apologizing for the faults and errors;
Gōng then withdrew his troops and returned to Jīngkǒu.
Guóbǎo's elder brother, the Palace Attendant Wáng Kǎi, and the Swift Cavalry Marshal Wáng Yú both requested to resign their posts;
Dàozǐ, considering that Kǎi and Yú were born of a different mother than Guóbǎo,
and had never been on good terms with him,
released them without further inquiry.
On the wùzǐ day,
a general amnesty was declared.
Yīn Zhòngkān, though he had agreed with Wáng Gōng,
hesitated and did not dare to move his troops;
upon hearing of Guóbǎo and others' deaths,
he then defiantly submitted a memorial and raised troops,
dispatching Yáng Quánqī to station at Bālíng.
Shěn Yuē said: Bālíng County,
was established in the first year of Jìnwǔdì's Tàikāng era,
belonging to Chángshā.
Lì Dàoyuán said: The Xiāng River flows north to Bāqiū Mountain and enters the Yangtze,
the mountain is on the right bank,
there is the old city of Bālíng,
originally the Wú's Bāqiū storehouse;
Jìn established Bālíng County,
later setting up Jiànchāng Commandery.
Zhòngkān then returned.
The heir of Kuàijī, Sīmǎ Yuánxiǎn,
at the age of sixteen,
possessed outstanding talent.
Serving as Shìzhōng,
he persuaded Sīmǎ Dàozǐ that Wáng Guó and Yīn Zhòngkān would ultimately become a threat,
and requested to secretly prepare against them.
Dàozǐ then appointed Yuánxiǎn as General Who Conquers the Caitiffs,
assigning to him the personnel from his own guard headquarters and the civil and military officials of Xúzhōu.
This laid the groundwork for Yuánxiǎn to campaign against Wáng and Yīn.
11 The King of Wèi, Tuòbá Guī, due to insufficient military provisions,
ordered the Duke of Dōngpíng, Tuòbá Yí, to leave Yè
and move his garrison to Jùlù,
accumulating grain taxes in Yángchéng.
Mùróng Xiáng led out six thousand infantry
to wait for an opportunity to raid the various Wèi garrisons;
Guī attacked and defeated them,
beheading five thousand,
and capturing seven hundred alive,
all of whom he released.
Releasing them
was a means to win over the hearts of the people within the city of Zhōngshān.
12 Earlier,
the Lúshuǐ Hú of Zhāngyè, Jǔqú Luóchóu,
was a descendant of the Xiongnu King of Jǔqú.
The Lúshuǐ Hú were distributed living in Āndìng and Zhāngyè,
and historians attached the name of the commandery where they resided to them.
Jǔ,
is pronounced Zǐyú.
The History of the Northern Dynasties states: The Jǔqú clan for generations lived in Línshōng, Lúshuǐ, in Zhāngyè.
The King of Liáng, Lǚ Guāng, appointed Luóqiú as Shàngshū,
and he accompanied Guāng on the campaign against Western Qín.
After Lǚ Yán was defeated and died,
Luóqiú's younger brother, the Administrator of Sānhé, Jǔqú Zhōu, said to Luóqiú:
Lǚ Guāng, having obtained Liángzhōu,
proclaimed himself King of Sānhé,
so this commandery was likely established by Guāng.
Xián's commentary states: Sānhé
refers to the Jīnchéng River, the Cìzhī River, and the Huáng River.
This commandery was probably established within the boundaries of the Hàn commanderies of Zhāngyè and Jīnchéng.
"Our ruler is aged and muddled, trusting slander.
Now the army is defeated and generals are dead,
precisely the time when he will be suspicious and jealous of the wise and brave.
We brothers will certainly not be tolerated.
Rather than dying without fame,
it would be better to lead our troops toward Xīpíng,
exiting Tiáodiào.
The Héxī Zhāng clan established Xīpíng Commandery,
which in Táng times was the territory of Shànzhōu.
Tiáodiào
is a place name,
located within the boundaries of Pānhé County, Zhāngyè Commandery of Hàn.
Diào,
is pronounced Tiáodiào.
Pān,
according to Rúchún, is pronounced Pán.
Liángzhōu can then be easily pacified."
Luóqiú said:
"What you say is indeed true.
However, our family for generations has been renowned in the western regions for loyalty and filial piety.
I would rather let others betray me,
than I cannot bear to betray others."
Guāng indeed listened to slander,
and on the charge of causing the army's defeat, executed Luóqiú and Zhōu.
Luóqiú's nephew, Jǔqú Méngxùn,
was heroic and outstanding, possessing strategic acumen,
and was widely read in books and history.
He took the remains of Luóqiú and Zhōu back for burial;
many tribes were connected to his clan by marriage,
and those attending the funeral numbered over ten thousand.
Méngxùn wept and said to the multitude:
"King Lǚ is benighted and tyrannical, without principle,
killing many innocents.
Our ancestors in earlier generations
dominated Héxī like tigers.
Méngxùn's forebears
for generations served as the Xiongnu Left Jǔqú.
Héxī
was the left territory of the Xiongnu.
For generations they lived in Lúshuǐ as tribal chiefs,
his great-grandfathers and grandfathers were all powerful and brave, renowned for their courage.
How about restoring the enterprise of our ancestors?"
The multitude all acclaimed "Wànsuì!"
Thereupon they swore an alliance and raised troops,
attacking Liáng's Línsōng Commandery,
and capturing it.
Línsōng Commandery
was established by Zhāng Tiānxí,
and later Zhōu abolished it, merging it into Zhāngyè County of Zhāngyè Commandery.
The Treatise on Geography of the History of the Five Dynasties states
that Shāndān County in Zhāngyè had Jīnshān.
The affairs of Jǔqú Méngxùn begin here.
13 The Left Chief Clerk of the Minister Over the Masses, Wáng Xīn,
was the grandson of Wáng Dǎo.
He resided in Wú due to his mother's mourning.
When Wáng Gōng campaigned against Wáng Guóbǎo,
he appointed Xīn by provisional tablet as Acting Administrator of Wú Commandery,
conferring office with a white tablet,
which was not an imperial appointment.
The Three Wú were all east of Jiànkāng.
Tens of thousands responded.
Not long after,
Guóbǎo died,
Gōng ceased military operations,
ordered Xīn to leave his post,
and return to mourning attire.
Xīn, having during the uprising
executed many who opposed him,
found the situation irreversible,
and thus became greatly enraged.
He did not accept Gōng's order,
but sent his son Wáng Tài to lead troops against Gōng,
and submitted a memorial to Sīmǎ Dàozǐ, Prince of Kuàijī,
detailing Gōng's crimes and evils;
Dàozǐ sent his memorial to Gōng.
In the fifth month,
Gōng dispatched Sima Liú Láozhī to lead five thousand men to attack Tài,
and beheaded him.
He also fought Xīn in Qū'ē,
Xīn's forces collapsed,
and Xīn fled alone on horseback,
his whereabouts unknown.
Yú Xiàofù was arrested and handed over to the Chamberlain for Law Enforcement,
but because his grandfather Yú Tán had rendered meritorious service,
Yú Tán had merit in the campaign against Sū Jùn.
Xià,
is pronounced Xiájià.
14 Yān's Kùnúguān Jì entered Zhōngshān
and fought with the Duke of Kāifēng, Mùróng Xiáng.
Mùróng Bǎo had sent Jì to assist in defending Zhōngshān,
and thus he fought with Xiáng.
Nú,
is pronounced Núwò.
They exterminated the entire Kùnúguān clan;
they also killed the Governor of Zhōngshān, Fú Mó,
and exterminated his clan.
Zhōngshān city had no fixed ruler,
and the people feared the Wèi troops would take advantage,
so men and women formed alliances,
each person fighting for themselves.
Had Mùróng Nóng and Mùróng Lóng been left in Zhōngshān and employed,
the outcome might have been different.
On the day Jiǎchén,
the King of Wèi, Tuòbá Guī, lifted the siege of Zhōngshān,
and went to Hèjiān for provisions,
overseeing the righteous grain taxes of the various commanderies.
On the day Jiǎyǐn,

he appointed the Duke of Dōngpíng, Tuòbá Yí, as Grand General of Agile Cavalry, Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs at Home and Abroad, Governor of the Six Provinces of Yǎn, Yù, Yōng, Jīng, Xú, and Yáng, and Left Chancellor,
and enfeoffed him as Prince of Wèi.
Mùróng Xiáng, believing himself capable of repelling the Wèi troops,
and that his prestige and virtue had already been established,
thereupon ascended the imperial throne,
changed the era name to Jiànshǐ,
and established the hundred officials.
He appointed the Duke of Xīnpíng, Kězúhún Tán, as General of Chariots and Cavalry and Prefect of the Masters of Writing,
"Tán"
should be
"Tán".
Gū had earlier been sent to Yān,
and was detained by Yān;
he was Guī's younger brother.
The officials in Yè urged the Prince of Fànyáng, Mùróng Dé, to assume the imperial title,
but then someone arrived from Lóngchéng,
and they learned that the Yān ruler Bǎo was still alive,
so they desisted.
15 The King of Liáng, Lǚ Guāng, sent the Duke of Tàiyuán, Lǚ Zuǎn, to lead troops to attack Jǔqú Méngxùn at Cōnggǔ,
and defeated him.
Cōnggǔ
was likely within the boundaries of Shāndān County.
Méngxùn's elder cousin, Nánchéng, was a general of Liáng.
Hearing of Méngxùn's uprising,
he also gathered a multitude of several thousand and garrisoned Lèguàn.
Lèguàn County
belonged to Jiǔquán Commandery in Hàn times,
and was later abolished by Zhōu and merged into Fúlù County.
Guàn,
is pronounced Gūhuān,
also Gǔwán.
The army was defeated,
and Chéng died.
Lěi
is a surname;
Chéng
is a given name.
Nán Chéng advanced to attack Jiànkāng,
and sent an envoy to persuade the Prefect of Jiànkāng, Duàn Yè, saying:
"The Lü clan's governance is in decline,
powerful ministers arbitrarily issue commands,
punishments and executions are arbitrary,
and people have no place to settle.
Within this single province,
rebels are visible everywhere,
the signs of disintegration are clearly before our eyes,
and the people are crying out with nowhere to turn.
Why, my lord, with your unparalleled talent,
would you wish to show loyalty to a state on the verge of collapse!
Nán Chéng and I have already raised the banner of great righteousness,
and we wish to invite you, my lord, to come and govern our humble province,
so that those who have suffered amidst the devastation
may receive the blessing of revival.
As the Book of Documents says: 'We wait for our lord;
when our lord comes, we shall revive.'
Duàn Yè did not comply.
After a stalemate of twenty days,
with no external relief arriving,
the commandery's people, Gāo Kuí and Shǐ Huì, urged Duàn Yè to accept Nán Chéng's request.
Duàn Yè had long been at odds with the Liáng court's Palace Attendant Fáng Guǐ and Vice Director Wáng Xiáng,
and fearing he could not secure his own safety,
he finally agreed.
Nán Chéng and the others recommended Duàn Yè as Grand Commander, General of the Soaring Dragon, Governor of Liáng Province, and Duke of Jiànkāng,
and changed the era name to Shénxǐ.
They appointed Nán Chéng as General Who Supports the State,
entrusting him with military and state affairs.
Méngxùn led his troops to submit to Duàn Yè,
and Duàn Yè appointed Méngxùn as General Who Guards the West.
Lǚ Guāng ordered the Duke of Tàiyuán, Lǚ Zuǎn, to lead troops to attack Duàn Yè,
but he was unsuccessful.
16 In the sixth month,
the Western Qín King Qīnguī summoned Péng Xīniàn, the Governor of Northern Hé Province, to serve as General Who Guards the Garrison;
he appointed the General Who Guards the West, Wūhóng Pòguāng, as Governor of Hé Province;
"Wūhóng"
should be
"Wūyǐn".
The Treatise on Officials and Clans in the Book of Wèi states,
among the surnames of those who entered internally, there was the Wūyǐn clan,
which later changed to the Fáng clan.
Zhāng Jùn partitioned Xīngjìn, Jīnchéng, Wǔshǐ, Nán'ān, Yǒngjìn, Dàxià, Wǔchéng, and Hànzhōng to form Hé Province.
Northern Hé Province
was established by the Qǐfú clan,
with its seat at Fúhǎn.
The General Who Guards the Garrison
was established by Liú Cōng.
He garrisoned Fúhǎn.
Zhāng Mào partitioned Wǔxīng, Jīnchéng, Xīpíng, and Āngù to form Dìng Province.
Xīngjìn Commandery was also established by the Zhāng clan.
Fúhǎn County
belonged to Jīnchéng Commandery in Hàn times,
to Lǒngxī Commandery in Later Hàn,
and was later partitioned to belong to Xīpíng Commandery.
Zhāng Jùn partitioned it to belong to Jìnxīng Commandery,
and later it was partitioned again to establish Xīngjìn Commandery.
Wēn,
pronounced wēn.
Fú,
pronounced fū.
17 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Mùróng Xiáng killed Kězúhún Tán.
Xiáng was addicted to wine, extravagant, and licentious,
showing no concern for his soldiers and people,
meting out punishments and executions without restraint.
He executed over five hundred people, from princes and dukes downward,
causing his subordinates to become disaffected.
The city suffered from famine and hardship,
and Xiáng would not allow the people to go out to gather grain,
so the dead lay piled upon each other.
The entire city plotted to welcome the King of Zhào, Mùróng Lín.
Xiáng sent the General Who Supports the State, Zhāng Xiāng, to lead over five thousand men to supervise tax collection in Chángshān.
Lín entered Zhāng Xiāng's army from the Dīnglíng region,
secretly attacked Zhōngshān,
found the city gates unbarred,
captured Xiáng,
and executed him.
Lín then assumed the imperial title,
and allowed people to go out in all directions to gather grain.
Once the people were full,
they sought to engage Wèi in battle,
but Lín refused,
and gradually they fell back into poverty and hunger.
The King of Wèi, Tuòbá Guī, stationed his army at Lǔkǒu,
and sent Chángsūn Féi to lead seven thousand cavalry to raid Zhōngshān,
penetrating its outer walls.
Lín pursued them to the Gū River.
The Gū River
is in Xīnshì County of Zhōngshān.
The Geographical Records state: The city of Lúnú faces the Kòu River to the north,
and the Gū River to the front.
Gū,
pronounced gōng hū fān.
In the eighth month,
on the first day, Bǐngyín,
the King of Wèi, Tuòbá Guī, moved his army to Jiǔmén in Chángshān.
Chángshān Commandery had Jiǔmén County.
Many people and livestock died,
and the officers and soldiers all longed to return home.
Guī asked his generals about the epidemic,
and they replied:
"Only four or five out of ten remain."
Guī said:
"This is simply fate's decree.
What can we do about it!
The people of the four seas
can all become subjects of a state;
it depends on how I govern them.
Why worry about lacking people!"
His ministers then dared not speak further.
He sent the General Who Pacifies the Army, the Duke of Lüèyáng, Tuòbá Zūn, to raid Zhōngshān,
penetrating its outer walls before returning.
18 Yān appointed the King of Liáoxī, Mùróng Nóng, as Commander of All Military Affairs Within and Without, Grand Marshal, and Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
19 The Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Grand Master of Ceremonies of Liáng, Guō Nún of Xīpíng,
was skilled in astronomy and numerology,
and the people of the state trusted and respected him.
It happened that Mars remained in the Well constellation,
and Guō Nún said to Vice Director Wáng Xiáng:
"In the division corresponding to Liáng,
there will be a great military conflict.
Our ruler is old and ill,
the crown prince is weak and incompetent,
and the Duke of Tàiyuán is fierce and violent.
Once the inevitable occurs,
disaster and turmoil are certain to arise.
The two of us have long held key positions within the court,
and he has always bitterly resented us;
we will be the first to be executed.
The Tiánhú chieftain Wáng Qǐjī's tribe is the strongest;
Tiánhú
is a type of Hú people.
He has many of his former followers.
I wish to join you, sir, in raising a great undertaking,
supporting Qǐjī as our leader.
The troops of the two park-cities
will then all be ours.
The seat of Liáng Province is Gūzāng,
which has Eastern and Western Park-cities.
We can discuss the rest later."
Wáng Xiáng agreed.
Guō Nún used the troops of the two park-cities to set fire to the Hóngfàn Gate at night,
with Wáng Xiáng acting as an insider;
the plot was exposed,
Wáng Xiáng was executed,
and Guō Nún then occupied the Eastern Park-city and rebelled.
Among the common people, it was said that when a sage raises troops,
nothing he undertakes fails,
and many followed him.
The King of Liáng, Lǚ Guāng, summoned the Duke of Tàiyuán, Lǚ Zuǎn, and ordered him to attack Guō Nún.
As Zuǎn was about to return,
his generals all said:
"Duàn Yè is sure to follow our army's rear,
we should move our troops secretly by night."
Zuǎn said:
"Duàn Yè lacks heroic talent;
he relies on his city walls for self-defense.
If we sneak away by night,
it would only serve to boost his morale."
He then sent an envoy to inform Duàn Yè:
"Guō Nún has rebelled,
I am now returning to the capital;
the capital refers to Gūzāng.
Envoy,
pronounced shū lì fān.
You may come out early to do battle."
He then led his troops back.
Duàn Yè did not dare to come out.
26. The twelve tribal chieftains of the Xiānbēi Tǔmò and others from Hé'nán [south of the river] all submitted to Tūfǎ Wūgū.
This refers to the Hé'nán in Jīnchéng.
27. A man from Yān who had traveled from Zhōngshān to Lóngchéng
reported that Tuòbá Shèguī was weak and declining,
and that Situ Dé was securely guarding Yèchéng.
Just then, Dé's memorial arrived,
urging the Yān ruler Bǎo to return south.
Bǎo thereupon conducted a grand review of his troops and horses,
planning to retake the Central Plains.
He sent the Hónglú Lǔ Suì to bestow upon Dé, by imperial edict, the titles of Chéngxiàng and Jìzhōu Mù,
and authorized all the dukes, marquises, regional inspectors, and grand administrators in the southern regions to receive appointments and titles according to the established system.
In the eleventh month,
on the Guǐchǒu day,
Yān proclaimed a general amnesty.
In the twelfth month,
after the mobilized troops had all assembled and
martial law was in place at the encampment,
Bǎo sent General Qǐ Lún south to assess the situation.
On the Yǐhài day,
Mùróng Lín arrived at Yè
and again proclaimed himself King of Zhào.
He advised Fànyáng Wáng Dé, saying:
"Since Wèi has captured Zhōngshān,
they will take advantage of their victory to attack Yè.
Although Yè has stored provisions,
the city walls are extensive and difficult to defend firmly.
Moreover, the people's hearts are fearful and terrified;
it cannot be held.
It would be better to head south to Huátái,
use the Yellow River as a barrier to await Wèi,
watch for an opportunity to act,
and then perhaps we can recover Héběi."
At that time, Lǔyáng Wáng Hé was garrisoning Huátái.
Hé was a younger cousin of Chuí.
He also sent an envoy to welcome Dé;
Dé agreed.
1. In spring, the first month, Yān's Fànyáng Wáng Dé led 40,000 households from Yè southward to migrate to Huátái.
Wèi's Wèi Wáng Yí entered Yè,
seized its granaries and storehouses,
and pursued Dé to the river,
but failed to catch up.
King of Zhào Lín urged Dé to assume the imperial title.
Dé followed the precedent of his elder brother Chuí,
and assumed the title King of Yān.
For the events, see the ninth year of the Xiàowǔ Emperor's Tàiyuán era in scroll 105.
He exercised imperial authority through the Office of the Commander-in-Chief.
The Office of the Commander-in-Chief meant that all regional commands were under the authority of the King of Yān's residence.
Exercising imperial authority meant issuing imperial decrees to conduct affairs.
He appointed King of Zhào Lín as Sīkōng and concurrently Shàngshū Lìng,
Mùróng Fǎ as Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn,
Mùyú Bá as Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè,
and Dīng Tōng as Yòu Púyè.
Lín again plotted rebellion;
Dé had him killed.
2. On the Gēngzǐ day, Wèi King Guī traveled south from Zhōngshān to Gāoyì,
where he found Wáng Yǒng's son Xiàn.
Delighted, he said:
"He is the grandson of Wáng Jǐnglüè!"
He appointed him as Zhōngzhèng of his native province.
Wáng Měng was from Jù County, Běihǎi, Qīngzhōu.
During the Tàikāng era, Jù was placed under the Dōngguǎn Commandery.
In the Jìn dynasty, Dōngguǎn belonged to Xúzhōu.
The Jìnshū Zǎijì records him as being from Běihǎi Jù County,
likely because Měng himself claimed the Hàn dynasty commandery and county.
However, his family resided in Wèi Commandery, and he lived in seclusion at Huáyīn,
from where he went over to Qín.
His son Yǒng garrisoned Yōuzhōu
and died in battle at Xiānglíng while following Fú Pī;
therefore, Xiàn was living as a refugee in Gāoyì.
Now Wèi appointed him as Zhōngzhèng of his native province,
but they had not yet obtained Qīngzhōu and Xúzhōu.
It was likely to have him evaluate and rank the scholars of the eastern regions.
He was also put in charge of the Ménxià bureau.
The Xuǎncáo bureau is the responsibility of the Lìbù Shàngshū.
The Ménxià bureau is the responsibility of the Shìzhōng, Chángshì, and Jǐshì Huángmén.
Xuǎn is pronounced xuǎn.
He established a Xíngtái.
Zhèng Qiáo said: Xíngtái existed since Wèi and Jìn times.
When Jìn Wénwáng campaigned against Zhūgě Dàn,
Sànqí Chángshì Péi Xiù and Shàngshū Púyè Chén Tài accompanied him with a Xíngtái.
When Dōnghǎi Wáng Yuè led troops to station at Xǔchāng,
he had a Xíngtái accompany him.
Later, Wèi called it Shàngshū Dà Xíngtái,
with separately established officials.
He, along with Zuǒ Chéng Jiǎ Yí, led 5,000 officials and soldiers to garrison Yè.
Since Hàn Emperor Guāngwǔ entrusted authority to the Shàngshū,
affairs were handled by the Táigé,
referring to the Shàngshū Shěng as the Shàngshū Tái.
When Jìn Emperor Huìdì moved west to Cháng'ān,
he established a Liútái in Luòyáng
to manage affairs left behind,
hence the name Liútái.
When the Tuòbá clan established Xíngtái,
they were set up according to need
to administer the affairs of a circuit.
The Wèishū Guānshì Zhì records that among the clans that entered from within were the Sùhé clan,
later changed to the Hé clan.
Xiāng is pronounced xiāng.
Guī returned from Yè to Zhōngshān,
intending to return north.
He conscripted ten thousand laborers to build a straight road,
cutting through the Hénglíng from Wàngdū to Dài, over five hundred lǐ.
Hénglíng refers to the ridges of Héng Mountain,
located northwest of Shàngqǔyáng,
which is the Dǎomǎguān road.
The Jìnshū Dìdào Jì calls it Hóngshàngguān.
Shěn Kuò said: The northern sacred mountain, Héngshān,
is what is now called Dàmào Shān.
The old temple to the mountain was at the foot of the mountain.
After the Later Jìn,
it gradually moved inward,
and the place is now called Shénpéng.
The current temple is in Qǔyáng.
North of the temple is the Wàngyuè Pavilion;
when the weather is clear after a fresh rain,
one can see Dàmào.
The Fēihú Road is west of Dàmào.
From the Yínyězhài, one goes north out of Dǎomǎguān,
then from Shíménzi and Lìngshuǐpù,
enters between the Píngxíng and Méihuí stockades,
and reaches Dàizhōu.
However, the Dàizhōu Shěn Kuò mentioned is Yānmén.
From there one could also reach Wèi's capital Dài,
but it likely was not the straight road.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: The Qíyí River emerges east of Píngshū County,
flows northeast past Lántíng to the south,
then northeast past Shíménguān to the north,
which was the old road leading out from the ancient pass of Zhōngshān.
The Wèi Tǔdì Jì states: Nine lǐ west of Dài City is Píngshū City.
This was the ancient Dài City.
Héng is pronounced héng.
If there were disturbances east of the mountains,
he would re-establish a Xíngtái at Zhōngshān,
ordering Wèi Wáng Yí to garrison it.
He appointed Fǔjūn Dàjiāngjūn Lüèyáng Gōng Zūn as Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè,
to garrison Hékǒu in Bóhǎi.
Yòu Jiāngjūn Yīn Guó was supervising tax collection in Jìzhōu.
Hearing that Guī was about to return north,
he plotted to attack Xìndū.
Ānnán Jiāngjūn Chángsūn Sōng captured Guó
and executed him.
3 Yān Qǐlún returned to Lóngchéng.
Last year, Bǎo sent Qǐlún south to observe the situation.
"Lún"
should be
"Lún",
pronounced Lú Kūn fān.
The Yān ruler Bǎo ordered the troops to cease action.
The Prince of Liáoxī, Nóng, said to Bǎo:
"Now the capital relocation is still new,
we cannot campaign south.
We should take advantage of the assembled army to attack the Kùmòxī,
seize their oxen and horses to replenish military supplies,
further assess the actual situation,
and wait until next year to discuss it."
Bǎo followed this advice.
Jǐwèi,
they marched north.
Gēngshēn,
they crossed the Jiāoluò River.
The Jiāoluò River,
is probably the Ráolè River.
Xián said: The river is north of present-day Yíngzhōu.
During the time of Táng Tàizōng,
the Xī submitted,
and the Ráolè Dūdū Fǔ was established.
It is said
"Shè Guī went west,
going west,
means from Zhōngshān taking the Hénglíng and returning west to Yún and Dài.
Shàng,
shí zhǎng fān.
Yán pursued Bǎo and caught up with him,
Bǎo was greatly pleased,
and that day led the troops back.
4 Xīnyǒu,
the Wèi ruler Guī departed from Zhōngshān,
relocating over 100,000 officials, commoners, and various tribespeople from the six provinces east of the mountains to populate Dài.
This is the strategy of Hàn Gāodì relocating powerful families from east of the passes to populate Guānzhōng.
During the Hàn period,
Zhāngwǔ City was within the boundaries of Bóhǎi Píngshū County;
in the first year of Tàishǐ of Jìn Wǔdì,
the Zhāngwǔ Principality was established,
later becoming a commandery;
Suí abolished it,
it belonged to Yíngzhōu,
and was incorporated into Píngshū County.
The Governor of Guǎngchuān, Hè Làilú,
was bold and vigorous by nature,
Guǎngchuān County,
in the Former Hàn belonged to the Xìndū Principality,
in the Later Hàn belonged to Qīnghé Commandery,
in Jìn belonged to Bóhǎi Commandery,
later divided to form Guǎngchuān Commandery.
Shǒu,
shì yòu fān.
He attacked Fǔ,
killed him,
forced the garrison soldiers,
plundered various commanderies like Yángpíng and Dùnqiū,
crossed the river south,
and fled to Nán Yān.
The Nán Yān ruler Dé appointed Làilú as Governor of Bìngzhōu,
enfeoffing him as Prince of Guǎngníng.
5 The Xī Qín ruler Qiánguī sent Qǐfú Yìzhōu to attack Liáng's three cities of Zhīyáng, Wǔ, and Yúnwú,
and captured them;
Zhīyáng and Yúnwú,
are both ancient Hàn counties,
belonging to Jīnchéng Commandery;
Wǔ City was likely between these two counties.
Zhāng Shí separated Zhīyáng to belong to Guǎngwǔ Commandery;
Yúnwú probably remained the seat of Jīnchéng Commandery.
Liú Xù said: Táng's Lánzhōu Guǎngwǔ County,
is Hàn's Zhīyáng County;
Shànzhōu Lóngzhī County,
is Hàn's Yúnwú County.
Yúnwú,
pronounced Qián Yá.
6 The Yān ruler Bǎo returned to the Lóngchéng palace,
ordered the various armies to take up positions,
"dùn" refers to
the places where armies halt and encamp during marches.
Civil and military officers and soldiers all had their families follow the imperial carriage.
Jià,
refers to the imperial carriage,
similar to what the Hàn people called the "chéngyú".
They believed the troops were weary and weak,
Wèi had recently gained advantage,
and they could not yet oppose them,
so they should nurture the troops and watch for opportunities.
Bǎo was about to follow this,
but the Fǔjūn General Mùyú Téng said:
"The common people can share in success,
but it is difficult to plan beginnings with them.
Using the meaning of Shāng Yāng's words.
Lè,
pronounced Luò.
Your Majesty should decide alone,
seize the opportunity to advance,
and not widely gather differing opinions to thwart grand plans."
Bǎo then said:
"My decision is made,
anyone who dares remonstrate will be executed!"
In the second month,
on Yǐhài,
Bǎo went out to take up position,
leaving Shèng in charge of rear affairs.
Jǐmǎo,
the Yān army set out from Lóngchéng,
with Mùyú Téng as the vanguard,
the Minister of Works Nóng as the central army,
and Bǎo as the rear army,
each separated by one "dùn",
considering the following text mentions a continuous encampment of a hundred lǐ,
probably thirty lǐ constituted one "dùn".
On Rénwǔ,
Bǎo reached Yǐlián,
the Chángshàng Duàn Sùgǔ, Sòng Chìméi, and others, taking advantage of the troops' fear of campaigning,
thus started a rebellion.
All guard soldiers took turns on duty;
"chángshàng" means
they did not rotate.
Under the Táng official system,
Huáihuà Zhíjǐ Chángshàng,
Guīdé Zhíjǐ Chángshàng,
were all military honorary ranks,
ninth grade.
The position of Chángshàng has existed for a long time.
Shàng,
shí zhǎng fān.
Together they forced Lóng's son, the Prince of Gāoyáng Chóng, to be their leader,
killing the Prince of Lèlàng Wēi Zhòu, the Duke of Zhōngmóu Xī Duàn Yì, and various princes of the imperial clan.
The Prince of Héjiān Xī had always been on good terms with Chóng,
and Chóng protected him,
so he alone escaped.
The Yān ruler Bǎo fled with over ten horsemen to the camp of the Minister of Works Nóng.
Nóng was about to go out to welcome him,
but his attendants held his waist,
stopping him, saying:
"We should wait a little for clarity,
meaning the troops were in chaos,
like turbid water;
we should wait a bit for it to settle,
like water becoming clear,
and not go out lightly."
Nóng drew his sword intending to strike them,
then went out to see Bǎo,
and also sent a message galloping after Mùyú Téng.
Guǐwèi,
Bǎo and Nóng led troops back towards the main camp,
the main camp,
refers to Bǎo's camp.
The soldiers in Nóng's camp were also weary of campaigning,
and all discarded their weapons and fled,
employing the people on pleasant roads,
they toil without complaint;
employing the people for the sake of life,
they die without resenting the one who kills them;
violating this,
few do not fail.
Bǎo and Nóng fled back to Lóngchéng.
The Prince of Chánglè Shèng heard of the rebellion,
led troops out to meet them,
and Bǎo and Nóng barely escaped.
7 Huìjī Prince Dàozǐ, wary of the pressure from Wáng and Yīn,
because the Prince of Qiáo Shàngzhī and his younger brother Xiūzhī had talent and strategy,
drew them close as confidants.
Shàngzhī persuaded Dàozǐ, saying:
"Now the regional commanders are strong,
the prime minister's authority is light,
we should secretly establish confidants in the provinces to serve as our protective screen."
Dàozǐ followed this,
appointing his Marshal Wáng Yú as Governor of Jiāngzhōu,
commanding the military affairs of Jiāngzhōu and the four commanderies of Yùzhōu,
using him as strategic support,
day and night consulting with Shàngzhī,
watching for opportunities from all sides.
This sets the stage for Yǔ Kǎi persuading Wáng and Yīn to raise troops again.
Shuō,
shū ruì fān.
Sì,
xiāng lì fān.
8 The Wèi ruler Guī went to the Fánzhì Palace.
Fánzhì County,
belonged to Yànmén Commandery,
Wèi built a palace here.
Early in the Tiānpíng era,
Fánzhì Commandery was established,
Suí restored it as a county,
Táng placed it under Dàizhōu.
Zhì,
pronounced Zhǐ.
Guī was hunting on Báidēng Mountain.
Lì Dàoyuán said: "Now, seventeen lǐ east of Píngchéng, there is a terrace,
which is Báidēng Terrace.
South of the terrace faces a ridge,
which is Báidēng Mountain."
He said to Champion General Yú Lìdī:
"Your name suggests bravery and strength;
can you wrestle with this?"
He replied:
"Beasts are lowly, humans are noble.
If I wrestle and do not win,
would it not be a waste to kill a strong man in vain!"
So he drove it before Guī,
shot it with arrows and captured it.
Guī turned and thanked him.
The tribal chief of Xiùróng Chuān, Ěrzhū Yǔjiàn, followed Guī in attacking Jìnyáng and Zhōngshān and achieved merit.
He was appointed as a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
The area around his residence
was granted to him, with three hundred lǐ of land.
This was Northern Xiùróng.
This laid the groundwork for Ěrzhū Róng's rebellion against Wèi.
The biography of Ěrzhū Róng states: Yǔjiàn's ancestors
had for generations been tribal chiefs,
residing in Ěrzhū Chuān,
and thus took the surname.
Guī initially thought the Southern Xiùróng Chuān had fertile plains,
and wanted them to settle there.
Yǔjiàn said:
"Our family has served the state for generations,
attending closely to the ruler.
Northern Xiùróng is already within the realm,
