relatively close to the capital.
How can we move to a distant land just because of fertile or barren soil!"
Guī agreed.
Thus, Northern Xiùróng was likely near Píngchéng.
Huán,
pronounced huàn.
Qiú,
pronounced cí yóu fān.
Zhǎng,
pronounced zhī liǎng fān.
Sàn,
pronounced xī dǎn fān.
Qí,
pronounced qí jì fān;
same below.
The Róurán repeatedly invaded Wèi's borders.
Secretary of the Central Army Lǐ Xiān requested to attack them;
Guī agreed,
and they heavily defeated the Róurán and returned.
9 Yáng Guǐ appointed his Marshal Guō Wěi as the Chancellor of Xīpíng,
leading twenty thousand infantry and cavalry north to join Guō Nún.
Tūfǎ Wūgū sent his younger brother, General of Chariots and Cavalry Nùtán, with ten thousand cavalry to assist Guǐ.
Guǐ arrived at Gūzāng,
and encamped north of the city.
10 The Yān Secretary, Dùnqiū King Lán Hàn, secretly conspired with Duàn Sùgǔ and others,
leading troops to encamp east of Lóngchéng;
the defending troops in the city were few,
so Chánglè King Shèng moved the nearby residents inside the city,
obtaining over ten thousand able-bodied men,
to man the walls for defense.
Sùgǔ and his conspirators numbered only over a hundred,
the rest were coerced,
with no will to fight.
In the third month,
on Jiǎwǔ,
Sùgǔ and others were about to attack the city.
Liáoxī Huánliè King Nóng feared they could not hold,
and being lured by Lán Hàn,
at night,
secretly went out to join them,
hoping to preserve himself.
Nóng was known for wisdom and strategy,
yet he wanted to join Duàn Sùgǔ to save himself,
not knowing it would hasten his death.
It was as if heaven had taken away his discernment.
Sùgǔ and others attacked the city,
the defenders on the walls resisted fiercely,
and Sùgǔ's forces suffered hundreds of casualties.
Sùgǔ then took Nóng along the city walls,
jiàng,
as pronounced,
meaning to lead,
to coerce.
The defenders in the city relied on him for strength,
but suddenly seeing him below the walls,
they were all shocked and disheartened,
and thus fled and scattered.
Sùgǔ entered the city,
allowing his troops to kill and plunder,
leaving corpses strewn about.
Bǎo, Shèng, along with Mùyú Téng, Yú Chóng, Zhāng Zhēn, Lǐ Hàn, Zhào Ēn, and others, fled south on light cavalry.
Sùgǔ imprisoned Nóng in the palace.
Chángshàng Ājiāoluó,
Sùgǔ's chief strategist,
thought Gāoyáng King Chóng was young and weak,
and wanted to install Nóng instead.
Chóng's trusted followers Zōng Ràng, Chūlìjiān, and others heard of this.
On Dīngyǒu,
they killed Luó and Nóng.
Even if Sùgǔ had installed Nóng,
he would have inevitably died at the hands of Lán Hàn,
for the situation was already lost,
and wisdom could not be applied.
Nóng's former subordinate, Left Guard General Yǔwén Bá, fled to Liáoxī.
On Gēngzǐ,
Lán Hàn attacked Sùgǔ,
along with his followers,
and killed them all.
He deposed Chóng,
installed Crown Prince Cè,
issued a general pardon by decree,
and sent an envoy to welcome Bǎo,
meeting him at Jìchéng.
Bǎo wanted to return,
but Chánglè King Shèng and others all said:
"Hàn's loyalty or deceit is unknown.
Now, if you go alone to him,
and if Hàn has ill intentions,
it will be too late for regret.
It is better to go south to join Fànyáng King,
gather forces to take Jìzhōu;
if unsuccessful,
gather the southern forces,
and slowly return to Lóngdū.
It would not be too late."
Bǎo agreed.
Lóngchéng,
the former capital of Yān,
was thus called Lóngdū.
Mùróng Shèng's wisdom far surpassed his father's.
11 The Hú chieftain of Líshí, Hūyán Tiě, and the Hú chieftain of Xīhé, Zhāng Chóng, were unwilling to move to Dài,
gathered a crowd, and rebelled against Wèi.
Wèi's General of Distant Pacification, Yǔ Yuè, suppressed them.
12 King Guī of Wèi summoned King Yí of Wèi to assist in governance,
appointing Duke Zūn of Lüèyáng to replace him in defending Zhōngshān.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on Rénxū,
he appointed General for Subduing Barbarians Mù Chóng as Grand Commandant,
and General for Pacifying the South Chángsūn Sōng as Minister of Education.
13. The ruler of Yān, Mùróng Bǎo, passed by Yè via a side road.
The people of Yè requested him to stay,
but Bǎo refused.
He traveled south to Líyáng,
and lay in ambush west of the river.
The river water, flowing from the Zhēhài Pavilion, curved and ran northeast,
passing south of Líyáng County.
The west bank of the river was within the boundaries of Líyáng,
while the east bank was within the boundaries of Huátái.
"The Emperor received the Chancellor's memorial in the second month,
and Bǎo appointed Mùróng Dé as Minister over the Masses,
hence he was referred to as the Chancellor.
When he reached Yǐlián,
the tribal chief rebelled,
and he lost his base, coming here.
What a ruler relies on
is power.
With the masses rebelling and his kin turning against him,
his great power had already dissipated,
and he lost what he relied upon.
Mùróng Zhōng,
a cousin of Dé,
was the first to urge Dé to assume the imperial title.
Upon hearing this, Dé was displeased,
arrested Sī, and imprisoned him,
then reported the situation to the King of Southern Yān, Mùróng Dé.
Dé said to his subordinates:
"You all, for the sake of the state's grand strategy,
urged me to act as regent;
I also, because the heir emperor was wandering in exile,
(wandering,
means fleeing,
moving.)
(Exile,
means far away,
running away.)
temporarily complied with your proposal to rally the people's hearts.
Now Heaven is repenting of the calamity,
and the heir emperor has returned.
I shall prepare the imperial carriage to welcome him,
confess my faults at the traveling palace,
how about that?"
Wherever the Son of Heaven travels, there is a traveling palace,

with the abundance of the Great and Small Yù Valleys,
hence this is said.
Fù,
pronounced Fúyòu;
same below.
His military discipline is lax,
easy to defeat.”
Then he advanced to attack Jī,
greatly defeating him.
Jī retreated and stationed at Lóngzhī Fort.
The Táng dynasty’s Shàn Province had Lóngzhī County.
Liú Xù said: Lóngzhī,
was the land of Yǔnyá County in Hàn times.
At this time, it should have been within Xīpíng’s borders.
He captured it,
and Jī fled alone on horseback to Jiāohé.
Jiāohé,
was Tǔyùhún territory,
Lǚ Guāng established it as a commandery,
the Suí and Táng dynasty’s Kuò Province was this land.
Jiāo,
pronounced Jiānyáo.
Water swirling back is called jiāo.
This commandery was likely established at a bend of the Táo River.
Dù Yòu said: Jiāohé City is at Hèlán Mountain in Dáhuà County, Kuò Province.
Liú Xù said: Kuò Province,
Suí dynasty’s Jiāohé Commandery,
administered Guǎngwēi County,
which was the land of the Shāodāng Qiāng in Later Hàn,
Former Liáng established Huánghé Commandery,
Later Wèi established Shíchéng Commandery,
Emperor Fèi established Huàlóng County due to Huàlóng Valley within the county,
Later Zhōu established Kuò Province,
in the first year of Tiānbǎo era of Táng,
changed to Guǎngwēi County,
under its jurisdiction was Dáhuà County.
The Tǔhún Jiāohé City,
is 120 lǐ west of the county.
Dù Yòu said: Jiāohé City,
was built by Tǔyùhún Āchái.
He appointed Tián Xuánmíng as Nèishǐ of Xīpíng.
Grand Administrator of Lèdū Tián Yáo,
Lèdū,
annotation already seen in the 26th scroll, first year of Hàn Xuāndì’s Shénjué era.
Wǔdài Zhì: Huánshuǐ County of Xīpíng Commandery,
Later Zhōu established Lèdū Commandery.
Observing this,
then the Lǚ clan had already established the commandery.
Dù Yòu said: Huánshuǐ is also called Lèdū River,
administered by Táng’s Shàn Province.
Lè,
pronounced Luò.
Grand Administrator of Jiāohé Wáng Zhì all surrendered with their commanderies,
and tens of thousands of Qiāng and Hú households south of the range submitted to Wūgū.
30. The King of Xīqín, Qiánguī, sent the Governor of Qín Province Yìzhōu, General Wǔwèi Mù Wù,
“Mù Wù,”
in the Jìnshū Zàijì written as
“Mùróng Wù.”
Mù Wù was likely also of the Qǐfú clan,
the Zàijì is mistaken.
31. Winter,
tenth month,
Guǐyǒu day,
Yān ministers again offered the imperial title,
Bǐngzǐ day,
King Chánglè Shèng began to ascend the emperor’s throne,
issued a great amnesty,
honored Empress Duàn as Empress Dowager,
and Grand Empress Dīng as Empress Xiànzhuāng.
Initially,
when Lán Hàn controlled the state,
Shèng followed the Yān ruler Bǎo in exile,
and Lán served Empress Dīng with increasing diligence.
After Hàn was executed,
Shèng, due to being implicated,
wanted to kill her;
Empress Dīng, due to her merit in preserving and protecting,
firmly argued for her,
and she was spared,
but ultimately was not made empress.
32. Great amnesty.
33. Yīn Zhòngkān received the imperial edict,
and was greatly enraged.
It was the edict demoting him to Guǎngzhōu.
Huán Xuán and others were pleased with the court's order,
and wished to accept it,
but hesitated and could not decide.
Zhòngkān heard of this,
and hurriedly returned south from Wúhú.
He sent an envoy to admonish the soldiers at Càizhōu, saying:
"If you do not each disperse and return home,
when I reach Jiānglíng,
I will exterminate all your families."
The subordinate general under Yáng Quánqī, Liú Xì, led two thousand men and returned first.
Xuán and the others were greatly frightened,
and in disarray retreated westward.
They pursued Zhòngkān to Xúnyáng,
and caught up with him.
Since Zhòngkān had lost his position,
he relied on Xuán and the others for support.
Xuán and the others also depended on Zhòngkān's troops.
Although inwardly they were suspicious and obstructive toward each other,
the situation compelled them to unite.
Therefore, they exchanged sons and younger brothers as hostages.
On the rénwǔ day,
they swore an alliance at Xúnyáng.
They all refused to accept the court's orders.
Jointly they submitted a memorial pleading Wáng Gōng's case,
requesting the execution of Liú Láozhī and Qiáo Wáng Shàngzhī.
They also appealed that Zhòngkān was innocent,
and had been unjustly demoted.
The court was deeply afraid of them,
and both inside and outside there was turmoil.
Therefore, they again dismissed Huán Xiū,
and returned Jīngzhōu to Zhòngkān.
They issued a gracious edict to console and instruct him,
seeking reconciliation.
Zhòngkān and the others then accepted the edict.
The Imperial Censor Zhōngchéng Jiǎng Jì impeached Huán Xiū, accusing him of acting solely for his own interests,
misleading the court.
He said that dividing Jiāng and Yōng to grant to Huán Xuán and Yáng Quánqī,
was Xiū taking Jīngzhōu for himself.
Impeach,
pronounced hù gài fān,
also hù dé fān.
Initially,
when Huán Xuán was in Jīngzhōu,
his actions were arrogant and unrestrained.
Zhòngkān's close associates all urged Zhòngkān to kill him,
but Zhòngkān would not listen.
When they were at Xúnyáng,
relying on his reputation and status—
reputation,
meaning prestige and influence;
status,
meaning family background—
Xuán became even more arrogant and haughty.
Yáng Quánqī was a proud and fierce man.
Xuán often treated him as a lowly scholar,
which Quánqī deeply resented.
He secretly advised Zhòngkān that Xuán would ultimately become a threat,
and requested to ambush him at the altar site.
Zhòngkān feared the bravery and strength of Quánqī and his brothers.
He worried that if Xuán were killed,
they could no longer be controlled,
so he strictly forbade it.
Thereupon, each returned to his own garrison.
Xuán also knew of Quánqī's plot,
and secretly harbored the intention to eliminate Quánqī,
laying the groundwork for Xuán later killing Yīn and Yáng.
He appointed Biàn Fànzhī, the Tàishǒu of Shǐ'ān from Jìyīn, as his Chángshǐ to serve as his chief strategist.
In the first year of the Gānlù era of Sūn Hào of Wú,
the southern part of Línglíng Commandery was separated to establish Shǐ'ān Commandery,
belonging to Guǎngzhōu.
During the reign of Emperor Chéng of Jìn, it was transferred to Jīngzhōu.
In Suí and Táng times, it was part of Guìzhōu.
Xià,
pronounced hù yǎ fān.
Jì,
pronounced zǐ lǐ fān.
The imperial edict alone did not pardon Yǔ Kǎi.
Xuán appointed Kǎi as the Tàishǒu of Wǔchāng.
Initially,
Xī Huī was resisting the western armies for the court.
Before Xuán obtained Jiāngzhōu,
he wanted to seize Huī's Yōngzhōu,
and appoint Huī to Guǎngzhōu.
Huī heard of this,
and was afraid.
He consulted his followers,
who all said:
"If Yáng Quánqī comes,
who would not exert all effort?
But if Huán Xuán comes,
I fear it would be difficult to oppose him."
The Huán clan had long resided in Xīchǔ,
hence the people feared them.
Therefore, he plotted with Lǘqiū Xiàn to raise troops and resist.
Lǘqiū Xiàn was then the Tàishǒu of Nányáng,
a subordinate of Yōngzhōu.
They spread word that Xuán was coming to enter Miǎn,
with Quánqī as the vanguard.
Huī's followers believed it,
and at the mere rumor, all scattered.
Huī requested to surrender.
Quánqī entered the headquarters,
executed Lǘqiū Xiàn,
and released Huī to return to the capital.
When he reached Yángkǒu,
Yīn Zhòngkān secretly had someone kill him,
along with his four sons,
claiming they were killed by bandits.
34. The Western Qín Qǐfú Yìzhōu fought with Tǔyùhún King Shìpí at Dùzhōu Chuān.
Dùzhōu Chuān
is west of Lónghé, beyond the Líntáo frontier.
Tǔ,
pronounced with the entering tone of tūn.
Gǔ,
pronounced yù.
He fled and defended Báilán Shān.
He sent his son Dàngqǐ as a hostage to Western Qín to request peace.
The Western Qín King Qiánguī married a clanswoman to him.
35. The Liáng Jiànwǔ General Lǐ Luán surrendered Xīngchéng to Tūfǎ Wūgū.
Xīngchéng is east of Lóngzhī Fort, southwest of Yúnwú County.
36. In the eleventh month,
Lángyá Wáng Déwén was appointed as General of the Guards, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
The Zhēnglǔ General Yuán Xiǎn was appointed as Zhōng Lǐngjūn.
The Lǐngjūn General Wáng Yǎ was appointed as Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè.
37. On the xīnhài day,
the Wèi King Guī ordered the Shàngshū Lìbù Láng Dèng Yuān to establish the official system,
harmonize musical tones and pitch-pipes,
and the Yícáo Láng Dǒng Mì from Qīnghé to formulate rituals and ceremonies.
The Sāngōng Láng Wáng Dé established laws and statutes.
The Lìbù Láng, Yícáo Láng, and Sāngōng Láng
were all positions established by Cáo Wèi.
The Lìbù Shàngshū Cuī Hóng oversaw and finalized them,
making them the permanent model.
Yuān
was the grandson of Dèng Qiāng.
Dèng Qiāng
was a famous general of Fú Qín.
38. Yáng Guǐ and Wáng Qǐjī led several thousand households and submitted themselves to the Western Píng King Wūgū.
When the ruler of Yān, Mùróng Bǎo, arrived at Líyáng,
(the matter is recorded in the previous volume, last year).
Mùróng Hé did not comply.
Lǐ Biàn was afraid,
so he secretly led the Jìn army to Guǎnchéng,
(this matter is also recorded in the previous volume, last year).
Afterward, Mùróng Dé did not emerge,
and Biàn grew increasingly uneasy.
When Dé went to suppress Fú Guǎng,
Biàn again urged Hé to rebel,
but Hé did not comply.
Biàn then killed Hé
and surrendered Huátái to Wèi.
The Wèi traveling secretariat minister Hé Bá was in Yè,
and he led light cavalry from Yè to rush there.
Upon arrival,
Biàn regretted his decision
and closed the gates to resist and defend.
Bá sent the secretary-lang Dèng Huī to persuade him,
(Dèng Huī was a secretary-lang of the Wèi Yè secretariat).
(To persuade,
shuì, read as shuō).
Bá confiscated all of Dé's palace personnel and treasury stores.
Dé sent troops to attack Bá,
but Bá counterattacked
and defeated them,
also defeating Dé's general, the Prince of Guìyáng, Mùróng Zhèn,
capturing over a thousand people.
Many people of Chén and Yǐng submitted to Wèi.
(Chén and Yǐng refer to Chén commandery and Yǐngchuān).
The Southern Yān right guard general Mùróng Yún beheaded Lǐ Biàn
and led over twenty thousand officers, soldiers, and their families out of Huátái to join Dé.
Dé wanted to attack Huátái.
Hán Fàn said:
"Previously, Wèi was the guest,
and we were the hosts;
now we are the guests,
and Wèi are the hosts.
People's hearts are fearful and alarmed,
we cannot fight again.
(Again,
fù, read as fù).
We should first establish a foundation,
then plan for further advances."
Without Hán Fàn's words,
if Dé had attacked Huátái,
he would certainly have met defeat and ruin;
indeed, one need not wait until the time of Mùróng Chāo for that.
"Péngchéng is the old capital of Chǔ.
(Xiàng Yǔ made Péngchéng his capital, hence the saying).
The Prince of Běidì, Mùróng Zhōng, and others all urged Dé to attack Huátái.
The secretary Pān Cōng said:
"Huátái is a place open in all directions.
(Huátái controls the vital crossing of the Yellow River.
When Wèi crosses the river from the north heading south toward Jìn,
coming from Qīngshuǐ into the Yellow River,
or Qín follows the Wèi down the Yellow River,
all converge at Huátái.
Moreover, the city has no mountains or hills to rely on nearby;
chariots, cavalry, and naval forces can all maneuver freely.
Therefore it is called a place open in all directions).
To the south is Jìn,
to the west is Qín;
occupying it, one would not have a single day of peace.
Péngchéng has vast land and sparse population,
flat and without strategic barriers,
and it is an old garrison of Jìn,
not easily taken.
Furthermore, it is close to the Jiāng and Huái rivers;
in summer and autumn there is much water.
Fighting from boats
is the strength of Wú
and our weakness.
Qīngzhōu has two thousand lǐ of fertile fields,
over a hundred thousand elite troops,
to the left it has the riches of the sea,
to the right it has the security of mountains and rivers.
(The city of Guǎnggù was built by Cáo Yí;
the terrain is rugged and steep,
sufficient to be an imperial capital).
The heroes of Sān Qí
have long desired to find an enlightened ruler under whom to achieve merit.
Pìlǘ Hún was formerly a minister of Yān.
(In the nineteenth year of Xiàowǔ's Tàiyuán era,
Pìlǘ Hún was defeated by Mùróng Nóng
and subsequently became a minister of Yān).
If our great army follows closely behind,
should they not submit,
taking them will be like picking up mustard seeds.
Annex the weak, attack the benighted,
seize the disordered, subdue the perishing—
since the time of the Three Dynasties, Zhònghuǐ already had these words.
When the Master compiled the Documents,
he did not delete them.
Later people, clinging to antiquity,
speak exclusively of the armies of a true king,
acting with benevolence and righteousness.
One can take Duke Xiāng of Sòng as a warning.
(To persuade,
shuì, read as shuō).
Then close the passes, nurture your strength,
and wait for an opportunity to act.
This is Your Majesty's Guānzhōng and Hénèi."
(Using Xún Yù's words to persuade Cáo Cāo).
(To wait for an opportunity,
sì, read as sì).
The Buddhist monk Zhú Lǎng was always skilled in divination and prognostication.
(Zhú is the secular surname of Lǎng).
Lǎng said:
"Respectfully examining the three strategies,
Secretary Pān's proposal
is speech that will revive the state.
Moreover, at the beginning of this year,
a comet arose at Kuí and Lóu,
sweeping Xū and Wēi.
(A comet is an omen of removing the old and establishing the new.
Kuí and Lóu correspond to Lǔ,
Xū and Wēi correspond to Qí.
According to the Jìn Astronomical Treatise: Kuí, Lóu, and Wèi correspond to Lǔ and Xúzhōu.
Xū and Wēi correspond to Qí and Qīngzhōu.
Comet,
huì, read as suì,
also xuán ruì,
also xú zuì).
Pacify and inspect Lángyá,
and by autumn head north to patrol the Qí lands—
this is the way of Heaven."
Dé further secretly inquired about the years and generations.
Lǎng divined using the Zhōu Yì and said:
"Yān will decline in gēngxū.
The years will be one cycle,
the generations will reach your son."
Later, Yān perished in the sixth year of Yìxī,
the year being Shàngzhāng Yānmào.
(Shàngzhāng is gēng;
Yānmào is xū).
Dé then led his army south,
and the various northern border commanderies and counties of Yǎnzhōu all surrendered to him.
Dé appointed governors and magistrates to pacify them
and forbade soldiers from plundering.
The common people were greatly pleased,
with oxen and wine lining the roads.
On the 13th, bǐngzǐ,
the Wèi ruler Tuòbá Guī sent the Jianyi general Yǔ Zhēn and the Yueqi colonel Xī Jīn to attack the three tribes of Kùdí, Yòulián, and Hóumòchén,
defeating them all.
Later, the surnames Kùdí and Hóumòchén both became noble and prominent,
while the lineage of Yòulián declined.
They established garrisons and returned.
On the 14th, jǐmǎo,
(the Jìn court) posthumously honored the emperor's birth mother, Lady Chén, as Empress Dowager Dé.
In summer,
the fourth month,
the Xiānbēi Diéjué Hénèi led five thousand households to surrender to Western Qín.
The Western Qín ruler Qīfú Gānguī appointed Hénèi as the Diéjué commander-in-chief
and gave him a clanswoman as wife.
(Diéjué is also a Xiānbēi tribe;
Hénèi is his name.
Jué,
read as jué.
To give as wife,
qī, read as qì).
On the 16th, jiǎwǔ,
Yān proclaimed a great amnesty.
Huìjī Prince Sīmǎ Dàozǐ was ill
and moreover was drunk every day without fail.
His heir, Yuánxiǎn, knowing that the court's regard for him was fading,
then hinted to the court to relieve Dàozǐ of his posts as Minister over the Masses and Governor of Yángzhōu.
On yǐwèi,
Yuánxiǎn was appointed Governor of Yángzhōu.
When Dàozǐ sobered up and learned of it,
he was furious
but could do nothing about it.
Yuánxiǎn took the Lújiāng Grand Administrator, Huìjī's Zhāng Fǎshùn, as his chief strategist,
extensively promoting and establishing his own clique and relatives,
and all the court nobles feared and served him.
(This sets the stage for Yuánxiǎn and Zhāng Fǎshùn both being executed later).
The Yān cavalier attendant-in-ordinary Yú Chāo and left general Gāo Hé, among others, were implicated in a plot to rebel
and were executed.
The Liang Crown Prince Shào and the Duke of Tàiyuán Zuǎn led troops to attack Northern Liáng.
Among the four commanderies west of the Yellow River,
Zhāngyè is the northernmost,
hence it was called Northern Liáng.
The character "將"
is pronounced with the falling tone.
Wūgū dispatched the General of Agile Cavalry Lìlùgū and Yáng Guǐ to rescue it.
Yè was about to engage in battle,
when Jǔqú Méngxùn advised:
"Yáng Guǐ relies on the strength of the Xiānbēi,
harboring ambitions to spy and covet.
Tūfǎ
was originally of Xiānbēi stock.
The character "沮"
is pronounced with the rising tone.
They have placed their troops in a death ground,
making them invincible.
If we do not fight now, we will have the security of Mount Tài;
if we fight, we will face the peril of piled eggs."
Yè followed his advice,
holding his troops and not engaging in battle.
Shào and Zuǎn led their troops back.
In the sixth month,
Wūgū appointed Lìlùgū as the Governor of Liáng Province,
stationing him in Xīpíng,
and summoned the General of Chariots and Cavalry Rùtán to enter and oversee the affairs of the prefecture and state.
The heir of Kuàijī, Yuánxiǎn, considered himself young,
and did not wish to immediately assume heavy responsibilities;
on the Wùzǐ day,
he appointed the Prince of Lángyá Déwén as Minister over the Masses.
The former Governor of Héjiān of Wèi,
Lú Pǔ, led his private army of several thousand households to seek provisions in Yúyáng,
and subsequently occupied several commanderies.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Jǐwèi day,
the Yàn ruler Shèng sent an envoy to appoint Pǔ as the Governor of Yōu Province.
This sets the stage for the subsequent events where Wèi dismissed Zhāng Gǔn and captured Lú Pǔ.
The character "帥"
is read as "率".
The character "使"
is pronounced with the departing tone.
On the Xīnyǒu day,
the Yàn ruler Shèng issued an edict stating:
"According to the Legal Precedents Statute,
if dukes and marquises commit crimes,
they may redeem themselves with gold and silk.
During the Warring States period,
Marquis Wén of Wèi's teacher Lǐ Kuī compiled and arranged the laws of various states,
composing the Canon of Laws.
He believed that in the governance of a true king,
nothing is more urgent than dealing with robbers and bandits.
Robbers and bandits must be investigated and captured,
hence he wrote the chapters on 'Nets' and 'Arrests'.
For offenses such as frivolous cunning, scaling city walls, gambling, borrowing under false pretenses, lack of integrity, licentious extravagance, and exceeding regulations,
he composed a miscellaneous chapter.
He also added provisions for increasing or decreasing penalties according to the law.
Thus, the six chapters he wrote
all pertained to the system of crimes and punishments.
Hàn's Xiāo Hé added the statutes on 'Raising [Armies]', 'Stables', and 'Households',
making a total of nine chapters.
Wèi's Chén Qún and others adopted the Hàn laws,
formulating a new code of eighteen chapters.
They collected examples of crimes into the 'Designation of Penalties',
placing it at the head of the code.
The 'Law on Robbery' included robbery, intimidation, and buying and selling people,
while the statutes included hostage-taking,
none of which were strictly robbery matters,
so they were separated to form the 'Law on Robbery'.
The 'Law on Banditry' included deception, fraud, exceeding fief boundaries, and forging imperial orders;
the 'Law on Imprisonment' included fraud and matters of life and death;
'Ordinance Bǐng' included falsely claiming exemption or remission;
as the categories were numerous,
they were separated to form the 'Law on Fraud'.
The 'Law on Banditry' included cutting down trees,
killing or injuring people, livestock, and losing official seals;
the 'Law on Metal and Cloth' included damaging or losing government property;
these were separated to form the 'Law on Damage and Loss'.
The 'Law on Imprisonment' included accusation and investigation, and retrial;
the 'Law on Stations' included reporting rebellion and arrest and reception;
the statutes included submitting petitions at the palace gate;
these were separated to form the 'Law on Accusation and Investigation'.
The 'Law on Imprisonment' contained methods for detaining prisoners, interrogating cases, and adjudicating cases;
the 'Law on Raising [Armies]' contained matters of submitting cases;
the statutes included investigating matters and reporting judgments;
these should be made into a separate chapter,
thus they were separated to form the 'Law on Detention, Interrogation, and Adjudication'.
The 'Law on Robbery' included accepting bribes from those under one's supervision and accepting wealth to pervert justice;
the 'Miscellaneous Law' included borrowing under false pretenses and lack of integrity;
'Ordinance Yǐ' included extorting money from people;
the statutes included envoys investigating bribes;
as these matters were similar,
they were separated to form the 'Law on Petitions and Bribes'.
The 'Law on Robbery' included sudden insults and strong bandits;
the 'Law on Raising [Armies]' included initiating corvée labor;
the 'Detailed Law' included selling out;
the statutes included undertaking construction of buildings;
these were separated to form the 'Law on Raising [Armies] and Initiating [Corvée]'.
The 'Law on Raising [Armies]' included failure to perform corvée and delay;
the 'Law on Banditry' included failure to prepare military supplies;
the 'Law on Stations' included military shortages and failure to raise [supplies], and the old statutes included not diligently upholding the law and not obeying imperial edicts;
these were implemented during the Hàn dynasty,
but should no longer be considered law,
so a separate 'Law on Delay' was created.
The Qín era originally had statutes on stations, relay carriages, auxiliary carriages, and kitchens;
later, the Hàn only established mounted relays,
without carriages or horses,
yet the law still contained these provisions,
making them empty stipulations,
so the 'Law on Stations' was abolished,
taking the usable parts that conformed to the statutes to form the 'Ordinance on Postal Relays'.

The 'Law on Accusation and Investigation' included reporting emergencies, ordinances on reporting urgent alarming matters, and the 'Law on Raising [Armies]' included beacon fires and statutory ordinances;
these were made into the 'Law on Alarming Matters'.
The 'Law on Robbery' included returning stolen goods to their owners;
the 'Law on Metal and Cloth' included fines, redemption payments, debts, and pricing with pure gold;
the statutes included offenses of average value for sitting on illicit goods;
these were made into the 'Law on Compensation for Stolen Goods'.
In the initial formulation of the laws,
there were no provisions for exemption from punishment.
Zhāng Tāng and Zhào Yǔ began creating precedents for supervisors and department heads who knowingly allowed offenses.
Those who knew but deliberately did not report or investigate
were sentenced to redemption;
those who did not see or know were not punished.
The statutes on exemption from punishment became numerous,
so it was appropriate to consolidate them into a general example of exemption,
to reduce statutory text,
hence it was revised to become the 'Law on Exemption from Punishment'.
At the beginning of the Jìn dynasty, Jiǎ Chōng determined the laws,
adding eleven chapters to the Hàn's nine chapters,
changing the old laws to 'Designation of Penalties' and 'Legal Precedents',
distinguishing the 'Law on Imprisonment' into 'Accusation and Investigation', 'Detention and Interrogation', and 'Adjudication',
dividing the 'Law on Robbery' into 'Petitions and Bribes', 'Fraud', 'Water and Fire', and 'Damage and Loss',
creating 'Palace Guards and Prohibitions' and 'Violation of Regulations' according to the nature of matters,
compiling the 'Offices of Zhōu' into the 'Law on Feudal Lords',
making a total of twenty chapters.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: In ancient times, redemption of crimes all used copper;
the Hàn began to use gold instead,
but reduced the weight,
making it equivalent in value to copper.
During the Hàn and later Wèi dynasties,
redemption of crimes all used gold.
Later, Wèi found gold difficult to obtain,
so one liǎng of gold
was exchanged for ten bolts of silk.
Now the law has again reverted to the ancient practice of redeeming with copper.
This is quite meaningless.
From now on, all shall be ordered to achieve merit to redeem themselves,
and shall no longer submit gold and silk."
The Chancellor of Western Qín, the Duke Xuān of Nánchuān, Chūlián Qǐdū, died.
Nánchuān
is a place name.
Xuān
is his posthumous title.
The Qín Duke of Qí, Chóng, and the General Who Guards the East, Yáng Fósōng, invaded Luòyáng.
The Governor of Hénán, Xīn Gōngjìng of Lǒngxī, defended the city and held firm.
The Governor of Yōng Province, Yáng Quánqī, sent an envoy to seek help from the Prince of Chángshān of Wèi, Zūn.
The Wèi ruler Guī appointed the Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Zhāng Jì of Xīhé as Zūn's Assistant Department Head to respond.
Quánqī asked Jì:
"When Wèi attacked Zhōngshān,
how many soldiers were there?"
Jì said:
"Over four hundred thousand."
This event is recorded in the 108th scroll, the 21st year of the Xiàowǔ era of Tàiyuán.
"With Wèi's strength,
a small Qiāng tribe is not worth destroying.
Moreover, Jìn and Wèi
were originally one family,
referring to the time when Yīlú rescued Liú Kūn.
In righteousness, there is nothing to hide.
Here, our troops are weak and provisions scarce;
the rescue of Luòyáng
depends solely on Wèi.
If it is preserved,
there will certainly be generous repayment;
if it is not held,
rather than letting the Qiāng obtain it,
it would be better to let Wèi obtain it."
As for someone like Yáng Quánqī,
how could he be entrusted with defending the borders!
In the eighth month,
Guī sent the Grand Commandant Mù Chóng with sixty thousand cavalry to rescue them.
The Yàn Governor of Liáoxī, Lǐ Lǎng, had been in the commandery for ten years,
and his authority extended throughout the region.
The Yàn Liáoxī commandery seat was at Lìngzhī.
He repeatedly refused summons to court.
As his family was in Lóngchéng,
he did not dare to openly rebel,
but secretly summoned Wèi troops,
promising to surrender the commandery to Wèi;
he sent an envoy galloping to Lóngchéng,
exaggerating the enemy's strength.
Shèng said:
"This is certainly deceit."
He summoned the envoy for interrogation,
and indeed there was no such fact.
Shèng exterminated Lǎng's entire clan;
on the Dīngyǒu day,
he dispatched the General Who Supports the State, Lǐ Hàn, to attack him.
In the winter of the 31st year,
in the tenth month,
on the jiǎwǔ day,
Yān’s Central Guard General Wèi Shuāng was found guilty of a crime,
and was ordered to commit suicide.
Lǐ Hàn returned,
and upon hearing of Shuāng’s death,
he became fearful,
abandoned his army, and fled.
When he reached Bǎn Xíng,
he turned back and surrendered himself to accept punishment.
The ruler of Yān, Shèng, restored his noble rank and position,
and said to his Attendant-in-Chief Sūn Qíng:
“Hàn, as a general, abandoned his army;
his crime is unpardonable.
However, in the past, when the late emperor was in distress,
and flesh and blood turned against each other,
and the high officials lost their integrity,
only Hàn, as a eunuch, remained loyal and diligent without slackening,
consistent from beginning to end.
The events are recorded in the second year of the previous scroll.
In the 32nd year, Xīn Gōngjìng firmly defended [the city] for over a hundred days.
When the Wèi reinforcements had not yet arrived,
the Qín army captured Luòyáng,
and captured Gōngjìng.
When Gōngjìng was brought before the Qín king Xīng,
he did not bow,
and said:
“I will not be a subject of the Qiāng bandits!”
Xīng imprisoned him,
but Gōngjìng escaped and returned.
North of the Huái and Hàn rivers,
many cities requested to surrender,
and sent hostages to Qín.
In the 33rd year, the ruler of Wèi, Guī, appointed Mù Chóng as the Inspector of Yùzhōu,
and stationed him at Yěwáng.
After Qín had captured Luòyáng,
Wèi established a garrison at Yěwáng,
to guard against their crossing the river and invading.
In the 34th year, Yuán Xiǎn, the heir of Kuàijī,
was by nature harsh and severe,
arbitrarily deciding life and death.
He conscripted men from the eastern commanderies who had been slaves and were made into clients,
and those who were slave households,
or those who had committed crimes and were confiscated as government slaves;

from the high officials down to the ninth-rank officials, as well as descendants of the imperial clan, state guests, former worthies, and scholar-officials’ sons and grandsons who had taken shelter as clients,
this is what is called “exempting slaves to become clients.”
He relocated them to the capital,
to fill military service obligations,
causing great turmoil and suffering in the eastern regions.
Sūn Ēn took advantage of the popular unrest,
and led his followers from the sea islands to kill the magistrate of Shàngyú.
Shàngyú County,
since the Hàn dynasty, has belonged to Kuàijī Commandery,
located over a hundred lǐ northwest of the commandery seat.
“Shuài”
is read as “lǜ.”
The Administrator of Kuàijī, Wáng Níngzhī,
was the son of Xīzhī,
and his family had long followed the Way of the Celestial Masters,
the Way of the Celestial Masters,
which is the tradition transmitted by Zhāng Dàolíng.
“Kuài”
is pronounced “guì.”
He also made no military preparations,
spending his days in the Daoist chamber kneeling and chanting prayers.
The Daoist chamber
is a room for Daoist worship.
“Qǐ”
is pronounced “qǐ.”
Níngzhī said:
“I have already petitioned the Great Dao,
and borrowed ghost soldiers to guard all the strategic passes,
each numbering tens of thousands,
so there is no need to worry about the bandits.”
When Ēn gradually drew near,
he then allowed troops to be sent out,
but Ēn had already reached the commandery seat.
On the jiǎyín day,
Ēn captured Kuàijī,
and Níngzhī fled,
but Ēn captured and killed him,
along with all his sons.
Níngzhī’s wife, Xiè Dàoyùn,
the daughter of Yì,
upon hearing that the bandits had arrived,
remained calm and composed,
ordered her maids to carry her in a sedan chair,
drew her sword, and went out the door,
personally killing several people,
before being captured.
The Administrator of Wúguó, Huán Qiān; the Administrator of Línhǎi, Xīn Qín Wáng Chóng;
the Jìn Shū records
“Xīn Cài Wáng Chóng.”
Chóng
was the great-grandson of Rǔnán Wáng Yòu,
and since his grandfather’s time,
had inherited the fief of Xīn Cài.
“Qín”
should be
“Cài.”
At this time, Xiè Zhēn of Kuàijī, Lù Huái of Wú Commandery, Qiū Wāng of Wúxīng,
Xǔ Yǔnzhī of Yìxīng, Zhōu Zhòu of Línhǎi, Zhāng Yǒng of Yǒngjiā, and others from eight commanderies including Dōngyáng and Xīn’ān,
rose up in arms simultaneously,
killing local officials to respond to Ēn.
Within ten days,
their numbers reached several hundred thousand.

The Administrator of Wúxīng, Xiè Miǎo; the Administrator of Yǒngjiā, Sīmǎ Yì; Duke Gù Yìn of Jiāxīng; Duke Xiè Mínghuì of Nánkāng; the Court Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, Xiè Chōng; Zhāng Kūn; and the Gentleman of the Central Secretariat, Kǒng Dào, were all killed by Ēn’s followers.
Miǎo and Chōng
were both nephews of Ān.
At that time, the Sān Wú region had enjoyed peace for a long time,
and the people were unaccustomed to warfare,
so the troops of the commanderies and counties all fled at the mere rumor of the enemy.
Ēn occupied Kuàijī,
proclaimed himself General Who Conquers the East,
forced prominent people to serve as his officials,
and called his followers
“Immortal People.”
Those among the people who did not join him
were killed, including infants and children,
resulting in seven or eight out of ten deaths.
He pickled the magistrates of the counties to feed to their wives and children,
and those who refused to eat
were dismembered.
Dismemberment
means cutting apart the limbs and joints,
like dissecting an ox.
He burned towns and houses,
set fire to granaries and storehouses,
felled trees,
and filled in wells.
Kǒng Ānguó said: “Kān”
means to chop down trees;
“yīn”
means to block up.
Women with infants who could not leave
threw them into the water,
saying:
“Congratulations on ascending to the immortal hall ahead of me;
I will follow you later.”
Ēn submitted a memorial listing the crimes of Sīmǎ Dàozǐ, the Prince of Kuàijī, and his heir Yuán Xiǎn,
and requested their execution.
Since the emperor’s accession to the throne,
internal and external affairs had been in discord,
with the area south of Shítóu all controlled by Jīng and Jiāng,
and the area west of it monopolized by Yùzhōu.
The river flows from the borders of Jīng and Jiāng commanderies into the territory of Yángzhōu,
all flowing northeast;
Lìyáng is on the west bank of the river,
and Jiànkāng is on the east bank.
Sūn Quán built Shítóu City,
likely to control the strategic crossing of the river.
The court’s governance
extended only to the Sān Wú region.
When Sūn Ēn rebelled,
all eight commanderies fell to Ēn.
The eight commanderies are: Kuàijī, Línhǎi, Yǒngjiā, Dōngyáng, Xīn’ān, Wú, Wúxīng, and Yìxīng.
Bandits rose up everywhere,
and Ēn’s followers also had agents hidden in Jiànkāng,
causing people to feel fearful and anxious,
constantly worried about sudden uprisings.
As a result, internal and external security was tightened.
Dàozǐ was granted the Yellow Axe,
and Yuán Xiǎn was appointed General of the Central Army.
The Inspector of Xúzhōu, Xiè Yǎn, was ordered to concurrently oversee military affairs in Wúxīng and Yìxīng to suppress Ēn;
Liú Láozhī also dispatched troops to suppress Ēn,
submitting a memorial and immediately setting out.
Láozhī was stationed at Jīngkǒu.
In the 35th year, Western Qín appointed Xīn Jìng, the Administrator of Jīnchéng, as Right Chancellor.
In the twelfth month,
on the jiǎwǔ day,
Gāo Hú, the Administrator of Yān Commandery of Yān, led three thousand households to surrender to Wèi.
Hú
was the son of Tài.
This sets the stage for Gāo Huān’s later usurpation of Wèi.
“Xiáng”
is pronounced “xiáng.”
On the bǐngwǔ day,
the ruler of Yān, Shèng, enfeoffed his younger brother Yuān as the Duke of Zhāngwǔ,
Qián as the Duke of Bólíng,
and his son Dìng as the Duke of Liáoxī.
On the dīngwèi day,
the dowager of Yān, Lady Duàn, passed away,
and was posthumously honored as Empress Huìdé.
In the 39th year, Xiè Yǎn attacked and killed Xǔ Yǔnzhī,
welcomed Wèi Yǐn back to the commandery,
advanced to attack Qiū Wāng,
defeated him,
and together with Liú Láozhī, fought their way forward,
triumphing wherever they went.
Yǎn remained stationed at Wúchéng,
Wúchéng County,
during the Former Hàn belonged to Kuàijī Commandery,
during the Later Hàn belonged to Wú Commandery,
and since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties, has belonged to Wúxīng Commandery.
They advanced to the Zhèjiāng River.
An edict appointed Láozhī as the Commander of Military Affairs of Wú Commandery.
In the beginning,
Liú Yù of Péngchéng,
was born and his mother died,
his father Liú Qiáo lived as a sojourner in Jīngkǒu,
the family was poor,
and he was about to abandon him.
The mother of Liú Huáijìng from the same commandery,
was Liú Yù's maternal aunt,
having given birth to Huáijìng not yet a full year,
ran to save him,
stopped nursing Huáijìng and nursed Yù instead.
When he grew up,
he was brave, strong, and had great ambition.
He barely knew characters,
made a living by selling shoes,
liked gambling,
and was despised by the local community.
When Liú Láozhī attacked Sūn Ēn,
he recruited Yù to join the military staff,
according to the systems of Jìn and Sòng,
staff officers not assigned to a specific bureau had no fixed quota.
They encountered several thousand bandits,
and immediately engaged them,
his followers all died,
and Yù fell down the riverbank.
The bandits approached the bank wanting to descend,
Yù vigorously wielded a long sword, looking up and hacking, killing several men,
then managed to climb up the bank,
still shouting loudly and chasing them,
the bandits all fled,
Yù killed and wounded many.
Liú Jìngxuān wondered why Yù had not returned for so long,
led troops to search for him,
saw Yù alone driving several thousand men,
they all sighed in admiration.
Thereupon they advanced to attack the bandits,
greatly defeated them,
beheaded and captured over a thousand men.
The affairs of Liú Yù begin here.
In the beginning,
Ēn heard that eight commanderies had responded,
said to his subordinates:
"There is nothing left to do in the world,
I should go with you gentlemen in court robes to Jiànkāng."
Meaning he intended to ascend the throne.
Court,
pronounced zhāo.
Said:
"If I cut off the area east of the Zhèjiāng River,
I won't fail to be a Gōu Jiàn!"
Meaning he wanted to be like King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè, preserving possession of Kuàijī.
Gōu,
pronounced gōu.
On the wùshēn day
Láozhī led troops across the river,
Ēn heard of it and said:
"I am not ashamed to flee."
The Jiāngbiǎo Zhuàn: When Zhōu Yú defeated the Wèi army,
Lord Cáo said:
"I am not ashamed to flee."
Therefore Ēn quoted this to speak.
They abandoned much treasure, children, and women on the road,
the government troops competed to seize them,
Ēn thereby managed to escape,
again fled into the sea islands.
Gāo Sù defeated Ēn's partisans at Shānyīn,
Shānyīn county belonged to Kuàijī commandery,
north of the commandery city was all within the county's boundaries.
Captured
the Wúxīng Grand Administrator Qiū Wāng and the Yúyáo Magistrate Shěn Mùfū of Wúxīng.
Yúyáo county belonged to Kuàijī commandery,
located over two hundred lǐ east of the commandery city.
The eastern lands suffered chaos,
hoping for the arrival of government troops,
but then Láozhī and others allowed the soldiers to plunder violently,
the gentry and commoners were disappointed,
in the commandery and county cities there were no longer any human traces,
after over a month some gradually returned.
The court worried Ēn would come again,
appointed Xiè Yǎn as Grand Administrator of Kuàijī, Commander of the Military Affairs of Five Commanderies,
leading Xúzhōu civil and military officials to garrison the coastal areas.
The five commanderies,
were Kuàijī, Línhǎi, Dōngyáng, Yǒngjiā, and Xīn'ān.
Now from Kānshān east to Lánfēng, Shíyàn, Mínghè, Sōngpǔ, Xièpǔ, Dìnghǎi,
are all coastal areas.
Lead,
read as shuài.
Appointed Yuánxiǎn as Lù Shàngshū Shì.
People at the time called Dàozǐ the Eastern Lù,
Yuánxiǎn the Western Lù;
the Western Mansion's carriages and cavalry crowded together,
the Eastern Residence's gate could spread a net.
Yuánxiǎn had no good teachers or friends,
those he trusted and was close to were all flattering sycophants,
some considered them outstanding heroes of the time,
some considered them refined and famous scholars.
Thereby Yuánxiǎn daily grew more arrogant and extravagant,
hinted to the ritual officials to propose,
that he, with high virtue and great prestige,
since being in charge of all affairs,
all officials should show him utmost respect.
Shùn brought him into all affairs.
Yǔ occupied all affairs.
The Zhōuguān says: Táng, Yú examined antiquity,
established offices numbering a hundred,
within there were the Bǎikuí and Sìyuè,
outside there were the Zhōumù and Hóubó.
All used Bǎikuí as an official title.
Kǒng Ānguó said: Kuí,
means to measure;
Shùn promoted the Eight Kǎi,
had them measure all affairs,
this explains the meaning of using Bǎikuí as an official title.
People of Jìn often used Bǎikuí to mean all officials.
When seeing Yuánxiǎn they all bowed.
At that time military campaigns arose frequently,
the state's resources were depleted and empty,
from the Minister Over the Masses down,
daily received seven shēng of grain,
yet Yuánxiǎn accumulated and extorted without cease,
his wealth surpassed the imperial household.
This sets the stage for Yuánxiǎn's destruction of the state and ruin of his family.
Frequently,
pronounced suǒ jiǎo fān.
Extort,
pronounced lì shàn fān.
40 Yīn Zhòngkān feared Huán Xuán's overbearingness,
thus with Yáng Quánqī formed a marriage alliance for support.
Quánqī repeatedly wanted to attack Xuán,
Zhòngkān each time restrained and stopped him.
Xuán feared in the end he would be destroyed by Yīn and Yáng,
thus informed the authorities,
requesting to expand his jurisdiction;
the authorities also wanted to sow discord,
to make them turn against each other,
thus added to Xuán Commander of the Military Affairs of Four Commanderies of Jīngzhōu,
the authorities,
meaning Yuánxiǎn.
The four commanderies of Jīngzhōu,
were Chángshā, Héngyáng, Xiāngdōng, and Línglíng.
Quánqī was resentful and fearful.
Yáng Guǎng wanted to resist Huán Wěi,
Zhòngkān did not listen,
sent Guǎng out as Grand Administrator of the two commanderies Yídū and Jiànpíng.
Yáng Zījìng had previously been Chancellor of Jiāngxià,
Xuán used troops to raid and seize him,
appointed him as Advisory Army Consultant.
Quánqī marshaled troops and raised his standard,
claiming to be reinforcing Luò,
wanting with Zhòngkān to jointly attack Xuán.
Zhòngkān, though outwardly allied with Quánqī, inwardly doubted his intentions,
earnestly stopped him;
still worried he could not restrain him,
sent his younger cousin Yù to camp in the northern border,
to block Quánqī.
Quánqī, since he could not act alone,
and could not discern Zhòngkān's true intent,
then disbanded his troops.
Zhòngkān was suspicious and indecisive,
Advisory Army Consultant Luó Qǐshēng said to his younger brother Zūnshēng:
"Lord Yīn is benevolent but indecisive,
surely will meet with disaster.
I have received his recognition and favor,
in duty I cannot leave,
certainly will die for him."
When Zhòng Kān fled,
none of the civil or military officials escorted him,
only Luó Qǐshēng followed.
Passing by his family home on the road,
his younger brother Zūnshēng said:
"To part like this,
how can we not clasp hands once!"
Qǐshēng turned his horse and offered his hand.
Zūnshēng was strong,
and thus pulled him down,
saying:
"At home we have an elderly mother,
where are you going to go?"
Qǐshēng, wiping away tears, said:
"In today's affair,
I am certain to die for it;
you all serve and care for her,
do not fail in your filial duties.
Within one household,
to have both loyalty and filial piety,
what regret is there then!"
Zūnshēng held him even tighter.
Zhòng Kān waited for him on the road.
Seeing Qǐshēng had no chance to break free,
he whipped his horse and left.
When Huán Xuán arrived,
none among the gentlemen of Jīngzhōu failed to call on Huán Xuán,
only Qǐshēng did not go,
instead managing the household affairs of Zhòng Kān.
Someone said:
"Like this,
calamity is sure to come!"
Qǐshēng said:
"Lord Yīn treated me as a man of state,
yet I was restrained by my younger brother,
unable to follow him to jointly exterminate the vile rebels.
What face have I to then seek life from Huán!"
Huán Xuán heard this and was angry.
However, he had always treated Qǐshēng generously,
so first sent someone to tell him:
"If you apologize to me,
I will release you."
Qǐshēng said:
"I am an official of Governor Yīn of Jīngzhōu.
Jīngzhōu is defeated,
I could not save it,
what apology is there to make!"
Huán Xuán then arrested him,
and again sent someone to ask Qǐshēng if he had any words.
Qǐshēng said:
"Emperor Wén killed Jī Kāng,
and Jī Shào became a loyal minister of Jìn.
The matter of killing Jī Kāng is seen in scroll 78, the third year of the Jǐngyuán era of Emperor Yuán of Wèi.
The matter of Jī Shào's death is seen in scroll 85, the first year of the Yǒngxīng era of Emperor Huì.
Huán Xuán then killed Qǐshēng but pardoned his younger brother.
41 The King of Liáng, Lǚ Guāng, was gravely ill.
He established his heir apparent, Shào, as Heavenly King,
and titled himself Retired Emperor;
he appointed the Duke of Tàiyuán, Zuǎn, as Grand Commandant,
and the Duke of Chángshān, Hóng, as Minister Over the Masses.
He said to Shào:
"Now the state faces many troubles,
three neighbors watch for an opening.
The three neighbors,
refer to Tūfā, Qǐfú, and Duàn Yè.
Trouble,
nǎi dàn fān.
Have Zuǎn command the six armies,
Hóng manage the court administration.
You, be reverent and do not act,
entrust weighty matters to your two elder brothers.
Then perhaps we can succeed.
If internally you suspect and envy each other,
then calamity within the walls,
will arrive in a morning or evening!"
He also said to Zuǎn and Hóng:
"Yǒngyè's talent is not for setting right disorder.
Lǚ Shào's courtesy name is Yǒngyè.
He unworthily occupies the position of sovereign.
You are the sovereign.
People's hearts are not yet settled.
If you brothers are harmonious and close,
then the throne will flow for ten thousand generations;
"Jí",
should be
"jí".
Otherwise, disaster will come before you can turn your heel!"
Zuǎn and Hóng wept and said:
"We dare not."
He also grasped Zuǎn's hand and admonished him, saying:
"Your nature is crude and violent,
this deeply worries me.
Properly assist Yǒngyè,
do not listen to slanderous words!"
That day,
Guāng died.
He was sixty-three years old.
Zuǎn pushed open the gate, entered and wailed,
expressed his full grief and then left.
Shào was afraid,
and offered the position to him,
saying:
"Elder brother's merit is high and years are long,
you should inherit the great succession."
Zuǎn said:
"Your Majesty is the state's legitimate eldest son,
how dare I usurp it!"
Shào firmly yielded,
Zuǎn did not accept.
The General of Agile Cavalry, Lǚ Chāo, said to Shào:
"Zuǎn has been a general for many years,
his prestige shakes both inside and outside.
Facing mourning, he shows no grief,
walks with high steps and gazes afar.
He surely has other intentions,
you should eliminate him early."
Shào said:
"The late emperor's words are still in my ears,
how can I disregard them!
I, in my weak years, bear a heavy responsibility,
and precisely rely on my two elder brothers to bring peace to the family and state.
Even if they plot against me,
I regard death as a return home,
and could never bear to have such an intention.
Do not speak of this again!"
Zuǎn met with Shào at the Zhànlù Hall.
Chāo held a sword and attended at his side,
looking at Zuǎn, requesting to arrest him.
Shào did not permit it.
This sets the stage for Chāo ultimately killing Zuǎn.
He was the son of Guāng's younger brother Bǎo.
Hóng secretly sent the Secretary, Jiāng Jì, to tell Zuǎn:
"The ruler is dim and weak,
unable to bear many troubles.
Elder brother's prestige and kindness have always been renowned.
You should make plans for the altars of grain and soil,
you cannot cling to minor principles."
Zuǎn then that night led several hundred strong men over the north city wall,
and attacked the Guǎngxià Gate.
Hóng led the multitude from the Eastern Park to axe open the Hóngfàn Gate.
Wáng Yǐn's Jìn Shū says: The Liángzhōu city walls are three lǐ east-west,
and seven lǐ north-south,
originally built by the Xiōngnú.
By the time of the Zhāng family,
they further built four additional city walls,
each enclosure one thousand paces;
the east city was named the Drill Ground,
the north city was named the Dark Warrior Garden,
both planted with orchard fruits,
and had palaces and halls.
The Guǎngxià Gate and Hóngfàn Gate,
are both gates of the inner city.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
Xià,
hù yǎ fān.
The guard asked him, saying:
"Who is it?"
The multitude said:
"The Duke of Tàiyuán."
The guard said:
"The state has a great change,
the ruler is newly established.
The Duke of Tàiyuán acts not according to the way,
entering the forbidden city at night.
Are you planning rebellion?"
Thereupon he drew his sword and went straight forward,
struck Zuǎn, hitting his forehead.
Zuǎn's attendants captured him.
Zuǎn said:
"He is a righteous man,
do not kill him!"
Shào sent the Leader of the Gentlemen of the Household of the Rapid as Tigers, Lǚ Kāi, to lead the palace guards to resist and fight at the Duānmén.
Lǚ Chāo led two thousand troops to aid him.
The multitude had always feared Zuǎn,
and all fled without fighting.
Zuǎn entered from the Qīngjiǎo Gate,
and ascended the Qiānguāng Hall.
The Qīngjiǎo Gate,
is likely the east gate of Liángzhōu's inner city.
The Qiānguāng Hall,
was built by Zhāng Jùn;
considering himself as one who ruled Héyòu autocratically yet for generations upheld the duties of a minister,
though humble yet glorious,
therefore he named the hall thus.
Lǚ Chāo fled to Guǎngwǔ.
Zuǎn feared Hóng's military strength,
and offered his position to Hóng.
Hóng said:
"I, Hóng, as Shào's younger brother, inherited the great succession,
but the hearts of the people were not compliant.
Therefore, I violated the late emperor's final command and deposed him,
shamed and indebted to the Yellow Springs!

Emperor Ān Dīng, Fifth Year of Lóng'ān (Xīnchǒu, 401)
His uncle, the Duke of Bāxī, Lǚ Tuó, and
his younger brother, the Duke of Lǒngxī, Lǚ Wěi, were both in the northern city.
Someone advised Lǚ Wěi, saying:
"Lǚ Chāo is committing treason and rebellion.
You, sir, as a close brother,
Dù Yù said: 'Jiè' means
'great'.
Shuō,
shū ruì fān;
same below.
Jiāng Jì and Jiāo Biàn are in the southern city,
Yáng Huán and Tián Chéng are in the eastern park,
all are our allies.
Why worry about not succeeding!"
Lǚ Wěi prepared his troops, intending to join Lǚ Tuó in attacking Lǚ Chāo.
Lǚ Tuó's wife, Lady Liáng, stopped him, saying:
"Lǚ Wěi and Lǚ Chāo are both sons of your brothers.
Why abandon Lǚ Chāo to help Lǚ Wěi,
making yourself the chief culprit of disaster!"
Lǚ Tuó then said to Lǚ Wěi:
"Lǚ Chāo's uprising has already succeeded.
He occupies the armory,
commands elite troops.
Planning against him is extremely difficult.
Moreover, I am old,
and incapable of action."
Lǚ Chāo's younger brother, Lǚ Miǎo, was favored by Lǚ Wěi.
He advised Lǚ Wěi, saying:
"The traitor Lǚ Zuǎn killed his brothers,
meaning he killed Lǚ Shào and also killed Lǚ Hóng.
Shuō,
shū ruì fān.
He truly wishes to honor and establish you, my lord.
Now, you, my lord, are the eldest son of the late emperor,
you should rule the state.
No one has other expectations.
What further doubt is there!"
Lǚ Wěi believed him.
He then formed an alliance with Lǚ Lóng and Lǚ Chāo,
and entered the city alone on horseback.
Lǚ Chāo seized and killed him.
He offered the throne to Lǚ Lóng.
Lǚ Lóng showed a reluctant expression.
Lǚ Chāo said:
"Now it is like riding a dragon to ascend to heaven.
How can one stop halfway!"
Lǚ Lóng then assumed the title of Heavenly King.
Lǚ Lóng,
styled Yǒngjī,
was the son of Lǚ Bǎo, younger brother of Lǚ Guāng.
He changed the era name to Shéndǐng.
Lǚ Chāo had previously obtained a small tripod in Pānhé,
considering it a divine auspice.
Therefore, he used it to mark the era.
He made his wife, Lady Yáng, empress.
He appointed Lǚ Chāo as Commander of All Military Affairs at Home and Abroad, Grand General Who Supports the State, and Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
enfeoffing him as Duke Āndìng.
He posthumously honored Lǚ Zuǎn as Emperor Líng.
When Empress Yáng, wife of Lǚ Zuǎn, was about to leave the palace,
Lǚ Chāo, fearing she would take treasures with her,
ordered her searched.
Lady Yáng said:
"You brothers are unrighteous,
slaughtering each other with your own hands.
I am a person who will die soon.
What use are treasures to me!"
Lǚ Chāo also asked where the imperial seal was.
Lady Yáng said:
"It has already been destroyed."
The empress was beautiful.
Lǚ Chāo intended to take her as his consort.
He said to her father, the Right Deputy Director Yáng Huán:
"If the empress commits suicide,
disaster will befall your clan!"
Yáng Huán told Lady Yáng.
Lady Yáng said:
"Father, you sold your daughter to the Dí to seek wealth and honor.
Once was already excessive,
how can it be done again!"
Quoting words from the Zuǒzhuàn.
She was posthumously honored as Empress Mù.
Yáng Huán fled to the King of Héxī, Lìlùgū.
Lìlùgū appointed him as Left Marshal.
5 In the third month,
Sūn Ēn headed north towards Hǎiyán.
Hǎiyán County was originally Wǔyuán Township.
The Qín established it as Hǎiyán County.
During the Hàn, it belonged to Kuàijī Commandery.
During the Later Hàn and Jìn, it belonged to Wú Commandery.
Now it is eighty lǐ southeast of Xiù Prefecture.
Qù,
qī yù fān.
He built a city at the old site of Hǎiyán.
Ēn came daily to attack the city.
Liú Yù repeatedly defeated him,
killing his general Yáo Shèng.
The city had few troops and could not withstand.
At night, Yù lowered flags and hid his men.
The next morning, he opened the gates,
having a few weak and sickly men climb the walls.
The rebels from afar asked where Liú Yù was.
They said,
"He fled last night."
The rebels believed it,
and rushed into the city.
Yù fiercely attacked,
greatly defeating them.
Ēn knew the city could not be taken,
so he advanced towards Hùdú.
Yù again abandoned the city and pursued him.
The magistrate of Hǎiyán, Bào Lòu, sent his son Bào Sìzhī leading one thousand Wú troops,
requesting to be the vanguard.
Yù said:
"The rebel troops are very skilled.
The Wú people are not accustomed to battle.
If the vanguard suffers defeat,
it will certainly defeat our army.
They should stay in the rear to create声势."
Sìzhī did not listen.
Yù then set up many flags and drums in ambush.
Once the vanguard engaged,
all ambushes emerged.
Yù raised flags and beat drums.
The rebels thought there were troops on all sides,
and retreated.
Sìzhī pursued them,
and died in battle.
Yù fought while retreating.
Those under his command were almost all dead or wounded.
When they reached the previous battlefield,
he ordered his attendants to take clothes from the dead to show leisure.
The rebels were suspicious,
and did not dare press.
Yù shouted loudly to fight again.
The rebels, afraid, retreated.
Yù then led his men back.
6 The King of Héxī, Lìlùgū, attacked Liáng.
He fought with the King of Liáng, Lǚ Lóng,
greatly defeating him,
and relocated over two thousand households before returning.
7 In summer,
the fourth month,
on Xīnmǎo,
the Wèi abolished the Yè branch secretariat.
The Wèi established the Yè branch secretariat,
see the second year of Lóng'ān in the 110th scroll.
They appointed Yǔ Yuè as governor.
The Wèi's Xiàng Prefecture governed six commanderies: Wèi, Yángpíng, Guǎngpíng, Jí, Dùnqiū, and Qīnghé.
Dù Yòu said: The Later Wèi established Xiàng Prefecture at Yè,
taking the name from Hédǎnjiǎ residing at Xiàng.
8 Qǐfú Gān'guī arrived at Yuànchuān.
He appointed Biān Ruì as Chief Clerk,
Wáng Sōngshòu as Marshal,
and demoted all dukes, ministers, generals, and commanders to staff officers and subordinate officers.
9 The King of Northern Liáng, Duàn Yè, feared Jùqú Méngxùn's bravery and strategy,
and wanted to keep him at a distance.
Méngxùn also deeply concealed himself.
Yè appointed the Gentleman of the Palace Gate, Mǎ Quán, to replace Méngxùn as Governor of Zhāngyè.
Quán was always heroic and outstanding,
favored and valued by Yè,
and often looked down upon and insulted Méngxùn.
Méngxùn slandered him to Yè, saying:
"The world is not worth worrying about,
only Mǎ Quán should be of concern."
Yè then killed Quán.
In my view,
Suǒ Sì and Mǎ Quán were both mediocre men.
Relying on their family backgrounds and acting arrogantly,
they were incapable.
Méngxùn said to Jùqú Nánchéng:
"Lord Duàn lacks the talent for discernment and decision.
Jiàn means
clarity;
duàn means
decision.
Duàn,
dīng luàn fān.
Previously, he only feared Suǒ Sì and Mǎ Quán.
Now they are both dead.
Suǒ Sì died in the fourth year of the previous scroll.
What do you think?"
Nánchéng said:
"Yè was originally a solitary guest,
established by our family.
Relying on us brothers is like a fish relying on water.
For a person to plot against those who trust him
is inauspicious."
Méngxùn then requested to be Governor of Xī'ān.
Yè was pleased that he was going outside,
and agreed.
Měngxùn made an appointment with Nánchéng to jointly sacrifice at Lánmén Mountain,
but secretly sent Simǎ Xǔ Xián to report to Yè, saying:
"Nánchéng intends to use the holiday leave to stage a rebellion.
If he requests to sacrifice at Lánmén Mountain,
my words will be proven true."
When the time came,
it indeed happened.
Yè arrested Nánchéng and ordered him to commit suicide.
Nánchéng said:
"Měngxùn first plotted rebellion with me.
Due to our brotherly bond,
I concealed it and did not speak out.
Now, because I am still alive,
he fears the troops will not follow him,
so he made an appointment with me to sacrifice at the mountain and instead falsely accused me.
His intention is for the king to kill me.
I beg you to falsely announce my death,
expose my crimes and evils,
then Měngxùn will certainly rebel.
After that, I will follow the king's command to attack him,
and there will be nothing we cannot overcome."
Yè did not listen,
and killed him.
Měngxùn tearfully told the crowd:
"Nánchéng was loyal to King Duàn,
yet King Duàn unjustly killed him without reason.
Can you gentlemen seek revenge for him?
Moreover, initially we jointly established King Duàn,
wishing to bring peace to the masses;
now the province is in chaos,
and it is not something King Duàn can save."
Nánchéng had always won the hearts of the people,
and the crowd was all indignant, weeping, and striving eagerly.
By the time they reached Dīchí,
Dīchí County,
which belonged to Zhāngyè Commandery in the Han dynasty,
was abolished in the Jin dynasty,
its territory falling within the boundaries of Táng's Gānzhōu Zhāngyè County.
Bǐ,
bì mèi fān,
means "to reach."
Dī,
dīng ní fān,
also pronounced dī.
Zhènjūn General Zāng Mòhái led his troops to surrender to him,
and many Qiāng and Hú people raised troops in response to Měngxùn.
Měngxùn advanced and threatened
Hóuwù.
Yè had previously suspected Right General Tián Áng,
and imprisoned him;
at this point, he summoned Áng,
apologized and pardoned him,
ordering him to join Wǔwèi General Liáng Zhōngyōng in jointly attacking Měngxùn.
Biéjiàng Wáng Fēngsūn said to Yè:
"The various Tiáns of Xīpíng,
have had rebels for generations.
Áng appears respectful but is treacherous at heart,
and cannot be trusted."
Yè said:
"I have suspected him for a long time;
but there is no one besides Áng who can attack Měngxùn."
When Áng reached Hóuwù,
he led five hundred cavalry to surrender to Měngxùn,
and Yè's army then collapsed.
Zhōngyōng also went to Měngxùn to surrender.
In times of danger, suspicion, and wavering loyalty,
using words is difficult,
and employing people is even more difficult.
At such a moment,
without clear strategy and decisive courage, one cannot succeed.
In the fifth month,
Měngxùn reached Zhāngyè.
Tián Áng's nephew Chéng'ài opened the city gates to let him in,
and Yè's attendants all scattered.
When Měngxùn arrived,
Yè said to Měngxùn:
"I am alone and isolated,
having been elevated by your family.
I wish to beg for my remaining life,
to be allowed to return east and see my wife and children."
Měngxùn beheaded him.
The Northern Liáng Duàn Yè perished after four years.
Yè,
was a Confucian scholar and an elder of good character,
lacking other strategic abilities.
His authority and prohibitions were not enforced,
and his subordinates acted on their own authority.
He particularly believed in divination and sorcerers,
hence his downfall.
Jùqú Nánchéng's younger brother, Fùzhàn General Jù Lěi, led five hundred households to surrender to Héxī King Lìlùgū.
Lěi,
was the son of Shízǐ.

"Sōng",

Wèi'ān person Jiāo Lǎng
Wèi'ān County was within the boundaries of Wǔwēi Chāngsōng County,

Later, Wèi established Wèi'ān Commandery.
"Since the Lǚ family's Martial Emperor passed away,
Lǚ Guāng's posthumous title was Yìwǔ Emperor.
Shuō,
lún ruì fān.
The administrative framework was not established,

Now, taking advantage of their usurpation period,

Shuòdé spoke to Qín King Xīng,

12 In the sixth month,
on Jiǎxū,
Sūn Ēn sailed across the sea and suddenly arrived at Dāntú.
Dāntú County,
was ancient Zhūfāng,
later called Gǔyáng,
Qín changed it to Dāntú,

The Geographical Records say: In Qín times,
those who observed celestial signs said the place had imperial aura,

and changed the name to Dāntú.
With over a thousand tower ships,
Jiànkāng was shocked and terrified.
On Yǐhài,
martial law was imposed inside and out,
all officials entered and resided within the government offices;
Guànjūn General Gāo Sù and others guarded Shítóu,

which is the mouth where the Qínhuái River enters the Yangtze.
Duàn,
dīng guǎn fān.
Guànjūn General Huán Qiān and others guarded Báishí,
Zuǒwèi General Wáng Gǔ and others stationed at Zhōngtáng,
and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Qiáo King Shàngzhī was summoned to enter and defend the capital.
Liú Láozhī led troops from Shānyīn to intercept Sūn Ēn,
but before he arrived, Ēn had already passed through,
so he sent Liú Yù from Hǎiyán to provide reinforcements.
Yù had fewer than a thousand soldiers,
yet he advanced by forced marches day and night,
arriving at Dāntú at the same time as Ēn.
Yù's forces were few,
and having traveled a great distance, they were exhausted,
while the defending troops at Dāntú had no fighting spirit.
Ēn led his men, beating drums and shouting,
and ascended Suànshān.
Suànshān,
now located three lǐ west of Zhènjiāng Prefecture's city walls,
had abundant garlic on the mountain,
hence the name.
Suàn,
read as Sū Guàn.
Yù led his troops in a swift attack,
routing them decisively,
with many
throwing themselves off cliffs or into the water,
and Ēn barely managed to escape back to his ships in disarray.
However, Ēn still relied on his large numbers,
and soon regrouped his forces to head straight for the capital.
The Rear General Yuán Xiǎn led troops to resist,
but suffered repeated defeats.
Huìjī Prince Dàozǐ had no other strategies,
and merely prayed daily at the Jiǎnghóu Temple.
The Jiǎnghóu Temple was located on Jiǎngshān,
eighteen lǐ northeast of Shàngyuán County in present-day Jiànkāng Prefecture.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty,
Mòlíng Commandant Jiǎng Zǐwén fought against bandits,
died in battle at the foot of the mountain,
and Sūn Quán of Wú established a temple for him.
Both court and commoners in Jiāngdōng prayed to him,
and he often responded with spiritual efficacy.
The common people were terrified and panicked.
Qiáo Prince Shàngzhī led elite troops and rushed to the scene,
directly stationing them at the Jīnǔ Hall.
Ēn's tower ships were tall and large,
and sailing against the wind, they could not move swiftly,
taking several days to reach Báishí.
Ēn had originally intended to take advantage of the dispersal of the various armies
to launch a surprise attack;
but upon learning that Shàngzhī was in Jiànkāng,
and hearing that Liú Láozhī had already returned,
reaching Xīnzhōu,
Xīnzhōu was in the middle of the great river west of Jīngkǒu,
believed to be present-day Zhūjīnshā.
Fù,
read as Fú Yòu.
He sailed north across the sea to Yùzhōu.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: Northeast of Qú County in Dōnghǎi, there is a large island in the sea,
called Yùzhōu,
which is what the Shānhǎijīng refers to
as "Yùshān in the sea."
He killed three thousand people.
General Níngshuò Gāo Yǎzhī attacked Ēn at Yùzhōu,
but was captured by Ēn.
The title General Níngshuò was likely established during the Jìn.
Huán Xuán trained his troops and drilled his soldiers,
constantly watching for opportunities from the imperial court,
and upon hearing that Sūn Ēn was threatening the capital,
he raised his standard and gathered forces,
submitting a memorial requesting permission to attack him.
Yuán Xiǎn was greatly alarmed.
As Ēn retreated,
Yuán Xiǎn issued an imperial edict ordering him to stop,
and Xuán then stood down his forces.
13 Liáng Zhōngyōng and others jointly recommended Jǔqú Méngxùn as Grand Commander-in-Chief, Great General, Governor of Liángzhōu, and Duke of Zhāngyè,
pardoning all within his territory,
and changing the era name to Yǒng'ān.
Méngxùn appointed his cousin Fúnú as Prefect of Zhāngyè and Marquis of Hépíng,
his brother Ná as General Jiànzhōng and Marquis of Dūgǔ,
Tián Áng as Prefect of Xījùn,
Zāng Mòhái as General Fǔguó,
Fáng Guǐ and Liáng Zhōngyōng as Left and Right Chief Administrators,
Zhāng Zhì and Xiè Zhènglǐ as Left and Right Military Commandants;
promoting and appointing talented individuals,

14 King of Héxī Lìlùgū ordered his ministers to speak frankly about strengths and weaknesses.
Xīcáo Cóngshì Shǐ Gǎo said:
"When Your Majesty commands generals to go on campaigns,
they are always victorious;
however, you do not prioritize pacification and stability,
focusing only on relocating the people;
the people are attached to their land and reluctant to move,
so many rebel and defect,
which is why you behead generals and capture cities but do not expand your territory."
Lìlùgū praised him.
15 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Wèi's Governor of Yǎnzhōu Chángsūn Féi
(Wèi had not yet gained Yǎnzhōu;
Féi was sent south as Governor of Yǎnzhōu to seize territory.)
advanced east to Péngchéng,
