16 Qín's Duke of Lǒngxī Shuòdé crossed the river from Jīnchéng,
heading straight for Guǎngwǔ,
and King of Héxī Lìlùgū withdrew the Guǎngwǔ garrison to avoid him.
The Qín army reached Gūzāng,
and Liáng King Lóng sent Grand General Fǔguó Chāo, General Lóngxiāng Miǎo, and others to engage them,
but Shuòdé routed them decisively,
capturing Miǎo alive,
and taking or killing tens of thousands.
Lóng barricaded himself in the city and held firm,
while Duke of Bāxī Tuó led twenty-five thousand troops from the Eastern Park to surrender to Qín.
Duke of Xīliáng Lǐ Gǎo, King of Héxī Lìlùgū, and Jǔqú Méngxùn each sent envoys to submit memorials and offer tribute to Qín.
Earlier,
Liáng general Jiāng Jì surrendered to King of Héxī Lìlùgū,
and Duke of Guǎngwǔ Tǎntán discussed military strategy with him,
greatly admiring and valuing him,
sitting together on joined mats,
riding together in the same carriage when going out,
and often talking
late into the night.
Lìlùgū said to Tǎntán:
"Jiāng Jì indeed has fine talent,
but his demeanor is unusual,
and he will surely not stay here long;
it would be better to kill him.
If Jì goes to Qín,
he will surely become a problem for others."
Tǎntán said:
"I treat Jì as a friend from commoner days,
and Jì will surely not betray me."
In the eighth month,
Jì led several dozen cavalry to join the Qín army.
The Tūfā brothers all praised Tǎntán's brilliant foresight,
but I, having examined Tǎntán's entire story,
dare not agree.
Furthermore, examining Jiāng Jì's journey from Liáng to Qín,
Jì appears to have been a treacherous and deceitful man,
yet Tǎntán admired and valued him.
Thus, Tǎntán was esteemed by his brothers for his talent and eloquence,
but his wisdom and strategy were insufficient,
which is why he lost his state.
"Lǚ Lóng is isolated in a city with no reinforcements;
if you, illustrious lord, lead a great army against him,
he will surely request to surrender;
however, he will only surrender in name,
and will not truly submit.
I request three thousand infantry and cavalry for Jì,
to join Wáng Sōngcōng with the forces of Jiāo Lǎng and Huá Chún.
Wáng Sōngcōng
was a Qín general;
Jiāo Lǎng and Huá Chún were both from Liáng.
Shuō,
read as Shū Ruì.
Huá,
read as Hù Huà.
Lóng is not worth capturing.
Otherwise,
with Tūfā to the south,
militarily strong and the state wealthy,
if they seize and occupy Gūzāng,
their power and influence will grow even stronger,
and Jǔqú Méngxùn and Lǐ Gǎo will be unable to resist,
and will surely submit to them.
In that case,
they will become a great enemy for our state."
Shuòdé then memorialized to appoint Jì as Prefect of Wǔwēi,
assigning him two thousand troops,
to station and hold Yànrán.
Bān Gù's Dìlǐzhì states,
in Wǔwēi's Xiūtú County,
Wáng Mǎng changed the name to Yànrán,
later reverting to Xiūtú.
During the Yǒngníng era,
Zhāng Guǐ established Wǔxīng Commandery northwest of Gūzāng,
and Yànrán County belonged to it.
Qín King Xīng, hearing of Yáng Huán's talent, summoned him,
and Lìlùgū dared not keep him.
The historian notes that the various Liáng states feared Qín's strength.
17 An edict appointed Liú Yù as Prefect of Xiàpī,
to attack Sūn Ēn at Yùzhōu.
After several battles,
he routed Ēn decisively.
Ēn was thus weakened,
and fled south again along the coast,
with Yù pursuing and intercepting him.
18. Yān King Mùróng Shèng, having learned from his father Mùróng Bǎo's loss of the state due to weakness and timidity,
was determined to enforce severe punishments and harsh laws.
He was also proud of his own intelligence and perceptiveness,
and was highly suspicious and jealous.
If any of his ministers had even the slightest hint of suspicion against them,
he would have them executed preemptively.
Because of this, the imperial relatives and meritorious veterans
felt that no one could ensure their own safety.
On the Dīnghài day,
Left General Mùróng Guó conspired with Palace Generals Qín Yú and Duàn Zàn
to lead the imperial guards in a surprise attack against Shèng.
(The Palace Generals were positions established by Mùróng Shèng,
named after the Palace Generals of the Jin dynasty.)
(Shuài,
read as "lead.")
Over five hundred people died.
On the Rénchén night,
Former General Duàn Jī, along with Qín Yú's son Qín Xīng and Duàn Zàn's son Duàn Tài, secretly raised a clamor and shouted within the palace grounds;
Shèng, hearing of the disturbance,
led his attendants out to fight,
and the rebels fled and scattered.
Jī was wounded
and hid among the side rooms.
Shortly after, a rebel struck Shèng from the darkness,
wounding him.
Shèng was carried by palanquin to the front hall,
where he issued orders to the palace guards.
After the situation was stabilized, he died.
He was twenty-nine years old.
Mùróng Shèng remained composed in the face of crisis;
this shows his heroic strategy was also exceptional.
However, he met his end due to suspicion, jealousy, and a penchant for killing.
Thus, the people of the world are certainly not such that one person can wield his intelligence and schemes to kill them all.
Central Garrison General Mùróng Bá and the Deputy Director of the Retinue Guō Zhòng reported to the Empress Dowager Dīng,
stating that the state faced many difficulties,
and it was appropriate to establish an elder ruler.
At the time, public expectation rested on Shèng's younger brother, the Minister over the Masses and Imperial Secretary, the Duke of Píngyuán, Mùróng Yuán.
However, the Duke of Héjiān, Mùróng Xī, had always been favored by Empress Dowager Dīng.
Dīng therefore deposed the Crown Prince Mùróng Dìng
and secretly welcomed Xī into the palace.
The next morning,
when the ministers entered court,
they only then learned of the change,
and consequently submitted a petition urging Xī to ascend the throne.
Xī yielded to Yuán,
but Yuán did not dare accept.
On the Guǐsì day,
Xī assumed the position of Heavenly King.
(Xī,
styled Dàowén,
was the youngest son of Mùróng Chuí.)
All were executed along with their three clans.
On the Jiǎwǔ day,
a general amnesty was declared.
On the Bǐngshēn day,
the Duke of Píngyuán, Mùróng Yuán, was ordered to commit suicide due to suspicion.
In the intercalary month,
on the Xīnyǒu day,
Shèng was buried at the Xīngpíng Mausoleum,
and given the posthumous title Zhāowǔ Emperor,
with the temple name Zhōngzōng.
While Empress Dowager Dīng was attending the funeral and had not yet returned,
Central Army Commander Mùróng Tí and Infantry Commandant Zhāng Fó plotted to install the former Crown Prince Dìng.
The plot was discovered,
and they were executed,
and Dìng was also ordered to commit suicide.
(Yān had established Dìng as Crown Prince;
see the fourth year of the previous scroll.)
On the Bǐngyín day,
a general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed to Guāngshǐ.
19. The Qín Duke of Lǒngxī, Yáo Shuòdé, had besieged Gūzāng for several months.
Many people from the east who were inside the city plotted to rebel and escape.
Wèi Yìduō again incited and agitated them,
intending to kill the Liáng King Lǚ Lóng and the Duke of Āndìng, Lǚ Chāo.
The plot was exposed,
and over three hundred families were implicated and executed.
Shuòdé pacified and accepted both the barbarians and the Huáxià people,
appointed local administrators,
rationed food and stored grain,
making plans for a prolonged campaign.
The ministers of Liáng requested to make peace with Qín,
but Lóng refused.
The Duke of Āndìng, Chāo, said:
"Now our supplies and reserves are exhausted internally,
and everyone from top to bottom is wailing in distress.
Even if Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng were reborn,
they would have no plan to offer.
(Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng
were men of wisdom and strategy,
hence the reference.)
Why begrudge a short letter and a single envoy to use humble words to repel the enemy!
After the enemy leaves,
we can cultivate virtuous governance to give the people rest.
If our divined reign is not yet exhausted,
why worry about not restoring our former enterprise!
(King Chéng of Zhōu established the tripods at Jiárǔ,
divining thirty reigns,
and seven hundred years.)
We can also preserve our clan intact.
If not,
sitting here awaiting destitution,
what will ultimately become of us?"
Lóng then followed his advice.
In the ninth month,
he sent an envoy to request surrender from Qín.
Shuòdé memorialized to appoint Lóng as General Who Guards the West, Governor of Liáng Province, and Duke of Jiànkāng.
Lóng sent his sons, younger brothers, and veteran civil and military officials such as Mùróng Zhù and Yáng Yǐng, over fifty families in total, to Cháng'ān as hostages.
(Mùróng Zhù
was a member of the Yān imperial clan.
After Fú Jiān destroyed Yān,
its imperial clan members were all assigned to border commanderies,
hence Zhù remained in Héxī.)
(Zhù,
pronunciation Zhāng Liù fān.)
(Zhì,
pronunciation zhì;
the same below where used as 'hostage'.)
(Shuòdé's army) did not commit the slightest offense,
sacrificed to former worthies,
and treated famous scholars with respect,
pleasing the western region.
The two commanderies of Jiǔquán and Liángníng under Jǔqú Méngxùn's jurisdiction rebelled and surrendered to Xīliáng.
(The seat of Jiǔquán Commandery was Fúlù County.
According to Wèi Shōu's Treatise on Geography,
Liángníng Commandery administered the two counties of Yuánchí and Gòngzé.)
(Méngxùn) was greatly afraid,
and sent his younger brother, General of Establishing Loyalty Jǔqú Ná, and the Chief Clerk of the Pastoral Office, Zhāng Qián,
(Méngxùn had proclaimed himself Governor of Liáng Province,
and established the position of Chief Clerk of the Pastoral Office.)
(Ná,
pronunciation Nǚ Jū fān.)
to request permission to lead his people eastward.
Shuòdé was pleased,
appointed Qián as Grand Administrator of Zhāngyè,
and Ná as Grand Administrator of Jiànkāng.
Qián urged Méngxùn to move east.
Ná privately said to Méngxùn:
"Gūzāng has not yet been captured,
the Lǚ clan still exists,
Shuòdé's provisions will run out and he will withdraw,
he cannot stay long.
Why abandon our own land,
to be controlled by others!"
Zāng Mòhái also believed this to be correct.
Méngxùn sent his son Xīniàn as a hostage to the Héxī King Tàfúlì Lùgū.
(Since Méngxùn did not move east,
he sent a hostage to Lùgū to seek aid.)
(Lùgū) said:
"Xīniàn is young;
you should send Ná."
In winter,
the tenth month,
Méngxùn again sent an envoy to submit a memorial to Lùgū, saying:
"Your subject previously sent Xīniàn to fully express my sincere intentions,
but Your Sacred Will was not yet clear,
and you further demanded my younger brother Ná.
Your subject humbly believes that,
if there is sincere trust,
then a son is not considered light,
but if there is no trust,
then a younger brother is not considered weighty.
Now the calamity of the enemy is not yet pacified,
and I cannot comply with the edict.
I hope Your Majesty will understand this."
Lùgū was angry,
and sent Marquis Zhāngsōng Jù Yán and Marquis Xīngchéng Wén Zhī to lead ten thousand cavalry to attack Méngxùn.
They reached Wànsuì and Línsōng.
(The Treatise on Geography of the Jìn History states
that Jiǔquán Commandery had Yánshòu County,
which was likely later renamed Wànsuì.
Zhāng Tiānxí established Línsōng Commandery.
The Five Dynasties Treatise states: Línsōng County had Línsōng Mountain,
and it was abolished into Zhāngyè County during the Later Zhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Suí Emperor Yáng merged Wànsuì into Shāndān County,
which belonged to Zhāngyè Commandery.)
(Jiàng,
pronunciation jí liàng fān.)
(Qí,
pronunciation qí jì fān.)
They captured over six thousand households of his people.
Méngxùn's paternal uncle Kǒng Zhē went to pay court to Lùgū,
promising to send Ná as a hostage.
Lùgū then returned the people he had plundered,
and recalled Jù Yán and the others.
(Wén Zhī
was Lùgū's younger brother.)
20. The Southern Yan ruler Bèidé held a banquet for his ministers at Yánxián Hall.
Bèidé
originally had the single name Dé.
After occupying the Qí region,
he added a character above,
becoming named Bèidé.
He said to his ministers:
"To which rulers of antiquity can I be compared?"
The Governor of Qīngzhōu, Jū Zhòng, said:
"Your Majesty is a sagely ruler who has restored the dynasty,
the equal of Shàokāng and Guāngwǔ."
Bèidé turned to his attendants and ordered that Zhòng be granted a thousand bolts of silk;
Zhòng, considering the gift too lavish,
declined it.
Bèidé said:
"You know how to jest with me,
do you think I do not know how to jest with you?
Your response was not truthful,
so I am also rewarding you with empty words."
Hán Fàn stepped forward and said:
"The Son of Heaven does not speak in jest.
In today's discussion,
both ruler and minister were at fault."
Bèidé was greatly pleased,
and granted Fàn fifty bolts of silk.
Bèidé's mother and elder brother Nà were both in Cháng'ān.
Bèidé sent Dù Hóng of Píngyuán to seek them out.
Hóng said:
"When I reach Cháng'ān,
if I do not receive news of the Empress Dowager's movements,
I will proceed west to Zhāngyè.
Dé served the Qín as the Grand Administrator of Zhāngyè,
and his elder brother Nà consequently settled his family in Zhāngyè,
hence Hóng intended to go to Zhāngyè to seek him.
My father, Xióng, is over sixty years old.
I beg for an official salary from his home district to fulfill the sentiment of the crow feeding its parent."
The filial crow feeds its parent in return,
hence the expression.
Lǐ Mì's "Memorial Expressing My Feelings" states:
"With the private feelings of a crow,
I wish to beg to be allowed to care for my parent to the end."
"Dù Hóng sought an official salary before even setting out on his mission;
his crime of coercing his ruler is great."
Bèidé said:
"Hóng is welcoming my mother for his ruler,
and seeking an official salary for his father.
He embodies both loyalty and filial piety.
What crime is there in that!"
He appointed Xióng as the Magistrate of Píngyuán.
When Hóng reached Zhāngyè,
he was killed by bandits.
21. In the eleventh month,
Liú Yù pursued Sūn Ēn to Hùdú and Hǎiyán,
and again defeated him,
capturing and beheading him by the tens of thousands.
Ēn then fled far out to sea from Jiákǒu.
22. In the twelfth month,
on the Xīnhài day,
the Wèi ruler Guī sent Chángshān King Zūn and Dìnglíng Duke Hé Bá to lead fifty thousand troops in a surprise attack against Mòyígān at Gāopíng.
Gāopíng
belonged to Āndìng in the Hàn,
according to Wèi Shōu's treatise, it belonged to Xīnpíng Commandery of Jīngzhōu.
Also, Yuánzhōu had a Gāopíng Commandery;
Lì Dàoyuán states: Gāopíng River is three hundred and forty *li* southwest of Āndìng.
Shuài
is read as shuài.
23. On the Yǐmǎo day,
the Wèi Tiger-Wielding General Sù Tàgān attacked Yān,
assaulting Lìngzhī.
On the Yǐchǒu day,
the Yān Central Army Commander Yǔwén Bá came to its rescue.
On the Rénwǔ day,
Sù Tàgān captured Lìngzhī and garrisoned it.
24. Lǚ Chāo attacked Jiāng Jì but could not overcome him,
so he then attacked Jiāo Lǎng.
Jiāng Jì was then holding Yànrán,
and Jiāo Lǎng was holding Wèi'ān.
Lìlùgū sent the Chariot and Horse General Rùtán to aid them.
By the time he arrived,
Chāo had already withdrawn,
and Lǎng closed his gates and refused him entry.
Rùtán was angered,
and prepared to attack him.
The General Who Guards the North, Jù Yán, remonstrated:
"Cherishing one's native land and being reluctant to move is
the common sentiment of people.
Lǎng holds an isolated city with no food.
If he does not surrender this year,
he will submit of his own accord next year.
Why must we kill many soldiers to attack him!
If we are not victorious,
he will certainly leave and join another state.
To abandon the people of our province and provide resources to a neighboring enemy
is not a good plan.
It would be better to admonish him with kind words."
Rùtán then made peace with Lǎng,
and subsequently displayed his military might at Gūzāng,
encamping at Húkēng.
Húkēng is west of Gūzāng.
Rùtán knew that Lǚ Chāo would certainly come to raid his camp,
and prepared fire to await him.
Chāo sent the Central Fortifications General Wáng Jí at night to lead two thousand elite troops to raid Rùtán's camp.
Rùtán calmly maintained strict order and did not rise.
When Jí entered the fortifications,
torches were raised both inside and out,
illuminating the area as bright as day.
They released their troops to attack,
beheading Jí and over three hundred armored soldiers.
Lǚ Lóng was afraid,
and pretended to establish friendly relations with Rùtán,
requesting to form an alliance within the imperial park.
Rùtán sent Jù Yán to enter and form the alliance.
Jù Yán suspected there was an ambush,
and tore down the park wall to enter.
Chāo's ambushing troops attacked him.
Jù Yán lost his horse and fled on foot.
The General Who Crosses Rivers, Guō Zǔ, fought fiercely to resist them,
and Jù Yán was then able to escape.
Rùtán was enraged,
and attacked Lǚ Lóng's Chāngsōng Grand Administrator Mèng Yī at Xiǎnměi.
Chāngsōng and Xiǎnměi
were both counties in the Hàn and Jìn,
belonging to Wǔwēi Commandery.
Lǚ Guāng changed Chāngsōng to Eastern Zhāngyè Commandery,
but soon restored it as Chāngsōng Commandery.
According to the "Treatise of the Five Dynasties,"
the Later Zhōu abolished Xiǎnměi and merged it into Gūzāng.
Yī
is pronounced Xǔ Wéi.
Ānguó and the General Who Pacifies Distant Lands, Shí Kě, led five hundred cavalry to rescue him.
Ānguó and the others feared Rùtán's strength,
and fled back.
25. Huán Xuán memorialized to have his elder brother Wěi appointed as Governor of Jiāngzhōu,
to guard Xiàkǒu;
Simā Diāo Chàng as General Who Supports the State and Commander of the Military Affairs of Eight Commanderies,
to guard Xiāngyáng;
and sent his generals Huángfǔ Fū and Féng Gāi to garrison Pénkǒu.
He relocated two thousand households of the Jù and Zhāng barbarians to south of the Yangtze River.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* says: The Jiāng, Hàn, Jù, and Zhāng
are the sacred rivers of Chǔ.
The *Shuǐjīng* states: The Jù River originates from Fánglíng in Hànzhōng,
flows southeast past Línjū,
then east past Zhījiāng County,
and south into the Yangtze.
The Zhāng River originates from Jīng Mountain east of Línjū County,
flows south to north of Zhījiāng County and enters the Jù.
The areas along these two rivers were all inhabited by barbarians.
Jù
is pronounced Zǐ Yú.
Zhāng
is pronounced Zhū Liáng.
He further gathered displaced people,
and established Suí'ān Commandery.
Suí'ān Commandery
administered Chángníng County.
The Suí abolished Chángníng and merged it into Chánglín.
Xuán detained them all and did not send them.
Xuán considered himself to possess two-thirds of the Jìn state.
He repeatedly had people present auspicious signs concerning himself,
wishing to confuse the masses.
He also sent a letter to the Prince of Kuaijī, Dàozǐ, stating:
"When the bandits approached the outskirts,
the wind prevented them from advancing,
the rain prevented them from using fire,
and their provisions were exhausted, so they left.
It was not due to being overpowered.
After Guóbǎo's death,
Wáng Gōng did not take advantage of this authority to enter and take control of the court's administration.
This is sufficient to see that his heart was not disrespectful towards Your Excellency,
yet he was called disloyal.
Among the important and trusted confidants of today,
who are those with contemporary reputations and pure esteem?
How can it be said there are no outstanding individuals?
It is simply that they cannot be trusted!
Among the gentlemen of Jiāngdōng,
those whose names and positions were prominent and illustrious at the time
were generally called outstanding and renowned.
This has led to the disaster of today.
Since then,
it is still said that it has been this way since.
I, Xuán, unworthily hold office in a distant region,
hence I have laid out the facts."
Yuánxiǎn saw this,
and was greatly afraid.
Zhāng Fǎshùn said to Yuánxiǎn:
"Huán Xuán relies on his family's resources,
has always had an arrogant spirit,
and now having annexed Yīn and Yáng,
exclusively controls Jīngchǔ;
Yīn and Yáng refer to Yīn Zhòngkān and Yáng Quánqī.
The annexation of Yīn and Yáng is recorded in the third year of Lóng'ān in the previous scroll.
Dì,
means mansion;
dìxià,
is similar to terms like ménxià or géxià.
The eastern lands are devastated,
both public and private resources are exhausted,
Xuán is certain to take advantage of this to unleash his treacherous villainy,
and I am secretly worried about it."
Yuánxiǎn said:
"What can be done about it?"
Fǎshùn said:
"Xuán has only just obtained Jīngzhōu,
the people's sentiments are not yet attached to him,
he is currently focused on pacifying and appeasing them,
and has no leisure for other plans.
If we take advantage of this moment to send Liú Láozhī as the vanguard,
and Your Excellency follows with the main army,
Xuán can be captured."
Yuánxiǎn considered this reasonable.
At that time, Wǔchāng Tàishǒu Yǔ Kǎi, because Xuán had created enmity with the court,
feared that the affair would not succeed,
and disaster would reach himself,
Yǔ Kǎi defected to Huán Xuán,
see the second year of Lóng'ān in scroll one hundred and ten.
said
"Xuán has greatly lost the people's favor,
the masses will not be used by him,
if the court dispatches troops,
I will act as an insider."
Yuánxiǎn was greatly pleased,
and sent Zhāng Fǎshùn to Jīngkǒu,
to consult with Liú Láozhī;
Láozhī considered it difficult.
Fǎshùn returned,
and said to Yuánxiǎn:
"Observing Láozhī's words and expression,
he is certain to betray us,
it would be better to summon him and kill him;
if not,
he will ruin our great affair."
Yuánxiǎn did not follow this.
Thereupon, they greatly built up the naval forces,
conscripted troops and outfitted warships,
to plan the campaign against Xuán.
First year of Yuánxīng (Rényín, 402)
1 Spring,
first month,
first day Gēngwǔ,
In the third month of this year,
Yuánxiǎn was defeated,
the Lóng'ān era name was restored,
Huán Xuán soon changed it to Dàhēng,
Xuán usurped the throne,
and changed it again to Yǒngshǐ.
The first year of Yuánxīng was changed in the first month of this year,
the Comprehensive Mirror continues to use the first year of Yuánxīng from this year until the first year of Yìxī,
not changing the first year of Yuánxīng,
not acknowledging Huán Xuán's usurpation,
to rectify the chaotic times and return to the proper order.
Appointed Shàngshū Lìng Yuánxiǎn as Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, Zhēngtǎo Dàdūdū, Dūdū Shíbā Zhōu Zhūjūnshì, and granted the Yellow Axe,
At that time, within Jìn's borders there were only eighteen provinces: Yáng, Xú, Nánxú, Yǎn, Nányǎn, Yù, Nányù, Qīng, Jì, Sī, Jīng, Jiāng, Yōng, Liáng, Yì, Níng, Jiāo, and Guǎng,
Yuánxiǎn oversaw all of them,
had he truly been able to execute Huán Xuán,
he would certainly have overstepped his superiors and usurped power.
Piào,
read as piào.
Jì,
read as jì.
Qián Jiāngjūn Qiáo Wáng Shàngzhī was appointed as the rear commander,
thereupon a great amnesty was declared,
the era name was changed,
internal and external precautions were enforced;
Ji Kuàijī Wáng Dàozǐ was appointed as Tàifù.
Yuánxiǎn wanted to exterminate all the members of the Huán clan.
Zhōnghùjūn Huán Xiū,
was the nephew of Piàojì Zhǎngshǐ Wáng Dàn,
Dàn was favored by Yuánxiǎn,
and thus explained that Xiū and others had different aspirations from Xuán,
Yuánxiǎn then stopped.
Dàn,
was the great-grandson of Dǎo.
Zhāng Fǎshùn said to Yuánxiǎn:
"Huán Qiān and his brothers often act as eyes and ears for the upper reaches,
they should be executed to prevent treacherous schemes.
Moreover, the success of the affair,
depends on the vanguard army,
and Láozhī is fickle,
if there is any change,
then disaster and defeat will arrive immediately,
we can order Láozhī to kill Qiān and his brothers to show he has no divided loyalties,
if he does not accept the order,
we should preemptively deal with him."
Preemptively deal with him,
means before the disaster arrives, plan for it in advance,
intending to kill Láozhī.
"Now, without Láozhī,
there is no one to oppose Xuán;
moreover, to kill a great general at the start of the affair,
will unsettle people's sentiments."
Repeatedly, it was not permissible.
Fǎshùn spoke to Yuánxiǎn repeatedly,
but in the end, it was considered not permissible.
Huán Chōng had left behind particular kindness,
and Qiān,
was Chōng's son,
so he was appointed from Piàojì Sīmǎ to Dūdū Jīng‧Yì‧Níng‧Liáng Sì Zhōu Zhūjūnshì, Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
intending to win over the hearts of the western people.
2 Dīngchǒu,
Yān's Mùróng Bá attacked Wèi's Lìngzhī garrison,
captured it,
Sù Tàgān fled,
and captured Wèi's Liáoxī Tàishǒu Nà Xié.
Yān appointed Bá as Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ,
to guard Lìngzhī,
and appointed Zhōngjiān Jiāngjūn Liáoxī Yáng Háo as the commandery Tàishǒu.
Dīnghài,
appointed Zhāngwǔ Gōng Yuān as Shàngshū Lìng,
Bólíng Gōng Qián as Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè,
Shàngshū Wáng Téng as Yòu Púyè.
3 Wùzǐ,
Wèi's Cáiguān Jiāngjūn Hé Tū attacked the various tribes of Chùfú, Sùgǔyán, etc.,
and defeated them.
Initially,
Wèi Zhǔ Guī sent Northern Region Dàrén Hè Dígān to offer a thousand horses to Qín to propose marriage,
Qín Wáng Xīng heard that Guī had already established Empress Mùróng
The establishment of Empress Mùróng is recorded in the fourth year of Lóng'ān in the previous scroll.
Mòyìgān, Chùfú, Sùgǔyán,
were all vassal states of Qín,
and Wèi attacked them,
thus creating a rift between Qín and Wèi.
Gēngyín,
Guī conducted a grand review of troops and horses,
and ordered the various commanderies of Bìngzhōu to store grain at Qiánbì in Píngyáng to prepare against Qín.
Wèi Shōu's Treatise on Geography,
Píngyáng Qínchāng County,
was Běiqū of Hàn and Jìn,
and had Qiánchéng.
Suí merged Qínchāng into Xiānglíng.
Also, according to the Records of Yáo Xīng,
Qiánbì is Qiánchéng.
Róurán Shèlún was currently on good terms with Qín,
and sent a general to rescue Chùfú and Sùgǔyán;
Xīnmǎo,
Hé Tū intercepted and attacked,
greatly defeating them,
Shèlún led his tribes far into retreat north of the desert,
seizing the lands of the Gāochē and settling there.
Húlǜ tribe leader Bèi Hóulì attacked Shèlún,
was greatly defeated by him,
Bèi Hóulì fled to Wèi.
Shèlún then attacked the remnant Xiongnu tribe Rìbáyějī to the northwest,
greatly defeating them,
and subsequently annexed the various tribes,
his troops and horses multiplied and flourished,
becoming powerful in the north.
His territory extended west to Yānqí,
east connecting to Cháoxiǎn,
south bordering the great desert,
and the small states on all sides were all subjugated and attached to him;
he proclaimed himself Dòudài Kèhán.
Wèi Shōu's book writes
"Qiūdòudài",
in Wèi language meaning to drive and expand.
Hán,
read as hán.
Dù Yòu said: The title Kèhán originated with Róurán Shèlún,
similar to saying emperor.
However, the ancestors of the Tuòbá clan,
in the Comprehensive Mirror, are all recorded as Kèhán,
which was before Shèlún.
He organized a thousand men as an army,
the army had a general;
a hundred men as a chuáng,
the chuáng had a leader.
Army generals and chuáng leaders,
were all Wèi institutions,
Shèlún likely imitated and established them.
Jiàng,
read as jiàng.
Chuáng,
read as chuáng.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
Those who were cowardly had stones thrown at their heads and were killed.
Róurán becoming a problem for Wèi began from this.
4 Tūfǎ Rùtán captured Xiànměi,
captured Mèng Yī and reprimanded him for not surrendering earlier.
Tūfǎ Rùtán had been attacking Xiànměi since last year,
and only now captured it.
"Yī received deep favor from the Lǚ family,
entrusted with authority to guard this territory;
if I had surrendered upon seeing your esteemed army's banners upon arrival,
I fear I would have incurred blame from those in charge."
Rùtán released him and treated him with respect,
relocated over two thousand households and returned,
appointing Yī as Left Marshal.
Yī declined, saying:
"The Lǚ family is about to perish,
the imperial court will certainly take the region west of the Yellow River,
everyone, wise or foolish, knows this.
But Yī, tasked with defending the city, failed to preserve it,
and to further accept a prominent appointment
would privately trouble my conscience.
If I may receive your grace,
allowing me to go to Gūzāng to face execution,
I would die without regret."
Rùtán, admiring his righteousness, sent him back.
5 The eastern regions suffered from the rebellion of Sūn Ēn,
leading to famine,
and grain transport was interrupted.
Huán Xuán blocked the river routes,
causing both public and private shortages,
so bran and acorns were given to the soldiers.
Xuán believed the court had many worries,
certainly having no leisure to attack him,
allowing him to conserve strength and watch for opportunities.
When the imperial army was about to set out,
his cousin, the Grand Tutor's Chief Clerk Shí Shēng, secretly informed him by letter;
Xuán was greatly alarmed,
and wanted to consolidate at Jiānglíng.
Chief Clerk Biàn Fànzhī said:
"Your illustrious might shakes both near and far,
Yuánxiǎn's mouth still smells of milk,
Liú Láozhī has greatly lost popular sentiment;
if our troops approach the capital region,
demonstrating fortune and misfortune,
a collapse can be expected by merely lifting a foot.
How can we allow the enemy to enter our territory,
bringing hardship upon ourselves!"
Xuán followed this advice,
leaving Huán Wěi to guard Jiānglíng,
submitted a memorial and issued a proclamation,
listing Yuánxiǎn's crimes,
and led troops eastward.
When the proclamation arrived,
Yuánxiǎn was greatly afraid.
In the second month,
on Bǐngwǔ,
the Emperor farewelled Yuánxiǎn at West Pond;
Yuánxiǎn boarded the ship but did not depart.
Yuánxiǎn inwardly feared Huán Xuán,
hence boarded the ship but did not depart.
6 On Guǐchǒu,
Wèi's Prince of Chángshān Tuóba Zūn and others reached Gāopíng.
Last year in the twelfth month,
Wèi sent Zūn and others to attack Gāopíng,
arriving now.
Leading several thousand cavalry, they pursued Liú Bóbó to Qínzhōu.
Qínzhōu's seat was at Shàngguī.
Leading,
read as "commanding."
Cavalry,
pronunciation according to Qíjì.
Failing to catch up, they returned,
seizing all the treasury's accumulated wealth,
over forty thousand horses,
and over ninety thousand miscellaneous livestock,
relocating the people to Dàidū.
Wèi made Píngchéng its Dàidū.
Píngyáng Prefect Èrchén again invaded Qín's Hédōng.
Surname genealogy: In the Spring and Autumn period, states of Èr and Zhěn,
later both became surnames.
Èr in Èrchén,
is a non-Han surname.
Again,
pronunciation according to Fúyòu.
Cities in Guānzhōng closed their gates by day,
Qín people selected troops and trained soldiers to plan an attack on Wèi.
7 King of Qín Yáo Xīng established his son Yáo Hóng as Crown Prince,
and issued a general amnesty.
Hóng was filial, friendly, tolerant, and harmonious,
fond of literature,
skilled in conversation and poetry,
but weak and often ill;
Xīng wanted to make him heir,
but hesitated and could not decide,
only establishing him after a long time.
This sets the stage for Yáo Hóng's weakness leading to Qín's downfall.
8 Gūzāng suffered a great famine,
one dǒu of rice cost five thousand coins,
people ate each other,
over a hundred thousand starved to death.
City gates were closed by day,
paths for gathering firewood were cut off,
people requesting to leave the city to become slaves of the non-Han tribes
numbered several hundred daily.
Lǚ Lòng, disliking how this dampened morale,
had them all buried alive,
corpses piled up filling the roads.
Jùqú Méngxùn led troops to attack Gūzāng,
Lòng sent an envoy to seek help from King of Héxī Tūfǎ Lìlùgū.
Lìlùgū sent Duke of Guǎngwǔ Rùtán to lead ten thousand cavalry to rescue him;
before arriving,
Lòng defeated Méngxùn's army.
Méngxùn requested an alliance with Lòng,
left over ten thousand hú of grain for him and returned.
Rùtán reached Chāngsōng,
heard Méngxùn had already retreated,
then relocated over five hundred households from Liángzé Duànzhǒng and returned.
Liángzé is the Zhūyě Marsh of the Tribute of Yǔ,
east of Wǔwēi County,
also called Xiūtú Marsh.
Returned,
pronunciation according to Cóngxuān.
Palace Attendant-in-Ordinary Zhāng Róng said to Lìlùgū:
Attendant,
pronunciation according to Xǐdǎn.
Cavalry,
pronunciation according to Qíjì.
"Jiāo Lǎng and his brother hold Wèi'ān,
secretly communicating with the Yáo clan,
repeatedly shifting allegiances;
if we do not take them now,
they will surely become a worry for the court later."
Lìlùgū sent Rùtán to attack them,
Lǎng bound himself and surrendered.
Jiāo Lǎng used Wèi'ān to summon Qín troops,
events seen last year in the fifth month.
Surrendered,
pronunciation according to Hùjiāng;
same below.
Relocated his people to Lèdū.
9 Huán Xuán set out from Jiānglíng,
worried about failure,
often planning to return west;
upon passing Xúnyáng,
seeing no imperial troops,
he was very pleased,
and the troops' morale also rose.
The historian notes Huán Xuán's timidity,
and that Liú Láozhī and others could not rely on righteousness to capture him.
General,
pronunciation according to Jíliàng;
same below.
Yǔ Kǎi's plot was exposed,
Xuán imprisoned him.
On Dīngsì,
an edict sent Prince of Qí Róuzhī with the zōuyú banner to proclaim to Jīng and Jiāng provinces,
ordering them to cease troops;
Xuán's vanguard killed him.
Róuzhī was Sīmǎ Zōng's son.
In the tenth year of Xiàowǔ's Tàiyuán era,
Róuzhī inherited the title Prince of Qí,
continuing the line of Yōu and Jiǒng;
Zōng was enfeoffed as Prince of Nándùn.
On Dīngmǎo,
Xuán reached Gūshú,
sent his general Féng Gāi and others to attack Lìyáng.
Yùzhōu's provincial seat was at Lìyáng.
Xuán's army cut off Dòngpǔ,
Dòngpǔ is Dòngkǒu,
where Wèi's Cáo Xiū defeated Lǚ Fàn.
Cut off,
pronunciation according to Dīngguǎn.
Yùzhōu Governor Prince of Qiáo Shàngzhī led nine thousand infantry to array at the shore,
sent Wǔdū Prefect Yáng Qiū to garrison Héngjiāng,
Qiū surrendered to Xuán's army.
Shàngzhī's forces collapsed,
he fled to Túzhōng,
Xuán captured him.
Tú,
same as Chú.
Abandoned the city and fled.
Liú Láozhī had long disliked General of Agile Cavalry Yuánxiǎn,
fearing that once Huán Xuán was eliminated,
Yuánxiǎn would become even more arrogant and unrestrained,
and also fearing his own merit and fame would grow too great,
not tolerated by Yuánxiǎn;
moreover, relying on his own talent and military prowess,
commanding strong troops,
he intended to use Xuán to eliminate those in power,
then watch for Xuán's weaknesses and take power himself,
hence unwilling to attack Xuán.
Yuánxiǎn was intoxicated day and night,
appointed Láozhī as vanguard,
Láozhī repeatedly went to his gate,
but could not see him,
and when the Emperor farewelled Yuánxiǎn,
only met him in the public seat.
Thereupon, Liáo Zhī gathered his officials and staff in large numbers,
to discuss occupying the region north of the Yangtze River to attack Xuán.
Army Advisor Liú Xí said:
"Among things that cannot be done, none is greater than rebellion.
General, in previous years you rebelled against Wáng, the Governor of Yǎnzhōu,
(Wáng, Governor of Yǎnzhōu,
refers to Wáng Gōng.)
and against the young lord Simǎ,
(refers to Yuán Xiǎn.)
One man rebelling three times,
how can he establish himself!"
When he finished speaking,
he hurried out,
and many of the subordinate officials scattered and fled.
Liáo Zhī became fearful,
and sent Jìng Xuān to Jīngkǒu to fetch his family,
but they failed to arrive by the appointed time.
Liáo Zhī thought the affair had already been exposed,
and that Jìng Xuān had been killed by Xuán,
so he led his troops northward in flight,
reaching Xīnzhōu,
where he hanged himself and died.
When Jìng Xuān arrived,
he had no time to mourn,
and immediately crossed the river, fleeing to Guǎnglíng.
The generals and officials jointly encoffined and buried Liáo Zhī,
and returned his remains to Dāndù.
Xuán ordered the coffin split open and the head severed,
exposing the corpse in the marketplace.
(Expose,
pronounced bù bǔ fān,
or also as the original character.)
10. A great amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed to Dàhēng.
11. Huán Xuán declined the titles of Chancellor, and the three provinces of Jīng, Jiāng, and Xú.
(Xuán, having already appointed his brothers to oversee the three provinces of Jīng, Jiāng, and Xú,
and having now obtained Jiànkāng,
grasped the court's power,
no longer considered the Chancellorship important,
therefore declined them all.)
He was appointed to oversee all affairs;
and Lángyé Prince Dé Wén was made Grand Tutor.
12. Sīmǎ Xiūzhī, Liú Jìngxuān, and Gāo Yǎzhī all fled to Luòyáng,
each sending their sons or younger brothers as hostages to Qín to seek aid.
The Qín ruler, Xīng, gave them tallies and credentials,
sending them within Guānzhōng
to recruit troops,
where they obtained several thousand men,
and returned again to station themselves in the Péngchéng area.
13. Sūn Ēn raided Línhǎi,
and the Línhǎi Grand Administrator Xīn Jǐng attacked and defeated him.
The men and women from Sān Wú whom Ēn had captured
were nearly all dead.
Ēn, fearing capture by the government troops,
then threw himself into the sea and died.
His followers and concubines who followed him in death numbered in the hundreds,
and they were called
"Water Immortals."
The remaining several thousand followers again chose Ēn's brother-in-law Lú Xún as their leader.
(Xún
was the great-grandson of Chén.
Lú Chén,
son of Lú Zhì,
initially followed Liú Kūn.
After Kūn's death,
he served the Duàn clan.
After Duàn Liáo's defeat,
he served Zhào.
Chén,
pronounced shì rén fān.)
He was exceptionally talented and skilled.
In his youth,
the Buddhist monk Huì Yuǎn once said to him:
"Although you, sir, embody refinement and simplicity,
your ambitions harbor disloyalty.
What is to be done?"
Grand Marshal Xuán, wishing to pacify the eastern regions,
then appointed Xún as Grand Administrator of Yǒngjiā.
(In the first year of the Tàiníng era of Emperor Míng,
Yǒngjiā Commandery was established from part of Línhǎi,
present-day Wēnzhōu.)
Yet his raiding and violence did not cease.
(The affairs of Lú Xún begin here.)
14. On the jiǎxū day,
Yān declared a great amnesty.
15. The Héxī King, Tūfā Lìlùgū, fell seriously ill,
and in his final decree entrusted state affairs to his younger brother, Rùtán.
Initially,
Tūfā Sīfùjiān loved and valued Rùtán greatly.
(Jiān,
pronounced jū yán fān.)
He said to his sons:
"Rùtán's capacity and insight
are not something any of you can match."
Therefore, the elder brothers did not pass it to their sons but to their younger brother.
(Wú Shòumèng considered his youngest son Jì Zhá worthy,
so his various sons and brothers passed it among themselves,
wishing to eventually pass the state to Jì Zhá,
yet Jì Zhá ultimately did not accept.
Tūfā Wūgū and Lìlùgū passing the state to Rùtán
is like the intention in Wú,
yet how could they know the state would perish by Rùtán's hand!)
He merely reigned passively.
(Passive reign
means hanging robes and folding hands, doing nothing.)
Lìlùgū died,
Rùtán succeeded to the position,
and changed his title to King of Liáng.
From this point, history refers to the Tūfā clan as Southern Liáng.
He moved the capital to Lèdū,
and posthumously honored Lìlùgū as King Kāng.
16. In summer,
the fourth month,
Grand Marshal Xuán went out to station troops at Gūshú,
resigning from the position of Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
An edict approved this;
yet all major policies were still referred to him for consultation,
while minor matters were decided by the Imperial Secretariat Director Huán Qiān and Biàn Fànzhī.
Since the Lóng'ān era,
people both inside and outside the court had grown weary of calamity and disorder.
When Xuán first arrived,
he dismissed the treacherous and flattering,
promoted the outstanding and worthy,
and the capital rejoiced,
hoping for a period of slight peace.
But soon Xuán became extravagant, arrogant, and unrestrained,
his policies and decrees inconsistent,
factions arose mutually,
they bullied and insulted the court,
reduced and cut back the supplies and ceremonial items for the imperial carriage,
and the Emperor nearly could not avoid hunger and cold.
Because of this, the hearts of the multitude were disappointed.
In Sān Wú, a great famine occurred,
the registered population was reduced by half,
in Kuàijī by three or four-tenths,
in Línhǎi and Yǒngjiā nearly entirely,
wealthy families all wore fine silks,
held gold and jade,
shut their doors and together starved to death.
This was certainly caused by the failure of governance by those above,
yet the depletion of people and exhaustion of things
is also part of the great cycle of Heaven and Earth.
("Of the remaining people of Zhōu,
not a single one was left";
viewing it from this,
such events can indeed occur.)
(Wear,
pronounced yú jì fān.)
17. Qǐfú Chìpán escaped from Xīpíng and returned to Yuànchuān.
(Qǐfú Gānguī sent Chìpán to Xīpíng;
see the fourth year of Lóng'ān in the previous scroll.)
Qǐfú Gānguī sent Chìpán to present himself at the Qín court,
and the Qín ruler Xīng appointed Chìpán as Grand Administrator of Xīngjìn.
18. In the fifth month,
Lú Xún entered Dōngyáng from Línhǎi.
Grand Marshal Xuán sent Army-Pacifying Central Army Advisor Liú Yù to lead troops to attack him.
Xún was defeated,
and fled to Yǒngjiā.
19. Gāogōulí attacked Sùjūn.
(Sùjūn City is northeast of Lóngchéng.
Gōu,
pronounced as the character,
also pronounced jū.
Lí,
pronounced lì zhī fān.)
The Northern Yān Provincial Governor of Píngzhōu administered Sùjūn.
20. The Qín ruler Xīng mobilized large armies from various regions,
dispatching Yìyáng Duke Píng, Imperial Secretariat Vice Director Dí Bózhī and others to lead forty thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Wèi.
Xīng personally led a large army to follow them,
appointing Imperial Secretariat Director Yáo Huǎng to assist the Crown Prince Hóng in guarding Cháng'ān,
Mòyígàn to temporarily guard Shàngguī,
and Guǎnglíng Duke Qīn to temporarily guard Luòyáng.
Píng attacked Wèi's Qiánbì for over sixty days,
and captured it.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Wèi ruler Guī sent Pílíng Prince Shùn and Provincial Governor of Yùzhōu Zhǎngsūn Féi to lead sixty thousand cavalry as the vanguard,
and personally led a large army to follow and attack them.
21. In the eighth month,
Grand Marshal Xuán hinted to the court that, for his merit in pacifying Yuán Xiǎn, he should be enfeoffed as Duke of Yùzhāng,
and for his merit in pacifying Yīn and Yáng, he should be enfeoffed as Duke of Guìyáng,
while retaining his original enfeoffment as Duke of Nánjùn.
Xuán enfeoffed Yùzhāng upon his son Shēng,
and Guìyáng upon his elder brother's son Jùn.
The Wei ruler Guī arrived at Yǒng'ān.
Yǒng'ān was originally the Hàn dynasty's Zhì County,
belonging to Hédōng Commandery.
Emperor Shùn changed its name to Yǒng'ān.
During the Jìn dynasty, it belonged to Píngyáng Commandery.
The Suí and Táng dynasties' Huòyì County of Jìn Prefecture was originally Yǒng'ān County.
Lì Dàoyuán said: Yǒng'ān
was the former capital of the Earl of Huò.
The county has Mount Huòtài.
Chángsūn Féi intercepted and attacked them,
capturing them all.
Píng retreated and fled.
Guī pursued him.
On the yǐsì day,
he caught up at Cháibì.
Píng barricaded himself within the city walls and defended firmly.
The Wei army besieged him.
The Qín king Xīng led an army of forty-seven thousand to rescue him,
intending to occupy Tiāndù to transport grain to supply Píng.
Cháibì is east of the Fén River.
Tiāndù is likely the name of a crossing on the Fén River,
located on the west bank of the Fén River.
"The Art of War states: Those occupying high ground can be 'perched upon' by the enemy;
those in deep positions can be 'imprisoned' by the enemy.
Now Qín is violating both principles.
We should, before Xīng arrives,
dispatch a surprise force to first occupy Tiāndù.
Then Cháibì can be taken without a fight."
Guī ordered the fortification of a double-layered encirclement,
internally to prevent Píng from breaking out,
externally to resist Xīng's entry.
General Ān Tóng of Guǎngwǔ said:
"East of the Fén River is the Méngkēng,
stretching over three hundred lǐ east to west,
with no accessible paths.
When Xīng comes,
he will certainly come from west of the Fén River straight to Cháibì.
If so,
the enemy's forces and momentum will connect,
and even if our double encirclement is solid,
we will not be able to control them.
It would be better to build a pontoon bridge,
cross to the west of the Fén,
and construct defensive positions to resist them.
When the enemy arrives,
they will have no way to apply their wisdom and strength."
Guī followed this advice.
Xīng reached Púbǎn,
but fearing Wei's strength,
he delayed for a long time before advancing his troops.
On the jiǎzǐ day,
Guī led thirty thousand infantry and cavalry to intercept and attack Xīng south of Méngkēng,
beheading over a thousand men.
Xīng retreated and fled over forty lǐ.
Píng also did not dare to come out.
Guī then divided his troops to occupy four strategic points,
preventing the Qín troops from approaching Cháibì.
Xīng encamped west of the Fén River,
relying on ravines to build fortifications.
He tied bundles of cypress wood and set them adrift from upstream on the Fén River,
intending to destroy the pontoon bridge.
The Wei soldiers hooked them all out and used them as firewood.
Coarse wood is called xīn,
fine wood is called zhēng.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Píng's grain was exhausted and his arrows spent.
At night,
he led all his troops in a breakout attempt through the southwestern encirclement to escape.
Xīng arrayed his troops west of the Fén,
lighting signal fires and raising a clamor in response.
Xīng wanted Píng to fight desperately to break out and escape.
Píng looked to Xīng to attack the encirclement and provide a link-up,
but they only shouted back and forth in response,
none daring to press close to the encirclement.
Píng could not break out.
With his plans exhausted,
he led his followers to drown themselves in the river.
Many of his generals followed Píng into the water.
Guī sent skilled swimmers to hook and capture them,
and none escaped.
They captured Dí Bózhī and the Commandant of the Rapid as Tigers Cavalry, Táng Xiǎofāng, among over forty others.
The remaining twenty-thousand-plus troops all surrendered and were taken prisoner.
Xīng watched helplessly as they met their end,
powerless to save them.
His entire army wailed in grief,
the sound shaking the mountains and valleys.
He repeatedly sent envoys to seek peace with Wei,
but Guī refused.
Riding the momentum of victory, he advanced to attack Púbǎn.
The Qín Duke of Jìn, Xù, defended firmly and did not give battle.
It happened that the Róurán were planning to attack Wei.
Guī heard of this,
and on the wùshēn day,
led his troops back.
Someone reported that the Grand Astrologer Cháo Chóng and his brother, the Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gates Cháo Yì, had secretly summoned Qín troops.
When Guī reached Jìnyáng,
he ordered Chóng and Yì to commit suicide.
23 Qín relocated over ten thousand households of powerful local families from Héxī to Cháng'ān.
24 Grand Marshal Xuán killed Wúxīng Grand Administrator Gāo Sù, General Zhú Qiānzhī, and Qiānzhī's elder cousin Lǎngzhī, Liú Xí, and Xí's younger brother Jìwǔ.
All were former generals of Liú Láozhī's Northern Headquarters.
Xí's elder brother, Jìzhōu Governor Liú Guǐ, invited Sīmǎ Xiūzhī, Liú Jìngxuān, Gāo Yǎzhī, and others to jointly occupy Shānyáng. Shěn Yuē said: Shānyáng
was originally territory of Shèyáng County.
During the Yìxī period, territorial reorganization
first divided Guǎnglíng Commandery to establish Shānyáng Commandery and Shānyáng County.
The Táng dynasty's Chǔ Prefecture is this area.
They intended to raise troops to attack Xuán,
but were unsuccessful and fled.
Generals Yuán Qiánzhī, Liú Shòu, Gāo Chángqìng, Guō Gōng, and others all went to join them,
planning to flee to Wei.
When they reached south of Chénliú,
they split into two groups: Guǐ, Xiūzhī, and Jìngxuān fled to Southern Yān,
while Qiánzhī, Shòu, Chángqìng, and Gōng fled to Qín.
The Wei ruler Guī initially heard that Xiūzhī and the others were coming,
and was greatly pleased.
Later, he wondered why they had not arrived,
and ordered the Governor of Yǎnzhōu to seek and inquire. (In the fifth year of Lóng'ān,
Wei appointed Chángsūn Féi as Governor of Yǎnzhōu
to campaign southward and seize territory,
but he did not yet hold Yǎnzhōu.)
He asked the reason,
and they all said:
"The prestige and reputation of the Wei court spread far,
therefore Xiūzhī and the others all wished to submit and join.
But then they heard that Cuī Chěng had been killed." (Cuī Chěng's death is recorded in the third year of the previous scroll.)
Guī deeply regretted this.
From then on, when scholars committed offenses,
they were often treated with leniency.
25 The Southern Liáng king Tǎntán attacked Lǚ Lóng at Gūzāng.
26 The Yān king Xī took as consorts the two daughters of the former Zhōngshān Prefect Fú Mó. (When the Yān king Bǎo first ascended the throne,
Fú Mó was Prefect of Zhōngshān.)
The elder was made a Noble Lady,
the younger, named Xùnyīng,
was made a Noble Consort,
and the Noble Consort was especially favored.
Empress Dowager Dīng was resentful and angry.
She plotted with her nephew, the Secretary Shàng Xìn, to depose Xī and install the Duke of Zhāngwǔ, Mùróng Yuān.
The plot was discovered.
Xī forced Empress Dowager Dīng to commit suicide,
buried her with the rites of an empress,
and gave her the posthumous title Xiàn Yōu Empress. (Empress Dowager Dīng had previously had an affair with Xī; the matter is recorded in the previous year.)
On the wùchén day,
he killed Yuān and Xìn.
On the xīnwèi day,
Xī went hunting at Běiyuán. (Běiyuán is north of Lóngchéng.)
The magistrate of Shíchéng County,
which belonged to Běipíng Commandery during the Hàn
and to Jiàndé Commandery during Yān,
Gāo Hé, was originally the magistrate of Shíchéng.
At that time, he was in Lóngchéng for the grand mourning.
He killed the Colonel-Director of Retainers Zhāng Xiǎn,
entered and plundered the palaces,
seized weapons from the armory,
coerced the military camps and offices,
closed the gates, and ascended the city walls.
Xī galloped back.
The men on the city walls all threw down their weapons and opened the gates.
He executed all the rebels,
only Hé escaped and got away.
On the jiǎxū day,
a general pardon was declared.
27 Wei appointed Yǔ Yuè as Minister of Works.
28 In the twelfth month,
on the xīnhài day,
the Wei ruler Guī returned to Yúnzhōng.
The Róurán Khagan Shèlún heard that Guī was attacking Qín,
and invaded Wei from Cānhépō,
reaching Cháishān. (Cháishān is north of Shànwú County.
In the sixth year of Wèi's Tiānxīng period,
a palace was built here.)
Lún is pronounced Lú Kūn.
The Wei Prince of Chángshān, Mùróng Zūn, led ten thousand cavalry in pursuit,
but failed to catch up and returned.
29 Grand Marshal Xuán sent the Censor Dù Lín to escort the Prince Wénxiào of Kuaijī, Sīmǎ Dàozǐ, to Ānchéng.
Lín, following Xuán's intention,
poisoned Dàozǐ,
killing him.
30 The Western Commandery Grand Administrator appointed by Jǔqú Méngxùn, Liáng Zhōngyōng, rebelled
and fled to Western Liáng.
Méngxùn heard of this
and laughed, saying:
"I treated Zhōngyōng
with the kindness of flesh and blood,
yet Zhōngyōng did not trust me.
He only betrayed himself.
How could I, alone, be in this one man!"
He then returned all of Zhōngyōng's wife and children to him.
The King of Southern Liáng, Tufa Rùtán, and Jǔqú Méngxùn each dispatched troops to attack Lǚ Lóng,
causing Lǚ Lóng great distress.
A strategist of Qín spoke to the King of Qín, Yáo Xīng, saying:
"Lǚ Lóng relies on the resources of his ancestors,
ruling exclusively beyond the Yellow River.
Although he is currently suffering from famine and hardship,
he can still sustain himself.
If he becomes prosperous in the future,
he will ultimately not be ours.
Liángzhōu is strategically remote and difficult to access,
with fertile and abundant land.
It would be better to take advantage of his crisis and seize it."
Yáo Xīng then sent an envoy to summon Lǚ Chāo to serve in the court.
Lǚ Lóng, realizing that Gūzāng could not sustain itself in the long run,
used Lǚ Chāo's request to seek refuge in Qín.

Yáo Xīng sent the Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Qí Nán, General Zhènxī Yáo Jié, Left Worthy King Qǐfú Gānguī, and General Zhènyuǎn Zhào Yào to lead 40,000 infantry and cavalry to welcome Lǚ Lóng west of the Yellow River.
The King of Southern Liáng, Tufa Rùtán, withdrew from the garrisons at Chāngsōng and Wèi'ān to avoid them.
Withdraw,
means to gather.
Rù,
is pronounced as nú wò.
When Qí Nán and others arrived at Gūzāng,
Lǚ Lóng, in a plain carriage with white horses, welcomed them by the roadside.
Lǚ Lóng urged Qí Nán to attack Jǔqú Méngxùn.
Jǔqú Méngxùn sent Zāng Mòhái to resist,
defeating Qí Nán's vanguard.
Qí Nán then formed an alliance with Jǔqú Méngxùn.
Jǔqú Méngxùn sent his younger brother, Ná, to offer tribute to Qín.
Qí Nán appointed Sima Wáng Shǎng as the acting Governor of Liángzhōu,
assigning him 3,000 soldiers to garrison Gūzāng.
He appointed General Yán Sōng as the Governor of Cāngsōng.
Cāngsōng
is the Hàn-era Chāngsōng County.
They divided the garrisons between the two cities
and relocated Lǚ Lóng's clan, officials, and 10,000 households to Cháng'ān.
The historical records state: From Lǚ Guāng to Lǚ Lóng, it lasted thirteen years before being destroyed.
Scatter,
is pronounced as xī dǎn.
Cavalry,
is pronounced as qí jì.
The remaining civil and military officials were promoted according to their abilities.
Initially,
Guō Nún often said
"The one who replaces Lǚ will be Wáng,"
so when he raised troops,
he first supported Wáng Xiáng,

"If you can withdraw your troops and disband your armor,
I will give you a fresh start,
appointing each of you to positions,
ensuring you do not lose your status."
Liú Yù appointed Zhūgě Chángmín to oversee the military affairs north of the Huái River,
stationing him at Shānyáng.
He appointed Liú Jìngxuān as the Governor of Jiāngzhōu.
In the 14th year, the Rouran Khan Shèlún's cousin Yuèdài Dàrǎnshè plotted to kill Shèlún,
but failed,
and fled to Wèi.
In the 15th year, the King of Yān, Mùróng Xī, built the Xiāoyáo Palace in the Lóngténg Garden,
with hundreds of connected rooms.
He excavated the Qūguāng Sea.
In the height of summer,
the soldiers were not allowed to rest,
and more than half died from heatstroke.
Last year, Xī had built the Lóngténg Garden.
"Yē"
is pronounced "yú xiē fān."
It means injury from heat.
In the 16th year, the heir of Xīliáng, Lǐ Tán, died.
In the 17th year, Liú Yì, Hé Wújì, Liú Dàoguī, and the Governor of Xiàpī, Mèng Huáiyù of Píngchāng, led their troops westward from Xúnyáng.
In the fifth month,
on the day Guǐyǒu,
they encountered Huán Xuán at Zhēngróng Zhōu.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Jiāng River flows east past Wǔkǒu,
then east again,
where on the right one reaches Lǐmǔ Pǔ,
which faces Zhēngróng Zhōu to the north.
This is where Liú Yì defeated Huán Xuán,
located between present-day Huángzhōu and Shòuchāngjūn.
Dù Yòu said: Zhēngróng Zhōu is in Wǔchāng County of Èzhōu.
"Zhēng"
is pronounced "shì gēng fān."
"Róng"
is pronounced "hù méng fān."
Huán Xuán had tens of thousands of soldiers,
and our troops feared them,
wanting to retreat to Xúnyáng.
Dàoguī said:
"No!
They are many, we are few;
the disparity in strength is great.
If we fear and hesitate to advance now,
we will certainly be overwhelmed by them.
Even if we reach Xúnyáng,
how could we hold it securely?
Although Huán Xuán has a reputation as a hero,
internally he is actually timid and cowardly.
Moreover, having already suffered defeat and flight,
his troops lack steadfast resolve.
In decisive battle between two armies,
victory goes to the side with the stronger general,
not necessarily the larger force."
Thereupon, he waved his troops forward to advance,
and Yì and others followed him.
Huán Xuán often kept a small boat tied to the side of his command ship in case he needed to flee in defeat,
which meant his troops lacked the will to fight.
Yì and others took advantage of the wind to set fires,
throwing all their elite forces into the fray and vying to be first.
Huán Xuán's army was utterly routed,
and he burned his baggage and fled by night.
Guō Quán went to Yì and surrendered.
Huán Xuán's former general Liú Tǒng, Féng Zhì, and others gathered a band of four hundred men and attacked and captured Xúnyáng city.
Yì sent the General Who Establishes Might, Liú Huáisù, to suppress and pacify them.
Huáisù
was the younger brother of Huáijìng.
Liú Huáijìng appears in the 111th scroll, in the third year of Lóng'ān.
Huán Xuán took the Emperor and fled west in a single boat,
leaving the Empress Hé of Yǒng'ān and Empress Wáng in Bālíng.
Empress Hé of Yǒng'ān
was Empress Zhāng of Emperor Mù.
Empress Wáng
was the Empress of Emperor Ān.
He requested a separate boat to gather scattered troops,
then rebelled against Huán Xuán,
escorted the two Empresses to Xiàkǒu,
and eventually returned to Jiànkāng.
On the Jǐmǎo day,
Huán Xuán and the Emperor entered Jiānglíng.
Féng Gāi advised him to go downriver and fight again,
but Huán Xuán did not listen.
He wanted to flee to Hànzhōng to join Huán Xī,
who was then the Governor of Liángzhōu.
However, his orders were not obeyed.
On the Gēngchén day,
in the middle of the night,
as he was making arrangements to depart,
chaos had already erupted within the city.
So, he and over a hundred close confidants rode horses out of the city and fled westward.
Upon reaching the city gate,
his attendants attacked Huán Xuán in the darkness,
but missed.
His followers then turned on each other, killing one another,
with corpses strewn everywhere.
Huán Xuán barely managed to reach a boat,
and his attendants scattered,
leaving only Biàn Fànzhī by his side.
On the Xīnsì day,
Wáng Kāngchǎn, the Assistant Governor of Jīngzhōu, escorted the Emperor into the prefectural residence of Nánjùn,
and the Grand Administrator Wáng Téngzhī led civil and military officials to serve as guards.
Huán Xuán intended to go to Hànzhōng;
Máo Xiūzhī, the Commandant of the Garrison Cavalry,
who was the nephew of Máo Qú,
lured Huán Xuán into Shǔ,
and Huán Xuán followed him.
Máo Fán, the Governor of Níngzhōu,
who was Máo Qú’s younger brother,
died in office.
Máo Qú sent his elder brother’s grandson Máo Yòuzhī and the Army Advisor Fèi Tián, leading several hundred men, to escort Máo Fán’s coffin back to Jiānglíng.
On the Rénwǔ day,
they encountered Huán Xuán at Méihuízhōu.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Jiāng River passes south of Jiānglíng County,
where there is an islet called Méihuízhōu.
Arrows rained down like a downpour,
and Huán Xuán’s favored attendants Dīng Xiānqī and Wàn Gài shielded him with their bodies,
both dying.
Féng Qiān, the Protector of Yìzhōu from Hànjiā, drew his sword,
stepped forward intending to strike Huán Xuán,
and Huán Xuán pulled out the jade hairpin from his head and gave it to him,
explaining that since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
caps and headscarves had hairpins,
and guides,
with the most honored using jade for them.
The guide,
meaning to lead,
was used to guide the hair into the cap or headscarf.
"Who are you,
to dare kill the Son of Heaven!"
Féng Qiān replied:
"I am killing the traitor to the Son of Heaven!"
He then beheaded him,
and also executed Huán Shíkāng, Huán Jùn, and Yǔ Zé.
He captured Huán Shēng and sent him to Jiānglíng,
where he was executed in the market.
The imperial carriage returned to Jiānglíng to restore order,
and Máo Xiūzhī was appointed as the Valiant Cavalry General.
On the Jiǎshēn day,
a general amnesty was declared,
and all those who had been coerced into following the rebellion were not questioned.
On the Wùyín day,
the ancestral tablets were placed in the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
This involved receiving the ancestral temple tablets sent from Xúnyáng.
The heads were displayed on the Great Bridge.
After Liú Yì and others had won the battle,
they thought the major events were settled,
and were not in a hurry to pursue,
and also encountered wind,
so their boats could not advance.
Nearly ten days after Huán Xuán’s death,
the various armies still had not arrived.
At that time, Huán Qiān was hiding in Jǔzhōng,
which refers to the area along the Jǔ River,
encompassing the territories of Línjū and Shànghuáng counties.
Jǔ,
pronounced zǐ yú fān.
Huáróng County had belonged to Nánjùn since the Hàn dynasty.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Jiāng River branches left to form Zhōngxiàkǒu,
and on the right, Zhōnglángpǔ emerges.
Huáróng County is now within the boundaries of Jiānlì County.
The Book of Jìn, Biography of Zhèn, says: He hid in the Yǒng area of Huáróng.
The Zuǒzhuàn states: Yán Áo wandered in Yǒng and escaped.
Dù Yù’s commentary notes: Yǒng River is in Huáróng County, Nánjùn.
Yǒng,
pronounced yǒng.
He sent someone to report to Huán Zhèn, saying:
"Huán Xīn has already captured the capital,
Féng Zhì has also taken Xúnyáng,
and Liú Yì’s armies have all been defeated and retreated along the way."
Huán Zhèn was overjoyed,
gathered a band of two hundred men,
and attacked Jiānglíng,
with Huán Qiān also gathering a crowd to respond.
In the intercalary month,
on the Jǐchǒu day,
they recaptured Jiānglíng,
killing Wáng Kāngchǎn and Wáng Téngzhī.
Huán Zhèn saw the Emperor in the temporary palace,
galloping his horse and brandishing his spear,
he went straight to the steps,
and asked where Huán Shēng was.
Upon hearing that he was already dead,
he glared at the Emperor and said:
"How has my family wronged the state,
that it should be slaughtered like this!"
Lángyé Prince Déwén stepped down from the bed and said to him:
"Was this ever the intention of us brothers!"
Huán Zhèn wanted to kill the Emperor,
but Huán Qiān strenuously stopped him,
so he dismounted,
composed himself, paid his respects, and left.
On the Rénchén day,
Huán Zhèn held a mourning ceremony for Huán Xuán,
set up a mourning hall,
and posthumously honored him as Emperor Wǔdào.
On the Guǐsì day,
Huán Qiān and others led the remaining officials to present the imperial seal to the Emperor, saying:
"The former ruler followed the example of Yáo abdicating to Shùn,
but now the Chǔ mandate has not endured,
and the hearts of the people have returned to Jìn."
They appointed Lángyé Prince Déwén as the Governor of Xúzhōu,
Huán Zhèn as the Commander of Military Affairs for the Eight Commanderies and Governor of Jīngzhōu,
Huán Qiān again as Palace Attendant and Guard General,
with additional duties as Governor of Jiāngzhōu and Yùzhōu.
The Emperor’s attendants and guards
were all Huán Zhèn’s confidants.
Huán Zhèn had been frivolous in his youth,
and Huán Xuán did not treat him as a nephew.
At this point,
he sighed and said:
"If you had employed me earlier,
this defeat would not have occurred.
If you were still here,
with me as the vanguard,
the empire could easily be pacified.
Now, acting alone like this,
where can I turn?"
He then indulged in wine and women,
and wantonly carried out killings.
Huán Qiān advised Huán Zhèn to lead troops downriver to fight,
while he himself guarded Jiānglíng.
Huán Zhèn had always looked down on Huán Qiān,
and did not heed his advice.
Liú Yì arrived at Bālíng,
and executed Wáng Zhìhuī.
Hé Wújì and Liú Dàoguī attacked Huán Qiān at Mǎtóu,
which is on the southern bank of the great Jiāng River,
facing north toward Jiāngjīnkǒu.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: East of Língxī is Lóngbēi,
which is over two hundred paces in circumference,
with deep waters,
and a dragon was seen within it,
hence the name Lóngbēi.
Huán Wèi,
was the son of Huán Mì.
Huán Mì appears in the 103rd volume, in the first year of Xiàowǔ’s Níngkāng era.
Hé Wújì wanted to take advantage of the victory and head straight for Jiānglíng,
but Liú Dàoguī said:
"The art of war speaks of advancing and retreating at the right time;
one cannot recklessly press forward.
The Huán family has lived in Western Chǔ for generations,
and even the young and lowly exert their utmost efforts for them;
Huán Zhèn’s bravery is unmatched in the army,
making it difficult to contend with him head-on.
We should rest our troops and build up strength,
and gradually devise strategies to contain him,
and we will surely overcome him."
Hé Wújì did not listen.
Huán Zhèn engaged them in battle at Língxī,
where the Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Jiāng River flows south from Jiānglíng County,
passes east by Yànwěizhōu,
and joins the Língxī River to the north.
At the confluence of the Jiāng and Xī rivers is the Língxī garrison,
backed by hills and facing the river,
with Língxī to the west.
Hé Wújì and others were heavily defeated,
with over a thousand dead.
They retreated to Xúnyáng,
and together with Liú Yì and others, submitted a memorial admitting their fault.
Liú Yù, holding Liú Yì responsible for commanding the armies,
relieved him of his post as Governor of Qīngzhōu.
Huán Zhèn appointed Huán Wèi as the Governor of Yōngzhōu,
to guard Xiāngyáng.
Liǔ Yuēzhī, Luó Shù, and Zhēn Jìzhī heard that Huán Xuán had died,
and advanced their troops from Báidì to Zhījiāng.
Zhījiāng County had belonged to Nánjùn since the Hàn dynasty,
but in our dynasty it was reduced to a town,
subordinate to Sōngzī County.
Zhēn,
is pronounced like zhī.
They also led their troops to retreat.
Soon after, Shù and Jìzhī both fell ill,
and Yuēzhī went to Huán Zhèn pretending to surrender,
intending to plot a surprise attack on Zhèn.
The matter was leaked,
and Zhèn killed him.
Yuēzhī's Sima, Shí Yánzǔ,
Shí,
is a surname.
defended Fúlíng.
In the sixth month,
Máo Qú sent a general to attack Hànzhōng,
and beheaded Huán Xī.
Qú himself assumed command of Liángzhōu.
18 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on Wùshēn,
Empress Yǒng'ān, née Hé, passed away.
19 The Zhāoyí of Yān, née Fú, fell ill,
and a man from Lóngchéng named Wáng Róng claimed he could cure her.
After the Zhāoyí died,
the King of Yān, Mùróng Xī, had Róng executed at the Gōngchē Gate,
dismembered and burned.
20 In the eighth month,
on Guǐyǒu,
Empress Mùzhāng was buried at Yǒngpínglíng.
21 Wèi established six Yèguan officials,
modeled after the ancient six ministers.
22 In the ninth month,
Diāo Chěng plotted rebellion,
was executed,
and the Diāo clan thus perished.
When Diāo Kuí was executed,
only Chěng was pardoned,
while Diāo Yōng managed to flee and defect to the north;
with Chěng also executed,
the Diāo clan in Jiāngnán was thus extinguished.
Their slaves and retainers ran rampant,
monopolizing mountains and marshes,
becoming a scourge in Jīngkǒu.
Liú Yù distributed their accumulated wealth,
allowing the people to take according to their strength,
and it took days to exhaust;
at that time, the provinces and commanderies were suffering from famine and hardship,
and the people relied on this to survive.
23 Qǐfú Gānguī and Yáng Shèng fought at Zhúlǐng,
southwest of Shàngguī there are Nánshān and Zhúlǐng.
24 The Duke of Xīliáng, Lǐ Gǎo, established his son Xīn as heir apparent.
25 The Wèi ruler, Tuòbá Guī, went to the Zhāoyáng Hall to reassign and supplement the officials,
summoning the civil and military courtiers,
personally evaluating and selecting them,
appointing them according to their talents.
Nobility ranks were divided into four levels: kings were enfeoffed with large commanderies,
dukes with small commanderies,
marquises with large counties,
and earls with small counties.
Their ranks were from first to fourth,
and old ministers who had merit but no nobility were posthumously enfeoffed.
Distant imperial clansmen and those of different surnames who inherited titles were demoted in rank accordingly.
They also established five ranks of honorary officials,
with ranks from fifth to ninth;
sǎn,
is pronounced sǎndǎn.
Their ranks also corresponded to the fifth to ninth;
when official positions were vacant,
they were filled from among them.
Many official titles did not follow the old Hàn and Wèi systems,
but imitated the ancient dragon officials and bird officials.
The Zuǒzhuàn records: Tánzǐ said: In ancient times, Tàihàoshì used dragons to mark the calendar,
so they had dragon masters and dragon names.
When our ancestor Shǎohàozhì was established,
phoenixes happened to arrive,
so they had bird masters and bird names: Fèngniǎoshì,
was the calendar official;
Xuánniǎoshì,
was in charge of the equinoxes;
Bózhàoshì,
was in charge of the solstices;
Qīngniǎoshì,
was in charge of beginnings;
Dānniǎoshì,
was in charge of closures;
Zhùjiūshì,
was the Minister of Education;
Jiūjiūshì,
was the Minister of War;
Shījiūshì,
was the Minister of Works;
Shuǎngjiūshì,
was the Minister of Justice;
Gǔjiūshì,
was in charge of affairs;
the five Jiū,
gathered the people.
The five Zhì were the five craft officials,
and the nine Hù were the nine agricultural officials.
Dù Yù's commentary says: Tàihàoshì had auspicious signs of dragons,
so they used dragons to name officials.
Yīng Shào said: They used dragons to mark their officials: the spring official was the Azure Dragon,
the summer official was the Red Dragon,
the autumn official was the White Dragon,
the winter official was the Black Dragon,
and the central official was the Yellow Dragon.
Zhāng Yàn said: When Fúxī was about to rise,
a divine dragon arrived bearing a chart,
so they used it to name officials and masters.
The Wèishū Guānshìzhì records
"various departments' messengers."
Those who served as surveillance officials were called White Egrets,
because they crane their necks to look far;
the rest were similar.
26 Lú Xún invaded Nánhǎi,
attacking Pānyú.
The Governor of Guǎngzhōu, Púyáng Wú Yǐnzhī, resisted and defended for over a hundred days.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on Rénxū,
Xún attacked the city at night and captured it,
burning down government buildings and civilian houses completely,
and capturing Wú Yǐnzhī.
Xún proclaimed himself General Who Pacifies the South,
acting as Governor of Guǎngzhōu,
gathered the burned bones into a common grave,
buried on an islet,
obtaining over thirty thousand skulls.
He also sent Xú Dàofù to attack Shǐxīng.
In the first year of Gānlù of Wú's Sūn Hào,
Shǐxīng Commandery was established from the southern part of Guìyáng's Dūwèi,
which became Sháozhōu in the Táng dynasty.
27 Liú Yù assumed the post of Governor of Qīngzhōu.
Liú Yì was relieved of Qīngzhōu,
and Yù assumed it himself.
Liú Jìngxuān was in Xúnyáng,
accumulating provisions and repairing ships,
never unprepared,
so even though Hé Wújì and others were defeated and retreated,
they relied on him to recover.
Huán Xuán's nephew Liàng proclaimed himself Governor of Jiāngzhōu,
and invaded Yùzhāng.
Jìngxuān attacked and defeated him.
Liú Yì, Hé Wújì, and Liú Dàoguī again advanced westward from Xúnyáng,
reaching Xiàkǒu.
Huán Zhèn sent General Who Guards the East Féng Gāi to defend the eastern bank,
General Who Spreads Martial Might Mèng Shāntú to occupy Lǔshān City,
and General Who Supports the State Huán Xiānkè to defend the Crescent Fortress,
with a combined force of ten thousand men,
supporting each other by water and land.
Yì attacked Lǔshān City,
Dàoguī attacked the Crescent Fortress,
and Wújì blocked the middle of the river.
From chén to wǔ,
both cities collapsed.
The Hànshuǐ meets the Jiāng southwest of Lǔshān,
to the left of the Hànshuǐ is the Quèyuè City,
also called the Crescent Fortress,
which was the old Qūlíng County,
later changed to the seat of Shāyí County.
Gāi fled to Shíchéng.
28 On Xīnsì,
Wèi granted a great amnesty,
and changed the era name to Tiāncì.
They built the Western Palace.
In the eleventh month,
the Wèi ruler Guī went to the Western Palace,
ordering the imperial clan to establish clan masters,
the eight states to establish grand masters and lesser masters,
and each province and commandery to also establish masters,
to distinguish clans and factions,
recommend talent and conduct,
similar to the Zhōngzhèng officials of Wèi and Jìn.
The Wèishū Guānshìzhì says: Because the surnames and clans of the eight states were difficult to distinguish,
each state established grand masters and lesser masters,
to distinguish their clans and factions,
and evaluate and recommend talent.
Beyond the eight states,
each commandery established a master,
with duties similar to those in the eight states,
comparable to today's Zhōngzhèng.
The imperial clan established clan masters,
also similar to the duties of the provinces, commanderies, and eight states.
Xíng,
is pronounced xiàmèng.
29. The King of Yān, Mùróng Xī, went on a hunting excursion with Empress Fú.
They traveled north and ascended Báilù Mountain.
To the east, they crossed Qīnglíng.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states: The Great Liáo River flows southeast past the west of Lìxiàn in Liáodōng Commandery.
It then joins with the Báiláng River on the right.
The Báiláng River originates southeast of Báiláng County in Yòuběipíng.
It bends north,
passes west of Báilù Mountain,
which is also called Báiláng Mountain.
Qīnglíng is also known as Qīngxíng.
It is located over four hundred *lǐ* southeast of Lóngchéng.
The *Wèi Shū: Dìxíng Zhì* records
that in Shíchéng County of Jiàndé Commandery, there was a shrine at Báilù Mountain.
The Cāng Sea is south of Hǎiyáng County in Liáoxī Commandery.
Huán,
follow the *xuān* reading.
Alternatively, read as usual.
30. In the twelfth month,
Liú Yì and others advanced and captured Bālíng.
Liú Yì's orders were strict and orderly,
and the common people along their route felt secure and pleased.
Liú Yù reappointed Liú Yì as Governor of Yǎnzhōu.
Huán Zhèn appointed Huán Fàngzhī as Governor of Yìzhōu,
stationing him at Xīlíng.
Wén Chùmào attacked and defeated him,
and Fàngzhī fled back to Jiānglíng.
31. Gāogōulí invaded Yān.
32. On the *wùchén* day,
the Wèi ruler, Tuòbá Guī, went to the Cháishān Palace.
33. This year,
people of Jìn fleeing the turmoil,
carrying their infants on their backs, headed north of the Huái River, their numbers filling the roads.
