Emperor Ān Jǐ
First Year of Yìxī (Year *yǐsì*, 405)
1. Spring,
first month,
the Administrator of Nányáng, Lǔ Zōngzhī of Fúfēng, raised troops and launched a surprise attack on Xiāngyáng.
Huán Wèi fled to Jiānglíng.
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
Liú Yì and the other armies reached Mǎtóu.
Huán Zhèn, holding the Emperor captive, went out and stationed his forces at Jiāngjīn.
The Jiāngjīn garrison was at Jiānglíng,
facing the riverbank to the south.
The *Jīngzhōu Jì* says: Three *lǐ* east of Jiānglíng County was Jīnxiāng.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states: South of Jiānglíng city was the Mǎmù Fortress.
This sandbar began from Méihuí and extended down to here,
over seventy *lǐ* long.
On the sandbar was Fèngchéng,
the seat of the Jiāngjīn Commandant.
He offered to send the Son of Heaven back;
Yì and the others refused.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
Zōngzhī defeated Huán Zhèn's general Wēn Kǎi at Zuòxī.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states: The Zuòxī stream originates north of Jiānglíng County.
It seems the various pools scattered their flow,
all converging here,
accumulating to form a river.
It flows east past the south of Lǔ Zōngzhī's fortifications,
then flows east into the Chuánguān Lake.
Jiàng,
read as *jíliàng*.
Zuò,
read as *cáigè*,
also pronounced *zuò*.
The *Jùn Guó Zhì*: Over ten *lǐ* north of Jiānglíng County was Jìnán City.
He led his troops to engage Zōngzhī in battle,
and was utterly defeated.
Liú Yì and others defeated Féng Gāi at Yùzhāngkǒu.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states: The Yangtze River passes Jiānglíng and flows east,
reaching Yùzhāngkǒu,
which connects to the Xià River.
To the northwest is Yùzhāng Ridge,
from which the place likely gets its name.
It is twenty *lǐ* from Jiānglíng city.
Yì and others entered Jiānglíng,
captured Biàn Fànzhī and others,
and executed them.
Huán Zhèn returned,
saw fires rising,
knew the city had fallen,
his troops all scattered,
and Zhèn fled to Yúnchuān.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states: The Yún River originates from the Dàhóng Mountain southeast of Càiyáng County in Nányáng Commandery of Hàn.
It flows southeast,
passes west of Suí County,
then flows south past west of Ānlù County in Jiāngxià,
then flows southeast into the Xià River.
Yún,
pronounced *yún*.
On the *yǐwèi* day,
an edict decreed that all major dispositions were entrusted to the Champion General Liú Yì.
On the *wùxū* day,
a general amnesty was declared,
the era name was changed,
only members of the Huán clan were not pardoned.
Because Huán Chōng had been loyal to the royal house,
his grandson Huán Yìn was specially pardoned.
Lǔ Zōngzhī was appointed Governor of Yōngzhōu.
Máo Qú was appointed General Who Conquers the West and Commander of the military affairs of the five provinces of Yì, Liáng, Qín, Liáng, and Níng.
Qú's younger brother Máo Jǐn was appointed Governor of Liáng and Qín Provinces,
and Máo Yuàn was appointed Governor of Níng Province.
Liú Huáisù pursued and beheaded Féng Gāi at Shíchéng.
Huán Qiān, Huán Yí, Huán Wèi, Huán Mì, Hé Dànzhī, and Wēn Kǎi all fled to Qín.
Yí
was the younger brother of Huán Hóng.
(The death of Huán Hóng is recorded in the previous year's section of the previous scroll.)
2. The King of Yān, Mùróng Xī, attacked Gāogōulí.
On the *wùshēn* day,
he attacked Liáodōng.
Just as the city was about to fall,
Xī commanded his officers and soldiers:
"None of you may ascend first.
Wait until the city walls are completely leveled,
then I and the Empress will enter by carriage."
Because of this, the city had time to strengthen its defenses thoroughly,
and he failed to capture it and withdrew.
(Later, Gāo Wěi of Northern Qí's attack on Jìnzhōu
was also like this.)
Huán,
follow the *xuān* reading.
Alternatively, read as usual.
The King of Qín, Yáo Xīng, honored the monk Jiūmóluóshí as Teacher of the State,
treating him like a deity.
He personally led his assembled ministers and Buddhist monks to listen to Jiūmóluóshí lecture on Buddhist scriptures.
He also ordered Jiūmóluóshí to translate over three hundred volumes of sūtras and treatises from the Western Regions.
He constructed many pagodas and temples on a large scale.
The number of monks engaged in seated meditation often reached a thousand.
Chán,
means stillness,
tranquility.
The *Chuándēng Lù* says: There are five types of *dhyāna*:
that of ordinary people,
that of non-Buddhists,
that of the Hīnayāna,
that of the Mahāyāna,
and that of the Supreme Vehicle.
Chán,
read as *shílián*.
From this, the commanderies and counties were transformed,
and nine out of ten households engaged in Buddhist practices.
3. Qǐfú Gānguī attacked the Tǔyùhún leader Dàhái,
defeated him utterly,
captured over ten thousand people, and returned.
Dàhái fled and died in Húyuán.
The *Jìn Shū: Tǔyùhún Zhuàn* states: The Tǔyùhún king Wūgēdī
also had the name Dàhái.
"Húyuán"
is written
as "Húguó" in some texts.
Hái,
read as *hékāi*.
Mòhéchuān is northeast of the Xīqīng Mountains.
Xīqīng
is also called the Jiāngtái Mountains.
Shuài,
read as *shuài*.
Shùluògān reduced corvée labor and taxes,
was trustworthy in bestowing rewards and strict in administering punishments.
The Tǔyùhún revived,
and the various tribes of Shā and Qiáng all submitted to him.
Duàn Guó said: Southwest of Jiāohé Commandery, one hundred seventy *lǐ*, is Huángshā,
one hundred twenty *lǐ* from north to south,
seventy *lǐ* from east to west,
reaching Dàyángchuān to the west.
Looking at it is like someone scattered chaff and husks on the ground.
No plants or trees grow there,
just barren yellow sand,
extending for several hundred *lǐ* around.
The Táo River originates northeast of the Jiāngtái Mountains,
and flows through Tǔyùhún territory.
Within the three hundred *lǐ* from Táo to Jiāng, north and south,
the ground is covered with dragon's beard grass,
but there is no firewood.
This is called Jiāngchuān.
Jiāng,
read as *qúliáng*.
4. The Duke of Western Liáng, Lǐ Gǎo, proclaimed himself Grand General, Grand Commander, and Governor of Qín and Liáng Provinces.
He declared a general amnesty,
changed the era name to Jiànchū,
and sent his attendant Huáng Shǐ and Liáng Xìng to travel covertly to present a memorial at Jiànkāng.
5. Second month,
on the *dīngsì* day,
the officials at the provisional capital prepared the imperial carriage to welcome the Emperor from Jiānglíng.
Liú Yì and Liú Dàoguī remained stationed at Xiàkǒu,
while Hé Wújì escorted the Emperor eastward back to the capital.
5. During the rebellion of Huán Xuán,
Guó Fán and Shū Fán, sons of Hàjiān King Tán, fled to Southern Yān.
After the death of Hàjiān King Yóng,
who had no heir,
Emperor Yuán appointed Róng, son of Péngchéng King Zhí, as Yóng's successor.
Upon Róng's death,
again with no son,
the Emperor subsequently appointed Qīn, son of Péngchéng King Shì, as Róng's successor.
Upon Qīn's death,
Tán succeeded him;
upon Tán's death,
Guó Zhèn succeeded.
Guó Fán was likely a brother of Guó Zhèn.
When Liú Yù rose to restore [the Jin],
his intention to usurp was not yet apparent.
Guó Fán could have, like Liú Jìngxuān and others, returned south.
Yet he attacked and harassed the Jin border.
Xiù, grandson of Qīn, succeeded to the title of Zhāngwǔ.
He was a cousin of Guó Fán.
Xiù was executed for plotting rebellion as the brother-in-law of Huán Zhèn,
which is why Guó Fán and his brother dared not return south.
How could they have known that Yù would certainly usurp!
Tán,
pronunciation: tán.
Fán,
pronunciation: fán.
On the jiǎxū day,
Guó Fán and others captured Yìyáng.
6. The Yān army marched over three thousand lǐ,
with soldiers and horses exhausted and frozen,
corpses lining the roads.
They attacked the Mùdǐ fortress of Gāogōulí,
but failed to capture it and withdrew.
Mùdǐ fortress was east of Nánsū,
where the Táng established Mùdǐ Prefecture.
Gōu,
pronounced as usual,
also pronounced jū.
Lí,
pronunciation: lí.
Moreover, fearing the tyranny of Yān King Xī,
he resigned from office due to illness.
This sets the stage for the later Yān people assassinating Xī and establishing Yún.
7. In the third month,
on the gēngzǐ day,
the Wèi ruler Guī returned to Píngchéng;
in summer,
the fourth month,
on the gēngshēn day,
he went again to Cháishān Palace;
on the jiǎwǔ day,
he returned to Píngchéng.
8. Róurán Shèlún invaded the Wèi border.
9. In the fifth month,
Qián, Duke of Bólíng, and Zhāo, Duke of Shàngdǎng, both sons of Yān ruler Bǎo,
were ordered to commit suicide due to suspicion.
10. In the sixth month,
Qín's Duke of Lǒngxī, Shuòdé, came to court from Shàngguī.
The Qín ruler Xīng declared a general amnesty for him;
upon his departure,
Xīng escorted him as far as Yōng,
before returning.
Xīng treated Duke Jìn Xù and Shuòdé with the etiquette due to family elders.
Regarding carriages, horses, clothing, and playthings,
he first offered them to his two uncles, taking inferior ones for himself.
On major state policies,
he consulted them before acting.
11. Tūfǎ Rùtán attacked Jǔqú Méngxùn,
who defended his city firmly.
Rùtán advanced to Chìquán and then withdrew.
Chìquán was north of Dīchí County in Zhāngyè.
The Qín ruler Xīng, considering him loyal,
appointed Rùtán as Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs West of the River, General of Chariots and Cavalry, and Governor of Liáng Province,
stationing him at Gūzāng,
and recalling Wáng Shàng to Cháng'ān.
People of Liáng Province like Shēntú Yīng and others sent Registrar Hú Wēi to Cháng'ān to request Shàng's retention,
but Xīng refused.
Wēi, meeting Xīng,
tearfully said:
"Our province has upheld the royal transformation,
for nearly five years now.
In the ninth month of the fifth year of Lóng'ān, Lǚ Lóng surrendered to Qín,
and it has not yet been five full cycles to this point.
Though imperial majesty does not reach us directly,
the officials and people, tasting gall and wiping blood,
together defended this isolated city;
looking up, we relied on Your Majesty's sage virtue,
looking down, we leaned on the benevolent governance of a good shepherd.
Thus we managed to preserve ourselves,
until today.
Why does Your Majesty now trade us for three thousand horses and thirty thousand sheep?
To value animals over people,
surely this cannot be right!
If the army and state require horses,
simply trouble the Department of State Affairs to issue an order.
The over three thousand households of our province,
each contributing one horse,
could fulfill it by evening if ordered in the morning—
what difficulty would there be!
In the past, Emperor Wǔ of Hàn exhausted the resources and strength of the realm,
to open up Héxī,
in order to sever the right arm of the Xiōngnú.
Now Your Majesty, without cause, abandons the loyal and good Hua clans of five commanderies,
to aid a violent foe.
Not only will the officials and people of our province be plunged into misery,
I fear it may become a source of anxiety for the sagely court, causing late meals."
Xīng regretted it,
sending Chē Pǔ of Xīpíng to gallop and stop Wáng Shàng,
and also sending an envoy to instruct Rùtán.
But by then, Rùtán had already led thirty thousand infantry and cavalry and encamped at Wǔjiàn.
Wǔjiàn,
was south of Gūzāng.
Chē,
pronunciation: chē.
Shǐ (envoy),
pronunciation: shǐ.
Shuài (to lead),
read as shuài.
Rùtán urgently forced Wáng Shàng to depart;
Shàng left through the Qīngyáng Gate,
while Rùtán entered through the Liángfēng Gate.
"Qīngyáng"
should be
"Qīngyáng".
The Liángfēng Gate
was the south gate of Gūzāng.
Assistant Inspector Zōng Chǎng escorted Shàng back to Cháng'ān.
Zōng,
is a surname.
In Hàn times, there was Nányáng's Zōng Zī.
"I have obtained over three thousand households in Liáng Province,
but the one upon whom my affections rest,
is you alone.
Why do you abandon me and leave!"
Chǎng said:
"Now escorting my former lord
is how I demonstrate loyalty to Your Highness."
Rùtán said:
"As the new shepherd of this esteemed province,
what strategy should I employ to pacify those near and win over those far?"
Chǎng said:
"Though the land of Liáng is impoverished,
it is a strategically advantageous place.
If Your Highness kindly comforts its people,
gathers its worthy and outstanding men to achieve merit and fame,
what goal could you not attain!"
Thereupon, he recommended over ten noted civil and military talents from the province;
Rùtán praised and accepted them.
When Wáng Shàng reached Cháng'ān,
Xīng appointed him as a Secretary.
Rùtán feasted his officials in the Xuāndé Hall.
Looking up, he sighed and said:
"The ancients had a saying: 'The builder does not reside,
the resident does not build.'
How true!"
Wǔwēi's Mèng Yī said:
"Formerly, King Wén of Zhāng first built this hall.
To this day, a hundred years later,
it has seen twelve lords.
After Zhāng Jùn's death,
he was privately given the posthumous title King Wén.
The Zhāng clan, from Jùn through Zhònghuá, Yàolíng, Zuò, Xuánjìng, and Tiānxī, totaled six lords.
Liáng Xī, Lǚ Guāng, Lǚ Shào, Lǚ Zuǎn, Lǚ Lóng, and Wáng Shàng make another six lords,
altogether twelve lords."
Yī,
pronunciation: yī.
Rùtán approved of this.
12. The Wèi ruler Guī planned the layout of Píngchéng,
wishing to emulate Yè, Luòyáng, and Cháng'ān,
and to expand the palace buildings.
As Jìyáng Grand Administrator Mò Tí had ingenious ideas,
Emperor Huì divided Chénliú to establish the Jìyáng principality,
later making it a commandery.
Jì,
pronunciation: jǐ.
Sī (idea),
pronunciation: sì.
He consulted with him on the project's scale.
Tí, having served long, grew somewhat negligent.
Guī grew angry,
and ordered him to commit suicide.
Tí
was the grandson of Hán.
This Mò Tí is not the same as the Duke of Gāoyì, Mò Tí.
Mò Hán appears in the 89th scroll, third year of Emperor Mǐn's Jiànxīng reign.
Wèi originally had eight tribal chiefs.
After gaining the Central Plains,
they established Píngchéng as the capital of Dài,
distributing the eight tribes within the capital region.
Lěi,
pronunciation: lěi.
They dug canals and ponds,
expanded parks and hunting grounds,
planned the outer city walls,
twenty lǐ square,
laid out markets and wards,
completing the work in thirty days.
In the autumn of the 13th year,
in the seventh month,
the Grand Commandant of Wèi, Duke Dīng of Yídū, Mù Chóng, passed away.
According to the Duke of Zhōu’s posthumous naming system, “Dīng” means “to uphold righteousness but fail to achieve it.”
In the eighth month,
Tūfǎ Rùtán appointed Marquis of Xīngchéng, Wén Zhī, to guard Gūzāng,
and returned to Lèdū himself.
Although he accepted the titles and commands of Qín,
his carriages, attire, rituals, and ceremonies
were all like those of a king.
On the jiǎchén day,
the ruler of Wèi, Guī, went to the Cháishān Palace,
and then proceeded to Shímò.
North of Yīnshān, it is all desert,
including White Desert, Black Desert, and Stone Desert.
The White and Black Deserts are named for their colors,
while Stone Desert likely refers to a place where the ground is all stone.
According to the History of the Northern Dynasties,
Shímò is located northwest of Wǔyào County in Dìngxiāng Commandery of Hàn, beyond the frontier.
Crossing north of the desert,
on the guǐsì day,
he returned south to Chángchuān.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: Chángchuān City is west of Róuxuán Garrison.
When Liú Yù heard that Qiáo Zòng had rebelled,
he sent General Lóngxiāng, Máo Xiūzhī, to lead troops along with Sīmǎ Róngqī, Wén Chùmào, and Shí Yánzǔ to jointly suppress him.
Xiūzhī arrived at Dàngqú.
Dàngqú County
belonged to Bā Commandery during Hàn,
was divided into Bāxī Commandery during Liú Shǔ’s rule,
and Emperor Huì re-divided Bāxī to establish Dàngqú Commandery.
According to the Records of the Five Dynasties,
Nánchōng County in Guǒ Prefecture formerly established Dàngqú Commandery,
and Shíjìng County in Hé Prefecture also established Dàngqú Commandery,
both along the route from Báidì to Chéngdū.
Dàng
is pronounced tàng.
Chéngzǔ proclaimed himself the Governor of Bā Province,
and Xiūzhī retreated to Báidì.
Tūfǎ Rùtán sought friendly relations with Xīliáng,
and Duke of Xīliáng, Hào, agreed.
Jǔqú Méngxùn attacked Jiǔquán,
reaching Ānzhēn.
Ānzhēn was Ānmí County of Hàn’s Jiǔquán Commandery.
Later generations abbreviated it,
writing
“mí”
as
“mǐ.”
Due to transcription errors,
it was further written
“mǐ”
as
“zhēn.”
Méngxùn withdrew and returned.
Gōngsūn Wǔlóu of Nányàn wanted to monopolize court authority,
and slandered Prince Zhōng of Běidì to the ruler of Nányàn, Chāo,
requesting his execution.
When Bèidé, the ruler of Nányàn, died,
Mùróng Fǎ did not attend the funeral.
Chāo sent an envoy to reprimand him.
Fǎ became fearful,
and plotted rebellion with Zhōng and Duàn Hóng.
When Chāo heard of this,
he summoned Zhōng.
Zhōng claimed illness and did not come,
so Chāo arrested his associates, including Attendant-in-Ordinary Mùróng Tǒng,
and executed them.
Sima of the Southern Expedition, Bǔ Zhēn, reported that Left Imperial Secretary Fēng Sōng frequently interacted with Fǎ,
suspecting conspiracy.
Chāo arrested Sōng and handed him over to the Court of Judicial Review.
The Empress Dowager, fearful,
tearfully told Chāo:
“Sōng repeatedly sent the Director of the Yellow Gates, Móu Cháng, to tell me: ‘The Emperor is not born of the Empress Dowager,
and I fear a repeat of the Yǒngkāng incident.’
I am a woman with shallow understanding,
and fearing the Emperor would kill me,
I told Fǎ.
Fǎ was misled in his plans,
what more can I say?”
Chāo then had Sōng torn apart by chariots.
General of the Western Central Army, Fēng Róng, fled to Wèi.
Chāo sent Mùróng Zhèn to attack Qīng Province,
Mùróng Yù to attack Xú Province,
and Right Imperial Secretary Jìyáng Prince Níng and Hán Fàn to attack Yǎn Province.
Nányàn’s Governor of Qīng Province was stationed in Dōnglái,
the Governor of Xú Province in Jǔchéng,
and the Governor of Yǎn Province in Liángfù.
Jì
is pronounced zǐlǐ.
Duàn Hóng fled to Wèi.
Fēng Róng and bandits attacked Shísài City,
killing the Great General Who Guards the West, Yú Yù,
causing panic throughout the state.
Jìyáng Prince Níng plotted to kill Hán Fàn,
and attack Guǎnggù.
Fàn learned of this,
mobilized troops to attack Níng,
and Níng fled to Liángfù.
Fàn then led his forces,
attacked Liángfù,
and captured it.
Fǎ fled to Wèi,
and Níng fled to Qín.
Mùróng Zhèn captured Qīng Province,
and Zhōng killed his wife and children,
escaping through a tunnel,
fleeing to Qín with Duke of Gāodū, Shǐ.
Qín appointed Zhōng as the Grand Administrator of Shǐpíng,
and Níng as Attendant-in-Ordinary.
The ruler of Nányàn, Chāo, liked to change old institutions,
causing discontent both in court and among the people.
He also wanted to restore corporal punishment,
adding boiling and dismemberment by chariot as penalties,
but due to opposition, he abandoned the idea.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Fēng Fú died.
When Mùróng Chāo ascended the throne,
although he was not a young ruler,
it was a time of national suspicion and ministers not yet loyal.
Chāo could not unite them with sincerity,
causing them to take up arms,
leading to their flight and exile.
With whom could Chāo stand?
Even before Liú Yù’s troops arrived,
it was certain he would be destroyed.
The Ministry of Personnel discussed the merits of establishing righteousness,
and petitioned to enfeoff Liú Yù as Duke of Yùzhāng Commandery,
Liú Yì as Duke of Nánpíng Commandery,
Hé Wújì as Duke of Ānchéng
Commandery,
with others receiving various enfeoffments and rewards.
The Governor of Liáng Province, Liú Zhì, rebelled,
and Liú Yì sent a general to capture him.
On the gēngshēn day,
the ruler of Wèi, Guī, returned to Píngchéng.
On the yǐhài day,
Left General Kǒng Ānguó was appointed Left Imperial Secretary.
In the eleventh month,
Tūfǎ Rùtán moved to Gūzāng.
Qǐfú Gānguī went to Qín to pay court.
In the twelfth month,
Hé Wújì was appointed Commander of Military Affairs of the Eight Commanderies of Jīng, Jiāng, and Yù Provinces, and Governor of Jiāng Province.
The eight commanderies
likely refer to Wǔchāng in Jīng Province,
Xúnyáng, Yùzhāng, Lúlíng, Línchuān, Póyáng, Nánkāng in Jiāng Province,
and Jìnxī in Yù Province.
This year,
Huán Shísuí, Sīmǎ Guófán, and Chén Xí gathered bandits at Hútáo Mountain.
Hútáo Mountain is likely within the boundaries of Lìyáng Commandery.
Fán
is pronounced fúyuán.
Shísuí
was the younger brother of Shíshēng.
In spring,
the first month,
on the xīnchǒu day, the first day of the month,
Yān proclaimed a general amnesty,
and changed the era name to Jiànshǐ.
The ruler of Qín, Xīng, because Qǐfú Gānguī was growing strong and difficult to control,
kept him as Master of Guests in the Ministry of Personnel.
Emperor Chéng of Hàn established four sections in the Ministry of Personnel,
the fourth being the Master of Guests,
responsible for affairs of foreign tribes and barbarians.
He supervised his tribal followers.
After this, Qín’s governance gradually declined,
while Chìpán grew stronger day by day,
and Gānguī could no longer be kept.
Chì
is pronounced chāngzhì.
Xiào
is pronounced hùjiào.
Jiān
is pronounced gōngxián.
In the second month,
on the jǐyǒu day,
Liú Yù went to Jiànkāng,
firmly declining his newly appointed official position,
and even intending to go to the Court of Judicial Review.
An edict allowed him to retain his original post,
and Yù returned to Dāntú.
The ruler of Wèi, Guī, enfeoffed his son Xiū as Prince of Héjiān,
Chùwén as Prince of Chánglè,
Lián as Prince of Guǎngpíng,
and Lí as Prince of Jīngzhào.
5 Yīn Zhòngwén had always possessed talent and reputation,
and he himself believed he should be in charge of court administration,
but he was discontented and unable to realize his ambitions;
"discontented"
means feeling anxious and uneasy.
Zhòngwén was a partisan of Huán Xuán,
and though he hoped for advancement due to his talent and reputation, he could not advance,
hence his unease.
"Court"
is pronounced zhí yáo fān.
He was especially unhappy.
Hé Wújì had long admired his fame;
Dōngyáng
was under Wújì's jurisdiction,
as Wújì was the commander of the five commanderies east of the Zhèjiāng River,
and Dōngyáng was one of them.
Wújì was pleased
and held him in high regard.
However, Zhòngwén, disheartened and distracted,
did not visit the headquarters;
"headquarters"
refers to the command headquarters,
which was Hé Wújì's administrative seat.
"Distracted"
is pronounced hū guǎng fān.
"Confused"
is pronounced hū.
Wújì was greatly angered.
At that time, the Southern Yān invaded,
and Wújì said to Liú Yù:
"Huán Yǐn and Yīn Zhòngwén are the real afflictions at the heart,
the northern barbarians are not worth worrying about."
In the intercalary month,
Luò Bīng, a general under Liú Yù's command, plotted a rebellion,
but the plot was discovered,
and Yù executed him.
He then claimed that Bīng had secretly colluded with Zhòngwén, Huán Shísōng, Cáo Jìngzhī, Biàn Chéngzhī, and Liú Yánzǔ,
plotting to install Huán Yǐn as ruler,
and they were all executed along with their clans.
6 The Yān king Mùróng Xī built the Chénghuá Palace for his empress Fú,
transporting soil from the north gate,
making soil as expensive as grain.
Dù Jìng, the commander of the Sùjūn garrison, carried a coffin to the palace to remonstrate vehemently,
but Xī executed him.
The Northern Yān's Yíngzhōu governor was stationed at Sùjūn.
Empress Fú once craved frozen fish in late summer,
but frying fish to make it frozen
is something many people can do today;
in the sixth month of late summer, when the heat is intense,
it cannot freeze.
The Běncǎo states: Dìhuáng leaves resemble gānlùzi,
its flowers resemble zhīmá flowers,
but with fine spots,
northerners call it niúnǎizi;
in the second and eighth months,
its roots are harvested and dried in the shade;
it relieves various fevers,
breaks up blood stasis,
and promotes menstrual flow.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the guǐchǒu day,
Empress Fú died,
and Xī wept so bitterly he fainted,
reviving after a long time;
he mourned her as if for his parents,
wearing the coarsest mourning garments,
and eating only porridge.
He ordered all officials to set up mourning stations within the palace and weep,
sending people to inspect the mourners,
punishing those without tears,
so the ministers all forced themselves to shed bitter tears.
Lady Zhāng, the Princess of Gāoyáng,
was Xī's sister-in-law,
the wife of Gāoyáng Prince Mùróng Lóng.
Xī wanted her to be buried alive with the empress,
but upon destroying her burial garments, he found worn-out felt in her boots,
and thus ordered her to commit suicide.
Wéi Qiú, the Vice Director of the Right, and others all feared being forced to die as attendants,
so they bathed and awaited their fate.
From nobles and officials down to soldiers and commoners,
each household was conscripted to build the tomb,
exhausting the treasury's resources.
The tomb's perimeter spanned several li,
and Xī said to the overseer:
"Build it well,
for I will follow her there."
From these words of Xī,
it is clear his death was imminent.
"Overseer"
is pronounced gōng xián fān.
On the dīngyǒu day,
the Yān Empress Dowager Duàn removed her honorary title,
and moved out of the main palace to live in an outer residence.
7 The Dí king Yáng Shèng appointed Píngběi General Fú Xuān as the Protector of Liángzhōu,
leading troops into Hànzhōng,
and the Qín Liángzhōu Assistant Inspector Lǚ Yíng and others raised troops in response;
Lǚ Yíng likely served as the Qín Liángzhōu Assistant Inspector,
as can be inferred from the later dispatch of the Southern Liángzhōu Governor Wáng Mǐn by the Qín king Yáo Xīng to observe Qiáo Zòng.
Yíng and others sought aid from Shèng,
and Shèng sent troops to the Jìnkǒu,
forcing Mǐn to retreat and garrison at Wǔxīng.
The Shuǐjīng states: The Miǎn River flows east past the Báimǎ Garrison to the south,
where the Jìn River joins it.
The commentary notes: The Jìn River originates in the Dí territory of Wǔdū to the north,
flows south past the east of Zhāng Lǔ's city,

—to watch for opportunities against Wèi.

The Wèi emperor Tuòbá Guī returned the captured Qín general Táng Xiǎofāng to Qín.
The Qín king Yáo Xīng requested the return of Hè Dígān,

Bóbō, upon hearing that Qín had resumed relations with Wèi, grew angry,

He reached Dàchéng,

He gathered all his forces, over thirty thousand men, under the pretense of hunting in the Gāopíng River area,

The Shǐjì and Hànshū both state that the Xiōngnú were descendants of Chúnwéi, who was himself a descendant of the Xià Hòu clan.

Chán:
pronunciation "chán".
He changed the era name to Lóngshēng,

He appointed his elder brother Yòudìdài as Chancellor,

Lì Sìtí as Grand General,

Chìyú Ālì as Imperial Censor-in-Chief,

Ruòmén as Prefect of the Masters of Writing,
Chìyǐjiān as Left Executive of the Masters of Writing,
and Yǐdǒu as Right Executive of the Masters of Writing.
Hè Dígān had long been in Cháng'ān,

Upon his return,

the Yān king Xī buried his consort Fú at Huīpínglíng.

Xī, with hair disheveled and barefoot,

Jiǎzǐ,
a great amnesty was declared.
Initially, the General of the Central Guard Féng Bá and his younger brother, Palace Attendant Sùfú, had both offended Xī.
Xī wished to kill them,

Xī's taxes and corvée were numerous and frequent,

Bá, Sùfú, and their cousin Wàn
Ní plotted, saying:

means to return and plead guilty.
Shǒu:
pronunciation "shì jiù fān".
If we join together to undertake a great endeavor,

Thereupon they rode together in a carriage,
had a woman drive,

When Xī went out to attend the funeral,

Bá had long been on good terms with Mùróng Yún,

Yún declined on grounds of illness.
Yún claimed illness; see the previous year.
"Héjiān is licentious and cruel,

You, sir,
are of the renowned Gāo family.

They supported him and brought him out.

Xī retreated into the Lóngténg Garden.

Bǐngyín,

"The words of Lord Yáo are divine!"

letting them exhaust each other,
without troubling the central realm's troops."
He also did not listen.
Xīng sent a letter to Rùtán, saying:
"Now I am sending Qí Nán to campaign against Bóbó,
fearing he might flee westward,
so I have ordered Bì and others to intercept him west of the river."
Rùtán believed this,
and thus did not prepare defenses.
Bì crossed from Jīnchéng,
crossing the river from Jīnchéng.
"Now the royal army claims to campaign against Bóbó,
Rùtán is hesitant,
and his defenses are not strict.
I request five thousand light cavalry
to surprise attack his city gates.
Then the people of the mountains and marshes will all be ours,
the isolated city will have no reinforcements,
and we can capture it effortlessly."
Bì did not follow this advice,
advancing to Mòkǒu,
Mòkǒu is within the boundaries of Chāngsōng Commandery,
called Chāngsōng Mòkǒu.
According to Wèi Shōu's Treatise on Geography,
Chāngsōng Commandery had Mòkǒu County.
Bì sent someone to persuade him to surrender,
but Bà said:
"You abandon your sworn oath and attack an allied state.
I would rather die
than surrender!"
Bì launched an attack,
killed him,
and advanced swiftly to Gūzāng.
Rùtán defended the city firmly,
launched surprise attacks against Bì,
defeated him,
and Bì retreated to hold Xīyuàn.
Wáng Zhōng and others within the city plotted to act as internal agents,
but the plot was exposed,
and Rùtán intended to execute only the ringleaders and pardon the rest.
Yīlì Yánhóu, the Front Army General, said:
"Now with strong enemies outside,
and traitors secretly acting within,
what danger could be greater?
If we do not bury them all,
how will we deter others in the future!"
Rùtán followed this advice,
killing over five thousand people.
He ordered the commanderies and counties to release all cattle and sheep into the wild,
and Liǎn Chéng allowed his troops to plunder;
Rùtán sent the Great General Who Guards the North, Jù Yán, and the General Who Guards the Army, Jìng Guī, among others, to attack them,
and the Qín troops were heavily defeated,
with over seven thousand heads taken.
Rùtán released cattle and sheep to bait the enemy,
and Liǎn Chéng plundered them,
which explains his defeat.
Rùtán attacked him,
but did not overcome him.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Xīng sent the Great General of the Guards and Duke of Chángshān, Yáo Xiǎn, leading twenty thousand cavalry as reinforcements for the various armies,
reaching Gāopíng,
he heard of Bì's defeat,
and hurried there by forced march.
Xiǎn sent skilled archers Mèng Qīn and four others to challenge at the Liángfēng Gate,
but before they could draw their bows,
Rùtán's Material Officer General Sòng Yì and others met them in battle,
and killed them.
Xiǎn then shifted blame onto Liǎn Chéng,
sent an envoy to apologize to Rùtán,
pacified the areas beyond the river,
and led his troops back.
Rùtán sent the envoy Xú Sù to Qín to apologize.
The Xià king Bóbó heard that Qín troops were approaching,
and retreated to defend Héqū.
Héqū is northeast of Shuòfāng;
the Yellow River winds for a thousand lǐ.
He allowed his troops to plunder the countryside;
Bóbó secretly led his troops to launch a surprise attack,
capturing and beheading over seven thousand men.
Nán led his troops to retreat,
Bóbó pursued him to Mùchéng,
captured him,
and took thirteen thousand of his officers and soldiers prisoner.
Subsequently, tens of thousands of Yí and Xià people north of the mountains submitted to Bóbó,
and Bóbó appointed governors and magistrates to pacify them.
Yáo Bì's defeat
did not yet make Tūfǎ a threat to Qín.
But Qí Nán's defeat
made Hélián's threat flare up.
11. Sīmǎ Shūfán from Fánchéng invaded Zōushān.
The governor of Lǔjùn, Xú Yōng, abandoned the city and fled.
Chējì Chángshǐ Liú Zhōng attacked and repelled him.
12. The King of Northern Yān, Mùróng Yún, enfeoffed Mùróng Guī as the Duke of Liáodōng,
and had him preside over the sacrifices of Yān.
13. Liú Jìngxuān, having entered the gorges,
which are the so-called Three Gorges,
personally led the Governor of Yìzhōu Bào Lòu, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Wén Chùmào, and Lóngxiāng Jiāngjūn Shí Yánzǔ, advancing from Diànjiāng through successive battles.
Qiáo Zòng sought aid from Qín.
The King of Qín, Yáo Xīng, dispatched Píngxī Jiāngjūn Yáo Shǎng and Nánliángzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Mǐn to lead twenty thousand troops to assist him.
Jìngxuān's army reached Huánghǔ,
five hundred *lǐ* from Chéngdū.
Huánghǔ is near Fúchéng.
They remained locked in stalemate for over sixty days.
Jìngxuān could not advance;
provisions were exhausted,
illness and plague spread in the army,
and more than half died.
He then led the army back.
Jìngxuān was dismissed from office as punishment,
with one-third of his fiefdom revoked.
The Governor of Jīngzhōu, Liú Dàoguī, as the supervising commander, was demoted in title to Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn.
This is in accordance with the principle in the *Spring and Autumn Annals* of holding the commander responsible.
Dàoguī was then the Commander-in-Chief for the campaign against Shǔ.
Liú Yù, because of Jìngxuān's defeat,
requested to resign from his position.
An edict demoted him to Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn,
but he retained the authority to establish his own administrative office as before.
Liú Yì wanted to use severe laws to punish Jìngxuān,
but Yù protected him.
Hé Wújì said to Yì:
"How can you let personal grievance harm the utmost public good!"
(The personal grievance is mentioned in the first year of the previous reign.)
14. Qǐfú Chìpán, because the Qín administration was gradually declining,
and fearing attacks from Qín,
in winter,
the tenth month,
gathered over twenty thousand men from various tribes and built a fortified city on Kāngláng Mountain to occupy it.
Dīng Dù said: Kāngláng Mountain is in the Western Qiāng region.
I believe that since the Qǐfú clan occupied Yuànchuān,
their territory extended west to Fúhǎn,
east to Lǒngdǐ,
north bounded by Hèlián,
and south bordered Tǔyùhún.
Kāngláng Mountain should be southwest of Yuànchuān.
The western border of the Sòng dynasty reached Qín and Wèi,
so Kāngláng Mountain was then within the Western Qiāng.
Kāng,
is pronounced *qiū gāng fān*.
Láng,
is pronounced *lú dāng fān*.
15. In the eleventh month,
Tūfǎ Rùtán again proclaimed himself King of Liáng,
issued a general pardon,
changed the era name to Jiāpíng,
and established all officials.
He established his wife, Zhéjué Shì, as Queen,
and his heir, Wǔtái, as Crown Prince,
and appointed him Lù Shàngshū Shì.
Wǔtái,
originally named Hǔtái.
The Tang compilers of the *Jìn Shū*,
avoiding the taboo of the Tang ancestor's name,
changed
"Hǔ"
to
"Wǔ".
The *Comprehensive Mirror* follows this.
The Marquis of Chāngsōng, Jùyán, was made Tàiwèi.
16. In Southern Yān, the Rǔ River dried up;
("Rǔ"
should be
while the Miǎn River did not freeze.
The *Commentary on the Water Classic* states: The Miǎn River originates east of Yíngchéng,
flowing northwest into the Shí River.
Yíngchéng is Línzī City.
The Shí River commonly has the name Miǎn River,
and is also called Shí Miǎn River.
The Shí River flows northeast into the Zī River,
and the Zī River further northeast joins the Zhuó River.
The Zhuó River flows northeast past the west of Guǎnggù City.
The Zhuó River is also sometimes commonly called the Miǎn River.
In the past, when Zhào attacked Guǎnggù,
those who observed the *qì* believed that because the Miǎn River encircled the city, it could not be captured.
If the Wǔlóngkǒu were blocked,
the city would certainly fall.
They referred to this water.
Miǎn,
is pronounced *shén líng fān*.
(The King) asked Lǐ Xuān,
who replied:
"The Miǎn River not freezing
is truly because it closely encircles the capital city,
being near the sun and moon."
Chāo was greatly pleased,
and bestowed upon him a full set of court robes.
17. In the twelfth month,
Qǐfú Chìpán attacked Péng Xīniàn at Fúhǎn,
but was defeated by Xīniàn and returned.
18. This year,
the ruler of Wèi, Tuòbá Guī, killed the Duke of Gāoyì, Mò Tí.
Initially,
when Tuòbá Kūduō attacked Guī,
(see the 106th scroll, the eleventh year of Xiàowǔ's Tàiyuán era),
(Mò Tí) secretly sent an arrow to Kūduō, saying:
"How can a three-year-old calf bear a heavy load!"
Guī harbored resentment in his heart.
By now,
someone reported that Tí's demeanor was arrogant and presumptuous, imitating that of a ruler.
Guī sent someone to show the arrow to Tí and said to him:
"How did the three-year-old calf turn out?"
Tí and his son wept facing each other.
The next morning,
they were arrested and executed.
(Text punctuated by Niè Chóngqí, proofread by Wáng Chóngwǔ)
Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command
Later Student from Tiāntāi
Emperor Ān Gēng
Yìxī Fifth Year (Jǐyǒu, 409)
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the *gēngyín* day, the first day of the month,
the ruler of Southern Yān, Chāo, held court with his assembled ministers,
and lamented the inadequacy of the Grand Music.
(In the third year,
Chāo presented the Grand Music performers to Qín,
hence he lamented its inadequacy.)
Cháo,
is pronounced *zhí yáo fān*.
The General of the Imperial Guard, Hán Yuē:
(Dīng Dù said: Yuē,
is pronounced *zhú jiǎo fān*.)
"The late emperor, because the old capital had fallen,
folded his wings in Sān Qí.
When Zhōngshān fell,
Mùróng Dé abandoned Yè
and held Huátái;
later, he also lost Huátái,
and then took the Qí lands in the east and occupied them.
(These events are all recorded earlier.)
Jí,
is pronounced *jí lì fān*.
He waited for an opportunity from Wèi,
to restore the former enterprise.
Yet now we further invade and plunder our southern neighbors, thereby broadening our enmity.
Is this permissible!"
Chāo said:
"My plan is already decided,
I will not discuss it with you."
(The historian records that Mùróng Chāo's obstinate rejection of advice led to invasion and his downfall.)
Sì,
is pronounced *xiāng lì fān*.
2. On the *xīnmǎo* day,
a general pardon was issued.
3. On the *gēngxū* day,
Liú Yì was appointed as General of the Guards and granted the authority to establish his own administrative office with the same honors as the Three Excellencies.
Yì loved talent and esteemed scholars,
and all the famous figures of the time flocked to him,
except for the Registrar of Yángzhōu, Zhāng Shào from Wújùn, who did not go.
Someone asked him why,
Shào said:
"My lord is a hero for the ages,
why trouble with many questions!"
(Liú Yù held the position over Yángzhōu,
hence he referred to him as 'my lord'.)
4. The King of Qín, Yáo Xīng, sent his younger brother, General Who Pacifies the North Yáo Chōng, and General Who Conquers Caitiffs Dí Bózhī, among others, to lead forty thousand cavalry
to attack the King of Xià, Hèlián Bóbó.
Chōng reached north of the mountains,
plotted to turn back and attack Cháng'ān,
but Bózhī did not agree and he stopped,
then poisoned Bózhī to silence him.
5. The King of Qín, Yáo Xīng, sent an envoy to again appoint Qiáo Zòng as Grand Governor, Chancellor of State, and King of Shǔ,
bestowing the Nine Distinctions upon him,
authorizing him to issue decrees and grant titles,
all according to the rituals of a king.
6 In the second month,
the Southern Yan generals Mùróng Xìngzōng, Húgǔ Tí, Gōngsūn Guī, and others led cavalry to raid Sùyù,
capturing it.
Sùyù City was north of the Huái River.
Emperor [of the Southern Dynasties] established Sùyù Commandery and Sùyù County;
because Emperor Dàizōng of the Táng dynasty had the personal name Yù,
it was changed to Sùqiān County,
belonging to Xúzhōu.
Sòng Bái said: Sùyù City was 180 lǐ southeast of Xiàpī.
It was originally the place where the people of Sòng were relocated.
After Sòng was destroyed,
it became a town.
During the Hàn dynasty, it was Qiúyóu County,
belonging to Línhuái Commandery.
Emperor Ān of Jìn established Sùyù County,
and the Táng dynasty changed it to Sùqiān County.
General,
read as jí liàng fān.
They selected 2,500 men and women and handed them over to the Imperial Music Bureau to be trained.
Guī [Gōngsūn Guī]
was the elder brother of Wǔlóu.
At this time,
Wǔlóu served as Palace Attendant, Imperial Secretary, and concurrently Commander of the Left Guard,
monopolizing court administration.
His clan relatives all held prominent positions,
and no one among the princes and officials, both inside and outside the court, did not fear him.
The Southern Yan ruler Chāo discussed the merits of the Sùyù campaign,
enfeoffing Húgǔ Tí and others as dukes of commanderies and counties.
The Prince of Guìlín,
Zhèn, remonstrated, saying:
"These few men,
exhausted the people and wore out the troops,
creating enmity for the state.
What merit do they have to be enfeoffed?"
Chāo was angry,
and did not reply.
The Chief Clerk of the Imperial Secretariat, Wáng Yǎn, flattered and served Wǔlóu.
The Hàn Imperial Secretariat had eighteen Clerks,
later increased to twenty-one.
Afterwards, the number of personnel increased further,
so a Chief Clerk was established to oversee them.
His official rank reached Left Assistant Director.
People of the state said of him:
"If you wish to become a marquis,
serve Wǔlóu."
Chāo also sent Gōngsūn Guī and others to raid Jǐnán,
capturing over a thousand men and women before leaving.
This Jǐnán Commandery was also an émigré administration established north of the Huái River.
Jǐ,
read as zǐ lǐ fān.
The people all fortified themselves in stockades for self-protection.
An edict ordered the Inspector of Bìngzhōu, Liú Dàolián, to garrison Huáiyīn to guard against them.
7 Qǐfú Chìpán went to Shàngguī to meet with the Duke of Tàiyuán of Qín, Yì.
Péng Xīniàn took advantage of the emptiness to attack him.
Chìpán heard of this,
was furious,
and without informing Yì, returned,
attacked Xīniàn,
defeated him,
and then besieged Fúhǎn.
Qǐfú Gānguī accompanied the Qín ruler Xīng to Píngliáng;
Chìpán captured Fúhǎn.
Péng Xīniàn had occupied Fúhǎn.
Fú,
pronounced fū.
Gānguī fled back to Yuànchuān.
Gānguī had been detained by Qín,
see the third year in the previous scroll.
Liú Jué of Féngyì gathered a crowd of several thousand,
occupied Wànnián and rebelled.
The Qín ruler Xīng was in Píngliáng,
so Jué took the opportunity to rebel.
[Yáo Hóng] beheaded Jué,
and pardoned his remaining followers.
The generals requested to issue a public proclamation,
announcing the display of the severed heads.
Hóng did not permit it,
saying:
"The sovereign entrusted me with rear affairs.
Being unable to suppress the rebel bandits,
I should blame myself and request punishment.
How dare I boastfully claim credit for myself!"
Yáo Hóng was leisurely and refined in literary pursuits.
From a Confucian scholar's perspective,
he seemed to have grasped the way of a son,
but he was not a talent for restoring order.
The Qín ruler Xīng went from Píngliáng to Cháonà,
and heard of Yáo Chōng's plot,
which was said to be about returning to surprise-attack Cháng'ān.
8 In the third month,
Liú Yù submitted a memorial opposing the campaign against Southern Yān.
Court discussions all considered it inadvisable,
only the Left Deputy Director Mèng Chǎng, the Cavalry General Simā Xiè Yù, and Army Advisor Zāng Xǐ believed it would certainly succeed,
and urged Yù to proceed.
Yù appointed Chǎng to supervise the affairs of the Central Army headquarters.
Supervising the affairs of the General of the Central Army's headquarters.
Chǎng,
read as chǒu liǎng fān.
Supervise,
read as gǔ xián fān.
He was the grandson of Ān's elder brother.
Initially,
after the defeat of the Fú clan,
Wáng Měng's grandson, Zhèn'è, came seeking refuge.
He was appointed Magistrate of Línlǐ.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn established Línlǐ County in the fourth year of Tàikāng,
belonging to Tiānmén Commandery.
Suí and Táng merged it into Lǐzhōu's Lǐyáng County.
Lǐ,
pronounced lǐ.
He was very weak at drawing a bow,
but had strategic insight,
was good at decisive judgment,
and enjoyed discussing military and state affairs.
Someone recommended Zhèn'è to Liú Yù.
Yù spoke with him,
was pleased,
and had him stay overnight.
The next morning,
he said to his aides:
"I have heard that from a general's family comes a general.
Zhèn'è truly is one."
He immediately appointed him as a Central Army Advisor.
9 Mount Héngshān collapsed.
10 In summer,
the fourth month,
Qǐfú Gānguī went to Fúhǎn,
left his heir Chìpán to garrison it,
gathered his followers, obtaining twenty thousand men,
and moved the capital to Dùjiān Mountain.
Dùjiān Mountain
was where Qǐfú's ancestor Sī Fán had resided.
11 Thunder struck the eastern corridor of the Tiān'ān Hall of Wèi.
The Wèi ruler Guī disliked this,
and ordered the Left Construction Office to use battering rams to attack the eastern and western corridors,
destroying them all.
Initially,
Guī took cold-food powder.
Many people of Jìn took cold-food powder.
Today, the Thousand Gold Prescriptions contain several formulas.
Sū Shì said: In the world, there are those who consume stalactite and aconite and indulge in wine and sensual pleasures to seek longevity.
This likely began with Hé Yàn.
Yàn was young and wealthy,
so he took cold-food powder to aid his desires.
All who took it
suffered from back abscesses and vomiting blood in succession.
When the drug acted,
his nature became mostly agitated and irritable,
with unpredictable fits of anger.
By now, it gradually worsened.
Moreover, disasters and anomalies frequently appeared.
Diviners mostly said there would be sudden changes arising close at hand.
Guī was worried and distressed, uneasy.
Sometimes he did not eat for several days,
or stayed awake all night.
He recounted the successes, failures, gains, and losses of his entire life,
talking to himself incessantly.
Suspecting that his close ministers and attendants were all untrustworthy,
whenever officials presented memorials before him,
he would recall their past wrongs,
and often kill them.
For others, if their complexion changed,
or their breathing was irregular,
(the air going in and out once is called a breath),
or if their speech was slightly mistaken,
he would consider it as harboring evil in their hearts,
manifesting outwardly,
and often personally beat them to death.
The historian says the Wèi ruler Guī's death was approaching.
People in the court could not ensure their own safety.
Officials merely sought to avoid punishment.
No one supervised or managed others.
Bandits and thieves operated openly.
In the lanes and alleys,
people became scarce.
Guī also knew this,
saying:
"I intentionally allowed it to become like this.
After this calamitous year passes,
I will then clear and govern it."
At this time,
close ministers feared punishment,
and most did not dare seek closeness.
Only the Editorial Director Cuī Hào was respectful and diligent without slacking,
sometimes not returning home all day.
Hào
was the son of the Minister of Personnel, Cuī Hóng.
Hóng never opposed the emperor's will,
nor did he flatter and fawn.
Therefore, only the father and son Hóng were not reprimanded.
12 The Xià ruler Bóbó led twenty thousand cavalry to attack Qín,
plundering and taking over seven thousand households of various Hú from Píngliáng,
and advanced to station at Yīlì Chuān.
Wèi Shōu's Treatise on Geography states: Píngliáng City was within the boundaries of Chúnyīn of Āndìng Commandery of Hàn,
and in Táng times, it was the territory of Yuánzhōu.
Yīlì Chuān must also have been southeast of it.
Liú Yù passed through Dà Xiàn,
and the Yān troops did not come out.
Yù raised his hand and pointed to the sky,
his joy showing on his face.
His attendants said:
"You have not yet seen the enemy, yet you are already joyful.
Why is that?"
Yù said:
"Our troops have already passed the dangerous terrain,
and the soldiers have the determination to fight to the death;
meaning they have already passed the danger of Dà Xiàn.
The men have no worries about shortages.
Meaning the Yān people did not cut down the grain crops.
In the sixth month,
on Jǐsì,
Yù reached Dōngguǎn.
Chāo had previously sent Gōngsūn Wǔlóu, Hè Làilú, and Left General Duàn Huī, among others, to lead 50,000 infantry and cavalry to station at Línqú;
upon hearing that the Jìn troops had entered Xiàn,
he personally led 40,000 infantry and cavalry to join them,
ordering Wǔlóu to lead cavalry to advance and occupy Jù Miè Shuǐ.
Jù Miè Shuǐ,
in the Guóyǔ, is called Jù Shuǐ,
Yuán Hóng called it Jù Mèi Shuǐ,
and the Shuǐ Jīng calls it Jù Yáng Shuǐ.
The water originates north of Tài Shān in Zhūxū County,
passes west of that county,
and then north past the east of Línqú County.
Up and down along the water,
are all the locations of Liú Yù's camps when he attacked Guǎnggù.
Defeating them,
Wǔlóu retreated and fled.
Yù used 4,000 chariots as left and right wings,
advancing slowly in parallel formation,
and fought the Yān troops south of Línqú.
As the sun was tilting westward,
the sun passing noon is called tilting westward.
Zè,
pronounced zǔlì fān.
Army Advisor Hú Fān said to Yù:
"Yān has sent out all its troops to fight,
the defenders left in Línqú city must be few.
I wish to lead a surprise force along a hidden path to take the city.
This is how Hán Xìn defeated Zhào."
Yù sent Fān, along with Advisory Army Advisor Tán Sháo, and General of Establishing Might, Hé Nèi's Xiàng Mí, to secretly lead troops behind the Yān army,
attacking Línqú,
claiming that light troops had arrived by sea.
Xiàng Mí donned armor and was first to ascend,
and thus captured it.
Chāo was greatly alarmed,
and rode alone to join Duàn Huī south of the city.
Chāo went from Línqú city out to the south of the city to join Huī.
The Yān forces were greatly defeated,
over ten great generals including Duàn Huī were beheaded,
Chāo fled back to Guǎnggù,
and his imperial seal, carriage, and leopard tail were captured.
Fú Qián said: The great procession has eighty-one subordinate chariots,
arranged in three rows,
with the Shàngshū and Yùshǐ riding in them.
The last chariot
hangs a leopard tail,
and all before the leopard tail are within the imperial precincts.
The Jìn records: The ceremonial procession has thirty-six subordinate chariots,
the last chariot hangs a leopard tail.
Xǐ,
pronounced sīshì fān.
On Bǐngzǐ,
the great city was captured.
Chāo gathered his forces and retreated to defend the small city.
Yù built a long siege wall to surround it,
the wall was three zhàng high,
and three layers of moats were dug;
he pacified and accepted surrenders,
selected and promoted the worthy and talented,
and both Huá and Yí were greatly pleased.
Thus, using the grain stores of the Qí region,
all grain transport from the Jiāng and Huái was halted.
Chāo sent Shàngshū Láng Zhāng Gāng to seek troops from Qín,
pardoned Guìlín Wáng Zhèn,
appointing him as Lù Shàngshū, Commander of All Military Affairs at Home and Abroad,
summoned him for an audience,
apologized to him,
and asked him for strategy.
Zhèn said:
"The hearts of the people
are tied to one person.
Now Your Majesty personally commanded the six armies,
but fled in defeat and returned.
The officials are disheartened,
the soldiers and people have lost morale.
I hear the Qín people have their own internal troubles,
meaning Qín has internal troubles from Hèlián.
Sàng,
pronounced xīlàng fān.
The scattered soldiers who have returned still number tens of thousands.
You should take out all gold and silk to entice them,
and fight one more decisive battle.
If Heaven's mandate aids us,
we will surely defeat the enemy;
if not,
to die is also beautiful,
compared to shutting the gates and waiting for the end,
is that not still better!"
Minister of Education, Lèlàng Wáng Huì said:
"That is not so.
The Jìn troops are riding on victory,
their momentum is a hundredfold.
For us to oppose them with defeated troops,
is that not difficult!
Although Qín is locked in struggle with Bóbó,
that is not enough to be a worry;
moreover, they share the Central Plains with us,
the situation is like lips and teeth.
How can they not come to our aid!
But if we do not send a high minister, we cannot obtain substantial troops.
Shàngshū Lìng Hán Fàn is esteemed by both Yān and Qín,
as seen in the third year of the previous volume.
Chāo followed this advice.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Liú Yù was appointed Governor of Běi Qīng and Jì Provinces.
After the Jìn clan crossed south,
they established Nán Qīng and Jì Provinces south of the Huái,
