"Jiāo Chén, Wáng Hóu, and others")
'Chén'
is pronounced 'shìrén'.
gathered over three thousand families,
occupied the southern city,
promoted Jiāo Lǎng as Grand Commander-in-Chief and General of the Soaring Dragon,
while Chén proclaimed himself Governor of Liáng,
and surrendered to Méngxùn.
Since Tántán occupied Gūzāng,
engaging in warfare with neighbors on all sides,
he suffered defeat wherever he went.
Not only did he lose Gūzāng,
he could not even secure Lèdū.
The Book of Songs says:
"Do not cultivate the great fields,
Lest the weeds grow tall and proud.
Do not think of distant people,
Lest your heart be weary and troubled."
This precisely describes such a situation.
10. Liú Yù arrived at Xiàpī,
and had the baggage and supplies transported by boat,
while he personally led the elite infantry on foot.
Upon reaching Shānyáng,
he heard that Hé Wújì had been defeated and killed,
and feared that the capital might fall.
He rolled up his armor and hastened his march,
arriving at the Huái River with only a few dozen men.
Lǐ Yánshòu's *Nán Shǐ* records this as
"the Jiāng River,"
which should be followed,
as by the time Yù reached Shānyáng, he had already crossed the Huái.
A traveler said:
"The rebels have not yet arrived.
If Lord Liú returns,
there will be nothing to worry about."
Yù was greatly pleased.
As they were about to cross the Jiāng,
the wind grew fierce,
and everyone found it difficult.
Yù said:
"If Heaven's mandate aids the state,
the wind will cease of itself;
if not,
what harm is there in capsizing and drowning!"
He immediately ordered them to board the boats,
and as the boats moved, the wind stopped.
After crossing the Jiāng,
they reached Jīngkǒu,
and the crowd was greatly reassured.
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Guǐwèi day,
Yù arrived at Jiànkāng.
Due to the fall of Jiāngzhōu,
he submitted a memorial returning his seal and ribbons,
but an imperial edict did not permit it.
The Governor of Qīngzhōu, Zhūgě Chángmín, the Governor of Yǎnzhōu, Liú Fān, and the Governor of Bīngzhōu, Liú Dàolián, each led troops to defend Jiànkāng.
Qīngzhōu, Yǎnzhōu, and Bīngzhōu
were all temporarily established between the Jiāng and Huái rivers at that time.
"Jiàng"
is pronounced as "liàng" according to the fǎnqiè spelling;
the same applies below.
The Governor of Yùzhōu was a younger cousin of Liú Yì.
Yì heard that Lú Xún was invading,
and was about to resist him when he fell ill;
after recovering,
he prepared to set out.
Liú Yù sent Yì a letter saying:
"I have long been accustomed to attacking demonic rebels.
Sūn Tài used heterodox teachings to deceive the masses,
and Sūn Ēn and Lú Xún were both his followers,
hence they are called demonic rebels.
'Yí'
is pronounced as "yú jì" according to the fǎnqiè spelling.
'Yāo'
is pronounced as "yú jiāo" according to the fǎnqiè spelling.
The rebels have recently gained illicit advantages,
and their momentum should not be taken lightly.
Now that the repair of our ships is nearly complete,
I should join forces with you, brother.
When victory is achieved,
the appointments in the upper reaches
will all be entrusted to you."
He also sent Liú Fān to go
and persuade Yì to stop.
Yì was angry,
and said to Fān:
"In the past, I deferred to him for a momentary achievement,
but do you think I am truly inferior to Liú Yù?"
He threw the letter to the ground,
and led a fleet of twenty thousand from Gūshú.
Yì was then stationed at Gūshú as the Governor of Yùzhōu.
"Shuài"
is read as "shuài."
When Xún first invaded,
he sent Xú Dàofù toward Xúnyáng,
while Xún personally led an attack on the various commanderies in Xiāngzhōng.
The various commanderies in Xiāngzhōng
were the areas of Hàn's Chángshā, Línglíng, and Guìyáng.
He was defeated at Chángshā.
Xún advanced to Bālíng,
intending to head toward Jiānglíng.
When Xú Dàofù heard that Yì was approaching,
he sent a swift messenger to report to Xún, saying:
"Yì's troops are very strong.
The success or failure of our endeavor
depends on this.
We should join forces to crush him;
if we achieve victory here,
Jiānglíng will be of little concern."
Xún set out from Bālíng that very day,
and joined forces with Dàofù to advance downstream.
In the fifth month,
on the Wùwǔ day,
Yì and Xún fought at Sāngluòzhōu.
Yì's troops were heavily defeated,
abandoning hundreds of boats,
and fled on foot with a few hundred men.
The remaining troops were all captured by Xún,
and the abandoned baggage and supplies piled up like mountains.
Earlier,
when Xún reached Xúnyáng,
he heard that Yù had returned,
but still did not believe it;
only after defeating Yì
did he obtain confirmation,
and he and his followers looked at each other in dismay.
Xún wanted to retreat to Xúnyáng,
attack and capture Jiānglíng,
and hold the two provinces to resist the court.
The two provinces
refer to Jīngzhōu and Jiāngzhōu.
Dàofù strongly argued against it.
Xún hesitated for several days,
and then followed his advice.
On the Jǐwèi day,
a general amnesty was declared.
Yù recruited men as soldiers,
rewarding them according to the same standards as those who had rallied to the cause at Jīngkǒu.
Yù had raised troops at Jīngkǒu to attack Huán Xuán,
and those who joined the righteous cause were rewarded more generously than usual at the time.
Some suggested dividing the troops to guard various key crossings,
but Yù said:
"The enemy is numerous, and we are few.
If we divide our troops to garrison and defend,
they will be able to gauge our strengths and weaknesses;
moreover, if one place suffers defeat,
it will dampen the morale of the entire army.
Now, if we gather our forces at Shítóu,
and respond flexibly as needed,
it will not only prevent them from estimating our numbers,
but also avoid dividing our strength.
If additional troops gradually assemble,
we can discuss further strategies then."
The court heard of Liú Yì's defeat,
and the people were terrified.
At that time, the northern army had just returned,
and the generals and soldiers were mostly wounded and sick.
The combat troops in Jiànkāng numbered less than several thousand.
Lú Xún, having conquered the two towns,
(the two towns
refer to Jiāng and Yù.)
had a continuous line of boats and carts stretching for a hundred lǐ.
His tower ships were twelve zhàng high,
and those who had fled after defeat vied to describe his strength.
Mèng Chǎng and Zhūgě Chángmín wanted to escort the imperial carriage across the river,
but Liú Yù refused.
At that time, there were no walled cities on either side of the river to rely on.
Chǎng and Chángmín wanted to escort the Son of Heaven across the river,
which would mean either fleeing east to Guǎnglíng
or holding Lìyáng to the west.
Chǎng,
pronounced as chǒu liǎng fān.
When Hé Wújì and Liú Yì went south to campaign,
Chǎng predicted they would certainly be defeated,
and indeed it turned out so.
By this time,
he again said that Liú Yù certainly could not resist Lú Xún,
and many quite believed him.
Only the General of Dragon-Soaring, Yúqiū Jìn of Dōnghǎi, refuted Chǎng and others in court,
believing it was not so.
The Central Army Advisor Wáng Zhòngdé said to Liú Yù:
"You, illustrious lord, are a protector appointed by fate,
having newly achieved great merit,
your might shakes the six directions.
(The Wèi Ministry of Personnel had a Central Army Gentleman;
the various ducal offices and military commands also accordingly established Central Army Advisors.)
(Newly achieved great merit
refers to the destruction of Yān.)
Once they hear of your triumphant return,
they will naturally flee and collapse;
but if you flee first yourself,
then your position will be no different from that of a commoner.
A commoner issuing commands—
how could that awe others!
If this plan is adopted,
I ask to take my leave from here."
Liú Yù was very pleased.
Chǎng persistently pleaded without cease,
and Liú Yù said:
"Now our important towns are lost externally,
and a powerful enemy presses internally.
The people are terrified and alarmed,
and none have firm resolve.
If we move once,
we will crumble and disintegrate on our own,
and how could we even reach the north bank of the river!
Even supposing we could reach it,
it would merely prolong our days a little.
Now, though our soldiers are few,
they are sufficient for one battle.
If we achieve victory,
then ruler and minister will share in fortune;
if ill fate must come,
I will lie dead before the temple gate,
fulfilling my long-held vow to devote myself to the state,
and will not hide in the wilds to beg for survival.
My decision is made;
do not speak of it again!"
Chǎng was angered that his words were not heeded,
and moreover believed defeat was certain.
He therefore requested death.
Liú Yù angrily said:
"You may first witness one battle,
(shēn means
again.)
Chǎng knew Liú Yù would ultimately not follow his advice,
so he submitted a memorial stating:
"When Liú Yù campaigned north,
the multitude did not agree,
only I supported Liú Yù's plan of action.
(The matter is seen in the previous year.)
Now the state is in peril and crisis—
this is my crime.
I humbly accept blame to apologize to the world."
After sealing the memorial,
he took poison and died.
On the yǐchǒu day,
Lú Xún reached Huáikǒu,
(the mouth where the Qínhuái River enters the Yangtze.)
The Prince of Lángyá, Sīmǎ Déwén, was made Commander of the Various Military Affairs of the Palace City,
and stationed at Zhōngtánghuáng.
(A hall without four walls is called huáng.)
The various generals each had their own garrison posts.
Liú Yù's son Liú Yìlóng was just four years old.
Liú Yù had the Advisory Army Counselor Liú Cuì assist him,
and garrison Jīngkǒu.
Cuì was a cousin of Liú Yì.
Liú Yù saw people by the water watching the enemy,
and found it strange.
He asked Army Advisor Zhāng Shào,
and Shào said:
"If your command had not returned,
the people would be fleeing and scattering without respite—
how could they be watching!
Now they should no longer be afraid."
Liú Yù said to his generals and aides:
"If the enemy advances directly from Xīntíng,
their vanguard will be irresistible,
and we should temporarily avoid them.
The outcome of victory or defeat cannot be predicted.
If they turn and moor at the western bank,
(the western bank
is Càizhōu.)
Xú Dàofù requested to burn their boats from Xīntíng to Báishí and advance,
attacking Liú Yù from several routes.
Lú Xún wanted to proceed with a surefire plan,
and said to Dàofù:
"Before our main army arrived,
Mèng Chǎng already took his own life at the mere rumor;
judging by the overall situation,
they should collapse in disorder within days.
Now to decide victory or defeat in a single morning,
recklessly seeking gain,
is not a sure way to victory,
and moreover will kill and wound our soldiers.
It is better to hold our troops and wait."
Dàofù thought Lú Xún was too hesitant and indecisive,
and sighed:
"I am ultimately misled by Lord Lú;
the affair certainly will not succeed.
Had I been able to serve a true hero,
the world would not be hard to pacify."
Liú Yù ascended the Shítóu Fortress to observe Lú Xún's army.
At first he saw them heading toward Xīntíng,
and turned pale looking at his attendants;
but then they turned and moored at Càizhōu,
and he was pleased.
(Càizhōu is on the western bank of Shítóu;
now, twenty-five lǐ west of Shàngyuán County in Jiànkāng Prefecture is Càizhōu.)
Liú Yù feared Lú Xún would invade and raid,
so he used Yúqiū Jìn's plan,
felling trees to build palisades at Shítóu and Huáikǒu,
repairing Yuèchéng,
and building three forts at Zhāpǔ, Yàoyuán, and Tíngwèi.
(Zhāpǔ is on the southern bank of the great river,
near the mouth of the Qínhuái.)
(Yàoyuán,
probably a place where medicinal herbs were grown.)
(Where the Tíngwèi court offices were located,
thus becoming a place name.)
(Zhā,
pronounced zhuāng jiā fān.)
According to the Imperial Annals of the Jìn History,
the three forts were all at Huáikǒu.)
Liú Yì had traveled through Mán and Jìn territories,
(the area inhabited by the Mán people up and down Xīyáng
is called Mán;
those who are subjects of the king and pay taxes and perform corvée
are called Jìn.)
and his followers were hungry and exhausted,
with seven or eight out of ten dead.
On the bǐngyín day,
he reached Jiànkāng,
and awaited punishment.
Liú Yù consoled and encouraged him,
and put him in charge of internal and external留守 affairs.
(In charge of the留守 affairs of the Commander-in-Chief of Internal and External Various Armies office.)
An edict demoted him to Rear General.
11. Wèi's Chángsūn Sōng reached the north of the desert and returned,
and the Róurán pursued and surrounded him at Niúchuān.
On the rénshēn day,
the Wèi ruler Túbá Sì attacked the Róurán northward.
The Róurán Khan Shèlún heard of it,
fled,
and died on the way.
His son Dùbá was still young,
and the tribesmen established Shèlún's brother Húlǜ,
titled Àidòu
gài Khan.
Sì led his troops back to Cānhépō.
12. Lú Xún concealed troops on the southern bank,
the southern bank,
which is the southern bank of the Qínhuái River estuary.
He claimed that all his forces would advance on foot from Báishí.
Liú Yù left his staff officer Shěn Línzǐ and Xú Chìtè to garrison the southern bank,
cutting off Chápǔ,
ordering them to hold firm and not move;
Yù, along with Liú Yì and Zhūgě Chángmín, went north to confront them.
Línzǐ said:
"The words of these treacherous rebels,
may not be truthful,
we should prepare deep defenses."
Yù said:
"Shítóu City is strategically secure,
and the defenses along the Huái River are very strong,
with you remaining in the rear,
it is sufficient to hold it."
Línzǐ
was the son of Mùfū.
Shěn Mùfū,
was from Wǔkāng, Wúxīng.
In the third year of Lóng'ān,
Sūn Ēn invaded Kuàijī,
and the three Wú regions responded.
Mùfū was in Kuàijī,
Ēn appointed him as magistrate of Yúyáo,
Ēn was defeated by Liú Láozhī,
and Mùfū was also killed.
On the Gēngchén day,
Lú Xún burned Chápǔ,
and advanced to Zhānghóu Bridge.
Xú Chìtè was about to attack them,
but Línzǐ said:
"The rebels claim to be heading to Báishí but repeatedly come to challenge us,
their true intentions are clear.
Our forces are outnumbered and cannot match them,
it is better to hold our strategic position and wait for the main army."
Chìtè did not listen,
and went out to engage in battle;
the ambush was sprung,
Chìtè was heavily defeated,
fleeing alone by boat to the north of the Huái River.
This is the northern bank of the Qínhuái River.
Zhū Língshí came to his rescue,
and the rebels then retreated.
Xún led elite troops in a major advance,
reaching Dānyáng Commandery.
Dānyáng Commandery,
was the seat of the Dānyáng Prefect.
Shàng,
is pronounced as shí zhǎng fān.
They beheaded Xú Chìtè,
removed their armor for a long time,
and then deployed their formation at Nántáng.
Nántáng,
is the southern bank of the Qínhuái River.
Chén,
is read as zhèn.
13. In the sixth month,
Liú Yù was appointed as Grand Commandant, Director of the Secretariat, and granted the Yellow Axe;
Yù accepted the Yellow Axe,
but firmly declined the other titles.
Yǔ Yuè, the Army Commander of the Chariot and Cavalry Central Army, was appointed as Governor of Jiāng Province.
Yuè,
was the son of Zhǔn.
Liú Yù was General of Chariots and Cavalry,
because Liú Jìngxuān failed in the campaign against Shǔ,
he requested to be demoted to General of the Central Army,
so the offices of Chariot and Cavalry and Central Army shared one Army Commander.
Yǔ Zhǔn,
was the grandson of Yǔ Liàng.
14. Sīmǎ Guófán and his younger brothers Shūfán and Shūdào fled to Qín.
The Qín king Xīng said:
"Liú Yù has just executed Huán Xuán,
and is assisting the Jìn court,
why have you come?"
They replied:
"Yù weakens the royal house,
and whenever any of our clan members show self-improvement or establish themselves,
Yù immediately eliminates them;
he is becoming a threat to the state,
even more so than Huán Xuán."
Xīng appointed Guófán as Governor of Yáng Province,
and Shūdào as Governor of Jiāo
Province.
15. Lú Xún plundered various counties but gained nothing,
and said to Xú Dàofù:
"Our army is weary,
it would be better to return to Xúnyáng,
combine our forces to capture Jīng Province,
occupy two-thirds of the realm,
and then gradually contend with Jiànkāng."
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on the Gēngshēn day,
Xún retreated south from Càizhōu to Xúnyáng,
leaving his follower Fàn Chóngmín with five thousand men to hold Nánlíng.
Nánlíng is west of Xuānchéng County in Xuānchéng Commandery,
Liáng established Nánlíng Commandery and Nánlíng County,
which was within the boundaries of Shíchéng County of the Hàn-era Dānyáng Commandery,
and is now the territory of Guìchí County in Chí Prefecture.
Xún, considering the uncertainties of warfare,
intended to return south to Pānyú,
so he had Chóngmín guard it to secure the mouth of Pénglí Lake.
Sòng Bái said: The opposite bank of Zhàjiāngkǒu is the old territory of Nánlíng County,
which is now Fánchāng County.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,

Yù sent Vice General Wáng Zhòngdé, Liú Zhōng the Administrator of Guǎngchuān, Kuǎi Ēn the Chamberlain for the Palace Garrison of Héjiān from Lánlíng, Mèng Huáiyù the Consultant Army Officer of the Central Army, and others to lead troops in pursuit of Xún.
16. On the Yǐchǒu day,
the Wèi ruler Sì returned to Píngchéng.
17. The Western Qín king Qiánguī attacked more than ten tribes including Yuèzhì and Qūjī,
Yuèzhì,
were a Xiānbēi tribe;
their chieftain was called Chìlí.
Chìlí's son was called Jiégūī,
who surrendered to Qiánguī in the sixteenth year of Xiàowǔ's Tàiyuán era,
and rebelled and surrendered to Qín in the twenty-first year.
Qūjī is Jiégūī,
the pronunciation is slightly corrupted.
They were relocated to Yuànchuān.
In the eighth month,
Qiánguī again made Yuànchuān his capital.
The Qǐfú clan originally had their capital at Dùjiān Mountain,
when Qiánguī grew powerful,
he first made Yuànchuān his capital.
After being defeated by Qín and surrendering to them,
Qín had him garrison Yuànchuān,
but he rebelled again,
and fearing an attack from Qín,
he returned to defend Dùjiān Mountain.
Now that his forces were gradually growing stronger,
and he no longer feared Qín,
he again made Yuànchuān his capital.
18. Jǔqú Méngxùn attacked Western Liáng,
and defeated the Western Liáng heir apparent Xīn at Mǎmiào,
In ancient times, they worshipped the horse ancestor,
later generations established a temple to worship him,
hence the place was named Mǎmiào.
The Liáng Duke Hào ransomed Yuánhǔ with two thousand catties of silver and two thousand taels of gold;
Méngxùn returned him,
and then made an alliance with Hào before returning.
19. Liú Yù returned to Dōngfǔ,
after Lú Xún retreated,
Yù then returned to Dōngfǔ.
He sent the General Who Establishes Might Sūn Chù from Kuàijī and the General Who Spreads Martial Might Shěn Tiánzǐ to lead three thousand troops by sea to attack Pānyú.
Tiánzǐ,
was the elder brother of Línzǐ.
Everyone thought
"the sea route is arduous and distant,
it will certainly be difficult to reach,
and moreover it divides and reduces our current strength,
which is not an urgent matter at present."
Yù did not listen,
and instructed Chù:
"The main army will certainly defeat the treacherous rebels around the twelfth month,
by the time you arrive,
first destroy their nest,
so that they have nowhere to flee."
20. Qiáo Zòng sent his Palace Attendant Qiáo Liáng and others to appear before Qín,
requesting troops to attack Jìn.
Zòng appointed Huán Qiān as Governor of Jīng Province,
and Qiáo Dàofú as Governor of Liáng Province,
leading twenty thousand troops to invade Jīng Province;
the Qín king Xīng sent the former General Gǒu Lín to lead cavalry to join them.
Since Lú Xún advanced east,
Jiānglíng had not received news from Jiànkāng,
and bandits rose up one after another.
The Governor of Jīng Province Liú Dàoguī sent his Army Commander Wáng Zhènzhī to lead Tán Dàojì the Administrator of Tiānmén,
In the sixth year of Yǒng'ān of Wú's Sūn Xiū, Tiānmén Commandery was established from part of Wǔlíng.
Chōng County had Sōngliáng Mountain,
on the mountain there was a rock,
where the rock opened for several tens of zhang,
its height was such that
even shooting upward with a crossbow could not reach it,
its upper part was called Tiānmén,
hence the commandery was named after it.
The Geographical Records: Shímén County in Lǐ Prefecture,
was ancient Tiānmén Commandery.
Shuài,
is read as shuài;
the same below.
Dàojì,
was the younger brother of Zhī.
Zhèn Zhī arrived at Xúnyáng,
but was defeated by Xún Lín.
Lú Xún, upon hearing this,
appointed Lín as the Colonel of the Southern Man,
allocated troops to him,
and sent him to attack Jiānglíng while riding the momentum of victory,
claiming that Xú Dàofù had already captured Jiànkāng.
Huán Qiān recruited old loyalists along the way;
the Huán clan had long resided in Jīngchǔ,
bound by old favors,
their loyalty never forgotten,
hence they were called old loyalists.
Qiān stationed his troops at Zhījiāng,
a county that since the Hàn dynasty belonged to Nánjùn,
and was the state of Luó during the Spring and Autumn period.
The Jiāng River branched off west of the county to form Tuó,
then rejoined the main river to the east,
hence the name Zhījiāng (Branch River).
In the sixth year of the Xīníng era of our dynasty,
Zhījiāng was downgraded to a town,
and incorporated into Sōngzī County.
With two enemies closing in,
many officials and people in Jiānglíng harbored disloyal thoughts.
Dàoguī then assembled his officers and soldiers and addressed them:
"Huán Qiān is now nearby,
and I hear some elders are considering leaving.
The civil and military officials who came with me from the east are sufficient to handle matters;
these eastern officials,
referring to Dàoguī's accompanying officers, aides, and soldiers.
I do not intend to stop anyone."
He then opened the city gates at night,
and left them open until dawn.
Everyone was awed and submitted,
and no one left.
The Governor of Yōngzhōu, Lǔ Zōngzhī, led several thousand troops from Xiāngyáng to Jiānglíng.
Some said Zōngzhī's intentions were unpredictable,
but Dàoguī rode out alone to meet him,
and Zōngzhī was moved and pleased.
Dàoguī assigned Zōngzhī to guard the city,
entrusting him with his innermost trust,
and personally led the armies to attack Qiān.
His officers and aides all said:
"Now, going far out to attack Qiān,
victory is uncertain.
Xún Lín is nearby at Jiāngjīn,
watching our movements.
If he comes to attack the city,
Zōngzhī may not be able to hold it;
should there be any misstep,
the grand cause will be lost."
Dàoguī said:
"Xún Lín is foolish and cowardly,
with no clever strategies.
Since we have not gone far,
he will certainly not dare to approach the city.
I will now capture Qiān,
and victory will be immediate upon arrival;
in the time it takes to hesitate,
I will already have returned.
Once Qiān is defeated, Lín will be terrified,
how could he find the time to come!
Moreover, with Zōngzhī holding the city alone,
why would he not last a few days!"
He then galloped off to attack Qiān,
advancing by both water and land.
Qiān and others deployed a large fleet of warships,
supplemented by infantry and cavalry,
and fought at Zhījiāng.
Tán Dàojì charged forward and broke through the enemy formation,
and Qiān and others were utterly defeated.
Qiān fled alone by boat to Xún Lín,
but Dàoguī pursued and beheaded him.
On his return,
he reached Yǒngkǒu,
as noted in the Water Classic Commentary: the Yǒng River flows from the Xià River south to join the Jiāng,
hence called Yǒngkǒu.
This is the place mentioned in the Spring and Autumn Annals and Zuo Tradition where Yán Áo wandered to Yǒng and escaped,
located east of Jiānglíng city.
Dù Yù said: the Yǒng River is in Huáróng County, Nánjùn.
Yǒng,
pronounced yǒng.
Lín fled,
and Dàoguī sent his Advisory Army Officer, Liú Zūn of Línhuái, to lead troops in pursuit.
Earlier,
when Qiān arrived at Zhījiāng,
officials and people of Jiānglíng had all written letters to Qiān,
detailing the city's weaknesses and strengths,
intending to act as insiders;
now these letters were discovered,
but Dàoguī burned them all without reading,
and everyone was greatly reassured.
21 The Governor of Jiāngzhōu, Yǔ Yuè, appointed Yúqiū Jìn, the Grand Administrator of Póyáng, as the vanguard,
who repeatedly defeated Lú Xún's troops,
advanced to occupy Yùzhāng,
and cut off Xún's supply routes.
In the ninth month,
Liú Zūn beheaded Xún Lín at Bālíng.
Huán Shísuǐ took advantage of Xún's invasion,
and raised troops at Luòkǒu,
as noted in the Water Classic Commentary: the Hàn River passes Ānyáng County of Wèixīng,
then east to south of Dǎngchéng,
where it merges with the Luògǔ River,
which flows north from Luògǔ,
a valley north connecting to Cháng'ān,
its waters flowing south into the Hàn River,
hence called Luòkǒu.
Wáng Tiān'ēn, the Magistrate of Zhēngyáng, declared himself Governor of Liángzhōu,
"Zhēngyáng",
should be
"Wēiyáng".
According to the Jìn Dynasty Geography Records: Wēiyáng County belonged to Shàngyōng Commandery.
Shěn Yuē said: Wèi established Jiànshǐ County,
and Emperor Wǔ of Jìn renamed it Wēiyáng.
When King Wǔ of Zhōu attacked Zhòu,
eight states—Yōng, Shǔ, Qiāng, Máo, Wēi, Lú, Péng, and Pú—followed him.
I suspect Wēiyáng County was named after the ancient state of Wēi,
though history lacks evidence for this.
The Governor of Liángzhōu, Fù Sháo, sent his son Hóngzhī, the Grand Administrator of Wèixīng, to attack Shísuǐ and others,
and all were beheaded,
thus extinguishing the Huán clan.
Sháo
was the grandson of Chàng.
22 The Western Qín King Qiánguī attacked the Qín commanderies of Lüèyáng, Nán'ān, and Lǒngxī,
capturing them all,
and relocated 25,000 households to Yuànchuān and Fúhǎn.
23 On Jiǎyǐn day,
the Wèi ruler Guī was buried at Shènglè Jīnlíng,
posthumously titled Xuānwǔ,
and temple-named Lièzǔ.
In the first year of the Yǒngchū era of Emperor Gāozǔ of Sòng,
Wèi changed Guī's posthumous title to Dàowǔ Emperor.
24 Liú Yì insisted on pursuing and attacking Lú Xún,
but Chief Clerk Wáng Dàn secretly advised Liú Yù:
"Yì has already suffered defeat,
he should not be allowed to achieve merit again."
Yù agreed.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Yù led Yǎnzhōu Governor Liú Fān, General of Nìngshuò Tán Sháo, and General of Guànjūn Liú Jìngxuān south to attack Lú Xún,
appointing Liú Yì as Supervisor of the Grand Commandant's留守 Office,
entrusting all subsequent matters to him.
On Guǐsì day,
Yù departed from Jiànkāng.
25 Xú Dàofù led 30,000 troops toward Jiānglíng,
suddenly arriving at Pòzhǒng.
Pòzhǒng is east of Jiāngjīn.
Qù,
pronounced qū.
The pursuit summons did not reach in time,
and morale was greatly shaken.
Rumors spread that Xún had already pacified the capital,
and sent Dàofù to serve as Governor,
but the people of Jiāng and Hàn, moved by Liú Dàoguī's act of burning the letters,
no longer harbored disloyal thoughts.
Dàoguī assigned Liú Zūn to lead a separate mobile force,
while he personally confronted Dàofù at Yùzhāngkǒu,
where the vanguard suffered a setback;
Zūn attacked from the flank,
crushing them,
beheading over ten thousand,
with nearly all the rest drowning in the water,
and Dàofù fled alone by boat back to Pénkǒu.
Earlier,
when Dàoguī assigned Zūn to lead the mobile force,
everyone thought that with a strong enemy ahead,
the only concern was having too few troops,
and they should not split their existing forces,
placing them in a useless location.
But after defeating Dàofù,
they ultimately relied on the mobile force,
and everyone's minds were put at ease.
26 The Xiānbēi Púhún, Qiāng Jùqǐ, Shūbào, and Dèng Ruò led 20,000 households to surrender to Western Qín.
The Xiānbēi had a Púhún tribe;
Jùqǐ, Shūbào, and Dèng Ruò were Qiāng tribes.
Jù,
pronounced gōu.
27 Wáng Zhòngdé and others, hearing that Liú Yù's main army was about to arrive,
attacked Fàn Chóngmín at Nánlíng;
Chóngmín's warships were stationed on both sides of the western
bank.
In the eleventh month,
Liú Zhōng personally went to scout the enemy,
but fog descended,
and the enemy hooked his boat.
Zhōng then led his men to attack the ship's hatch,
the ship's hatch,
now called the horse gate by boatmen.
Zhōng slowly retreated,
and together with Zhòngdé attacked Chóngmín,
who fled.
With Chóngmín's flight,
Yù could advance directly,
and Xún lost the strategic advantage of Húkǒu.
On the 28th day, Guichou,
Bào Lòu, the Inspector of Yìzhōu, died.
Qiáo Dàofú captured Bādōng,
killing the defending generals Wēn Zuò and Shí Yánzǔ.
Wēn Zuò was originally the Administrator of Bādōng.
Shí Yánzǔ had been stationed in Bādōng since the retreats of Liú Jìngxuān and Huáng Hǔ.
Jiàng,
is pronounced as liàng.
29 The troops of Lú Xún guarding Guǎngzhōu did not anticipate danger from the sea route.
On the Gēngxū day,
Sūn Chù suddenly arrived by sea,
taking advantage of heavy fog,
he attacked from all sides,
and captured the city that same day.
Sūn Chù pacified the original inhabitants,
executed Lú Xún's close associates,
stationed troops to guard strictly,
and dispatched Shěn Tiánzǐ and others to attack the various commanderies in the Lingbiǎo region.
30 Liú Yù's army was at Léichí.
Lú Xún proclaimed that he would not attack Léichí,
but would instead sail directly downstream;
Liú Yù knew he intended to fight.
In the twelfth month,
on the Jǐmǎo day,
he advanced his army to Dàléi.
Dù Yòu said: The Jìn dynasty's Dàléi garrison,
is in Shūzhōu's Wàngjiāng County,
now west of Wǎnkǒu there is Léijiāngkǒu,
which is that place.
The Sòngshū records state: On the western bank of Wàngjiāng County is the Dàléi River,
from Xúnyáng Cháisāng along the current for three hundred lǐ it enters the river,
which is Wàngjiāng County.
On the Gēngchén day
Lú Xún and Xú Dàofù led tens of thousands of troops, blocking the river as they sailed downstream,
so numerous that the ends of the fleet could not be seen.
Liú Yù deployed all his light warships,
leading his entire army to attack in unison;
he also divided infantry and cavalry to station on the western bank,
first preparing fire tools.
Liú Yù used powerful crossbows to shoot at Lú Xún's army,
taking advantage of the wind and water conditions to press them.
Lú Xún's warships all moored at the western bank,
where the troops on the bank threw fire to burn them,
smoke and flames filled the sky;
yān,
is the same as yān (smoke).
yán,
is read as yàn (flame).
They fled back to Xúnyáng.
Intending to head for Yùzhāng,
they then used all their strength to build barricades and block Zuǒlǐ;
Zuǒlǐ is so named because its location is on the left (east) bank of the Zhāng River,
hence the name.
Dù Yòu said: Zuǒlǐ is the Pénglí Lake mouth in Xúnyáng County, Jiāngzhōu.
duàn,
is pronounced dīng guǎn fān.
On the Bǐngshēn day
Liú Yù's army reached Zuǒlǐ,
but could not advance.
Liú Yù waved his command flag, about to engage in battle,
when the flagpole he held broke,
and the banner sank into the water,
causing everyone to feel strange and fearful.
Liú Yù laughed and said:
"In the battle of Fùzhōu years ago,
referring to the time he fought against Huán Xuán and Huán Qiān, etc.
zhé,
is pronounced ér shè fān.
chén,
is pronounced chí lín fān.
Now it is the same again,
the rebels are sure to be defeated."
He then attacked the barricades and advanced,
although Lú Xún's troops fought desperately to the death,
they could not stop them.
Lú Xún escaped on a single boat,
those killed and those who jumped into the water to drown totaled over ten thousand people.
Liú Yù accepted those who surrendered and submitted,
pardoned those who had been coerced,
and dispatched Liú Fān and Mèng Huáiyù with light troops to pursue them.
Lú Xún gathered his scattered soldiers,
still numbering several thousand,
and directly returned to Pānyú;
Xú Dàofù fled to defend Shǐxīng.
Liú Yù appointed the General Who Establishes Might, Chǔ Yùzhī, as Inspector of Guǎngzhōu.
Yùzhī,
was the great-grandson of Chǔ Póu.
Chǔ Póu,
was the father of Empress Dowager Chóngdé.
póu,
is pronounced pú hóu fān.
Liú Yì disliked Liú Mùzhī,
often casually telling Liú Yù that Liú Mùzhī's power was too great,
but Liú Yù instead grew closer and trusted him more.
31 The Yān dynasty's Duke of Guǎngchuān, Wàn Ní, and Duke of Shànggǔ, Rǔ Chén,
considering themselves members of the imperial clan,
with great achievements,
at the death of Mùróng Xī,
Wàn Ní and Rǔ Chén both had merit.
The King of Yān, Mùróng Bá, because these two feudal lords held important positions,
for a long time did not summon them,
Mùróng Bá appointed Wàn Ní as Governor of Yōu and Píng Provinces,
stationed at Féirú;
Rǔ Chén as Governor of Bìng and Qīng Provinces,
stationed at Báiláng.
This year,
Rǔ Chén secretly sent someone to tell Wàn Ní:
"Rǔ Chén has an excellent plan,
I wish to discuss it with my uncle."
Wàn Ní then fled to Báiláng,
and together with Rǔ Chén rebelled.
Mùróng Bá sent the Duke of Jíjùn, Mùróng Hóng, and Zhāng Xìng to lead twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to suppress them.
Mùróng Hóng first sent an envoy to explain the consequences of good and bad actions;
Wàn Ní wanted to surrender,
but Rǔ Chén would not agree.
Zhāng Xìng said to Mùróng Hóng:
"The rebels will come out to fight tomorrow,
tonight they are sure to come to raid our camp,
we should prepare for it."
Mùróng Hóng then secretly ordered people to prepare ten bundles of grass,
storing fire and setting an ambush to wait for them.
That night,
Rǔ Chén indeed sent over a thousand strong men to raid the camp,
all the fires were lit together,
the ambushing troops intercepted and attacked,
capturing and beheading them all without exception.
Wàn Ní and Rǔ Chén, afraid, came out and surrendered,
Mùróng Hóng beheaded them both.
Mùróng Bá appointed the Duke of Fànyáng, Sù Fú, as Grand Marshal,
changing his title to Duke of Liáoxī;
Mùróng Hóng as General of Agile Cavalry,
changing his title to Duke of Zhōngshān.

Sīmǎ Guāng
Compiled by Imperial Order
Later Student from Tiāntái
Emperor Ān Xīn
Yìxī Seventh Year (Xīnhài, 411)
1 Spring,
first month,
on the Jǐwèi day,
Liú Yù returned to Jiànkāng.
2 The Qín dynasty's Duke of Guǎngpíng, Yáo Bǐ, was favored by the Qín King Yáo Xīng,
served as Governor of Yōng Province,
stationed at Āndìng.
The Later Qín of Yáo divided the five commanderies north of the ridge to establish the Governor of Yōng Province,
stationed at Āndìng.
yōng,
is pronounced yú yòng fān.
He urged Yáo Bǐ to befriend those around Yáo Xīng in order to seek entry to the court.
Yáo Xīng summoned Yáo Bǐ to serve as Prefect of the Masters of Writing, Palace Attendant, and Great General.
Yáo Bǐ then devoted himself to befriending court officials,
gathering reputation and influence,
in order to oppose the Crown Prince;
the people of the state hated him.
At that time, Yáo Xīng, because there were many rebellions in the northwest,
wanted to appoint an important general to pacify the region;
the Administrator of Lǒngdōng, Guō Bō, requested that Yáo Bǐ be sent out to garrison;
Wèi Shōu's Treatise on Geography records the Lǒngdōng Commandery,
governing the counties of Jīngyáng, Zǔlì, and Fǔyí,
but does not record when the commandery was established,
likely established during the Fú or Yáo regimes.
The Western Wèi established Lǒngdōng at Qiānyuán,
which is the Táng dynasty's Lǒng Province.
He appointed the Minister of Ceremonies, Suǒ Léng, as Grand Commandant and concurrent Administrator of Lǒngxī,
sending him to pacify and recruit the Western Qín.
This sets the stage for Suǒ Léng's surrender to the Western Qín.
suǒ,
is pronounced xī gè fān.
They confessed their crimes and requested to surrender.
Referring to the commandery administrators and county magistrates captured last year from Nán'ān, Luèyáng, Lǒngxī, and other commanderies.
shǐ,
is pronounced shū lì fān.
xiáng,
is pronounced hù jiāng fān.
Various Hu military affairs, General Who Conquers the West, Governor of Hé Province, Chanyu, Prince of Hénán,
Crown Prince Qìfén as General Who Pacifies the West, Wise Prince of the Left, Duke of Píngchāng.
Yáo Xīng ordered his ministers to search for and recommend talented individuals.
The Right Deputy Director, Liáng Xǐ, said:
"I have repeatedly received the imperial edict but have not found the right person,
one could say the world lacks talent."
Yáo Xīng said:
"Since ancient times, when emperors and kings rose to power,
they never sought ministers from people of the past,
nor awaited generals from the future,
but appointed talent according to the times,
and all were able to achieve good governance.
It is you who lack discernment in selecting and promoting,
how can you falsely accuse all under heaven?"
The ministers were all pleased.
Yáo Xīng's refutation of Liáng Xǐ was indeed correct,
but which of the ministers, understanding Yáo Xīng's intention, actually promoted those of humble origin?
This is what is called liking empty reputation without practical use.
3. Qín's Yáo Xiáng was stationed at Xìngchéng,
but was pressured by Xià King Bóbó,
and fled south to Dàsū;
Bóbó sent General Píngdōng Lù Yìgān to pursue and behead him,
capturing all his troops.
Bóbó then attacked Āndìng to the south,
defeating Shàngshū Yáng Fúsōng at the Qīngshí Northern Plain,
and forcing the surrender of 45,000 of his troops;
he advanced to attack Dōngxiāng,
captured it,
and relocated over 3,000 households to Èrchéng.
Qín's Zhènběi Cānjūn Wáng Màidé fled to Xià,
and Xià King Bóbó asked him for a strategy to destroy Qín.
Màidé said:
"Although Qín's virtue has declined,
its frontier garrisons remain strong.
I suggest we conserve our strength and wait for the right moment."
Bóbó appointed Màidé as Jūnshī Zhōnglángjiàng.
Màidé thus became a strategic advisor for Xià.
Not long after,
they stationed troops at Xìngchéng.
4. Liú Fán led generals such as Mèng Huáiyù in pursuing Lú Xún to the southern mountain regions.
In the second month,
on the Rénwǔ day,
Huáiyù captured Shǐxīng,
and beheaded Xú Dàofù.
5. Hénán King Qiánguī relocated over 3,000 households of the Xiānbēi Púhún tribe to Dùjiānchéng.
(Púhún's surrender to Qiánguī is recorded in the previous volume, last year.)
Dùjiānchéng was the Dùjiān Mountain City, the former capital of the Qǐfú clan.
Qǐfú Qiánguī originally established his state with the name Qín,
so he established Qínxīng Commandery at Dùjiān Mountain.
6. Jiāo Lǎng still held Gūzāng.
(Lǎng's occupation of Gūzāng is recorded in the previous volume, last year.)
They captured Lǎng but pardoned him;
appointing his younger brother Ná as Qínzhōu Cìshǐ,
to guard Gūzāng.
They then attacked Nánliáng,
besieging Lèdū,
but failed to capture it after thirty days;
Nánliáng King Tántán sent his son Ānzhōu as a hostage,
and they withdrew.
7. Tǔyùhún Shùluògān attacked Nánliáng,
defeating Nánliáng Crown Prince Hǔtái.
8. Nánliáng King Tántán wanted to attack Jǔqú Méngxùn again.
Hánchuān Hùjūn Mèng Kǎi advised:
"Méngxùn has recently annexed Gūzāng,
his ferocious momentum is at its peak,
he cannot be attacked."
Tántán did not listen,
advancing along five routes,
reaching Fānhé and Tiáodiào,
plundering over 5,000 households before returning.
General Qū Yòu said:
"Now that we have gained profit,
we should return by forced march,
crossing dangerous passes early.
Méngxùn is skilled in using troops;
if his light forces arrive suddenly,
with a strong enemy pressing from outside,
and the relocated households rebelling within,
this is a dangerous path."
Wèiwèi Yīlìyán said:
"They are on foot, we are on horseback,
the situation is not comparable.
Now returning by forced march would show weakness,
and moreover, we would abandon our plundered wealth,
this is not a good plan."
Soon, there was dark fog and wind and rain,
Méngxùn's troops arrived in great force,
and Tántán was defeated and fled.
Méngxùn advanced and besieged Lèdū,
Tántán defended the city walls and held firm,
sending his son Rǎngān as a hostage to request peace,
and Méngxùn then withdrew.
9. In the third month,
Liú Yù began to accept the positions of Tàiwèi and Zhōngshū Jiān.
(His appointment as Tàiwèi is recorded in the previous volume, fifth year.)
(His appointment as Zhōngshū Jiān is recorded in the sixth year.)
Chénjùn's Yīn Jǐngrén became Xíng Cānjūn.
(Xíng Cānjūn
did not have the same rank as Cānjūnshì,
as noted previously.)
"Who among Mèng Chǎng's staff is worthy to enter my office?"
Mùzhī recommended former Jiànwēi Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Xiè Huì.
Huì
was the great-grandson of Ān's elder brother Jù.
Mèng Chǎng was Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn,
and recruited Huì as Zhōngbīng Cānjūn.
Yù once interrogated prisoners;
that morning,
the Xíngyù Cānjūn was ill,
so Huì replaced him;
in the carriage, he glanced through the interrogation records,
and quickly issued judgments.
The ministerial office had many affairs,
and legal cases piled up heavily;
Huì responded to inquiries and handled matters,
without any errors or mistakes;
Yù thus considered him extraordinary,
and on that same day appointed him as Xíngyù Zéicáo.
(Xíngyù likely divided into Míncáo and Zéicáo,
Zéicáo handled matters of theft and banditry.
According to Sòng records,
various ministerial offices' Cānjūn included Chángliú Zéicáo, Xíngyù Zéicáo, and Chéngjú Zéicáo;
Xíngyù did not have Míncáo.
Xiè Huì as Cānjūn
did not initially hold a Cáo position,
now he was promoted and appointed.)
He was good at conversation and laughter,
knowledgeable and broadly proficient,
Yù deeply appreciated and favored him.
10. Lú Xún, while marching, gathered troops and reached Pānyú,
then besieged it,
Sūn Chǔ defended and held out for over twenty days.
Shěn Tiánzǐ said to Liú Fán:
"Although Pānyú's city is strategically solid,
it was originally the bandits' nest;
now that Xún is besieging it,
there may be internal changes.
Moreover, Sūn Jìgāo's forces are few and weak,
(Sūn Chǔ,
courtesy name Jìgāo.)
If the bandits return to occupy Guǎngzhōu,
their ferocious momentum will revive."
In summer,
the fourth month,
Tiánzǐ led troops to rescue Pānyú,
attacked Xún,
defeated him,
killing over ten thousand.
Xún fled,
Tiánzǐ and Chǔ pursued him together,
and again defeated Xún at Cāngwú, Yùlín, and Níngpǔ.
(Cāngwú and Yùlín
were ancient Hàn commanderies.
Níngpǔ Commandery
was established by Wú, carved out of Hépǔ Commandery.
Cāngwú
was Táng's Yùzhōu;
Yùlín,
Táng's Yùlínzhōu;
Níngpǔ,
Táng's Héngzhōu.)
Unable to advance further,
Xún fled to Jiāozhōu.
Initially,
the Jiǔzhēn Prefecture governor Lǐ Xùn rebelled.
Jiǔzhēn,
an ancient commandery of the Hàn,
was the Táng's Àizhōu.
After Duàn Huīyuàn died,
the imperial court appointed his son Duàn Huìdù as the Jiāozhōu Regional Inspector.
Before the imperial edict arrived,
Lú Xún attacked and captured Hépǔ.
Hépǔ,
an ancient commandery of the Hàn,
was the Táng's Liánzhōu.
Huìdù led the civil and military officials of the regional government to resist Xún at Shíqí,
and defeated him.
Xún still had about three thousand remaining troops,
and Lǐ Xùn's remaining partisans, such as Lǐ Tuō, gathered five thousand more Lǐ and Liáo people to respond to Xún.
On the Gēngzǐ day,
Xún arrived at the southern ferry of Lóngbiān in the morning;
Lóngbiān County of Jiāozhǐ Commandery,
where both the regional and commandery governments were located.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: In the 23rd year of the Jiàn'ān era of the Hàn,
at the beginning of establishing the region,
a flood dragon coiled around the northern and southern ferries,
so they changed the name from Lóngyuān to Lóngbiān.
I note that both Hàn histories record
"Lóngbiān",
perhaps because Yán Shígǔ and Lǐ Xián avoided the Táng taboo,
and thus also changed
"yuān"
to
"biān"
They engaged Xún in battle,
throwing pheasant-tail torches to burn his warships.
Pheasant-tail torches,
are bundles of grass tied at one end,
fitted with an iron arrowhead,
while the grass tail spreads out like a pheasant's tail,
lit on fire and thrown at the enemy.
Warship,
pronunciation: hù àn fān.
Xún's warships all caught fire,
and his troops suffered a great collapse.
Knowing escape was impossible,
Xún first poisoned his wife and children,
then summoned his singing girls and concubines, asking:
"Who is willing to die with me?"
Most said:
"Sparrows and mice cling to life,
truly it is hard to face death."
Some said:
"My lord is about to die,
how could I wish to live!"
So he killed all those who declined to die,
and then threw himself into the water.
Huìdù retrieved his corpse and beheaded it,
along with his father and son, and Lǐ Tuō and others,
placed the seven heads in boxes and sent them to Jiànkāng.
11 Initially,
when Liú Yì was in Jīngkǒu,
impoverished,
he was practicing archery with acquaintances in the Eastern Hall.
Yǔ Yuè was the Right Chief Clerk of the Minister Over the Masses,
arriving later,
he seized their archery hall;
everyone else avoided him,
but Yì alone did not leave.
Yuè's kitchen prepared a lavish feast,
but none was given to Yì;
Yì asked Yuè for roasted gosling,
Yuè angrily refused to give it,
and Yì henceforth bore a grudge.
At this time,
Yì requested to additionally supervise Jiāngzhōu,
and the edict granted it.
He then submitted a memorial stating:
"Jiāngzhōu is an inland region,
its duty is to govern the people,
it should not maintain a military headquarters that exhausts the people's strength,
it is proper to abolish the military headquarters and move the garrison to Yùzhāng;
and since Xúnyáng borders the Man tribes,
a thousand soldiers from the regional headquarters can be assigned to assist the commandery garrison."
Thereupon, Yuè was relieved of his Commander and General titles,
and as Regional Inspector he garrisoned Yùzhāng.
Yì had his trusted general Zhào Huī lead a thousand soldiers to guard Xúnyáng;
the three thousand civil and military officials of Yuè's headquarters all entered Yì's headquarters,
and the summons and arrests were severe.
Summons and arrests,
refers to orders issued to Jiāngzhōu to pursue and arrest.
Upon reaching Yùzhāng,
Yuè died from a carbuncle on his back.
12 The King of Hénán, Qiánguī, relocated the tribal people of the Qiāng leader Jù Qǐ and others, over five thousand households, to Diélán City.
Jù Qǐ's surrender to Qiánguī was seen in the previous year's scroll.
Diélán City is southwest of Dàxià,
and northeast of Kāngláng.
At the end of the Hàn,
the Dí king of Xīngguó, Ā Guì, occupied Xīngguó City,
within the boundaries of Lüèyáng Commandery,
and Qǐfú established a commandery based on that place name.
He also appointed his son Mùyìgān as Wǔwēi Grand Administrator,
garrisoning Kāngláng City.
Kāngláng City,
in the fourth year,
was built by Qǐfú Chìpán.
Also,
pronunciation: fú yòu fān.
13 On the Dīngmǎo day,
the Wèi ruler Sì visited the Jīnlíng tombs,
with the Marquis of Shānyáng, Xī Jīn, remaining in charge.
The King of Chānglí, Mùróng Bó'ér, plotted rebellion;
on the Jǐsì day,
Xī Jīn arrested and executed him along with his partisans.
14 In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Yān ruler Fá appointed his heir apparent, Yǒng, to concurrently hold the title of Grand Chányú,
and established four assistants.
The heir apparent concurrently holding the title of Grand Chányú began with Liú Hàn,
at that time only left and right assistants were established,
Fá added front and rear assistants.
Chán,
pronunciation: chán.
The Róurán Kèhán Húlǜ sent an envoy to offer three thousand horses to Fá,
kè,
pronunciation follows entering tone.
hán,
pronunciation: hán.
envoy,
pronunciation: shū lì fān.
Fá ordered his ministers to deliberate.
The Duke of Liáoxī, Sùfú, said:
"Previous generations all married imperial clan women to the Six Barbarians,
we should agree to give him a daughter of a concubine,
the Lèlàng Princess should not be lowered to marry someone not of our kind."
Fá said:
"I am just now promoting trust among different customs,
how can I deceive them!"
So he married the Lèlàng Princess to him.
Fá was diligent in governmental affairs,
encouraging agriculture and sericulture,
reducing corvée labor,
lightening taxes;
whenever appointing a governor or magistrate,
he would personally summon them for an audience,
asking about the essentials of governance,
to observe their ability.
The Yān people were pleased with him.
15 The King of Hénán, Qiánguī, sent the Duke of Píngchāng, Chìpán, and the Central Army General Shěn Qián to attack Southern Liáng.
Shěn Qián
was Qiánguī's son.
In the eighth month,
Chìpán's troops crossed the river,
this refers to crossing the Jīnchéng River.
Chì,
pronunciation: chāng zhì fān.
The Southern Liáng troops were defeated,
and over a hundred thousand oxen and horses were captured before returning.
16 Jǔqú Méngxùn led light cavalry to raid Western Liáng,
the Duke of Western Liáng, Hào, said:
"There is a way for troops to defeat the enemy without fighting,
by blunting their sharpness.
Méngxùn recently made an alliance with us,
as seen in the previous year's scroll.
If I close the gates and do not engage him in battle,
waiting until his sharp energy is exhausted and then attack him,
there is no way I will not overcome him."
After a while,
Méngxùn's provisions ran out and he withdrew,
Hào sent his heir apparent Xīn to lead seven thousand cavalry to intercept and attack him,
Méngxùn was badly defeated,
and his general Jǔqú Bǎinián was captured.
17 The King of Hénán, Qiánguī, attacked the Qín's Liàoyáng Grand Administrator Yáo Lóng at Bǎiyáng Fortress,
and captured it;
in winter, the eleventh month,
he advanced to attack the Nánpíng Grand Administrator Wáng Jǐng at Shuǐluò City,
the Shuǐjīng Zhù states: Shuǐluò Pavilion is west of Lǒng Mountain,
within the boundaries of the Hàn's Liàoyáng County.
Zhèng Jiǎn said: Shuǐluò City controls the Lǒng Ridge to the west, connecting the road to Qínzhōu,
two rivers from Lǒng encircle the city and flow west,
winding around and connecting to the Wèi River,
the plain is level and the soil fertile,
extending several hundred lǐ.
The Yuánfēng Jiǔyù Zhì states: Déshùn Army has Shuǐluò City one hundred lǐ to the southwest,
built by Liú Hù under Zhèng Jiǎn's orders during Emperor Rénzōng's reign.
Jǐng,
pronunciation: jū yǒng fān.
He relocated over three thousand households of people to Tánjiāo.
Tánjiāo is northwest of Zhìchéng.
In the twelfth month,
the Western Qiāng leader Péng Lìfā launched a surprise attack and occupied Fúhǎn,
proclaiming himself Grand General and Hézhōu Governor,
Qiánguī attacked him,
but did not overcome him.
18 This year,
the Bīngzhōu Regional Inspector Liú Dàolián was appointed as Běixúzhōu Regional Inspector,
and moved his garrison to Péngchéng.
1 In spring,
the first month,
Hé Nán King Qián Guī again attacked Péng Lìfā,
reaching Nú Kuí Valley.
Lìfā abandoned his followers and fled south,
Qián Guī dispatched General Zhèn Wēi Qǐfú Gōngfǔ to pursue him to Qīng Shuǐ,
and beheaded him.
He captured twelve thousand three hundred Qiāng households,
appointed Qǐfú Shěn Qián as Hé Zhōu Regional Inspector,
garrisoned Fú Hǎn, and then returned.
2 In the second month,
on Bǐng Zǐ day,
Wú Xīng Grand Administrator Kǒng Jìng was appointed as Deputy Director of the Right of the Imperial Secretariat.
3 Hé Nán King Qián Guī moved his capital to Tán Jiāo,
ordering Duke Píng Chāng Chì Pán to garrison Yuàn Chuān.
Qián Guī attacked Tǔyùhún Ā Ruògān at Chì Shuǐ,
and forced his surrender.
Wǔ Dài Zhì: In the fifth year of the Suí dynasty's Dà Yè era, Tǔyùhún was pacified,
and Hé Yuán Commandery was established at the ancient Chì Shuǐ City,
which was near Jī Shí Mountain.
Wèi Shōu's Dì Xíng Zhì states: Lín Táo Commandery had a Chì Shuǐ County.
Shuǐ Jīng Zhù states: Chì Shuǐ City was also called Lín Táo East City.
To surrender,
the pronunciation is "hù jiāng fān."
4 In summer,
the fourth month,
Liú Dàoguī requested to return due to illness,
and it was granted.
Dàoguī had been in Jīng Zhōu for many years,
from the first year,
Dàoguī governed Jīng Zhōu.
Upon his return,
the government treasury and curtains
remained exactly as they were before.
Two armored soldiers accompanying him moved mats onto the boat,
and Dàoguī had them executed in the marketplace.

The Later General and Yù Zhōu Regional Inspector Liú Yì was appointed as General of the Guards, Commander of the military affairs of Jīng, Níng, Qín, and Yōng provinces, and Jīng Zhōu Regional Inspector.
Yì said to Left Guard General Liú Jìngxuān:
"I am unworthy of this western appointment,
but I wish to trouble you to serve as my Chief Clerk for the Southern Man,"
meaning the Chief Clerk of the Southern Man Colonel's office.
Jìngxuān was afraid,
and informed Grand Marshal Yù,
who laughed and said:
"Just ensure that Elder Brother remains safe,
there is certainly no need for excessive worry."
Yì's nature was stubborn and self-willed,
he considered his merit in establishing righteousness to be equal to Yù's,
and was deeply self-congratulatory and boastful;
although he outwardly deferred to Yù in matters of authority, he was inwardly unsubmissive;
this can be seen from his reply to his brother Fán last year.
He was often discontented and frustrated.
Yù always treated him gently and compliantly,
causing Yì to become increasingly arrogant and unrestrained.
He once said:
"I regret not encountering Liú or Xiàng,
to contend with them for the Central Plains!"
After his defeat at Sāng Luò,
an event recorded in the sixth year of the previous scroll,
he became even more resentful and agitated.
Yù had never studied much,
while Yì was quite well-versed in literature and refinement,
so many court officials of good reputation sided with him.
He formed deep alliances with
Deputy Director of the Imperial Secretariat Xiè Hùn,
and Dān Yáng Governor Xī Sēngshī.
Sēngshī
was the nephew of Xī Chāo.
Since Yì now controlled the upper reaches,
he secretly harbored plans against Yù.
He requested concurrent supervision over Jiāo and Guǎng provinces,
and Yù granted it.
Yì also petitioned to appoint Xī Sēngshī as Colonel of the Southern Man and Rear Army Marshal,
and Máo Xiūzhī as Nán Commandery Grand Administrator.
Yù also approved this,
appointing Liú Mùzhī to replace Sēngshī as Dān Yáng Governor.
Yì submitted a request to go to Jīng Kǒu to bid farewell at his ancestral tombs,
and Yù went to meet him at Ní Táng.
General Níng Yuǎn Hú Fán said to Yù:
"Does Your Excellency believe General Liú of the Guards will ultimately remain subordinate to you?"
Yì was General of the Guards,
hence the title.
After a long pause,
Yù said:
"What do you think?"
Fán replied:
"Commanding a million troops,
attacking with certainty of success,
fighting with certainty of victory,
Yì respects you for this;
but as for dabbling in historical records,
Shī Gǔ explained: 'Shè'
is like wading through water;
'liè,'
is like hunting animals;
meaning to browse through them,
not specializing deeply.
'Zhuàn,'
is pronounced 'zhí liàn fān.'
He prides himself on being a hero;
thus, scholars and refined gentlemen flock to him.
I fear he will never remain subordinate to you,
it would be better to seize him during this meeting."
Yù said:
"Yì and I both share the merit of restoration,
his faults are not yet evident,
we cannot plot against each other."
Although Yù answered Fán with these words,
he secretly had plans for dealing with Yì.
5 Qǐfú Chì Pán attacked Southern Liáng's Sān Hé Grand Administrator Wú Yīn at Bái Tǔ,
and captured it,
appointing Qǐfú Chū Lěi to replace him.
Shuǐ Jīng states: The Huáng Hé passes south of Hán Chuān City,
then flows east past Lín Jīn City north and Bái Tǔ City south.
Kàn Yǐn's Shí Sān Zhōu Zhì states: Sixty lǐ west of Zuǒ Nán Ford,
there is Bái Tǔ City,
north of the great river,
serving as a crossing point along the river.
'Lěi,'
is pronounced 'lì zhuī fān.'
Wèi Shōu states: Bái Tǔ County
belonged to Shàng Commandery in the Hàn,
to Jīn Chéng Commandery in the Jìn,
and to Xīn Píng Commandery in the Later Wèi.
I believe the Bái Tǔ of Later Wèi's Xīn Píng was the Bái Tǔ of Hàn's Shàng Commandery,
while the Bái Tǔ of Jìn's Jīn Chéng was the Bái Tǔ west of Zuǒ Nán,
each being a different place.
Wǔ Dài Zhì states: Bīn Zhōu's Xīn Píng County was formerly called Bái Tǔ,
this is the Bái Tǔ of Hàn's Shàng Commandery and Later Wèi.
Southern Liáng's Bái Tǔ should have been within the boundaries of Táng's Shàn Zhōu.
In the sixth month,
Qǐfú Gōngfǔ assassinated Hé Nán King Qián Guī.
Gōngfǔ
was the son of Guó Rén,
and because he was not made heir,
he committed regicide.
He fled and held Dà Xià.
Duke Píng Chāng Chì Pán dispatched his younger brother, General Guǎng Wǔ Zhì Dá, and General Yáng Wǔ Mù Yìgān, leading three thousand cavalry to attack him;
he appointed his younger brother Tán Dá as General Zhèn Jīng
[Guardian of the Capital],
to garrison Tán Jiāo.
Qǐfú made Tán Jiāo his capital,
considering it the imperial city,
hence he established the General Zhèn Jīng to garrison it.
'Shuài,'
is read as 'lǜ.'
'Qí,'
is pronounced 'qí jì fān';
same below.
'Tán,'
is pronounced 'tú hán fān.'
Chì Pán led over twenty thousand households of officials, soldiers, and civilians to move to Fú Hǎn.
Many in Qín urged King Xīng of Qín to take advantage of the chaos to seize Chì Pán,
but Xīng said:
"Attacking others during mourning
is contrary to ritual propriety."
King Bóbó of Xià wanted to attack Chì Pán,
but Army Advisor and Central General Wáng Mǎidé admonished:
"Chì Pán
is our ally state,
now suffering from mourning and turmoil.
If we cannot offer aid,
and instead rely on our military strength to attack him,
even a commoner would be ashamed to do such a thing,
let alone a ruler of ten thousand chariots!"
Bóbó then desisted.
6 In the intercalary month,
on Gēng Zǐ day,
Duke Liè Wǔ of Nán Commandery, Liú Dàoguī, died.
7 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on Jǐ Sì, the first day of the month,
the Wèi ruler Sì toured east,
establishing four Great Generals and twelve Lesser Generals;
appointing Marquis Shān Yáng Jīn and Marquis Yuán Chéng Qū to act as Left and Right Chancellors.
Xī Jīn was enfeoffed as Marquis Shān Yáng,
Tuòbá Qū as Marquis Yuán Chéng.
On Gēng Yín day,
Sì reached Rú Yuán,
and toured the northwestern tribal areas.
8 Qǐfú Zhì Dá and others defeated Qǐfú Gōngfǔ at Dà Xià.
Gōngfǔ fled to Dié Lán City,
to join his younger brother Ā Chái;
Zhì Dá and others attacked and captured it,
beheading Ā Chái and his five sons.
Gōngfǔ fled to Kāng Láng Southern Mountain,
was pursued and captured,
along with his four sons,
and executed by dismemberment at Tán Jiāo.
In the eighth month,
Qǐfú Chì Pán proclaimed himself Great General and King of Hé Nán.
Chì Pán
was Qián Guī's eldest son.
He changed the era name to Yǒng Kāng;
buried Qián Guī at Fú Hǎn,
posthumously titled Wǔ Yuán,
and temple name Gāo Zǔ.
9 Empress Wáng passed away.
On the 10th day of the Gēngxū year,
the Wei ruler Sì returned to Píngchéng.
This was after an inspection tour.
In the 9th month,
the King of Hénán, Chìpán, appointed the Minister of Works Zhái Qíng from Wǔshǐ as his Chancellor of State,
and the Palace Attendant and Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent, Zhào Jǐng, as the Censor-in-Chief.
He abolished the positions of Minister of Works, Vice Minister, the Six Ministers of the Ministry of Works, Palace Attendants, and other offices.
On the Guǐyǒu day,
Empress Xī was buried at the Xiūpíng Mausoleum.
Liú Yì arrived at Jiānglíng,
where he made many changes to the local administrators.
He arbitrarily took over ten thousand troops from the civil and military officials of Yùzhōu and the military forces of Jiāngzhōu to accompany him.
At that time, Liú Yì fell seriously ill.
Xī Sēngshī and others, fearing that if Liú Yì died,
their faction would be in danger,
advised Liú Yì to request that his cousin, the Governor of Yǎnzhōu, Liú Fán, serve as his deputy.
Grand Marshal Liú Yǔ pretended to agree.
Liú Fán came to court from Guǎnglíng.
On the Jǐmǎo day,
Liú Yǔ issued an edict listing Liú Yì’s crimes,
stating that he had conspired with Liú Fán and Xiè Hùn to commit treason.
Liú Fán and Xiè Hùn were arrested and ordered to commit suicide.
Earlier,
Xiè Hùn had been on intimate terms with Liú Yì.
Xiè Hùn’s elder cousin Xiè Dàn was often worried about this
and gradually distanced himself from Xiè Hùn.
He said to his younger brother Xiè Pú and his nephew Xiè Zhān:
"With this temperament of Yìshòu,
he will eventually bring ruin to the family."
Yìshòu
was Xiè Hùn’s childhood name.
He was the grandson of Xiè Ān.
On the Gēngchén day,
an edict was issued granting a general amnesty.
The former Administrator of Kuàijī, Sīmǎ Xiūzhī, was appointed as the Governor of Jīng, Yōng, Liáng, Qín, Níng, and Yì Provinces and the Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
The Inspector of Běixúzhōu, Liú Dàolián, was appointed as the Inspector of Yǎn and Qīng Provinces,
stationed at Jīngkǒu.
The Inspector of Běixúzhōu was based in Péngchéng.
Liú Dàolián was stationed at Jīngkǒu
to serve as an important northern defense for Jiànkāng.
Liú Yǔ suspected that Zhǎngmín would be difficult to manage alone,
so he appointed Liú Mùzhī as General of Establishing Military Might,
assigned him staff officers,
and provided him with resources and troops to guard against him.
By this time, Liú Yǔ already had the intention to kill Zhǎngmín.
On the Rénwǔ day,
Liú Yǔ led his armies from Jiànkāng.
Army Advisor Wáng Zhèn’è requested a hundred boats to serve as the vanguard.
On the Bǐngshēn day,
they arrived at Gūshú.
Wáng Zhèn’è was appointed as General Who Inspires Awe,
and together with General of the Soaring Dragon Kuǎi Ēn, he led a hundred boats ahead.
Liú Yǔ instructed them:
"If the enemy can be attacked,
attack them.
If not,
burn their ships and boats,
and remain stationed by the water to wait for me."
Wáng Zhèn’è then advanced day and night,
spreading the word that Inspector Liú of Yǎnzhōu was coming.
In winter,
the 10th month,
on the Jǐwèi day,
Wáng Zhèn’è arrived at Yùzhāngkǒu,
twenty *li* from Jiānglíng City.
He disembarked and proceeded on foot.
Kuǎi Ēn’s troops were in front,
with Wáng Zhèn’è following behind.
One or two men were left on each boat,
with six or seven banners erected on the shore opposite the boats.
Drums were placed beneath the banners.
He told the men left behind:
"When you estimate that we are about to reach the city,
beat the drums vigorously,
making it appear as if a large army is following."
"Beat the drums vigorously" means to sound the drums.
Wáng Zhèn’è advanced directly to attack the city.
He told the soldiers in the front ranks:
This means he informed the soldiers in the front ranks.
"If anyone asks,
just say that Inspector Liú of Yǎnzhōu has arrived."
The ferry guards and the common people were all at ease and unsuspecting.
When they were still five or six *li* from the city,
they encountered Liú Yì’s trusted general Zhū Xiǎnzhī.
"Trusted general" refers to a general who is close to the commander and holds a key military position.
He asked:
"Where is Inspector Liú of Yǎnzhōu?"
The soldiers replied:
"He is behind."
Zhū Xiǎnzhī went to the rear of the army but did not see Liú Fán.
Instead, he saw soldiers carrying shields and other combat equipment.
"Péng pái" refers to what is now called "páng pái," used to ward off arrows and blades.
Sǔn Miǎn said: "Lǔ" means "Péng pái."
The *Shìmíng* states: "Péng pái" is a military weapon.
"Péng" means "páng" (side),
as it is used to fend off enemies and defend against attacks from the side.
The sound of drums beating vigorously was very loud.
Realizing that this was not Liú Fán’s arrival,
he immediately galloped away on horseback
and informed Liú Yì, ordering the city gates to be closed.
Wáng Zhèn’è also galloped forward.
Before the gates could be fully closed,
the soldiers managed to enter the city.
The Chief Clerk of the Guard Army, Xiè Chún, went to pay his respects to Liú Yì.
Subordinates paying respects at the government office is called "cān chéng."
His attendants wanted to take his carriage back.
Xiè Chún rebuked them, saying:
"I am an official of the people,"
meaning he served as an official for the people.
He then galloped back into the government office.
Xiè Chún was the grandson of Xiè Jù, the elder brother of Xiè Ān.
Wáng Zhèn’è fought with the soldiers inside the city
and attacked the inner city.
The inner city within a city was called the "golden city" during the Jìn and Sòng periods.
The time after midday is called "bū."
"Mid-bū" refers to the exact Shēn hour.
The end of the Shēn hour is called "late bū."
Wáng Zhèn’è breached the golden city and entered.
He sent someone to show Liú Yì the edict, the amnesty document, and Liú Yǔ’s handwritten letter.
Liú Yì burned them all without looking
and, together with Sima Máo Xiūzhī and others, urged the soldiers to fight fiercely.
The people inside the city still did not believe that Liú Yǔ had come personally.
However, the soldiers who had come from the east with Liú Yì
had many cousins and relatives among the imperial army.
As they fought, they talked,
and upon learning that Liú Yǔ had come personally,
morale collapsed in fear.
By nightfall,
the soldiers in front of the audience hall had all scattered.
Liú Yì’s brave general Zhào Cài was killed.
Liú Yì’s remaining soldiers still closed the eastern and western gates and resisted.
Wáng Zhèn’è, concerned that they might injure each other in the darkness,
led his troops out and surrounded the golden city,
leaving the southern side open.
Liú Yì, fearing that there were ambushes to the south,
at midnight,
led about three hundred of his followers
and broke out through the north gate.
Máo Xiūzhī said to Xiè Chún:
"Just follow me."
Xiè Chún refused
and was killed by others.
Liú Yì fled at night to the Niúmù Buddhist Temple.
The Niúmù Temple was located twenty *li* north of Jiānglíng City.
When Huán Wèi was defeated,
as recorded in the 114th scroll, first year.
Wèi is pronounced as "yū wù fān."
Monk Chāng had hidden him,
but Liú Yì killed Chāng.
This time,
the temple monks refused him, saying:
"Our late abbot sheltered Huán Wèi,
and he was killed by General Liú of the Guard Army.
Now we truly dare not shelter a stranger."
Liú Yì sighed and said:
"To be trapped by one’s own laws—
it has come to this!"
The *Records of the Grand Historian* records that when Lord Shāng offended the state of Qín,
he fled to the pass and wanted to stay at an inn.
The innkeeper did not know he was Lord Shāng
and said:
"According to Lord Shāng’s laws,
innkeepers who lodge guests without proper identification will be punished."
Lord Shāng sighed and said:
"Alas!
To be trapped by one’s own laws—
it has come to this!"
The next day,
the residents reported him,
and he was beheaded in the marketplace.
His sons and nephews were also executed.
Liú Yì’s elder brother Liú Mó fled to Xiāngyáng,
but Lǔ Zōngzhī captured and beheaded him, sending his head to the capital.
Earlier,
Liú Yì's paternal uncle Liú Zhènzhī was living in retirement at Jīngkǒu,
not responding to summons for official appointment,
and often said to Yì and Liú Pān:
"Your talents and capabilities
are sufficient to achieve your ambitions,
but I fear it will not last long.
I will not seek wealth and rank from you,
nor will I share in your punishments and troubles."
Whenever he saw Yì or Pān arriving at his gate with their entourage and guards,
he would berate them.
Yì was very respectful and fearful of him;
when still several hundred paces from his residence,
he would dismiss all his ceremonial guards,
and proceed with only a few men in plain clothes.
After Yì's death,
the Grand Marshal Liú Yù memorialized to appoint Zhènzhī as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.
Sàn,
read as sǎn.
Qí,
read as jì.
14 The Duke of Chóuchí, Yáng Shèng, rebelled against Qín.
In the first year of Yìxī,
Shèng surrendered to Qín,
now he rebelled again.
The Qín king Yáo Xīng sent the Jianwei General Zhào Kūn as the vanguard,
with the Lijie General Yáo Bóshòu following him,
the Former General Yáo Huī advancing from Jiùxiá,
the Qín Province Governor Yáo Sōng advancing from Yángtóuxiá,
and the Right Guard General Hú Yìdù advancing from Qiānchéng,
to attack Shèng.
Xīng personally went from Yōng to join them,
meeting with the various generals at Lǒngkǒu.
This is the entrance to the Lǒng road.
Jiàng,
read as jiàng.
The Tiānshuǐ Grand Administrator Wáng Sōnghū said to Sōng:
"The late emperor's divine strategies were matchless,
and Xú Luòshēng, with his heroic martial prowess assisting the mandate,
twice entered Chóuchí,
yet returned without success;
Yáo Cháng also attacked Chóuchí twice,
this should be examined.
It is simply because the terrain is dangerously fortified.
Now, with Zhào Kūn's troops
and Your Excellency's authority,
compared to the previous dynasty,
I truly do not foresee success.
Your Excellency fully understands the strategic advantages,
why not memorialize and report this!"
Sōng did not listen.
Shèng led his troops to confront Kūn,
Bóshòu was timid and did not advance,
Kūn's forces were outnumbered and no match,
and he was defeated by Shèng.
Xīng executed Bóshòu and returned.
Xīng appointed Yáng Fúsōng as the Governor of Yōng Province,
leading the troops from north of the mountains to attack Xià.
The Qín Yōng Province governed the five commanderies north of the mountains,
with its seat at Āndìng.
Xiàn,
read as xiàn.
Xīng said to his courtiers:
"Fúsōng, whenever he sees the enemy,
becomes uncontrollably brave,
so I always restrict his troops to no more than five thousand.
Now that he commands many more,
he will certainly be defeated when encountering the enemy.
He has already gone far,
and it is too late to pursue him;
what shall we do?"
Fúsōng battled the Xià king Bóbó,
was indeed defeated,
captured by Bóbó,
and had his throat cut, dying.
15 Qín established the Lady of Handsome Fairness Qí as empress.
16 Jǔqú Méngxùn moved to Gūzāng.
17 In the eleventh month,
on the day Jǐmǎo,
the Grand Marshal Yù arrived at Jiānglíng,
and executed Xī Sēngshī.
Earlier,
although Máo Xiūzhī served as Liú Yì's subordinate,
he had always attached himself to Yù,
so Yù specially pardoned him.
He bestowed upon Wáng Zhèn'è the title of Marquis of Hànshòu.
Yù asked Yì's Advisory Army Counselor Shēn Yǒng:
"What should be implemented today?"
Yǒng replied:
"Eliminate old grievances,
double benevolent favors,
and arrange official appointments according to family rank.
Since Wèi and Jìn times,
it has been customary to base the order of official appointments on the level of family status;
'guàn xù' means
to arrange in order,
like stringing coins on a thread.
That is all."
Yù accepted this,
issuing an edict to reduce taxes and levies,
lighten corvée labor and mitigate punishments,
ceremoniously summon famous scholars to office,
and the people of Jīng were pleased.
18 Zhūgě Chángmín was arrogant, unrestrained, greedy, and extravagant,
his actions often unlawful,
causing trouble for the people,
and he constantly feared that Grand Marshal Yù would investigate him.
After Liú Yì was executed,
Chángmín said to his close associates:
"'Last year, Péng Yuè was minced into sauce;
this year, Hán Xìn is killed.'
Words of Hàn's Xuē Gōng.
Bèi,
read as bèi.
Then, dismissing others, he asked Liú Mùzhī:
"Widespread rumors
all say that the Grand Marshal is at odds with me;
how did it come to this?"
Mùzhī said:
"The Duke campaigned far upstream,
entrusting his elderly mother and young children to Your Excellency;
if there were the slightest negligence,
how could he tolerate it!"
Chángmín's mind was somewhat eased.
Chángmín's younger brother, the Assistant State Protecting General Liú Límín, urged Chángmín:
"The demise of the Liú clan
is also a cause for fear for our Zhūgě clan;
we should take advantage of Yù not having returned yet to plot against him."
Chángmín hesitated and did not act,
then sighed:
"In poverty and lowliness, one often thinks of wealth and honor;
with wealth and honor, one inevitably treads upon crisis.
Now, to wish to be a commoner in Dāntú,
how could it be possible!"
Chángmín,
was from Yángdū in Lángyá,
but resided in Dāntú.
"Pánlóng was cruel, violent, arbitrary, and domineering,
bringing destruction upon himself.
As the different factions are about to be eliminated,
and the path of the world is becoming level,
matters of wealth and honor
we shall share together."
Jìngxuān replied:
"Since the Yìxī era,
I have undeservedly held posts in three provinces and seven commanderies;
Jìngxuān, after returning from the north,
was appointed Grand Administrator of Jìnlíng,
transferred to Jiāng Province,
stationed at Xúnyáng,
concurrently administering commandery affairs,
summoned and appointed as Neishi of Xuānchéng,
holding the post of Grand Administrator of Xiāngchéng,
transferred to Protect the Army Pacifying the Man,
Grand Administrator of Ānfēng,
Neishi of Liáng Principality,
then transferred to Governor of Qīng Province,
soon changed to Jì Province.
I think of avoiding fullness and residing in deficiency.
The purport of wealth and honor
is not something I dare aspire to."
Moreover, he had the letter presented to Yù,
Yù said:
"Ā Shòu indeed does not betray me."
Jìngxuān,
courtesy name Wànshòu,
hence Yù called him Ā Shòu.
Liú Mùzhī worried that Chángmín would cause trouble,
and dismissing others, asked the Grand Marshal's Acting Army Counselor Dōnghǎi Hé Chéngtiān:
"Will the Duke succeed in his current undertaking?"
Chéngtiān said:
"Jīng Province need not worry about not being pacified in time;
pàn,
means to decide.
When the Duke returned from Zuǒlǐ into Shítóu last year,
it was very relaxed;
referring to the time after defeating Lú Xún and returning.
Tuō ěr,
means returning lightly and relaxed,
without strict preparations.
Now greater caution is appropriate."
Mùzhī said:
"If not for you,
I would not have heard these words."
While Yù was in Jiānglíng,
the Assistant State Protecting General Wáng Dàn requested Yù's permission to go down first,
Yù said:
"Zhūgě Chángmín seems to have suspicions about himself;
how can you just leave!"
Dàn said:
"Chángmín knows that I enjoy your regard,
now if I go down alone lightly,
he will certainly think there is nothing to worry about,
and thus his mind can be slightly eased."
Yù laughed and said:
"Your courage surpasses Bēn and Yù."
Then he allowed him to return first.
19 Jǔqú Méngxùn ascends the throne as King of Héxī.
Jǔqú Méngxùn
was a Hú person from Línsōng of the Lúshuǐ region.
His ancestors served as the Zuǒ Jǔqú (Left Master of the Imperial Stud) for the Xiōngnú,
and thus took the official title as their surname.
He changed the era name to Xuánshǐ,
and established a bureaucracy following the precedent of Liáng Wáng Lǚ Guāng when he became King of Sānhé.
Lǚ Guāng proclaimed himself King of Sānhé,
see the fourteenth year of the Xiàowǔ Tàiyuán era, scroll 107.
20 Grand Commandant Yù planned to attack Shǔ,
but had difficulty selecting a commander-in-chief.
Considering that Zhū Língshí, the Grand Administrator of Xīyáng, possessed both military capability
and administrative experience,
he wished to employ him.
Everyone believed Língshí's qualifications and reputation were still too junior,
and that he would find it difficult to shoulder such a heavy responsibility;
Yù did not listen.
In the twelfth month,
he appointed Língshí as the Governor of Yìzhōu,
commanding General Nìngshuò Zāng Xǐ, Grand Administrator of Héjiān Kuǎi Ēn, Grand Administrator of Xiàpī Liú Zhōng, and others to attack Shǔ,
assigning half of the main army, twenty thousand men, to him.
Xǐ
was the younger brother of Yù's wife,
and his rank was superior to Língshí's,
yet he was also placed under his command.
Yù and Língshí secretly planned the advance,
saying:
"Liú Jìngxuān in previous years advanced from Huánghǔ,
but retreated without success.
The event is seen in the fourth year, scroll 114.
They will likely anticipate that we will come unexpectedly, still via the Inner River route.
Yǔ Zhòngyōng said: The Jiāngzhōu county of Bā commandery faces the confluence of two rivers,
the right one is the Fú,
the Inner River;
the left one is the Shǔ,
the Outer River.
They will certainly station heavy troops at Fúchéng to guard against the inner route.
If we head towards Huánghǔ,
we will fall right into their trap.
Now, we will take the main force via the Outer River to capture Chéngdū,
while sending a diversionary force via the Inner River.
This is an ingenious strategy to control the enemy."
However, he worried that this plan might leak out prematurely,
allowing the enemy to ascertain our true dispositions.
He separately prepared a sealed letter to be given to Língshí,
writing on the envelope:
"Open only upon reaching Báidì."
Thus, although the various armies advanced,
they did not know the details of the plan.
Máo Xiūzhī persistently requested to go;
Yù feared that if Xiūzhī reached Shǔ,
he would certainly carry out many killings,
and as the local people bore a grudge against the Máo clan,
they would also certainly fight to the death to defend themselves,
so he did not permit it.
This was because Máo Qú's family had been exterminated by the people of Shǔ.
21 Ten commanderies were separated from Jīngzhōu to establish Xiāngzhōu.
In the third year of the Chéngdì Xiánhé era,
Xiāngzhōu was abolished and merged into Jīngzhōu,
and now it was re-established.
22 Grand Commandant Yù was additionally appointed Grand Tutor and Governor of Yángzhōu.
23 On Dīngsì,
the Wèi sovereign Sì toured north,
reaching the Great Wall before returning.
This was the Great Wall built by Qín.
1 Spring,
second month,
Gēngxū,
the Wèi sovereign Sì went to Gāoliǔchuān;
Jiǎyín,
he returned to the palace.
2 Grand Commandant Yù returned east from Jiānglíng.
He sent his baggage train ahead in continuous relays, traveling day and night,
and had previously set a date for his arrival,
but each time he delayed and did not advance.
Zhūgě Chángmín and the high officials waited for him day after day at Xīntíng,
but he repeatedly missed the scheduled time.
On the last day of the month, Yǐchǒu,
Yù proceeded swiftly by light boat,
and secretly entered the Eastern Administration.
The concerns that Liú Mùzhī and Hé Chéngtiān had,
Yù had already clearly in mind.
At dawn on the first day of the month, Bǐngyín,
Chángmín heard of this,
and rushed in alarm to the gate.
Yù had hidden strong warriors, including Dīng Wǔ, behind curtains,
then led Chángmín into a private room for conversation,
discussing all matters that had not been fully addressed in their lifetime.
Chángmín was very pleased.
Dīng Wǔ emerged from behind the curtain,
dragged him from his seat and killed him,
then carried the corpse and handed it over to the Commandant of Justice.
His brother Límín was arrested;
Límín was always brave and fierce,
and died fighting.
His younger brother, Army Consultant to the Grand Marshal, Yòumín, and his cousin, General Nìngshuò Xiùzhī, were also killed.
3 On Gēngwǔ,
the Qín sovereign Xīng sent an envoy to Wèi to repair relations.
4 Grand Commandant Yù submitted a memorial stating:
"Grand Marshal Wēn, considering that 'the people lacked a fixed base,
deeply harming governance,'
implemented the Gēngxū land registration to unify their occupations;
the Gēngxū regulation is seen in the second year of the Āidì Xīngníng era, scroll 101.
The benefits indeed stem from this.
From then until now,
it has gradually fallen into disuse and laxity,
I request to reaffirm the former regulation."
Thereupon, land registration was carried out according to boundaries,
with the exception of those from Xú, Yǎn, and Qīng provinces residing in Jìnlíng,
who were not included in the registration;
the Governors of Xú, Qīng, and Yǎn provinces all had their administrative seats in Jìnlíng,
hence it was difficult to apply land registration there.
Registration,
pronunciation: duàn, dìng luàn fān.
Merge.
On Wùyín,
Yù was additionally appointed Governor of Yùzhōu.
Yù firmly declined the posts of Grand Tutor and Provincial Governor.
This refers to declining the appointments from the previous winter.
5 Fàn Húdá of Línyì raided Jiǔzhēn,
Dù Huìdù attacked and beheaded him.
6 The King of Hénán, Chìpán, sent General Zhèndōng Tán Dá and General Píngdōng Wáng Sōngshòu to lead troops east to attack Xiūguān Quán Xiǎoláng and Lǚ Pòhú at Báishíchuān,
defeating them heavily,
capturing over ten thousand men and women,
and advancing to occupy Báishíchéng and Xiǎnqīn.
Xiūguān Quán Xiǎochéng, Lǚ Nújiā, and others, comprising over twenty thousand households, occupied Báikēng and refused to submit;
