Tán Dá attacked and beheaded them,
and the Xiūguān in Lǒngyòu all surrendered.
Qín's Grand Marshal Suǒ Léng surrendered Lǒngxī to Chìpán.
In the seventh year,
Qín ordered Suǒ Léng to guard Lǒngxī to pacify and recruit Qǐfú.
Suǒ,
pronunciation: xī gè fān.
Surrender,
pronunciation: jiàng, hù jiāng fān.
7 The Xià sovereign Bóbó proclaimed a great amnesty,
and changed the era name to Fèngxiáng;
he appointed Chìgān Ālì to concurrently hold the post of Superintendent of Palace Buildings,
and mobilized one hundred thousand Yí and Xià people from north of the mountains to build a capital city north of Shuòfāng River and south of Hēishuǐ River.
The *Shuǐjīng Zhù* states: Shēyán River is also called Shuòfāng River,
its source is at Chìshāfù southwest of Shēyán county,
flowing northeast past the old city south of Shēyán county.
Hèlián built Tǒngwànchéng south of this river.
Shēyán River flows further east,
where Hēishuǐ joins it,
the water emerges from Hēijiàn in Shēyán county,
passes southeast through Shālíng,
and empties into Shēyán River.
Tǒngwànchéng was the seat of the Dìngnán military governor of Xiàzhōu in the Táng dynasty.
Xià,
pronunciation: xià, hù yǎ fān.
"I am about to unify the world,
and rule over all states,
thus the new city should be named Tǒngwàn (Unify Myriad)."
Ālì was ingenious but cruel,
he steamed earth to build the walls,
and if an awl could penetrate even one inch,
he would kill the builder and have him mixed into the wall.
Bóbó considered him loyal,
and entrusted him with authority.
Whenever weapons were completed,
and presented to him,
workers were certain to die: if an arrow could not penetrate armor, the bow-maker was beheaded;
if it penetrated, the armor-maker was beheaded.
He also cast a large bronze drum,
with figures like Fēilián, Wēngzhòng, bronze camels, dragons, and tigers,
adorned with gold,
arrayed in front of the palace halls.
In total, several thousand craftsmen were killed,
and as a result, all implements were exquisitely sharp and effective.
Bóbó considered that his ancestors had taken their mother's surname, Liú,
which was improper.
The *Zàijì* states: Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn gave a daughter of the imperial clan in marriage to the Chányú Mòdú of the Xiōngnú,
and they swore an oath as brothers,
therefore his descendants assumed the surname Liú.
Thus he changed his surname to Hèlián,
saying that the imperial lineage is connected to Heaven as its sons,
its majesty is linked with Heaven;
those who were not of the main line
were all to take Tiěfá as their surname.
Bóbó's father, Wèichén, was originally of the Tiěfú clan,
so he changed the surname of those not of the main line to Tiěfá.
Meaning they are all capable of conquering others.
8 In summer,
in the fourth month,
on the Yǐmǎo day,
the Wei ruler Sì toured westward,
ordering the Zhèngbing General Xī Jīn,
"Zhèngbing,"
the Northern History writes as
"Dūbīng."
Dà Féi
was a Róurán person.
The Hóngfēi General
was an office created by the Tuòbá clan.
General,
read as jiàng.
The Róurán surname was Yùjiǔlǘ,
now called Lǘ,
for brevity and convenience.
Mount Bánà was likely beyond the frontier of Guǎngníng Commandery.
9 The King of Hénán, Chìpán, sent the General of Pacifying the North Wū Dìyán and the Champion General Zhái Shào to attack the Tǔyùhún separate commander Jù Páng at Qìqín
River,
and inflicted a major defeat on him.
10 The King of Héxī, Méngxùn, established his son Zhèngdé as heir apparent,
additionally appointing him as General of Guarding the Garrison and Manager of the Affairs of the Masters of Writing.
11 The King of Southern Liáng, Rùtán, attacked the King of Héxī, Méngxùn.
Méngxùn defeated him at Ruòhòu Wù,
and again defeated him at Ruòliáng.
He then advanced to besiege Lèdū,
but after twenty days could not capture it.
The Administrator of Huánghé of Southern Liáng, Wén Zhī, surrendered his commandery to Méngxùn,
and Méngxùn appointed Wén Zhī as Administrator of Guǎngwǔ.
Méngxùn again attacked Southern Liáng,
and Rùtán gave the Grand Commandant Jù Yán as a hostage,
after which Méngxùn withdrew.
Méngxùn went west to Tiáodiào,
and sent the Champion General Fú Ēn with ten thousand cavalry to raid the two tribes of Bēihé and Wūtí,
inflicting a major defeat on them.
The Hàn had the Bēihé Qiāng,
who dwelled at Freshwater Sea.
Méngxùn was resting at the New Terrace,
when the eunuch Wáng Huáizǔ struck Méngxùn, wounding his foot.
Méngxùn's wife, Lady Mèng, captured and beheaded him.
Méngxùn's mother, Lady Chē, passed away.
12 In the fifth month,
on the Yǐhài day,
the Wei ruler Sì went to the old palace at Yúnzhōng.
The Táng Protectorate of the Danyu governed one county, Jīnhé,
which was the Yúnzhōng of Qín and Hàn times.
The New Book states: Jīnhé was originally the capital of Dàowǔ of Later Wei.
On the Bǐngzǐ day,
a great amnesty was declared.
The Hú of Xīhé, Zhāng Wài and others, gathered a crowd and became bandits.
On the Yǐmǎo day,
Sì sent the Duke of Kuàijī, Chánglè Liú Jié and others to station at Xīhé to summon and attack them.
According to this, from Yǐhài to Bǐngzǐ is nearly forty days,
and it is clear that the fifth month has no Yǐmǎo day,
so it is likely Jǐmǎo.
Kuài,
read as guì.
Sì went to Wǔyuán.
13 Zhū Língshí and others arrived at Báidì and opened the sealed letter,
which said:
"All armies are to take Chéngdū via the Outer River,
Zāng Xī is to take Guǎnghàn via the Middle River.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Luò River emerges south of Zhāng Mountain in Luò County,
passes south of the old city of Luò County,
which was the seat of Guǎnghàn Commandery,
then passes south through Xīndū County where it joins the Bóshuǐ River,
and also joins the Jiān River,
also called the Pí River.
It then passes through the Niúbǐ River in Qiánwéi,
and east through Zīzhōng County,
where it is called the Bóshuǐ River.
The Bóshuǐ River reaches the foot of Fāng Mountain in Jiāngyáng County and enters the Jiāng,
at the mouth called the Bóshuǐ Estuary,
known as the Middle River.
Proceed from the Inner River toward Huánghǔ."
Thereupon, the various armies advanced with double speed.
Qiáo Zòng indeed ordered Qiáo Dàofú to lead a heavy force to garrison Fúchéng,
to guard against the Inner River.
Língshí reached Píngmó,
two hundred lǐ from Chéngdū.
Zòng sent the Inspector of Qín Province, Hóu Huī, and the Master of Writing of the Right, Qiáo Shēn, to lead over ten thousand troops to station at Píngmó,
building fortifications on both banks to resist them.
Língshí said to Liú Zhōng:
"Now the weather is extremely hot,
and the enemy has deployed troops strictly and fortified the dangerous points.
Attacking them may not necessarily succeed,
and would only increase our exhaustion.
Moreover, I wish to nurture our vigor, rest the troops, and wait for their opening.
What do you think?"
Zhōng said:
"That is not right.
Previously we loudly proclaimed that the main force was heading for the Inner River,
so Qiáo Dàofú dared not leave Fúchéng.
Now our heavy army has suddenly arrived,
catching them by surprise.
Hóu Huī and his ilk are already terrified.
The enemy's reliance on troops to guard the dangerous points
is because they are afraid and dare not fight.
Taking advantage of their fear and terror,
we should attack with our full elite force.
The situation is certain to result in victory.
After conquering Píngmó,
we can naturally advance with drums beating,
and Chéngdū will certainly be unable to hold.
If we delay our troops and maintain a standoff,
they will come to know our true situation.
If the Fú army suddenly arrives,
and they combine forces to resist us,
once their morale is settled,
and their good generals are gathered—
'good generals' refers to Qiáo Dàofú.
Read as jiàng.
Then we will seek battle but not obtain it,
our army's provisions will have no source,
and over twenty thousand men will all become captives of the Shǔ people."
Língshí followed his advice.
The various generals, considering the northern city across the water to have difficult terrain and many troops,
wanted to first attack its southern city.
Língshí said:
"Now, if we slaughter the southern city,
it will not be enough to break the northern one.
If we use our full elite force to capture the northern city,
then the southern city will disperse without even a wave of the hand."
In autumn,
in the seventh month,
Língshí led the various armies in a fierce attack on the northern city,
captured it,
and beheaded Hóu Huī and Qiáo Shēn.
He then led his troops back to head for the southern city,
and the southern city collapsed on its own.
Língshí abandoned the boats and advanced on foot.
Qiáo Zòng's senior general, Qiáo Fǔzhī, was stationed at Niúpí.
"Niúpí"
should be
"Niúbǐ."
Mèng Kāng said: Bǐ
is pronounced bì.
Master Yán said: Pronounced bì'ěr.
Niúbǐ County had belonged to Qiánwéi Commandery since Hàn times.
Hé Chéngtiān said: In the Jìn, Emperor Mù transferred it to belong to Shǔ Commandery.
Nowadays, on the west bank of Jiǎn Province there is an ancient Niúbǐ garrison city.
Dǎbí Mountain is located over ten lǐ south of Péngshān County in Méi Province today.
The mountain rises in isolation,
facing the river water to the east.
Common saying: In the past, a Zhōu tripod sank here,
and someone saw its nose,
hence the name.
Sāi,
read as sè.
He was beheaded.
Xiǎo Gǒu heard of this,
and also collapsed.
Thereupon, the various camps and garrisons of Zòng, seeing the situation, fled one after another.
On the Wùchén day,
Qiáo Zòng abandoned Chéngdū and fled.
Shàngshū Lìng Mǎ Dān sealed the government storehouses to await the Jìn army.
On the Rénshēn day,
Zhū Língshí entered Chéngdū,
executed Qiáo Zòng's relatives of the same paternal lineage,
while the rest of the populace was left undisturbed,
allowing them to resume their livelihoods.
When Qiáo Zòng left Chéngdū,
he first bid farewell at his ancestral tombs.
His daughter said:
"Flight will surely not bring escape,
it will only bring disgrace;
since death is inevitable regardless,
it would be better to die at the tombs of our ancestors."
Zòng did not heed her.
Qiáo Dàofú heard that Píngmó had not been held,
and led troops from Fú to come to its aid.
Zòng went to join him.
Dàofú, upon seeing Zòng,
angrily said:
"A great man such as you, possessing such achievements, yet you abandon them!
Where do you think you are going to return to!
Who among men does not die?
How exceedingly cowardly you are!"
Thereupon, he threw his sword at Zòng,
striking his saddle.
Zòng then departed
and hanged himself.
Wáng Zhì of Bāxī beheaded him and sent his head to Língshí.
Dàofú said to his followers:
"The survival or destruction of Shǔ
truly rests with me,
not with the Prince of Qiáo.
Now that I am here,
we are still sufficient for one battle."
His followers all assented;
Dàofú distributed all his gold and silk to bestow upon his men,
who accepted them and then fled.
Dàofú fled among the Lǎo tribes,
but a man of Bā named Dù Jǐn captured and delivered him.
He was beheaded at the army gate.
In the first year of the Yìxī era,
Qiáo Zòng occupied Shǔ,
and was destroyed after nine years.
Jǐn,
pronounced Qú Lìn.
Dān said to his followers:
"Marquis Zhū will not send me to the capital,
he wishes to silence me,"
meaning Língshí took many items from the storehouses,
and killed Dān to silence him.
He then washed, lay down,
took a rope, and died.
Shortly after,
Língshí's envoy arrived,
and mutilated his corpse.
An edict appointed Língshí to oversee the military affairs of the six commanderies of Liáng and Qínzhōu,
and bestowed upon him the title of Marquis of Fēngchéng County.
14. Wèi's Xī Jīn and others defeated Yuèqín west of Bónà Mountain,
and relocated over twenty thousand households to Dàníng.
15. The Héxī Hú leader Cáo Lóng and others, leading a tribal following of twenty thousand men, came and entered Púzǐ.
Zhāng Wài surrendered to them,
and they elevated Lóng to Great Chányú.
16. On the Bǐngxū day,
the Wèi sovereign Sì went to Dìngxiāng Commandery's Dàluò City.
The Records of the Two Hàn Dynasties state: Dìngxiāng Commandery had a Luò County.
17. The King of Hénán, Chìpán, attacked the Tǔyùhún leader Zhī Páng at Chángliǔ Chuān,
capturing Páng and five thousand of his households, then returned.
18. In the eighth month,
on the Guǐmǎo day,
the Wèi sovereign Sì returned to Píngchéng.
19. Cáo Lóng requested to surrender to Wèi,
captured and delivered Zhāng Wài,
who was executed.
20. On the Dīngchǒu day,
the Wèi sovereign Sì went to the Cháishān Palace;
on the Guǐwèi day,
he returned.
21. In the ninth month,
the Tàiwèi Liú Yù was again appointed as Tàifù and Governor of Yángzhōu;
he firmly declined.
22. The King of Hénán, Chìpán, attacked the Tǔyùhún separate commander Jué Kuí at Kěhún Chuān,
greatly defeating him,
and capturing twenty-three thousand men and women.
In winter,
the tenth month,
Jué Kuí led his remaining followers to surrender to Chìpán.
23. The Tǔjīng Hú and Líshí Hú leader Chū Yǐjuàn rebelled against Wèi.
The Wèi sovereign Sì ordered the Marquis of Yuánchéng, Qū, to supervise the Duke of Kuaìjī, Liú Jié, and the Marquis of Yǒng'ān, Wèi Qín, to campaign against them.
On the Dīngsì day,
Chū Yǐjuàn led Xià troops to intercept and attack Jié,
captured him, and presented him to Xià;
Qín died in battle.
Sì, because Qū had lost two generals,
wished to execute him;
but later pardoned him,
and had him act as Governor of Bìngzhōu.
When Qū arrived at the province,
he indulged in drink and neglected affairs.
Sì accumulated his former and recent crimes,
had him transported back in a cage cart,
and executed him.
When the Wèi sovereign Sì ascended the throne,
Qū's son Mó Hún had merit in this;
Qū relied on this and became arrogant.
To accumulate his evils and then execute him
is not the way to protect the households of meritorious officials.
24. In the eleventh month,
the Wèi sovereign Sì sent an envoy to request a marriage alliance with Qín.
The Qín sovereign, Yáo Xīng, agreed.
25. This year,
Suǒ Miǎo of Dūnhuáng was appointed as Governor of Liángzhōu,
and Fú Xuān then returned to Chóuchí.
Fú Xuān had entered Hànzhōng,
see the first year in scroll 114.
Miǎo had resided in Hànchuān,
and had a grudge with Biéjià Jiāng Xiǎn.
After fifteen years in total, Miǎo was stationed in Hànchuān;
Xiǎn then bared his upper body to welcome him.
Miǎo showed no sign of anger,
and treated him with even greater kindness.
Upon retiring, he said to others:
"I once resided here,
frustrated for many years.
If I were to take vengeance on Jiāng Xiǎn,
many would be fearful.
It is simply better to submit to it oneself,
why must one vent one's will!"
Upon hearing this, the entire region was pleased.
Jū Xiàn's pacification of Dōnglái was also like this.
Those in the world who cultivate grievances leading to disaster
do so because they do not know this principle.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the Xīnyǒu day,
Wèi proclaimed a great amnesty,
and changed the era name to Shénruì.
On the Xīnsì day,
the Wèi sovereign Sì went to Fánzhì;
in the second month,
on the Wùxū day,
he returned to Píngchéng.
2. The Xià sovereign, Hèlián Bóbó, invaded Wèi's Hézhōng at Púzǐ.
3. On the Gēngxū day,
the Wèi sovereign Sì went to the Cháishān Palace.
4. Wèi's Governor of Bìngzhōu, Lóu Fúlián, launched a surprise attack and killed the Tǔjīng Protector and its garrison troops appointed by Xià.
The Wèishū Guānshì Zhì states: Among the surnames of those who entered internally was the Pǐlóu clan,
later changed to the Lóu clan.
Last year,
Xià defeated Tuòbá Qū,
and consequently stationed garrison troops at Tǔjīng.
5. Sīmǎ Xiūzhī was in Jiānglíng,
and had won considerable favor among the people of the Jiāng and Hàn regions.
His son, the Prince of Qiáo, Wénsī, was in Jiànkāng.
Wénsī
was Xiūzhī's eldest son.
The Prince of Qiáo, Shàngzhī, died during the disaster of Huán Xuán.
When the Emperor restored order,
he had Wénsī inherit the princedom.
He was fond of associating with frivolous knights-errant;
the Tàiwèi Liú Yù disliked him.
In the third month,
the relevant officials reported that Wénsī had personally beaten and killed a state official.
An edict ordered the execution of his faction but pardoned Wénsī.
Xiūzhī submitted a memorial acknowledging his fault,
requesting to be relieved of his post,
but it was not permitted.
Yù seized Wénsī and sent him to Xiūzhī,
ordering him to discipline and admonish him himself,
intending for Xiūzhī to kill him;
but Xiūzhī only submitted a memorial to depose Wénsī,
and also sent a letter to Yù explaining and apologizing.
Yù was therefore displeased,
setting the stage for Yù's later campaign against Xiūzhī.
The six commanderies of Yùzhōu
were Xuānchéng, Xiāngchéng, Huáinán, Lújiāng, Ānfēng, and Lìyáng.
6. In summer,
the fifth month,
on the Xīnyǒu day,
the Wèi sovereign Sì returned to Píngchéng.
7. Qín's Rear General Liǎn Chéng campaigned against rebelling Qiāng tribes,
was defeated by the Qiāng,
and, fearing punishment,
fled to Xià.
8. The Qín sovereign, Yáo Xīng, was ill.
The sorcerer-rebel Lǐ Hóng and the Dí leader Chóu Cháng rebelled at Èrchéng.
Xīng, despite his illness, went in person to campaign against them,
beheaded Cháng,
captured Hóng, and returned.
9 The Left General of Qin, Yáo Wénzōng, was favored by Crown Prince Hóng.
The Duke of Guǎngpíng, Bì, detested him,
and falsely accused Wénzōng of harboring resentful words.
The King of Qin, Xīng, grew angry,
and ordered Wénzōng to commit suicide.
As a result, the ministers feared Bì and looked at him askance.
Whenever Bì spoke to Xīng,
his words were always followed.
He appointed his close associate, Yǐn Chōng of Tiānshuǐ, as Gentleman Attendant at the Palace Gate,
and Táng Shèng as Imperial Secretary.
Those in charge of confidential and important matters around Xīng
were all his partisans.
The Right Deputy, Liáng Xǐ, the Palace Attendant, Rèn Qiān, and the Governor of the Capital Region, Yǐn Zhāo, seized an opportunity to speak to Xīng, saying:
"Between father and son,
it is difficult for others to speak;
however, the duty between ruler and minister
is no less than that between father and son.
Therefore, we, your ministers, cannot remain silent.
The Duke of Guǎngpíng, Bì,
secretly harbors the ambition to seize the position of heir apparent.
Your Majesty favors him excessively,
lending him authority and power.
Treacherous and unscrupulous individuals flock to attach themselves to him.
Everyone on the roads is saying that Your Majesty is planning to depose and establish a new heir.
Is this true?"
Xīng said:
"How could such a thing exist!"
Xǐ and the others said:
"If it does not exist,
then Your Majesty's love for Bì
is precisely what will bring disaster upon him.
We hope you will remove those around him
and reduce his authority and power.
In this way,
it is not only for Bì's safety,
but also for the security of the ancestral temple and the state."
Xīng did not respond.
The Grand Minister of Agriculture, Bǎo Wēn, and the Left Chief Clerk of the Minister over the Masses, Wáng Bì, both secretly submitted memorials urging Xīng to establish Bì as Crown Prince.
Although Xīng did not follow their advice,
he also did not reprimand them.
Xīng fell critically ill.
Bì secretly gathered several thousand men,
plotting to stage a rebellion.
Yáo Yù sent messengers to inform his elder brothers stationed in the frontier commands of Bì's rebellious actions.
Thereupon, Yáo Yì marshaled troops at Púbǎn,
and the General Who Pacifies the East and Governor of Yùzhōu, Yáo Shào, marshaled troops at Luòyáng.
Yì and Shào
were both sons of Xīng.
(Note on pronunciation: Zhì is pronounced zhí.
Shào is pronounced gū huáng.
) They all intended to march to Cháng'ān to punish Bì.
It happened that Xīng's illness took a turn for the better.
He met with his ministers,
and the General Who Conquers Caitiffs, Liú Qiāng, tearfully reported the situation to Xīng.
Liáng Xǐ and Yǐn Zhāo requested that Bì be executed,
and said:
"If Your Majesty cannot bear to kill Bì,
you should at least strip him of his authority and position."
Xīng had no choice
and dismissed Bì from the post of President of the Imperial Secretariat,
ordering him to return to his residence with only his general's title and ducal rank.
(Bì held the title of Grand General
and was enfeoffed as Duke of Guǎngpíng.)
Yì, Shào, Chén, and Yáo Xuān all came to the court.
They sent Yù to speak to Xīng,
requesting an audience.
Xīng said:
"You all merely wish to discuss Bì's affair.
I already know about it."
Yù said:
"If there is anything to discuss about Bì,
Your Majesty should deign to listen.
If what Yì and the others say is incorrect,
then simply subject them to punishment.
How can you refuse them in advance!"
Thereupon, he summoned Yì and the others for an audience in the Consultation Hall.
Xuān spoke with tears, stating his case to the utmost.
Xīng said:
"I will handle this myself,
it is not something for you all to worry about."
The East Section Officer of the Army Pacification, Jiāng Qiú, submitted a memorial stating:
"The Duke of Guǎngpíng, Bì,
has committed offenses and his rebellion is evident.
Everyone on the roads knows it.
In the past, under King Wén's transformation,
he set an example for his wife;
(The Ode "Sī Qí" says: He set an example for his wife,
and extended it to his brothers.)
starting from his beloved son.
Although one may wish to endure and conceal it,
his rebellious faction ceaselessly incites and deludes others.
How can Bì's rebellious heart be reformed!
You should expel and disperse his vicious followers
to cut off the source of disaster."
Xīng showed Qiú's memorial to Liáng Xǐ, saying:
"Everyone in the world uses my son as a topic of conversation."
(Kǒng Ānguó said: 'Topic of conversation' means something constantly on people's lips.)
Xǐ said:
"If what Qiú says is true,
Your Majesty should make an early decision."
Xīng remained silent.
(The historian remarks that Yáo Xīng did not heed the words of his ministers and sons,
thus fostering the disaster of Hóng and Bì contending for the state.)
10 The Tuòqìhàn, Yǐfú, and other tribes all rebelled against Southern Liáng.
The King of Southern Liáng, Tàntán, wished to campaign against them.
The Army Protector of Hánchuān, Mèng Kǎi, admonished him, saying:
"Now, with consecutive years of famine,
we are pressed by Chìpán to the south,
and by Méngxùn to the north.
The people are unsettled.
Even if a distant campaign is victorious,
there will surely be future troubles.
It would be better to form an alliance with Chìpán and exchange grain,
pacify and soothe the various tribes,
ensure sufficient food and repair weapons,
and await the right moment to act."
Tàntán did not listen.
He said to Crown Prince Hǔtái:
"Méngxùn has recently left and cannot come suddenly.
What concerns me day and night
is only Chìpán.
However, Chìpán has few troops and is easy to defend against.
You carefully guard Lèdū.
I will certainly return within a month."
Thereupon, he led seven thousand cavalry to attack the Yǐfú,
defeating them soundly,
and capturing over four hundred thousand horses, cattle, and sheep.
The King of Hénán, Chìpán, heard of this
and wanted to attack Lèdū.
His ministers all considered it inadvisable.
The Chief Clerk of the Grand Treasury, Jiāo Xí, said:
"Tàntán disregards nearby troubles and covets distant gains.
(Nearby troubles refer to Méngxùn and Chìpán;
distant gains refer to the Yǐfú.)
If we cut off his western route
(the western route from Lèdū,
this is the route Tàntán would take to return from the Yǐfú to Lèdū),
then Hǔtái will be left alone guarding an isolated city,
and we can capture him effortlessly.
This is a time when Heaven is destroying them.
We must not miss this opportunity."
Chìpán followed his advice,
leading twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Lèdū.
Hǔtái relied on the city walls to resist and defend.
Chìpán attacked from all four sides.
The Gentleman of the Army Pacification of Southern Liáng, Wèi Sù, said to Hǔtái:
"The outer city is vast and difficult to defend.
Your Highness should rather gather our people to guard the inner city.
('Our people' refers to the tribes of the Xiānbēi Tūfā clan.)
Even if we are not victorious,
we can still preserve ourselves."
Hǔtái said:
"Chìpán is a petty bandit.
He will flee any day now.
Why are you so excessively worried!"
Hǔtái suspected that the Jìn people had different intentions.
(The barbarians called the Huá people 'Jìn people'.)
Mèng Kǎi wept and said:
"Chìpán is taking advantage of our weakness to invade internally.
The state is in as much danger as a pile of eggs.
We, Kǎi and others, wish to advance to repay your kindness,
and, retreating, consider our wives and children.
Everyone thinks of exerting themselves to the death,
yet Your Highness suspects us to such an extent!"
Hǔtái said:
"How could I not know of your loyalty and sincerity?
I fear that others might entertain thoughts beyond consideration.
I am using you to reassure them."
One evening,
the city walls collapsed.
Chìpán entered Lèdū.
He sent the General Who Pacifies Distant Lands, Jié Qián, to lead five thousand cavalry in pursuit of Tàntán.
He appointed the General Who Pacifies the South, Qián Tún, as Commander of All Military Affairs West of the River and Governor of Liángzhōu,
to garrison Lèdū.
(Jié Qián and Qián Tún were both of the Qǐfú tribe.)
He garrisoned Xīpíng.
He appointed Zhào Huī as Grand Administrator of Guǎngwǔ,
to garrison Guǎngwǔ.
He appointed the General Who Glorifies Martial Prowess, Wáng Jī, as Grand Administrator of Jìnxīng,
to garrison Hàomén.
He relocated Hǔtái and over ten thousand households of his civil and military officials and common people to Fúhǎn.
(Fùdān was the son of Wūgū.)
11. Chǔ Kuāng of Héjiān said to the Yān king Féng Bá:
“Your Majesty ascended the throne in Liáo and Jié,
yet your old clan and kinsmen
turn their heads toward the rising sun,
saying that just as the sun rises in the east,
so Féng Bá rose in Liáo and Jié.
Those of your clan in Chánglè
turn their heads and gaze eastward.
Jié,
read as yè.
I request to go and welcome them.”
Bá said:
“The road is several thousand lǐ long,
and it crosses foreign states;
how can they be brought here?”
Kuāng said:
“Zhāngwǔ borders the sea.
Bá’s ancestors
were from Xìndū in Chánglè,
and Zhāngwǔ Commandery was established by the Jìn from the Hàn’s Bóhǎi Commandery.
From Xìndū to Zhāngwǔ,
one can sail by sea to Liáoxī.
Emerging at Línyú in Liáoxī
is not difficult.”
Línyú County
belonged to Liáoxī Commandery in the Hàn.
Shī Gǔ said: Yú,
pronounced yù.
The Shuǐjīng says: Jiéshí is south of the county.
Bá appointed Kuāng as Guerrilla General and Vice Director of the Central Secretariat,
providing him with ample funds for the journey.
Kuāng, along with Bá’s elder cousin Féng Mǎi and younger cousin Féng Dǔ,
led over five thousand households from Chánglè back to Hélóng.
Emperor Gāo of Hàn established Xìndū Commandery,
which in the second year of Emperor Jǐng became the Kingdom of Guǎngchuān,
renamed Lèchéng by Emperor Míng,
changed to Ānpíng by Emperor Ān,
and renamed Chánglè by the Jìn.
Lè,
pronounced luò.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
Bá appointed their chief as the King of Guīshàn.
Bá’s younger brother Féng Pī had taken refuge in Gāogōulí to avoid turmoil;
Bá summoned him
and appointed him Left Vice Director,
enfeoffing him as Duke of Chángshān.
12. The Róurán kèhán Húlǜ was about to marry his daughter to Yān.
Kè,
read in the entering tone.
Hán,
pronounced hán.
“My young daughter is marrying far away and will be homesick;
I request that the daughters of ministers like Shùlí and others accompany her as bridesmaids.”
Húlǜ refused.
Bùlùzhēn went out
and said to Shùlí and others:
“Húlǜ wants to make your daughters bridesmaids,
sending them far away to another state.”
Shùlí, fearing this,
conspired with Bùlùzhēn to have warriors lie in ambush behind Húlǜ’s yurt at night,
waiting for him to emerge and seize him.
They sent him and his daughter to Yān,
and installed Bùlùzhēn as kèhán, with himself as minister.
Earlier,
when Shèlún relocated the Gāochē,
see the events in the first year of Yuánxīng, scroll 112.
Lún,
pronounced Lú Kūn.
Shèlún was grateful to him,
appointing him as a chief.
Bùlùzhēn and Shèlún’s son Shèbá went together to Chìluòhóu’s home,
where they violated his young wife.
The wife told Bùlùzhēn:
“Chìluòhóu intends to support Dàtán as ruler.”
Dàtán was
the son of Shèlún’s younger uncle Púhún,
commanding a separate tribe guarding the western border,
and was widely popular.
Bùlùzhēn returned and raised troops to besiege Chìluòhóu,
who committed suicide.
He then led troops to attack Dàtán,
but Dàtán counterattacked,
defeated him,
captured Bùlùzhēn and Shèbá,
executed them,
and proclaimed himself kèhán,
taking the title Móuhángéshenggài Kèhán.
Wèi Shōu said: In Wèi language, it means ‘victorious.’
Húlǜ arrived at Hélóng,
where the Yān king Bá enfeoffed Húlǜ as Marquis of Shànggǔ,
housed him in Liáodōng,
treated him with guest rites,
and took his daughter as a Zhāoyí.
Húlǜ submitted a letter requesting to return to his state.
Bá said:
“Now you have abandoned your state ten thousand lǐ away,
and there is no internal support;
if I send a large escort,
supply lines will be difficult to maintain,
but with few troops, success is unlikely.
How can you return?”
Húlǜ insisted,
saying:
“No need for a large force;
I only request three hundred cavalry
to escort me to the Chìlē state.
The people will surely welcome me joyfully.”
Bá then sent the Former Assistant to the Chányú, Wàn Líng, to lead three hundred cavalry and escort him.
Líng dreaded the distant journey;
upon reaching Hēishān,
Hēishān is north of Táng’s Zhènwǔ frontier,
also known as Shāhú Shān.
Dàtán also sent envoys to present three thousand horses and ten thousand sheep to Yān.
13. In the sixth month,
Tàishān Grand Administrator Liú Yán and others led over seven thousand households of refugees, and the Héxī Hú chief Liú Zhē and others led over ten thousand households of tribesmen,
all surrendering to Wèi.
14. On Wùshēn,
the Wèi ruler Sì went to the Cháishān Palace;
on Dīnghài,
he returned to Píngchéng.
15. After the collapse of Lèdū,
the Southern Liáng General of Pacifying the West, Fán Ní, fled from Xīpíng to inform the Southern Liáng king Tàntán.
Tàntán said to his followers:
“Now our wives and children have all been captured by Chìpán,
and retreat offers no refuge.
Can you join me in using the resources of Yǐfú
to seize Qìhàn and ransom our families?”
He then led his troops west;
many fled back,
and Tàntán sent General of Guarding the North Duàn Gǒu to pursue them,
but Gǒu also did not return.
Thus, the officers and soldiers all scattered,
leaving only Fán Ní, General of the Central Army Hébó, General of the Rear Army Luò Gōng, and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Yīn Lìlù who did not leave.
Sàn,
read as sǎn.
Qí,
read as jì.
“Méngxùn and Chìpán once submitted to me.
Méngxùn pledged allegiance to Lìlùgū;
see the fifth year of Lóng’ān, scroll 112.
Chìpán and his father submitted to Lìlùgū;
see the fourth year, scroll 111.
Zhì,
read as zhì.
Is this not shameful!
The world is vast,
yet there is no place for me;
how painful this is!
Rather than gathering and dying together,
it is better to separate and perhaps survive.
Fán Ní
is the son of my eldest brother.
Fán Ní was likely Wūgū’s son.
Zhǎng,
read as zhǎng.
Our people in the north number nearly ten thousand households;
Méngxùn is currently recruiting and comforting the people,
preserving the perishing and continuing the severed.
You should follow him;
Hébó and Luò Gōng should also go with Ní.
I am old;
no place will accept me.
I would rather see my wife and children and die!”
He then surrendered to Chìpán,
with only Yīn Lìlù accompanying him.
Tàntán said to Lìlù:
“All my relatives have scattered;
why do you alone remain?”
Lìlù said:
“My elderly mother is at home;
it is not that I do not wish to return.
But having pledged myself as your subject,
the ways of loyalty and filial piety
are difficult to fulfill both.
I lack talent,
unable to weep blood and seek aid from neighboring states for Your Majesty,
how dare I leave your side!”
Tàntán sighed:
“Truly, understanding people is not easy.
My ministers and relatives have all abandoned me;
today, the only one who remains loyal and righteous from beginning to end,
without fail, is you alone!”
All of Nùtán's cities surrendered to Chìpán,
except for Wèi Xiánzhèng, who was stationed at Hàomén,
holding firm and refusing to surrender.
Chìpán sent someone to tell him:
"Lèdū has already fallen,
your wife and children are all in my hands,
what do you hope to achieve
by defending a single city all alone?"
Xiánzhèng replied:
"I have received great kindness from the King of Liáng,
and serve as a shield for the state.
Although I know Lèdū has been captured,
and my wife and children taken prisoner,
and that those who submit first will be rewarded,
while those who submit later will be executed;
yet I do not know whether my sovereign is alive or dead.
The sovereign
refers to Nùtán.
My wife and children are a minor matter,
how could they sway my heart!
If I were to covet temporary gain,
and forget the heavy responsibility entrusted to me,
how could Your Majesty possibly use someone like that!"
Chìpán then sent Hǔ Tái with a handwritten letter to persuade him,
but Xiánzhèng said:
"You are the heir apparent,
yet you failed to fulfill your duty,
allowing yourself to be bound and captured,
abandoning your father and forgetting your lord,
ruining the legacy of ten thousand generations.
I, Xiánzhèng, am a man of principle;
how could I possibly follow your example!"
Upon hearing that Nùtán had reached Zuǒnán,
he then surrendered.
The *Thirteen Provinces Gazetteer* by Kàn Yīn states: Zuǒnán City is located sixty *li* east of Báitǔ County in Jīnchéng.
The *Jìn History* records: The Zhāng clan established the Jìnxīng Commandery,
to which Zuǒnán County belonged.
This county was also established by the Zhāng clan.
When Chìpán heard that Nùtán had arrived,
he sent an envoy to greet him outside the city,
and treated him with the courtesy due to a distinguished guest.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Chìpán appointed Nùtán as General of Agile Cavalry,
enfeoffing him as the Duke of Zuǒnán.
The civil and military officials of Southern Liáng
were appointed according to their abilities.
A little over a year later,
Chìpán had someone poison Nùtán;
his attendants urged him to take an antidote,
but Nùtán said:
"How could my illness possibly be cured!"
He then died,
and was posthumously titled King Jǐng.
The *Annals* record: From Tūfà Wūgū to Nùtán, three generations passed,
and the state was destroyed after nineteen years.
Nùtán's sons Bǎozhōu and Hè,
Jùyán's son Fùlóng,
Lìlùgū's grandson Fùzhōu,
and Wūgū's grandson Chéngbō,
all fled to the King of Héxī, Méngxùn.
After some time,
they fled again to Wèi.
Wèi appointed Bǎozhōu as the King of Zhāngyè,
Fùlóng as the Duke of Jiǔquán,
Hè as the Duke of Xīpíng,
Fùzhōu as the Duke of Yǒngpíng,
and Chéngbō as the Duke of Chāngsōng.
The Wèi ruler Sì admired Hè's talent,
and said to him:
"Your ancestors and I share the same origin,"
and bestowed upon him the surname Yuán.
This laid the foundation for the Yuán clan's prominence in Wèi.
On the sixteenth day of the eighth month,
the day Wùzǐ,
the Wèi ruler Sì sent the Marquis of Mǎyì, Lòu Sūn, as an envoy to Qín.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
he sent the Court Gentleman Yú Shímén as an envoy to Yān,
and Yuè Lìyán as an envoy to Róurán.
When Yú Shímén reached Hélóng,
he refused to enter and see the king,
saying:
"The great Emperor of Wèi has issued an edict;
I must wait for King Féng to come out to receive it,
and only then dare I enter."
The King of Yān, Bá, sent people to drag him inside;
Shímén, upon seeing Bá, did not bow.
Bá had people press down on his neck,
but Shímén said:
"If King Féng bows to receive the edict,
I will naturally show the respect due between guest and host.
Why must you force me like this!"
Bá was enraged,
and detained Shímén without sending him back.
Shímén repeatedly insulted him in front of the crowd.
His attendants requested that Shímén be killed,
but Bá said:
"He is merely serving his own lord."
He then imprisoned Shímén,
hoping to make him surrender,
but Shímén never yielded.
After a long time,
his clothes and cap were nearly completely worn out,
and lice swarmed all over him;
Bá sent him new clothes and a cap,
but Shímén refused to accept them.
The Wèi ruler Sì appointed the Erudite Wáng Liàng as a Pingnán Army Advisor,
and sent him with a letter from General Pingnán and Governor of Xiāngzhōu, Wèi Tàizhēn, to communicate with Grand Commandant Yù.
Tàizhēn
was the younger brother of Gǔzhēn.
In the ninth month,
on the first day, Dīngsì,
there was a solar eclipse.
In winter,
the tenth month,
the King of Hénán, Chìpán, once again declared himself King of Qín,
and established all the officials.
When Chìpán succeeded to the throne,
he had styled himself King of Hénán;
now, having annexed Southern Liáng,
he resumed the title King of Qín.
The Yān ruler Bá made peace with Xià,
and the King of Xià, Bóbó, sent the Palace Secretary Wūluò Gū to Yān to oversee the alliance.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
when various states resolved their enmities and established friendly relations,
if the two rulers could not meet in person to form an alliance,
they would always send their ministers to oversee the alliance.
The *Zuǒzhuàn* records: Chén Wǔfù went to Zhèng to oversee the alliance.
Dù Yù commented: "Lì"
means "to oversee."
In the eleventh month,
on the day Rénwǔ,
the Wèi ruler Sì sent envoys to tour the various provinces,
to inspect and audit the assets of the governors and magistrates.
Any property not brought from their own households
was recorded as illicit gains.
The King of Western Qín, Chìpán, established a woman of the Tūfà clan as his queen.
She was the daughter of Nùtán.
In the twelfth month,
on the first day, Bǐngxū,
the Róurán Khan Dàtán invaded Wèi;
on the day Bǐngshēn,
the Wèi ruler Sì went north to attack him.
Dàtán fled,
and Sì sent Xī Jīn and others to pursue him.
They encountered heavy snow,
and two or three out of ten soldiers froze to death or had their fingers frostbitten.
A man from Hénèi named Sīmǎ Shùnzǎi declared himself King of Jìn.
The Wèi people attacked him,
but could not defeat him.
The Duke of Liáoxī of Yān, Sùfú, died.
The King of Yān, Bá, attended his funeral seven times before the burial.
In ancient times, when a high minister died,
the ruler would attend his funeral three times.
"Bì"
is pronounced bì mèi fān,
meaning "to reach."
In this year,
Sīmǎ Guófán and his brothers gathered a crowd of several hundred, secretly crossed the Huái River,
and entered Guǎnglíng City at night.
The *Zhī Biography* says: They crossed the Huái River from the border of Běixúzhōu.
"Fán"
is pronounced fú yuán fān.
Guófán's troops went straight up to the audience hall,
and Zhī rushed out in alarm,
intending to resist them.
He was shot and wounded, and retreated inside.
He said to his attendants:

Hào likely based this on the Outer Commentary to the Zuǒzhuàn of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
The Outer Commentary states:
"In the fifteenth year of King Huì of Zhōu,
a spirit descended at Shēn,
the king asked Nèishǐ Guò about it.
He replied: 'It must be Dānzhū.'
The king said: 'Who will receive it?'
He replied: 'In the land of Guó.'
The king said: 'How long will Guó last?'
He replied: 'In the past, Yáo ruled the people for five generations.
Now his descendant appears.
The appearance of a spirit
does not exceed its allotted time.
If we judge from this,
it will not exceed five years.'
In the nineteenth year,
Jìn captured Guó."
Commentary,
pronounced zhuàn.
On the days Gēngwǔ
and Xīnwèi,

the disappearance of Mars
should have occurred on these two days.
Gēng and Wǔ
both correspond to Qín;

Gēng and Xīn belong to the west,
hence they correspond to the western barbarians.
Mars is certain to enter Qín."
The others all angrily said:

More than eighty days later,

"Departing and returning again
is called forming a hook."
The Treatise on Astronomy in the Book of Jìn states:
"Mars signifies chaos,
treachery,
disease,
mourning,
famine,
and war,
and the state where it resides suffers calamity.
If it encircles and forms a hook,
with its rays shaking and changing color,
moving forward and back,
left and right,
the calamity is even greater."
Hook,
read as gōu.
Forming a hook,
means moving in an encircling path like a hook,
also forming the character 'jǐ'.
The Kūnmíng Pond dried up,

pronounced xiáng.
He garrisoned Chìshuǐ.
34. The younger brother of the Minister over the Masses of Yān, Sūn Hù, named Bórén, was Governor of Chānglí,
and along with his younger brother Chìzhī Yǐbá, both were talented and brave.
They had rendered meritorious service following the King of Yān, Féng Bá, in raising troops,
referring to the time they killed Mùróng Xī,
events seen in the 114th scroll, third year.
They made resentful remarks,
and Bá executed them both.
He promoted Hù to Excellency of the Palace with Special Powers and Imperial Secretary,
to console his heart,
but Hù was discontented and unhappy,
so Bá poisoned him to death.
The Grand Administrator of Liáodōng, Wùyíntí, believing himself meritorious,
was sent out to a border commandery,
harbored resentment,
plotted to rebel,
and Bá also executed him.
After Wànní and Rǔchén died,
Sūn Hù and his brothers and Wùyíntí were also executed,
showing Féng Bá also had little kindness.
35. Línyì invaded Jiāozhōu,
and the provincial general repelled them.
1. In spring,
the first month,
on the day Jiǎshēn,
the ruler of Wei, Tuòbá Sì, went to Cháishān Palace;
on the day Wùzǐ,
he returned to Píngchéng.
2. The Grand Commandant Liú Yù was additionally appointed Governor of Yǎnzhōu and Commander of Nánqínzhōu,
commanding a total of twenty-two provinces;
the twenty-two provinces: Xú, Nánxú, Yù, Nányù, Yǎn, Nányǎn, Qīng, Jì, Yōu, Bìng, Sī, Yǐng, Jīng, Jiāng, Xiāng, Yōng, Liáng, Yì, Níng, Jiāo, Guǎng, and Nánqín.
3. The King of Qin, Yáo Xīng, sent Lǔ Zōngzhī to lead troops to raid Xiāngyáng,
but he died before arriving.
His son, Lǔ Guǐ, led the troops in the raid,
but the Governor of Yōngzhōu, Zhào Lúnzhī, defeated him.
4. The King of Western Qin, Qìfú Chìpán, attacked the Duke of Táoyáng of Qin, Péng Lìhé, at Qiángchuān,
and Jūqú Méngxùn attacked Shíquán to rescue him.
Chìpán reached Tàzhōng,
then withdrew.
In the second month,
Chìpán sent the Marquis of Xiāngwǔ, Tándá, to rescue Shíquán,
and Méngxùn also withdrew.
Méngxùn then made peace and formed a marriage alliance with Chìpán.
Since Chìpán destroyed the Tūbá clan,
he and Méngxùn had been neighboring enemies,
fighting yearly,
but now they made peace.
11. Several tens of thousands of households of the Hú in Bīngzhōu rebelled against Qín,
entering Píngyáng.
They elected the Xiōngnú Cáo Hóng as the Great Chányú.
Cáo Hóng was likely a descendant of Cáo Gǔ's son Cáo Yín, the Xiōngnú Right Virtuous King,
the so-called Eastern Cáo.
Chán,
pronounced like "chán" (蝉).
This was a place where Xiōngnú tribes gathered for mutual protection,
hence the name.
They captured Hóng
and sent him to Cháng'ān.
Fifteen thousand households of their powerful and prominent families were relocated to Yōngzhōu.
The seat of Qín's Yōngzhōu was at Āndìng.
12. The Dí chieftain Yáng Shèng attacked Qín's Qíshān,
capturing it,
and advanced to threaten Qínzhōu.
Qín's Rear General Yáo Píng went to its rescue;
Shèng led his troops in retreat,
and Píng, together with the defending general of Shàngguī, Yáo Sōng, pursued him.
The Xià king Bóbó led 40,000 cavalry to raid Shàngguī.
Before he arrived,
Sōng engaged Shèng in battle at Zhú Lǐng,
was defeated and died.
The Shuǐjīng Zhù states: The Jí River passes through Dāngtíng Chuān,
then flows southeast,
merging with the Zhú Lǐng River.
This river originates from the Zhú Lǐng in the southern mountains,
flowing northeast into the Jí River.
The Jí River flows northeast into Shàngguī County.
After twenty days,
Bóbó captured Shàngguī,
killing the Qínzhōu Governor Yáo Jūndū and over 5,000 officers and soldiers,
and then destroyed the city walls.
He advanced to attack Yīnmì.
Yīnmì,
the ancient state of the Mì people,
is referred to in the Shī as
"The people of Mì show no respect,
daring to resist the great state."
Since the Hàn dynasty, it has been a county,
belonging to the Āndìng Commandery.
The Kuòdìzhì states: The old city of Yīnmì
is west of Chúngǔ County in Jīngzhōu.
Its eastern part connects to the county town,
which is the ancient state of Mì.
Bóbó appointed his son Chāng as Governor of Yōngzhōu,
to guard Yīnmì.
The Qín Northern Expedition General Yáo Huī abandoned Āndìng,
fleeing back to Cháng'ān.
The people of Āndìng, such as Hú Yǎn, led 50,000 households to occupy the city and surrendered to Xià.
Bóbó sent the Eastern Garrison General Yáng Gǒur to lead 5,000 Xiānbēi to garrison Āndìng.
He then attacked the Qín Western Garrison General Yáo Chén at Yōngchéng.
Chén abandoned his post and fled to Cháng'ān.
Bóbó occupied Yōng,
and advanced to plunder Méichéng.
The Qín Duke of Dōngpíng Yáo Shào and the General Who Conquers Caitiffs Yǐn Zhāo, among others, led 50,000 infantry and cavalry to attack him.
Bóbó retreated towards Āndìng.
Hú Yǎn closed the city gates against him,
killed Yáng Gǒur and the Xiānbēi under his command,
and again surrendered Āndìng to Qín.
Shào advanced and attacked Bóbó at Mǎ'ān Bǎn,
defeating him,
and pursued him as far as Cháonà,
but failing to catch up, returned.
Bóbó returned to Xìngchéng.
Yáng Shèng again sent his nephew Juàn to attack Qín,
reaching Chéncāng.
The Qín general Liǎn Mànwéi attacked and repelled him.
The Xià king Bóbó again sent his nephew Tí to invade southward Xièyáng.
The Jìnshū Zǎijì records it as
"Chíyáng",
which should be followed.
Chíyáng County belonged to the Fúfēng Commandery,
and in Táng times was the Jīngzhào Yúnyáng County.
Fù,
pronounced fú yòu fān.
13. The Liáng Minister of War Suǒ Chéngmíng submitted a memorial advising Duke Lǐ Hào of Liáng to attack the King of Héxī Méngxùn.
Hào summoned him for an audience,
and said to him:
"Méngxùn is a scourge to the people;
how could I forget him!
But I consider that our strength is not yet sufficient to eliminate him.
If you have a strategy that will surely capture him,
you should present it to me;
merely advocating grandiose words,
urging me to launch an eastern campaign,
how is this any different from saying
'Shí Hǔ is a petty upstart,
he should be executed in the marketplace'!"
Chéngmíng, ashamed and fearful, withdrew.
14. In autumn,
the seventh month,
the Wèi ruler Sì conducted a great hunt at Niúchuān,
reaching the Yīnfán River before returning.
The Běishǐ states: He ascended Fǔshān,
overlooking the Yīnfán River.
The Kuòdìzhì states: Fǔshān is three lǐ north of Huáiróng County in Guīzhōu.
On the Wùxū day
he arrived at Píngchéng.
15. In the eighth month,
on the Bǐngwǔ day,
a general amnesty was declared.
16. Níngzhōu presented an amber pillow to the Grand Commandant Liú Yù.
Amber comes from the Āiláo tribes.
The Guǎngyǎ states: Amber is formed in the earth,
where no grass grows above or around it.
At depths of eight or nine chǐ,
pieces as large as a hú measure are found.
After removing the outer layer,
the amber inside is like a dǒu measure.
Initially, it is like peach resin,
which solidifies and hardens to become amber.
The Bówùzhì states: Pine resin sinks into the earth,
after a thousand years transforms into poria cocos,
and after another thousand years, poria cocos transforms into amber.
Nowadays, Tàishān has poria cocos but no amber,
while Yǒngchāng has amber but no poria cocos.
Yù was greatly pleased upon receiving it,
and ordered it to be crushed and distributed among the generals and soldiers of the northern expedition.
Yù appointed his heir apparent Yìfú as Central Army General,
to oversee the affairs of the Grand Commandant's留守 office.
Liú Mùzhī was appointed Left Vice Director,
concurrently holding the posts of Army Supervisor of the Supervisor of the Army and Central Army offices.
The Supervisor of the Army
refers to Yìfú,
who supervised the army of the Grand Commandant's留守 office.
Jiān,
pronounced gōng xián fān.
He was in overall charge of internal and external affairs.
The Grand Commandant's Left Minister of War, Xú Xiànzhī of Dōnghǎi, was appointed as Mùzhī's deputy.
The Left General Zhū Língshí was responsible for guarding the palace and government offices.
The Xúzhōu Governor Liú Huáishèn was responsible for guarding the capital.
The Assistant Officer of the Yángzhōu Administration, Zhāng Yù, was entrusted with handling the affairs of the留守 prefecture.
Entrusted with handling the affairs of the留守 prefecture,
means he was entrusted with the留守 affairs of Yángzhōu.
He was the younger brother of Huáijìng.
Liú Mùzhī handled internal court administration,
and externally supplied the military campaigns.
His decisions were swift as flowing water,
and affairs never stagnated.
Guests and visitors converged like spokes to a hub,
with all manner of requests and appeals.
Internal and external reports and petitions
filled the steps and rooms;
filling the steps and rooms,
refers to the documents of reports and petitions.
He wrote replies to letters with his hand,
listened to reports with his ears,
and responded verbally with his mouth,
all simultaneously without interference,
and all were handled competently.
He also enjoyed having guests,
engaging in conversation, appreciation, and laughter,
tirelessly throughout the day.
Whenever he had a moment of leisure,
he would personally copy books by hand,
perusing and collating them.
He was extravagant and lavish by nature,
his meals always covered a square zhàng,
and every morning he would prepare food for ten people,
never dining alone.
He once said to Yù:
"My family was originally poor and humble,
and provisions were often lacking.
Since I have presumptuously held office,
although I have always intended to be frugal and reduce expenses,
the daily necessities
have become slightly excessive.
Beyond this, I have not burdened you in the slightest."
The Central Army Consultant and Adjutant Zhāng Shào said to Yù:
"Human life is precarious and fragile,
one must plan for the long term.
If something unfortunate were to unexpectedly befall Mùzhī,
who could replace him?
Your esteemed enterprise is as it is,
esteemed enterprise,
refers to the achievements Yù has already accomplished;
'esteemed'
is a term of respect.
How will you arrange matters?"
Yù said:
"This I leave entirely to Mùzhī and to you."
Yì then raised troops and proclaimed himself emperor,
issuing proclamations to the various commanderies and prefectures,
intending to transport grain from the Xiōngnú Fort to supply the garrison troops.
The Xiōngnú Fort was located in Píngyáng.
The garrison troops
were the forces under Yì's command stationed at Púbǎn.
Yì used humble words to entice them,
sending his personal dagger as a pledge,
but Chéngdū did not comply.
Yì dispatched the Valiant Cavalry General Wáng Guó to lead several hundred armored soldiers to attack Chéngdū,
but Chéngdū counterattacked and captured him.
He then sent an envoy to reprimand Yì, saying:
"You, Illustrious Lord, hold a weighty responsibility due to your close kinship,
yet when the state was in peril, you could not save it,
and instead harbor improper ambitions;
will the spirits of the Three Ancestors
be willing to bless you, Illustrious Lord?
(Yáo Yìzhōng's temple name was Shǐzǔ,
Yáo Chǎng's was Tàizǔ,
and Yáo Xīng's was Gāozǔ,
these are the so-called Three Ancestors.)
I will go to see you, Illustrious Lord, by the river."
Púbǎn bordered the river,
hence the phrase "by the river."
He explained the principles of rebellion and loyalty,
and mobilized troops and supplies to campaign against Yì.
Yì also called for troops from the various cities,
but none responded,
only several thousand households from Línjìn answered Yì's call.
Chéngdū led his troops across the river,
attacked the rebels in Línjìn,
and defeated them.
The garrison troops, including Guō Chún from Āndìng, rose up and besieged Yì.
The Duke of Dōngpíng, Shào, entered Púbǎn,
captured Yì,
and executed Sūn Chàng and others.
27 This year,
the Wèi General of the Guards, the Filial and Principled King of Ānchéng, Shūsūn Jùn, died.
The Wèi sovereign Sì deeply mourned him,
and said to his wife, Lady Huán:
"We shared honor in life,
can we not share sorrow in death?"
Lady Huán then hanged herself and was buried alongside him.
When Sì ascended the throne,
Shūsūn Jùn had rendered meritorious service,
as recorded in the fourth year of the 115th scroll.
28 The Dīnglíng, Zhái Měngquè, drove off and plundered officials and commoners,
entering Báijiàn Mountain to cause rebellion;
Báijiàn Mountain was likely located west of Huòzé County in Hàndōng.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: Huòzé River originates from Báijiàn Ridge west of Huòzé City,
flowing east past Huòzé.
Huòzé
corresponds to Yángchéng County in Táng's Zé Prefecture.
Shī Gǔ said: Huò
is pronounced wū huò fān.
Dàoshēng,
was Sōng's nephew.
Dàoshēng wanted to advance and attack Měngquè,
but Pú said:
"The officials and commoners did not willingly join the rebellion,
they were coerced by Měngquè.
If we do not distinguish between them now,
and attack them all together,
even if they wish to return to good,
they will have no way to do so,
and will certainly unite their efforts,
relying on the dangerous terrain to resist the government troops,
making it difficult to quell them quickly.
It would be better to first send an envoy to instruct them,
declaring that those who did not conspire with Měngquè will not be punished,
then they will surely be pleased and disperse."
Dàoshēng followed this advice,
and several thousand households surrendered,
allowing them to resume their former occupations.
Měngquè and over a hundred of his followers fled,
Pú and others pursued and beheaded Měngquè;
the Left Department Minister Zhōu Jǐ thoroughly pursued the remaining followers,
and executed them all.

Later Scholar from Tiāntái
Emperor Ān, Guǐ
Yìxī thirteenth year (Dīngsì, 417)
1 Spring,
first month,
jiǎxū, first day,
there was a solar eclipse.
2 The Qín sovereign Hóng held court with all officials in the front hall,
and due to the internal and external crises pressing upon them,
the sovereign and his ministers wept together.
Internally, brothers were creating calamities,
externally, they were pressured by Jìn and Xià.
They burned their dwellings,
and moved from Běiyōng Prefecture towards Cháng'ān.
Qín divided the five commanderies north of the ridge into Běiyōng Prefecture,
garrisoning Āndìng.
Hóng did not heed the advice of the Duke of Dōngpíng, Shào, and Yì Héng, which led to chaos.
Shuài
is read as shuài.
Yōng
is pronounced yòng fān.
Qū
is pronounced qī yù fān.
They issued proclamations to the commanderies and prefectures,
intending to eliminate the wicked at the sovereign's side;
the General Who Spreads Might, Jiāng Jì, led his troops to join them,
and the General Who Establishes Integrity, Péng Wándū, abandoned Yīnmì and fled back to Cháng'ān.
Huī reached Xīnzhī,
and Jiāng Jì advised Huī, saying:
"The state's important generals and main armies are all in the east,
the capital is empty,
if you quickly lead light troops to attack it,
you will certainly capture it."
Huī did not follow this advice,
and instead attacked Méichéng to the south;
the General Who Guards the West, Yáo Chén, was defeated by Huī,
causing great alarm in Cháng'ān.
Hóng urgently sent an envoy to summon the Duke of Dōngpíng, Shào,
and dispatched Yáo Yù and the General Who Assists the State, Hú Yìdù, to station west of Lǐ.
There is no Lǐ River in Guānzhōng,
"Lǐ"
should be
"Fēng".
The Fēng River originates from Fēng Valley south of Hù,
flowing north past the Shanglin Park into the Wèi.
Shǐ
is pronounced shū lì fān.
The Duke of Dōngpíng, Shào, led the various armies back west,
and confronted Huī at Língtái.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Hàn Língtái was south of the Qín Ēpáng Palace,
with the Hào River flowing north of it.
They guarded Tóngguān,
and also led troops back.
Huī's troops, seeing the various armies gathering from all sides,
all became fearful;
his general Qí Huáng and others went to the main army and surrendered.
Huī advanced his troops to pressure Shào,
Zàn attacked him from behind,
Huī's troops were greatly defeated,
and Huī and his three brothers were killed.
Hóng wept for him bitterly,
and buried him with ducal rites.
3 The Grand Marshal Yù led the naval forces from Péngchéng,
leaving his son, the Duke of Péngchéng, Yìlóng, to guard Péngchéng.
An edict appointed Yìlóng as Supervisor of Military Affairs of the Four Prefectures of Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, and Jì, and Governor of Xú Prefecture.
4 The Duke of Liáng, Hào, fell seriously ill,
and on his deathbed instructed the Chief Clerk Sòng Yáo, saying:
"After I die,
my heir is like your own son,
guide him well."
In the second month,
Hào died.
The officials supported the heir, Xīn, as Grand Commander, Grand General, Duke of Liáng, and concurrently Governor of Liáng Prefecture.
A general amnesty was declared,
and the era name was changed to Jiāxīng.
Xīn's mother, Lady Yǐn of Tiānshuǐ, was honored as Empress Dowager;
Sòng Yáo was appointed to oversee the affairs of the three offices.
The three offices
are the offices of the Grand Commander,
the Grand General,
the Duke of Liáng,
and the Governor's office.
His temple name was Tàizǔ.
5 The Western Qín General Who Pacifies the East, Mù Yìgān, attacked the Tǔyùhún Shù Luògān,
defeating his brother Āchái at Yáogān River.
Yáogān River was beyond the frontier.
Gān
is pronounced jū hán fān,
also jū àn fān.
Shù Luògān fled and held Báilán Mountain,
where he fell ill from shame and indignation.
On the verge of death,
he said to Āchái:
"My son Shí Qián is young and weak,
I now entrust this great matter to you."
Shù Luògān died,
Āchái succeeded him,
proclaiming himself General of Agile Cavalry and Governor of Shā Prefecture.
Shù Luògān was posthumously titled King Wǔ.
Āchái gradually used military force to annex the neighboring small tribes,
his territory extending several thousand li,
and thus became a powerful state.
6 The King of Héxī, Méngxùn, sent his general to attack the Wūtí tribe,
and greatly defeated them;
the Wūtí captives lived west of Jīnshān in Shāndān County, Zhāngyè.
Jiàng
is pronounced jí liàng fān.
They surrendered.
The Bēihé Qiāng lived in Xīhǎi.
Xiáng
is pronounced hù jiāng fān.
7. Wáng Zhèn'è advanced his army to Miǎnchí.
He sent Máo Dézǔ to launch a surprise attack on Yǐn Yǎ at Lǐwúchéng,
capturing him.
The Qin state had appointed Yǎ as the Grand Administrator of Hóngnóng,
stationed at Lǐwúchéng.
According to the historical records,
Lǐwúchéng should be located west of Yíyáng.
Sòng Bái said: Lǐwúchéng,
in the early period of the Later Wei, still belonged to Hóngnóng,
and since the Táng dynasty, it has been the seat of Miǎnchí County's administration.
I note that Lǐwú is originally the name of a pavilion within the boundaries of the Hàn dynasty's Qīnghé Kingdom,
this is Lǐchéng,
not Lǐwúchéng.
The Comprehensive Mirror likely inherited the error from the Book of Jìn.
Zhèn'è led his troops straight forward,
reaching Tóngguān.
Tán Dàojì and Shěn Línzǐ crossed the Yellow River north of Shǎn,
captured Xiāngyì Fortress,
and the Qin's Héběi Grand Administrator Xuē Bó fled to Hédōng.
Xiāngyì Fortress was in Héběi County of the Héběi Commandery,
which during the Hàn and Jìn dynasties belonged to Hédōng Commandery,
and the Qin state separately established Héběi Commandery.
They did not succeed.
Another general attacked the Xiōngnú Fortress,
but was defeated by Yáo Chéngdū.
On the Xīnyǒu day,
the Róngyáng garrison commander Fù Hóng surrendered Hǔláo to the Wei state.
The Qin ruler Yáo Hóng appointed the Duke of Dōngpíng, Yáo Shào, as Grand Steward, Grand General, and Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs,
granted the authority of the Yellow Axe,
changed his title to Duke of Lǔ,
and ordered him to oversee General of the Martial Guard Yáo Luán and others, commanding fifty thousand infantry and cavalry to guard Tóngguān.
He also sent another general, Yáo Lǘ, to rescue Púbǎn.
Shěn Línzǐ said to Tán Dàojì:
"Púbǎn has strong city walls and many troops,
it cannot be captured quickly,
attacking it would cause heavy casualties among our forces,
and defending against it would prolong the campaign.
Wáng Zhèn'è is at Tóngguān,
his situation is isolated and his strength is weak,
it would be better to combine forces with Zhèn'è and strive together for Tóngguān;
if we capture it,
Yǐn Zhāo will collapse without a fight."
Dàojì followed this advice.
In the third month,
Dàojì and Línzǐ arrived at Tóngguān.
The Qin's Duke of Lǔ, Yáo Shào, led his troops out to engage in battle,
Dàojì and Línzǐ fiercely attacked,
greatly defeating him,
killing and capturing thousands.
Shào retreated and stationed his troops at Dìngchéng.
Guō Yuánshēng's Record of Campaigns says: Dìngchéng is thirty lǐ from Tóngguān,
with a city on each side of the road,
and the Wèi River flows north of it.
He said to his generals:
"Dàojì and the others have few troops,
they have advanced deep into enemy territory in isolation,
they can only fortify their positions and await reinforcements.
If we divide our forces to cut off their supply route,
we can capture them without much effort."
He then sent Yáo Luán to station at the main road to cut off Dàojì's supply route.
Entering the pass from west of Miǎnchí,
there are two routes.
The southern route goes via Huíxī Bǎn,
which was the route used before the Hàn dynasty.
Cáo Cāo disliked the danger of the southern route,
so he opened a northern route,
and thus the northern route became the main road.
The historical records say: Shào left Luán to guard the strategic point to cut off Dàojì's supply route.
Although Luán stationed at the main road,
he also occupied a strategic position to intercept the supply route.
Shào initially sent Hú Yìdù to occupy Dōngyuán,
likely to form a mutual support with the main road,
which is what is meant by occupying a strategic position.
When Shěn Línzǐ attacked Luán's camp,
why could Yìdù not come to the rescue?
Why?
Because people's hearts were filled with fear and panic,
and they were facing enemies on all sides.
Luán sent Yǐn Yǎ to lead troops and engage the Jìn forces south of the pass,
south of the pass,
meaning south of Tóngguān.
They were about to kill him.
Yǎ said:
"I should have died the other day,
fortunately I escaped and survived until now,
so I am willing to die.
However, although the barbarians and the Huáxià are different,
the duty between ruler and subject is the same.
The Jìn is launching a campaign based on great righteousness,
can it not allow the Qin to have ministers who uphold integrity!"
So they spared him.
On the night of the Bǐngzǐ day,
Shěn Línzǐ led elite troops in a surprise attack on Luán's camp,
beheaded Luán,
and killed several thousand of his soldiers.
Shào again sent the Duke of Dōngpíng, Yáo Zàn, to station at the river to cut off the water route;
Shěn Línzǐ attacked him,
Zàn was defeated and fled,
returning to Dìngchéng.
Xuē Bó, based at Héqū, came to surrender.
The Yellow River flows south from Púbǎn to Tóngguān,
then turns sharply and flows east,
the area between Púbǎn and Héběi,
is called Héqū.
The Grand Marshal Liú Yù led the naval forces from the Huái and Sì rivers into the Qīnghé River,
intending to sail west up the Yellow River,
first sending an envoy to request passage from the Wei state;
the Qin ruler Yáo Hóng also sent an envoy to request rescue from the Wei state.
The Wei ruler Tuòbá Sì had his ministers deliberate on the matter,
they all said:
"Tóngguān is a natural fortress,
it is very difficult for Liú Yù to attack it with naval forces;
if he lands on the northern shore to invade,
the situation would be much easier for him.
Yù claims to attack Qin,
but his true intentions are hard to gauge.
Moreover, Qin,
is a state related to us by marriage,
we cannot not rescue them.
A Qin princess married into Wei,
see the eleventh year of the previous scroll.
Do not allow him to proceed west."
The Erudite Sacrificial Officer Cuī Hào said:
"Yù has been planning against Qin for a long time.
Now Yáo Xīng is dead,

During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Luò Xiàhóng, Xiānyú Wàngrén, and Gěng Shòuchāng created the celestial sphere to examine calendrical measurements.
During the reign of Emperor Hé,
Jiǎ Kuí further added the ecliptic.
During the reign of Emperor Shùn,
Zhāng Héng again constructed the armillary sphere,
equipped with inner and outer circles, the ecliptic and celestial equator, north and south poles,
arranged the twenty-four solar terms, twenty-eight lunar mansions, inner and outer star officials, as well as the sun, moon, and five planets,
using water clock to rotate it within the palace chamber,
the stars rising and setting,
corresponded with the heavens.
Afterwards,
Wú's Lù Jì created the armillary sphere,
Wáng Fān constructed the celestial sphere.
The old armillary sphere used two fēn as one degree,
with a circumference of seven chǐ, three cùn, and half a fēn.
Zhāng Héng recreated it,
using four fēn as one degree,
with a circumference of one zhàng, four chǐ, and six cùn.
Wáng Fān considered the ancient design too small,
the stars too densely packed,
Héng's instrument too large,
difficult to move,
so he recreated the armillary sphere,
using three fēn as one degree,
with a circumference of one zhàng, nine cùn, and three-fifths of a fēn.
Zhōulǐ: The Grand Minister of Education uses the method of the sundial to measure the depth of the earth,
correct the sun's shadow,
to seek the center of the earth.
If the sun is south, the shadow is short and there is much heat;
if the sun is north, the shadow is long and there is much cold;
if the sun is east, the shadow is in the evening and there is much wind;
if the sun is west, the shadow is in the morning and there is much cloudiness.
The shadow at the summer solstice,
is one chǐ and five cùn,
this is called the center of the earth.
The annotation says: The sundial is used to obtain the shadows of the four seasons, sun, and moon.
Zhèng Sīnóng said: Measuring the depth of the earth,
refers to the depth of north, south, east, and west.
Sun south,
means the gnomon is placed too far south,
close to the sun.
Sun north,
means the gnomon is placed too far north,
far from the sun.
Shadow evening,
means the sun is past noon when the shadow is centered,
the gnomon is placed too far east,
close to the sun.
Shadow morning,
means the shadow is centered before the sun reaches noon,
the gnomon is placed too far west,
far from the sun.
Xuán said: At midday, place the sundial,
observe the yīn and yáng,
examine its north and south.
If the shadow is shorter than the sundial,
it is called sun south,
meaning the earth is closer to the sun in the south.
If the shadow is longer than the sundial,
it is called sun north,
meaning the earth is closer to the sun in the north.
East of the sundial is called sun east,
meaning the earth is closer to the sun in the east.
West of the sundial is called sun west,
meaning the earth is closer to the sun in the west.
If so,
then cold, heat, cloudiness, and wind will be biased and not harmonious,
meaning the desired result is not achieved.
Generally, the sun's shadow on the earth varies by one cùn per thousand lǐ.
Zhèng Sīnóng also said: The length of the sundial is one chǐ and five cùn,
on the day of the summer solstice, erect an eight-chǐ gnomon,
its shadow exactly matches the sundial,
this is called the center of the earth.
Now Yǐngchuān Yángchéng is such a place.
Jìn Yúfúzhì: The odometer drum chariot,
drawn by four horses,
is made like the south-pointing chariot.
Cuī Bào's Gǔjīnzhù said: The Dàzhāng chariot is used to mark the distance of the road,
originating from Xījīng,
also called the odometer chariot.
The chariot has two levels,
both with wooden figures,
traveling one lǐ,
the lower level strikes a drum;
traveling ten lǐ,
the upper level strikes a bell.
The Yellow Emperor created the south-pointing chariot.
Jìn Yúfúzhì: The south-pointing chariot,
also called the guide chariot,
drawn by four horses.
Its lower part is made like a tower,
three levels and four corners,
with golden dragons holding feather tassels.
Carved wood into an immortal,
wearing feather garments,
standing on the chariot,
though the chariot turns,
the hand always points south.
When the imperial procession travels,
it is the vanguard vehicle.
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn said: The south-pointing chariot,
has a roof built over the four sides of the compartment,
the guide figure's skirt and robe, celestial garments are inside the compartment,
above, the four corners all have dragon-shaped railings,
with colored edges;
genuine peacock feathers,
black cloth double curtains,
lacquered painted wheels,
drawn by oxen,
all decorated with bronze fittings.
The odometer drum chariot is made like the guide chariot,
with a canopy above,
embroidered garments and lacquered paintings,
the drum mechanism is all inside.
Hún,
is pronounced hù běn fān.
All were distributed as rewards to the generals and soldiers.
Qín's Duke Píngyuán Pú and Bīngzhōu Cìshǐ Yǐn Zhāo surrendered with Púbǎn,

Sent Yáo Hóng to Jiànkāng,
and executed him in the market.
In the ninth year of Xiàowǔ's Tàiyuán era,

changed the era name to Báiquè,

Advisor Cānyù Wáng Zhòngdé said:

and will inevitably cause alarm.
Now the army has been exposed for a long time,
the soldiers long to return home,
the plan to move the capital,
cannot be discussed."
Yù then stopped.
Over a hundred thousand Qiāng people fled west to Lǒngshàng,
Shěn Línzǐ pursued and attacked them to Huáilǐ,
capturing tens of thousands.
The Yáo clan,
were Qiāng;
since the Yáo clan was destroyed,

Héxī King Méngxùn heard that Grand Commandant Yù had destroyed Qín,

Ménxià Xiàoláng Liú Xiáng entered to report matters,
since Cáo Cāo and Sūn Quán established the Xiàoshì to monitor ministers,

Méngxùn said:

Then he executed him.
Initially,
Xià King Bóbó heard that Grand Commandant Yù was attacking Qín,

Moreover, his brothers rebelled internally,

Yù will certainly take Guānzhōng.
However, Yù cannot stay long,

I will take it as easily as picking up a mustard seed."
Then he fed the horses and sharpened the weapons,
trained and nurtured the soldiers,

Yù sent an envoy to deliver a letter to Bóbó,

facing Yù's envoy,

Yù read the text,
and sighed:
"I am not his equal!"
History says that barbarian leaders are often cunning.
16 Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ Xiè Xīn died;

Sīmǎ Xiūzhī, Sīmǎ Wénsī, Sīmǎ Guófán, Sīmǎ Dàocì, Lǚ Guǐ, Hán Yánzhī, Diāo Yōng, Wáng Huìlóng, and Huán Wēn's grandsons Dàodù and Dàozǐ, along with clansmen Huán Mì and Huán Suì, and Yuán Shì of Chénjùn Commandery, all went to surrender to Chángsūn Sōng of Wei.

Fán,

In winter,
the tenth month,

General Who Establishes Righteousness,
Wei used this title to honor Diāo Yōng,

Ài,
was the garrison commander of Shàngguī for Qín.
Commander,
pronounced as Jiàng.

In the twelfth year,

after Shàngguī surrendered,

On the 20th day, in the eleventh month,
Wei's Shūsūn Jiàn and others attacked the Dīnglíng leader Zhái Shǔluòzhī and others in the Western Mountains,

Western Mountains,

On the 21st day, Xīnwèi,

Initially,
Yù wanted to remain in Cháng'ān to manage affairs in the northwest,

When Mùzhī died,
Yù felt there was no one to entrust with the foundation at home,

When Mùzhī died,
the court was fearful and anxious,

The Central Army's Advisory Army Officer Zhāng Shào said:

Yù wanted Wáng Hóng to replace Mùzhī.
Attendant Officer Xiè Huì said:

Wáng Hóng,
courtesy name Xiūyuán.
Frivolous,

He took over the responsibilities of the remaining post.
Thus, all major court matters that had previously been decided by Mùzhī

Yù appointed his second son, the Duke of Guìyáng, Yìzhēn, as Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of the Three Provinces of Yōng, Liáng, and Qín, General Who Pacifies the West, and concurrent Governor of Yōng and Eastern Qín Provinces.
Yìzhēn was twelve years old at the time.
He appointed the Grand Commandant's Advisory Army Officer, Jīngzhào's Wáng Xiū, as Chief Clerk,
Wáng Zhèn'è as Marshal and concurrent Administrator of Féngyì,
Shěn Tiánzǐ and Máo Dézǔ as Central Army Officers,
and additionally appointed Tiánzǐ as concurrent Administrator of Shǐpíng,
Dézǔ as concurrent Governor of Qín Province and Administrator of Tiānshuǐ,
and Fù Hóngzhī as Clerk of the Bureau of Administration for Yōng Province.
Previously,
displaced households from Lǒngshàng residing in Guānzhōng
hoped to rely on military might to return to their homeland;
but when Eastern Qín Province was established,
at that time Yù had not yet gained Tiānshuǐ,
Eastern Qín Province was concurrently governed by Máo Dézǔ.
Some say,
Yù established Eastern Qín Province,
and had Yìzhēn concurrently govern it.
Previously,
pronounced as Xiān.
They all sighed in disappointment.
The people of Guānzhōng had long respected Wáng Měng,
and when Yù captured Cháng'ān,
Wáng Zhèn'è's contributions were the greatest,
which made the southerners all jealous of him.
Shěn Tiánzǐ, because of his victory at Yáoliǔ,
harbored resentment and competed for credit with Zhèn'è.
When Yù was about to return,
Tiánzǐ and Fù Hóngzhī repeatedly said to Yù:
"Zhèn'è's family is in Guānzhōng,

Yù said:

Say no more."
Yù privately said to Tiánzǐ:
"The reason Zhōng Huì could not carry out his rebellion
was because of Wèi Guàn.
The affairs of Huì and Guàn are recorded in the 78th scroll, in the first year of Xiánxī of Emperor Yuán of Wei.
With more than ten of you,
why fear Wáng Zhèn'è!"
This sets the stage for Shěn Tiánzǐ killing Wáng Zhèn'è.
Your subject Guāng remarks: The ancients had a saying:
"If you doubt someone, do not employ them;
if you employ them, do not doubt them."
Since Yù entrusted Zhèn'è with Guānzhōng,
yet later spoke to Tiánzǐ in such a manner,
he was inciting them to cause trouble.
How regrettable,
that an enemy of a hundred years,
and a territory of a thousand miles,
gained with such difficulty,
was lost so hastily,
causing the capitals of Fēng and Hào to fall back into enemy hands.
Xúnzǐ said:
"Conquest is easy,
but consolidation is difficult."
How true!
On the 22nd day, when the elders of the Three Qín heard that Yù was about to return,
they went to his gate in tears and pleaded:
"We, the remnant people, have not been touched by royal influence,
for a hundred years now,
and only now have we seen the robes and caps of civilization,
with everyone celebrating.
The ten imperial tombs in Cháng'ān are your family's graves,
and the palaces of Xiányáng are your family's homes,

Emperor Gāozǔ's Chánglíng, Emperor Huì's Ānlíng, Emperor Wén's Bàlíng, Emperor Jǐng's Yánglíng, Emperor Wǔ's Màolíng, Emperor Zhāo's Pínglíng, Emperor Xuān's Dùlíng, Emperor Yuán's Wèilíng, Emperor Chéng's Yánlíng, Emperor Āi's Yìlíng, and Emperor Píng's Kānglíng,
are all in Guānzhōng,
totaling eleven tombs;
saying ten
is a round number.
The palaces of Cháng'ān and Xiányáng are all remnants of the Hàn dynasty.
Yù,
as a descendant of the Liú clan,
is why the elders spoke these words to persuade him to stay.
Yù was moved to pity by this,
and comforted them, saying:
"I have received orders from the court,
and cannot stay long.
I truly appreciate your sentiment of longing for your homeland,
and now I leave my second son
second son,
meaning the second son.
to strive and live with you."
In the twelfth month,
on the Gēngzǐ day,
Yù departed from Cháng'ān,
entered the Yellow River from Luò,
and returned via the opened Biàn Canal.
On the 23rd day, the Dí chieftains Xú Hàinú and Qí Yuánzǐ, leading a tribe of thirty thousand in Yōng,
sent envoys to surrender to Wei.
The Wei ruler Sì sent General Wáng Luòshēng and Administrator of Hénèi, Yáng Shēng, to march west to respond to them.
On the 24th day, in the intercalary month,
on the Rénshēn day,
the Wei ruler Sì went to Dàníng Chángchuān.
On the 25th day, over a thousand households from Qín and Yōng, led by the Magistrate of Xiāngyì, Kòu Zàn of Shànggǔ, surrendered to Wei,
Zàn,

people from Qín and Yōng who had migrated to Wei's Hénán, Xíngyáng, and Hénèi

Zàn was skilled in recruitment and安抚,
and the number of displaced people who returned to him
tripled from the initial count.
In the summer, King Bóbó of Xià heard that Grand Commandant Liú Yù had returned east,
and was greatly pleased.
A skilled commander observes opportunities and then acts.
"I wish to seize Guānzhōng.
You, sir, try to explain the strategy for it."
Wáng Mǎidé said:
"Guānzhōng is a strategically advantageous location,
yet Yù has left his young son to guard it.
He hurriedly returned in disarray,
precisely because he is eager to swiftly accomplish his usurpation.
He has no leisure to again concern himself with the Central Plains.
The true intentions in Liú Yù's heart,
both Cuī Hào and Wáng Mǎidé understood them.
Fù,
fú yòu fān.
This opportunity must not be lost.
Qīngní and Shàngluò
are the strategic passes controlling the north-south routes.
We should first dispatch mobile forces to cut them off;
block Tóngguān in the east,
severing his water and land routes;
then issue proclamations to the Sānfǔ region,
applying both authority and virtue.
Then Yìzhēn will be caught in the net,
and will not be difficult to capture."
Bóbó defeated Yìzhēn and seized Guānzhōng,
ultimately following Mǎidé's plan.
Gǔ,
yīn gǔ.
He led twenty thousand cavalry towards Cháng'ān.
His Front General Chāng garrisoned Tóngguān.
He appointed Mǎidé as Right Chief Clerk to the Army Pacifier,
garrisoning Qīngní.
Liú Yù obtained Luòyáng but could not prevent the bandit Zàn from watching covetously at his side.
He had Yìzhēn guard Guānzhōng but could not prevent the Xià troops from cutting off Tóngguān and Qīngní.
He returned south to Péngchéng,
and before his seat had even warmed, Yìzhēn was defeated.
After he abandoned the realm,
before his flesh was cold, the four garrisons were lost.
It was fitting.
27. This year,
the Wèi Capital Sitting Grand Official, Marquis Zhāng'ān Fēng Yì, died.

first month,
Dīngyǒu, first day.

Shuài,
dú yuē shuài.

3. Summer,
Hèlián Guī reached Wèiyáng.
The people of Guānzhōng surrendering to him lined the roads.
Dragon Soaring General Shěn Tiánzǐ led troops to resist him,
but fearing the enemy's great numbers,

He sent a messenger back to report to Wáng Zhèn'è.
Zhèn'è said to Wáng Xiū:
"The Duke entrusted a ten-year-old child to us.
We ought to together think of exerting our utmost strength;
yet he holds troops and does not advance.
How can the barbarians be pacified!"
The messenger returned
and reported this to Tiánzǐ.
Tiánzǐ and Zhèn'è had long harbored intentions to scheme against each other,
and from this, his anger and fear increased.
Before long,
Zhèn'è and Tiánzǐ both went out to Běidì to resist the Xià troops.
